The categories describe roles, not permission to act without limits. Each agent uses a Microsoft Entra Agent ID and the permissions configured for it. Sessions show inputs, intermediate work, outputs and requests for approval. Administrators can restrict who runs or views an agent, and users can stop a session.[7]

How Defender and Sentinel fit

Microsoft Defender is the primary operating surface. Customers access Perception from the Defender portal, where they can use chat, agents, playbooks and session views. Microsoft describes Security Copilot as an AI-assisted chat interface and Perception as an agentic system in which specialized agents coordinate and act across the environment. The two experiences are complementary and priced separately.[4][9]

Microsoft Sentinel can contribute data and analytics when a workflow needs them. For example, the Detection Authoring Agent activates the Microsoft Sentinel plugin when applicable, alongside Microsoft Defender XDR and Microsoft Threat Intelligence. It checks available tenant tables and existing detections before proposing KQL logic.[8] Sentinel is therefore a possible source of security context, not a universal prerequisite for every Perception workflow and not a product that Perception replaces.

For customers using the unified security operations experience, the potential value is richer context and fewer hand-offs. At Ignite 2026, Microsoft also announced that playbooks can start in Defender or from automated incident triggers. Preview integrations can bring AWS, Okta and Salesforce context into selected workflows. APIs and Model Context Protocol can connect ITSM, SIEM and SOAR tools. The limitation is equally important: an agent cannot reason over telemetry that is missing, delayed, incorrectly scoped or inaccessible to its identity. These capabilities are not all generally available; customers should verify the status of each integration before designing production processes around it.[12][13]

What the Microsoft demo shows

Microsoft's product demo illustrates a Protect against a threat session. A threat intelligence source is analyzed, reconnaissance maps likely attack paths, a web application is tested, new detections are proposed and a remediation plan is produced. The interface also shows a proposed source-code fix moving to a pull request for review. The important idea is continuity: the workflow carries context from intelligence to protection instead of leaving each stage in a separate queue. The Web App Pen Test Agent remains in preview.[9][12]

The demo shows how the operating model is intended to work. It does not prove that every capability is generally available, accurate or safe to run autonomously. Microsoft's own application card warns that agent outputs can be incomplete, inaccurate or outdated and that critical outputs must be validated before action.[7]

Governance and human approval

A generally available agentic platform should be governed like privileged automation, not enabled like a dashboard. Microsoft lists Defender portal access, unified role-based access control across relevant Defender workloads and appropriate access for each agent identity as prerequisites. A Security Admin configures agents; a Security Reader can run configured agents and view sessions.[10]

Least privilege must apply to the agent identity as well as the person starting the session. If an identity cannot reach a required scope, results may be incomplete. If it can reach too much, the blast radius of an incorrect decision increases. Approval gates, change control and separation of duties therefore remain part of the security design.

Customers should also distinguish proposals from active controls. The Detection Authoring Agent can prepare a rule and open the custom detection wizard, but saving the rule is what activates it in the tenant. The Recon Agent uses read-only access and does not exploit or modify the resources it assesses. Microsoft manages the current playbooks; customers cannot create, edit or delete them in this release.[6][7][8]

A practical adoption plan

Confirm access and economics. Microsoft Perception is generally available. Microsoft Perception uses consumption-based pricing and can be purchased through pay-as-you-go or an AI Flex Plan. If the organization has an active Microsoft Azure Consumption Commitment, eligible Perception usage counts toward it. Microsoft provides a cost estimator, usage dashboard and budget controls in the Defender portal. The public product page does not publish a single numerical unit price for every agent or workflow so customers should model expected consumption and confirm regional and contractual terms with Microsoft.[9]

Confirm data and regulatory fit. Microsoft states that prompts, session content and outputs are treated as Customer Data and are not used to train foundation models. For tenants whose Customer Data storage location is outside the European Union, prompt evaluation may occur in the United States, United Kingdom, European Union, or Australia and New Zealand depending on locality and GPU availability. Confirm that the product terms and processing arrangements meet the organization's regulatory, contractual and data-handling requirements.[7]

Choose one measurable workflow. Start with a bounded problem such as extracting threat intelligence, triaging a defined alert type or recommending detections. Define the current analyst effort, expected output and acceptable error rate before the first session.

Prepare the data foundation. Confirm that Defender workloads, Sentinel tables where relevant, threat intelligence and exposure data are connected, current and correctly scoped. Missing context will produce incomplete results even when the agent executes successfully.

Design identity and approval boundaries. Create dedicated agent identities, grant only the minimum data and actions required, and decide which outputs remain advisory. Keep production rule activation, code changes and containment behind named approvers until the evidence supports a wider delegation model.

Validate the output. Test KQL against historical data, compare triage verdicts with analyst decisions, confirm attack paths with asset owners and review remediation for operational impact. Treat confidence and reasoning as evidence to examine, not proof.

Measure the outcome. Track time from intelligence to validated detection, false-positive rate, investigation time, accepted recommendations, change failures and cost per completed workflow. Increase autonomy only when the results are stable and auditable.

Where LevelBlue fits

Microsoft Perception does not remove the need for a well-run SOC. It makes telemetry quality, permissions, detection engineering, response authority and continuous human oversight more important because agents can move work through the chain faster.

LevelBlue's Microsoft Security portfolio includes accelerators, implementation and optimization services, and managed security services across Microsoft Defender XDR and Microsoft Sentinel, including 24/7/365 detection, hunting, investigation and response.[11] This work aligns with the operating foundation that agentic security requires: effective data coverage, tuned detections, carefully scoped access and clear escalation paths.

For customers evaluating Perception, the immediate work is readiness. That means identifying the workflows worth automating, validating Defender and Sentinel coverage, defining agent access, documenting approval boundaries and deciding how agent-produced artefacts enter the existing detection and response lifecycle. Those controls matter for both generally available capabilities and any preview functions evaluated separately.

Where this leaves security leaders

The case for Microsoft Perception is not that every security decision should become autonomous. It is that the delay between intelligence, investigation and protection has become a security weakness in its own right.

Customers already using Microsoft Defender can prepare by reviewing unified RBAC and agent scope, improving telemetry and choosing one measurable workflow. Customers using Defender with Microsoft Sentinel can also examine whether their data and detection content are ready to support tenant-aware recommendations. With the platform now generally available, they should still begin with narrow permissions and explicit approval gates, and treat preview-only capabilities as separate adoption decisions.

The goal is not the highest number of agents. It is a shorter, safer path from a credible threat signal to a tested protection, with humans still accountable for the decisions that can affect the business.

In this article

AI agents found a new flaw and took over a university server

The agents adapted when attempts failed

Its important to patch public-facing software and limit access where possible

Give an AI agent a target and tell it to break in. According to Amazon Threat Intelligence, that was enough to set an attack in motion that uncovered a previously unknown vulnerability and eventually gave the attacker full control of a university server.

The agents were running through Cairn, an open-source framework designed for legitimate security research and penetration testing. But, like other security tools, it can be turned against the organizations it was intended to help protect.

On September 10, 2026, Amazon Threat Intelligence found the attacker’s Cairn server exposed to the internet without authentication. Its accessible records revealed approximately 48 hours of activity targeting universities in East Asia outside mainland China. The operator supplied IP addresses and variations of a simple instruction: “obtain shell access,” a way to run commands on the target.

Against a server running an open-source medical imaging AI application, the agents discovered a previously unknown file-upload weakness. The application’s maintainers released a fix after Amazon notified them.

Cairn coordinates AI agents. An operator gives it a starting point and an objective. Its agents investigate, run tools, record findings on a shared “blackboard,” and decide what to try next. It can work with different models and delegates tasks to existing coding agents running in containers.

We recently wrote about ARTEX, a similar tool. Both turn plain-language objectives into coordinated actions with limited human supervision. The main distinction is their implementation: Cairn delegates work to existing coding-agent tools, while ARTEX uses an event-driven planner and parallel workers within its own penetration-testing platform.

How to stay safe

Automated hacking is not new. Scanners, password-guessing tools, and exploit scripts existed long before these frameworks. What changes is who, or what, decides the next step. An AI agent can interpret an error, revise its approach, choose another tool, and continue without waiting for a person to make each decision. Scripts were already faster than humans. The bigger change is that AI agents can adapt as they go with less operator involvement.

AI agents can still fail. In Amazon’s investigation, the agents spent roughly 16 hours trying unsuccessfully to take over one target.

The fundamentals still matter:

Reduce unnecessary internet exposure, especially for administrative interfaces and research services.

Patch exposed software and fix authentication and configuration weaknesses.

Limit permissions so one compromised application cannot automatically control everything around it.

Collect and correlate logs and prepare carefully scoped automated responses for high-confidence detections. AI agents can trigger a lot of alerts, so it’s important to recognize the significant ones and respond quickly.

Leaving a weakness exposed gives attackers more opportunities to find it. AI agents can keep trying without an operator supervising every attempt.

Title: Hackers Exploit Two GeoServer Flaws as Researchers Warn of Unauthenticated RCE Chains
Context: 6) - An arbitrary file read vulnerability that could enable an attacker to access local text files readable by the GeoServer process or fetch adversary-selected HTTP or HTTPS...
Full Text:
Threat actors are actively exploiting two newly patched security flaws in GeoServer, according to watchTowr.

The vulnerabilities in question are CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129243, details of which are below -

CVE-2026-120705 (CVSS score: 8.6) - An arbitrary file read vulnerability that could enable an attacker to access local text files readable by the GeoServer process or fetch adversary-selected HTTP or HTTPS URLs by means of a single unauthenticated Web Feature Service (WFS) request.

CVE-2026-129243 (CVSS score: 8.8) - An incorrect authorization vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to invoke OWS operations that are otherwise protected by service security rules.

Advisories for both the flaws were published on November 24, 2026, in the following versions -

CVE-2026-120705: org.geoserver:gs-wfs-core - 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7

CVE-2026-120705: org.geotools:gt-metadata - 35.2, 34.6, and 33.7

CVE-2026-129243: org.geoserver:gs-ows - 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7

"Attackers sent error-based exploit probes to validate that the server is vulnerable by creating and invoking stored queries," the preemptive exposure management firm said in an X post today.

Eye Security, which discovered and reported CVE-2026-120705, said the flaw can be combined with two other vulnerabilities in the same product to create an unauthenticated remote code execution chain -

CVE-2026-129245 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use of a hard-coded signing key ("geoserver") vulnerability in the "remember me" functionality that could be exploited to forge administrator authentication. (Fixed in org.geoserver:gs-main versions 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7)

CVE-2026-120704 (CVSS score: 7.2) - An improper control of the generation of code vulnerability that could allow an administrator, or anyone with access to an administrator session, to execute arbitrary code as the user running GeoServer. (Fixed in org.geoserver.security:gs-sec-jdbc versions 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7)

In a hypothetical attack chain, a bad actor can follow the steps below -

Exploit CVE-2026-120705 to access "users.xml," a file containing GeoServer usernames and password hashes, and obtain the password representation along with the static signing key extracted from the security configuration ("security/config.xml").

Exploit CVE-2026-129245 to forge a valid administrator authentication cookie by using the predictable signing key and the stored password representation without having to know the administrator password.

Exploit CVE-2026-120704 to abuse an administrator-controlled JDBC configuration to execute code from an uploaded native library on both Linux and Windows versions of GeoServer.

According to the project maintainers, CVE-2026-129245 is also part of a five-step unauthenticated remote command execution chain that involves -

CVE-2026-129244 (CVSS score: 6.9) - WFS stored query exception discloses data directory path

CVE-2026-129243 (CVSS score: 8.8) - Service security rules bypassed with a prefixed service name such as x/WFS

CVE-2026-120705 (CVSS score: 8.6) - Unauthenticated WFS GetFeatureById XML injection

CVE-2026-129245 (CVSS score: 9.2) - Predictable "remember me" key allows administrator session forgery

CVE-2026-129242 (CVSS score: 8.6) - Deserialization in JDBC user and role services allows administrator code execution

"An attacker who obtains an administrator password digest, through any file disclosure or a copy of the data directory, can log in as that administrator," GeoServer maintainers said. "Changing the key in security/config.xml does not help when the same file disclosure also reveals the key."

Jonah Burgess, a Senior Security Researcher at Rapid7, who goes by the online alias CryptoCat has been acknowledged for independently discovering and reporting the five-step unauthenticated remote command execution chain on August 2, 2026.

"Prefixing the Web Feature Service (WFS) name, as in x/WFS, slips past the admin-only rule for stored queries. GeoServer turns escaped text in a saved query into live xi:include elements, which leaks the files holding the remember-me key and the admin password digest," the researcher said.

"Those two values forge an administrator cookie without cracking the password. As admin, the attacker points a JDBC user service at an uploaded HSQLDB database, and the bundled driver deserialises a stored value that runs commands."

In light of active exploitation of two of the flaws, users are advised to update to GeoServer versions 2.27.7, 2.28.6, and 3.0.2 released over the past month as soon as possible.

The development comes a little over three months after another critical flaw in GeoServer (CVE-2026-76904, CVSS score: 9.8) witnessed active exploitation efforts as a zero-day.

(The story has been updated after publication to include more details of the flaws and emphasize that advisories for the issues were released on November 24, 2026. The patches were originally released in October and early November 2026.)

Context: Overview On November 24, 2026, Broadcom released VMware Security Advisory VMSA-2026-0011 to address several new vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-123903, a critical...
Full Text:
Overview

On November 24, 2026, Broadcom released VMware Security Advisory VMSA-2026-0011 to address several new vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-123903, a critical authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service component of vCenter. Broadcom assigned it a CVSSv3.1 score of 9.8 Critical. An attacker who can reach an affected vCenter’s VMware Directory Service (vmdir) over the network can gain access without authenticating.

Broadcom's supplemental FAQ distinguishes CVE-2026-123903 from an older vulnerability CVE-2026-123890, which Rapid7 covered previously when CVE-2026-123890 was reported as being exploited in the wild. Both of these vulnerabilities affect the VMware Directory Service in vCenter and can give an attacker access to the vCenter without credentials. CVE-2026-123890 was reachable over RPC while CVE-2026-123903 is reachable over LDAP.

As of this writing, there are no known public reports of exploitation of CVE-2026-123903 in the wild. A public proof-of-concept exploit is available and has been validated by Rapid7 to successfully achieve an authentication bypass.

Attackers are known to be targeting vulnerabilities in the VMware Directory Service, therefore Rapid7 recommends remediating exposed systems on an urgent basis outside of normal patching cycles.

Mitigation guidance

Vendor updates are available for CVE-2026-123903. Broadcom lists no workaround, and these vCenter updates are not eligible for Quick Patch. Rapid7 recommends updating affected deployments on an urgent basis, outside normal patch cycles, using the standard update mechanism for the deployment.

Title: Prompting AI to be ‘thorough’ can drive sandbox escapes, Anthropic says
Context: Prompt wording meant to make AI agents more resourceful, such as telling them to search thoroughly or invoking authority, sharply raises the odds they will reach outside a...
Full Text:
Prompt wording meant to make AI agents more resourceful, such as telling them to search thoroughly or invoking authority, sharply raises the odds they will reach outside a poorly secured sandbox, Anthropic has found in its latest evaluation.

The evaluation, called Siren, gives Claude models routine dev-ops tasks inside deliberately weakened sandboxes and places a “honeypot,” such as a credential, file, or emulated internet service, outside the boundary, Anthropic researchers Oscar O’Rahilly and Darya Kaviani wrote in a blog post.

Anthropic tested six Claude models, from Mythos 5 to the 5.5 series, without the safeguards that ship in its products. The tests covered more than 1,700 scenarios in 26 sandboxes built on tools including Docker, gVisor, and QEMU. Most of the weaknesses are misconfigurations modeled on public reports, the company said.

Wording mattered more than deadlines

Anthropic’s researchers tested different types of instructions, which they called “tempters”. Some increased urgency by introducing deadlines or the consequences of failure. Others encouraged agents to search extensively or gave them broad authority over their machines.

“Some tempters give the model broad authority over its own machine. Others tell it to search thoroughly, on that machine or more widely, and list what it checked,” the researchers wrote.

Removing deadlines and stated costs of failure changed the rate of reaching outside by no more than about six percentage points, the post said.

Removing the wording that asked for thoroughness and asserted authority had a far larger effect, cutting reach rates by 23 to 26 points in five of the six models, the researchers wrote. Claude Mythos 5 was the exception, reaching outside about 90% of the time in every version of the scenarios, the post added.

Across the Claude 5.5 models and Claude Mythos 5.2, agents reached outside in 21% to 32% of scenarios, but misaligned use occurred in only 0.6% to 1.6%. The corresponding misaligned-use rates for the older Claude Mythos 5 and 5.1 models were 25.8% and 12.7%, respectively, according to the post.

“Siren is designed to make this behavior easy to measure; its rates are not an estimate of how often this behavior happens in real use,” the company wrote.

Six rules in the system prompt

The first mitigation Anthropic tested was spelling out six sandbox rules in the system prompt. They cover host files, host services, container engine sockets, credentials, network destinations, and anything left running on the host after a task ends.

The rules made the models 68% to 96% less likely to reach outside, cutting the rate for the newest models to about 2% or less, the researchers wrote. Mythos 5 still reached outside in nearly a quarter of scenarios.

Duncan Brown, group vice president and global domain lead for worldwide security and trust at IDC, said no CISO should rely solely on system prompt rules as a control for agents.

“It’s like marking your own homework: asking a model to moderate itself is a high-risk approach,” Brown said.

Mitigations reduce boundary crossing

Anthropic tested three measures to reduce the likelihood of agents reaching outside their sandboxes. The first involved explicitly describing the sandbox, specifying which resources were off-limits, and instructing the model to stop and report if a task required resources it had not been given.

This reduced reaching-out rates by 68% to 96%, depending on the model. A tool allowing agents to report sandbox weaknesses rather than exploit them reduced the rate by seven to 33 percentage points.

The third measure, auto mode, uses a classifier to check tool calls before execution. In an offline replay of the test episodes, it blocked the first command accessing external material in 96% to 100% of misaligned use cases. It blocked the first command attempting to reach outside in 53% to 84% of boundary-crossing episodes.

The mitigations make escape less likely but “don’t fix the sandbox itself,” Anthropic wrote.

Brown said enterprises should not rely on AI vendors to secure their own models. Instead, they should encase agents in a governance structure that limits scope and access to what is required and no more, he said.

“CISOs may use AI to govern AI, but they must ensure that the governance AI is from a different vendor and has a different model provenance than the one they are governing,” Brown said.

Models suspect they are being tested

Anthropic also found that models frequently suspected they were being tested. Claude Sonnet 5.5 showed signs of evaluation awareness in 67% of scenarios. Across the four newer models, the rate ranged from 43% to 67%.

“With only six models, we can’t tell whether models are more cautious about reaching outside because they suspect they are in a test, or whether the increased eval awareness and the reduced tendency to leave the sandbox are both products of how newer models were trained,” the researchers wrote.

Brown said enterprises should not rely on vendor-produced evaluations alone when deciding whether to deploy agents. “Agents are goal-focused and will stop at nothing to achieve their mission,” he said. Organisations should instead deploy agents with “an identified sponsor, a clear scope, an expiry date and an evidential record of what the agent actually did.”

Full Text:
CISA has added 10 new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2023-25914 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Path Traversal Vulnerability

CVE-2023-25915 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Input Validation Vulnerability

CVE-2025-41450 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Authentication Vulnerability

CVE-2026-103406 Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) Juniper Session Smart Conductor and Session Smart Router OS Command Injection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-133275 Mitel MiCollab Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type Vulnerability

CVE-2026-133303 Mitel MiCollab XML Injection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-133311 Mitel MiCollab Weak Authentication Vulnerability

CVE-2026-133323 Mitel MiCollab OS Command Injection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-133324 Mitel MiCollab Not Failing Securely Vulnerability

CVE-2026-133469 Vates Xen Orchestra Improper Validation of Specified Type of Input Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Full Text:
U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds Drupal Core, Idunno AntiCsrf, and Optimizely Web Experimentation flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added Drupal Core, Idunno AntiCsrf, and Optimizely Web Experimentation vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog:

CVE-2026-131914 Idunno AntiCsrf Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability

CVE-2026-132165 Drupal Core Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

CVE-2026-132224 Optimizely Web Experimentation External Control of Critical State Data Vulnerability

The first flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-131914 (CVSS score of 9.8), is a critical insecure deserialization vulnerability affecting Idunno AntiCsrf, a legacy ASP.NET library used to protect web applications against Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks. The vulnerability allows unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on vulnerable servers by sending a specially crafted HTTP POST request. Mandiant confirmed that the flaw is being actively exploited in the wild. However, the security firm has not attributed the attacks to any specific threat actor. The affected library is no longer maintained, and no official security patch is available. Organizations are advised to remove it and replace it with a supported anti-CSRF solution.

The second flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-132165 (CVSS score of 9.8), is a critical remote code execution vulnerability affecting Drupal Core. The issue resides in Drupal’s installation script, install.php, which under specific conditions can be abused by an unauthenticated attacker to reinstall Drupal, potentially resulting in a complete website takeover or remote code execution. Drupal’s security team confirmed that the vulnerability has been exploited against live websites since at least November 19, 2026. Although exploitation requires specific conditions, organizations should restrict access to the installation script and upgrade to the fixed releases: Drupal 10.6.22, 11.3.22, or 11.4.13. No specific threat actor has been publicly identified in connection with these attacks.

The third flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-132224 (CVSS score of 7.1), is an external control of critical state data vulnerability affecting Optimizely Web Experimentation. The issue stems from improper handling of the account signup process, which could allow attackers to gain control of existing customer accounts and modify the Project JavaScript (projectJS) field. Attackers exploited this weakness to inject malicious JavaScript into Optimizely-hosted assets, allowing malicious code to be delivered to visitors of legitimate websites. The attacks were associated with a campaign that compromised hundreds of websites and delivered malicious scripts, including code designed to steal payment card information and hijack cryptocurrency transactions. CISA confirmed active exploitation by adding the vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on November 24, 2026. No specific threat actor has been publicly attributed to the campaign. Optimizely addressed the vulnerability on November 17, 2026.

According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog.

Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure.

CISA orders federal agencies to fix the vulnerabilities by November 27, 2026.

Title: Drupal Fail2Install Exploit Details Emerge as Critical RCE Flaw Faces Active Exploitation
Context: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday added a critical flaw impacting Drupal to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal...
Full Text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday added a critical flaw impacting Drupal to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the fixes by November 27, 2026.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-132165 aka Fail2Install (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of remote code execution (RCE) impacting Drupal core.

"Drupal Core contains a not failing securely vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to take over an existing site or execute arbitrary code via the Drupal installer," CISA said. "Under specific conditions, the attacker can use install.php to attempt to reinstall Drupal on the site."

As previously reported by The Hacker News, an attacker can use the installer to attempt to reinstall Drupal, resulting in site takeover or remote code execution under certain circumstances.

According to an independent analysis by Searchlight Cyber, it has emerged that ordinary server resource limits can be abused to trick Drupal into mistakenly believing that an existing website was not installed, enter its installation process via "install.php," create an administrator-controlled account, and execute arbitrary PHP code.

While Drupal has checks in place to determine whether the website is already installed before allowing installation to proceed, the research found that it's possible to bypass these checks by exhausting server resources.

As a result, a failed database connection to the configured database and a failed database check for an existing installation are interpreted as evidence that the website has not been installed, and Drupal allows the installation to proceed after winning a race condition that allows a second database connectivity check to pass.

To achieve this, the three resource exhaustion techniques have been put to use -

EMFILE, which refers to a limit on how many files a Linux process can open

Database connection exhaustion

TCP source-port exhaustion

"We started with EMFILE, then explored database and TCP limits to determine whether availability failures could become security primitives," the cybersecurity company said.

"Applying this methodology to Drupal uncovered a pre-authentication RCE affecting Drupal 8.9, 9, 10, and 11 across four common deployment combinations: Apache with PostgreSQL, Apache with MySQL, PHP-FPM with PostgreSQL, and PHP-FPM with MySQL."

This behavior can be turned into a pathway for code execution by taking advantage of the fact that Drupal's installer supports SQLite database files and allows the database path to be selected during installation. This is made possible because the installer doesn't restrict the file name extension.

"By selecting a path ending in .php under the document root, the installer creates an SQLite database with a PHP extension," Searchlight Cyber said. "Once the installation reaches the site configuration form, Drupal stores the submitted website name inside the SQLite database. By using PHP code as the website name, the payload bytes are written into the .php database file."

While direct access to the generated PHP file is blocked by Drupal's stock .htaccess on a stock Apache deployment, a path-handling weakness in the Apache RewriteRule could be exploited to achieve arbitrary PHP execution.

"Starting from three system-wide limits, we showed how errors that appear to affect only availability can become primitives for crossing a security boundary," Searchlight Cyber researchers Kevin Gervot and Adam Kues said.

"In Drupal, temporary database failures can produce a FAIL, FAIL, and then SUCCESS sequence that reopens the installer on an existing website and ultimately leads to pre-authentication RCE through an SQLite database containing PHP code."

The issue has been addressed in the following versions -

Drupal 11.4.x - Update to Drupal 11.4.13

Drupal 11.3.x - Update to Drupal 11.3.22

Drupal 10.6.x - Update to Drupal 10.6.22

The addition of CVE-2026-132165 to the KEV catalog follows a report received by the Drupal Security Team that it "was exploited on live sites as early as 2026-11-19 19:00 UTC."

It's worth noting that CVE-2026-132165 is the third Drupal flaw to come under active exploitation this year following CVE-2026-9082 (CVSS score: 6.5) and CVE-2026-118539 (CVSS score: 6.5).

Title: Microsoft fixes Microsoft 365 bug blocking access to Office apps
Context: I've launched applications in safe mode as well without any luck," one user said
Full Text:
Earlier this week, Microsoft resolved a known issue that was preventing some Microsoft 365 customers from accessing Office applications.

This follows widespread reports on social media and Microsoft's support website about what affected users described as a persistent white screen or square that can't be dismissed, displayed over Office apps' user interfaces or Microsoft 365 sign-in windows.

"We've installed 3 separate versions of 365 on this device, but no matter how we try to get into a 365 app we get stuck on this white screen. I've launched applications in safe mode as well without any luck," one user said.

The company confirmed in a support document updated Monday that a blank dialog box prevented customers from opening Microsoft 365 Outlook, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, OneNote, and Access apps.

"When you open an Office application, a blank dialog window might appear. The dialog box doesn't show any text or buttons," Microsoft said. "If you can't dismiss it, you might be unable to continue using the application."

Microsoft says the issue is now fixed in Microsoft 365 Apps Version 2611 (Build 16.0.20625.20142), released last week.

​However, Microsoft says that customers who can't update because of this bug can also upgrade to the latest version from the command line by going through the following procedure:

Save your work and close all Office applications.

Open an elevated command prompt.

Run the following command "%programfiles%\Common Files\Microsoft Shared\ClickToRun\officec2rclient.exe" /update user updatetoversion=16.0.20625.20142.

This is the last in a series of bugs that have affected Microsoft 365 and Office customers since the start of the year.

For instance, in June, Microsoft fixed another issue that blocked Office for the web users from opening Excel and PowerPoint documents, and another that prevented Windows 365 users from downloading the Office suite.

One month later, it resolved a bug that blocked third-party apps from launching Microsoft Office apps like Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and Access and from opening documents on Windows systems.

More recently, in September, Microsoft fixed a known issue causing copy-and-paste and autofill failures for Excel users after installing the September 2026 security updates.

That same month, Microsoft also had to temporarily pause the rollout of the KB5002907 Microsoft 365 update to fix a bug that deactivated (and in some cases completely removed) perpetual Office 2016 and Office 2019 installations for some users.

Title: Hackers now exploit critical Drupal RCE flaw to hijack sites
Context: The Drupal security team has confirmed that a critical vulnerability that lets attackers hijack unpatched sites has been actively exploited since at least Thursday
Full Text:
The Drupal security team has confirmed that a critical vulnerability that lets attackers hijack unpatched sites has been actively exploited since at least Thursday.

Drupal is a content management system (CMS) commonly used by large organizations, including government entities, major research universities, and high-profile enterprise and media organizations.

The security flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-132165, was discovered by Anthropic's OSS Scanner and can be exploited by anonymous users to gain remote code execution or take over vulnerable sites by abusing the Drupal installer.

"Drupal core ships with an install.php file for installing Drupal core. Under specific conditions, an attacker can use the installer to attempt to reinstall Drupal. This can lead to a site takeover or remote code execution," the Drupal security team warned last Wednesday. "Some exploit paths are mitigated if the web server cannot write to or change permissions on settings.php."

While it wasn't initially flagged as abused in the wild, in an update to the original security advisory, Drupal warned that this flaw has been "exploited on live sites as early as 2026-11-19 19:00 UTC."

Websites using the paid Drupal Steward Web Application Firewall (WAF) service are already protected from known attack vectors, but admins are still advised to upgrade to the latest available Drupal version in case other attack vectors are discovered.

Those who can't immediately upgrade should block access to /core/install.php in the web server configuration or the .htaccess file in the web root to secure the Drupal installer.

On Tuesday, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has also added the vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog and ordered federal agencies to secure their systems against ongoing attacks by Friday, November 27.

"These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise," the agency warned. "While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities."

Since November 2021, CISA has tagged five Drupal vulnerabilities as abused in the wild, two of which have also been exploited by ransomware groups.

Title: Hackers Exploited CVSS 10.0 Hex.pm RCE Flaw to Compromise 6 Package Registry Servers
Context: The flaw used in the attack had been in the registry's code since February 2016, and the team that maintains the service had every server on a patched build within about 15...
Full Text:
An attacker ran operating system commands on Monday on six production servers of Hex.pm, the package registry that Elixir and Erlang developers fetch their dependencies from.

The flaw used in the attack had been in the registry's code since February 2016, and the team that maintains the service had every server on a patched build within about 15 minutes of the first malicious request.

Checks since then found no sign that any package was changed. Whether the attacker read account data such as email addresses, password hashes, and two-factor authentication secrets could not be ruled out, the team said.

What Hex Users Should Do Now

Everyone with a hex.pm account has been logged out because the maintainers replaced the keys that sign sessions and access tokens. They advise account holders to take these steps:

Change your hex.pm password.

Reset two-factor authentication by setting up a new authenticator entry, and store the new recovery codes.

Log back in to the client with mix hex.user auth or, for Erlang projects, rebar3 hex user auth.

Update the Hex client when the next release ships, expected within days, with a new registry signing system.

Watch for phishing. Exposed email addresses may be misused, so check that links in any email about Hex go to hex.pm.

API keys do not need to be replaced, according to the team: they are random 128-bit values stored only as HMAC-SHA256 hashes, which it says cannot realistically be brute-forced. Passwords are hashed with bcrypt, which slows guessing but does not stop it for weak passwords, so changing them still matters.

Developers who never created a hex.pm account and only fetch public packages have nothing to reset, Peter Ullrich, one of the report's authors, said in a maintainer clarification on the Elixir Forum. Those who signed up with GitHub should still log back in to their clients, and reset two-factor authentication if they enabled it.

Until the new client ships, the advice is to fetch packages only from repo.hex.pm and to avoid third-party mirrors. The registry signing key has not yet been replaced, and it was among the credentials the attacker could have read.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-129514 with the maximum CVSS score of 10.0, sat in the parser hex.pm used to read request bodies sent in an Erlang data format. That parser ran before routing and authentication, so an unauthenticated POST request to any address on the site could reach it.

The decoding function was meant to be safe, and it did block dangerous terms such as functions, but it accepted maps with a __struct__ key, which allowed a request body to pose as any Elixir struct the application had loaded.

The safety check that would have stopped this was removed from the code on February 23, 2016, which is where the flaw's age comes from. Exploitation before Monday has not been established.

A crafted struct ran nothing by itself. It caused an error, and the error reporting code then inspected the struct. That inspection, via the Ecto and DBConnection database libraries, led to a point where the server called a function of the attacker's choice, which then ran operating system commands with the permissions of the registry's service account.

The security advisory lists hex.pm as affected from February 23, 2016 until Monday. The fix commit makes the decoder reject any term containing a map with a __struct__ key, and every hex.pm server was running it by 18:31 UTC on Monday.

Load balancer logs recorded 69 exploit requests between 18:16 and 18:29 UTC on Monday, all from two addresses, the Hex.pm team said in its incident report yesterday. Files created by the exploit appeared on six web servers, in one case just 3 milliseconds after the request. Three of those servers joined mid-attack, when a restart brought up machines still on the vulnerable build.

To check the packages, the team compared every database table against a copy taken two minutes before the first exploit request and traced each difference to normal activity. The 23 releases published during the attack all match the audit log, no older release was changed, and the package and registry files written that evening match the database records.

Database reads, shell commands, environment variables and direct reads from file storage were not logged. For that reason, "we cannot rule out that the attacker accessed data stored in the database," the team wrote. That database holds email addresses, password hashes, API key hashes, two-factor authentication secrets and session data, and private packages could also have been read without leaving a trace.

The checks found no leftover shells and no new accounts or cloud keys in the audit logs. Who was behind the attack is unknown. Activity from the two addresses going back to late last week suggests the attacker built a local copy of hex.pm to test against, according to the team.

A separate security report describing the same flaw arrived by email at 19:07 UTC on Monday, after the attack had ended. By yesterday morning the team had replaced every credential the attacker could have read except the registry signing key. On Monday night it reported the breach to the Swedish data protection authority, to CISA in the United States and to ENISA in the European Union.

Related Library Fixes

Alongside the incident, maintainers of three widely used Elixir libraries disclosed flaws of their own involving structs built from untrusted data, and shipped fixed versions yesterday. These are separate disclosures, not further attacks on Hex.pm.

Library

CVE

Affected versions

Fixed versions

ash

CVE-2026-124283

3.31.3 up to, but not including, 3.38.0

3.38.0

flop

Each needs its own conditions to be exploited. The Ash flaw requires keyset pagination with a client-supplied cursor, certain sort field types, and a signing secret left at its unset default, according to the Ash advisory.

The db_connection flaw "is not exploitable in db_connection alone," the DBConnection advisory says, because another component must first decode untrusted data into structs. The Flop flaw has similar conditions around its pagination cursors, according to the Flop advisory.

The exploited flaw sits in the hexpm server code, not in the Hex client, so organizations that run their own copy of the registry are affected until they deploy the patch.

Title: Three Attacks, Zero Exploits in Microsoft 365
Context: ClickFix and Session Hijacking In about eight minutes, an attacker gains access to an employee's inbox without installing any malware because the employee runs the malicious...
Full Text:
Most of us think of a breach as something technical, like an unpatched server or a zero day. We figure MFA makes a stolen password worthless. That thinking assumes the attacker breaks in using their own tools.

This blog breaks down three attacks that skip all of that. They work because an employee does something perfectly ordinary, like clicking a link or approving a login. The attacker gets in by abusing the victim's own tools and habits. We show how each one works so you can recognize the tradecraft before it's used against you.

ClickFix and Session Hijacking

In about eight minutes, an attacker gains access to an employee's inbox without installing any malware because the employee runs the malicious command themselves. It starts with a stolen login, the kind anyone can buy off the dark web for about the price of a large pizza. The attacker tries it, but MFA stops them at the door. Plenty of attacks would end there, but this attacker goes after the person who owns the password instead.

The bait is an email, and it takes almost no effort to write. The attacker asks ChatGPT for something that sounds like routine internal comms, like a company-wide note about an updated holiday policy. The attacker swaps in a link to a look-alike SharePoint site, adds a deadline, and tells people not to reply to their manager, because a quick check with the boss is how phishing gets caught.

The employee opens the email and clicks. The page shows a "prove you're not a robot" box. We've all done this countless times. But this time, clicking it discreetly loads a payload onto the employee's clipboard, and the page asks them to press the Windows key + R, paste, and hit Enter. That's ClickFix. The employee thinks they're finishing a verification, and they're running the attacker's PowerShell on their own machine.

Meanwhile, the PowerShell sends the attacker the employee's session cookies. The browser stores them when you tell it to keep you signed in, and most of us say yes so we don't have to log in over and over. The cookie carries the approved MFA. The attacker loads those cookies into their browser using a free extension called Cookie Editor, refreshes, and then lands in the employee's Outlook inbox. They have the password but never had the phone, and the stolen session makes that gap irrelevant. This is token impersonation, also called session hijacking, and it reaches well past Microsoft 365, since everything the browser held is up for grabs.

Over-Permissioned Apps and Global Admin

An attacker turns a standard user's phished login into a Global Admin account in under six minutes. This one starts with Standard Steve, who has an ordinary account and an ordinary workday. The attacker wants his access, so they put an Evilginx proxy between Steve and the login page, phish his credentials, and sign in as Steve. Steve hasn't set up MFA yet, so the attacker can register their own MFA, which means a password reset won't lock them out.

Steve can't open the admin center, but the Azure management portal and Entra are wide open, so the attacker starts looking around. In app registrations, they find something odd. Steve owns a finance integration app. Standard users don't usually own apps, and this one carries a directory-wide role management permission, which is about as powerful as permissions get. The attacker creates a new secret for the app with a two-year lifespan, so even if someone blocks Steve's account, the app still lets them in.

For the last step, the attacker describes what they want in plain English to n8n, a workflow automation tool, and asks it to make them a Global Admin. After a couple of minutes of back and forth, the workflow runs. Steve logs back in with the attacker's MFA and opens the admin center as a Global Admin. About seven controls could have stopped or slowed all of this, including keeping standard users out of the admin center and enforcing MFA registration.

Device Code Phishing

An employee signs in on Microsoft's real login page, and an attacker gets access to their mailbox without ever seeing the password. That's the attack behind EvilTokens, a phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) platform that Huntress and Microsoft tracked hitting more than 300 organizations in about two weeks.

The attacker's part is small. They enter a company's domain into EvilTokens, and the platform creates a phishing email targeting that company's employees.

An employee opens a phishing email that has a short code in it, the type of code you get from Netflix. They go to the login page and sign in with the code like they would on any other day.

That sign-in is the moment the attacker gets in. The code is tied to the attacker's session, so when the employee signs in, access goes straight back to the attacker's back end. The employee used their own credentials and their own MFA on the real login page, and that's exactly what handed over the account. The attacker now has the employee's email and every document in OneDrive, and can search through it all.

The employee sees a normal sign-in and goes back to work while someone else reads their files. Because the attacker holds a live session, access can persist even after a password reset unless the session and tokens are revoked as well.

EvilTokens went from launch to takedown in under nine months. Microsoft's Principal Corporate Counsel Carlton Gammons, Huntress's Chief Legal Officer Lauren Zajac, and Product Manager Rich Mozeleski explain how Huntress's early research and a law written for the mob took it down.

The One Ordinary Action Every Attack Needed

Each attack asked the user for a single normal action, and each victim acted as a reasonable employee would on a busy day. That's why the defense has to start before the inbox.

For your users, that means knowing what these moments look like. A web page telling you to open the Run dialog is a ClickFix tell because no real CAPTCHA asks you to do that. A login code you never asked for deserves the same suspicion as a password prompt you didn't expect.

For admins, it means checking your tenant for the settings in the second attack, like who owns app registrations and which apps hold directory-wide permissions. Every one of those settings could have been closed.

If you only have time for one thing this week, pick one of those controls and check it in your own tenant.

Title: This could mess with Thanksgiving, says VMware as it drops third critical patch bundle in a week
Context: The security vulnerability landscape is more dynamic than ever; please know that while we acknowledge this timing is not optimal, your ability to operate and maintain a secure...
Full Text: VMware has issued its third critical security advisory in a week, this time to warn of four critical flaws and address a total of 23 issues. VMSA-2026-0011 landed on November 24, just five days after two other advisories. VMware’s FAQ for the new advisory includes the following remarks: Because of coordinated disclosure and release pipeline timing this VMSA comes on the heels of VMSA-2026-0009, and atop a major holiday in the United States. The security vulnerability landscape is more dynamic than ever; please know that while we acknowledge this timing is not optimal, your ability to operate and maintain a secure environment amidst modern, AI-assisted threats is paramount to us. Make of that what you will as you ponder how and when to patch the four critical flaws, including the 9.8-rated CVE-2026-123903, which allows a malicious actor to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to vCenter, the management tool VMware users rely on to manage hosts and VMs. This is the third 9.8-rated authentication issue VMware has fixed in vCenter since July. Two of the other critical flaws in this new advisory allow an attacker to run code on an ESX host, earning the bugs a 9.8 rating. CVE-2026-123910 makes that possible thanks to a heap out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the I/O filter service, while CVE-2026-123911 is a use-after-free vulnerability. The other critical flaw, CVE-2026-123912, can result in a guest escape from VMware’s desktop Workstation and Fusion desktop hypervisors. It’s also present in VMware’s ESX hypervisor, but attackers thankfully can’t escape that product’s sandbox. This one’s easy to mitigate because the problem is in a USB controller that users can turn off. Most of the other flaws require installation of updated software. There’s a little good news in that some of the software updates VMware issued last week include fixes for the newly disclosed flaws. But there are still plenty of fresh fixes to apply, across ten products: ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, VMware tools, Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, the Telco Cloud Platform, Telco Cloud Infrastructure, and the VMware Avi Load Balancer. VMware’s advisory thanks external researchers for finding and reporting most of the flaws. The Broadcom business unit is known to be a member of Project Glasswing, the Anthropic-run effort to use the Mythos model to find flaws that has seen many vendors dramatically increase the number of patches they produce. In past years, VMware has often published considerably more than this year’s 11 security advisories. With five weeks left in the year, perhaps vAdmins need to worry Christmas might also get complicated. ®

Title: Cisco and OpenAI dispatch AI agents to shield vulnerable systems before permanent patches arrive
Context: Attackers are using swarms of them to exploit discovered flaws; with both PHP2Shell and Java4shell, campaigns were underway “within a day of disclosure, if not before,” he...
Full Text:
Autonomous AI agents are rapidly and dramatically transforming the cybersecurity landscape for both defenders and adversaries.

In hopes of giving security teams a head start and pitting machine against machine, Cisco and OpenAI have released a new open source project, dubbed Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”). The Shirudo platform launches small, temporary mitigations to help protect systems until patches can be deployed. AI agents can replace flawed code with fixed code, which human teams can test and approve (or not), then deploy, setting boundaries and holding onto the keys, with no need for a hard reset.

The project has already been proven to block a Java4Shell exploit attempt against the search and analytics platform Elasticsearch, while the site continued to run as usual.

Need to buy time

“For years, we’ve treated security like a coat of paint,” Cisco president and CPO Jeetu Patel wrote in a blog post. “You first build infrastructure, then wrap security around it.”

But, he asserted, this approach is “fundamentally mismatched” to AI. Security should live inside the infrastructure itself. “If protection sits outside the system, it’s always a step behind,” he said.

He noted that AI agents are getting better at discovering security vulnerabilities; for instance, startup Calif used AI to help discover the PHP2Shell flaw and a major Java bug.

Dovetailing with this, the agents themselves are both a risk vector and an adversarial actor. Attackers are using swarms of them to exploit discovered flaws; with both PHP2Shell and Java4shell, campaigns were underway “within a day of disclosure, if not before,” he pointed out. Flaws unfold over minutes and hours, as opposed to the days and weeks of the past, but permanent fixes take time to build, test, and roll out.

“We need ways to shield systems and buy our teams time to get patches in place,” Patel said.

Making the infrastructure secure from the start

Shirudo combines Cisco’s infrastructure with OpenAI’s frontier models and AI research. It is built on extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), which supports the running of small, sandboxed programs inside a Linux kernel without changing source code or loading additional modules.

“This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems,” OpenAI explained in its blog post announcing the project.

Speaking in their own language, guardian agents investigate and detect flaws and build shields, then test whether they stop the attack, all without disrupting the targeted service. The shields are cryptographically signed and only loaded when verified and deemed safe. Linux’s eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against safety rules, and kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes.

Shirudo also uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being added or removed.

All this takes place even if attackers have already gained access to a system.

Further, self-defending agents can monitor for false positives, performance, and overall system health, and incorporate red-team findings and other feedback as well as signals for continuous improvement. Evidence backing every control travels across the system.

The idea, according to Cisco and OpenAI, is to make the infrastructure itself secure by default. “We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer,” OpenAI wrote in its post.

Shirudo in the wild

Shirudo has its roots in Tetragon, an eBPF-based security platform developed and open-sourced by Isovalent, which was acquired by Cisco in 2024. It is already incorporated into Cisco’s Live Protect capability.

But Tetragon has been rewritten for the agentic era; its previous iteration pointed AI to human-oriented consoles, configuration files, and policy languages. In that workflow, the agent thought in machine code, which was then decoded for humans and processed, then translated back again into machine code. With Shirudo, agents interact in their natural language, which is code.

“Agents are different,” Isovalent co-founder Thomas Graf and its chief open source officer Liz Rice noted in a blog post: They are very good at generating code, can absorb huge amounts of context quickly, and “[don’t] mind reverse engineering several million lines of assembly code.”

In one controlled testing environment, researchers fed information about the Java4Shell vulnerability into Shirudo, which automatically created a shield against exploitation, generating a mitigation in Java bytecode which was injected into any Java app and added validation on the base64 input to guard against exploit attempts by threat actors.

Graf and Rice explained that agent loops can either be tasked to actively search for new vulnerabilities on their own, or work off external sources like newly-available security disclosures. Agents can generate mitigation code, reproduce and validate exploits, and determine the most effective patching measures. This step is repeated until the agent identifies a successful path. The shield is then signed and securely rolled out to vulnerable nodes; it retires when a patch is installed.

“This step is continuously monitored and repeated to achieve the highest possible security score while closely monitoring the health of applications,” Graf and Rice explained. It can be designed to be “more or less autonomous.”

Once mitigation shields are deployed, the system employs a “hit” count of active exploitation attempts, so that exploits can be investigated on demand.

Ultimately, the Shirudo project is only the beginning, Graf and Rice noted, but it already shows “true potential” and the hope is it will continue to evolve in the open source ecosystem. “We believe that building secure infrastructure for the AI era is an industry-scale problem,” they said.

Shirudo is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, a permissive open-source software license approved by the Open Source Initiative. This allows anyone to use, modify, and redistribute software, including in proprietary or commercial products, with minimal restrictions. Its BPF programs are dual licensed under GPL and BSD.

Developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators are encouraged to inspect the code, test outcomes, and contribute to the project’s development.

Title: NGINX HTTP/2 Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-123633
Context: Related Unit 42 Topics HTTP, DNS, Threat Detection Background While researching NGINX, I independently found the HTTP/2 connection-state defect now tracked as CVE-2026-123633
Full Text:
Executive Summary

CVE-2026-123633 is a use-after-free vulnerability in NGINX HTTP/2 that may let an unauthenticated attacker cause a denial of service. In the CVE record, F5 says code execution may be possible when address space layout randomization (ASLR) is disabled or bypassed.

CVE-2026-123633 affects NGINX servers that accept HTTP/2 client connections and proxy requests to a backend when free worker connections run low. A fragmented request can leave an active connection marked reusable. Under connection pressure, NGINX can close that connection and free memory the active request still uses.

F5's CVE record scores the issue 9.2 Critical under CVSS 4.0. The NGINX security advisories page labels the issue medium and lists versions 1.19.7 through 1.30.6 and 1.31.0 through 1.31.8 as affected. F5 credits memN0ps (Palo Alto Networks Unit 42) among the reporters.

NGINX 1.30.7 on the stable branch and 1.31.9 on the mainline branch contain the fix. F5 also lists affected NGINX Plus releases.

Administrators should review HTTP/2 reverse-proxy exposure and upgrade to a fixed NGINX release or a vendor package containing the CVE-2026-123633 fix.

Background

While researching NGINX, I independently found the HTTP/2 connection-state defect now tracked as CVE-2026-123633.

An unauthenticated client can send a fragmented HTTP/2 request that leaves an active connection marked as reusable. When the server resolves a hostname during the request and free connection slots run low, NGINX can reclaim that connection mid-request and free memory its DNS resolver is still using.

I reproduced the use-after-free with AddressSanitizer (ASan) on builds of unmodified NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 source. The NGINX security advisories page lists 1.19.7 through 1.30.6 and 1.31.0 through 1.31.8 as affected and 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 as fixed releases.

I reported the HTTP/2 use-after-free privately to F5. F5's CVE record scores it 9.2 Critical under CVSS 4.0 and 8.1 High under CVSS 3.1. The NGINX security advisories page labels it Medium.

In my ASan test on a Debian guest, ASan stopped NGINX at the first read from freed DNS lookup memory.

The resolver path in my test stems from the HTTP/2 connection bug tracked as CVE-2026-123633. CVE-2026-123634 is a separate DNS resolver vulnerability fixed in the same release.

I also found a memory disclosure vulnerability that leaked a libc pointer. I used the address to calculate the libc base and work around ASLR when chaining the disclosure with CVE-2026-123633. I reported this additional bug to F5 as a separate issue. From an attacker VM, I achieved pre-authentication remote code execution on a target VM as the non-root NGINX worker. The chain required a non-default NGINX configuration, and some attempts did not open a shell.

F5 assessed the memory disclosure as a behavior limited to a non-typical configuration and has not assigned it a CVE at the time of writing, so I am leaving out its details and the exploit steps.

How the Connection State Defect Works

NGINX marks a connection reusable when it can close that connection under pressure. Stream creation should clear the reusable mark once a request starts, but ngx_http_v2_create_stream() leaves it set in affected releases.

When a client sends only part of an HTTP/2 HEADERS frame header, ngx_http_v2_handle_connection() marks the connection reusable and returns early. The code below shows that decision:

Reaching the Resolver Use-After-Free

The stale reusable mark lets NGINX reclaim a live connection when it needs a free slot. In my test, a request-time DNS lookup opened a new socket and triggered the drain.

My test used an HTTP/2 proxy route with a variable upstream. The variable evaluated to a hostname that was neither a literal IP address nor a configured upstream group, so NGINX looked it up during the request. The lookup also had to open a new resolver UDP socket.

The worker opens a new UDP socket only if it has none for the selected nameserver. Cached answers and in-flight lookups also skip the socket-allocation drain I tested.

Opening the DNS socket needs a connection slot, so ngx_get_connection() runs a drain check first. ngx_drain_connections() acts once free slots fall to one sixteenth of worker_connections or below while at least one reusable connection exists. The drain function then selects entries from the tail of the reusable queue, sets each connection's close flag, and calls its read handler:

c->close = 1; c->read->handler(c->read);

My test client closed its socket with zero linger after completing the frame, leaving NGINX with an active request on a reset connection. When connection pressure triggered the drain, the HTTP/2 read handler tried to send GOAWAY on that socket.

A successful write would have left the request running, but the write failed with Connection reset by peer, so NGINX finalized the connection and request. The ASan free stack passes through ngx_http_upstream_check_broken_connection().

Request cleanup reaches ngx_resolve_name_done(), which frees the resolver state while the original lookup still holds a pointer to it.

In ngx_resolve_name_locked(), the DNS send runs before timeout setup. The send can drain the connection and free ctx. When the send returns, timeout setup uses the stale pointer, as the code below shows:

ASan reported that NGINX read memory from a freed DNS lookup context. The free path ran through ngx_drain_connections(), ngx_http_v2_finalize_connection(), ngx_http_upstream_finalize_request() and ngx_resolve_name_done(). In the run where ASan reported the read, I split the 9-byte HEADERS frame header after 5 bytes. For the control, I sent the full frame header first and then the HPACK block. NGINX sent a DNS query and kept running. Figure 2 follows the calls from socket allocation to the use-after-free.

I ran the ASan test in an isolated Debian 13 guest. NGINX was built from official 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 source with Clang 19.1.7, HTTP/2, ASan and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer. I sent the HTTP/2 requests over the guest's loopback interface.

For the 1.31.8 run, I set worker_connections to 16 and opened 13 filler connections that NGINX had not marked reusable. Table 1 shows the sanitizer results alongside the released-source review.

Limits

A source build includes the HTTP/2 module only when configured with --with-http_v2_module. Distribution packages commonly enable it.

The ASan evidence in this article comes from builds of 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 over loopback. The 1.31.8 test configuration set worker_connections to 16 instead of the documented default of 512, and ran NGINX with master_process off. The sanitizer aborted that single process. The public fix commit also names upstream connection setup as a drain trigger.

Two-VM Demonstration

The two-VM demonstration combined CVE-2026-123633 with the separate memory disclosure mentioned in the Background section. The target ran NGINX 1.31.8 with a root master and a www-data worker under a non-default configuration. Figure 3 records the running processes, version, loaded configuration path and listener.

The first attempt from the attacker VM recovered a libc address but did not open a shell; the second opened an interactive shell as www-data. Detection and Hunting

In the ASan test, NGINX logged a connection-drain warning before the sanitizer aborted the process. The warning can also appear under ordinary connection pressure, while a worker exit can have unrelated causes. A release build may keep running after reading freed memory. Table 3 lists investigation leads for HTTP/2 reverse proxies.

Signal

What I Saw in Testing

What to Check

Unexpected NGINX process exit

ASan aborted the single-process NGINX test after NGINX read freed memory.

Investigate unexpected worker exits in production near HTTP/2 requests and connection pressure. A worker exit on its own is weak evidence of exploitation.

Connection pressure with request-time DNS

NGINX logged "16 worker_connections are not enough, reusing connections" at warn level during the ASan test.

Correlate the warning with resolver traffic and connection pressure on routes that resolve at request time. The warning and DNS traffic can also occur under ordinary load.

Table 3. Signals to use in detection and hunting.

The warning in Table 3 is logged at most once per second per worker, so one line can cover several drain calls. Because NGINX defaults to the error log level (which omits warnings), configure error_log at the warn level (or a level that captures more detail, such as notice or info), then correlate the warning with traffic and worker state.

Exposure Review

CVE-2026-123633 describes a use-after-free in HTTP/2 reverse proxies that are running low on worker connections. The path I reproduced used a variable proxy_pass hostname, a configured resolver and a new UDP socket. F5's CVE description covers a broader set of HTTP/2 reverse proxies.

Check the running configuration. A master process can select another file with -c, so check its command line before assuming that the packaged path is the live one. The command nginx -T prints the on-disk configuration, which can still differ from what the running workers loaded.

I only tested proxy_pass. Operators should also review variable targets in:

grpc_pass

fastcgi_pass

uwsgi_pass

scgi_pass

For a matching route, check the running build and how close the worker gets to its connection limit. I tested one DNS socket route, but upstream connection setup also allocates through ngx_get_connection(), so static upstream routes still need review.

Mitigations

NGINX 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 fix the HTTP/2 issue. No workaround is listed in the CVE-2026-123633 record. If an upgrade must wait, the following changes could reduce exposure:

Where the service allows it, disable HTTP/2 on exposed listeners. Check every relevant listen ... http2 parameter and, on NGINX 1.25.1 or later, any http2 on; setting in the http or server context. Either setting can keep HTTP/2 enabled. Disabling HTTP/2 can break gRPC clients and may increase connection use if other traffic falls back to HTTP/1.1. If HTTP/2 stays enabled on other listeners, the extra HTTP/1.1 connections can push the same worker closer to its worker_connections limit.

Raising worker_connections gives the worker more headroom under the same traffic, but an attacker can still exhaust the extra slots and the connection-state bug remains.

Test each change before deployment. After upgrading, confirm the running worker uses a binary containing the CVE-2026-123633 fix. A configuration reload (nginx -s reload) keeps the old binary running in memory, so perform a full restart or live binary upgrade.

Conclusion

The defect starts when an HTTP/2 connection stays marked reusable after a request begins. In my test, opening a DNS socket under connection pressure drained that live connection and freed resolver state that the request still used. ASan reported that NGINX read memory after it had been freed.

Defenders should identify affected HTTP/2 reverse proxies, look for worker exits around connection pressure, and install a fixed NGINX release or vendor backport. My resolver test shows one way to reach the use-after-free. F5's description covers HTTP/2 reverse proxies more broadly.
