Title: 'God Mode' Flaws Could Wreak Border-Control Havoc
Socket Releases Free Patches for 100% of Critical CVEs in RubyGems
Context: Earlier this month, we released a free security fix for a critical Rails Active Storage vulnerability, tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 (CVSS 9
Full Text:
We've completed security patches for 100% of patchable critical-severity CVEs in the RubyGems ecosystem, and we're making those fixes available to everyone for free. Developers can now remediate these vulnerabilities without upgrading their existing dependency versions, even when an upstream fix requires a breaking change.

The milestone follows an intensive engineering sprint focused on expanding RubyGems patch coverage. During the effort, our team also made substantial improvements to the systems used to generate, test, validate, and publish security fixes.

Socket identifies six critical vulnerabilities with available patches in a sample Ruby project.

Fixing Vulnerabilities Without Dependency Upgrades #

Upgrading to a secure upstream version is generally the simplest way to address a vulnerability. But upgrades aren't always straightforward, particularly for applications that depend on older versions of libraries.

Some Ruby applications have been running for a decade or longer and still serve important functions. Their dependencies may have been abandoned, or upgrading to a supported version may require substantial changes to the application itself. In some cases, a compatible upstream fix simply doesn't exist.

Socket Certified Patches provide another option. We develop targeted security fixes for the dependency versions developers already use, often by backporting fixes from newer releases. These changes address the vulnerable code while preserving the package version and minimizing changes to its existing behavior.

For applications that depend on abandoned libraries, this can extend the useful life of software that might otherwise need to be replaced or extensively rewritten. For actively maintained applications, patches allow teams to remediate known vulnerabilities without having to coordinate an immediate dependency upgrade. They can continue upgrading on their own schedule, with time to test compatibility and address breaking changes.

Security patches don't replace the benefits of ongoing dependency maintenance. Upstream releases still provide bug fixes, new features, and compatibility improvements. But a vulnerability doesn't necessarily have to dictate when an application undergoes a larger upgrade, and in some cases, a targeted patch may be the most practical long-term solution.

Earlier this month, we released a free security fix for a critical Rails Active Storage vulnerability, tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 (CVSS 9.8). The vulnerability could allow unauthenticated attackers to write arbitrary files through specially crafted uploads and, under certain configurations, potentially achieve remote code execution.

Our patch gives applications affected by the vulnerability an alternative to immediately upgrading Rails. Developers can apply the security fix to their existing dependency while planning and testing a broader upgrade separately.

The RubyGems coverage milestone extends this approach across the ecosystem's patchable critical vulnerabilities.

New Hosted and Vendored Delivery Options #

We've also expanded the ways developers can install remediated packages. Previously, Socket's patching workflow primarily involved modifying dependency files after installation. Our new hosted and vendored modes integrate directly with existing package management workflows.

Hosted mode lets developers install remediated gems through Bundler. The socket-patch CLI updates the lockfile to reference patched packages served through patch.socket.dev and, when necessary, adds source: settings to the affected gem declarations in Gemfile. The dependency versions remain unchanged, and Bundler installs the patched gems through its normal installation process.

Vendored mode stores the remediated packages directly in the application's repository under .socket/vendor/. Subsequent installations use those local packages without contacting Socket's infrastructure.

Vendored patches are yours to keep. They stay in your repository and go wherever your application goes, even if you stop using Socket.

Neither mode requires an installation hook or the Socket CLI on build machines. Once the dependency changes are committed, developers can continue installing their dependencies normally.

Both options preserve the existing dependency version. They also eliminate the need to run a separate patching step after every dependency installation. Developers can continue using the original in-place patching mode if they prefer that workflow.

These delivery options are particularly useful for organizations that need to control how dependencies enter their build environments or cannot introduce a new step into existing CI/CD pipelines.

We recently expanded support for Ruby gems containing native extensions as well. With socket-patch CLI 5.1.0, native extensions are rebuilt after patching, allowing us to remediate vulnerabilities in packages such as nokogiri, where a source-level change alone would not update the compiled code that applications execute.

Socket's dashboard provides instructions for obtaining a security patch for a critical Nokogiri vulnerability without upgrading the dependency.

Testing Security Fixes Against Existing Package Behavior #

A successful security patch needs to eliminate the vulnerability without introducing regressions elsewhere in the package.

Our validation process includes reproducing the vulnerability against the original dependency and verifying that the same exploit fails after patching. We also run regression tests, differential tests comparing the original and patched versions, compatibility checks against supported runtimes, and performance benchmarks.

We've expanded this testing to include downstream dependents, allowing us to exercise patches against software that actually relies on the affected library. This helps identify compatibility problems that may not be exposed by the package's own test suite.

Developers can inspect individual patches and their verification results on Socket, including test outcomes, exploit validation, performance measurements, and the code changes made.

These checks are especially important when backporting fixes into older library versions. A change that works correctly in the latest upstream release may depend on other changes introduced in the intervening years. Those differences must be accounted for before publishing a patch for an older release.

Some Vulnerabilities Require Different Remediation #

Our 100% critical-CVE coverage applies to vulnerabilities that can be safely patched. We generally consider three types of vulnerabilities unpatchable:

Malicious packages: The correct remediation is to remove the malicious dependency, not attempt to repair it.

Misattributed vulnerabilities: An advisory may identify a package that doesn't contain the vulnerable code because the vulnerability actually exists in another dependency. In those cases, we focus on fixing the package that contains the vulnerability.

Breaking changes: Some vulnerabilities are inherent to a package's design or public interface. Fixing them would require incompatible changes, potentially making dependency replacement or reachability analysis necessary.

We evaluate these cases individually and can make exceptions for particularly serious vulnerabilities where a breaking change may be warranted. Our current assessment is that roughly 95% of RubyGems CVEs are patchable under these criteria.

Free Critical CVE Patches Are Available Now #

All Socket patches for critical-severity CVEs are free, including for developers and organizations without a Socket account or paid subscription.

To get started, install the standalone socket-patch CLI:

curl -fsSL https://install.socket.dev/patch | sh

From a Ruby project's root directory, preview the available fixes without modifying any files:

socket-patch scan --dry-run

To apply patches in the default hosted mode and install the remediated gems:

socket-patch scan bundle install

Alternatively, use vendored mode to store the patched packages in the repository:

socket-patch scan --mode vendored bundle install

The CLI identifies available security fixes for the specific dependency versions in the project and reports which vulnerabilities they address. Patches for high-, medium-, and low-severity vulnerabilities are available through Socket's Enterprise plan.

For more information about patch validation, delivery options, and supported package managers, see our Certified Patches documentation and installation guide.

We're continuing to expand RubyGems coverage across all severity levels while improving our ability to generate, validate, and distribute security fixes. The free critical patches are available now.

Tenable Enclave Security leverages third-party software to help provide underlying functionality. Several of the third-party components (simpleSAMLphp, libcurl, OpenSSL, Apache HTTP Server, libssh2, Go, golang.org/x/crypto, klauspost/compress, Traefik, jackson-core, jackson-databind) were found to contain vulnerabilities, and updated versions have been made available by the providers.

Title: VMware vCenter Hit by Another Critical 9.8-Rated Auth Bypass Flaw After Zero-Day Exploitation
Context: The critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123903, is rated 9
Full Text:
Broadcom has shipped patches to address 23 vulnerabilities impacting VMware ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, and Avi Load Balancer, including one critical bug that could be abused to bypass authentication.

The critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123903, is rated 9.8 out of 10.0 on the CVSS scoring system. It resides in the VMware Directory Service ("vmdir").

"A malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system," Broadcom said in an advisory released today.

The company credited sglab of QiAnXin, Qi Qin (@LeoQ7_) of depthfirst, and VulTeam, XGTP from ThreatBook for independently reporting the flaw.

Also patched in vCenter are four high-severity flaws, including an arbitrary file write vulnerability while processing certain archives that could be exploited to achieve code execution on the appliance (CVE-2026-123904, CVSS score: 7.5).

The remaining three vulnerabilities relate to denial-of-service in the VMware Directory Service (CVE-2026-123905, CVE-2026-123906, and CVE-2026-123907, CVSS scores: 7.5).

The issues have been addressed in the following versions -

VMware Cloud Foundation and VMware vSphere Foundation 9.1.x.x - Fixed in 9.1.2

VMware Cloud Foundation and VMware vSphere Foundation 9.0.x.x - Fixed in 9.0.2.0300

VMware vCenter 8.0 - Fixed in 8.0 U3m

VMware vCenter 7.0 (Contact Broadcom Support, if on extended support contract)

VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x - Fixed in 5.2.5

VMware Telco Cloud Platform - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2)

VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2)

The fixes arrive days after Broadcom shipped updates for CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8), another authentication bypass flaw impacting the VMware Directory Service that was exploited as a zero-day by a suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group called Armory Castle. VMware has noted that CVE-2026-123903 is a distinct issue and is not related to CVE-2026-123890.

While Broadcom makes no mention of any of the newly disclosed flaws as being exploited in the wild, it's essential that customers apply the updates for optimal protection.

Title: Rapid7 Analysis: VMware vCenter SRP Authentication Bypass to Root (CVE-2026-123890)
Context: The attack recovered the directory database and its Security Token Service (STS) signing key, forged an administrator API session, and used appliance administration features to...
Full Text:
Overview

An unauthenticated attacker can retrieve the session key for an in-progress administrator login to VMware vCenter's directory service. The attacker then uses that key to complete the login without knowing the account's password. The vulnerable interface is exposed through DCE/RPC on TCP port 2012.

The issue, tracked as CVE-2026-123890, combines a Secure Remote Password (SRP) session-key getter that is callable before authentication with an RPC context lookup that does not enforce ownership. The context handles use predictable UUIDv1 values. By creating two reference contexts around a pending login, an attacker can narrow the hidden login handle to a short timestamp window and ask the server for its key.

We reproduced the bypass against vCenter Server Appliance 8.0.2.00400, build 23929136, running Photon OS 4.0, and leveraged the resulting administrator connection through to root command execution. SSH and Bash access were initially disabled. The attack recovered the directory database and its Security Token Service (STS) signing key, forged an administrator API session, and used appliance administration features to create an account and enable SSH. Neither the existing SSO password nor the root password was an input to that chain.

Impact

The attacker needs network access to TCP 2012 and the name of an existing SSO principal. Our PoC uses the default SSO administrator principal, administrator@vsphere.local; deployments using a different SSO domain need the corresponding account name. The attack does not depend on an existing authenticated connection or an administrator being online. The attacker initiates the login attempt in order to recover its session key.

The authenticated connection can call the directory database-copy interface. Its raw database contains the STS private signing key, allowing the attacker to sign administrator assertions that vCenter trusts. Our attack workflow used a forged assertion to create a local appliance superAdmin account, enable SSH and Bash, and execute commands as root through sudo. This final part requires access to the HTTPS API on TCP 443 and SSH on TCP 22, in addition to TCP 2012. It uses the administrative privileges obtained through the original bypass; no second vulnerability is needed once you have administrative RPC access.

Technical Analysis

Returning the key before checking the proof

// vmdir/server/vmdir/rpcsrpserv.c long Srv_rpc_srp_verifier_get_session_key( handle_t hServer, srp_verifier_handle_t hSrp, rpc_p_srp_bytes_container ret_key_cont) { // ... struct SRPVerifier ver = (struct SRPVerifier *) hSrp; //[A1] rpc_p_srp_bytes_container key_cont = NULL; if (!ver) { sts = rpc_s_invalid_handle; goto error; } key = srp_verifier_get_session_key(ver, &key_len); // [A2] if (!key || key_len == 0) { sts = rpc_s_auth_nokey; goto error; } sts = _srp_bytes_container_allocate(key, key_len, &key_cont); if (sts) { goto error; } *ret_key_cont = key_cont; // [A3] // ... }

The SRP RPC getter receives an SRP verifier at [A1], obtains its session key at [A2], and returns a copy at [A3]. It checks whether the verifier and key exist. It does not check whether the caller has authenticated, whether the caller owns the verifier, or whether the SRP client has supplied a valid password proof.

The value at [A1] is a server-side pointer that the RPC runtime resolves from the context handle supplied in the request. Each newly created verifier context receives its own UUID, so the attacker needs the handle for the specific pending login they want to complete. These context UUIDs identify individual verifier instances; the fixed interface UUIDs identify the available RPC interfaces.

UUIDv1 values contain a timestamp, clock sequence, and node identifier. The attacker creates a verifier immediately before starting the target login and another immediately afterward, obtaining both reference UUIDs without authenticating. On the tested service, the reference UUIDs share their clock sequence and node identifier. The attacker reuses those fields and searches the intervening timestamps for the pending login's live verifier, keeping the login connection open throughout the search.

// vmdir/thirdparty/csrp/srp.c int srp_verifier_is_authenticated(struct SRPVerifier *ver) { return ver->authenticated; // [A4] } // ... const unsigned char *srp_verifier_get_session_key( struct SRPVerifier *ver, int *key_length) { if (key_length) *key_length = hash_length(ver->hash_alg); return ver->session_key; // [A5] }

The underlying SRP library exposes the authentication flag separately at [A4]. Its key getter at [A5] does not consult that flag. The server has already computed the shared key while generating its challenge, because it needs that key to verify the client's proof. Returning it at this stage gives the client the secret needed to produce that proof.

Resolving another connection's context

// dcerpc/idl_lib/ctxeectx.c void rpc_ss_ee_ctx_from_wire( ndr_context_handle *p_wire_context, rpc_ss_context_t *p_context, volatile error_status_t *p_st) { // ... p_uuid = &p_wire_context->context_handle_uuid; // [B1] // ... nil-handle check and table lock ... this_link = &context_table[dce_uuid_hash(p_uuid, (error_status_t *)p_st) % CALLEE_CONTEXT_TABLE_SIZE]; // [B2] while (!dce_uuid_equal(p_uuid, &this_link->uuid, (error_status_t *)p_st)) { this_link = this_link->next_context; // ... reject a missing entry ... } *p_context = this_link->user_context; /* [B3] */ // ... }

The RPC runtime takes the supplied UUID at [B1], searches a process-wide table at [B2], and returns the associated context at [B3]. There is no comparison with the requesting connection or its authenticated identity. Although context creation records a client for lifetime management, that client is not part of this lookup's authorization decision (hooray!!).

We confirmed the boundary directly: one anonymous RPC connection created an SRP verifier, and a second anonymous connection retrieved that verifier's key before any password proof was sent. The first connection's context handle was enough to make the second connection's request succeed.

The service registers the helper with a secure-interface flag and an authentication callback. On the tested TCP path, however, the RPC executor retrieves those registration values and dispatches the server stub without enforcing the callback. Other directory handlers perform their own access checks. The SRP key getter has no equivalent check, leaving it reachable before authentication.

Predictable handles make the lookup usable

// dcerpc/uuid/uuidsys.c void uuid__get_os_time(dce_uuid_time_t *uuid_time) { // ... if (gettimeofday(&tp, (struct timezone *)0)) // [C1] { perror("uuid__get_os_time"); exit(-1); } uuid__uemul((long)tp.tv_sec, UUID_C_100NS_PER_SEC, &utc); uuid__uemul((long)tp.tv_usec, UUID_C_100NS_PER_USEC, &usecs); // [C2] UADD_UVLW_2_UVLW(&usecs, &utc, &utc); // ... add the UUID epoch offset ...

The UUID timestamp generator reads the wall clock at [C1] and converts its microseconds into 100-nanosecond UUID ticks at [C2]. The resulting UUIDv1 handle also contains a clock sequence and node identifier. In our captures, those latter fields remain stable while newly created contexts advance through the timestamp space.

vmdir manages this SRP authentication exchange through the Generic Security Service API (GSS-API), which provides a common interface for authentication mechanisms. Starting the login creates an SRP verifier internally, but the login client does not receive its context handle.

An attacker can obtain reference handles by creating ordinary SRP verifiers through the helper interface. Creating one immediately before the GSS-API login and another immediately afterward bounds the timestamp of its hidden verifier. The shared node and clock-sequence fields then let the attacker construct candidate UUIDs within that interval.

The default search advances in increments of ten UUID ticks, matching the clock's microsecond resolution. The generator also supports uniqueness adjustments within a clock tick, so the PoC includes a one-tick search mode. Clock changes, concurrent activity, and the chosen search bounds can affect recovery; exhausting the window does not establish that a target is patched.

Exploit

Narrowing the Search Window for a Pending Login

The service exposes two relevant RPC interfaces on port 2012:

Interface

UUID

Operations used

SRP verifier helper

c7e94609-6ab0-4767-8e92-b6485bff1649

Create verifier, retrieve key, delete verifier

vmdirdbcp

72c780fe-af6b-42ba-9b02-f61f4ccc98ed

SRP-authenticated bind, directory state, and database open/read/close

The helper's operation numbers are 0 for verifier creation, 1 for key retrieval, and 4 for deletion. GetState is operation 4 on the separate vmdirdbcp interface. The interface UUID is therefore part of identifying an operation; the operation number alone is ambiguous.

The client first creates a reference verifier, starts a separate SRP login as the target principal (e.g. administrator@vsphere.local), and creates the second reference verifier. It keeps the login connection open while querying candidate handles over another anonymous connection. These are all connections controlled by the attacker.

GSS does not return the handle for its own verifier. A reference verifier for the same principal has a different session key, so retrieving that reference key does not complete the pending GSS login. We need the key from the verifier associated with the login connection; the reference handles only narrow the search for it.

In the final standalone PoC test, the reference handles were:

Before: 1d98c67a-e468-11f1-b101-000c29451b35 Hidden: 1d99c43a-e468-11f1-b101-000c29451b35 After: 1d9a8a14-e468-11f1-b101-000c29451b35

The interval between the reference timestamps was 115,610 UUID ticks, or about 11.56 milliseconds. The search recovered the hidden handle shown above after 5,083 queries. Four workers issued the queries in that Python test, so the count includes requests that were already in flight when the match was found.

The SRP verifier helper returns the pending login's actual 20-byte session key. The attack does not need a weak password, a password hash from disk, or an invalid SRP public value.

Completing SRP with the disclosed key

M1 = SHA1((SHA1(N) XOR SHA1(g)) || SHA1(I) || s || A || B || K) HAMK = SHA1(A || M1 || K)

Here, I is the requested principal, N and g are the SRP group parameters, s is the server's salt, and A and B are the public values exchanged during login. The server sends s alongside B in its initial SRP challenge, before the client supplies a password proof. The salt is public: a legitimate client uses it with the password to derive the values needed for authentication.

The client already has all of these inputs except K. Once the key getter supplies K, the client can calculate the normal client proof, M1, and verify the server's response, HAMK.

The attack does not need a weak password, a password hash from disk, or an invalid SRP public value. Our client uses the valid public value A = 2 in the normal 2048-bit group. The reference verifiers use the cheaper 1024-bit group only to obtain the timing bounds.

The implementation hashes minimal big-endian integer representations. On the tested build, the returned B is 276 bytes because CSRP serializes k*v + g^b without first reducing the sum modulo N. Reducing or truncating that returned value while building the transcript produces the wrong proof.

The successful mechanism on this build is the legacy SRP OID 1.2.840.113554.1.2.10. Its token framing also differs from a conventional GSS wrapper: the outer length covers the OID, with the SRP state token following it. The client carries the exchange in SPNEGO bind and ALTER_CONTEXT messages, using RPC packet privacy. Matching that framing is necessary to reach the vulnerable authentication flow.

Proving the authenticated connection

The client derives packet-protection keys from the recovered SRP key using the server's normal implementation. PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA1 expands the key into 64 bytes using the principal as salt and 128 iterations. Those bytes supply an IV, material for the Kerberos AES-256 string-to-key operation, and a 16-byte HMAC key. RPC stubs are encrypted with AES-CBC and authenticated with HMAC-SHA1 over the ciphertext.

PoC output:

{"time": "2026-11-19T22:25:25.919835+00:00", "event": "session_key_disclosed", "uuid": "1d99c43a-e468-11f1-b101-000c29451b35", "key": "1f1476617a050b8e30388e0f58ed80d83f01aa02", "guesses": 5083, "seconds": 0.8774298130301759} {"time": "2026-11-19T22:25:25.952425+00:00", "event": "srp_authentication_complete", "username": "administrator@vsphere.local", "M1": "af03ad96cb799381bf8e9a30a412b4371e24729d", "HAMK": "537b2d5753f213304824551077bddd51ed6693ae", "password_supplied": false} {"time": "2026-11-19T22:25:26.226964+00:00", "event": "protected_rpc_result", "operation": "RpcVmDirGetState", "state": 3, "status": 0, "plaintext": "0300000000000000"}

We used RpcVmDirGetState to test the resulting connection to 192.168.1.81. An anonymous request returned status 5, ACCESS_DENIED. The authenticated request above returned 0300000000000000: the little-endian directory state, 3 (Normal), followed by the operation's success status, 0. The PoC checked the server's SRP proof and the encrypted response's MAC before accepting the result.

Key recovery took approximately 0.88 seconds in this run. The complete test retained the original RPC traffic and a packet capture with 15,343 packets and zero kernel drops. This brings us to the end of exploiting CVE-2026-123890. We have demonstrated how we can authenticate to VMware vCenter's directory service as the administrator user and will now outline how that access can be used to get root access to the device.

Reading the directory database

vmdir/server/vmdir/rpcserv.c, Srv_RpcVmDirOpenDatabaseFile:

// vmdir/server/vmdir/rpcserv.c UINT32 Srv_RpcVmDirOpenDatabaseFile( handle_t hBinding, PWSTR pwszDBFileName, vmdir_dbcp_handle_t *ppFileHandle) { // ... DWORD dwRpcFlags = VMDIR_RPC_FLAG_ALLOW_TCPIP | VMDIR_RPC_FLAG_REQUIRE_AUTH_TCPIP | VMDIR_RPC_FLAG_REQUIRE_AUTHZ; // ... dwError = _VmDirRPCCheckAccess(hBinding, dwRpcFlags, pszDomainDn, &pAccessToken); // [D1] BAIL_ON_VMDIR_ERROR(dwError); // ... validate arguments and convert the filename ... dwError = _VmDirRemoteDBCopyWhiteList(pszDBFileName); // [D2] BAIL_ON_VMDIR_ERROR(dwError); // ... if ((pFileHandle = fopen(pszDBFileName, "rb")) == NULL) { // ... report the open failure and take the error path ... } *ppFileHandle = pFileHandle; // [D3] // ...

The database-copy handler requires authentication and authorization at [D1]. The earlier bypass satisfies those checks as the SSO administrator. The filename passes a database-path allowlist at [D2], and the handler returns a file context at [D3]. We requested /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb through that interface.

The IDL assigns operation 0 to open, 1 to read, and 2 to close. The open request carries a reference wide string and an initially empty context handle. Each read supplies the returned context, a byte count, and an empty output container. Reads continue until the server returns a zero byte count.

Our first complete export contained 16.22 MB. We used 2,048-byte reads so the response, encryption padding, and verifier fit into a single RPC fragment. The directory stayed in state 3, Normal; we did not call RpcVmDirSetBackendState or take the service offline. These calls copy the live file rather than producing a transaction-consistent backup. The downloaded file contained the signing credential needed for the next step.

Signing an administrator API assertion

The TenantCredential-1 record in data.mdb contains the STS RSA private key and its certificate chain. Metasploit already provides extraction and SAML-signing code in vcenter_offline_mdb_extract and vcenter_forge_saml_token. We reused those implementations, matched the signing certificate to the recovered private key, and verified its VMCA issuer.

The signed assertion identifies administrator@vsphere.local and carries the existing template's administrator group claims, including SystemConfiguration.Administrators. The issuer uses the appliance's STS identity, and the assertion includes a short validity window. Once the XML is signed, changing its whitespace can invalidate the digest, so the client preserves its compact serialization.

lib/msf/core/exploit/remote/http/vmware_vcenter.rb, API login:

token = Base64.strict_encode64(Zlib.gzip(assertion)) # [E1] response = vcenter_api_request( 'POST', %w[com vmware cis session], port: port, host: host, headers: { 'Authorization' => "SIGN token=\"#{token}\"" } ) session_id = vcenter_api_value(response) # [E2]

The client gzip-compresses and Base64-encodes the assertion at [E1], following the vendor REST SDK's SAML login example. A successful POST /rest/com/vmware/cis/session returns the API session ID at [E2]. Subsequent requests carry it in the vmware-api-session-id header. Our forged assertion returned HTTP 200 and authorized reads of the appliance's SSH and Bash settings.

From the appliance API to root

The authenticated API session gives us a way to create credentials that SSH will accept. We created a fresh local account through the appliance local-accounts API, assigning the superAdmin role. This is an operating-system account on the appliance; creating it does not require changing an existing account's password.

The tested build accepts the account-creation request through the legacy REST route POST /rest/appliance/local-accounts/<username>, with its configuration inside a config object. The configuration supplies the generated password, roles: ["superAdmin"], and enabled: true. The same API session enables SSH with PUT /rest/appliance/access/ssh and {"enabled":true}, then enables Bash with PUT /rest/appliance/access/shell and {"config":{"enabled":true,"timeout":600}}.

/etc/sudoers.d/applmgmt on the tested appliance:

%superAdmin ALL= PASSWD: ALL, NOPASSWD: OPERATOR_N, ADMINISTRATOR_N

That sudo rule allows the new account to run commands as root using its own generated password. An SSH login initially enters the appliance CLI, so the client requests a PTY and starts shell /bin/bash. After answering the appliance's sudo password prompt, it starts sudo -n /bin/bash -i on the same terminal. The sudo timestamp from that authentication permits the retained root shell.

We verified uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),4044(shellaccess) through the resulting SSH connection. This account and password were created by the forged API session; the supplied lab root credentials were used separately for inspection and were not used to obtain this shell. Using the sessions in Metasploit

[*] 192.168.1.81:2012 - Recovered the pending session key after 17337 guesses in 8.12 seconds [*] 192.168.1.81:2012 - Recovered context 688f5878-e487-11f1-b101-000c29451b35, key f56a33e23fad8b8d340c8ca0887aebe1fb793bab [+] 192.168.1.81:2012 - Authenticated as administrator@vsphere.local without a password; protected directory state: 3 [+] 192.168.1.81:2012 - Saved authentication evidence to /Users/jheysel/codex_research/vsphere_armory_castle_20261119/metasploit/config/loot/20261119190933_default_192.168.1.81_vmware.vmdir.srp_059381.json [*] VMware directory RPC session 3 opened (192.168.1.70:61547 -> 192.168.1.81:2012) at 2026-11-19 19:09:34 -0700 [*] 192.168.1.81:2012 - Interacting with vmdir session 3; use background to return to msfconsole vmdir > whoami Authenticated SSO principal: administrator@vsphere.local vmdir > state Directory state: 3 vmdir > state Directory state: 3

The Metasploit module separates the inexpensive key-disclosure check from the full authentication attempt. check creates an owned verifier and asks for its key through a second anonymous association. run then performs the pending-login search, completes SRP, and verifies the protected operation.

The module's default RPC action retains the authenticated association and exposes a vmdir > prompt with state and whoami commands. Selecting ACTION SHELL continues through database export, SAML API authentication, and SSH to a root command shell. The fresh end-to-end test produced the following output:

[+] 192.168.1.81:2012 - Root execution verified: uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),4044(shellaccess) [*] Command shell session 1 opened (192.168.1.70:62059 -> 192.168.1.81:22) at 2026-11-20 07:48:25 -0700 ... [*] 192.168.1.81:2012 - Interacting with shell session 1; use background to return to msfconsole ... root [ /home/sebastian-fritsch ]# id uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),4044(shellaccess)

CreateSession defaults to true for either action. We resumed the root shell and ran id to show root access before exiting.

The shell action saves the generated account credentials and original SSH/Bash settings before changing the appliance. It retains the temporary account and access settings while the session is open. On exit, it closes SSH, restores the original settings, and deletes its account through the API. The order matters: the appliance refuses to delete an account that still has running processes, and disabling SSH terminates active connections. Closing the console abruptly can prevent cleanup; the saved recovery details identify the account and settings to restore.

Detection opportunities

The unauthenticated key queries are visible before the client establishes packet privacy. Useful network evidence includes repeated calls to operation 1 on the SRP helper interface, with no RPC authentication verifier and context UUIDs that differ mainly in their timestamp fields. In our reproduction, those queries occur between the pending login's initial bind and its SRP proof continuation.

The helper interface UUID, operation number, authentication state, query volume, and UUID pattern are useful together. A connection to port 2012 or an administrator SRP login on its own does not establish exploitation.

The appliance also retains evidence of the database export and subsequent administration. We recovered the following records from the same vCenter 8.0.2.00400 appliance after the test accounts had been removed.

/var/log/vmware/vmdird/vmdird-syslog.log:

2026-11-20T14:45:46.792144+00:00 info vmdird t@140450245629504: Remote DB transfer (/storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb) granted.

The directory service records this message when its filename allowlist grants a remote database-copy request. It identifies the requested database, but does not include the caller's address or prove that the transfer completed. An unexpected grant for data.mdb provides a timestamp to correlate with network traffic and the later API activity; legitimate directory replication can also use this interface. The SRP bypass can occur without a database-copy request, so this entry identifies the export stage.

/var/log/vmware/vapi/endpoint/endpoint-access.log:

2026-11-20T14:48:08.065Z | vAPI-I/O dispatcher-0 | e97ae44e-a503-4b58-9b68-1168c80e89c6 | 192.168.1.70 - - [20/Nov/2026:14:48:07 +0000] "POST /rest/appliance/local-accounts/sebastian-fritsch HTTP/1.1" 200 0 "-" "Mozilla/5.0 (iPad; CPU OS 17_7_2 like Mac OS X) AppleWebKit/605.1.15 (KHTML, like Gecko) Version/17.4.1 Mobile/15E148 Safari/604.1" 233

The API access log records the source address, request path, status, and user-agent. This request creates the account used by the root-shell stage. The same file contains our POST /rest/com/vmware/cis/session, PUT /rest/appliance/access/ssh, PUT /rest/appliance/access/shell, and eventual account-deletion requests. An HTTP 200 on a settings request does not reveal which value was applied, so the appliance management log supplies the next part of the sequence.

/var/log/vmware/applmgmt/applmgmt.log:

2026-11-20T14:48:07 PM UTC [47843]INFO:vmware.appliance.localaccounts.localaccounts_impl:Administrator@VSPHERE.LOCAL created the local account user sebastian-fritsch 2026-11-20T14:48:09 PM UTC [47843]DEBUG:root:com.vmware.appliance.version1.access.ssh.set(enable=True) 2026-11-20T14:48:10 PM UTC [47843]DEBUG:root:com.vmware.appliance.version1.access.shell.set(config=Structure('ShellConfig', dict(enabled=True, timeout=600))) 2026-11-20T14:49:34 PM UTC [47843]INFO:vmware.appliance.localaccounts.localaccounts_impl:Administrator@VSPHERE.LOCAL deleted the local account user sebastian-fritsch.

These records identify Administrator@VSPHERE.LOCAL as the account creator and show SSH and Bash being enabled. The configuration values appear in DEBUG-level records on the tested appliance; the account creation and deletion records are INFO-level. The forged SAML session is treated as an administrator session, so that identity alone does not distinguish it from legitimate administration.

/var/log/audit/sshinfo.log.1.gz, decompressed:

2026-11-20T14:48:12.368544+00:00 node-1w7jr9qrllzwd9vncrrr8zlf9 sshd[592859]: Accepted password for sebastian-fritsch from 192.168.1.70 port 62059 ssh2 2026-11-20T14:48:17.298091+00:00 node-1w7jr9qrllzwd9vncrrr8zlf9 sudo: sebastian-fritsch : TTY=pts/0 ; PWD=/home/sebastian-fritsch ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/bin/bash -i 2026-11-20T14:49:34.208901+00:00 node-1w7jr9qrllzwd9vncrrr8zlf9 userdel[593806]: delete user 'sebastian-fritsch'

The SSH and sudo records tie the new account to the API client's address and a root Bash shell. They also retain the deletion performed during cleanup. Search sshinfo.log and its rotated copies; these entries had moved into sshinfo.log.1.gz by the time we collected them. Matching records are also available through the system journal.

/var/log/audit/audit.log:

type=EXECVE msg=audit(1795186087.886:3732): argc=6 a0="/usr/sbin/useradd" a1="-m" a2="-G" a3="superAdmin" a4="--" a5="sebastian-fritsch" type=EXECVE msg=audit(1795186097.286:3767): argc=4 a0="sudo" a1="-n" a2="/bin/bash" a3="-i"

Linux audit records preserve the command arguments for adding the user to superAdmin and invoking sudo -n /bin/bash -i. These examples come from a rotated audit log. They remain available after the account and its home directory are removed, subject to log retention.

For this reproduced path, correlate an unexpected database-transfer grant with creation of a local administrator, SSH/Bash enablement, and an SSH login followed by sudo. The database-copy grant appears at 14:45:46 UTC, account creation at 14:48:07, and the root-shell command at 14:48:17. These are administrative operations that can occur legitimately; their sequence and whether they fit expected activity determine their value as indicators. The account name, source address, user-agent, UUIDs, and session values shown here belong to our lab run and are not fixed attacker identifiers.

Mitigation

Broadcom identifies vCenter 8.0 U3m as the fixed release for the 8.0 branch in VMSA-2026-0009 and its accompanying FAQ. Other release branches have their own guidance. Apply the vendor's supported update for the deployed product and keep the directory-service management interfaces reachable only by the systems that need them.

The failed boundary spans both the SRP helper and the RPC runtime: a pending authentication key is exposed, and a connection can resolve a context that it does not own. Replacing predictable UUIDs alone leaves that ownership problem in place. We did not compare the vendor's fixed binaries, so this analysis does not attribute a particular code change to the patch.

Additionally, A Security found that DeepSeek V4.1 Flash cost a fraction of what other models required, at $0.81 per validated finding, when the closed models cost between $9.54 (for Gemini 3.8 Flash) and $31.85 (GPT 5.6 Sol).

GLM 5.3, however, was not as cost-efficient, at $10.49 per validated finding, slightly more than the cheapest closed model.

Study Caveats: Cost Scope and Provider Variables Complicate the Results

While the A Security test is another example showing a rising interest in Chinese open-weight AI models, the results of the study, released on November 23, do not mean these models are always better, or cheaper, at finding vulnerabilities.

In addition, the Israeli company specified that cost figures covered only the four exploitation agents and exclude discovery, browser use, reporting, advisor calls and other orchestration costs, partly because advisor configurations varied across runs. A full scan would cost more, and costs will vary by setup.

The pricing basis also differs: GLM 5.3 was priced at its official token rates, while the other models used recorded provider spend. DeepSeek ran on a pinned provider route after earlier runs through another provider had heavy fallback, and timings reflect the specific inference providers and configurations used, so they should not be read as fixed model-level speed rankings.

DeepSeek also drifted the most, reporting findings outside its assigned lead on at least 4.5% of leads, versus under 2.5% for the other models. While A Security researchers noted that such considerations matter little for attackers, it raises scope-control concerns for defenders, as an agent straying from its lead could touch assets outside an engagement's authorized scope.

Title: Google Researcher Shows How a Single Bit Change in .NET Files Bypassed Windows Code Integrity
Context: NET Framework loads a program file let a local attacker run untrusted code past two separate protections on Windows built to block it, Google Project Zero researcher James...
Full Text:
A quirk in how the .NET Framework loads a program file let a local attacker run untrusted code past two separate protections on Windows built to block it, Google Project Zero researcher James Forshaw showed in a write-up published yesterday.

The same loading behavior bypassed Oracle VirtualBox's process hardening on Windows hosts, tracked as CVE-2026-87268, and Windows code integrity, tracked as CVE-2026-108398.

Oracle fixed the VirtualBox flaw in September, and Microsoft fixed the Windows one on October 13, both before the write-up appeared.

VirtualBox on Windows monitors the system calls that load program files into its virtual machine processes, so a less-trusted user on the same computer cannot push code into them. Forshaw got past that watch through the .NET Framework.

The framework can run a .NET program file from a plain copy in memory when the normal way of loading it, as an executable image, fails. Version 4 of the framework takes that fallback on one specific error, and the memory copy skips the image checks a loaded program would face.

The VirtualBox check returned that error for any .NET file compiled as AnyCPU, a form meant to run on any processor, so an unchanged file loaded through the path the hardening never inspects.

To get the file loaded while a virtual machine was started, he registered a COM object in the current user's settings that a protected VirtualBox process would pull in, a method known as COM hijacking. He set out the mechanism in his technical analysis.

Oracle rates the flaw, CVE-2026-87268, as a local problem that needs low privileges and no user interaction, scores it 7.8, and lists VirtualBox 7.2.16 on Windows hosts as affected. Its security advisory says a successful attack can result in the "takeover of Oracle VM VirtualBox."

The code runs inside the protected VirtualBox process. It is not a break out of a guest virtual machine onto the host, and the attacker begins as an ordinary user on that host.

The same idea worked against Windows' own code-integrity checks, which decide what user-mode code is allowed to run. There is no VirtualBox hook here, only the system call that maps a file as an image.

The researcher found that clearing a single bit in a .NET file's header, the IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE flag, made that call reject the file while .NET still loaded and ran it.

"This single bit change is all you need to load an untrusted .NET assembly," he wrote. He tried it on Windows 11 S Mode, which enables User Mode Code Integrity (UMCI), the policy that limits which user-mode programs can run. A logic error in .NET's own policy check let the file load even with UMCI enforced.

The flaw, CVE-2026-108398, works through the .NET Framework version 4 loading path and needs a program willing to load the assembly. It is not a way to seize any Windows machine over the internet.

Microsoft rates it a local, low-privilege security-feature bypass, scores it 8.8, and fixed it on October 13. The company lists it as publicly disclosed but not used in attacks.

The same file reached a more sensitive target as well. Protected Process Light, or PPL, is a kind of Windows process that ordinary programs, even ones with administrator rights, are not meant to enter. By hijacking a COM object that WerSecureFault.exe loads, he ran his test code inside a PPL process at the highest protection level without administrator rights.

The older Protected Process type resisted the technique because the .NET runtime files lack the page hashes it requires. The October fix corrects the policy check for UMCI but does not change loading for protected processes, so that PPL route should still work, according to the researcher. It carries no separate CVE.

What to patch

On Windows hosts, update VirtualBox to a build that carries the September fixes. The affected versions are 7.2.16 and 7.2.18, and 7.2.18 shipped on September 15 with that set. An upstream code fix is not the same as a released binary, so check the running version rather than assume an older build already has it.

.NET systems need the October 13 update that matches the exact Windows and .NET Framework version in use, not one shared package. The update release notes list the right KB for each. On Windows 11 version 26H2, for example, it is KB5127694.

Forshaw first presented the Windows code-integrity bypass at the 44Con conference in September, having judged it fell outside Microsoft's rules for what gets fixed. After .NET developers told him the behavior he had counted on was accidental, he reported it in late September. The fix arrived in October's Patch Tuesday, less than a month later.

Title: Familiar weaknesses, exploited faster: defending against agentic cyber attacks
Context: We recently blogged about unlocking the potential of agentic cyber defence across a range of areas including enhanced threat detection and automated incident response
Full Text:
The NCSC believes the adoption of AI-enabled cyber can close the gap between attackers and defenders. We recently blogged about unlocking the potential of agentic cyber defence across a range of areas including enhanced threat detection and automated incident response. However, it will take time for defensive AI-driven programmes to mature, so organisations can’t sit back and wait for agentic defence to protect them. AI-enabled cyber defence is not the sole answer to agentic attacks; the foundations of cyber security and basic cyber hygiene remain the priority.

As we stated in the NCSC’s 2026 ‘The State of the Cyber Nation’ Annual Review, AI does not make established cyber security controls obsolete. In fact building strong foundations has never mattered more. AI is making weaknesses easier to find and faster to exploit; a forgotten key or an unprotected API which might once have gone unnoticed for years can be found in minutes.

Nearly everything the NCSC has seen can be prevented by implementing cyber security best practice, the application of modern cyber security approaches like zero trust, and by the diligent application of technical controls in line with your organisation's technologies and processes. For organisations seeking a structured approach:

zero trust principles can help protect against agentic attacks; explicitly verify identity, ensure least privilege everywhere, and deploy controls as if attackers are already inside your network

the Cyber Assessment Framework helps organisations responsible for essential services or critical functions assess and improve their cyber resilience

the NCSC’s Cyber Essentials sets out the minimum technical controls for organisations, as recommended by the government

Although they may not always be applied in the right place, the controls that mitigate the threat from agentic offensive frameworks will already be familiar to many organisations. Today's frameworks may be replaced by quieter, more capable ones, and tools will change. But the cyber security fundamentals won't.

This is your chance to get ahead of the threat. Consider how your organisation would answer the questions above, and make sure your answers hold up against an attacker that never needs a break and never gets tired of asking.

Kris B, Incident Handler, Incident Management

Ellen T, Lead Data Scientist, Vulnerability Management Team

David Chismon, CTO for Architecture

Title: OpenAI and Cisco Release Open-Source Tool to Shield Unpatched Linux Systems
Context: OpenAI and Cisco have released Shirudo, an open-source Linux security tool designed to temporarily block exploitation of known vulnerabilities until organizations can install...
Full Text:
OpenAI and Cisco have released Shirudo, an open-source Linux security tool designed to temporarily block exploitation of known vulnerabilities until organizations can install permanent patches.

In a November 23 announcement, OpenAI said that Shirudo could guard live systems without forcing a restart.

Greg Brockman, president and co-founder of OpenAI, commented, "Finding a bug today doesn't mean you can patch every system tomorrow."

How the Shields Work

Shirudo is built on extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), which allows vetted mini-programs run inside the Linux kernel, the core of the operating system.

Each shield was designed to target only the one operation an exploit needed, leaving normal requests untouched, and operators could trial a proposed protection before approving it. OpenAI said shutting off a risky function entirely could cause an outage, because the same function could serve both attackers and legitimate users.

Shields carried a cryptographic signature that was verified before it could load. A Trusted Platform Module (TPM), a hardware security chip, kept a log of every protection added or removed, giving teams evidence of what had been active on a system.

Isovalent, a Cisco-owned company, described Shirudo as a rewrite of Tetragon, the open-source eBPF security platform it released in 2022. It said Tetragon already powered Live Protect, which Cisco uses to mitigate flaws in its own products.

Read more on Linux flaws: Linux Flaws Exposed Before Fixes as Root Exploit Goes Public

Java4Shell Test and Early Limits

In a single controlled test, a shield written by OpenAI's Codex inserted validation into Java's Base64 decoding routine.

Attached to an Elasticsearch instance that was already running, it stopped a Java4Shell exploit attempt while the application stayed online. Isovalent said the mitigation "appears to be effective" and would protect affected applications until OpenJDK was patched.

The result came from a test designed and run by the project builders rather than an independent evaluation.

Isovalent engineer John Fastabend said at a Linux kernel summit in 2026 that his team often came across vulnerabilities with no suitable point in the kernel where a shield could attach, LWN reported.

Shirudo's GitHub repository described the project as pre-release, with production use requiring a Linux kernel carrying Shirudo's kernel patches and a TPM 2.0 chip.

OpenAI said it hoped eventually to release shields that had already been tested at the same time flaws were disclosed. It added that the two companies were designing Shirudo so AI agents could investigate flaws, write shields and check that they worked and called automatically generated least-privilege policies a longer-term aim.

Title: CISA Adds Three Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
Context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
Full Text:
CISA has added three new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-131914 Idunno AntiCsrf Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability

CVE-2026-132165 Drupal Core Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

CVE-2026-132224 Optimizely Web Experimentation External Control of Critical State Data Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Title: Attackers exploited an Azure API Management flaw to steal secrets, Microsoft warns
Context: Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) subsequently linked cyberattacks against two energy companies to the vulnerability, providing evidence of exploitation in an...
Full Text:
Microsoft is warning customers that attackers exploited a flaw in Azure API Management Classic tiers to steal stored secrets, an intrusion that Norway’s National Security Authority has linked to breaches at two energy companies and says organizations should assume exposed credentials were compromised.

Microsoft said in an Azure Service Health security advisory sent to customers that it identified the vulnerability on Nov. 18 and deployed a mitigation the following day. The advisory, tracking ID MZK9-GH0, said the exposure began before Microsoft found the flaw, reported Bleeping Computer.

The company said in the advisory that “an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances.”

The potentially exposed information includes secrets stored in Named Values, client secrets associated with identity providers and OpenID Connect providers, subscription keys, and tokens used to call direct management APIs, the report added.

Microsoft warned that its mitigation does not invalidate previously compromised credentials and that affected customers must rotate potentially exposed secrets and investigate suspicious activity. The advisory said only the Classic tiers of the service are affected, not Azure API Management v2, the report added.

The potential exposure was not limited to a theoretical security risk. Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) subsequently linked cyberattacks against two energy companies to the vulnerability, providing evidence of exploitation in an operational environment.

Norway tells customers to assume exposure

In a security advisory published November 20 and updated November 23, NSM said an unidentified actor had actively targeted access tokens, secrets, and Named Values stored in Azure API Management.

“Earlier this week, NSM became aware of a vulnerability in Azure API Management (APIM) that affects several Norwegian businesses,” NSM said in the advisory, translated from Norwegian.

It said the vulnerability should now be closed, but asked organizations to take measures anyway.

“Anyone with Azure API Manager must assume that their secrets and named values ​​are out of whack,” the advisory added. “This means that the business must roll back all tokens and secrets.”

In the advisory, NSM’s director of operational cybersecurity, Martin Albert-Hoff, said the vulnerability was first discovered by Norway’s energy sector. The agency identified Equinor and Skagerak Energi among the affected organizations and said the vulnerability had also affected organizations in other countries and sectors.

Equinor disclosed a cyberattack against some of its IT systems on November 17. In an update published November 20, the company said the attack had been stopped, production was running normally, and there was no indication that data had been stolen or altered.

A day later, Skagerak Energi reported an attempted cyberattack against some of its IT systems. The company said the incident had not affected its operations or production and that there was no indication that information had been compromised.

NSM warned that public disclosure of the vulnerability could encourage additional threat actors to attempt exploitation.

“When a vulnerability becomes known, multiple actors may attempt to exploit it,” the agency said in its advisory (translated from Norwegian), adding that the rapid escalation in the use of artificial intelligence was affecting the threat environment.

Neither Microsoft’s advisory nor NSM’s notice includes a CVE identifier for the flaw.

Urgent need to rotate credentials

Microsoft’s mitigation closed the unauthorized management-plane access path, but it advised customers to investigate whether their APIM instances were accessed before the fix and whether stored credentials could have been exposed, the report added.

In a November 21 post on its Azure Integration Services blog, Microsoft published guidance on identifying and rotating credentials configured in Azure API Management.

The guidance covers subscription keys, Named Values containing secrets, backend credentials, OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect client secrets, connection strings, and credentials written directly into API policies.

Microsoft recommended that organizations rotate credentials at the systems where they were originally issued, rather than simply updating their values in APIM.

“Updating the value in API Management alone does not invalidate the old credential,” the company said in the blog post, as per the report.

NSM has issued more extensive recommendations, advising organizations using Azure API Management to assume that their secrets and Named Values may have been exposed and to rotate all associated tokens and secrets.

The agency also published a patch check. According to NSM, instances on the 0.52.x branch are patched from build 31936, and those on 0.53.x are from build 31938. V2 and Consumption tier instances are not vulnerable, the agency said.

Organizations with unpatched instances should contact Microsoft directly, and those that see signs of compromise should contact NSM, the advisory said.

Cloud security researcher Anders Kristiansen, who published detection and hunting guidance after the advisories, said patching alone is not enough.

“If you run APIM, patching isn’t the end of it,” Kristiansen wrote in a blog post.

His rotation list includes backend credentials, app registration secrets, subscription keys, the Key Vault secrets the service references, and tenant access keys. Microsoft did not immediately respond to CSO’s request for comment.

Title: Microsoft Fixes Azure API Management Classic Flaw as Actor Targets Customer Secrets
Context: "It is still uncertain how extensive the exploitation of the vulnerability is, and has been
Full Text:
Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) has disclosed that it became aware of a security vulnerability in Microsoft's Azure API Management (APIM) that has affected multiple businesses in the country, including energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi.

"An unknown actor has been actively looking for access tokens, secrets, and named values ​​in APIM," NSM said. "It is still uncertain how extensive the exploitation of the vulnerability is, and has been."

The security agency said it has so far seen no evidence that has had any impact on Norwegian businesses.

According to a non-public advisory issued by Microsoft, the issue is said to affect the APIM classic tier. Instances on v2 tiers are not affected.

"On 18 November 2026, Microsoft identified a security issue affecting Azure API Management Classic tiers that could allow unauthorized access to certain management functionality if the service was not configured according to documented security best practices," Microsoft said in the advisory.

"Microsoft closed the access path on 19 November 2026. Our investigation found that customers were exposed and an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the security issue."

As a result, credentials or configuration secrets associated with the API Management resources may have been accessed by an unauthorized third-party if the service has not been configured as per security best practices. The information that may have been accessed could include -

Secrets stored in Named Values Client secrets associated with identity providers

Client secrets associated with OpenID Connect providers

Subscription keys

Tokens used to call direct management APIs

As of November 21, 2026, the Windows maker has released guidance for customers to help identify and rotate the secrets and credentials configured in their Azure API Management instances. It did not disclose how many customers were affected.

"If someone obtains a credential from that configuration, they may be able to use it directly against the service it protects," security researcher Anders Kristiansen said. "What they can reach depends on the credential's permissions and whether it is still valid."

NSM has also warned that the vulnerability affects several sectors in Norway and other entities outside of the country, adding it's working with national and international partners and businesses about the matter.

Title: WHMCS SQL Injection Could Expose Customer Data and Admin Password Hashes without Login
Context: Fixes are available only for supported versions, so installations on the 8
Full Text:
A flaw in WHMCS's shopping cart, the billing and automation platform many web hosting companies use to run their businesses, could allow anyone on the internet to retrieve customer records and administrator password hashes from an installation's database. No login is needed.

The company disclosed the SQL injection yesterday along with two other flaws that need a logged-in client, and released fixed versions. It has not reported attacks using any of the three.

Because no login is needed, the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-82981 (CVSS score: 8.7), is within reach of anyone who can load the shopping cart of a vulnerable installation over the internet.

The records an attacker could pull include clients' personal and support information as well as admin accounts with their hashed passwords, according to the company's advisory. A stolen hash is not a working password, but it gives attackers something to try to crack offline.

The 9.0.10 and 8.13.8 updates shipped yesterday, and the release notes list them as maintenance releases. For the 9.1 series, the security advisory names 9.1.2 as the fix, but that build had not yet appeared on the company's 9.1 release notes page at publication time.

Fixes are available only for supported versions, so installations on the 8.0 to 8.12 series must upgrade to a fixed release.

Installing the updates falls to self-hosted administrators, since WHMCS Cloud installations are updated automatically, according to the company's updating documentation.

The second SQL injection, CVE-2026-82979 (CVSS score: 7.1), sits in the Client Area and needs a logged-in client that holds the View & Manage Contacts permission. That client could read other customers' personal, billing, and support information, as well as the same admin records and password hashes, the second advisory says.

The third flaw, CVE-2026-93700, lies in how email campaigns process client-supplied data. A logged-in client could use it to read sensitive configuration files on the server, including database credentials, and to run code on the server, its advisory says.

It carries the highest score of the three, 9.0, though its CVE record uses the older CVSS 3.1 scale while the other two use CVSS 4.0. That record's vector indicates that some user interaction is required, and the company has not said what else exploitation entails.

All three flaws were reported by a single researcher who uses the handle alakazamspooon.

For the email-campaign flaw, updating is not the whole job. The email-campaign advisory also tells administrators to:

Delete every planned or ongoing campaign under Utilities > Email Campaigns, using Delete in each campaign's Manage Campaign menu.

Clear the template cache under Utilities > System > System Cleanup, using Empty Template Cache.

Update to a fixed release.

The advisory does not explain why existing campaigns must go, leaving open the question of whether updating alone is enough.

This is at least the third round of WHMCS security fixes this year. The company patched an authorization flaw in the Client Area on May 12, described in its May advisory, and an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw on September 3, described in its September advisory.

Title: Patching vCenter Zero-Day Is Only Step One
Context: 20, 2026 ThreatDefence, VMware vCenter CVE-2026-123890 Zero-Day: Patching and Hunting The Cyber Sec Guru, How ARMORY CASTLE Used a vCenter Zero-Day to Reach ESXi Rescana, VMware...
Full Text:
CVE-2026-123890 is a critical authentication bypass in VMware vCenter's directory service, rated 9.8 out of 10. An attacker who can reach vCenter on the network can become administrator@vsphere.local without a password. A suspected China-nexus espionage group, ARMORY CASTLE, exploited it as a zero-day from early September 2026. Broadcom patched it on Nov. 19, and CISA gave U.S. federal agencies until Nov. 23 to fix it.

Install the patch today. Then plan for the harder job. If anything that could reach your vCenter was compromised at any point since September, the patch closes the door but doesn't take back what went through it. In the intrusion researchers investigated, that included vCenter's SAML signing key, its master encryption key and Active Directory credentials copied straight out of virtual machine disks.

Let's see how the attackers used this flaw, which builds fix it, and the hunting and credential rotation that should follow the patch.

What Is CVE-2026-123890

Broadcom disclosed the flaw last week, in advisory VMSA-2026-0009, which fixes five vulnerabilities across vCenter, SDDC Manager and VMware Tools for Windows. CVE-2026-123890 is the critical one. An authentication bypass using an alternate path (CWE-288) in the VMware Directory Service, the component behind vCenter's single sign-on. Mandiant found it and reported it privately.

The bug lives in a remote procedure call interface that vCenter's directory service exposes on TCP port 2012. Its Secure Remote Password login generates predictable identifiers based on timestamps, and according to researchers, an attacker can use that to recover the shared session key without knowing any password. The result is an authenticated session as administrator@vsphere.local, the most powerful account in a vSphere environment.

From there, an attacker can run commands and copy files through the directory service, including data.mdb, the database that holds the SSO domain's accounts and the private key vCenter uses to sign SAML login tokens. It is not a virtual machine escape. It's worse in a different way - it hands over the console that manages every host and VM.

Two things make it easy to get wrong:

It's a different bug from CVE-2026-59309, the vCenter authentication bypass Broadcom fixed in July. Mandiant observed attackers using CVE-2026-123890 against a vCenter that was already patched for the July flaw.

There is no workaround. Broadcom's only fix is the update, which its own FAQ treats as an emergency change.

How ARMORY CASTLE used it from a support box to domain credentials

Mandiant's write-up shows why vCenter being reachable only from the internal network didn't protect it. The attackers never touched vCenter from the internet. They worked their way to it from the inside.

ARMORY CASTLE's path from a remote-support appliance to Active Directory credentials

Break in at the edge. The group, formerly tracked as UNC5221, first exploited a separate zero-day in BeyondTrust Remote Support, CVE-2026-102764.

Find the VMware estate. From the support appliance, it scanned the internal network for VMware ports, including 443, 2012, 5480 and 9080, then moved to internal Linux appliances that had no endpoint detection and response (EDR) tooling. It dropped two web shells and became root by setting the SUID bit on /bin/env with the gdb debugger.

Take vCenter. A custom Go tool Mandiant calls BONESAW exploited CVE-2026-123890 over port 2012, created a new SSO administrator account, copied the directory database and extracted the token-signing key.

Forge logins. A second tool, SAWSNAKE, used the stolen key to sign SAML tokens as the administrator, a "Golden SAML" attack that bypasses passwords and MFA.

Drop into the appliance. The group switched on SSH through vCenter's appliance management API, logged in with its new account, stole vCenter's master encryption key and its PostgreSQL database password, then switched SSH off again.

Reach the hosts and the domain. It logged in to ESXi hosts as vpxuser and root, added its own SSH key, and used a Python tool to extract the Active Directory database (NTDS.dit) and registry hives straight from a virtual machine's disk. The files left through the original support appliance.

Two backdoors kept the door open: BEARBONES, a modified Dropbear SSH server that accepts a hardcoded password, and LAZYBONES, which takes commands through Slack. The timing matters too. BONESAW's build timestamp is July 13, 2026, and the attackers used it in early September. Go build timestamps can be faked, but Mandiant reads it as a tool built for broader operations, not a one-off.
