Title: Attackers Exploit Optimizely Flaw To Inject Malicious JavaScript
Context: IntroductionOn November 16, 2026, an attacker exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely's Web Experimentation account signup flow
Full Text: IntroductionOn November 16, 2026, an attacker exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely's Web Experimentation account signup flow. Optimizely is a platform used to create, manage, test, and personalize digital content and websites. The flaw allowed the attacker to edit the Project JavaScript (projectJS) field. Customers use this field to add custom code that runs on pages that load the Optimizely snippet. By abusing this mechanism, the attacker injected malicious JavaScript into customer projects. The code was then delivered to visitors’ browsers through the Optimizely snippets, including snippets served from Optimizely’s content delivery network (CDN).The attack highlights the continued risk posed by third-party script dependencies and software supply chain compromises, particularly when websites rely on trusted third-party platforms to deliver JavaScript that runs in visitors’ browsers.Optimizely reported that it blocked the vulnerable path, deployed a fix, removed the injected code from affected projects, ended active sessions, revoked tokens, reset access for affected accounts, and notified impacted customers.The malicious payload was designed to replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses, skim payment card details, steal cookies, capture page screenshots, and deliver iOS exploits to iPhones and iPads. Organizations using Optimizely, or similar third-party JavaScript platforms, should treat this incident as a reminder to review third-party script governance, monitoring, and browser-side security controls. ThreatLabz ObservationsThreatLabz identified more than 450 unique domains and more than 3,000 URLs serving the malicious script. These findings suggest a broader impact across organizations and industry verticals than previously reported. The affected domains span industries including the following:Airlines and TravelAutomotiveBanking and FinanceE-commerceInsuranceNews and MediaProperty and Real EstateRetail and FashionSmart HomeSportsTechnology and SaaSTelecommunications RecommendationsFor end users who visited affected sitesMonitor bank and credit card statements for suspicious activity.Review cryptocurrency transactions made on or around November 16, 2026.Be cautious of unexpected account activity on sites visited during the incident.Update iOS and iPadOS devices to the latest available security version.Change passwords for accounts used on potentially affected websites, especially if the same credentials are reused elsewhere.For organizations using OptimizelyReview Optimizely project configurationAudit all Project JavaScript fields for unauthorized or unexpected code.Review recent changes, user activity, account creation events, and administrative access.Confirm whether any project snippets were modified during the exposure window.Verify that production pages load only approved versions of Optimizely snippets.Rotate and reset accessReset credentials for affected Optimizely administrative users.Rotate API tokens, session tokens, and integration keys associated with Optimizely.Enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all users with access to experimentation or web personalization platforms.Deploy Content Security Policy (CSP) in enforcement mode where possibleRestrict script execution to approved domains.Limit where pages can send requests and load images and frames using connect-src, img-src, frame-src, and related CSP directives.Use CSP reporting to identify unexpected browser-side activity.Reduce third-party JavaScript riskMaintain an inventory of third-party scripts loaded across websites.Review whether each third-party script is still required.Apply least-privilege principles to third-party tags and tag management platforms.Monitor third-party script changes and unexpected behavior. How It WorksOptimizely Web Experimentation allows site owners to run A/B tests, personalization logic, and other front-end experiments by loading JavaScript on customer websites. The Project JavaScript field is designed to let customers add custom JavaScript that executes on any page that loads the Optimizely snippet.Public reporting indicates that the attacker injected malicious JavaScript into the Project JavaScript field of affected customer projects. The injected code was then delivered through legitimate Optimizely snippets. As a result, when visitors loaded a page with a modified snippet, the injected JavaScript could run in their browsers.Scope of script activity: The observed JavaScript activity is primarily limited to the browser context of the website where the scripts are loaded. The wallet replacement, clipboard manipulation, form monitoring, card-skimming, screen capture, and network-hooking behaviors operate inside the current page, its accessible DOM, same-origin frames, page-initiated requests, and JavaScript-accessible cookies or browser APIs. By design, this JavaScript cannot directly inspect other browser tabs, unrelated websites, other sites’ cookies, local files, or global browser activity. The main exception is the iOS/iPadOS exploit-delivery branch: if one of the delivered exploit chains succeeds, the resulting impact could potentially exceed normal web-page sandbox restrictions.Attack chainThe figure below shows how malicious JavaScript reached website visitors through Optimizely snippets.Figure 1: Attack chain showing how a threat actor injected malicious JavaScript into Optimizely customer projects.Initial access and injectionAs stated above, the attacker exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely’s Web Experimentation account signup flow. This flaw allowed unauthorized write access to the Project JavaScript field for multiple customer projects. Modified snippets were served through existing delivery paths, including Optimizely’s CDN (including cdn.optimizely.com) and, in some cases, customer domains. This made the attack more effective because many affected websites already trusted and allowed Optimizely scripts.Malicious JavaScript payloadIn most affected snippets, the injected code acted as a loader that fetched a second-stage JavaScript payload named track.js from attacker-controlled infrastructure such as 1688360[.]cc. The JavaScript payload provided the main malicious functionality, and ran in the visitor’s browser within the context of the affected website.The following flowchart shows what track.js does after it runs in a visitor’s browser. Figure 2: Clipboard hijacking, card skimming, cookie theft, screen capturing, and attempted exploit delivery on iOS and iPadOS.Cryptocurrency address replacement The script monitors page content, clipboard operations, and network-transmitted data for cryptocurrency wallet addresses. Targeted cryptocurrencies include Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tron, Solana, Litecoin, Toncoin, Bitcoin Cash, and Dogecoin. When the script detects a valid wallet address, the script attempts to replace it with an attacker-controlled wallet address. Cookie theft and screen capture Cookie theft and screen capture happens only when a valid crypto wallet address is replaced and the element is visible. In that case, the JavaScript payload script loaded the legitimate html2canvas.min.js to capture a screenshot of the page, along with the page URL, cookies, original wallet address, and other metadata. This data is sent to the attacker endpoint https://1688360[.]cc/hit.php, likely so the operator can validate successful replacement activity and capture the victim’s session context. The JavaScript payload could collect browser cookies from the affected website, with some exceptions such as if the HttpOnly flag was set. This could cause users to unknowingly send cryptocurrency to the attacker instead of the intended recipient.Payment card skimmingLater versions of the payload added payment card skimming functionality. The script monitors input and textarea elements, keyboard events, form submissions, and web requests for payment card numbers, expiration dates, and CVV values on the compromised website. Captured card data was to an attacker-controlled endpoint (1688360[.]cc/card.php). Note the skimmer could not read payment details entered inside secure cross-origin payment iframes, such as hosted payment fields from providers like Stripe or Adyen.Attempted iOS exploit delivery For visitors using iPhones or iPads, the malware reportedly attempted to load the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits. The payload used device and browser checks to decide whether to attempt iOS-specific exploitation. When the payload identified a visitor’s device as an iPhone or iPad, it added two script elements to the page to load external JavaScript files. Indicators of these pages are the elements data-channel-code, data-chain-url, and data-cfasync attributes.The script injected a hidden iframe in some cases (hxxps://eil786npto9u5bq[.]icu/JIUJIU888/weifile[.]html) on devices it identified as running iOS 18.6 or earlier. The iframe is positioned off-screen with zero width and height, suggesting it is not intended to be visible to the user. iOS exploit delivery componentstrack.js is the browser-side payload. It checks for iOS or iPadOS and loads additional components when it detects either operating system.boot.js is the main iOS loader. It uses Safari and iOS version information to select the next delivery path.weifile.html provides a separate delivery path for selected iOS and iPadOS versions. It loads index.js.index.js initializes an obfuscated loader, decodes embedded modules, reports device and domain metadata, and may fetch additional modules (if required). The following table summarizes the two modules embedded in index.js.Embedded Module IdentifierDescription57620206d62079baad0e57e6d9ec93120c0f5247Utility/runtime helper module providing encoding, binary parsing, numeric conversion, URL normalization, and typed-array/DataView helpers.14669ca3b1519ba2a8f40be287f646d4d7593eb0Browser environment profiling and anti-analysis module that checks runtime capabilities, storage behavior, WebRTC, MathML rendering, WebAssembly behavior, and automation indicators such as navigator.webdriver.Table 1: Functions of the two modules embedded in index.js. ConclusionThe Optimizely incident highlights how attackers can compromise trusted third-party JavaScript supply chains to reach users across many websites at once. By abusing a legitimate experimentation feature, the attacker delivered injected JavaScript through snippets that affected websites already trusted. Note the malicious JavaScript code can run in visitors’ browsers without any obvious change to the page. The card-skimming and wallet-replacement behavior should be understood as page-context activity, not browser-wide monitoring. These scripts act within the compromised site where they are loaded. Broader impact would depend on successful exploitation by the iOS/WebKit exploit chain. Title: NGINX2Root (CVE-2026-123007): Frequently asked questions about five critical NGINX vulnerabilities
Context: A bug is only exploitable if the relevant feature is in use
Full Text:
Frequently asked questions about five critical NGINX remote code execution vulnerabilities and five additional flaws fixed in F5’s November 18 out-of-band release.

Key takeaways

NGINX2Root is associated with five critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, and a separate, unpatched Linux kernel local privilege escalation (LPE) flaw that can be chained with the NGINX bugs to gain root.

CVE-2026-123007 is the most urgent of the five. It is an unauthenticated RCE flaw in NGINX’s HTTP/2 implementation and requires only HTTP/2 over TLS to be enabled. A PoC is publicly available on GitHub.

F5’s November 18 release fixed the five NGINX2Root vulnerabilities and five additional NGINX flaws.

Background

Tenable’s Research Special Operations (RSO) team has compiled this blog to answer Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) regarding NGINX2Root, a set of five critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, and five additional NGINX flaws that F5 fixed in an out-of-band security release on November 18, 2026.

FAQ

What is NGINX2Root?

NGINX2Root is the name Xint (Theori) gave to five critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, and a separate, unpatched Linux kernel local privilege escalation (LPE) flaw that Xint says can be chained with the NGINX bugs to gain root. The NGINX flaws are memory-corruption bugs in HTTP/2, HTTP/3, the resolver, and the mail proxy module. Exploitation depends on the specific feature being active, and achieving code execution generally requires ASLR to be absent or defeated. The name is not used by F5 or nginx.org.

This includes escaping Docker containers to compromise the host kernel. Xint is withholding most technical details pending a kernel patch.

Which one is the most urgent?

The most urgent is CVE-2026-123007 because it only needs HTTP/2 to be enabled. It has been in the code since HTTP/2 support arrived in 1.9.5 in 2015, and Wiz confirmed code execution against an NGINX instance serving only static content, with no application logic or additional modules involved. Wiz Research, Rapid7, Xint and others reported it independently.

When were the NGINX vulnerabilities first disclosed?

On November 18, F5 released an out-of -band security update for 10 vulnerabilities in the NGINX Plus, NGINX Open Source.

Was this exploited as a zero-day?

There is no evidence of the five NGINX vulnerabilities being exploited as zero-days. Xint says it found the bugs on October 11, 2026, reported them to F5 via HackerOne on October 16, and published them after the coordinated release. No source reviewed reports exploitation in the wild, and the CVEs are not on CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog as of November 18.

Are threat actors exploiting these CVEs?

There are no reports of threat actors exploiting these CVEs as of November 18.

Is there a proof-of-concept (PoC) available for these vulnerabilities?

Yes for CVE-2026-123007. Rapid7 published a technical analysis of CVE-2026-123007 on November 18, and its author, Stephen Fewer, released a public PoC on GitHub at sfewer-r7/CVE-2026-123007. The repository includes a minimal crash-level trigger script and a full unauthenticated remote code execution exploit, demonstrated against NGINX 1.31.8 in a Docker container with HTTP/2 over TLS. Rapid7 describes the exploit as constrained: it depends on a glibc memory-copy routine specific to x86-64 builds, requires roughly 128 gigabytes of HTTP/2 traffic, and needs to defeat ASLR by recovering heap addresses from server responses. Execution lands in the NGINX worker process. The exploit is also unlikely to succeed against servers behind HTTP/2-terminating proxies or on connections too slow to deliver the required data volume before NGINX's one-hour connection limit is reached.

Xint published demo videos and said it intentionally omitted the final steps needed to reproduce the full exploits. Wiz confirmed working exploits exist but has chosen not to publish them.

Are patches or mitigations available for the NGINX2Root vulnerabilities?

Yes. Patching is the fix. Mitigations are a temporary stopgap, and each covers only some of the vulnerabilities. Upgrade to the fixed versions in the table below. Title: NGINX2Root: Five RCE bugs in NGINX, a Linux kernel path to root, and how to detect exploitation
Context: The Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) reviewed the disclosures and tested post-exploitation activity in a lab to help defenders understand who is exposed, what they can do...
Full Text:
On November 18, 2026, F5 published CVE records for five memory-safety bugs in NGINX, and the project shipped fixes the same day in NGINX 1.31.9 (mainline) and 1.30.7 (stable). Each bug allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to corrupt memory in an NGINX worker process, and all five carry a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2.

Xint, one of the teams that reported the bugs, published a write-up dubbing the set of vulnerabilities “NGINX2Root.” Xint also chained one of the NGINX bugs with a previously unknown Linux kernel bug in the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) to get root on the host, including from inside a Docker container running the official NGINX image.

At the time of publication for this blog, there has been no public proof-of-concept (PoC) or reported in-the-wild exploitation. However, several teams found the HTTP/2 bugs independently, and both Xint and Wiz researchers say they’ve built working exploits that bypass address space layout randomization (ASLR). Also, the Linux kernel bug has not yet been assigned a CVE, nor has a fix been released.

The Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) reviewed the disclosures and tested post-exploitation activity in a lab to help defenders understand who is exposed, what they can do before a fixed package reaches every host, and what runtime detection can see. This blog covers the five NGINX bugs, the kernel half of the chain, and what defenders can do now.

All five CVE records have been assigned the same scores: 8.1 (High) on CVSS 3.1 and 9.2 (Critical) on CVSS 4.0. NGINX2Root is network-based, doesn’t require authentication, and is relatively complex. F5 describes the impact as a worker crash or memory corruption, with code execution where ASLR is disabled or can be bypassed. All five are data-plane bugs, and F5 states there is no control-plane exposure.

The fixed releases are NGINX 1.31.9 and 1.30.7. For NGINX Plus, they are 37.3.0.1 and 37.0.8.1 (37.2.0.1 and 37.0.7.1 fix CVE-2026-123633). The same release fixes five more NGINX CVEs, including CVE-2026-118899, an infinite loop while reading a client request body over TLS 1.3, which NGINX rates as major. Upgrading to these versions fixes all 10 bugs.

Any NGINX version before 1.31.9 (mainline) or 1.30.7 (stable) is vulnerable if it has one of the features in the vulnerability table above enabled. How you check depends on where your NGINX comes from. There are four factors to consider for exposure:

Distribution packages: Distribution packages keep their version string when they backport a fix, so nginx -v won’t tell you whether you're patched. Ubuntu 24.04 ships NGINX 1.24.0, Ubuntu 22.04 ships 1.18.0, Debian 12 ships 1.22.1 and Debian 13 ships 1.26.3. Fixes for these will arrive as new package revisions. For example, Xint notes that Ubuntu 22.04's package went from 1.18.0-6ubuntu14 to 1.18.0-6ubuntu14.22 while still reporting 1.18.0. As of November 18, Debian and Ubuntu list every supported release as vulnerable to CVE-2026-123007, with no fixed package yet. NGINX.org packages, official images, and source builds report the upstream version, so nginx -v will provide an accurate patch status. The official nginx:1.31.9 image is available.

Container images: Images are only fixed when they are rebuilt on a fixed NGINX and redeployed. A running container doesn't change when the host is patched. Patch and redeploy.

Kubernetes ingress-nginx: The project was archived on March 24, 2026. Its README says there will be "no further releases, no bugfixes, and no updates to resolve any security vulnerabilities." The controller image includes its own NGINX build, so the project will not ship these fixes.

NGINX-derived software: Software built on NGINX's code, such as OpenResty, Tengine and Angie, is not named in the advisories. Check with those maintainers for possible exposure.

For scale, Xint counted 56.7 million hosts in Shodan identified as NGINX on November 10, 2026. Of the 11.94 million hosts that reported a version, 98.9% fell inside the 1.9.5 – 1.31.8 range vulnerable to CVE-2026-123007. Because of backports and feature requirements, a version banner doesn't prove a host is vulnerable. However, it does show how few public servers are on a current release.

Why teams should prioritize CVE-2026-123007

This is the bug with the widest reach. It needs only HTTP/2, which is a common setting on public HTTPS servers. Researchers have reported that serving ordinary static files is enough to reach the vulnerable code: No backend application or third-party module is needed. They have also confirmed RCE with an ASLR bypass on official NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds, over HTTP/2 with TLS on 64-bit systems. For example, Xint ran its exploit against a public HTTPS endpoint on AWS. The flaw itself dates back to NGINX 1.9.5, the release that added HTTP/2 support.

F5 credits four independent reporters for this CVE, and researchers describe exploitation as difficult. However, when four teams find the same bug independently, regardless of how challenging exploitation is, it is reasonable for defenders to assume that they’re not the only ones looking.

Understanding the other four NGINX2Root CVEs

Each of the other bugs requires a specific feature to be turned on, which narrows the potential list of exposed users:

CVE-2026-123633 also needs HTTP/2, plus proxying to an upstream. Turning off HTTP/2 blocks both HTTP/2 bugs.

CVE-2026-123634 needs a proxy_pass destination built from request variables, a resolver, and a subrequest from mirror or SSI. Researchers note that turning off mirror alone is not enough, because SSI also creates subrequests. Setting mirror_request_body on does not fix it either.

CVE-2026-121810 affects only servers with HTTP/3 enabled.

CVE-2026-113425 affects only servers that run the NGINX mail proxy with auth_http.

SCTP and the Linux kernel bug

The "to root" part of NGINX2Root is a separate bug. Researchers found a use-after-free and double-free in the Linux kernel's SCTP code, introduced by Linux 4.15 in 2018. According to Xint, it leaks kernel memory to defeat kernel ASLR and lets an attacker call an arbitrary kernel function. This bug currently has no CVE or patch, and researchers are withholding further details until a fix exists.

It’s important to note that hosts that never use SCTP are exposed, too. On most distributions, the sctp kernel module is not loaded until a process opens an SCTP socket, and then the kernel loads it automatically. So an attacker running code as an unprivileged NGINX worker can load the vulnerable code into the kernel themselves. In the Sysdig TRT lab, a single SCTP socket opened from the NGINX worker was enough to load sctp.ko. Once loaded, the module stays loaded until the next reboot.

Containers don't change this, because they share the host's kernel. Researchers ran the chain from inside a Docker container built from the official nginx:1.31.8 image and got root on the underlying host.

Blocking the module closes this path on hosts that don't need SCTP. With install sctp /bin/false in a file under /etc/modprobe.d/, the NGINX worker's SCTP socket call failed with EPROTONOSUPPORT in the Sysdig TRT lab, and the module was not loaded.

The block has three limits, however: It doesn't unload a module that is already loaded, it doesn't help where SCTP is compiled into the kernel, and it breaks workloads that use SCTP, such as telecom signaling and some Kubernetes network plugins.

The impact of NGINX2Root

Worker crashes and memory corruption: F5 describes the impact as a worker crash or memory corruption. An attacker can send crafted traffic to an exposed NGINX server without credentials.

Code execution as the NGINX worker: Researchers report working exploits that bypass ASLR. Normally, code execution in an NGINX worker is limited to the worker's unprivileged user.

Root on the host and container escape: The SCTP kernel bug turns a worker compromise into root on the host, including from inside a Docker container, because containers share the host's kernel.

A patch gap: The fix is released, but most fleets haven't received it yet. Most NGINX in production comes from a distribution package or a container base image. For those, the fix arrives when the distribution ships a backport and the image is rebuilt. Expect a gap of days or more between the upstream release and the build you actually run.

What this means for defenders

The fix is released, but most fleets haven't received it yet. Most NGINX in production comes from a distribution package or a container base image. For those, the fix arrives when the distribution ships a backport and the image is rebuilt. Expect a gap of days or more between the upstream release and the build you actually run.

The configuration workarounds are narrow and effective. Turning off HTTP/2 blocks the two most reachable bugs, including CVE-2026-123007. The other three need features that many deployments don't use. Find out which features your servers actually have enabled, so you know how much exposure you have before a fixed package arrives.

The kernel bug makes a worker compromise much worse. Normally, code execution in an NGINX worker is limited to the worker's unprivileged user. The SCTP bug turns that into root on the host, and an escape from the container. Blocking the sctp module costs nothing on hosts that don't use it. Today, this is the only mitigation for the kernel half of the chain.

Reloading isn't enough. A configuration reload leaves existing connections on the old worker processes. After you upgrade or change the configuration, restart NGINX, or confirm that every old worker has exited.

How to detect NGINX2Root

No public exploit code has been released and there is no reported in-the-wild exploitation, so the attack itself can't yet be replayed. Instead, the Sysdig TRT ran post-exploitation payloads from inside a real, vulnerable NGINX 1.31.8 worker process, in a container and on the host, which are the steps an attacker would take after gaining code execution.

However, researchers have confirmed RCE with an ASLR bypass, ran an exploit against a public HTTPS endpoint on AWS, and chained an NGINX bug with the SCTP kernel bug to get root on the host. These exploits have been described as difficult, but they are possible. Four teams found the CVE-2026-123007 vulnerability independently, so defenders should assume threat actors are working on it as well.

Threat intelligence

Sysdig Secure customers can use the Sysdig Threat Intelligence feed to find hosts and workloads that run an affected NGINX version, including NGINX bundled in other software. The feed checks versions, not enabled features. A host fixed by a distribution backport can stay listed until the feed is updated.

Runtime detection

Sysdig Secure customers can also detect attacker activity at each of these stages:

A shell started by the NGINX worker: Run shell untrusted.

A reverse shell from the worker: Reverse Shell Detected, and Redirect STDOUT/STDIN to Network Connection in Container.

A second-stage binary dropped and run: Drop and execute new binary in container, and Execution from /tmp.

Ordinary NGINX activity did not trigger any of these rules in our testing. This includes plain requests, HTTP/2 load, proxying, resolver and mirror traffic, configuration reloads, and the fixed NGINX 1.31.9 image.

Security teams should expect some alerts on patch day, because legitimate maintenance can resemble post-exploitation activity in some cases. For example, when we upgraded NGINX in place with its live binary upgrade (rather than a restart) in our lab, this triggered Sysdig Secure’s Non sudo setuid and Container Run as Root User rules. A configuration reload didn’t trigger these rules. If you upgrade this way, you’ll likely see similar alerts from your runtime detection tool. Scope any tuning to the maintenance window instead of suppressing the rules permanently to reduce the noise.

Researchers also suggest watching for these signs, though they note that these are general warning signs to be weighed together, and not confirmed indicators of vulnerability exploitation:

NGINX worker crashes and segmentation faults in error.log or coredumpctl.

Commands run by the NGINX worker's user.

Long-lived HTTP/2 connections that receive a large amount of data and send back very little.

Detecting NGINX2Root with open source Falco

Falco sees syscalls, not HTTP requests. It can't see the malicious request itself, but it can see what the request causes on the host. Use the Falco open source ruleset to detect post-exploitation activity such as a shell or a new binary started by an NGINX worker.

Recommendations

Patch

Upgrade to NGINX 1.31.9 or 1.30.7, or NGINX Plus 37.3.0.1 or 37.0.8.1. Then, restart NGINX rather than reloading it, and confirm that every old worker process has exited.

Follow your distribution's advisory, not the upstream version number. Install the fixed package revision when it ships.

Rebuild and redeploy container images that include NGINX once a fixed base image is available.

Plan a migration off ingress-nginx. The project will not ship these fixes.

Temporary mitigation if you can’t patch right away

Disable HTTP/2 until you're patched. On NGINX 1.25.1 and later, set http2 off; in each affected server block and remove http2 from listen. On 1.9.5 through 1.25.0, remove http2 from listen. Turn it back on after upgrading.

Remove request-time DNS lookups. Point proxy_pass at a fixed upstream group rather than a variable, and turn off mirror and SSI where you don't need them.

Disable HTTP/3. Remove quic listeners, set http3 off;, send Alt-Svc 'clear', and block UDP on the port.

Contain the blast radius, investigate, and audit

Block the SCTP module on hosts and Kubernetes nodes that don't use SCTP: add install sctp /bin/false to a .conf file in /etc/modprobe.d/. Run lsmod | grep sctp to check whether it's already loaded. If it is and nothing on the host uses it, the block takes effect after the next reboot.

Restrict the mail proxy. Bind the IMAP, POP3, and SMTP listeners to loopback, or allow only trusted sources through the firewall.

Watch for NGINX worker crashes and for processes started by NGINX workers.

Conclusion

NGINX2Root combines five NGINX bugs that already have a fix with one Linux kernel bug that doesn't.

The NGINX half is a patch-management problem: The upstream fix is out, but distribution packages and container images will take time to catch up, and the configuration workarounds can cover that gap. The kernel half requires immediate attention, and turns the compromise of an unprivileged worker into root on the host.

Although no public exploit has been released as of this blog’s publication, researchers already claim to have working POCs. The time for teams to patch is now.

Title: NGINX HTTP/2 Vulnerabilities: How to Identify Affected Images and Apply Security Updates
Context: Aquasec products are not affected, and detection for both vulnerabilities is available in Aquasec’s Online and Offline CyberCenter vulnerability feeds to help customers identify...
Full Text:
TL;DR: Two critical vulnerabilities in NGINX’s HTTP/2 implementation, CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely on affected servers. Both vulnerabilities carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 and require HTTP/2 to be enabled. Organizations should identify affected NGINX deployments and apply available security updates immediately.

Aquasec products are not affected, and detection for both vulnerabilities is available in Aquasec’s Online and Offline CyberCenter vulnerability feeds to help customers identify potentially vulnerable container images.

What are the critical NGINX HTTP/2 vulnerabilities?

Two critical vulnerabilities have been disclosed in NGINX’s HTTP/2 implementation, potentially exposing affected servers to remote code execution (RCE) without authentication.

The vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, affect NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus, as well as potentially other products that incorporate vulnerable NGINX versions.

Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled, although the additional conditions required for exploitation differ. Successful exploitation could allow an attacker to gain unauthorized access to an affected server, potentially exposing sensitive data or disrupting services.

NGINX is widely used as a web server, reverse proxy and Kubernetes ingress component, making it important for organizations to assess deployments beyond standalone web servers.

For NGINX Plus, versions 37.0.8.1 and 37.3.0.1 address both vulnerabilities on their respective release tracks. Customers running older NGINX Plus branches should upgrade to a supported release containing the appropriate fixes.

Organizations using NGINX through operating system packages, container images or third party distributions should consult their provider’s security advisories for the applicable fixed versions, including any backported security updates.

How can organizations identify and remediate affected NGINX deployments?

Organizations should prioritize internet facing NGINX deployments and review both installed versions and HTTP/2 configurations to determine potential exposure.

Recommended actions include:

Identify affected deployments. Review NGINX servers, container images, reverse proxies and Kubernetes ingress controllers to locate potentially vulnerable versions.

Verify HTTP/2 configuration. Confirm whether HTTP/2 is enabled on affected services, since both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 for exploitation.

Apply available security updates. Upgrade to the appropriate patched NGINX release or follow the guidance provided by the operating system or product vendor.

Consider temporary mitigation. If immediate patching is not possible, consider disabling HTTP/2 on affected listeners. Test application compatibility before making changes, particularly for services that depend on HTTP/2, such as gRPC.

Verify remediation. Restart or redeploy affected services after updating, confirm the running NGINX version and review vulnerability scanning results.

Organizations running F5 NGINX Ingress Controller should upgrade to version 5.8.0, while those using NGINX Gateway Fabric should upgrade to version 2.9.0.

The archived community Kubernetes ingress nginx project also includes vulnerable NGINX versions and has no planned security fix. Organizations using this project should review their HTTP/2 configurations and plan migration to a maintained alternative.

How does Aquasec help identify images affected by the NGINX vulnerabilities?

Aquasec has completed its assessment of CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007 and confirmed that Aquasec products are not affected. No Aquasec product updates or remediation are required.

Detection for both vulnerabilities is now available in Aquasec’s Online and Offline CyberCenter vulnerability feeds.

Customers can rescan potentially affected NGINX container images and use Aquasec’s native vulnerability scanning and Image Assurance Policies to identify images with matching CVE findings.

Detection coverage may depend on the availability of vulnerability information from individual operating system and package vendors. An image without a CVE finding should not automatically be considered unaffected.

Customers should continue to verify their NGINX versions and HTTP/2 configurations against the applicable vendor advisories, even when vulnerability scanning does not report either CVE.

For detailed information on detection coverage and recommended actions, refer to the Aquasec Knowledge Base.

What should organizations do next?

The immediate priority is to identify affected NGINX deployments and apply the available security updates. Because both vulnerabilities could enable unauthenticated remote code execution, organizations should prioritize internet facing services and verify that patched versions are running in production.

Aquasec customers can use the updated Online and Offline CyberCenter vulnerability feeds to help identify potentially affected images, while continuing to validate NGINX configurations and vendor security guidance.

For additional technical details and remediation information, consult the official NGINX security advisories.

FAQs

Are Aquasec products affected by CVE-2026-123633 or CVE-2026-123007?

No. Aquasec has confirmed that its products are not affected by either vulnerability. No Aquasec product updates or remediation are required.

Can Aquasec detect the NGINX HTTP/2 vulnerabilities?

Yes. Detection for CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007 is available in Aquasec’s Online and Offline CyberCenter vulnerability feeds. Customers can rescan container images to identify matching vulnerability findings.

Does disabling HTTP/2 mitigate these NGINX vulnerabilities?

Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled. Disabling HTTP/2 on affected listeners can be considered as a temporary mitigation when immediate patching is not possible. Organizations should test application compatibility before making changes and apply the available security updates as the recommended remediation.

Are Kubernetes ingress controllers affected by the NGINX vulnerabilities?

Potentially. Products that incorporate vulnerable NGINX versions may be affected. Organizations should review the versions used by their ingress controllers and follow the applicable vendor security guidance.

Does a clean Aquasec vulnerability scan mean an NGINX image is unaffected?

Not necessarily. Detection coverage depends on available vulnerability information from operating system and package vendors. Organizations should verify installed NGINX versions and HTTP/2 configurations even when no matching CVE finding appears.

Title: AI unearths ‘internet breaker’ flaws in Nginx web server
Context: Xint’s researchers, who used the company’s own autonomous AI harness, found five of the flaws and discovered a separate Linux kernel vulnerability in the SCTP subsystem that can...
Full Text:
Nginx, the web server estimated to power a third of the internet, has shipped fixes for multiple vulnerabilities, including a critical unauthenticated remote code execution flaw that puts millions of websites at risk and has existed in the code for over a decade. Researchers from several security firms independently found some of the same flaws by using AI agents, adding to a string of recent AI-discovered vulnerabilities in widely used internet technologies such as PHP, Node, OpenSSH, and Java.

The most severe flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-123007, lets an attacker manipulate flow-control windows in the HTTP/2 protocol implementation to trigger an out-of-bounds memory copy that researchers from Xint.io turned into command execution with Nginx worker privileges. The vulnerability affects every official Nginx release for more than 10 years since version 1.9.5, which originally added HTTP/2 support in 2015.

A second HTTP/2 flaw, CVE-2026-123633, is a use-after-free vulnerability affecting releases 1.19.7 through 1.31.8. Both are fixed in Nginx 1.31.9 and 1.30.7, which F5 released along with fixes for eight other vulnerabilities.

Xint’s researchers, who used the company’s own autonomous AI harness, found five of the flaws and discovered a separate Linux kernel vulnerability in the SCTP subsystem that can be chained with any of those flaws to gain root privileges on the server. The company has dubbed the collection nginx2root.

In their tests the exploit chain escaped a Docker container running Nginx and obtained root on the underlying host. The kernel flaw has existed since Linux 4.15, released in 2018, and has no CVE or patch so the company is withholding details until distributions can ship a fix.

The exposure of web servers on the internet is vast with the Shodan search engine showing 56.7 million hosts running Nginx, and 98.9% of those that disclose their version report one in the vulnerable range. F5 recommends updating immediately or disabling HTTP/2 on affected ports, which blocks the two most severe flaws but not Xint’s other findings — CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-121810, and CVE-2026-113425 — which are in other components.

The CVE-2026-123007 flaw was reported to F5 by researchers from Rapid7, Wiz, Xint, and Ikotas Labs, while CVE-2026-123633, dubbed Drainbreak, was discovered and reported by researchers from Metnir, Wiz, and Xint. Only Rapid7 senior principal security researcher Stephen Fewer doesn’t mention AI in his write-up. The other four teams used AI agents and harnesses, with Xint’s CEO Brian Pak saying that his team’s platform scanned “50,000 lines of code in just 90 minutes” to surface “a critical vulnerability that gave an unauthenticated user a RCE path — essentially an internet breaker.”

Exploitation is likely

No one has exploited either flaw in the wild yet, according to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s assessment of both CVEs, but every research team built working exploits, and two describe the flaws as readily exploitable.

Xint called CVE-2026-123007 highly exploitable, saying an externally reachable TLS/HTTP/2 port was enough to corrupt the send window, disclose addresses, and execute commands, and validated the attack over public IPs on AWS, GCP, and Azure under concurrent traffic.

Metnir ran its exploit for CVE-2026-123633 with ASLR enabled, taking about 10 minutes, nearly all of it spent on defeating memory layout randomization, and reproduced the use-after-free in OpenResty, crashing the shipped binaries of Kong, Apache APISIX, NGINX Gateway Fabric, and community ingress-nginx, all of which enable HTTP/2 by default.

Rapid7’s Fewer calculated that running his exploit requires transmitting roughly 128GB of HTTP/2 data to the target. That takes about two minutes on a 10Gbit/s network and 17 minutes on 1Gbit/s. The technique also relies on a memory-copy routine in glibc that is used only on CPUs with AVX-512 extensions, but these are common on servers.“Exploitation is by no means a walk in the park, as the vulnerable systems must be directly exposed to the internet with no WAF or CDN terminating HTTP/2,” Yordan Ganchev, principal threat intelligence specialist at watchTowr, told CSO. “Memory corruption can also be tricky, as an effective exploit must properly groom and shape the memory heap and handle different NGINX versions, builds, and configuration variants. And when the system is internet-facing and under load, exploitation can cause more crashes than successful code execution.”

Patch and check what you’re actually running

Nginx Plus users should also update to 37.3.0.1 on the newer release line or 37.0.8.1 on the 37.0 line. The older R33 through R36 release line will never receive a fix because those versions have reached the end of technical support.

Disabling HTTP/2 comes with costs, as services that depend on it, such as native gRPC, stop working. Xint’s other three flaws require specific configurations. The resolver flaw affects setups that pick their backend per request and use the mirror directive, the HTTP/3 flaw affects QUIC listeners, and the mail proxy flaw affects deployments that use proxy on with auth_http. Xint published per-flaw mitigations in its technical write-up.For the accompanying Linux flaw, until a kernel patch is released, administrators who don’t use SCTP can block the module from loading by adding install sctp /bin/false to a file under /etc/modprobe.d.Administrators should also investigate unexpected Nginx worker crashes or commands launched by Nginx workers, Wiz noted.

“The real risk with this nginx bug isn’t the 11 years it went unnoticed, it’s how many teams will think they’ve patched when they haven’t,” Daniel Shechter, co-founder and CEO of Miggo Security, told CSO. “The version number can be wrong because distros backport fixes without changing it, a reload doesn’t swap out the running code, and the attack happens in HTTP/2 traffic that WAFs and access logs never see. If you can’t prove the fix is actually running, assume you’re still exposed.”

Title: NGINX2Root: Five nginx Flaws, Led by CVE-2026-123007. How to Find, Mitigate, and Patch Now
Context: That gives your team owners and deadlines to work with before the VMDR detection QIDs below are released
Full Text:
Executive Summary

NGINX2Root is a set of five nginx vulnerabilities disclosed on November 18, 2026. The lead flaw, CVE-2026-123007, is a memory corruption bug in the way nginx handles HTTP/2 connections. F5, which maintains nginx, rates it 9.2 under CVSS v4.0 and 8.1 under CVSS v3.1. An attacker with no credentials can crash nginx worker processes, and researchers have demonstrated remote code execution with the privileges of the nginx worker. Where the worker runs without root privileges, an attacker would need an additional escalation path to gain root. This could involve chaining the NGINX vulnerability with a suitable local privilege-escalation flaw. Unpatched builds of NGINX Open Source from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8, and unpatched NGINX Plus builds, are in scope when HTTP/2 is enabled. Fixes shipped in NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 and 1.31.9, and turning off HTTP/2 closes this exposure where patching has to wait. A separate Linux kernel flaw that the researchers used to go from the worker account to root has no patch yet. Start with internet-facing nginx servers that accept HTTP/2, and assign an owner and a deadline to every system still unpatched.

What’s at Risk

A Flaw in nginx Could Hand Attackers the Front Door to Your Applications. nginx is often the first system a web request reaches. It runs as a web server, a reverse proxy (a server that passes requests to the applications behind it), a load balancer, and the entry point to Kubernetes clusters. CVE-2026-123007 is in nginx’s own HTTP/2 code, so no application behind it has to be at fault.

HTTP/2 lets a client tell the server how much data it is allowed to send. nginx can lose count of that allowance when a client cancels requests at the right moment. The bad count later makes nginx copy memory it should not touch.

F5 says the result is typically a crash of the nginx worker, the process that handles live traffic. F5 also says code execution is possible where ASLR, the memory-address randomization that makes exploits harder, is disabled or bypassed. Xint, the team that named NGINX2Root, reports doing exactly that: it leaked memory addresses and then ran commands as the nginx worker over a public HTTPS port.

In Qualys TRU’s assessment, three outcomes matter to the business:

Exposure of traffic and keys. Code running in the worker can read requests and responses after nginx decrypts them, including passwords and session tokens. It may also expose TLS private keys that are held in software and accessible to the worker.

A foothold behind the perimeter. Backend systems usually trust the proxy in front of them. An attacker on that proxy starts from a trusted position.

Outages. A failed attempt can still crash workers and drop connections.

Workers normally run under a restricted account. An attacker gets whatever privileges the worker actually has, so if it already runs as root, no further escalation is needed in that environment. Where it does not, the researchers chained a separate flaw in the Linux kernel’s SCTP code to get root. SCTP is a network protocol, like TCP, that the kernel supports. They report root on the host, including from nginx running inside a Docker container. That kernel flaw has no CVE and no patch yet, so patching nginx removes the remote entry point but not the step to root.

NGINX2Root covers four more nginx flaws. F5 scores all five 9.2 under CVSS v4.0 and 8.1 under CVSS v3.1, and the same nginx releases fix them. Each needs a different configuration:

The rest of this post focuses on CVE-2026-123007, the flaw with the widest reach.

Why NGINX2Root Is Also an Application Security Problem

NGINX2Root is an infrastructure flaw, but its impact lands on the applications behind nginx. Where nginx terminates TLS and proxies requests, every login, API call, and session cookie bound for those applications passes through the worker process in clear text. An attacker running code in that worker sits between users and the applications they trust:

Credentials and tokens become reusable. Passwords, session cookies, API keys, and bearer tokens read from the worker can be replayed directly against the applications and APIs behind the proxy, where they look like legitimate user traffic.

Trust placed in the proxy becomes the attacker’s. Backend services, internal APIs, and admin interfaces are often reachable only from the proxy. Applications that accept identity or client details from headers the proxy sets, such as X-Forwarded-For or user headers added after single sign-on, trust whatever the compromised proxy sends.

Application traffic can be altered in transit. Requests and responses pass through the worker, so the attacker is positioned to change what users receive and what the backend processes, with no change to application code.

One proxy, many applications. A shared reverse proxy or Kubernetes ingress controller often fronts dozens of applications owned by different teams. A worker crash takes all of them offline at once.

For application security teams, the scoping question is not only which hosts run a vulnerable nginx build, but which applications and APIs depend on them, what data those applications handle, and who owns them.

Are You Affected?

A system is in scope only when both conditions are true. For an attack to work, the attacker must also be able to open an HTTP/2 connection to nginx itself.

NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 and 1.31.9. Releases before 1.9.5, which predate HTTP/2 support. Builds compiled without the HTTP/2 module. Any vendor build that contains the fix

The checks below come from the researchers’ write-up. Run them on the nginx host. The first shows whether the build includes HTTP/2. The second shows whether the configuration turns it on.

Run this one from outside your network. ALPN protocol: h2 means the server accepts HTTP/2 from the internet.

openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST -alpn h2 </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E ‘ALPN protocol:|No ALPN negotiated’

Three cautions when scoping:

Do not rely on nginx -v alone. Distributions often fix a flaw without changing the nginx version number. Compare the full package version with the distribution’s advisory.

Check where the HTTP/2 connection ends. If a CDN or load balancer handles HTTP/2 in front of nginx, an outside test only reaches that device. Test the nginx port directly.

Use internet exposure to order the work, not to close findings. An internal nginx with HTTP/2 on is still reachable by an attacker who is already inside the network.

Exploitation Status

As of November 18, 2026, we have not seen public confirmation of exploitation in the wild.

Working exploit code is public. The team behind NGINX2Root also reports its own exploit working over public IP addresses on AWS, GCP, and Azure, and is holding back the final steps.

The public exploit is hard to use. It sends a very large number of HTTP/2 control messages over one long-lived connection for several minutes, has to reach nginx directly, and depends on a specific memory-copy routine in the standard Linux C library on 64-bit Intel and AMD processors.

These limits slow mass exploitation. In Qualys TRU’s assessment, they do not protect a specific internet-facing server from a capable attacker, and other techniques may follow.

What to Do Now

Updating nginx is the only complete fix. F5 released fixed builds on November 18, 2026.

Linux distributions publish on their own schedules. As of November 18, 2026, Ubuntu and Debian had not shipped fixed packages. Use your vendor’s advisory to identify the fixed package and confirm it addresses CVE-2026-123007.

Restart nginx after you update. A reload applies configuration changes but keeps the old program running, so the flaw stays in memory until a restart.

If you cannot patch today, turn off HTTP/2 on every affected listener. F5 states the flaw affects only configurations that use HTTP/2, and the researchers recommend this as a temporary measure. For the exact steps, see nginx’s documentation for the http2 directive, CERT-EU’s advisory, and section 3.3 of the researchers’ write-up. Clients fall back to HTTP/1.1. Services that need HTTP/2, such as gRPC, will stop working, so test first. This covers CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633 only, and it does not replace the patch.

Advice for Risk and Vulnerability Management Teams

Qualys TRU’s advice for the teams running this response:

Do not let the score set the deadline: Under CVSS v3.1 this flaw is 8.1, which many remediation policies file as High. Public exploit code and a server that faces the internet matter more than the number. Handle vulnerable nginx deployments with externally reachable HTTP/2 as an emergency.

Close findings on evidence: A server is done when the fixed build is installed, nginx has been restarted, and the vendor’s advisory confirms the package covers all five CVEs. Report patched, temporarily mitigated, not exposed by configuration, and unknown as separate states, and do not count unknown as safe.

Fix the template as well as the server: Update container images, Helm charts, machine images, and autoscaling templates. Otherwise the next scale-out or failover brings the vulnerable build back.

Map each nginx instance to the applications and APIs behind it. A host inventory shows where a vulnerable build is installed; it does not show which applications, owners, and data depend on it. Use that mapping to set priority and to notify application owners, not to close findings.

Put an end date on every workaround: Turning off HTTP/2 covers two of the five flaws, and the next configuration push can undo it. Record who owns each exception and when it ends.

Decide what to do with nginx that will not get a fix: The community ingress-nginx project is archived, and the older NGINX Plus R-series branches have no fixed build listed, although fixed NGINX Plus 37.x releases exist. These need a migration plan or a signed risk acceptance.

Treat privilege escalation flaws as part of this response: Where the worker runs without root privileges, an attacker would need an additional escalation path to gain root. The newly disclosed SCTP flaw is one such path, and any other local privilege-escalation flaw that can be exploited from the worker’s context could serve the same purpose. Patch known local privilege-escalation flaws on nginx hosts, in the kernel and elsewhere, with the same urgency. A current kernel does not mean the SCTP flaw is fixed, because that flaw has no patch yet.

How Qualys Can Help

Qualys CyberSecurity Asset Management (CSAM) lists every asset with nginx installed, along with the version of each installation, so teams can quickly scope NGINX2Root remediation. Because NGINX Open Source 1.9.5 through 1.31.8 is affected, the version tells you which installations are in range. It does not tell you whether HTTP/2 is turned on or whether a Linux distribution has backported the fix, so check those separately. nginx bundled in containers, Kubernetes ingress controllers, and appliances may not appear in a standard inventory, so check those separately too.

Title: AI found more critical bugs in another widely used technology running 225M websites
Context: “AI has changed not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how quickly longstanding risks can become real threats
Full Text: Hot on the heels of serious vulnerabilities in seemingly every other widely used software powering the entire internet, F5 today released emergency patches for 10 bugs in open source NGINX. These include critical remote code execution flaws that let attackers hijack NGINX servers with HTTP/2 enabled, as well as the millions of websites running NGINX, to steal sensitive data and disrupt services. As with all of the other recently disclosed vulnerabilities in foundational technologies like PHP, Apache, and Java, these critical NGINX bugs were uncovered by researchers using AI. One of them has been hiding in the code for at least 10 years. Tomer Schwartz, Wiz’s chief technology officer of exposure management and AppSec, helped find the bug, along with researchers from Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint working independently. Schwartz told The Register that this wave of AI-discovered flaws “point to a new reality.” “We need to treat every internet-connected system as potentially vulnerable,” Schwartz said. “AI has changed not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how quickly longstanding risks can become real threats.” NGINX is the world’s most widely used open source web server, handling HTTPS requests and routing incoming traffic to the right application or API. It powers about a third of all websites (around 225 million), and F5 maintains the open source version. On Wednesday, F5 published an out-of-band security notification that addressed 10 CVEs in open source NGINIX. If you run NGINX, update to 1.31.9 as soon as possible. CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007 Two of the vulns are especially serious as they allow a remote attacker to execute code on the NGINX server without authentication. These two, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, both received a critical, 9.2 CVSS rating, and CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. All of the security shops listed earlier independently found at least one of these two CVEs - most, if not all, with an AI assist - and reported them to F5. “Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues in how NGINX handles HTTP/2 traffic,” Schwartz and fellow Wiz kid Nir Ohfeld said in a Wednesday blog about the two bugs. “In CVE-2026-123633, a connection's memory is freed while a request still needs it, creating a use-after-free. In CVE-2026-123007, incorrect flow-control accounting leads to an invalid memory copy.” Rapid7’s team also published a proof-of-concept to demonstrate leveraging CVE-2026-123007 for unauthenticated remote code execution against a vulnerable linux/amd64 Docker image running nginx version 1.31.8. Xint found three other NGINX flaws, plus a separate vulnerability in the Linux kernel that can be chained with any of the five NGINX vulnerabilities to gain root privileges on the host. The research team dubbed the six bugs “nginx2root.” The AI-powered offensive security firm also published videos demonstrating attacks using CVE-2026-123007 to execute commands as the NGINX worker inside a container, and then using the kernel vulnerability to escalate to root on the host. These attacks work on AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform, and bare-metal servers. AI-powered bug hunting for the win? "While preparing for ZeroDay Cloud 2026, a Xint researcher found CVE-2026-123007," the company said in a Wednesday blog. "A few days later, a fully automated Xint scan found the other four without human guidance." All of these newly-disclosed CVEs point to a larger security issue - especially in light of Tuesday’s Java4Shell, found by AI-bug-hunting-outfit Calif, PHP2Shell (Calif was one of the firms that also used AI to find and weaponize these critical vulns in PHP), and a critical Apache flaw under active exploitation . “AI is also accelerating vulnerability discovery faster than existing infrastructure was designed to absorb,” Schwartz told us. “Even after a vendor ships a fix, security teams still face heavy manual work in terms of locating vulnerable versions and configurations, testing patches, deploying interim mitigations (such as disabling HTTP/2), and coordinating all of these rollouts.” There is light at the end of the tunnel, he believes. “In the long run, AI-powered vulnerability research will harden foundational software.” But in the meantime, it’s a nightmare for security teams, vulnerability managers, and system administrators, who are drowning in the near-daily deluge of CVEs to patch before attackers find and exploit these vulnerabilities. “Continued collaboration between security researchers, maintainers, and defenders is crucial to absorb the speed and scale of these disclosures,” Schwartz said.®
