Full Text:
Overview

Today, both Rapid7 and F5 are disclosing CVE-2026-123007, a critical integer underflow vulnerability affecting nginx HTTP/2, which can allow for unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) against affected servers under certain conditions.

CVE ID

Description

CWE

CVSSv4

CVE-2026-123007

HTTP/2 flow-control memory corruption permitting worker-context RCE

CWE-191 (Integer Underflow)

9.2 (Critical)

nginx can miscalculate how much response data an HTTP/2 client has allowed it to send. A remote, unauthenticated client can exploit this error by cancelling queued response data, then make nginx use an invalid length when copying a later response. The resulting memory corruption can disclose data, interrupt service, and execute code with the nginx worker process's permissions.

Impact

Rapid7 has developed a proof-of-concept to demonstrate leveraging CVE-2026-123007 for unauthenticated RCE against a vulnerable linux/amd64 Docker image running nginx version 1.31.8, as shown below in Figure 1. The target nginx server’s configuration had http2 on and TLS enabled. Note that for brevity, video playback is at 8x speed.

Figure 1: Video demonstrating unauthenticated RCE against NGINX 1.31.8 via CVE-2026-123007

Leveraging CVE-2026-123007 for RCE requires a significant amount of network traffic to be transmitted, approximately 128 GB of HTTP/2 data. Both available network bandwidth and connection timeouts will place practical limitations on Internet exploitation. In the above example shown in Figure 1, exploitation takes two and a half minutes. The approximate timings to transmit the required network data over a 10 Gbit/s network is two minutes, while on a 1 Gbit/s network it is seventeen minutes. Due to nginx’s default one hour connection lifetime, a network slower than approximately 300 Mbit/s will take over the one hour connection limit threshold and will not be able to succeed. Additionally, should an HTTP/2 connection be proxied, the precise attacker-controlled HTTP/2 frames being transmitted will likely not be retransmitted in a way that satisfies exploiting the vulnerability.

Finally, the exploitation strategy developed depends on a specific x86-64 glibc EVEX/YMM memcpy implementation selected at runtime, based on the avx512f and avx512vl CPU features. Alternative RCE exploitation strategies may be viable, but none are currently known.

Credit

This vulnerability was discovered by Stephen Fewer, Senior Principal Security Researcher at Rapid7, and is being disclosed in accordance with Rapid7's vulnerability disclosure policy.

Technical analysis

The version of nginx tested was a linux/amd64 Docker image for nginx version 1.31.8 (nginx@sha256:5ab5b0b01097420873a3f3330f44248e34a3c2a3e8d5ee30658aeae8cb7435da), and ran with an exposed HTTPS service and http2 enabled.

How a client controls HTTP/2 response data

HTTP/2 carries messages called frames over a connection. Each request and response belongs to a numbered stream, so one connection can carry several exchanges at once. Response-body bytes are carried in DATA frames.

For this vulnerability, nginx is the sender and the remote client is the receiver. The client grants nginx permission, or flow-control credit, to send a certain number of DATA bytes. nginx tracks the remaining credit in two counters: one for each stream and one shared by the connection. Sending DATA must be permitted by both counters. These HTTP/2 counters are separate from TCP's receive window.

The client grants more credit by sending a WINDOW_UPDATE frame containing a positive increment. A stream identifier of zero increases the connection’s send credit. A nonzero stream identifier increases the send credit for the stream with that specific nonzero identifier. HTTP/2 limits the increment and the resulting window to 2^31-1 bytes, or 2,147,483,647 (0x7FFFFFFF). This report calls that maximum MAX.

The client can also send a SETTINGS frame containing a SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE parameter. This changes the starting credit for new streams. nginx must also adjust each active stream's remaining credit by the difference between the old and new setting values. It does not change the connection's credit. A reduction can therefore leave an active stream with negative credit until the client grants more. The connection window has no equivalent reduction: it must remain between zero and MAX. RFC 9113, section 6.9 defines these limits and the required errors.

nginx stores the connection counter in h2c->send_window, where h2c is the HTTP/2 connection record. Its size_t type is an unsigned integer: on the verified 64-bit build it can hold values from zero to 2^64-1. The size_t type can therefore hold values above HTTP/2's maximum connection window of 2^31-1 bytes (MAX). nginx must enforce that protocol limit in its own logic.

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2.h #define NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW ((1U << 31) - 1) // <--- [1] struct ngx_http_v2_connection_s { // ... size_t send_window; // <--- [2] // ... }; struct ngx_http_v2_stream_s { // ... ssize_t send_window; // ... };

The rule that the connection counter at [2] must never exceed MAX at [1] is the connection-window invariant. The separate stream counter, stream->send_window, is explicitly declared as ssize_t, a signed 64-bit integer on the verified build. That allows SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE to make a stream's credit temporarily negative. The connection counter remains unsigned. The later unsafe conversion occurs when the output filter treats excessive connection credit as a signed 64-bit off_t response length.

Leveraging vulnerability has four main stages:

By slowing its reading of server output, the client keeps selected DATA frames queued and unstarted. It raises the connection's credit to MAX and the selected streams' credit to just below MAX. A SETTINGS frame that increases SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE enough to exceed the stream limit makes nginx close those streams while leaving the connection usable. Request cleanup then restores the reserved credit above MAX.

An unsigned subtraction in the next connection WINDOW_UPDATE check underflows. Repeated accepted WINDOW_UPDATE frames can then raise the counter into the upper half of its 64-bit range without requiring the addition to wrap.

On the verified 64-bit build, nginx interprets that excessive counter as a negative response length and creates an invalid buffer. Buffered TLS output then passes a huge unsigned byte count to the memory-copy function memcpy, causing out-of-bounds reads and writes.

These constrained memory accesses depend on the build and selected copy routine. With a suitable memory layout, an attacker can use disclosed addresses and controlled overwrites to execute code with the nginx worker process's permissions.

Cancelling queued DATA restores too much credit

When nginx queues a DATA frame at [3], it subtracts the frame's DATA length from the connection's credit counter at [4] and then from the stream's credit counter. This reserves the credit before the bytes reach the client and prevents other streams from spending the same connection credit:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2_filter_module.c // ngx_http_v2_send_chain() // ... ngx_http_v2_queue_frame(h2c, frame); // <--- [3] h2c->send_window -= frame_size; // <--- [4] stream->send_window -= frame_size; stream->queued++;

An attacker can keep a later response queued by slowing or stopping its reading of earlier server output. Once the transport cannot accept more output, nginx must wait. This condition is transport backpressure. The attacker needs enough of it to keep the selected DATA frame unstarted: none of that frame's bytes have yet entered TLS output or the socket. Stopping response reads does not prevent the client from sending control frames in the other direction.

While the DATA remains queued, the client sends a connection WINDOW_UPDATE that raises nginx's reduced counter to MAX. The problem appears when the request that owns the queued DATA then closes. Its request-cleanup handler removes the unstarted DATA and returns the reserved credit:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2_filter_module.c // ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup() // ... for ( ;; ) { frame = *fn; if (frame == NULL) { break; } if (frame->stream == stream && !frame->blocked) { // <--- [5] *fn = frame->next; window += frame->length; // <--- [6] if (--stream->queued == 0) { break; } continue; } fn = &frame->next; } // ... h2c->send_window += window; // <--- [7]

The test at [5] selects removable, unstarted frames for that request. The local variable window totals their DATA lengths at [6]. The addition at [7] does not check whether restoring those bytes takes the connection counter above MAX.

For example, restoring 1,393 bytes after the counter has reached 2,147,483,647 (0x7FFFFFFF) produces 2,147,485,040 (0x80000570). This value is invalid under HTTP/2 as it exceeds MAX, although it still fits in a 64-bit size_t; the addition has not yet wrapped around. The unchecked restoration at [7] is the first invalid state in the vulnerability. The attacker still needs a way to close the selected requests while preserving the connection, so the excessive counter can be used again.

A SETTINGS error closes the stream but leaves the connection usable

When a SETTINGS frame increases SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE enough that an active stream's credit would exceed MAX, nginx terminates that stream but leaves the HTTP/2 connection usable. A client can create this condition by first sending a stream WINDOW_UPDATE to put the selected stream just below MAX. It then sends a SETTINGS frame that increases the initial stream-window setting. For example, changing the setting from 65,535 to 65,537 adds two bytes to every active stream. A stream already at MAX-1 would become MAX+1, even though the new setting value itself is allowed.

RFC 9113 requires this condition to end the connection with FLOW_CONTROL_ERROR. nginx instead calls ngx_http_v2_terminate_stream() for each affected stream. That function sends RST_STREAM, which ends an individual stream, and causes the request to be cleaned up. The loop then continues using the same connection:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2.c // ngx_http_v2_adjust_windows() // ... if (delta > 0 && stream->send_window > (ssize_t) (NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - delta)) { if (ngx_http_v2_terminate_stream(h2c, stream, NGX_HTTP_V2_FLOW_CTRL_ERROR) == NGX_ERROR) { return NGX_ERROR; } continue; // <--- [8] }

Here, delta is the difference between the new and old setting values. Request cleanup performs [5] through [7], while continue at [8] leaves the HTTP/2 connection open. The attacker can now send further frames on the connection whose credit has exceeded MAX.

The next WINDOW_UPDATE causes an integer underflow

When another connection WINDOW_UPDATE arrives, nginx tries to calculate how much additional credit is still allowed:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2.c // ngx_http_v2_state_window_update() // ... if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window) { // <--- [9] // ... return ngx_http_v2_connection_error(h2c, NGX_HTTP_V2_FLOW_CTRL_ERROR); } h2c->send_window += window; // <--- [10]

In this function, window is the increment received from the client. The subtraction at [9] is safe only while the stored counter is no greater than MAX. If cleanup has restored R excess bytes, the intended allowance is MAX - (MAX + R), or -R. Unsigned arithmetic cannot represent that negative result. On the verified 64-bit build it wraps to 2^64 - R, a very large positive number. This is the integer underflow identified by CWE-191.

The incorrect allowance lets further client increments pass the check. By sending many increments, each no greater than MAX, the client can raise the counter to 2^63 or above without wrapping the addition itself, shown at [10] above. Such a value has the top bit of its 64-bit representation set. It is still an unsigned value, but it no longer fits in a signed 64-bit integer. That distinction matters when nginx prepares the next response.

This amplification accounts for the large traffic requirement. A connection WINDOW_UPDATE occupies 13 HTTP/2 bytes: a nine-byte frame header and a four-byte payload. The credit granted by that frame is not data actually transmitted. Starting from the small over-credit state described above, reaching 2^63 by maximum-size increments takes about 2^32 frames, or 52 GiB. Reaching the near-2^64 values used for the confirmed read/write path takes about 2^33 increments, or 104 GiB. nginx also limits control-frame traffic relative to other received data. The current code-execution reproduction sends about 15 GiB of additional request-header traffic to stay within that limit, bringing its reported plaintext total to about 119.02 GiB. TLS and network overhead increase the actual wire traffic. These figures describe this 64-bit amplification route, not a universal minimum for every possible exploit.

Excessive credit becomes a negative response length

The client can make an active stream with available credit process an ordinary response body. nginx's HTTP/2 output filter decides how many body bytes to include in a DATA frame. Before following that calculation, it is useful to define the buffer it will create.

An in-memory nginx buffer is described by a ngx_buf_t record. Its pos pointer is the memory address of the next byte to send. Its last pointer is the address immediately after the available data. For four available bytes, last must be four bytes after pos; subtracting pos from last gives the length, four. A valid buffer therefore cannot have last before pos. nginx links these buffer records together into an output chain, which is a list of data waiting to be sent.

In ngx_http_v2_send_chain(), the byte limit is an off_t, a signed 64-bit integer on the verified build. The excessive unsigned connection counter is converted to that signed type at [11]. On this build, a value of 2^64 - d, where d is a small positive byte count, becomes -d:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2_filter_module.c // ngx_http_v2_send_chain() // ... if (limit == 0 || limit > (off_t) h2c->send_window) { limit = h2c->send_window; // <--- [11] } if (limit > stream->send_window) { limit = (stream->send_window > 0) ? stream->send_window : 0; } // ... if ((off_t) frame_size > limit) { frame_size = (size_t) limit; // <--- [12] } // ... rest = frame_size; while ((off_t) rest >= size) { // <--- [13] // ... } if (rest) { cl = ngx_http_v2_filter_get_shadow(stream, in->buf, offset, rest); // <--- [14] // ... }

The stream-window check does not reject a negative limit: it only reduces a limit that is too large. At [12], the negative limit becomes a huge unsigned frame_size. Casting the same value back to off_t makes it negative again, so [13] skips the loop that would normally consume and bound the available body bytes. At [14], nginx passes the invalid length to a helper whose size parameter is also a signed off_t.

That helper creates a shadow buffer: a new metadata record referring to part of the existing response data, without copying the response body itself. It sets the new end pointer using the supplied length:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2_filter_module.c // ngx_http_v2_filter_get_shadow() static ngx_chain_t * ngx_http_v2_filter_get_shadow(ngx_http_v2_stream_t *stream, ngx_buf_t *buf, off_t offset, off_t size) { // ... ngx_memcpy(chunk, buf, sizeof(ngx_buf_t)); // ... if (ngx_buf_in_memory(chunk)) { chunk->pos += offset; chunk->last = chunk->pos + size; // <--- [15] } // ... }

Because size is negative, [15] places last before pos. The response body has not become larger; its buffer metadata is now invalid. The next output stage trusts that metadata.

Buffered TLS output copies beyond the buffers

For buffered TLS output, ngx_ssl_send_chain() gathers bytes from the output chain into a temporary staging buffer before encryption. It calculates each input buffer's length using last - pos. The invalid buffer produces a negative signed length at [16]:

// src/event/ngx_event_openssl.c // ngx_ssl_send_chain() // ... ssize_t send, size, file_size; // ... size = in->buf->last - in->buf->pos; // <--- [16] if (size > buf->end - buf->last) { size = buf->end - buf->last; } if (send + size > limit) { size = (ssize_t) (limit - send); } // ... ngx_memcpy(buf->last, in->buf->pos, size); // <--- [17] buf->last += size; in->buf->pos += size;

Both checks only reduce lengths that are too large. Neither rejects a negative length. memcpy takes an unsigned size_t byte count, so [17] converts -d back into the huge value 2^64-d. The actual source and destination buffers are far smaller. This is where the invalid connection credit first reaches an out-of-bounds native memory access.

A copy that actually traversed such an enormous range would normally encounter inaccessible memory and crash the worker. In the tested x86-64 glibc implementation, however, certain lengths just below 2^64 cause the machine-level end-address calculations to wrap (Please see Addendum A below for more details on this unexpected behavior). For a length of 2^64-d, adding the length to a start address can produce an address d bytes before it. The optimized copy uses these end addresses in its loop conditions, so it can finish after a limited number of reads and writes that reach outside the intended buffers. The copy can return if all locations it actually accesses are accessible; other lengths, memory layouts, or copy implementations can fault immediately. If it returns, nginx also moves both buffer positions backward by the negative signed length.

Exploitation

The invalid copy can both read and overwrite worker memory. It does not give the client an HTTP/2 field in which it can simply choose any memory address. The useful addresses depend on where nginx allocated the response and TLS buffers, how much output is already buffered, and which copy routine the C library selected. These are constrained read and write capabilities, not an unconditional arbitrary read or write.

After creating the invalid DATA buffer, ngx_http_v2_send_chain() updates its position in the original response and records the bytes that remain to be sent:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2_filter_module.c // ngx_http_v2_send_chain() // ... offset += rest; // <--- [18] size -= rest; // ... if (offset) { cl = ngx_http_v2_filter_get_shadow(stream, in->buf, offset, size); // <--- [19] // ... in->buf = cl->buf; // ... }

Here, offset is the position within the original body and size is its remaining length. Starting at offset zero, the same unsigned value representing -d makes [18] move the offset backward by d and increase the remaining length by d on the verified build. The shadow buffer created at [19] therefore has a positive length, but starts d bytes before the original response and ends at its original end. If the oversized copy and connection survive, later ordinary DATA frames can carry those preceding bytes to the client through TLS. They can include pointers into the heap, where nginx dynamically allocates request data, or into loaded libraries. Those pointers disclose addresses that address-space layout randomization (ASLR) would otherwise hide.

On the write side, nginx stores client-supplied request data in heap allocations. With a suitable allocation layout, the oversized copy can pick up those attacker-selected bytes and replace fields in a nearby live heap object. One useful field is a callback: a stored function pointer that nginx intends to call later. An attacker who knows the relevant process addresses and can overwrite that field may redirect normal nginx processing to existing executable code. The overwrite need not contain new machine code. This explains the general route from disclosed addresses and controlled bytes to code execution; it does not claim that every build exposes the same object or callback. Execution has the worker's permissions; execution as the master process or root has not been established.

The proof-of-concept first recovers heap addresses and pointers into nginx and the GNU C Library (glibc) from memory preceding the original response body. It uses those addresses and the overwrite to forge nginx request and response-buffer objects that return selected parts of glibc's loaded image over HTTP/2. The returned ELF metadata is parsed to resolve system() despite ASLR, then a request-pool cleanup callback is redirected to invoke an attacker-chosen command.

Addendum A: Why an oversized memcpy can return

The TLS copy via ngx_memcpy (shown at [17] above) receives a byte count of 2^64-d, where d is a small positive distance. A routine that actually traversed that entire range would normally fault. This addendum explains why one optimized glibc implementation can instead finish after a limited number of out-of-bounds accesses.

glibc chooses among optimized copy routines according to the CPU's capabilities. The tested x86-64 routine uses EVEX/YMM instructions, which can move 32 bytes at a time. In the corresponding glibc 2.41 source, the EVEX wrapper includes a shared memcpy/memmove implementation, and its vector configuration sets VEC_SIZE to 32. A vector is the block of bytes handled by one such instruction.

The following excerpt uses AT&T assembly syntax, in which the source operand comes first. The CPU register %rdi holds the original destination address, called D below; %rsi holds the source address, Q; and %rdx holds the byte count, n. One route enters this backward-copy branch when D and Q are different and the unsigned difference D-Q is smaller than n. This includes the ordinary case where D is above Q and n is close to the unsigned 64-bit maximum.

// glibc 2.41: sysdeps/x86_64/multiarch/memmove-vec-unaligned-erms.S // Function: CPU-selected memcpy implementation, backward-copy branch // ... L(more_8x_vec_backward): // ... leaq (VEC_SIZE * -4 + -1)(%rdi, %rdx), %rcx // <--- [20] // ... andq $-(VEC_SIZE), %rcx // <--- [21] // ... L(loop_4x_vec_backward): // ... load and store four 32-byte vectors addq $(VEC_SIZE * -4), %rcx // <--- [22] cmpq %rcx, %rdi // <--- [23] jb L(loop_4x_vec_backward) // ... store the previously loaded leading and trailing vectors VZEROUPPER_RETURN // <--- [24]

The full glibc assembly source shows the omitted loads and stores. At [20], leaq calculates an address without reading memory. Its 64-bit result keeps only the low 64 bits. At [21], andq rounds that address down to a 32-byte boundary. Calling the resulting destination address cursor, the calculation is:

cursor = align_down_32((D + n - 129) modulo 2^64) = align_down_32(D - d - 129), when n = 2^64-d

Here, align_down_32 means rounding down to the nearest address divisible by 32; it is explanatory notation, not a glibc function. For an ordinary heap address and a small d, the calculated cursor is already below D.

The loop starts by copying one 128-byte block. Instruction [22] then moves the cursor backward by another 128 bytes. The comparison and unsigned jump at [23] repeat the loop only while D < cursor. Because the cursor is already below D, the jump is not taken. The routine writes its remaining leading and trailing vectors, then returns at [24]. It has not copied the enormous requested range: the wrapped address has made the loop stop after a small set of accesses. Those accesses can still read and overwrite memory outside the actual buffers.

Remediation

The following vendor supplied fixes are available.

Product

Vulnerable Versions

Title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): Who’s Exposed and How to Fix It
Context: The flaw isn't in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, Canada's Cyber Centre said it wasn't aware of attacks, and Calif is holding back its exploit code
Full Text:
Java4Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, is a heap overflow in Java's hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder. Researchers at Calif say it can let attackers without an account run code on Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak and other Java applications. Oracle and the OpenJDK project shipped fixes on Nov. 17, 2026, and CISA urged organizations to patch immediately. No exploitation in the wild has been reported.

Patch it, but read the conditions before you rank it next to Log4Shell. The vulnerable code runs only on x86-64 servers whose processors support AVX-512 VBMI, so a server's exposure depends on its CPU as much as its Java version. The same container image can be vulnerable on one host and safe on the next, and that is the detail most patch plans will miss.

Which Java versions and servers are affected?

A server is exposed only when three conditions hold at once.

1. A vulnerable Java build. Java 17.0.6 and later on the 17 line, plus Java 21, 25 and 27 before the November fixes. Standard Java 8 and 11 don't contain the flawed code, but the Java SE 8 Performance Pack build 8u511b33-perf does, as do recent GraalVM builds.

2. The right CPU. The vulnerable path runs only on x86-64 chips with AVX-512 VBMI: Intel Xeon Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids and Granite Rapids, and AMD Zen 4 or newer. ARM64 servers, including AWS Graviton, don't run it. On Linux, this command should print all four flags if the chip qualifies:

grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$'

3. A reachable decoder. An attacker has to get malformed Base64 into Java's standard decoder. Many servers decode Base64 before checking who you are, in HTTP Basic login headers, SAML artifacts and CSRF tokens, which is what makes the attack possible without a login.

Calif reports pre-authentication code execution under default settings on Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and with a login on Apache Kafka, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. It says the list is incomplete.

Java build

Oracle Java SE 17 (17.0.6 and later)

17.0.21.1

Oracle Java SE 21

21.0.13.1

Oracle Java SE 25

25.0.5.1

Oracle Java SE 27

27.0.1.1

Amazon Corretto 17, 21, 25, 27

17.0.21.1.2, 21.0.13.1.2, 25.0.5.1.2, 27.0.1.1.4

Azul Zulu 17, 21, 25, 27

17.70.201, 21.54.201, 25.38.201, 27.30.201

Red Hat build of OpenJDK and RHEL 8, 9, 10

Not yet released as of Nov. 18

Products that bundle their own Java runtime, from CI servers to appliances, need an update from their vendor, not just a new system JDK.

How Java4Shell works

When a method runs often enough, Java's JIT compiler swaps the standard Base64 decoding loop for a hand-tuned assembly routine, an "intrinsic," that uses AVX-512 VBMI instructions. That routine miscalculates the output size when the input ends with an unexpected = padding character. Wiz gives the example of 64 A characters followed by a single =.

The result is a write of 62 or 63 bytes past the end of the output array on the Java heap. Java does reject the malformed string, but only after the write has happened. That ordering is the whole bug: input validation in your application can't help, because the damage is done inside the decoder.

The overflowed bytes are fixed by the decoder, which is why early readings predicted a crash, not code execution. Calif's researchers got around that by arranging heap memory so the overflow enlarges a neighboring array. They then used that array to write chosen bytes and a second array to read memory back, a step they call JavaBleed, and worked from there to code execution.

There is no universal exploit. Each application needs its own memory layout and timing, and some attempts are sensitive to network delay. A failed attempt usually crashes the JVM, and an attacker can often try again.

One uncomfortable footnote: a pull request to OpenJDK on Sept. 9 described an overflow in the same decoder and included a triggering input. It was closed unmerged in early November after eight weeks of inactivity.

Is Java4Shell being exploited, and why do the scores disagree?

As of Nov. 18, 2026, no exploitation has been reported. The flaw isn't in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, Canada's Cyber Centre said it wasn't aware of attacks, and Calif is holding back its exploit code.

Independent labs have confirmed the dangerous part, though. Upwind reproduced the memory corruption on an Intel Ice Lake server on AWS until Java crashed. Blackpoint Cyber crashed a test Spring Boot app with about 28,300 malformed login requests in roughly 20 seconds, without logging in, and used the JavaBleed technique to read a secret from memory in all 30 local runs. Neither reproduced remote code execution.

That split explains the scores:

Source

Score

What it emphasizes

Calif

9.2 (CVSS 4.0)

Demonstrated pre-auth code execution on six apps

Red Hat

9.8 (preliminary)

No login required

Amazon

8.8

JVM crash for unauthenticated users; code execution for low-privileged users in some environments

Oracle / OpenJDK

8.1 (CVSS 3.1)

No login required, but hard to exploit

The practical read: a pre-auth crash of any affected Java service is easy today. Reliable code execution takes per-target work, but the researchers have shown it can be done, and the triggering input has been public since September. Treat it as urgent.

How to fix and mitigate Java4Shell

Find every affected runtime. Inventory Java 17 and later, including runtimes bundled inside products. Then check the CPU on each host with the command above. Mixed fleets and autoscaling groups can change exposure from one instance to the next.

Patch. Install the fixed build for your distribution from the table above, then restart Java services and rebuild and redeploy container images so the running process actually uses it. Red Hat users need the workaround until Red Hat ships fixes.

If you can't patch yet, turn off the vulnerable path. Start the JVM with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, which removes only the faster Base64 code. -XX:UseAVX=2 disables AVX-512 entirely, but use it only on x86-64, because Java on ARM64 won't start with it. Upwind warns that -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock on its own stops Java from starting. Remove the flag once the fixed build is in.

Reduce exposure at the edge. CISA recommends validating Base64 input at application boundaries, enforcing input-size limits and limiting unauthenticated access. A reverse proxy that buffers complete requests, as nginx does by default, blocks some attacks but not all.

Hunt for attempts. Look for Base64 tokens of 32 characters or more that end in = and whose length isn't a multiple of four, especially in Authorization headers; bursts of IllegalArgumentException from java.util.Base64$Decoder; and unexplained hs_err_pid crash logs or restart storms. None of these proves a compromise, and their absence doesn't prove you're safe.

Frequently asked questions

What is Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938)?

Java4Shell is a heap buffer overflow in the AVX-512 Base64 decoder of OpenJDK's HotSpot JVM on x86-64. Malformed Base64 ending in an extra = makes the decoder write 62 or 63 bytes past its output buffer. Calif, which disclosed it on Nov. 17, 2026, demonstrated unauthenticated code execution against six widely used Java applications.

Which Java versions are affected?

Java 17.0.6 and later on the 17 line, and Java 21, 25 and 27 before the November 2026 fixes. Fixed Oracle builds are 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1. The server must also have an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 VBMI, such as Intel Xeon Ice Lake or later, or AMD Zen 4 or later.

Are Java 8 and Java 11 affected?

Standard Java 8 and 11 builds don't contain the vulnerable code. The exception is the Java SE 8 Performance Pack build 8u511b33-perf, which is affected; Oracle's latest Performance Pack build is 8u513.

Is CVE-2026-114938 being exploited?

No exploitation in the wild had been reported as of Nov. 18, 2026, and the flaw wasn't in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Independent labs have reproduced crashes and memory reads but not remote code execution.

Is Java4Shell as bad as Log4Shell?

It's narrower. Log4Shell could be triggered by almost any logged string on any hardware with a simple, reliable exploit. Java4Shell needs specific CPUs, a reachable Base64 decoder and target-specific exploitation work. A pre-auth crash is easy, though, so treat it as urgent.

How can I mitigate Java4Shell without patching?

Start the JVM with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to disable the vulnerable decoder path, or -XX:UseAVX=2 on x86-64 only. Add input-size limits and Base64 validation at the edge, and remove the JVM flag once you've installed a fixed build.

Title: Java4Shell Vulnerability Allows Remote Attacks on Major Java Apps
Context: Java4Shell: A Hardware-Bound Exploit Despite the criticality and widespread impact of Java4Shell, several security firms noted that the vulnerability is difficult to exploit
Full Text:
Weeks after PHP2Shell, another critical vulnerability has been leaked before its planned disclosure and authorities are now urging organizations to apply patches.

The new vulnerability, known as ‘Java4Shell’ and tracked as CVE-2026-114938, is a memory corruption vulnerability in Open Java Development Kit (OpenJDK), an open-source implementation of the Java Platform, Standard Edition (Java SE) co-maintained by Oracle and a global community of developers and companies, such as Red Hat, Amazon and Microsoft. OpenJDK runs most Java applications.

The vulnerability was found by California-based security firm Calif, which published details on November 17 after some information was leaked before coordinated disclosure.

The flaw affects OpenJDK 17, 21, 25 and 27 and is rated with a high-severity score of 8.1 by Oracle (using CVSS v3.1) and a critical severity score of 9.2 by Calif (using CVSS v4.0).

The exploitation of Java4Shell can allow unauthenticated attackers corrupt memory in Java servers with a single malformed message.

According to a write-up from Calif, the blast radius of a potential exploit could be broad, with many Java-based applications built on OpenJDK also vulnerable.

Services vulnerable to a remote code execution (RCE) attack which has exploited Java4Shell include Keycloak, Atlassian’s products like Jira and Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate as well as many distributions based on OpenJDK:

Amazon Corretto

Eclipse Temurin

Microsoft Build of OpenJDK

Azul Zulu

BellSoft Liberica

SAP SapMachine

Red Hat OpenJDK

Oracle OpenJDK

Oracle Java SE

Oracle GraalVM for JDK

Other services can also be vulnerable to a Java4Shell exploit, but only if the attacker is able to authenticate. These include Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker.

Maintainers of OpenJDK have published a fix, but each Java vendor will ship its fixed build on its own schedule.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) published an emergency advisory on November 17 urging organizations to apply patches as soon as they are available.

Java4Shell: A Hardware-Bound Exploit

Despite the criticality and widespread impact of Java4Shell, several security firms noted that the vulnerability is difficult to exploit.

In two separate reports, VulnCheck and Endor Labs highlighted that exploitation of the vulnerability is hardware-specific, depending on the Java version, the underlying server processor and the application running on it.

Both research teams noted that the flaw affects CPUs supporting AVX-512 VBMI instructions, while ARM-based servers, including AWS Graviton, are not affected.

VulnCheck said its researchers had successfully reproduced the vulnerability on Ice Lake hardware, adding that processors without AVX-512 VBMI and BW support use an alternative decoding path that does not contain the defect.

Endor Labs noted that the affected processors include recent Intel and AMD server chips, which account for much of current cloud capacity.

As of November 18, no attacks exploiting the vulnerability had been reported in the wild.

CISA Mitigation Recommendations

CISA recommended the following mitigation measures:

Identify affected Java installations: review software inventories for Java Development Kits (JDKs) and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications, container images and appliances, as they may not appear as separate inventory entries

Apply security patches: install relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they become available, prioritizing internet-facing systems

Implement safeguards: where immediate patching is not possible, implement temporary safeguards, such as validating and restricting Base64 input at application boundaries, enforcing input-size limits and limiting unauthenticated access

Review vendor guidance: consult Oracle’s security advisory for additional patching instructions and recommendations

Monitor for suspicious activity: watch for indicators of potential exploitation, including rogue Java runtimes, unexpected Java Virtual Machine (JVM) crashes and suspicious Java processes

Context: 2 (Critical), according to Calif, which discovered the flaw, and 8
Full Text:
Key findings

CVE-2026-114938, which has been dubbed Java4Shell, is a critical heap overflow in the Base64 decoder of the OpenJDK HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM) on x86-64. It has a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v4.0 score of 9.2 (Critical), according to Calif, which discovered the flaw, and 8.1 (High) on CVSS 3.1 per OpenJDK's advisory.

A remote, unauthenticated attacker who can deliver crafted Base64 input to a vulnerable Java process can corrupt heap memory and achieve remote code execution (RCE). No user interaction is required for server-side attacks.

Only hosts with AVX-512 Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions (VBMI) are exposed. That means Intel Ice Lake or newer, or AMD Zen 4 or newer. ARM64 hosts, Java 11 and standard OpenJDK 8 are not affected.

Security company Calif demonstrated pre-authentication RCE in test configurations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate.

Oracle and OpenJDK released fixes on November 17, 2026. Fixed builds end in ".1", and the same version number without the suffix remains vulnerable.

No in-the-wild exploitation had been reported as of publication, but a proof-of-concept trigger is public. Symantec and Carbon Black Security Response is investigating, and up-to-date protection information will be added to our Protection Bulletin.

Overview

A critical vulnerability in OpenJDK, CVE-2026-114938 (aka Java4Shell), was disclosed on November 17, 2026. The flaw sits in the optimized Base64 decoder that the HotSpot JVM uses on x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI support. Oracle and OpenJDK have released patches, and the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) urged immediate patching. At time of writing on November 18 there has been no evidence found of in-the-wild exploitation of this bug.

Java4Shell is significant because Base64 decoding is routine in server software. Authentication headers, JSON Web Tokens (JWT), Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) assertions, file uploads and API fields are all Base64 encoded, so internet-facing login and API services decode attacker-controlled data by design. Calif, the security firm that first reported the flaw, published a standalone trigger and said product-specific exploit chains would be held back until upgrades are more widespread. Details about the flaw became public before patches were available.

How the vulnerability works

The store mask used by the decoder is wrong when the Base64 input ends in padding. As a result, the calculated output length underflows, and the decoder writes a full 64 bytes into a buffer that is smaller than that. According to Calif, a 65-byte input overflows the heap by 62 bytes, which corrupts adjacent Java objects, allowing an actor to gain heap read and write primitives, which makes the bug remotely exploitable.

Exploitation of the heap overflow depends on the layout of the target application, and a failed attempt can crash the JVM. A crash would result in denial of service, but Calif reported that retries often succeed. Heap memory disclosure is also possible. A client-side variant exists: a Java application that connects over Transport Layer Security (TLS) to a malicious server can be compromised.

Who is affected?

Affected versions are OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later (including 17.0.6 to 17.0.21), Java 21 before 21.0.13.1, Java 25 before 25.0.5.1 and Java 27. Oracle also lists Java SE 8 8u511b33-perf. Builds from Oracle, Corretto, Temurin, Microsoft, Zulu, Liberica, SapMachine, Red Hat and GraalVM are affected. Hosts must also run on an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI, which includes Intel Ice Lake and newer and AMD Zen 4 and newer. Java 11, standard OpenJDK 8, ARM64 hosts and x86 processors without AVX-512 VBMI are not affected.

Enterprise and server deployments carry the most risk, particularly identity, application lifecycle, build pipeline, artifact and data platforms. Popular Java-based applications such as Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Keycloak, Kafka and Elasticsearch could be affected. Many of these products ship their own bundled Java runtime, so organizations should check each vendor for updated releases and should not rely on the host's Java version alone. Consumers are mainly exposed through Java client applications.

Exploitation status

No in-the-wild exploitation had been reported as of November 18, 2026. However, Calif published a trigger that reproduces the overflow. It also showed pre-authentication RCE in Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Keycloak, JFrog Artifactory and PingFederate, as well as post-authentication RCE in Apache Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. Fake proof-of-concept repositories are likely to appear, and unpatched internet-facing Java services on AVX-512 hardware should be treated as potentially exposed.

Patching

Oracle released fixes in its November 2026 Critical Patch Update, alongside an OpenJDK advisory of the same date. Fixed builds are:

Java 17: 17.0.21.1

Java 21: 21.0.13.1

Java 25: 25.0.5.1

Java 27: 27.0.1.1

Java SE 8 (-perf builds): see the Oracle advisory

A running JVM keeps the vulnerable code until it is restarted, so every Java process must be restarted after upgrading. Containers should be rebuilt on patched base images. Downstream vendors are rolling out their own fixes, and fixed builds for several of them were not yet published at time of writing. CISA also advised identifying all Java installations, including those bundled in third-party applications, containers and appliances, and prioritizing internet-facing systems.

Interim mitigations

Where patching is not immediately possible, Calif lists two JVM options. Both require a restart and neither replaces patching.

Add -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to disable the Base64 intrinsics. This may slow Base64-heavy workloads.

Add -XX:UseAVX=2 to disable AVX-512. Use this on x86-64 hosts only, because the JVM will not start with it on ARM.

Do not set -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock on its own. It breaks JVM startup and can cause an outage if pushed fleet-wide.

CISA also recommended compensating controls such as validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input size limits and limiting unauthenticated access. Defenders can look for Base64 tokens that contain an equals sign and whose length is not a multiple of four, decoder exceptions such as “Input byte array has wrong 4-byte ending unit” in application logs, and unexpected JVM crashes or new hs_err_pid log files. The exception is thrown after the overflow, so it indicates an attempt and not a blocked attack.

Protection

Symantec and Carbon Black Security Response is investigating this vulnerability, guidance and reproduction steps. Full protection information is in the Symantec Protection Bulletin for Java4Shell. The bulletin will be updated continuously as new information becomes available.

Title: Three AI Models Agree on Just One of 121 Potential Code Flaws
Context: " If an attacker hunts with one model and a defender relies on another, he said, "the defender might never even see the vulnerability the attacker is about to exploit
Full Text:
Three frontier AI models given the same open source code to audit have produced vulnerability findings that barely overlap, according to new frontier AI research. Of 121 distinct potential issues, Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5.1, OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol and Z.ai's GLM-5.3 all flagged just one, software security firm Echo found.

Echo published the comparison in its November 18 research. Each model worked through two Maven libraries and one npm package with Echo's own hunting framework and the same validation process. Echo reached GPT-5.6 Sol through Daybreak, the program OpenAI runs for vetted security teams.

Of the 121 issues, 83% (100), came from a single model and 20 from the other two.

Read more on AI vulnerability discovery: AI Cuts Vulnerability Discovery from Nine Months to 90 Hours

Where the AI Models Disagreed

Claude Mythos logged the most validation passes overall, with 25, against nine for GLM-5.3 and eight for GPT-5.6 Sol. But GPT-5.6 Sol accounted for six of the seven passes on one Maven library, and GLM-5.3 found six validated issues on the other that its rivals missed.

Severity ratings split too. GLM-5.3 rated one flaw in an npm package with more than 350 million monthly downloads as Critical, Claude Mythos put it at High and GPT-5.6 Sol treated it as documented behavior rather than a bug. Automated validation rated it Low.

GPT-5.6 Sol finished its hunts in about 24 minutes, against roughly 198 for Claude Mythos and 174 for GLM-5.3. GLM-5.3 was the cheapest overall, with its three hunts costing about $22, against $303 for Claude Mythos and $30 for GPT-5.6 Sol, though Echo said the costs reflected its own access terms.

How Many AI Findings Held Up

The nine runs produced 446 initial findings, cut to 152 after cleanup. Of those, 74 were rated High or Critical, and 55 went through automated proof-of-concept testing after duplicates were set aside. Forty-two passed.

Echo cautioned that the 42 were not necessarily distinct bugs, since an issue found by more than one model could be credited to each. Findings rated Medium or Low were never tested, so a previously known flaw that Claude Mythos rated Medium never reached validation.

Echo security researcher Yuval Saggie said the race to find the best model was "the wrong question." If an attacker hunts with one model and a defender relies on another, he said, "the defender might never even see the vulnerability the attacker is about to exploit."

Each model ran only once, and Echo called the exercise "a controlled comparison rather than a comprehensive benchmark." It said automated validation did not amount to confirmation from the projects' maintainers.

Echo said the projects would stay unnamed, and technical details unpublished, until their maintainers had been notified.

Title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): Check Your Java Services Now
Context: Check Point IPS protection for the public PoC is available now, but patching is still the only complete fix
Full Text:
Bottom line: A single malformed Base64 string can give an attacker code execution on unpatched Java runtimes, often without logging in. Fixes were released on November 17, 2026. Inventory your Java runtimes, patch identity providers first, and use a startup flag where you cannot patch today. Check Point IPS protection for the public PoC is available now, but patching is still the only complete fix. Our full advisory has every detail.

What we see

The flaw: On recent Intel and AMD x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI, Java’s hand-tuned Base64 decoder miscalculates the output length for the padded tail of a short malformed input. The result is a write of 62 or 63 bytes past the end of its buffer, depending on the padding. Java rejects the input, but only after the write.

The impact: The bytes written are fixed, so on its own the overflow usually crashes Java. Calif, the firm that found the flaw, reports shaping server memory so the overflow enlarges a neighboring array, which gives read and write access and then code execution. It demonstrated this without authentication against default installations of Keycloak, self-managed Atlassian Jira and Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate, and with a login against Apache Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker. The same corruption can also expose heap memory, including private keys, session tokens, and credentials, without any code execution.

Why login is often not needed: Applications decode Base64 before authentication, in HTTP Basic authentication headers, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens, and file uploads.

Side effects: Failed attempts often crash the Java process, and an attacker can often retry. Calif also reports that a Java client can be compromised by connecting over TLS to a malicious server.

Exploitation status (as of November 18, 2026):We are not aware of confirmed exploitation. However, the root cause is public, and a triggering input has been visible since September 9, 2026. Several independent teams have reproduced crashes and the memory leak in lab conditions, though not code execution as of November 18.

Important Note : There is no universal exploit, because each product needs its own memory layout and timing. That slows mass exploitation but does not protect a specific, high-value target such as an identity provider.

Are you affected?

A system is vulnerable only when all three conditions are true: an unpatched runtime, a specific processor, and attacker-controlled Base64 that reaches Java’s standard decoder.

Condition

Affected

Not affected

Java runtime

Unpatched OpenJDK-based builds from 17.0.6 onward on Java 17, and all Java 21, 25, and 27 builds before the fix, from any vendor. Oracle also lists its Java 8 performance build.

Java 17 releases before 17.0.6, standard Java 8 and Java 11, and fixed builds (Oracle: 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, 27.0.1.1)

Processor

x86-64 with AVX-512 VBMI, including Intel Xeon Ice Lake through Granite Rapids and AMD EPYC and Ryzen Zen 4 and newer. The CPU must expose avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi, and bmi2

ARM64, and x86-64 processors without AVX-512 VBMI

Reachability

Attacker-controlled Base64 reaches Java’s standard decoder (login headers, tokens, uploads)

No path for external input to reach the standard Base64 decoder

How to check

Runtime: Build an inventory of the runtime each application actually uses. Bundled runtimes do not get OS updates, so check the one each application ships with.

Processor: Run the Linux command in the advisory. A host is affected only if avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi, and bmi2 all appear in its CPU flags (/proc/cpuinfo). Use the result to prioritize, not to dismiss a finding, because a cloud resize can silently move a workload onto an affected processor.

Reachability: This is the hardest to settle from the inside, because it depends on how each application is deployed and what sits in front of it.

What else is in scope

Self-managed Jira and Confluence: The risk applies to self-managed Data Center deployments. Atlassian manages the Java runtime for Atlassian Cloud. Atlassian installers typically ship their own bundled runtime, so operating system patches alone do not fix a self-managed instance.

Spring Boot: Treat every Spring Boot service on an affected runtime as in scope. Researchers reached code execution in sample Spring Boot applications, where login handling, tokens, and file uploads often decode Base64 before a user is authenticated.

Apache Tomcat: It was not tested and no advisory links it to this CVE. It runs a large share of Java web applications and is embedded in Spring Boot by default, so include every Tomcat server in your inventory.

Anything else: If you cannot rule out that attacker input reaches Java’s built-in Base64 decoder, assume it does. Vendor advisories cover only Java 17, 21, 25, and 27, so move any other release to a fixed build rather than assuming it is safe.

What to do: patch first

Updating the Java runtime is the only complete fix.

Fix availability (as of November 18, 2026)

Fixed builds shipped: Oracle, Amazon (Corretto), Azul (Zulu). For Oracle, only builds ending in .1 are patched.

Not yet released: Red Hat and Eclipse Temurin

Status unconfirmed: Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, BellSoft Liberica. Check each vendor’s page.

Bundled runtimes: Products that ship their own Java runtime need an update from the product vendor.

Patch in this order

Identity providers: Keycloak and PingFederate

Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, and Artifactory (for Jira and Confluence, apply Atlassian’s update or the startup flag)

Other internet-facing Java services that handle logins, tokens, or uploads

Internal systems and Java clients

If you cannot patch today

Add -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to the Java startup options and restart the service. This turns off only the accelerated Base64 decoder. Applications that decode large volumes of Base64 may slow down, so test first.

Alternatively, use -XX:UseAVX=2. It turns off AVX-512 entirely, at a broader performance cost. Java on ARM64 rejects this option and will not start.

Remove either option after you have patched.

Avoid: -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock on its own. It can stop Java from starting.

Verify: A patch or a flag takes effect only after Java restarts. Confirm on the running process:

jcmd <pid> VM.version

jcmd <pid> VM.flags

VM.version should show a fixed build. For Oracle that is a version ending in .1, such as 17.0.21.1, and other vendors use their own version strings. If you set the startup flag, VM.flags should list -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics.

Elasticsearch

Elasticsearch ships with a bundled Java runtime, and Calif demonstrated code execution against it after login. Some attacks depend on a request arriving in pieces, so a reverse proxy that waits for complete requests (nginx does by default) blocks those. This attack works in a single complete request, so request buffering does not stop it. Treat clusters with anonymous access or weak credentials as exposed without a login. Apply Elastic’s update, or add -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics in a new .options file under config/jvm.options.d/ (/etc/elasticsearch/jvm.options.d/ for DEB and RPM installs) and restart each node. Do not edit the root jvm.options file.

Block known exploit attempts at the gateway

Check Point has released an IPS protection, [protection name / ID], that detects and blocks the public proof-of-concept for CVE-2026-114938. Make sure it is set to Prevent on your Quantum gateways, especially for traffic going to internet-facing Java services. This reduces exposure while you patch. It does not replace the runtime update, because it targets the known triggering input and not every possible variant

How to spot attempts

Failed attempts often crash Java, so watch for unexpected service restarts and new hs_err_pid<pid>.log files, which the JVM writes on a fatal crash. Crashes during garbage collection are also a known sign of this corruption. Then list every place where attacker-controlled Base64 reaches Java before login: HTTP Basic headers, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens, and file uploads.

Find the Java services you expose to the internet

Check Point Exposure Management can identify internet-facing assets that appear to run Java, including the version, so you know where to start. This is a passive check of technologies and versions. It does not exploit anything or send attack traffic to your services.

A technology check shows where Java is present. It cannot confirm the processor or whether attacker-controlled input reaches Java’s Base64 decoder, so use the results to prioritize and still run the runtime and processor checks above.

Beyond this flaw, Exposure Management helps you find, prioritize, validate, and fix the exposures that matter most across your environment:

Threat Intelligence: Know which threats and vulnerabilities attackers are targeting.

CAASM: Get a continuously updated view of your assets and where they are exposed.

Vulnerability Prioritization: Focus on the exposures with real risk, not the longest list.

Agentic Exposure Validation (AEV): Test whether an exposure is exploitable.

Safe Remediation: Fix confirmed exposures without disrupting the business.

Title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): Frequently asked questions about OpenJDK remote code execution vulnerability
Context: Later that day, Oracle released its November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update (CSPU), and the OpenJDK Vulnerability Group published its own advisory
Full Text:
Java4Shell is a flaw in how Java decodes Base64 data. Calif, which found it, says it can let attackers run code on widely used Java applications without logging in. Oracle released fixed Java builds on November 17, and Calif is withholding its exploits for individual applications for now.

Key takeaways

CVE-2026-114938, dubbed Java4Shell, is an OpenJDK memory corruption vulnerability that Oracle scores 8.1 on CVSS 3.1, and Calif says its testing showed attackers could run code without logging in on applications such as Atlassian Jira and Jenkins.

As of November 17, Tenable is not aware of any reports that attackers have exploited this flaw, though Calif has published a PoC that triggers the bug without taking control of the system and a second researcher reports building a working exploit.

Oracle released fixed builds on November 17, and according to Calif, only systems running an affected Java version on x86-64 processors that support AVX-512 VBMI can be affected.

Background

Tenable's Research Special Operations (RSO) team has compiled this blog to answer Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) regarding Java4Shell, a vulnerability in OpenJDK that was patched on November 17, 2026.

FAQ

When was Java4Shell first disclosed?

On November 17, security firm Calif said on X that it had found and reported the flaw, and that details of Java4Shell, as Calif named it, had leaked ahead of a fix. Later that day, Oracle released its November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update (CSPU), and the OpenJDK Vulnerability Group published its own advisory. Calif then published its technical write-up. Oracle credits Quang Luong of Calif.io and Albert Yang for reporting the vulnerability.

Since the vulnerability has leaked: Calif discovered and reported Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938).We're publishing technical details by 1 PM Pacific today, after Oracle releases a patch.Stay tuned! https://t.co/No5hJXK1Zx

— Calif (@calif_io) November 17, 2026

What is CVE-2026-114938?

CVE

Description

CVSSv3.1

CVE-2026-114938

OpenJDK Base64 Decoder Memory Corruption Vulnerability (Java4Shell)

8.1

CVE-2026-114938 is a memory corruption vulnerability in the part of Java that decodes Base64, a common format that applications use to send data such as login details and file uploads. Oracle assigned it a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1 and rates its attack complexity as high. Calif says it scores 9.2 under CVSS 4.0. An attacker does not need to log in to exploit it remotely. According to Oracle, the flaw can only be exploited when an application passes untrusted data to the affected Java APIs, such as through a web service.

Is CVE-2026-114938 among the Java fixes in Oracle's November 2026 CSPU?

Yes. CVE-2026-114938 is addressed by one of the 11 Java SE security patches in Oracle's November 2026 CSPU, released November 17. For a breakdown of all the patches in this release, see our blog post on Oracle's November 2026 CSPU.

What is known about CVE-2026-114938?

The flaw is in a performance shortcut that Java uses to decode Base64 data faster on certain Intel and AMD processors. When the shortcut receives a specially crafted Base64 string, it writes data beyond the memory it set aside. That can corrupt other information the application is holding in memory.

According to Calif, an attacker can use this flaw in two ways. The first, which Calif calls "JavaBleed," lets an attacker read the application's memory. That memory may hold secrets such as keys and tokens. The second lets an attacker run their own code on the server. Calif also says that each application needs its own exploit, and that a failed attempt can crash the application, though an attacker can often try again.

Exposure depends on the processor as well as the Java version. According to Calif, Java uses the affected code only on x86-64 processors that support a feature called AVX-512 VBMI. These include Intel Xeon processors from the Granite Rapids, Emerald Rapids, Sapphire Rapids and Ice Lake families, as well as AMD processors based on Zen 4 or newer. Calif says systems with ARM64 processors are not affected. On Linux, a system meets this requirement when its processor reports all four of the avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi and bmi2 flags.

Which versions of Java are affected?

The OpenJDK Vulnerability Group lists the Java 17, 21, 25 and 27 release lines as affected by CVE-2026-114938. Calif says OpenJDK 17.0.6 and newer are affected. Oracle lists the following Oracle builds as affected:

Product

Affected versions (and likely earlier)

Oracle Java SE

Oracle GraalVM for JDK

17.0.21.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3

Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition

21.3.20.0.3

Oracle lists only builds it supports and says earlier versions are likely also affected. The Java 8 build on Oracle's list is its Enterprise Performance Pack. The OpenJDK advisory does not list standard Java 8 or Java 11 as affected by this vulnerability.

I don't use Oracle's Java builds. Am I affected?

Possibly. The flaw is in OpenJDK code, and according to Calif, the following Java distributions built from OpenJDK are also vulnerable:

Amazon Corretto

Oracle OpenJDK

Each vendor releases fixed builds on its own schedule, so check with your distribution's vendor for its fixed versions.

Which applications are known to be affected?

Calif says its initial testing showed that an attacker could run their own code on the following applications in their default configurations, when they run on an affected version of Java on a processor that supports AVX-512 VBMI. The list is not exhaustive, according to Calif.

Calif also said it ran its own code on sample applications built on frameworks including Apache Struts and Spring Boot. Calif adds that everyday functions, including authentication and file uploads, can lead to the vulnerable code, so more applications than the ones Calif tested may be exposed. Calif says researcher samczsun gave it a client-side exploit, and that a Java program can be compromised when it connects over TLS to a server an attacker controls, even if the program offers no service of its own. Calif says it will publish its exploits for individual products at a later date.

Has Java4Shell been exploited in the wild?

As of November 17, we are not aware of any reports of exploitation of CVE-2026-114938, and it is not listed in the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

Is there a proof-of-concept (PoC) available?

Yes. Calif published a PoC alongside its write-up that triggers the flaw without taking control of the system. It shows whether a given Java version and processor reproduce the bug. It does not show whether a particular application is exposed.

On November 17, Kevin Breen of Immersive said on X that they had developed a working exploit for CVE-2026-114938. According to Breen, the exploit has to be adapted to each application. It works only on a vulnerable version of Java running on a processor that supports AVX-512 VBMI, and only against applications that decode Base64 data. Breen also said that Apache Tomcat's Basic authentication and the java-jwt library provide ways to exploit the flaw before a user logs in. The post does not say that the exploit has been released.

Have a functional exploit POC for CVE-2026-114938 aka Java4Shell. This is not a generic exploit and will need to be application specific, you need a CPU with AVX-512 VBMI support, vulnerable JDK Version, and the app needs to use Base64, note that tomcats basic auth and java-jwt…

Yes. On November 17, Oracle released the following fixed builds:

Are there any mitigations?

Calif identified two Java startup options that keep the vulnerable code from running. The first, -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, turns off the Base64 shortcut. The second, -XX:UseAVX=2, turns off AVX-512 instructions. According to Calif, the second option applies only to x86-64 systems, and Java on ARM processors fails to start with it. Neither Oracle nor the OpenJDK Vulnerability Group mentions these options in its advisory.

Has Java been targeted historically?

Yes. CISA's KEV catalog includes 13 vulnerabilities in Oracle Java SE and the Java Runtime Environment (JRE), six of which are known to have been used in ransomware campaigns. Those six are:

Has Tenable Research classified this vulnerability as part of Vulnerability Watch?

Yes. CVE-2026-114938 has been classified as a "Vulnerability of Interest" as part of Vulnerability Watch.

Are Tenable products affected by this vulnerability?

Tenable is aware of this vulnerability and is investigating whether it affects any Tenable products.

Has Tenable released any product coverage for this vulnerability?

A list of Tenable plugins for this vulnerability can be found on the individual CVE page for CVE-2026-114938 as they're released. This link will display all available plugins for this vulnerability, including upcoming plugins in our Plugins Pipeline.

How can Tenable customers find affected assets?

Tenable One Vulnerability Management customers can go to Explore > Software to view installed software across their assets, then filter by product name and version to look for Java installations to compare against the affected versions above. Exposure also depends on the processor, as described above. Software data comes from credentialed and agent scans. For details, see Use the Software Page.

Tenable One Vulnerability Management customers can also use the Java Visibility and Exposures report, which lists Java installations and the hosts where they were detected.

Tenable One Attack Surface Management customers can find internet-facing assets running Java with the filter Programming Languages contains Java. Those assets can then be scanned with other Tenable sensors to check whether they are affected by CVE-2026-114938.

Title: CVE-2026-114938: Critical vulnerability in OpenJDK Java
Context: This vulnerability does require a specific subset of processors that support AVX-512 VBMI; these include commonly deployed processors from both Intel and AMD, resulting in a...
Full Text:
Cisco Talos is tracking the disclosure of a critical vulnerability in OpenJDK Java (CVE-2026-114938), dubbed “Java4Shell,” with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 that may lead to unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). This vulnerability can be triggered by sending a malformed Base64 input to affected JVMs, which can result in RCE.

Details

This vulnerability affects OpenJDK Java versions 17.0.6 and later running on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI (Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions) support enabled. These vulnerabilities have already been tested against a suite of Java applications with success, but the attack surface is likely much larger as additional targets are tested and confirmed.

This vulnerability does require a specific subset of processors that support AVX-512 VBMI; these include commonly deployed processors from both Intel and AMD, resulting in a large potential attack surface of vulnerable systems, including both on-premise and cloud environments.

Cisco Talos would like to thank Calif.io for sharing the details of the vulnerability in advance of public disclosure.

Observed exploitation

Talos has not observed in-the-wild exploitation of this vulnerability yet. However, we anticipate probing attempts may pick up soon after public disclosure. Talos will continue to monitor for exploitation attempts and will provide updates accordingly.

Recommendations and guidance

Talos recommends applying the software update for this vulnerability. If immediate patching is not possible, other mitigations can be implemented in the interim. The primary mitigation is starting the JVM with AVX-512 support disabled. This can be done by starting the application with “=XX:UseAVX=2”. Note that this is only applicable for x86-64 systems, as ARM-based processors will not recognize the command, likely resulting in failure to start.

Cisco is following its well-established process to evaluate its products and will provide updates shortly. Customers should reach out to their sales teams with specific questions

Coverage

Snort2: 1:67502 - 1:67513

Snort3: 1:301754, 1:67502 - 1:67513

These rules detect malformed base64 data in specific HTTP request fields associated with the vulnerability. This vulnerability is implementation specific. Title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): Pre-auth RCE in OpenJDK, and the challenge of image and feature bloat
Context: Calif, the firm that discovered the vulnerability, says that with 64 A characters and one =, a remote attacker with no credentials can overwrite heap memory, leak it Heartbleed-...
Full Text:
DISCLAIMER: This blog reflects public findings as of 1:36 UTC, Nov. 18, 2026, and it will be updated as new information is released.

Java promised that users would never have to think about memory again. Java's Base64 decoder, however, had other plans.

On November 17, 2026, Oracle and OpenJDK shipped fixes for Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a heap memory corruption bug in the AVX-512 accelerated Base64 decoder. Calif, the firm that discovered the vulnerability, says that with 64 A characters and one =, a remote attacker with no credentials can overwrite heap memory, leak it Heartbleed-style, and in the products they tested, get remote code execution (RCE).

Calif made a suggestion that Java4Shell’s Base64 optimization and the Squidbleed flaw that they also discovered are calls for vibe-uncoding, or the use of AI to find and remove system bloat to reduce an attack surface. This is the same point that’s been made in multiple Sysdig Cloud Native Security and Usage Reports since 2023 with regard to image bloat.

Let’s explore what's confirmed, what's still theoretical, and why after combating and cleaning up image bloat for years, the next fight appears to be feature bloat.

Important facts to know now about Java4Shell

What: Heap out-of-bounds write in OpenJDK's x86-64 Base64 intrinsic. Pre-authentication on common login paths.

Who: OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later (17, 21, 25, 27) on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI. ARM is out. Java 11 and standard Java 8 are out. Oracle also lists the Java 8 performance build (8u511b33-perf) as vulnerable.

Severity: 9.2 critical on CVSS 4.0 per Calif, and 8.1 on CVSS 3.1 per OpenJDK's advisory.

Exploitation: Calif confirms working RCE in Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate without authorization, plus five more post-auth. The researcher says OpenAI Codex helped find the bug in an hour and build an exploit in two hours for less than $200. Calif stated the exploit will not be publicly shared until organizations have patched the vulnerability.

Fix: Oracle builds ending in .1, or -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics as the bridge.

What happened

Time

Event

Nov 12

Oracle's pre-release notice: 11 Java SE fixes, all remotely exploitable without authentication, max CVSS 3.1 of 8.1. No CVE IDs.

Nov 17

Calif says the bug leaked ahead of the patch and moves its disclosure to 1 p.m. PT (21:00). Confirmed discussions about the report appear on X as early as 10:22.

Nov 17, 17:44 UTC

OpenJDK's advisory lists CVE-2026-114938 as hotspot/compiler, affecting 17, 21, 25, and 27.

Nov 17, 17:53 UTC

CISA KEV catalog is released. CVE not included.

A lab reproduction of the overflow is published and says RCE isn't proven.

Nov 17, 21:00 UTC

Calif publishes its write-up, with RCE demos across named products.

Who's affected by Java4Shell

Calif's list of vulnerable builds is broad because everything downstream of OpenJDK inherits the code: Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine, Red Hat OpenJDK, Oracle OpenJDK, Oracle Java SE, and Oracle GraalVM for JDK.
