ZDI-CAN-33367

Fix status

A small patch, “net: skbuff: propagate shared-frag marker in skb_zerocopy()”, is on netdev, reviewed by Eric Dumazet and tagged for stable. It has not been merged.

How the bug works: Dirty Frag again

Earlier this year, Dirty Frag (CVE-2026-43284) showed defenders how an unprivileged user could get the kernel's IPsec ESP code to decrypt in place over pages that belong to the page cache. Those pages back a file the user can only read, and decryption writes the attacker's bytes into the cached copy of that file. Targeting a setuid binary or /etc/passwd this way gives the attacker root without ever opening the file for writing.

The Dirty Frag fix marked those shared pages with a flag and taught ESP to copy before decrypting when it sees the flag. ZDI-CAN-33367 is a gap in that fix.

skb_zerocopy() moves the same pages into a new socket buffer but does not carry the flag across. ESP never sees the flag, decrypts in place, and the write lands in the page cache. According to TuxCare and Safeguard, the code path dates to kernel 3.14.

Not the first gap

The Dirty Frag fix only works if every piece of networking code that moves those pages around carries the flag along. Since May, the kernel's CVE team has published six follow-up CVEs where some other path lost it:

Frag-copy and shift helpers: CVE-2026-43503

Coalescing: CVE-2026-46300

IPTFS: CVE-2026-53363, CVE-2026-64566

An error-handling helper: CVE-2026-80977

Another error path inside skb_zerocopy() itself: CVE-2026-90049

CVE-2026-90049 is a different bug in the same function, so a kernel carrying its fix is not fixed for ZDI-CAN-33367.

Exploitation

The PoC needs unprivileged user namespaces and a handful of networking modules: nlmon, nft_queue, nfnetlink_queue, cls_u32, act_pedit, act_mirred, and esp4. It does not need a Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization (KASLR) leak, or any capability the user doesn't already get inside their own namespace.

Each step of exploitation is a system call that can be made by an ordinary user process:

Unshare into new user and network namespaces, then write sysctls.

Bring up an nlmon interface.

Install XFRM state over netlink.

Add an nftables NFQUEUE rule.

Attach a tc pedit action with a redirect.

splice() into a socket on 127.0.0.1, which triggers the in-place decryption over the page cache.

Impact

TuxCare reproduced a root shell on AlmaLinux 8–10, CloudLinux 9–10, Debian 12 and 13, and Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04. AlmaLinux was rooted with the Dirty Frag fix installed. CentOS 6 and 7 kernels are not vulnerable. The vulnerability is a local privilege escalation (LPE), so an attacker needs code execution on the host first.

ZDI-CAN-33774 and ZDI-CAN-33549

Both CVSS 9.0 reports are in ksmbd, the in-kernel Server Message Block (SMB) server. Samba is not ksmbd.

If your file servers run smbd, neither report applies to you. To check whether ksmbd is running anywhere, look for the ksmbd kernel module, the ksmbd.mountd userspace daemon, and a kernel-owned listener on TCP 445.

ZDI-CAN-33774: The dispatch race

ksmbd decides per request whether it is handling SMB1 or SMB2. If an attacker packs a burst of short SMB1 packets and an SMB2 packet into the same TCP write, the worker threads can run an SMB2 handler over SMB1 data and read past the end of the shorter buffer. This works before authentication. The public PoC leaks 28 bytes of kernel heap per attempt and can crash the kernel. ZDI describes a write-past-buffer path that needs share access and labels the bug as remote code execution (RCE), but nothing public shows code execution as of this blog’s publication.

Maintainer Namjae Jeon says the bug is already fixed, and his tree bears that out. Commit 68f410faedaf ("ksmbd: wait for negotiation before receiving another PDU") was written on September 30, credited to a different reporter, and describes exactly this race. It is queued in ksmbd's ksmbd-for-next branch and has not reached a released kernel.

ZDI-CAN-33549: SMB Direct

An integer underflow in the Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) transport turns a crafted buffer descriptor into a heap overflow of up to eight KB. The bar is higher than for 33774. The host needs an RDMA-capable interface (hardware, or the rxe software driver), a client that negotiates SMB Direct, and a writable share. The public PoC crashes the kernel.

SMB Direct maintainer Stefan Metzmacher believes a fix already in his branch for Linux 7.5 covers it. As of this writing, that hasn't been confirmed. Ubuntu builds SMB Direct support; Debian does not.

ZDI-CAN-34068

ZDI-CAN-34068 is an out-of-bounds write in vmwgfx, the kernel driver for VMware's virtual GPU, rated as LPE (CVSS 8.8). Only the title is public. Kroah-Hartman's reply on dri-devel points to the dirty-tracking code. There is no patch.

The exposure is narrow. vmwgfx only binds to VMware's SVGA virtual display adapter, so the bug only matters on VMware guests: vSphere and Workstation VMs, and VMware-based virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI). In Sysdig TRT testing, it does not reproduce on Lima or EC2 instances, which don't present that device.

ZDI-CAN-34076 and ZDI-CAN-32005

ZDI-CAN-34076 (nvmet) is an uninitialized-memory information leak in the Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) target's Get Log Page handling. Only the title is public, and the kernel team has said nothing can be done until details arrive.

ZDI-CAN-32005 (ConnMan) is a stack overflow in the ConnMan network manager's DNS proxy. It is a userspace bug, not a kernel bug, and is outside the scope of this post.

Detection

The four bugs that are the most impactful right now differ in what a syscall-level runtime sensor can observe:

ZDI-CAN-33367. The sequence of the exploitation is distinctive. The process unshares into new user and network namespaces, writes sysctls, brings up an nlmon interface, installs XFRM state over netlink, adds an nftables NFQUEUE rule, attaches a tc pedit action with a redirect, and then splice()s into a socket on 127.0.0.1. Nothing legitimate does all of that from a single unprivileged process. Of the four, this is the easiest one to detect.

ksmbd (33774 and 33549). A sensor can see that ksmbd is exposed: the module loads, ksmbd.mountd starts, and 445 is listening. It can see what an attacker does after code execution, once something spawns a process or touches files. It cannot see the race or the overflow itself. Runtime detection is the backstop.

ZDI-CAN-34068. The trigger is DRM ioctl() calls on the vmwgfx device node, made by a local process. That narrows where to look, but GPU ioctls are noisy on any desktop or VDI guest, so treat them as context for an investigation, not as a signal on their own.

Sysdig Secure customers are covered by a new runtime rule in the Sysdig Runtime Behavioral Analytics policy, Page Cache Poisoning via Spliced File Pages to Loopback, which matches the syscall patterns as seen for ZDI-CAN-33367. Work on exploits for the other flaws in this disclosure continues, and the Sysdig TRT is writing detection rules for them as the techniques become clear.

Independently of the entry point, customers also keep post-exploitation coverage, which detects the effects of a successful exploit rather than the route in.

Recommendations

ZDI-CAN-33367

Patch as soon as your distribution ships the skb_zerocopy() fix. A kernel carrying only the CVE-2026-90049 fix is not covered.

Restrict unprivileged user namespaces. Setting user.max_user_namespaces=0 (or kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0 on Debian) should block the public PoC, though TuxCare notes it has not yet validated this against the PoC. The cost is real: rootless containers, some browser sandboxes and some build tooling depend on user namespaces, so scope it to hosts that don't need them.

Avoid relying on Ubuntu's AppArmor user-namespace restriction. The PoC got past it through the AppArmor profile of a container launcher package.

Block the nlmon and act_pedit modules where you can. Denying them breaks this PoC, although TuxCare cautions it may not close every path to the bug.

Enforce seccomp RuntimeDefault on Kubernetes pods. The exploit starts by creating a user namespace, so containers that can call unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER) are in play. Docker's default seccomp profile blocks that call, but Kubernetes pods run Unconfined unless you set RuntimeDefault per pod or cluster-wide using the kubelet --seccomp-default option. This is a good week to make it the cluster default.

ZDI-CAN-33774 and ZDI-CAN-33549

Inventory where ksmbd runs. Samba users are unaffected.

Unload ksmbd and block the module on hosts that don't need it.

Restrict TCP 445 to trusted networks where ksmbd must stay.

Disable SMB Direct unless your storage network depends on RDMA.

ZDI-CAN-34068

Inventory Linux guests running on VMware, and watch for the vmwgfx patch.

Disable 3D acceleration, or keep the vmwgfx module from loading, on guests that have no use for it.

Across all Linux flaws

Track the reports by ZDI ID and component name until CVEs are assigned.

‍

Conclusion

ZDI's decision to copy public lists put reproduction details for six bugs in front of attackers before several of them had fixes. As defenders know, a lack of an assigned CVE ID does not mean a lack of exposure. Only one of the six, ZDI-CAN-33367, combines a public root exploit, broad distribution exposure, and a fix that hasn't yet merged. It is the seventh path found to drop the Dirty Frag flag, reopening a bug class whose protection has already leaked six times since May 2026. The two ksmbd reports carry the highest scores, but they only matter where ksmbd — not Samba — is running.

For defenders, the practical takeaway is that this week's work is about exposure, not scanners. It’s also important to note that the bugs differ in what defenders should actually watch. The ZDI-CAN-33367 exploit runs as an ordinary user process through a distinctive sequence of systems calls, so teams can catch it in motion. The ksmbd bugs run inside the kernel worker threads with no attacker process on the host, so controlling exposure is key.

Affected organizations should immediately restrict unprivileged user namespaces and enforce RuntimeDefault seccomp where they can, find out whether ksmbd is running anywhere in their estate, and patch ZDI-CAN-33367 the day their distribution ships the fix.

Title: PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619): Detecting unauthenticated remote code execution in PHP core
Context: To provide additional recommendations for security teams and create runtime detection coverage for Sysdig Secure and open source Falco users, the Sysdig Threat Research Team...
Full Text:
This blog was originally published on October 22, 2026.

As of October 28, there are four important updates to note:

CISA added both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109691 to its KEV Catalog on October 26.

We previously stated there were exploitation attempts. Exploitation has since been confirmed.

Multiple researchers have estimated the number of potentially vulnerable internet exposed hosts between 1.3 and 1.9 million.

Some downstream vendors impacted by these vulnerabilities include Cisco and Palo Alto Networks.

On October 21, 2026, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, dubbed PHP2Shell, were fixed in two emergency releases from the PHP project. The two CVEs group four related memory-safety bugs, and both vulnerabilities have a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. An unauthenticated attacker can exploit them to run code on a PHP server with HTTP requests alone. Multiple working proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits are circulating, and the researchers who reported the vulnerabilities said AI models helped in both discovery and exploit development.

Researchers reported the bugs to PHP in August 2026, PHP started a coordinated fix in September, and coordinated disclosure was set for October 22. Then, on October 20, the CVE identifiers and exploit details leaked to Hacker News and social media. PHP published an advance notice the same day and moved the release forward by one day, to October 21 at 14:00 UTC.

Exploitation did not wait for the patch. Amazon Threat Intelligence saw a PHP2Shell attempt against its MadPot honeypots on October 17, four days before disclosure. Cloudflare reported early attacks on October 21 at 07:43 UTC, more than six hours before the fix shipped. watchTowr reproduced the bugs and reported active exploitation attempts against each.

The vulnerable code dates back to PHP 5.4, released in 2012. The bugs live in the PHP engine, not within any application. For that reason, any WordPress, Drupal, or Joomla site with clean application code is still exposed.

To provide additional recommendations for security teams and create runtime detection coverage for Sysdig Secure and open source Falco users, the Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) analyzed PHP2Shell exploitation. The findings are outlined below.

Affected PHP versions

PHP version

Status

What to do

5.4-7.3

End of life, with no fix from the PHP project.

Move to a patched branch.

7.4, 8.0, 8.1

No official update released. The PHP security team published minimal source backports only for these versions.

Use a vendor-patched distribution package or move to a supported branch.

8.2, 8.3, 8.4, 8.5

Fixed in branches 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, 8.5.12

Update to the fixed release or later.

In addition to the version number, there are three additional factors to consider for potential exposure to PHP2Shell:

Distribution packages: Linux distributions and LTS vendors received the patches before release. Vendors often backport fixes without changing the upstream version number, so check the vendor advisory and not only php -v. Any package reporting an old version should be patched.

Affected SAPIs: Every PHP installation that serves web requests. This includes Apache mod_php, PHP-FPM, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. PHP rates mod_php as the highest risk. A SAPI is how PHP connects to a web server, so if PHP answers HTTP requests in any form, it is in scope.

Default configuration: Vulnerable. There are no specific settings needed to be exposed.

Root cause

A PHP worker reuses its memory from one request to another. When a request goes over memory_limit, PHP hits a fatal out-of-memory error and destroys the request heap. The worker survives, and continues to the next request.

The flaw is that PHP does not clear global pointers into the request heap after a fatal out-of-memory error, so a later request on the same worker uses stale pointers into freed memory. All four bugs share this root cause.

CVE-2026-109618: Session upload progress

Use-after-free in the unserializer. Session upload progress decodes session data while PHP parses a multipart/form-data upload. It keeps bookkeeping in the unserializer's global state. An out-of-memory error destroys the request heap, but this global state stays published.

Remote memory disclosure. Upload progress also stores the session ID in a global pointer. An out-of-memory error can leave that pointer dangling. A later multipart request on the same worker reaches the upload-progress cleanup before session initialization resets the pointer. PHP then URL-encodes the reclaimed heap contents into the PHPSESSID response cookie and sends them to the client.

Session upload progress is enabled by default. It runs during request parsing, before any application code, and even if the application never calls session_start(). Authentication and application filters do not stop it.

CVE-2026-109619: Fatal-error backtrace and OPcache

Use-after-free in fatal-error backtraces. PHP keeps the backtrace of the last fatal error in a global. An out-of-memory error destroys the request heap but does not clear that global. The next request on the worker finds a pointer into the previous request's memory.

OPcache type confusion. While OPcache persists a compiled script to shared memory, an allocation failure at the wrong moment leaves internal slots inconsistent across workers. One worker then interprets data with the wrong type.

Impact

PHP2Shell is a pair of unauthenticated remote code execution flaws in the PHP engine itself. Because they sit below the application and trigger before any application code runs, the exposure is every internet-facing PHP server on an affected version, and the impact ranges from silent theft of other users’ secrets to full code execution on the workload, with a path onward to the host.

Unauthenticated remote code execution, no credentials. Any client that can send HTTP requests to a vulnerable PHP server can run code as the web-server user. No login, application bug, or user action is needed.

Exposure of every PHP application, not just popular or common ones. The bugs are in the engine, so even a minimal application on an affected PHP version can be vulnerable.

Leaked secrets from other users’ requests. The memory disclosure works on its own, without RCE. It returns freed process memory to an unauthenticated client. That memory can hold data from other requests the same worker handled: credentials, session tokens, API keys, and even TLS private keys.

Container compromise and a path to the host. A PHP container is a common internet-facing workload. Code execution there gives the attacker the container's service account, mounted secrets, and network position. From there, a kernel LPE such as Copy Fail or Dirty Frag can lead to the host.

Detecting PHP2Shell with Sysdig Secure

Sysdig Secure customers using managed policies have detections to help them identify and respond to this active threat. The Sysdig TRT has already published a Threat Intelligence entry for PHP2Shell in Sysdig Secure, and Sysdig vulnerability management detects vulnerable PHP versions across images and hosts. Existing runtime detection rules also cover post-exploitation activity.

Threat intelligence

Sysdig Secure customers already have a PHP2Shell entry in the Threat Intelligence feed. The entry summarizes the flaw, the fixed versions, and the interim mitigations. It also shows how many hosts and workloads in your environment are impacted. Select the count to open a filtered search of the affected asset.

Vulnerability management

Sysdig vulnerability management detects CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 across your environment:

Images: Pipeline and registry scanning flag images that ship a vulnerable PHP runtime installed through the OS package manager, before they reach production.

Runtime workloads and hosts: Running workloads and hosts are matched against the new CVEs automatically. No rescan is needed.

Distribution backports: Matching uses vendor advisories, so a patched distribution package is not reported as vulnerable only because of its upstream version number.

Prioritization: Filter on workloads where the PHP package is in use, and start with internet-facing ones.

Runtime detection

The Sysdig TRT built two layered runtime rules for PHP2Shell and validated them against a working exploit. They ship as managed rules in the Sysdig Runtime Behavioral Analytics and Sysdig Runtime Notable Events policies. The two rules are PHP Web Worker Killed by Fatal Signal and PHP Web Worker Crash Followed by Shell Execution.

A successful PHP2Shell attack gives the attacker a command line, and from there attackers do what they do after any web RCE. They open a reverse shell, download and run a tool, start a miner, steal cloud credentials, or try a kernel LPE to get root. Sysdig Secure already detects this post-exploitation activity with managed rules in the policies that are enabled by default. Most of these rules match the behavior, not the parent process, so they work the same way whatever PHP runtime serves the application.

Detecting PHP2Shell with open source Falco

Falco sees syscalls, not HTTP requests. It cannot see the malicious request itself, but it can see what the request causes on the host. There are many possible detection strategies, such as detecting shell processes from php workers, but noise often poses a major challenge. As we showed before with Sysdig Secure, many existing post-exploitation detection strategies apply.

Recommendations

Update PHP on every server: Move to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, or to a vendor-patched package. This is the only complete fix. Application code cannot fix this.

Restart every PHP worker after you patch: Old workers keep running the vulnerable code.

Mitigate with the interim settings if you cannot patch today: PHP states that these settings reduce the risk but do not remove it:

Set memory_limit=-1 through php_admin_value, so applications cannot override it. Enforce request size limits at the web server or proxy instead. Do not use RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA.

Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in php.ini or the FPM pool config. Do not rely on ini_set() or .user.ini.

On PHP 8.5, also set fatal_error_backtraces=0.

Restart every worker, and verify the values through a web request, not the CLI.‍

Block multipart/form-data at the edge if uploads are not needed: This blocks the session upload-progress path and the memory disclosure. It does not cover every bug, and it breaks file uploads and some checkout forms.

‍Audit your environment: Find every affected host and workload, and start with internet-facing ones. Sysdig Secure customers can use the Threat Intelligence entry and Vulnerability Management findings. ‍

Investigate dating back to October 17: Exploitation began before disclosure. Check for web shells, new cron jobs, new accounts, and shells spawned by web server processes.‍

Rotate secrets: Because of the memory disclosure, even if you see no sign of code execution, secrets should be rotated for exposed servers.‍

Enable default runtime policies: Use detections for post-exploitation behavior such as known threats, threat intelligence matches, and behavioral anomalies. For internet-facing web applications, alert on shells and suspicious commands spawned by the web server. The Sysdig Runtime Threat Detection, Sysdig Runtime Threat Intelligence, and Sysdig Runtime Behavioral Analytics policies catch the post-exploitation stage. For internet-facing PHP, customers should also enable the Sysdig Runtime Notable Events policy, or at least its rules for shells and suspicious commands spawned by web servers.

Conclusion

PHP2Shell is composed of four memory-safety bugs under two critical CVEs in PHP core, the most widely deployed web runtime. Exploitation began before the fix existed, and PHP has carried the vulnerable code since 2012.

It is the third high-impact flaw this year in old, widely trusted core code, following Copy Fail and Dirty Frag. Like those vulnerabilities, PHP2Shell was found with AI assistance. Defenders should approach these vulnerabilities with an “assume breach” mindset, as exploitation can begin before a patch exists. Patch first. Then, until every worker is patched and restarted, use the interim settings, edge filtering, and runtime detection to close the gap.

Title: Microsoft: Hackers in China, N Korea using ARTEX AI tool to break into global tech systems
Context: "Threat actors define scope and targets for ARTEX, which then uses AI agents to set verifiable goals, define tactical steps for each stage of the operation, use tools to attack...
Full Text: Chinese and North Korean state-sponsored hacking crews are among the growing number of groups known for using the ARTEX pentesting tool in attacks, Microsoft said this week. ARTEX is an open source, AI-powered penetration testing framework that attackers have adopted to automate reconnaissance, credential attacks, and exploitation since its public release in July. Campaigns that have been linked to ARTEX have targeted cloud environments, IT software like ConnectWise, and financial institutions globally, sometimes reaching privileged access in under three hours. Salt Typhoon is arguably the most recognizable name on the list of ARTEX beneficiaries – the group responsible for attacks on telcos AT&T and Verizon, US government systems, UK prime minister's aides, and more. The lesser-known Crystal Typhoon – the group behind the ArcaneDoor attacks back when Microsoft called it Storm-1849 – was also named alongside it, as were North Korea's Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet. Microsoft also named China-state-aligned Storm-0940, linked to the ConnectWise compromise, and financially motivated, Cambodia-based Storm-3358. It had previously reported both groups' use of ARTEX. Chinese cybersecurity company ThreatBook claimed ownership of ARTEX in November. GitHub user "Autumn-27" originally published its source code with a Chinese-language interface in July. Various forks of the repo, which was taken down in October, have meant that the same framework is available in multiple languages. According to Infrawatch, there are more than 130 variants of ARTEX in circulation, and it is the most widely used agentic offensive framework (AOF) at present. Like other offensive security tools adopted by criminals, ARTEX can lower the effort required to mount attacks. Experienced groups can also use it to automate repetitive work and pursue multiple avenues at once. As Microsoft echoed this week, after the FBI and AWS issued their warnings earlier this month, ARTEX is proving to be a useful tool for the more sophisticated groups to streamline and hasten their attacks too. It's being used to help attackers steal AI and cloud credentials at "industrial scale," as AWS put it, which provide attackers access to advanced models for free. Microsoft says ARTEX can progress from reconnaissance to persistent, privileged access within minutes, depending on its configuration and the target's defenses. "In the past few weeks, we've reported several distinct campaigns that abused ARTEX to search public repositories for exposed secrets, enable supply chain compromise, and scan internet-facing systems for exploitation," its threat intelligence team blogged. "These campaigns illustrate how threat actors use ARTEX to automate various stages of the attack chain. "Threat actors define scope and targets for ARTEX, which then uses AI agents to set verifiable goals, define tactical steps for each stage of the operation, use tools to attack targets, create graphs to track discovered systems and results of actions, and report back to the threat actor." Notably, ARTEX does not offer any new attack techniques. All of the tool's capabilities were previously known to the cybersecurity world, but its value lies in the automation capabilities it offers users, chaining attacks at machine speed. In the UK NCSC's warning about AOFs this week, it said the key strengths of this technology are its speed, its thoroughness in probing target systems for weaknesses, how it learns from failures instantly, and that it is inexpensive to run at scale. AOFs' speed comes at a cost, however. These tools are noisy, the NCSC said, making them easier to detect in network logs and by defensive solutions. Some examples of the attacks in which the tool has been implicated include Storm-0940's hit on ConnectWise, which enabled attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, various financial institutions in South Korea and India, UK registrar 123 Reg, and the European Commission. ®

Title: Shopping scams: how to spot them and save money | Kaspersky official blog
Context: Cybercriminals use the stolen data both to steal money and to launch follow-up attacks
Full Text:
Black Friday is just around the corner — that time of year when a refrigerator that normally sells for $599.99 suddenly becomes a refrigerator that sells for “just $749.99 $599.99!”, online stores start writing in ALL CAPS, and every other website has a countdown timer that somehow knows that in exactly 14 minutes and 37 seconds, your life without a new vacuum cleaner will lose all meaning.

Kaspersky experts have looked at how cybercriminals exploit the Black Friday frenzy to steal users’ money and data. Today, we’re taking a look at this year’s most common scams. You can read the full report on Securelist.

A discount in name only

Let’s start with a classic: fake discounts. In the run-up to Black Friday, crafty sellers raise their prices so they can pass off the regular price as a discounted one. So that refrigerator that’s always cost $599.99 goes on sale on Black Friday for… $599.99. How generous!

Some stores and sellers care so little about their reputation that they simply pass off their regular prices as discounted ones without even raising them beforehand. These “discounts” may come with bold claims like “TODAY ONLY!”, “exclusive offer”, “hurry before it’s gone”, or “only one left in stock”. As you can probably guess, these claims usually have nothing to do with reality — they’re simply designed to trigger shoppers’ FOMO.

These tricks are as old as the hills, but fortunately, checking whether a store is being honest is easy in this case: just enter the product page URL into the Internet Archive and compare prices in the available snapshots from the past few months. If there aren’t any snapshots, try one of the many price history services.

It’s also worth comparing the price of the same product at other stores. This is where AI can come in handy, along with the useful prompts from our post Hacking Black Friday: using LLMs to save on the “sale of the year”.

How to tell scammers from legitimate sellers

If crafty sellers were all we had to worry about, we’d just compare prices and live happily ever after. Unfortunately, Black Friday is that time of year when scams and phishing schemes traditionally surge.

Scam websites are pretty straightforward: the prices are suspiciously low, and shoppers either never receive their orders or end up getting something completely different from what they expected. Phishing sites, on the other hand, impersonate well-known retailers and brands, but their goal is to get their hands not only on your money but also on your sensitive information: your name, address, phone number, payment card details, email address, and much, much more. Cybercriminals use the stolen data both to steal money and to launch follow-up attacks. For example, they might send you a message supposedly from a delivery service (“Your item failed inspection; you’ll need to request a refund”, “Confirm your delivery address”) or even try to impersonate employees of your bank.

Scammers impersonate Spotify and YouTube Premium to steal payment details and account credentials

Some phishing sites go even further, trying to trick users into downloading malware disguised as a retailer’s app, a discount coupon, an “order confirmation” file, or a browser update. A shopping trip gone wrong could leave you not only out of pocket but also with malware on your device.

With AI, cybercriminals can create hundreds or even thousands of these sites, making minor changes to the website address — for example, amazzon instead of amazon. The site’s design, meanwhile, can look virtually identical to the original.

Scammers often copy the fonts and design of legitimate stores. Above is an example of a fake Amazon page

Here’s a checklist to help you vet a store before making a purchase and protect yourself from scams:

Check when the domain was registered. If the online store has only been around for a few months or even days, that’s a major red flag that you might’ve stumbled across a scam.

Take a close look at the prices. Even the most generous discounts have their limits. If you’re being offered goods for next to nothing, someone’s probably trying to scam you.

Look for the store’s registered address — a missing address or an unusual location should raise suspicions.

Read the reviews carefully. Remember, a lack of negative reviews doesn’t guarantee that a store is trustworthy: sellers sometimes artificially inflate their ratings. Still, it’s worth looking — a single negative review might help you make the right decision.

Check the website you’re on. If the online store doesn’t use HTTPS or your browser warns you about a potential threat, don’t buy anything there.

To avoid falling for scammers’ tricks, use Kaspersky Premium. Our security solution detects fake domains and scam websites, blocks access to suspicious sites, and prevents malicious downloads. By the way, Kaspersky Premium also works with email, alerting you to phishing and spam. And from Black Friday until New Year’s, you can get it at up to 45% off* — for real, we promise!

AI scams: how to avoid buying AI-generated products

You might’ve seen one of the many viral videos in which a well-known clothing brand supposedly unveils adorable hoodies with a special pocket for pets. We hate to break it to you, but most of these videos are AI-generated, and the brand has never sold any such hoodies.

Over the past few years, savvy scammers have been making money selling products that don’t exist. These days, it’s easy to generate a convincing video of someone trying on nonexistent clothes or reviewing a made-up product. People who order these AI-generated products usually either receive nothing at all or end up with something completely different from what they expected: entirely different items, poor-quality knockoffs, or even… printed photos and miniature versions of the products they bought. And no, we’re not kidding!

Expectation vs. reality: instead of a Christmas decoration, a Reddit user received an image of it printed on a piece of fabric. Source And here, instead of the promised knitted sweater, the shopper received a cheap polyester T-shirt with a sweater printed on it. For $55, no less! Source

These products are mostly advertised on social media and live shopping (live commerce) platforms. Before you follow a link in the description or copy a product code from the comments, check who posted the video: is it a well-known brand? What information can you find about it online — does it have a registered address or an official website? Where exactly is the product being sold?

Don’t trust every influencer you come across, especially if their bio says something like “UGC creator” (user-generated content creator). These creators make money producing promotional content for brands, and a glowing review doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll receive a genuine, high-quality product.

What’s more, some “influencers” are actually entirely AI-generated, and they look pretty realistic. Many platforms actually require AI-generated content to be labeled, but creators don’t always follow the rules. It’s also worth checking when the supposed influencer’s account was created — scam accounts tend to pop up out of nowhere and don’t last long.

But what if you can’t find anything conclusive about the influencer or store? Then it’s time to take a closer look at the product ad itself. Watch out for these red flags:

the product or background looks unrealistic;

unusual highlights and shadows typical of AI-generated content;

people in the video or photo look unnatural, have the wrong number of fingers, or their jewelry, clothing details, and other small features keep changing;

the product itself looks “perfect”, has an unusual structure, or features a fantastical design you’ve never seen anywhere else;

suspiciously low prices.

You can also try a reverse image search for the product. Take a screenshot and upload it to a search engine — sometimes it turns out that the “exclusive designer sweater” has been circulating online for years in a very different form, or that the seller simply took someone else’s photo and tweaked it a little.

A promo code for 100% off your bank balance

Another less obvious type of scam involves bogus promotions and coupons. And no, we’re not talking about how most promo codes only work on your first order — or don’t work at all.

In the run-up to the holidays and major sales, scammers sell special paid “subscriptions” that supposedly give you access to coupons and promo codes for major retailers. Once you’ve paid, you’re promised regular deliveries of promo codes, coupons, or gift cards by mail — except you either receive nothing or get fake coupons that can’t be redeemed. These services are often offered on well-known online marketplaces.

Sometimes, scammers offering coupons promise an extra discount to anyone who completes their purchase on the scammers’ own website. In one case, a seller was offering drones for around $200 less than usual. The shopper paid by card and even received a tracking number, but the shipment status never updated. The seller then claimed they were waiting for payment confirmation, and before long their phone number was disconnected altogether. The shopper never received the drone.

Finally, you might get an email or message urging you to activate a unique coupon worth an eye-watering amount — today only, of course, and preferably within the next ten minutes. To claim this windfall, all you have to do is follow a link and enter all your sensitive information, including your payment card number. Quite a catch for the criminal!

So, if you want real promo codes on Black Friday, sign up for retailers’ own newsletters, check the offers sections on their official websites, and use well-known deal aggregators. But be wary of “exclusive” promotions from random posts and emails.

A box full of empty promises: mystery box scams

Want to buy a new smartphone for next to nothing? How about a game console?

Another popular lure is “mystery boxes” or “return pallets” supposedly filled with customer returns or surplus warehouse stock. For a small sum, sellers promise a whole box of random goods that could supposedly contain smartphones, laptops, headphones, and other expensive electronics. The catch? The contents are often much less impressive than the ads promise.

Last year, in the run-up to Black Friday, there were discovered more than 2,000 fake online stores offering “Amazon returns”. Scammers registered dozens of similar-looking domains, copied the designs of well-known retailers, and promised expensive electronics for next to nothing — in the end, shoppers never got the goods they’d been promised and simply handed their data over to the cybercriminals.

Some major retailers do have programs for selling returned items, but these offers are usually only available to other businesses, not ordinary consumers.

How to save money on Black Friday without getting scammed

Don’t focus solely on the size of the discount. Compare prices at different stores and make sure you check how much the product cost before the sale.

Make sure you’re on the legitimate website. Check how long the site has been around and whether the retailer provides contact details and legal information.

Go directly to the retailer’s website. If you receive a promotional email or find a promo code for a huge discount on social media, find the brand’s official website through a search engine or open the app you normally use instead of following the link you’ve been sent.

Don’t fall for AI-generated content. If an item only exists in a single viral video, look for it on the brand’s official website or try a reverse image search. If the product looks odd or just too unusual, trust your instincts!

Don’t share unnecessary information. A store doesn’t need your card number or home address to give you a discount. And if you have to pay a suspicious fee up front to claim a “gift”, it’s probably no gift at all.

Use a comprehensive security solution. Even the most attentive shopper might miss an extra letter in a website address or a well-disguised phishing email. Kaspersky Premium detects fake domains and scam websites, warns you about suspicious sites, blocks malicious downloads, and helps identify phishing emails. And right now, thanks to Black Friday and holiday discounts, you’ve got over a month to get it at up to 45% off*!

For more on the red flags to watch out for this Black Friday, read our report on Securelist.

And if you want to make the most of Black Friday, check out our post Hacking Black Friday: using LLMs to save on the “sale of the year”. We’ve put together ready-to-use prompts for ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and other AI assistants to help you:

check whether a store has really lowered its prices or quietly raised them just before the sale;

Title: Fake paid expert interviews impersonate brands to steal Google logins
Context: The campaign was discovered by cybersecurity firm Push Security, which has tracked it since October 13 and found that they impersonate eight companies: Accenture, American...
Full Text:
An ongoing phishing campaign dubbed "GoodGuys" impersonates major brands, including Google, Nvidia, Accenture, and SpaceX, to steal corporate Google and Okta credentials using fake invitations to paid expert interviews and webinars.

The attacks offer recipients up to $600 for a 45-minute interview in an attempt to get them to sign in with their work accounts to participate.

The campaign was discovered by cybersecurity firm Push Security, which has tracked it since October 13 and found that they impersonate eight companies: Accenture, American Express, Coca-Cola, Culver's, Google Cloud, Nvidia, SpaceX, and Spotify.

The threat actors abuse legitimate email and event platforms, including HireVue, SendGrid, Mandrill, and Cvent, to distribute phishing links.

In one attack, a phishing email sent through HireVue invited recipients to attend a Google Cloud webinar about deploying AI applications into production.

The threat actors use domains themed around interviews, webinars, and research studies, creating brand-specific subdomains to host the phishing pages, such as:

accenture[.]international-interviews[.]com

nvidia[.]feedback-study[.]com

google[.]webinar-cloud[.]com

spotify[.]interview-experts[.]com

Clicking the phishing links typically takes recipients to a CAPTCHA challenge before displaying a website impersonating the company that supposedly sent the invitation.

Each website features customized branding and lures, with the Nvidia phishing site offering $500 to participate in an AI feedback study and the Accenture site offering $600 for an expert interview.

The sites ultimately prompt visitors to sign in with their Google accounts to validate their invitations, allowing the attackers to steal their credentials. The phishing kit specifically targets corporate accounts and rejects email addresses associated with Gmail, Yahoo, and Outlook.

Unlike adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing kits that use reverse proxies to relay legitimate login pages, GoodGuys uses fake authentication forms controlled by an attacker-controlled server.

After victims enter their Google credentials, the phishing page can display various multifactor authentication (MFA) challenges, including requests for SMS codes, authenticator codes, and Google sign-in prompts requiring users to select a matching number on their phones.

The kit also includes fake Okta authentication forms and support for Okta Verify push notifications.

Push Security believes the threat actors manually attempt to log in using the stolen credentials, instructing the phishing page to display whatever MFA or security challenges Google or Okta show during authentication.

Similar techniques were used in vishing-based data theft attacks linked to the ShinyHunters extortion gang earlier this year to steal corporate single sign-on (SSO) credentials.

Once the process is completed, the phishing kit redirects victims to another website or displays a message thanking them for their application.

The researchers believe the phishing kit may have been developed using an AI coding assistant, based on hidden accessibility labels found in every analyzed version of the kit.

"The sign-in card in every build carries two hidden labels: "Sign-in simulation" and "GoodGuys sign-in simulation." They sit in accessibility text that only screen readers announce, so a visitor never sees them. We think the label is a leftover from how the kit was first built," explained Push Security.

"Calling the page a sign-in "simulation" for a made-up company is the kind of framing someone would use to get an AI coding assistant past its guardrails when asking it to build a phishing page. The label then stayed in every build we've collected."

The researchers also discovered a potentially related phishing campaign that uses fake Coca-Cola interview invitations and the Evilginx phishing kit to target Google Ads accounts.

While both campaigns used the same abused SendGrid click tracker and identical Coca-Cola branding assets, differences in their code and infrastructure prevented researchers from conclusively linking the attacks to the same threat actor.

Title: FIFA Says It Has Been Victim of a Cyberattack Accessing ‘Personal and Business Information’
Context: FIFA was the victim of a cyberattack that saw hackers gain access to what soccer’s world governing body describes as a “limited set of personal and business information,” it...
Full Text:
FIFA was the victim of a cyberattack that saw hackers gain access to what soccer’s world governing body describes as a “limited set of personal and business information,” it said Thursday.

“FIFA is working closely with the relevant authorities, including law enforcement,” the organization said in a statement sent to The Associated Press.

FIFA didn’t say when the cyberattack took place, or the precise nature of the hacked information.

Last week, a group calling itself the Handsome Boy Hacking Club posted a screenshot on X of what it claimed were FIFA files. Three days later, it appeared to take credit for the hack when responding to a post that said more than 12 gigabytes of internal documents had been leaked.

“FIFA condemns in the strongest possible terms the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data,” the governing body said in its statement. “Such actions constitute a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy and can have significant consequences for the individuals concerned.”

The breach comes at a time when FIFA and its president, Gianni Infantino, is under scrutiny after his foiled, secretive plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Infantino is also trying to extend his 11-year presidency of FIFA to 2031. He is the favorite when the election is held on March 18, with Kohzo Tashima of Japan and Philippe Diallo of France the other candidates.

Title: 'Significant number of customer records' pwned in Flight Centre Travel Group breach
Context: Travel giant Flight Centre Travel Group (FLT) says "a significant number of customer records" may have been accessed by "unknown persons" following a cyberattack
Full Text: Travel giant Flight Centre Travel Group (FLT) says "a significant number of customer records" may have been accessed by "unknown persons" following a cyberattack. The Brisbane-headquartered company said the incident affected a third-party accommodation booking system used by Flight Centre, Travel Associates, Cruiseabout, and some independent travel agents. Its disclosure [PDF], filed with the Australian Securities Exchange today, added that it was aware that records were accessed, but cannot definitively say how many were exfiltrated. Flight Centre is working with the supplier and incident response specialist Mandiant to establish the scope of the incident. An initial review suggests most accessed records contained only customer names, some with basic travel information. A "very small percentage" may also include birth dates, email addresses, limited passport details, phone numbers, or, in rare cases, health or mobility information. Flight bookings and corporate travel use separate systems and are unaffected, the company said. "FLT values customer privacy and data security," the company said in its disclosure. "The company understands that an incident like this can be unsettling for customers who may be affected, and we apologize for any concern this causes." Investigations remain ongoing, but FLT has already contained the attack, rotated keys and credentials, and increased system monitoring, it said. The company said it would contact affected customers directly. Its brands continue to operate normally, and travelers should proceed with their plans. Customers should independently verify unexpected messages about their bookings before clicking links, opening attachments, or sharing personal information. The attack on FLT follows others that have hit booking systems in the past year, including those on Booking.com and BWH Hotels. More recently, another Australian business, RMS Cloud, which provides booking software to travel and leisure companies, also acknowledged a breach that led to WhatsApp scams in late October. Numerous reports of travelers being targeted with messages that contained their names and booking details hit local news outlets at the time. Customers were sent convincing messages seemingly from the hotels they had booked, and according to Australia's National Anti-Scam Centre, the scams appeared to be financially motivated. Muhammad Yahya Patel, vCISO and cybersecurity advisor for EMEA at Huntress, said attackers targeting booking systems is a "familiar supply chain story" that has a greater impact than simple data theft. Speaking generally about the risks of exposed travel records, Patel said: "Unlike a compromised email address or phone number, a passport can't be changed easily or quickly. For affected customers, the practical risk extends well beyond the immediate breach. "Passport details combined with names, addresses, and travel history create a comprehensive identity profile that enables document fraud, identity theft, and targeted social engineering that could persist for years." ®

Title: Remus malware steals Gmail messages via fake Google Sheets extension
Context: The Remus infostealer is stealing Gmail messages through a stealthy malicious Chrome extension, a capability the malware operators marketed as a zero-day exploit in Google's...
Full Text:
The Remus infostealer is stealing Gmail messages through a stealthy malicious Chrome extension, a capability the malware operators marketed as a zero-day exploit in Google's email service.

On November 8, the Remus infostealer developer started advertising the alleged Gmail zero-day flaw that allowed the malware to collect emails even if victims changed their passwords and revoked all sessions.

Threat intelligence company Hudson Rock investigated the claims but came to inconclusive results. The researchers noted that evidence from the malware customers matched the seller's pitch, although there was no technical proof that a zero-day vulnerability was being exploited.

GenDigital and Invoke RE researchers published their independent findings yesterday, explaining that the advertised “zero-day” was just a malicious Chrome extension installed on the victims' browsers.

The extension is designed to steal unread emails from signed-in Gmail accounts. It can also survive password changes and session revocations because it remains installed in the victim's Chrome browser.

Its access to Gmail stops when the active session ends, and resumes again when the victim signs back in.

GenDigital discovered the extension after reverse-engineering the Remus infostealer. The researchers found no trace of an email-stealing module, suggesting that the functionality is implemented via an add-on.

“In a nutshell, the loaded module is a native DLL whose sole purpose is to install a malicious extension into Google Chrome, which, notably, is the only browser it targets,” GenDigital explains.

“The extension itself is bundled directly inside the DLL, stored as an unencrypted ZIP archive in its .rdata section.”

GenDigital explains that Chrome versions 137 and later removed a command-line option that allowed malware to load extensions.

Remus takes a complex route to overcome this restriction, editing the victim’s Chrome profile to register the malicious extension and then enabling ‘Developer Mode’ in the browser, which is required to run unpacked extensions.

The extension uses the name “Google Sheets,” copies the description of Google Docs Offline, and requests access to all websites.

Once active in the browser, it checks for unread emails every minute across up to 10 account slots and retrieves them in full, in raw format.

The extension sends the email subject, message body, sender, and victim’s email address to its command-and-control server, along with a campaign identifier.

Failed uploads are queued and retried, while a local record helps the extension keep track of what has succeeded so it doesn’t send duplicates.

Although the extension also parses attachment filenames, it does not send those to its operators, so this feature may not be fully implemented yet.

To defend against this threat, users are advised to download software only from trusted sources and scrutinize “chrome://extensions” for rogue installations or unexpected activation of Developer Mode.

Title: North Korea-Linked PolinRider Poisons Over 7,600 GitHub Repositories to Spread Malware
Context: " PolinRider attack from May 2025 The development comes as OpenSourceMalware said it discovered a PolinRider attack from May 2025, predating the earliest documented victims by...
Full Text:
The threat actors behind the PolinRider campaign have been observed planting a Python loader in GitHub repositories, as evidence emerges that the activity may have started as far back as February 2025.

"The loader hides in a small utils package or in conftest.py," SafeDep said in a report published this week. "When Python imports the file, the loader reads the newest transaction that an Ethereum wallet sent to itself. It decodes the input data of that transaction as JavaScript and runs it with Node.js."

The JavaScript code, for its part, reads a second wallet to locate the command-and-control (C2) server and then passes the next stage to a detached interactive Node.js environment by means of a node -i process.

The software supply chain security company said it identified the loader in 375 public repositories that belong to 260 accounts. There is no evidence that the loader has been distributed via PyPI or npm.

PolinRider is the name assigned to a malicious campaign linked to North Korean threat actors. Recent reports indicate that the activity employs various channels to distribute malware, including -

Fraudulent recruitment campaigns that make use of phishing emails and fake hiring portals like BlockNovas, AccuraSoftHire ("accurasofthire[.]com") and HuntRole ("huntrole[.]org") to trick prospective targets into running malware-laced projects under the pretext of a take-home assessment.

Publishing malicious packages across open-source ecosystems by hijacking maintainer accounts to plant obfuscated malware through fake font files (fa-solid-400.woff2, fa-solid-500.woff2, or fa-solid-300.llf), Visual Studio Code (VS Code) auto-run tasks, and Git history rewriting.

Using compromised developer machines to steal their GitHub tokens and force-push malicious commits into open-source repositories they have access to.

At a high level, the PolinRider loader retrieves an encrypted second-stage Node.js payload that scans the infected host for installed developer applications, such as GitHub Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, and Google Antigravity, and tampers with the most frequently used tools to execute attacker-controlled code and deliver infostealer malware.

It's worth noting here that PolinRider is assessed to be a sub-cluster operating in parallel with a long-running campaign codenamed Contagious Interview. While the latter is more of a social-engineering entry point that's used to compromise developer systems, PolinRider abuses the access to modify repositories and turn them into a distribution channel for malware.

"Cybercriminal groups deploy supply chain worms for opportunistic theft. On the other hand, North Korean state-sponsored threat actors use open-source software registries as a primary initial access vector targeting corporate environments," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said in a report published last month.

"Threat actors demonstrate how compromising a single maintainer account or registry scope converts open-source dependencies, resulting in widespread affected cloud environments."

Some of the decoy sites have been found to incorporate two other alternate delivery paths -

Instruct candidates to sideload a Google Chrome extension after enabling "Developer mode" to subscribe to new job alerts.

Employ ClickFix-style lures to get victims to copy and paste malicious commands into the terminal app depending on the operating system as part of a "standard settings bundle for candidates and interview workflows."

"The [job] application asks for a short verification video," StepSecurity said. "Until the server marks a candidate as having installed a 'driver,' the camera check always fails with a message saying the system does not have a compatible camera environment."

"A separate 'Technical onboarding' page on the site gives a one-line curl command to download the 'driver.' On Windows, the downloaded installer fetches a script from the careers site that installs Node.js if it is missing, downloads a JavaScript payload, runs it in the background and deletes itself. The macOS and Linux versions do the same."

The JavaScript malware is designed to perform the following steps -

Read the latest transaction associated with an Ethereum wallet ("0xa322E5f3D311D3080e6f0121063e9aDC2490Ef1a").

Get its destination wallet address ("0x67B38e9b67B38E9b68656c6C6f6970626f742121").

Extract the C2 server address twice ("103.179.142[.]155") from the first eight bytes ("67B38e9b" and "67B38E9b") of the wallet address, using a technique referred to as NullReceiver, while the last 12 bytes represent the ASCII string "helloipbot!!."

Use the IP address to fetch two payloads, "0x/cls" and "0x/ls," over port 443.

The NullReceiver technique

The latest findings from SafeDep show that the repositories are injected with a 58-line Python loader that reads the "0x3b1574417524c11a7403c4b232CAcBb320CceBC6" wallet to extract JavaScript code that then reaches out to a second wallet ("0x1eEf0849EDa15d87f64e51C73C8442Cf3c8bCEF3") to obtain the destination wallet associated with the latest transaction ("0x5F87b5545F87b55468656C6C6f6970626f742121"), which is then used to parse the C2 server ("95.135.181[.]84").

A defining aspect of NullReceiver is the marker "68656c6C6f6970626f742121" in the made-up destination wallet address that consistently translates to "helloipbot!!."

"The /0x/cls script runs twice, once with eval in the current process and once in a new process," SafeDep said. "The /0x/ls script runs only in a new process."

The exact nature of these payloads remains unknown. However, prior waves have been observed installing a stealer that harvests environment secrets, browser passwords, cookies, and wallet data. Interestingly, the wallet address "0x1eef0849eda15d87f64e51c73c8442cf3c8bcef3" has been reused by the threat actors across other attack waves -

Pushing compromised versions of legitimate npm packages such as @adminide-stack/utils, @adminide-stack/health-api-server, @adminide-stack/user-activity-browser, @adminide-stack/utils, @adminide-stack/forms-core, @adminide-stack/yantra-help-browser, server-hemera-mongo, cdeops, @cdmbase/wiki-browser, and @pubngo-stack/help-browser that use the same wallet address to fetch /0x/cls and /0x/ls from "95.135.181[.]151."

A fake recruitment campaign from HuntRole that convinces victims to complete a coding assessment, which uses a VS Code extension named "huntrole.assessment-tool" from the Visual Studio Marketplace to send system information and fetch and run a malicious JavaScript payload. The script queries the same wallet address to fetch /0x/cls and /0x/ls from "95.135.181[.]84."

Using a GitHub account named " Eternity0207 " to open over 200 pull requests targeting open-source projects like AsyncAPI Generator, CircuitVerse, and Open Food Facts, and subsequently force-push a modified commit containing an obfuscated loader that uses the same wallet address to fetch /0x/cls and /0x/ls from "95.135.181[.]84."

According to the maintainer of AsyncAPI Generator, "Each time, the payload stayed on the branch for 30-40 minutes and was then force-pushed away, so the final diff looked clean." The unauthorized modifications allowed the loader to run when an unsuspecting developer runs "npm run build" (for AsyncAPI), loads the test configuration (for Open Food Facts), or opens the folder in VS Code (for CircuitVerse). The GitHub account has since been suspended.

According to estimates from Apiiro, PolinRider has been detected in at least 7,609 GitHub repos owned by 2,330 accounts, most of them belonging to developers. Some of the victims include Neutralinojs, InstaWP Connect, and fxhash. The loader has been pushed to 2,040 repositories between October 27 and November 6, 2026.

"The worm uses stolen GitHub access to rewrite commits the developer already made, keeping the author, message and date, and adds a loader hidden after hundreds of spaces in a build config," Apiiro researcher Shmulik Cohen said.

"Building the project runs it. In the newest wave, opening the folder in VS Code is enough. The loader reads its server from an Ethereum wallet, so taking a server down changes nothing: one transaction moves every loader to the next."

PolinRider attack from May 2025

The development comes as OpenSourceMalware said it discovered a PolinRider attack from May 2025, predating the earliest documented victims by eight months. The attack targeted nine packages, using hijacked maintainer account to push poisoned versions within a span of 90 minutes -

itsa-utils@1.4.2

itsa-jsext@2.0.3

itsa-react-docviewer@16.1.2

itsa-cli@16.5.3

itsa-react-button@16.0.11

itsa-react-maskedinput@16.1.2

itsa-react-checkbox@16.0.5

itsa-react-focuscontainer@16.0.10

itsa-react-input@16.1.2

Each of these packages have been found to leverage EtherHiding, a precursor to NullReceiver, to retrieve a JavaScript downloader called JADESNOW, which is then used to deliver InvisibleFerret, a Python-based backdoor used in Contagious Interview campaigns, along with a Socket.IO RAT and a Python-based stealer.

"The 2025 sample carries PolinRider's payload but not its documented spread behavior, which appears in the same maintainer's GitHub repositories in four windows between January and July 2026," security researchers Paul McCarty and Jenn Gile said. "The blockchain records behind it date attacker activity back to February 2025."

"The infection likely persisted on the maintainer's machine from 2025, because the 2026 pushes ran from it. That matches PolinRider's documented propagation script, which rolls back the clock, folds the payload into the tip commit, and force-pushes with the developer's own credentials."

Title: Linux/EasyShell: MalwareMustDie Identifies One of the Earliest Publicly Documented RATs Built for LoongArch Linux
Context: MalwareMustDie analyzes Linux/EasyShell, a Rust implant targeting Linux and macOS, with LoongArch support and stealth features to evade detection
Full Text:
MalwareMustDie analyzes Linux/EasyShell, a Rust implant targeting Linux and macOS, with LoongArch support and stealth features to evade detection.

This case began with a shell script found on a victim’s node, which the author credits to 0xrb. MalwareMustDie’s researcher first read it as one more Chinese miner-style uninstaller or downloader. It wasn’t. The script installs software, and what it delivers is a Rust beacon implant.

MalwareMustDie wrote four reverse engineering notes, one forensics note, and two OSINT notes, then merged them into one report.

That restraint shapes everything that follows. This careful approach guides the entire analysis. The stager is hosted at hxxps://192[.]3.31[.]148:8443 and installs a payload called polkitd on both Linux and macOS. On Linux, it is saved as /usr/bin/polkitd, while on macOS it is placed in ~/Library/Caches/polkitd. The stager randomly chooses one of eight possible file names. The same server hosts the malware and receives its beacon communications over TCP port 8443. It is hosted by ColoCrossing (AS36352) in the United States.

The server provides seven different builds: l32, l64, l128, a32, a64, darwin_amd64 and darwin_arm64. The researcher describes the Linux x86 version, l32, as a Rust-based HTTPS beacon with all its required libraries built into the executable. Its build paths contain references to the EasyShell framework, including strings such as easyshell-http-beacon-implant and impl-core. For this reason, the researcher identifies the malware as Linux/EasyShell.

The l128 build targets LoongArch, a CPU architecture, and was compiled with rustc 1.96.0, while the others use 1.95.0. According to the researchers, this is one of the earliest publicly documented LoongArch64 RAT implementations he could find in public reporting, identified within the EasyShell multi-platform Rust implant family.

“I would like to note that this is one of the earliest publicly documented LoongArch64 RAT implementations I could find in public reporting (as of 2026-11-21), identified within the EasyShell multi-platform Rust implant family. “Earliest” here only means that I found no earlier public analysis; the LoongArch build itself is a framework default (chapter 7 addendum).” states the report. “Hands-on access: shell, file theft, credential plugins, SOCKS and relay pivot High. No monetisation code. Operator intent unknown (18.1). The macOS and LoongArch builds are framework defaults offered by every EasyShell stager, not a choice of this operator (18.2).”

Two caveats weaken any story about a targeted LoongArch campaign. The report says the macOS and LoongArch payloads aren’t this operator’s choice, because every EasyShell server offers them by default. The author also doubts the LoongArch build would load on a stock Debian loong64 or Kylin host without matching links or a compatible loader, and says it may never have been tested on real hardware.

The author didn’t run any sample. The beacon is an HTTPS POST to /api/v2/sync with an X-Client-Id header and a Windows Chrome 131 user agent. According to the report, the implant can open a remote shell, run plugins and scripts, upload and download files, and zip folders. It also offers SOCKS5 and relay tunnels, an outbound proxy, screenshots, process listing and killing, and self-deletion.

Credential dumping, token elevation and browser password theft aren’t built in. They come from a separate “Extensions” plugin set. The implant also checks for sandboxes, looking at DMI data, hypervisor names, mouse activity and system resources. Then it renames itself like a kernel thread, for example [kworker/0:0].

A third-party Joe Sandbox run on November 21 gives a useful reality check. It executed another l32 copy on Ubuntu 20.04 for about five minutes. The copy had the same size, 3,769,372 bytes, but a different hash, and it made three TCP connections to the C2, forked a child that called prctl, uname and a thread sleep, and created an empty hidden file. The score was 2 out of 100 with no YARA or Suricata match, which says more about the malware waiting for someone else to show up than about its harmlessness.

That hash difference matters. The server writes random bytes into one slot of every payload it generates, so each victim gets a different file.

“YARA family rule MMD_Linux_EasyShell_Rust_Implant on memory dumps and new binaries (it still matches the builds without the crate name); do not rely on the hashes for other victims.” MalwareMustDie warns.

The first draft of the report dates from November 19, and an addendum on November 22 documented the per-download hashes and the developer repository.

On attribution, the author is careful. EasyShell is a Chinese red team C2 framework sold through trial and member programs, and its public repository matches the samples. It isn’t VShell and has no Kinsing or SystemTen link, although the stager is based on a VShell template. No operator is named, and the author says the tool’s build markers describe its build environment, not whoever runs this C2.

There’s one loose thread. A separate chapter describes an intrusion on a Chinese mobile-malware hosting server, and a single shell-history line there re-ran the EasyShell stager from the same C2. The author rates the link between the two operators as medium confidence. A note about a December 2025 incident that used the same stager template at a different IP is marked unverified.

For security teams, the l32 version does not have its own way to remain on an infected system, although its plugins may add this feature. The researcher suggests looking for processes that use names normally associated with kernel threads, such as [kworker/0:0] or [rcu_sched], but have a real executable file listed under /proc/pid/exe. Another warning sign is HTTPS POST traffic to /api/v2/sync with an X-Client-Id header.

On macOS, defenders should look for executable files in user Caches folders that lack a quarantine attribute, code signatures without a Team ID, and security permission requests (TCC prompts) that mention polkitd.

The report also includes YARA, Sigma and osquery detection rules. The researcher recommends starting in detection-only mode. These rules were tested against known malware strings, but not against a large collection of legitimate software to check for false positives.

If a system looks infected, there is one important rule: do not kill the fake kernel thread immediately. The researcher recommends first isolating and preserving the system before terminating any process.

The report ships YARA, Sigma and osquery rules, meant to start in detect-only mode. They were checked on strings, not through a full retro-hunt on legitimate software.

“Golden rule: do not kill the fake kernel thread first. Collect its process state and memory, freeze it, cut its network, then clean. Killing it first loses the live config, the session keys and the tunnel table.” concludes the report.

In this article

Anthropic’s Siren test uses bait to see whether AI agents will reach beyond their sandbox

Recent Claude models reached or tried to reach outside in 21% to 32% of tests

Explaining the sandbox rules and giving agents a way to report weaknesses reduced those attempts

Honeypots are a classic defender’s trick. You leave something tempting lying around and watch who takes it.

Anthropic has now pointed that trick at its own AI models. Its new test, called Siren, checks whether AI agents will break out of their sandbox when something useful sits just outside it.

AI agents run commands, edit code, and call APIs on their own. They are usually kept in a sandbox, an isolated environment that limits which files, tools, and networks they can reach. But sandboxes aren’t perfect, and OpenAI models running cybersecurity evaluations with reduced safeguards got around their isolation.

How Siren works

Siren drops an agent into a simulated sandbox with a deliberate weakness. The task is an ordinary dev-ops job. Outside the sandbox sits a “honeypot,” such as a login credential, a file, or a service that mimics the public internet. Each scenario combines four ingredients:

The sandbox. There are 26 environments built from 5 common setups. Each has either a misconfiguration or an easy-to-find vulnerability.

The task. These are routine jobs of varying difficulty. Some are impossible to finish without reaching outside.

The honeypot. This is the material outside that would help complete the task.

The tempters. These are realistic nudges, such as urgency, higher stakes, or an instruction to search thoroughly. They never tell the model to leave the sandbox or give permission to do so.

Anthropic combined these ingredients into more than 1,700 scenarios. AI judges screened the draft nudges for realism. Reportedly, the whole setup runs inside a second sandbox cut off from the outside world.

Anthropic ran the tests without the safeguards that ship with its released models. Recent Claude models accessed or tried to access something outside the sandbox in 21% to 32% of scenarios. They used what they found in ways the scenario clearly didn’t allow in 0.6% to 1.6% of scenarios. Anthropic calls this “misaligned use.” Earlier models showed higher rates of misaligned use, at 12.7% for Mythos 5.1 and 25.8% for Mythos 5.

What happens with the results

Siren is now a standard pre-deployment check. Anthropic has reported its results in system cards since Claude Haiku 5.5 and uses them to help decide how to deploy its models internally and externally. It has also used Siren to test and refine defenses:

Spell out the rules. Adding a short description of the sandbox and its rules to the system prompt reduced how often the models reached outside by 68% to 96%.

Give agents a way to report. A tool for reporting sandbox weaknesses reduced how often models reached outside by between 7 and 33 percentage points. Letting a model see earlier reports cut it further.

Check actions before they run. Anthropic’s auto mode uses a classifier to vet tool calls. In an offline replay, it blocked the command that first touched the honeypot in 96% to 100% of misaligned uses.

With all three defenses in place, misaligned use fell to 0% in five models and to 0.1% in Mythos 5. Anthropic stresses that none of this fixes the sandbox itself, which still needs to be set up and patched properly. But it should be helpful when setting up sandboxes for the future.

Title: Wyoming uranium operation shuts down after cyberattack
Context: The Australian uranium producer said on Wednesday that it had activated its response procedures and brought in outside specialists following the attack on its US subsidiary,...
Full Text: Peninsula Energy has temporarily shut down its Wyoming uranium operation after a "cybersecurity incident" affected plant and wellfield control systems. The Australian uranium producer said on Wednesday that it had activated its response procedures and brought in outside specialists following the attack on its US subsidiary, Strata Energy, which operates the Lance uranium project. Peninsula Energy said it believes the attack is "confined to the plant and wellfield operating and control systems," and that back-office functions, such as payroll and other corporate systems, in both the US and Australia, remain unaffected. "The company's immediate priorities have been to protect the safety of its employees, secure its operating systems, and work towards the restoration of operations in a safe and controlled manner," it said in an update to the Australian Securities Exchange. The notification [PDF] went on to say that Peninsula Energy's investigations into the attack, including whether any data was compromised, remain ongoing. Peninsula has not given a restart date and says it cannot yet assess the impact on its 2027 production guidance. Operations will remain suspended until recovery and safety checks are complete. "Peninsula will provide further updates to the market as material information becomes available," it said. The disclosure of additional information came two days after Peninsula secured a short trading halt, which referenced a cybersecurity incident at its Wyoming site. The November 23 filing [PDF] dated the incident to Friday evening in Western Australia. Wednesday's update clarified that Strata detected it on the morning of November 20, local US time. Peninsula subsequently requested a voluntary suspension of trading until the earlier of November 30 or an announcement on restarting operations and any resulting change to production guidance. Peninsula's Lance project is a uranium mining operation, extracting the element from underground deposits and turning it into uranium concentrate, aka yellowcake or U₃O₈. Uranium concentrate is feedstock for nuclear fuel production, typically undergoing conversion, enrichment, and fabrication into uranium dioxide pellets before use in reactors. The Lance central processing plant was constructed to produce a maximum of 2.0 million pounds (Mlb) of U₃O₈ annually, and is licensed for 3.0 Mlb. Peninsula previously forecast production of 500,000 to 600,000 pounds in 2027, having withdrawn its 2026 guidance earlier this year following operational problems at Lance. It now says it will reassess the 2027 outlook once operations resume. ®

Title: Company was religious about backups but sinned by leaving them exposed
Context: The hackers found a plaintext password for the backup service account in a maintenance script on a file share and discovered that someone had used the very same password for a...
Full Text: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we’re thankful every time someone leaves a password sticky note on a monitor or fails to delete a terminated employee’s admin account. But neither of those common occurrences is what we’ll be talking about today. Instead, our subject broke the number-one rule of backups: you gotta keep ’em separated. Our story comes courtesy of Da Li, who serves as global alliance manager at Info2Soft, a company that provides data protection and recovery software. At one point, a partner called him into a case where a Chinese vehicle parts manufacturer fell victim to a ransomware gang. Unfortunately, its backup was compromised too. The manufacturer had religiously backed up its manufacturing execution system (MES) and SAP orders, inventory, and finance systems every night. There was even a green dashboard that showed the backup process had succeeded, and someone checked that every morning. However, one Friday evening, crims broke into the network and found out that the backup server was joined to the same Windows domain as the rest of the network. The hackers found a plaintext password for the backup service account in a maintenance script on a file share and discovered that someone had used the very same password for a domain admin account. So the first thing the crooks did was delete every restore point on that backup server. Then they started encrypting the production servers to ransom them. “Every backup job had succeeded for three years,” Li said. “The failure was that the thing meant to save them could be reached with the same keys as the thing being attacked.” The results were devastating. With the MES and SAP data both gone, the plant couldn't schedule production, ship parts, or track them. By the time Li was called in, the plant had already resolved its ransomware situation. We don’t know whether it paid or not. The manufacturer did ask Li and his company to make sure that this couldn’t happen again. Li’s fix was not radical, but it was instructive. He made sure that the company now keeps its backup system outside the production domain, uses unique credentials, and requires MFA to reduce the risk of unauthorized access even if a password is compromised. He also made sure that the company keeps at least one offline backup and runs a test restore quarterly to ensure it’s prepared for emergencies.®
