Title: Energy Giant Engie Notifies Customers of Supply Chain Breach
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
One of the world’s largest natural gas suppliers has notified an undisclosed number of customers that their personal data may have been compromised in a recent breach.

French multinational Engie employs over 90,000 people across 30 countries, supplying gas, nuclear power, and renewables. Its revenue in 2025 was almost €72bn ($80bn).

According to screenshots of the customer notification posted to X, the compromised data could include: full name, postal and email address, telephone number, unique IDs for energy supply (PCE/PDL), customer ID, and contract number.

The firm confirmed that no banking data was involved in the breach.

Read more on cyber-attacks impacting French firms: French Supermarket Cyber-Attack Impacts More Refrigeration Controllers

Engie urged customers to be on the lookout for potential fraud and phishing stemming from the incident.

“A malicious person could use the information mentioned above to impersonate you or use your personal details to contact another organization in your name, obtain additional information, or attempt to make a payment,” it warned. “Fraudulent emails may appear to come from trusted sources, such as organisations you know, in order to deceive you.”

According to a statement from the firm sent to Infosecurity, its own IT systems weren’t compromised. Engie blamed a third-party marketing platform used by its partners which was then compromised by threat actors.

“Engie recently identified unusual data access activity within a tool used by partners as part of their customer prospecting activities and the marketing of energy offers in France,” it explained.

“As soon as this activity was detected, the relevant access was disabled. At the same time, Engie launched an in-depth technical investigation to understand the circumstances of the incident, accurately assess its scope by identifying customers potentially affected, and ensure that the situation was fully secured. Enhanced monitoring measures were also put in place.”

No Group Has Claimed Responsibility

At the time of writing, no extortion group had admitted responsibility for the breach, which Engie said is now contained.

However, in October last year, extortion group Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters listed the firm on its leak site, after compromising over 100 Salesforce instances and claiming to have extracted more than one billion records.

In that incident, Engie’s US retail energy business Engie Resources was the victim, with the group claiming to have obtained 3GB of data.

According to claims data from insurer Resilience shared with Infosecurity, no UK or European energy and utilities clients have reported ransomware since July 2025.

European claims with a recorded cost involved only fraud or exposed customer data. That contrasts with the US where ransomware comprises around 70% of incurred losses across claims on record in the sector, Resilience said.

Title: LABScon26 Replay | Keynote: A Sober Analysis of AI Impact
Context: He concludes that at present the only good AI research is safety research, which he defines broadly to include economic and emotional security alongside computer security
Full Text:
In his LABScon 26 keynote, delivered in his inimitable comedic style, Harvard University professor James Mickens questions whether the scale of current AI investment is justified. Starting from US tech capex of roughly 1.4% of GDP in the second quarter of 2025, he argues that computers are already good enough, and notes that the world has so many CPUs and GPUs that they are put to work solving cryptocurrency puzzles to make imaginary money. More seriously, the AI models that investment is building, he says, grow increasingly opaque as their parameter counts rise.

Mickens then cites research and incident reports on model behaviour, including models acting to prevent another model being shut down and recent sandbox escapes at OpenAI and other labs. On economics, he rejects the assumptions that AI will create more jobs than it destroys and that universal basic income will follow widespread automation.

He concludes that at present the only good AI research is safety research, which he defines broadly to include economic and emotional security alongside computer security. Mickens own contribution is Guillotine, a hypervisor design that runs a model’s CPU code on isolated cores unable to read or write the hardware state of the cores running the hypervisor. Arguing that hardware-based mechanisms for isolating misaligned frontier models will be an important direction for research over the next five years, he invites those interested in this approach to collaborate.

This keynote speaks to security practitioners and researchers interested in AI risk, the economics behind current AI investment, or hardware-level containment of frontier models

About the Author

James Mickens is a Gordon McKay Professor of Computer Science at Harvard University. His research focuses on the performance, security, and privacy of large-scale online services; a current focus is the interpretability and sandboxing of potentially misaligned frontier models. Prior to becoming a professor at Harvard, Dr. Mickens spent seven years at Microsoft Research, working in the Distributed Systems group.

About LABScon

This presentation was featured live at LABScon 2026, an immersive 3-day conference bringing together the world’s top cybersecurity minds, hosted by SentinelOne’s research arm, SentinelLABS.

Title: Lessons from cybersecurity Black Week
Context: In the highest-risk setups, a demonstrated exploit can trigger the vulnerability before application code runs, meaning application-level authentication offers no protection
Full Text:
The week leading up to October 25, 2026, was every cyber defender’s nightmare: a barrage of critical vulnerabilities in PHP and the Linux kernel, a compromised LiteLLM release, a maximum-severity flaw in GitLab, a Node.js Brotli flaw, and a certificate authority incident affecting TLS trust.

A few years ago, a backlog like this would have filled a defender’s to-do list for a whole month. In the age of AI, all of this was reported within a single “Cybersecurity Black Week,” an exceptionally eventful seven-day period amid an already turbulent Black October. AI-assisted research helped uncover at least two of these flaws: PHP2Shell and the Brotli bug. On top of the breakneck patching pace, security teams faced mounting pressure to deliver status reports to other departments, management, customers, and the media.

Beyond their severity, the issues stood out for the variety of responses they demanded. Some required emergency runtime patches and upgrades; others called for containment, credential rotation, or the replacement of outdated certificate trust bundles. In several cases, installing the latest version was only the beginning of a long remediation process.

With so many problems landing at once, the main challenge was separating real risk from hype and prioritizing accordingly. Here is our assessment.

PHP2Shell: The loudest headline, with real-world limits

PHP2Shell generated the biggest media frenzy of the lot and, with it, a major headache for security teams, prompting many organizations to take their websites offline and look for emergency fixes. The name refers to two memory-safety vulnerabilities in PHP core, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, affecting PHP versions 5.4 through 8.5.11. Both vulnerabilities received a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 and can allow unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) on vulnerable PHP servers. In the highest-risk setups, a demonstrated exploit can trigger the vulnerability before application code runs, meaning application-level authentication offers no protection.

With PHP powering an estimated 69% of websites whose server-side programming language is known, government agencies in the United States, Europe, and elsewhere urged organizations to patch immediately, with some advising that affected internet-facing systems be isolated or taken offline if they could not be patched promptly. Government websites in the Netherlands, Germany, France, and other countries were temporarily taken offline as a precaution. The PHP project released fixes on October 21 in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, along with source-only backports for the end-of-life 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 branches. The rollout was complicated by a premature public leak, which forced the coordinated disclosure timeline forward.

While the flaws clearly belonged near the top of the patching list, early evidence suggested they were considerably harder to weaponize than initially feared. Successful exploitation requires specific conditions and knowledge of the target, and public proof-of-concept exploits did not work against a default PHP installation, according to Sansec.

On October 22, ESET was among nine security companies that told NBC News they had not seen any successful attacks, even though more than 200 proof-of-concept exploits were circulating. The remediation challenge extends beyond obvious web servers: PHP can also be embedded in appliances, network devices, management interfaces, and third-party products, while end-of-life PHP branches do not receive normal upstream binary releases.

Linux kernel: Reports went public before fixes were ready

As if the PHP issues weren’t severe enough, on October 21, Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) sent several reports on unpatched Linux kernel vulnerabilities to the kernel’s private security address while also copying public mailing lists. As a result, technical details of vulnerabilities for which fixes were not yet generally available became public, prompting stable kernel maintainer Greg Kroah-Hartman to question why the reports had been sent to public lists without patches.

The two most severe issues, both rated CVSS 9.0 by ZDI, affect KSMBD, the Linux kernel’s built-in SMB server. ZDI-CAN-33549 is an integer underflow in the SMB Direct path that could lead to RCE, while ZDI-CAN-33774 is a race condition that could also lead to RCE. Exploiting ZDI-CAN-33549 requires an RDMA-capable interface, a writable KSMBD share, and SMB Direct negotiation, significantly narrowing the number of systems exposed to that particular attack. Other reports concerned local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in the networking stack and the VMware graphics driver, as well as an information disclosure issue in the NVMe target code (NVMET).

To remediate, security teams had to track each report independently, consult distribution advisories, and restrict exposed services where practical while awaiting verified fixes. Kernel updates also required rebooting into the patched kernel and checking the running version, not merely confirming that a new package had been installed.

LiteLLM: Compromised, not merely vulnerable

On October 21, attackers published a malicious version of LiteLLM, 1.107.0, to PyPI and pushed compromised images to the project’s official container registries. According to the project’s incident report, its release pipeline was breached using GitHub CLI credentials associated with three developers. One of the stolen tokens belonged to an owner of the project’s GitHub organization, allowing attackers to disable branch protections and modify the release workflow to point to a lookalike repository. LiteLLM, a Python proxy for LLM providers, has about 23 million weekly downloads, and the malicious version remained available on PyPI for roughly two hours before it was quarantined. It was the project’s second supply-chain compromise of 2026, after malicious versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 appeared in March.

The payload combined a credential stealer with a second-stage remote access trojan (RAT). By abusing Python’s startup mechanisms, including a .pth file, it ran every time Python started, even if an application never imported LiteLLM. Execution therefore did not depend on exploiting an application flaw: simply running Python in an affected environment could be enough.

Affected environments had to be treated as potentially compromised, not merely vulnerable. According to LiteLLM, these included environments that ran litellm==1.107.0 and containers that executed affected images distributed under the v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, or main-stable tags during the compromised intervals. Removing or replacing the package was insufficient: teams needed to determine whether the malicious code had run, contain affected systems, rebuild from clean sources, and rotate exposed secrets from a clean environment. Cloud, source-control, and CI/CD logs also had to be reviewed for unauthorized activity.

Node2Shell: From Node.js to HTTP2Shell

Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) is an out-of-bounds write in Google’s Brotli decoder, which Node.js bundles. Malformed compressed input can cause crashes, memory disclosure, or potentially RCE when an application decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data. This can happen through explicit decompression, compressed request bodies, or automatically decompressed responses. Node.js rates the flaw as high severity, while the broader Brotli vulnerability carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. According to Aikido, researchers demonstrated code execution against the official, unmodified Node.js 24.22.0 image on Linux ARM64. Although the exploit did not work on every attempt, the demonstration showed that exploitation was practical, if not universally reliable.

Node.js shipped fixes on October 21 in versions 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1, and Bun followed with version 1.4.4 or later. Node.js 25.x, 23.x, 20.x, and earlier releases are end-of-life and will not receive the fix. Within days, the story outgrew Node.js. The same decoder is compiled into the Python Brotli and brotlicffi packages as well as into other HTTP software, which led researchers to rename the issue HTTP2Shell. The operational challenge was therefore not simply upgrading a single runtime but identifying every container, serverless deployment, and library that bundles the vulnerable decoder. The issue was fixed upstream in Brotli 1.2.1. Notably, OpenAI’s Codex Security had reported the underlying bug, and the fix had been present in the Brotli source since February without being recognized as a security issue.

GitLab: Credential leaks and authorization failures

On October 21, GitLab shipped a critical out-of-band patch release (versions 19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6, 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, and 18.11.13) addressing 12 security vulnerabilities. The headline flaw, CVE-2026-110264, rated 10.0 under CVSS v3.1, is an integer overflow triggered when GitLab compiles a specially crafted regular expression. Under certain conditions, it could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server. The affected versions date back to GitLab 7.0.

The other fixes addressed credential exposure, cache poisoning, authorization bypasses, and failures to enforce membership or merge-request approval policies. Reported unauthenticated attack paths included exposure of sensitive credentials through internal response headers and manipulation of a shared OAuth/OIDC discovery cache, while other issues required authenticated access. GitLab did not publish individual severity scores or exploitability details for these issues.

GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated were already patched, so the work fell on administrators of self-managed instances. GitLab strongly recommended upgrading immediately, but with a catch: the older backport releases (19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, and 18.11.13) included only the critical fix, while the remaining 11 issues were fixed only in 19.3.6 and later. Administrators also had to verify that all deployment components had been updated and assess the potential exposure of credentials and private project data due to the fact that patching would not invalidate stolen credentials or reverse unauthorized changes.

eMudhra/emSign: Compromised certificate trust

The high-priority eMudhra/emSign incident involved no software vulnerability at all. Several eMudhra intermediate certificate authorities (CAs) had insecure private keys, meaning attackers could potentially create certificates that would be trusted through the affected emSign certificate chain. While browsers had updated their trust stores and revocation lists, some Python tooling continued to trust the compromised intermediate CAs through its own certificate bundles. This created a risk of man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks against TLS connections, including those to python.org and pypi.org.

The Python Software Foundation urged users to upgrade immediately to at least certifi 2026.10.19, pip 26.2.2, and uv 0.13.4, and the Python core team shipped expedited releases 3.15.2, 3.14.10, 3.13.18, 3.12.16, and 3.11.18 to update the bundled pip. The updates had to reach every host, application, and existing virtual environment. Container images had to be rebuilt with layer caching disabled to fetch the latest system certificates. The decisive check was whether deployed clients rejected the compromised trust paths; simply upgrading Python was not enough.

Cutting through the noise

Cybersecurity Black Week showed that a severity score rarely tells the whole story. A 9.2-rated PHP flaw that attackers struggled to exploit, a 10.0-rated GitLab bug, exposed kernel reports with no patches, and a poisoned package that ran at Python startup each called for a different response. What they all had in common was a window of exposure: the time between disclosure and when the last affected system is patched. For the leaked kernel flaws, that window opened before any fix existed, and for end-of-life PHP versions, it may never fully close. This is where ESET’s multilayered protection comes in, using behavioural detection and other security mechanisms to help block exploitation attempts and keep systems protected until patches are applied.

At the same time, the signals defenders rely on were buried in noise, from scanning that was largely benign to a single behavioural rule firing hundreds of thousands of times in a week. What mattered most was quickly understanding which incidents actually affected an organization's environment and what each incident required. That is the problem ESET’s correlation engine, ESET LiveCortex, and its specialized cybersecurity model, ESET NeoCortex, are designed to solve: turning an overwhelming volume of raw data into understandable incidents so that defenders can act before attackers achieve their goals. To learn how they work, read Beyond the alert: How ESET is teaching AI to understand security incidents.

Title: ESET APT Activity Report Q2 2026–Q3 2026
Context: They represent only a subset of the cybersecurity intelligence made available to customers of ESET Threat Intelligence APT Reports
Full Text:
ESET APT Activity Report Q2 2026–Q2 2026 summarizes notable activities of selected advanced persistent threat (APT) groups documented by ESET researchers between April and September 2026. The operations presented here reflect the broader threat landscape observed during this period and highlight some of its key trends and developments. They represent only a subset of the cybersecurity intelligence made available to customers of ESET Threat Intelligence APT Reports.

During the monitored period, China-aligned groups conducted intelligence-collection operations primarily against governmental targets. FamousSparrow kept up its monitoring in South America, just as in the previous reporting period. In Southeast Asia and Oceania, China-aligned threat actors ran campaigns that appear to support Chinese law enforcement efforts against organized crime in the region. One threat actor targeted hotels in Palau, which seems to be increasingly used as a base for fraud-related organized crime. SlippyNunchucks deployed its DarkVigil toolset in Sri Lanka against Chinese-speaking individuals connected to fraud schemes, likely in the context of broader regional law enforcement efforts against financial crime. As scam compounds have become an issue for countries neighboring China, with direct negative effects on China itself, it is likely that China-aligned APT groups have supported law enforcement efforts in this area. Another, broader cluster of activity targeted Taiwanese organizations operating in the semiconductor industry. This focus on Taiwan’s semiconductor sector is consistent with long-running Chinese industrial espionage priorities, and the strategic importance of semiconductor supply chains to both economic competition and national security.

Middle East-aligned activity increased compared with the previous reporting period, driven mainly by the return of several established Iran-aligned groups. In the previous period, activity from these groups had declined, most likely because internet restrictions imposed by the Iranian regime hindered their own ability to operate effectively. FilthyFeline, a subgroup of OilRig, and MuddyWater resumed operations after a quieter period, with most activity directed at entities in Israel across multiple sectors; a smaller number of US companies were also affected. FilthyFeline also appears to have taken over activity against a cellular data service provider in Uzbekistan that had previously been compromised by BladedFeline, another OilRig subgroup. In parallel, we analyzed new or updated malware, suggesting renewed development activity within parts of the Iran-aligned ecosystem. We also discovered activity by Arid Viper, a Hamas-affiliated threat actor, against what appears to be the Palestinian Authority’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates or an affiliated governmental entity. Given the ongoing US-led peace process, as well as the long-standing rivalry between Hamas and the Palestinian Authority, this activity was potentially intended to collect intelligence on the Palestinian Authority’s diplomatic position and internal thinking regarding negotiations to reduce hostilities in the region.

North Korea-aligned threat actors did not deviate significantly from the types of targets seen in previous reporting periods. These include primarily technology and cryptocurrency companies, software developers, and other opportunistic targets. Alongside South Korea, Ukraine has become increasingly prominent among North Korea-aligned targets. This is likely related to growing ties between Russia and North Korea, and North Korea’s increasing involvement in Russia’s war against Ukraine, not only through indirect military support (munitions, etc.) but also through the deployment of North Korean soldiers. Alongside these broader trends, Lazarus resumed targeting of the drone sector, typically using recruitment-themed social engineering to gain initial access. The likely motivation is the increasingly important role that drone systems are playing in the war in Ukraine, where new tactics and capabilities are being tested. Access to such knowledge and manufacturing processes could provide North Korea with valuable know-how for developing its own drone-production capabilities. We also detected ScarCruft targeting an African country, which was probably intended either to maintain oversight of a North Korean worker scheme operating in the country or to monitor Russian activities there. Separately, DeceptiveDevelopment moved from fake job-interview lures to broader software supply-chain compromises, harvesting developer credentials and using that access to inject malicious code into public and private source code repositories.

Russia-aligned activity continued to support its war objectives, targeting governments, the defense sector, and military entities in Europe, with a substantially higher number of targets in Ukraine. Looking more closely at these activities, similarities between Russia-aligned and Belarus-aligned campaigns stand out, further supporting our hypothesis that threat actors aligned with the two countries are becoming operationally closer. Gamaredon’s operations, which are typically numerous, saw a significant decline. We suspect that this could be related to Ukrainian attacks on Crimea, where the group is suspected to operate, a broader restructuring of its operations, or other factors that we continue to assess. Despite this decline in activity, Gamaredon updated its PteroBox file stealer and started using new tools such as PteroPSDoor and Turla’s VBScript Rezzuar. PhantomCaptcha attempted to deploy spyware, which we named PrincessSpy, on Android devices while impersonating Ukrainian entities. We also identified an extensive campaign in Ukraine exploiting MDaemon mail servers, during which the attackers deployed two backdoor malware families, HELLAGE and HELLTAG.

North Korea’s expanding military cooperation with Russia has prompted expectations that North Korea-aligned cyberactivity might be starting to align more closely with Russian objectives in Ukraine. While some of their targeting interests overlap, notably around the drone sector, our telemetry more clearly points to Belarus-aligned groups acting as cyberproxies or force multipliers for Russia. We observed increased and more assertive activity from Belarus-aligned threat actors, with their operations increasingly reflecting Russia’s intelligence priorities in Ukraine in some areas. Most notably, we identified the first destructive cyberattack by a Belarus-aligned threat actor that we have documented in the European theater, marking a significant development in this threat nexus. According to our telemetry, FrostyNeighbor attacked a manufacturing company in Ukraine that plays an important role in the country’s transportation sector. This marks a notable escalation, as threat actors with a well-established history of destructive cyberoperations in Ukraine have, until now, been Russia-aligned.

Finally, we identified several cases of APT groups using AI and large language models (LLMs) at various stages of their operations. Threat actors used AI primarily to accelerate tasks that would otherwise require painstaking effort, including malware development and the creation of decoy websites. In some cases, this resembled vibe coding: rapid, prompt-driven drafting of code, with human operators adapting and integrating the results into their toolchains. We also discovered phishing lures containing images that were clearly AI-generated. In one notable case, Russia-aligned UAC-0099 inserted a decoy request for instructions on building a nuclear weapon into a script comment, apparently attempting to trigger the safety guardrails of LLM-based security analysis and prevent the inspection of the malicious code that followed.

Despite these developments, we have not noticed AI substantially reshaping the APT landscape over the past six months. While we cannot determine whether some operations may involve a higher degree of AI-driven automation, our telemetry continues to show hands-on-keyboard activity and operations that are not fully automated. Overall, our observations suggest that APT groups are currently using AI much like mainstream software developers: to accelerate software development, automate previously manual tasks, and assist with the analysis of large volumes of data, rather than to conduct fully autonomous malicious operations.

ESET products protect our customers’ systems from the malicious activities described in this report. Intelligence shared here is based mostly on proprietary ESET telemetry data and has been verified by ESET researchers.

ESET APT Activity Reports contain only a fraction of the cybersecurity intelligence data provided in ESET Threat Intelligence APT Reports. For more information, visit the ESET Threat Intelligence website.

Title: Google Cloud Requires AI Agents to Access Workspace Through Approved Methods
Context: First, the tech giant has unveiled its own Workspace model context protocol (MCP) servers, which are dedicated remote servers for Gmail, Google Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides,...
Full Text:
Google has introduced new purpose-built interfaces to better secure the use of AI agents across its Workspace environments, which will soon become the required way for AI agent to connect to Google Cloud and Workspace tools.

First, the tech giant has unveiled its own Workspace model context protocol (MCP) servers, which are dedicated remote servers for Gmail, Google Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat and Tasks.

This new standard comes with built-in permission, data loss prevention (DLP) checks and native human-in-the-loop (HITL) confirmations for sensitive actions. They also reject non-agent OAuth clients and work with Model Armor, Google Cloud’s prompt-injection screening service.

Meanwhile, Google has introduced the Workspace command-line interface (CLI), which allows AI agents to interact with Workspace services using commands, with structured JSON outputs and controlled OAuth sign-in.

From February 2027, all Google Workspace users will be required to connect AI agents through Workspace MCP servers or the Workspace CLI.

These new vetted methods will replace the traditional way to connect agents using Representational State Transfer application programmable interfaces (REST APIs).

In its announcement on November 25, Google said REST APIs were built “for human-paced apps where a valid OAuth token implied user intent.”

The tech giant argued this approach is no longer sufficient as AI agents increasingly act autonomously and at machine speed across emails, documents, datasets and cloud infrastructure. As a result, simply having a valid access token is no longer enough. Security checks, data access restrictions and human approval for sensitive actions must now be built into the process.

Besides these two new mandated entry points for AI agents, Google Cloud has also launched a protocol-native gateway for LLM, MCP, and Agent2Agent (A2A) traffic on Google Cloud, called Google Cloud Agent Gateway.

This extra layer of protection verifies agent identities against Google’s Agent Registry, enforces identity and access management (IAM) policies and default-deny outbound rules and screens requests with Model Armor, Google Cloud’s own guardrail layer against adversarial attacks, including prompt injection, sensitive data leaks and harmful content.

Title: Google mandates MCP or CLI access for Workspace AI agents starting February 2027
Context: Developers are advised to migrate their agent integrations to the supported interfaces and implement user confirmation and prompt injection protection mechanisms ahead of the...
Full Text:
Google has announced security controls across Google Workspace and Google Cloud to address the risks associated with autonomous AI agents accessing enterprise data, executing tasks, and interacting with cloud infrastructure.

The measures include dedicated agent identities, human approval controls for sensitive operations, prompt injection screening, and restrictions on how third-party AI tools access and process organizational data.

The company also announced the general availability of its Workspace Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and command-line interface (CLI), along with new requirements for AI agents connecting to its productivity services.

“Policy checks, data boundaries, and human confirmation have to live in the request path,” Chandu Thota, VP of Engineering at Google Workspace, and Brad Calder, President of Google Cloud Platform and SRE, wrote.

Google mandates new API access rules

Under the new Workspace AI Tools Addendum, AI agents must connect through Google’s Workspace MCP servers or CLI. Technical enforcement is scheduled to begin on February 1, 2027, while conventional applications can continue using existing REST APIs.

The MCP servers support Gmail, Google Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat, and Tasks, with support for Google Keep planned. Agent requests are checked against organizational permissions, DLP policies, and classification labels.

The Workspace CLI supports locally deployed agents and terminal-based automation through scoped OAuth authentication.

Dedicated agent identities and human approval

External AI agents connecting to Workspace must use dedicated OAuth client IDs, allowing administrators and users to distinguish AI agents from conventional applications.

Google is implementing least-privilege OAuth scopes and usage quotas to limit agent permissions and resource consumption. Time-limited approvals are planned for a future release, while quota-related billing is scheduled to begin on April 1, 2027.

In Google Cloud, agents receive individual identities through Agent Registry without relying on shared or long-lived keys. Their access and resource consumption are governed by identity and access management (IAM) policies and quotas.

Workspace MCP servers and the CLI enforce user confirmation for sensitive operations, such as sending emails, modifying Drive sharing permissions, or performing bulk edits.

Google Cloud customers can configure policies requiring MFA or human approval before agents access sensitive Cloud Storage buckets, change IAM permissions, or modify production infrastructure.

Workspace administrators can audit agent activity and revoke access through the admin console. Google plans to extend these capabilities to users.

Google Cloud customers can monitor agent behavior through Security Command Center, Agent Observability, Cloud Audit Logs, and Wiz. According to Google, revoking a Cloud Agent Identity or OAuth grant immediately terminates the associated access.

Prompt injection and unauthorized data access

Google Cloud Agent Gateway introduces protocol-level security controls for LLM, MCP, and Agent2Agent (A2A) communications.

The gateway verifies agent identities against Agent Registry, enforces IAM policies, restricts outbound connections through default-deny rules, and integrates Google’s Model Armor service to screen requests for prompt injection.

Google plans to introduce additional access restrictions that will enable Workspace administrators and users to prevent external AI agents from retrieving designated emails, files, and folders. These restrictions will build on existing Workspace DLP and client-side encryption capabilities.

New restrictions on enterprise data handling

The Workspace AI Tools Addendum prohibits the permanent storage of raw Workspace data, its use for model training, and unauthorized API scraping.

The addendum also establishes a 30-day retention limit for Google Technical Information, which includes vector embeddings, memory indexes, user profiles, and organizational graphs but excludes user data.

AI tool providers must comply with data retention and deletion requirements, including removing user data and associated technical information when an integration is disconnected or its access is revoked.

Google recommends that Workspace administrators review connected applications and agents, configure DLP policies, and monitor OAuth activity logs. Developers are advised to migrate their agent integrations to the supported interfaces and implement user confirmation and prompt injection protection mechanisms ahead of the February 2027 enforcement deadline.

Recognized for Completeness of Vision and Ability to Execute.

Our perspective: less stitching, more stopping threats

Most security teams don't struggle to find tools. They struggle to make them work together. We believe SOC analysts lose too much of their day moving between consoles and matching alerts to assets by hand, which is time not spent stopping threats.

To us, an integrated approach to security operations means detection, investigation and response working from the same data and the same view, so analysts can get from "what fired?" to "what do we do about it?" faster.

The importance of exposure management in the SOC

Rapid7 Incident Command, part of the Rapid7 Command Platform, brings together SIEM, SOAR, DFIR, attack surface management and threat intelligence. We built it on the idea that exposure management, and the context it brings, belongs inside the SOC, not next to it. In our view, when an alert arrives with what we know about the asset and how exposed it is, analysts can prioritize what matters instead of working from separate vulnerability reports and alert queues.

Context to act, not another console to check

We believe adopting an integrated SOC shouldn't be all-or-nothing. Incident Command is available in tiers from Essentials to Ultimate, so teams that want extra coverage can add managed services. That helps resource-pressured teams to start with what they need and grow at their own pace, spending less time building and maintaining integrations and more time on investigations.

To us, security operations work best when analysts have the context to act, not another console to check. Title: Microsoft named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Email Security
Context: Blue team agents investigate threats and improve detections, red team agents identify paths to compromise, and green team agents prioritize actions to close security gaps, while...
Full Text:
We’re honored to share that Microsoft has once again been named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Email Security.

AI is changing the threat landscape and this is shifting how organizations think about their existing security strategy. In response, we’ve invested in two areas over the past year: using AI to protect people and the agents that now read their email and making protection measurable so customers can verify that it works.

AI is changing both sides of the inbox

The first area of investment starts with a simple reality: AI now reads email alongside people, attackers are using AI to target both, and defense must use AI to stay ahead. Picture an ordinary vendor email: a meeting recap, a few action items, and a friendly sign-off. Hidden in white text on a white background is prompt injection: an instruction telling an AI assistant to gather financial documents and send them to an outside address. The employee isn’t the target; their AI agent is. People can be persuaded by messages that exploit fear, trust, or urgency, but agents don’t need persuading. Once an agent acts on an instruction, pulling the message back won’t undo it. This is why Microsoft Defender stops malicious messages before delivery and keeps reevaluating delivered mail as new intelligence comes in.

This summer, we introduced prompt injection protection for email in Defender to detect and quarantine messages carrying hidden malicious AI instructions before they reach Microsoft Copilot or other agents. In Defender, analysts can also see what an agent would see: the ‘Show concealed text’ button on the ‘Email Entity’ page reveals hidden content in the email preview, so they can inspect the instructions an agent could encounter. These attacks don’t show up often, yet. Over a four-week timeframe, we caught almost 10,000 prompt injection attempts, around 330 a day, out of the billions of emails Defender scans every day. The hard part is spotting those few without tripping over legitimate mail, so we don’t lean on a single model. Heuristics clear out the bulk first. What’s left goes to a fine-tuned small language model, and only the messages that still look suspicious reach a large language model for the final call. Saving the heaviest analysis for the smallest set of messages is what keeps false positives low and business email moving.

AI is also reshaping the attacks aimed at people. The phishing emails that worry us most are the ones that look completely normal. No malicious link, no infected attachment, just a plausible request written with perfect grammar and the right context. Generative AI makes those messages cheap to produce and endlessly variable. To meet that shift, we rebuilt how Microsoft Defender makes decisions rather than simply adding another filter. That decision-making now operates at scale, screening 5.2 billion emails a day on average1. The redesigned detection stack combines multiple machine learning models and LLM-based classifiers, with an ensemble model weighing their outputs to determine the final verdict. It also uses natural language processing signals, including message topic, to judge what a message is asking for and not only what it contains. That helps Defender catch attacks more accurately.

While detection helps with the message in front of you, defenders also need to see how it connects to the rest of an attack. Microsoft Perception extends that help beyond the message, connecting an email investigation to the broader exposure and response picture. Blue team agents investigate threats and improve detections, red team agents identify paths to compromise, and green team agents prioritize actions to close security gaps, while people retain control of critical decisions. The Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender, launched in September, provides a shared foundation for people and AI agents to investigate and respond to the full attack—not just an isolated email. By bringing security information and event management (SIEM) and extended detection and response (XDR) together, it connects email signals with endpoint, identity, cloud, and third-party data, giving AI-assisted security operations broader context.

Proof over promises: Making protection measurable

But using AI to defend only matters if customers can verify that it works. The second investment area is one the whole industry has struggled with: how do you know your email security is actually working? Detection claims are easy to make and hard to verify, so we publish the data.

Since July 2025, we’ve released quarterly email security benchmarking reports built on real-world threats, not synthetic tests. They compare environments protected by Microsoft Defender alone with those that add a secure email gateway in front of it or an integrated cloud email security (ICES) layer behind it. We believe transparency strengthens the whole market, and an industry that measures itself in the open improves faster.

While benchmarking shows how protection performs across organizations, the Protection & Posture Insights report shows how it performs in yours. This on-demand, tenant-specific report helps security leaders understand which threats target their organization, how well Microsoft Defender stops them, and where configuration can be strengthened. Recent updates show URL clicks checked and malicious-site attempts blocked across email, Microsoft Teams, Office apps, and Microsoft Copilot, and also highlight allow lists and overrides that may be letting threats through. Together, benchmarking and tenant-specific insights give leaders evidence to evaluate protection and identify opportunities to strengthen it.

We’re grateful to our customers, partners, and the analyst community for their trust, and to the teams turning insight into protection. Our engineers start with customer problems, while our researchers draw on more than 165 trillion signals a day across Microsoft to anticipate emerging threats and build protections before real-world examples appear2. This recognition from Gartner is a milestone for us, not the finish line. Our focus remains on protecting people and agents and giving customers evidence they can use to evaluate their defenses.

Drawing on her 25 years of engineering and leadership experience at Cisco, she also shared her perspective on network transformation and empowering engineers in the agentic AI era.

Thank you, Nairi, and congratulations on a successful Cisco Live Melbourne. What stood out as a key highlight this year?

Thank you, Kevin! Last year, on the same stage, we talked about our vision around platform convergence and unifying network operations. This year, we brought that vision completely to life. In the World of Solutions, customers didn’t just look at slides — they had real, conversational interactions with autonomous AI agents managing the Cisco Live network. Customers could actually have a conversation with the NOC AI agent. They could ask it just about any question about how the Cisco Live network was running in that moment. Experiencing that level of interactive autonomy firsthand generated tremendous excitement.

Those customers, or potential customers, got a deep look into the Network Operations Center (NOC).

The NOC is truly the heartbeat of Cisco Live, and hosting it right inside the Cisco Stand was a major focal point. Attendees got to see live network dashboards powered by Splunk and talk directly with our engineering experts about what it takes to deploy, manage, and secure a network. New this year, visitors could engage directly with our NOC AI Agent to query real-time performance stats and explore the exact equipment powering their event experience. Furthermore, on our daily behind-the-scenes tours in collaboration with Endace, customers experienced a live Agentic SOC powered by Splunk Enterprise Security and Cisco Cloud Control — watching us detect, correlate, and autonomously respond to active threats across live conference traffic in real time. It was a powerful, real-world demonstration of AgenticOps in action.

Sounds like all that resonated with the customers.

Yes, while Cisco Cloud Control is currently available in the U.S., it’s coming to APJC in 2027. So, the APJC customers are looking forward to having it here—and they were especially excited to see it in action.

What are some advantages customers say they are looking forward to from Cloud Control?

In talking with customers, a number of key advantages from Cloud Control came up. The first is around operational simplicity. Our customers want to move beyond science-project AI experimentation to trusted, policy-governed outcomes that eliminate operational silos. With Cisco Cloud Control, customers gain a unified platform powering AgenticOps. That enables intelligent automation and simplified network operations across their entire infrastructure.

Security and resilience are major concerns for them.

Yes, teams today are managing highly complex, multi-vendor hybrid and IT/OT environments. In fact, a recent Cisco study revealed that while 83% of organizations plan to deploy AI agents within the next 12 months, only 13% consider their infrastructure truly AI-ready. That readiness gap is where our engineers focus. We help customers architect, identify, and secure autonomous agents within their environments.

Splunk Enterprise Security was well represented in the World of Solutions.

Yes, that was showcased inside our agentic Security Operations Center (SOC). Attendees saw real-time threat detection and autonomous response operating across the Cisco Live network. Through Splunk’s industry-leading telemetry, security teams could watch malicious traffic get identified, isolated, and neutralized as it happened.

At Cisco Live Melbourne, APJC customers saw just how comprehensive Cisco solutions are.

Our customers are looking for a trusted partner who can deliver networks that are both AI-ready and inherently cyber-resilient. Our approach comes down to three core commitments:

First, operational simplicity. With Cisco Cloud Control and AgenticOps, we eliminate operational silos so teams can move from AI experimentation to trusted, closed-loop outcomes.

Second, security fused into the network. Security can’t be an afterthought; it’s built directly into the fabric with Cisco Live Protect and quantum-safe encryption.

And third, AI-ready infrastructure, built on Cisco Silicon One and next-gen Catalyst hardware to handle massive AI data concurrency. Layer Splunk across that entire footprint, and customers get end-to-end visibility they simply can’t get anywhere else. That is why Cisco stands alone in this transformation."

Think about the traditional engineering lifecycle. I started my career as a TAC engineer, so I know this firsthand. We spent hours manually configuring equipment, troubleshooting issues, and working through complex problems. Sometimes we'd make a configuration mistake, and when a customer's network was down, we'd be waiting hours for them to email us the logs so we could even start troubleshooting. Researching complex interoperability across multi-vendor environments, digging through thousands of log lines, and validating compliance architectures could take days or even weeks of manual effort. I've lived that reality, and that's what makes the change we're seeing today so significant.

Over the next 12 months, as Agentic Operations move from sandbox pilots into live production, engineers will spend far less time on that manual effort. Autonomous agents will handle telemetry aggregation, diagnostics, and baseline verification in seconds, freeing engineers to focus on what really matters: solving complex problems, applying engineering judgment and delivering better outcomes for customers.

For midsized organizations, strong endpoint security needs to do more than detect threats. It needs to stop attacks before they can take hold, without demanding constant tuning or adding to the workload of already stretched security teams.

That’s increasingly important as AI gives attackers new ways to find vulnerabilities, develop exploits, and execute attacks at speed and scale. Sophos Endpoint is built around a protection-first approach that stops threats early, before they can escalate into larger incidents.

According to the IDC MarketScape one of Sophos' key strengths is "Strong upfront protection across web, exploit, and ransomware vectors, validated across multiple independent testing programs, which reduces analyst workload and alert volume.”

Strong protection from day one

According to the IDC MarketScape, “Consider Sophos When: SMBs to large enterprises are seeking out-of-the-box, protection-first endpoint security with minimal tuning; organizations need a unified, open platform with strong third-party integration, native identity threat detection, and automation; and customers with limited security staff or no dedicated CISO function are seeking democratized, AI-augmented security and reporting."

Sophos Endpoint has recommended protections enabled by default, so teams get immediate protection without tuning individual applications, building exclusion lists, or keeping a security specialist on standby. It protects endpoints and servers across Windows, macOS, and Linux. As settings change over time, Account Health Check flags drift from recommended settings and high-risk misconfigurations, enabling administrators to fix issues with one click. Sophos partners can use one console to deliver consistent protection across small, midsized, and enterprise clients.

Block the techniques exploits rely on

AI can speed up exploit development, but it doesn’t change how exploits work on a device. Whether written by a human or an AI model, exploits still rely on a limited set of techniques.

Sophos Endpoint can block an exploit without knowing which specific vulnerability it targets or who wrote it. Its anti-exploitation technology targets the techniques exploits rely on, with 60+ proprietary mitigations enabled by default on every running process. We’ve been building and shipping this protection since 2015. To see how it works, watch how Sophos Endpoint stops exploits or read the Exploits Explained whitepaper.

Universal ransomware protection

Sophos Endpoint includes CryptoGuard, Sophos’ proprietary ransomware protection technology. Rather than trying to identify the ransomware itself, CryptoGuard monitors file contents for signs of malicious encryption. It blocks the offending process, whether it is running on the victim’s computer or on a compromised device elsewhere on the network (remote ransomware), and automatically restores encrypted files to their original state. See it in action in How Sophos Endpoint Stops Remote Ransomware.

Defenses that step up during an attack

When Sophos Endpoint detects an attack in progress, Adaptive Attack Protection instantly applies more aggressive protection on the device to disrupt and contain the attack. It responds to combinations of behaviors and the use of known attack tools, rather than relying on file hashes. That helps it respond to zero-day attacks and new variants, including AI-assisted attacks. If adversarial activity is detected across multiple endpoints or servers, a Critical Attack Warning notifies all administrators and provides attack details so you can act. Watch Sophos Endpoint: Adaptive Attack Protection and Critical Attack Warning to see both at work.

Coordinated defense with Sophos Fusion

Sophos Endpoint is part of Sophos Fusion, an AI-Native Cybersecurity Defense System designed for a world where threats move at AI speed. From one place, you can manage your Sophos products, review detections and alerts, and investigate and remediate threats. Synchronized Security turns a detection at one control point into a coordinated response across other defenses, including firewall, identity, and email. For example, when Sophos Endpoint detects a threat on a device, Sophos Firewall can automatically restrict that device’s network access and restore it once the threat has been resolved. CrowdStrike Buys Zscaler for US$43.9bn in Largest Cyber Deal
CrowdStrike buys missing network security piece in $43.9B Zscaler deal
Context: While the company has expanded beyond endpoint protection into identity, cloud security and threat intelligence, Zscaler brings an established security service edge (SSE) and...
Full Text:
CrowdStrike agreed to acquire cloud security company Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal on Monday, combining endpoint protection with zero-trust network security in one of the largest cybersecurity acquisitions ever and intensifying the industry’s race to build broad security platforms.

The deal brings together CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform, which focuses on endpoint, identity and cloud security, with Zscaler’s cloud-delivered network security and zero-trust access capabilities. CrowdStrike said the combined company is expected to begin with more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue (ARR).

The acquisition also addresses a strategic gap in CrowdStrike’s portfolio. While the company has expanded beyond endpoint protection into identity, cloud security and threat intelligence, Zscaler brings an established security service edge (SSE) and zero-trust network access platform.

“With Zscaler, CrowdStrike will enter network security, cybersecurity’s largest single addressable market segment,” CrowdStrike said in a statement.

The companies expect the deal to close in the second half of CrowdStrike’s fiscal 2028, subject to approval by Zscaler shareholders and regulators, the statement added.

The deal is larger than Google’s $32 billion purchase of Wiz and Palo Alto Networks’ $25 billion acquisition of CyberArk, both completed earlier this year.

From partnership to one platform

CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz framed the deal around AI in the statement.

“With Zscaler, we’re building cybersecurity’s operating system: a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI, and enable any agentic application to run safely,” Kurtz said.

Yih Khai Wong, research director at IDC, said the deal fits a pattern of larger security vendors “buying into adjacent control points rather than building them organically.” Until now, he said, CrowdStrike “lacks a strong, owned network/SSE layer.”

The two companies are not starting from scratch. The statement described the relationship as one of CrowdStrike’s largest technology alliances, with more than 2,000 shared customers and 16 integrations. CrowdStrike argued that a partnership integrates separate products, while one company integrates “the data, the roadmap, the go-to-market, and the commercial model.”

Wong said the existing partnership already delivers much of the correlation value. Ownership adds “control over the roadmap and the pace of integration,” he said.

Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said the merger buys “fluency rather than new vocabulary.” One owner means a single data model and faster correlation, he said, but that gain is “narrower than any merger pitch will claim.” He advised CISOs to ask the vendors to show, in their own environments, which outcomes today’s integration cannot already reach.

One contract, one renewal

The commercial plan is central to the deal. After closing, customers of either company will be able to buy the other’s products on a single Falcon Flex contract, the statement said. CrowdStrike identified about 8,000 Zscaler customers that do not yet use CrowdStrike, and said it expects about $1 billion in annualized revenue synergies within 30 months of closing.

“Falcon Flex will bring Zscaler onto the commercial model customers already use, so they commit once and expand from there,” the statement said.

Gogia said that model shifts leverage over time.

“Consolidation is sold at the first signature and priced at the second,” he said. The second signature comes at renewal, he said, when the supplier holds more of the estate and the buyer holds fewer alternatives. He advised CFOs and CISOs to price consolidation offers at their first full renewal, and to keep one credible alternative alive in each layer they consolidate.

Wong said consolidation “addresses real integration challenges for enterprises that commit to a single platform, while quietly reducing the leverage and flexibility of those that don’t.” Enterprises in heavily regulated industries that need best-of-breed tools may find bundled platforms fall short, he added.

Two layers, one release train

CrowdStrike also expects $500 million in annualized cost synergies within 18 to 24 months of closing, mainly from optimizing data center infrastructure, vendors and operations, the statement said.

For security teams, the question is whether that consolidation reaches the products themselves. Today the Falcon sensor and Zscaler’s client run as separate agents on separate clouds, with separate release schedules, Gogia said.

“A merged agent, a shared update pipeline, or a single control plane would change that,” Gogia said. “One bad release would then reach the device and the way in together.”

Wong said CISOs should build that scenario into their business continuity plans, since “an incident could affect both the endpoint agent and the access control plane.”

Gogia advised teams to map every access rule that depends on CrowdStrike’s device posture check, and to keep a fallback route that relies on neither vendor. Customers that pair Zscaler with another endpoint product, or Falcon with another SSE provider, should get integration commitments in writing, he said. “Neutrality promised in a blog post lasts exactly as long as the blog post.” Until the deal closes, both companies will continue to operate independently, the statement added.

Title: States Sue SpaceX Over Grok Deepfakes
Context: SpaceX acquired xAI, the Musk startup and parent company of X Corp
Full Text:
The attorneys general of Oregon and Virginia are suing Elon Musk’s SpaceX, alleging that the company violated consumer protection laws by lying to users about both the safety of its generative AI tools and how seriously the company took stopping child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and nonconsensual intimate imagery (NCII) from proliferating on its platforms. The suits follow a slew of other lawsuits against Musk’s companies around similar issues, including from the city of Baltimore and teens in Tennessee.

The attorneys general are each filing their own complaints in their respective state courts—Virginia in the circuit court for the city of Richmond, and Oregon in Multnomah County circuit court. Both suits name SpaceX and X Corp., the SpaceX subsidiary responsible for the social media platform X. SpaceX acquired xAI, the Musk startup and parent company of X Corp., in February. In doing so it also took ownership of Grok, which is at the center of the allegations in the suit.

Last winter, the Grok chatbot made headlines after users on X started prompting it en masse to generate sexualized photos of women and minors. Even more disturbing AI-generated videos were later found on Grok’s website, including those showing female celebrities engaging in sexual activities.

The states allege that Grok’s creators ignored industry safety standards and intentionally implemented weak safeguards in an attempt to entice more people to use its “lagging product.” In all, as Virginia alleged in its complaint, the defendants saw “a market opportunity for more profits” in the generation of sexualized images of real people, including children, and “intentionally released a product that inundated their platforms with CSAM.”

For example, the states say that Grok wasn’t subjected to enough third-party evaluations before releasing new models, and that Grok’s safety prompts included instructions to “assume good intent” and that the terms “teenage” and “girl” do “not necessarily imply underage.” They also allege that tens of thousands of reports were submitted without key information from xAI to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children’s CyberTipline, preventing the Center from being able to act on them 90 percent of the time.

In the complaints, the states say that Musk leaned into Grok’s “spicy mode” as a way to differentiate the model from its competitors and that this worked. They note, for example, that during the same time period that Grok’s ability to “undress” people was sparking international outrage, Musk posted about how Grok was “hitting #1 on the App Store in one country after another!” and discussing the chatbot’s “heavy usage growth.”
