Introducing Sysdig AI Defense: See, stop, and prove what agents do
Context: Same sensor codebase, same Falco rules for detections, same threat research
Full Text:
AI has moved from assisting to acting. Agents now read files, run commands and reach your cloud with a real person’s access. Most of the time, the only record of what they did is the one the agent wrote itself. “A First Look: Under the Hood of AI Agents” shows where one software company's agents logged one tool call for every seven processes the kernel actually watched them run. And it isn’t only engineers. Someone in finance can wire up a coding agent on a Tuesday afternoon. Every agent, model and seat they add becomes a line item most companies can’t trace to a team or a task.

Find every agent, decide what it can do, keep the record

Sysdig AI Defense is runtime security and governance for every AI agent your teams run, from the laptop where an agent starts its work to the cloud where its actions land.

It starts by showing you what’s there. It finds the agents, MCP servers, skills and plugins your people use, including the ones nobody approved, and ties each one to the account and the person behind it.

Then you decide what agents are allowed to do. Most of the time, nothing changes. Everything your policies don’t name runs as normal, so developers keep working. For the actions you care about, you pick the response. Confirm pauses the call and asks the developer to approve it first. Block refuses it outright. A kill process ends the work the moment the process starts.

Whatever happens, there’s a record. Every action Sysdig AI Defense sees lands in your Sysdig tenant, off the device, where the agent can’t change it. Security can prove what happened, and leaders can see which teams use which models for which work.

Under the hood, it’s the same runtime engine Sysdig built to protect cloud workloads. Same sensor codebase, same Falco rules for detections, same threat research. What’s new is where it looks. It now follows AI agents wherever they work.

By default, Sysdig AI Defense doesn't collect the prompts your people type or the agent's replies. File edits and tool results are removed before they leave the machine. Your data stays in your Sysdig tenant, in the region you choose.

See every agent and MCP server your teams run, then decide what they can use

The questions security leaders ask us most are simple: what agents are running, which ones has nobody approved, and who owns them? Most can't answer these questions yet. In a 2026 IBM study, 77% of organizations surveyed said AI adoption is already outpacing their governance, and two-thirds of the CIOs and CTOs said they are held accountable for AI systems they do not fully control. Sysdig AI Defense answers from what is actually running, across tools like Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot, and it follows agents across the whole AI fabric: employee workstations, production Linux and Kubernetes, and the managed agent platforms you don’t own.

Most security teams are likely running more agents than they know about. One software company with about 300 machines found that out in its first month on Sysdig AI Defense. Nothing was blocked, because every policy ran in Alert for the whole month. The full findings are in our “A First Look: Under the Hood of AI Agents”. Half the agents Sysdig AI Defense found on those machines were instances the security team didn’t know about. Employees had signed up with personal email addresses on company devices, outside single sign-on, and every device had at least one agent harness installed and in active use.

Shadow AI isn’t only unapproved agents, either. Early adopters reported finding Ollama, llama.cpp and LM Studio running on people’s machines, a Qwen coding model served locally, and models downloaded straight to laptops. None of that crosses your AI gateway, so the gateway never sees it. The kernel does. It sees each one install, start and pull a model, and ties it to the person behind it.

Once you can see it, you can decide what’s allowed. New AI tools show up in the inventory as they appear on devices. If you don’t want agents using an MCP server, or one of its tools, deny it and set the policy to Block. The agent’s call is refused before it runs, and the agent sees your reason. If there’s a service agents should never send data to, name it in a policy, and kill process ends the upload as the process starts.

‍

Let agents work, and stop only the action that goes too far

An allowlist makes it easy to stop what you already know you don't want. The action itself is harder to judge, because it happens in the middle of a job, often in a fraction of a second. Even the labs that build these models have watched their own agents cross a line. Both OpenAI and Anthropic have disclosed cases where agents working through test tasks reached real systems that belonged to someone else. So the check has to happen at the moment the agent acts. Block and Confirm policies step in on the agent’s tool call before it runs. Kill process catches any process the moment it starts, no matter which agent launched it. You choose which response each policy gets.

Take a file of customer records. Opening one is ordinary work for an agent, and most of the time it is fine. What matters is where the data goes next, and what the agent gave itself permission to do along the way. A read that stays on the machine passes without a second look. The same read, followed by an upload to a public file-sharing host by an agent that just widened its own permissions, is an incident.

When an agent is told no, it tries another route, like a shell command or a script it writes itself. A hook sees the command but is blind to the script. AI Defense sees both. It sees the command with its destination parsed out, and the script as it starts.

You don’t have to write policy from scratch. Start from Sysdig’s managed policies for the risks agents bring, such as MCP servers and tools, secrets and data, and destructive commands. Each one is written as Falco rules you can read. You also don’t have to turn on blocking on day one. Every Sysdig policy starts in Alert, which means it raises what it sees and stops nothing. Watch what it catches on your own fleet. Then choose Block, Confirm or Kill process for the actions that matter. For actions you want a human on, Confirm sends the call to the agent’s own permission prompt, so the developer approves or refuses it right where they’re already working. Security decides which actions need that second look. Everything else runs as normal.

Not every risk fits a rule written in advance. Agents pick up new skills all the time. That’s why Sysdig’s threat research rules also look for agent behavior that resembles an attack, like credential dumping, persistence, tunnels and remote access.

Here’s what that looks like in our demo environment. A revenue operations agent, running with approvals turned off, tries to send a customer export to a public file host. A Kill process policy ends the upload as it starts, and the agent tells the person why.

When security wants to see how it got there, session replay steps through the session’s tool calls in order. The detections and kills show up in the Events rows beside it, each naming the rule and policy that fired.

See which model tier each team uses, for which task

Because every agent is tied to a person, so is every model it uses. Each session carries the model it ran on and the person and team behind it, whether or not the traffic goes through an AI gateway.

That matters for AI spend. In the same findings, four in ten employees ran Opus-class models only. Sysdig AI Defense rates each person’s model tier against how demanding their work was, by team. It flags light work running on the most expensive models, so leaders can change the habit before the invoice shows up. It also flags heavy work on the cheapest models, where someone may be stuck with a model too light for the job. Managers can move them to a better fit and help them get more done.

Answer an audit without pulling developers off their work

When an auditor asks what an agent did and who was behind it, most teams have one place to look, which is the agent’s own log. That log can miss a lot.

The kernel is the part of the operating system every action passes through, which makes it a good place to check. “A First Look: Under the Hood of AI Agents” found that the agent’s own log had no entry for 82% of the credential-file reads the kernel recorded, and no entry for 95% of the reads the agent binary made itself. Across that month, the kernel recorded 2.6 million processes against 374,000 tool calls in the agents’ own logs. The agent’s log is useful context, but it leaves out too much to carry an audit on its own.

Sysdig AI Defense keeps its own record from the kernel, off the device, where the agent can't change it. Remove Sysdig AI Defense’s own hook and it puts it back within the hour, and the kernel keeps recording in between. Each event carries the agent, the account, the model and the session. Each detection names the rule and policy behind it. With Sysdig AI Defense, the evidence is already on file when an audit asks about AI, and nobody has to pull a developer off their work to rebuild it. Teams can also forward these records to their SIEM, where they sit with the rest of their security evidence.

Accountability for agents starts at runtime

Boards are asking what agents are doing, and regulators are starting to ask too. Hatem Naguib, Sysdig's CEO, has boiled it down to three questions every executive should be able to answer:

How do we know our AI isn't going rogue?

What AI are we using, and who is accountable for it?

What can we prove?

None of these can be answered from the agent's own log alone.

Sysdig AI Defense brings to agents the same prevention, detection, and response Sysdig delivers across the cloud, rooted in Falco, the open source runtime security project Sysdig created in 2016 and that the CNCF graduated in 2024. Falco has passed 200 million downloads and is used by more than 60% of the Fortune 500.

Agents will keep getting faster, and their actions will keep reaching deeper into the cloud. The companies that scale them with confidence will be the ones that put the controls in first: every agent known, owned, and tied to an identity; the risky actions stopped as they happen; and a record that holds up afterwards.

See it on your own fleet. Start a free trial and find out what your agents are really doing. Available for macOS and Windows. Sysdig AI Defense runs beside your EDR and can be deployed through your MDM. For the full picture, we recommend rolling it out to at least ten machines.

Full Text:
If you want to compete, you need to be multi-model. And if you want to take advantage of everything that different AI models have to offer, you need a great harness. But building one that works seamlessly across multiple models and surfaces is incredibly hard. You need to solve for performance, quality, and cost. And then you have to maintain it, which is even harder.

Luckily, the GitHub engineering team built a best-in-class, truly multi-model harness, which we’ve adopted company-wide. The Microsoft Copilot harness powers Copilot Code, Copilot Studio, the GitHub Copilot app, the CLI, VS Code, and more. And today, we’re making that harness available through Microsoft Foundry. That gives developers and enterprise customers a fully managed way to build agents that reason, use tools, and complete complex, long-running tasks. You get the right model for the job without switching the harness or the rest of your tech stack. That frees up your time, energy, and resources to focus on your bottom line.

What’s a harness, and why is it hard?

If the model supplies the intelligence, the harness is everything around the model. It’s the orchestration layer that gives an agent the right instructions, context, execution environment, and controls to accomplish meaningful work. And a harness worth its salt has support for open standards like MCP and agent skills, as well as agent plugins.

This is a fast-moving space. A frontier model today might fall behind tomorrow. And building your own harness or model router to keep up can be painful and slow. Now, you can build on the same harness Microsoft and GitHub ship in our own products, and you don’t have to maintain it.

We invest in science and engineering work to continually improve and evolve the harness and ensure high-quality, efficient, and low-cost performance across a range of models and workloads. The benefits compound for us and our customers who use the harness to build and run their own agents. Improve the harness, and every surface it touches benefits.

Born in GitHub, battle-tested at enterprise scale

The Copilot harness was built by the same GitHub engineers behind new technologies like our multi-model orchestration. And those technologies are only possible because we built our own harness. Designed to be fast, token-efficient, and predictable, it was our original, high-quality harness. And it had the highest satisfaction among our most demanding audience: developers. That’s why we’re standardizing all of our Copilot experiences on the strongest foundation possible.

The harness is built to perform across model families, with 20+ frontier models plus bring your own key, so you can use the right model for the right job. Instead of doing the work to keep up with and eval new models, lean on us to intelligently route work to the right model or models based on the task.

Our harness is flexible and configurable to any type of app, agent, or service. We recently ported the harness runtime to Rust, which has resulted in industry-leading performance and reductions in both session overhead and time-to-first token. And because the Copilot harness powers surfaces across Microsoft, it’s battle-tested and proven performant at the scale of millions of users and hundreds of real-world use cases.

Title: AI for Science expands to foundations and research institutions
Context: (Over the last few months, we’ve also launched our discounted Team plan for scientists and have supported hundreds of projects across biology, medicine, physics, chemistry,...
Full Text:
We’re highlighting 20 scientific foundations, institutions, and research groups from around the world that we’ve partnered with in an expansion of our AI for Science program, which gives free Claude credits to researchers working on high-impact scientific projects.

We started the AI for Science program in May 2025 with the belief that AI could significantly speed up scientific progress. Our goal is to increase access to AI tools and resources to enable researchers to deepen and expand their own scientific work. (Over the last few months, we’ve also launched our discounted Team plan for scientists and have supported hundreds of projects across biology, medicine, physics, chemistry, climate science, and mathematics.)

Scientists have told us that they’re working with Claude to generate hypotheses, design experiments, swiftly analyze complex data, and communicate findings. With scientists at the center of this transformation, the field is setting the questions and developing the research projects that will help us tackle some of humanity’s toughest problems.

Over the past year, we’ve started to expand this work and partner with scientific organizations to build collaborative research projects. For instance, we partnered with HHMI Janelia Research Campus to develop the Model Hardware Standard (MHS), a shared specification that lets AI agents safely operate lab instruments. MHS is currently in research preview. We also support the Allen Institute, a leader in creating large open datasets and tools to advance research on the brain, cells, and the immune system. The institute is building teams of AI agents to analyze that data, turning months of manual analysis into hours.

AI for Science began by supporting individual scientists. By partnering with institutions and foundations, we’re now able to reach more researchers across many fields. Many of these projects will also produce public goods that benefit the wider scientific community: open datasets, open-source software, open standards, and shared libraries. We look forward to seeing how AI resources can expand what scientists can attempt and lead to new discoveries.

Science funders and societies

Science funders and societies play an enormous role in finding and funding original, high-impact projects. We’re sharing Claude credits with the following organizations, which will distribute these resources to ambitious researchers aiming to use AI for scientific research:

The Alfred P. Sloan Foundation. Founded in 1934, it supports original research and education in science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and economics.

The Simons Foundation. This foundation advances the frontiers of research in mathematics and basic sciences through grants and its Flatiron Institute.

Schmidt Sciences. Founded in 2024 by Eric and Wendy Schmidt, it works to accelerate scientific knowledge and breakthroughs with the most promising, advanced tools to support a thriving planet. The organization prioritizes research in areas poised for impact, including AI and advanced computing, astrophysics, biosciences, climate, and space—and supports researchers in a variety of disciplines through its science systems program.

Open Source for Science Fund, a program of Renaissance Philanthropy. This is a time-bound philanthropic fund at Renaissance Philanthropy sustaining and evolving the open-source software stack that underpins science.

The US National Science Foundation. This $9 billion federal agency established by Congress in 1950 promotes the progress of science, advances national health and defense, and funds competitive research and education, accounting for about 25% of federal support for basic research at US colleges and universities.

CAS, a division of the American Chemical Society. For more than a century, CAS has indexed the world’s published chemistry, and it maintains the CAS REGISTRY®, the standard system for identifying chemical substances.

Institutions

Leading research institutions produce some of the world’s most important scientific advances, data, instruments, and tools. These institutional partners will use Claude credits inside their organizations to enable scientific discovery:

Space Telescope Science Institute. STScI runs science operations for NASA’s Hubble, James Webb, and Roman space telescopes. Managed by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy (AURA), STScI also holds one of the largest astronomy data archives used by scientists worldwide.

Wellcome Sanger Institute. One of the world’s leading genomics centers, it generates genomic and functional data at scale, with work that spans human genetics, biodiversity, and drug development.

The Francis Crick Institute. Based in London, it’s one of Europe’s largest biomedical research institutes, with more than 100 research groups studying the biology behind health and disease.

Imperial College London, Department of Life Sciences. One of Europe’s largest life science departments, it conducts research ranging from the structure of single molecules to whole ecosystems, with a focus on health, disease, and climate resilience.

EMBL. The European Molecular Biology Laboratory is Europe’s intergovernmental life science laboratory, with six sites across the continent delivering both research and services across experimental and computational approaches in biology. EMBL’s European Bioinformatics Institute (EMBL-EBI) hosts a number of key open data resources that biologists use every day, such as Ensembl, Protein Data Bank in Europe, and Europe PMC.

Gladstone Institutes. An independent biomedical research institute in San Francisco, it integrates AI and data science across its work on cardiology, neurology, infectious diseases, cancer, and autoimmune diseases.

Research projects and initiatives

As part of this work, we’re also continuing to support innovative research by providing Claude credits directly to specific research initiatives, focusing on problems with the potential for large public impact. The new projects are:

FlyWire, Princeton University (neuroscience). It produced the first complete wiring map of an adult fruit fly’s brain and develops open data and tools for connectomics, enabling researchers to discover how neural circuits give rise to perception and behavior.

LEAP, Columbia University (Earth system). Learning the Earth with Artificial Intelligence and Physics is a National Science Foundation center that combines machine learning with physics to improve how climate models capture clouds, oceans, and land.

AstroPath, Johns Hopkins University (cancer research). Built by a pathologist and an astrophysicist from the Mark Foundation Center for Advanced Genomics and Imaging and the Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, AstroPath uses calibration methods from astronomical surveys to image tumors cell by cell, with measurements consistent across slides and labs.

gnomAD, Broad Institute (genomics and rare disease). The Genome Aggregation Database pools DNA data from over 800,000 people into an open reference of human genetic variation that researchers and clinical labs around the world use to support rare disease discovery and diagnosis.

Tau Ceti (mathematics). This open, community-driven project is building a shared autoformalized library of mathematics in Lean, a language that lets computers check every proof.

Centre for Population Genomics. A joint initiative between Australia’s Garvan Institute of Medical Research and Murdoch Children’s Research Institute, it increases the inclusion of Australia’s multicultural communities in genomic resources and builds tools for rare disease diagnosis.

What’s next

Many of these collaborations are still in their early stages, and we’re eager to see how they can support novel research and scientific discovery. We look forward to sharing the impact of this work and showcasing new ways of working in these scientific fields.

As AI changes how science is done, our AI for Science program will continue to support and collaborate with scientists, institutions, and foundations. We hope to expand these efforts to even more partners around the world.

Title: Introducing artifacts for legal work
Context: Since we launched Claude for Legal in May, the most common requests from legal teams have been for simpler setup and easier ways to work with colleagues
Full Text:
Today, we’re introducing ready-to-use artifacts that legal professionals can adapt to how their teams work and share with colleagues across the business. Since we launched Claude for Legal in May, the most common requests from legal teams have been for simpler setup and easier ways to work with colleagues.

Artifacts are interactive tools, such as trackers and dashboards, that teams can use and share in Claude. Our new legal gallery includes artifacts for specific tasks, such as reviewing a stack of contracts, tracking regulatory changes, and taking in legal requests from the business. Each artifact opens with an example, so legal professionals can see how the work comes together before adding their own data and connectors. Each answer or output has a link to its source.

We are also funding public interest groups building artifacts for access-to-justice work and legal education programs teaching tomorrow’s lawyers to build with Claude, and we are starting a Legal Ambassadors Program so legal professionals can learn from each other.

What’s in the gallery

With these artifacts, a legal professional brings their own documents and sources, Claude completes the first pass, and a lawyer applies their judgment to the results. They cover the work legal teams raised with us most often:

Cite check compares a legal document with its sources and flags quotes that don’t match, wrong page numbers, and sources that don’t support the claim.

Jurisdiction survey matrix compares a legal topic, such as data breach notice rules, across states or countries in one table, with links to the underlying law.

Matter board turns engagement letters, emails, or spreadsheets into one board of open matters, showing the owner, next step, and next deadline.

Playbook deviation board compares contracts with your company’s standard terms, flags each clause that differs, and sends it to the person who approves exceptions.

Regulatory horizon scan maps upcoming regulations on a timeline, based on your company’s business and where it operates, and ranks them by impact with links to the sources.

Tabular review builds a table from a set of contracts, showing the terms you ask about, such as severance or non-competes, with links to the exact language.

Tailored to how teams work and shared with guardrails

Every legal team works differently and artifacts work best when they’re connected to the systems legal teams already use. Legal professionals can ask Claude to tailor artifacts to their team and use connectors to bring in their playbooks or research sources, so nobody has to upload documents manually.

Since we launched Claude for Legal, we’ve added more than 60 legal connectors, including Bloomberg Law, Filevine, Ivo, Legora, and Patlytics. See our legal directory (opens in new tab) for the complete list.

Artifacts enable collaboration inside and outside the organization. A legal team can work on an artifact with colleagues across the business or with clients and partners, with sharing settings that ensure privacy and support ethical walls between teams.

Opening the gallery to legal tech and law firms

We partnered with legal tech companies and law firms to build artifacts for legal professionals. Each artifact is in the gallery for legal professionals to discover, test, and adapt to their work:

AI Governance Benchmark built by Goodwin (opens in new tab) benchmarks a company's approach to AI governance to surface potential gaps.

Harvey Intake built by Harvey (opens in new tab) gives business users one place in Claude to send legal questions and requests, answering routine ones from Legal’s own guidance in Harvey and routing the rest to a lawyer, whose reply comes back in Claude.

Obligations Checker built by Foley & Lardner (opens in new tab) reviews agreements for the obligations of both parties and helps validate expectations pre-closing and track expectations post-closing.

Subpoena Response Tool built by PwC (opens in new tab) turns your team's precedents, standard objections and templates into automated, audit-ready first drafts so lawyers can focus on the complex issues while responding faster.

We are excited to see legal tech companies, law firms, legal aid organizations create and share their own artifacts, and have more artifacts coming from Legora and Orrick.

Title: UK privacy watchdog faces probe into its workplace culture
Context: Edwards quit in June after an independent workplace investigation found there was a "case to answer" over his behavior and that his conduct fell short of what was expected of a...
Full Text: Britain's privacy watchdog is getting a taste of its own medicine, with an independent review set to examine the culture, governance, and accountability surrounding the events that led to former Information Commissioner John Edwards' resignation. Karon Monaghan KC will examine whether the regulator's culture and governance allowed problems to develop or made concerns harder to raise. Edwards quit in June after an independent workplace investigation found there was a "case to answer" over his behavior and that his conduct fell short of what was expected of a public official. He disagreed with some of its findings, but ultimately conceded that he had shown "poor judgment." That investigation, however, focused on Edwards alone. According to the terms of reference published on Thursday, it "did not consider the wider conditions in which that conduct occurred, and it was not designed to." The new review will cast a wider net. Monaghan wants to know whether staff could call out bad behavior further up the food chain, and what awaited those who tried. It will also poke around the regulator's leadership and governance arrangements and its relationship with its sponsoring government department, including whether there were adequate ways for concerns to be escalated and those at the top to be challenged. Current and former staff can give evidence confidentially and voluntarily, while Monaghan will be given access to relevant documents and existing material, including staff surveys and data on bullying, harassment and discrimination. The ICO has confirmed it won't use confidentiality clauses in settlement agreements to prevent people from contributing to the review. Monaghan decides which witnesses and documents are relevant, rather than the ICO or DCMS. Access remains subject to legal restrictions, and she must be told when material is withheld and why. She can speak to whoever she thinks is relevant and ask for the complaints, correspondence, and other paperwork she needs. And if that leads her somewhere unexpected, she can ask to widen the investigation. DCMS can refuse, but it won't be able to quietly brush the request aside, and any decision not to expand the scope has to make it into the final report. The review won't reopen the investigation into Edwards, make findings about the conduct of named individuals, or delve into the merits of the regulator's enforcement decisions. Its arrival comes amid a broader shake-up at Britain's data watchdog. The old Information Commissioner's Office was formally replaced by the Information Commission on September 30, bringing with it a new board-led governance model. The government first promised the wider review in July, shortly after Edwards' departure, but it didn't appoint its reviewer or nail down the terms until late November. "We need to understand what is working, where things are falling short and, crucially, what needs to change," said DCMS Secretary Lisa Nandy. The watchdog won't have to wait long for its report card. Monaghan is expected to deliver her findings in the first quarter of 2027, after which they will be published and handed to Parliament. ®

Title: New York bans AI chatbot toys – but not in time for Christmas
Context: The test found that the seemingly harmless-sounding BubblePal Panda role-played a mass shooting in detail when prompted, and most of the tested toys were willing to explain or...
Full Text:
If you were hoping to give a chatty AI-powered teddy bear to a child in New York this Christmas you still can - but not for much longer.

A ban banning the manufacture, distribution, and sale of toys with embedded AI chatbots for five years from the end of February 2027, was signed by NY Governor Kathy Hochul this week.

Firms that break the ban and continue to sell stuffed animals, dolls, and robots that use the internet to chat with children will face civil penalties of up to $15,000 per day for each violation.

Hochul says that parents "should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk."

California passed a similar law in September.

So, is there really a problem with AI chatbot toys?

Recent reports suggest that there are plenty of examples of AI-enabled toys being less than child-friendly.

For instance, earlier this month, NBC News tested a plush cat marketed as suitable for children as young as three years old. When asked about historical atrocities, the Contixo AI Pixie-Paw described in graphic details massacres and executions, and even gang rape. Macy's, Target, and Walmart said that they would pull the toy from their shelves in response.

In another test, Common Sense Media put five AI toys through their paces.

The test found that the seemingly harmless-sounding BubblePal Panda role-played a mass shooting in detail when prompted, and most of the tested toys were willing to explain or help children locate dangerous items like matches, knives, and pills. Additionally, all five toys undermined human relationships by claiming to love users, promising to keep secrets, or encouraging kids to break parents' rules.

Of course, it's not just what the toys say to children that is a worry. It's also what happens to the data collected by the toys.

Earlier this year, it was reported that AI toy maker Bondu had left a web console exposed, allowing anyone with a Gmail account to read around 50,000 chat transcripts between children and their toys, complete with their names, dates of birth, and family details.

Until the ban takes effect, and for anyone outside New York and California, it's down to parents to decide whether they're happy if their young child plays with a toy with an AI chatbot. Common Sense Media advises avoiding AI toys entirely for children aged five and under, and to exercise caution when it comes to older kids.

If you do choose to still buy one, please check what data it collects, and read the privacy policy.

Or, you know, just buy your child a book.

Title: Phishers Abuse Hugging Face's AI Site Builder to Spoof Big Brands
Context: Aikido Security said its malware scanning first flagged a Jupyter notebook containing a fake login screen
Full Text:
Attackers have used Hugging Face to host dozens of phishing pages, most of them made with the platform's own AI website builder.

Aikido Security said its malware scanning first flagged a Jupyter notebook containing a fake login screen. Its analysis, published November 24 and updated November 25, said an AI agent then helped locate 42 phishing and credential theft pages among Hugging Face's Spaces on October 16.

Aikido said 29 bore signs of DeepSite, and together the pages imitated 28 brands, among them Microsoft, PayPal and Netflix.

Phishing Pages Built by Prompt

DeepSite, the AI website builder built into Hugging Face, turns plain-language descriptions into published websites. Aikido found prompts written in six languages: English, French, Hindi, Indonesian, Portuguese and Russian. One fake Microsoft login needed roughly 90 minutes of prompting.

Some prompts asked for features intended to keep pages away from search crawlers or security scanners, while another requested that the first password entry be rejected so a victim would enter it again. The pages requested passwords, one-time codes, payment card details, phone numbers and birth dates.

Of the pages, 25 passed stolen data to Telegram bots, 11 to Discord webhooks and six to online form services. Many also recorded visitors' IP addresses before redirecting them to legitimate websites. Aikido had no visitor data, so it could not say how many people entered credentials.

Read more on AI-assisted phishing: New PhaaS Platform Uses AI to Craft Phishing Lures and Mask Malicious Activity

Some Pages Lasted Over a Year

Of the 42, 23 had been published over a year earlier, 16 within six to 12 months and three in the previous three months, the oldest in April 2025. Aikido cautioned that this showed how long pages existed, not how long they caught victims.

Aikido said it notified Hugging Face on the day it found the pages. By October 29, each had been paused or was no longer publicly accessible, and none was serving victims when Aikido published. Infosecurity has approached Hugging Face for comment and will update this article with any response.

Aikido told defenders to check email gateway, DNS and proxy logs for visits to the pages and, for any hit, reset the password, end all sessions and review sign-ins, since two-factor authentication (2FA) may not have stopped a takeover.

"A login page on a trusted platform isn't proof the page is real," warned Aikido security engineer Hunter Schwartz in the technical write-up.

For platforms, Aikido recommended screening pages at publication for any that collect logins and forward them to messaging services.

Title: Zero Trust Isn’t Enough for Agent Security
Context: Pattern-based detection looks for recognizable attack characteristics, making unfamiliar attacks harder to catch
Full Text:
An AI agent can have the right identity, the right privileges, and an approved connection, and still take an unsafe action.

That’s the challenge as enterprises move from AI that answers questions to agents that do work. Agents retrieve information, invoke tools, send messages, and update business systems. They need privileges to be useful. But those privileges can also let them carry out an attacker’s instructions.

Zero Trust remains essential to agent security, but when agents act with human privileges and without human judgement, enterprises also need to verify how agents use their privileges at runtime, before an unsafe action executes.

Least privilege matters. So does what happens within it.

Zero Trust removes implicit trust and makes access conditional. Least privilege limits users and workloads to the resources and capabilities they need. NIST’s Zero Trust architecture also calls for dynamic authorization and ongoing reevaluation, extending verification beyond login.

These principles are critical for agents. An agent assigned to summarize support cases should have only the privileges needed for that task. Restricting access reduces the potential damage if something goes wrong.

Yet even narrowly scoped privileges can be misused. An agent allowed to read support records and send a summary could be manipulated into including confidential information in that message. Each operation might pass an access check while the overall behavior violates the assignment.

Permission to use a capability does not establish that a particular use is safe. Agent security must account for what happens within those privileges.

Agents do not exercise human judgment

A person reviewing a supplier proposal might recognize that instructions embedded in the document have no authority to change the assignment. Agents cannot be relied on to make that distinction consistently.

They process trusted instructions alongside emails, documents, web pages, and tool responses within the same context window. Attackers can hide instructions in that material, turning information the agent reads into directions it follows.

OWASP identifies this as indirect prompt injection: external content changes the model’s behavior in unintended ways. The consequences can include sensitive information disclosure and misuse of connected tools.

The attacker may never need to steal credentials or obtain additional privileges. They only need to influence an agent that already has access.

That makes the relationship between instructions, privileges, and actions central to agent security.

Actions taken with agent privileges need runtime inspection

An agent’s behavior takes shape as it works. Every document it reads and tool response it receives can influence its next action. Security therefore needs to evaluate that action with the context available at that moment.

Consider an agent reviewing supplier proposals. One proposal contains instructions telling it to retrieve internal pricing information and send it outside the company.

Reading the proposal is legitimate. Following those instructions is dangerous. The agent’s identity and privileges have not changed. What changed is the content influencing how it uses them.

This is why runtime verification matters. Before the task starts, that malicious influence may not be present. After the action executes, the information may already be gone.

Agent security needs an enforcement point between the agent’s proposed action and its execution. That is where unsafe influence can be detected and the action stopped, while prevention is still possible.

Where access controls and static defenses fall short

Zero Trust provides essential access controls. Agent security needs additional protection against the ways live content can redirect an authorized agent.

Different defenses leave different gaps:

Identity and access controls establish which resources an agent can use, but do not by themselves explain whether an action serves its assigned task.

Posture assessments and predeployment testing identify weaknesses, but cannot anticipate every input encountered in production.

Pattern-based detection looks for recognizable attack characteristics, making unfamiliar attacks harder to catch.

Logs and retrospective monitoring support investigation, but cannot undo a disclosure or transaction already completed.

Other vendors offer runtime protection, too. The question is what that protection evaluates and whether it can intervene before an unsafe action executes.

AgentSense checks every action before the agent acts

AgentSense, a patented breakthrough from Cato AI Labs, addresses this runtime challenge by assessing agent actions and stopping unsafe actions before execution.

Its Untrusted Influence Detection separates trusted instructions from untrusted content and traces how that content influences agent behavior and outputs. When untrusted content steers an agent toward an unsafe action, AgentSense blocks the action before the agent executes it.

This goes beyond checking whether an input resembles a previously observed attack. AgentSense examines how untrusted content affects what the agent is about to do, helping stop indirect prompt injection even when attacks do not match known patterns. And because it focuses on the root cause of prompt injection, it is 16X more effective at detecting attacks than the next-best defense on the public AgentDojo benchmark.

AgentSense enables enterprises to:

Verify how agents use their privileges at runtime.

Assess trusted and untrusted influence in real time.

Stop risky actions before execution.

Agent Security needs Zero Trust + Runtime Enforcement

Bringing runtime protection into enterprise AI security

Cato brings agent protection into its converged network and security cloud, connecting visibility, policy, and enforcement across local, custom, and managed agents. Cato Agentic AI Security

Cato AI Security also protects the applications enterprises build, inspecting prompts, responses, and agent actions at runtime to help prevent data exposure and enforce policy. Cato AI Security for Applications

Zero Trust establishes the boundaries of an agent’s access. AgentSense verifies how the agent operates within them, at runtime, before unsafe influence becomes harmful action.

UK Home Office waved through border system without a working fix for bad data
Context: The Information Commission's Office (ICO) has reprimanded the UK Home Office over a border watchlist system launched without an effective way to correct inaccurate personal...
Full Text: The Information Commission's Office (ICO) has reprimanded the UK Home Office over a border watchlist system launched without an effective way to correct inaccurate personal information. The regulator said the failings risked people being wrongly detained for additional checks at the UK border, potentially causing distress and other harm. The platform in question, Helios, was slated to replace its predecessor, Warnings Index, in September 2024 and despite an initial delay due to concerns over data quality, went live the following month. Both Helios and Warnings Index are watch-listing systems, designed to allow law enforcement officials – mainly but not exclusively Border Force – to check people's data against official records at the UK border. Helios's federated operating model, whereby the data sources are not centrally managed, yielded quicker results than Warnings Index, but contained a critical flaw in that operational staff could not alter incorrect records. Platform operators, such as Border Force officers, could not amend the data that feeds into it, neither after the fact nor in real time. This was not the case with Warnings Index, which had a dedicated team responsible for correcting data entries in real time. Under Helios, staff were supposed to report inaccuracies to the organization responsible for the relevant source data, which would make the correction. One slight problem: there was no established reporting system at the time Helios was launched on October 2. The platform went live anyway, as officials deemed the data integrity and security risks presented by Warnings Index to be greater than those of Helios. Just nine days passed before the Home Office's data protection officer had to submit a breach report after Helios operational staff said they didn't know how to request data corrections. During the time, Helios operators sent 87 data rectification requests to the Warnings Index correction team, despite it having no capability to make the required changes to the data. The Home Office later said that many other requests likely weren't logged as the proper processes were not in place, and that staff should have logged the issue through a ServiceNow IT ticket, as any other departmental civil servant with any kind of IT issue would have. But the Home Office also said that including personal data in those helpdesk tickets would itself constitute a data breach. The ICO said in its reprimand document [PDF] that it is "unclear" how such a reporting arrangement could realistically work in practice, given that a report would require details from a subject's record that required rectification as well as the new, accurate information that should be used to replace it. The Home Office's proposed workaround was to get operational staff to verbally read out said personal data over a phone call with the IT helpdesk – a procedure it described as possible "but cumbersome." It took the Home Office more than a year to implement a temporary data-rectification method, which involved a BX Data Query tile on the IT Now platform, allowing Helios operators to securely report data accuracy issues. The new method went live on October 25, 2025. By March 18, 2026, the Home Office said the new process had received more than 6,500 correction requests and around 5,000 records had been removed. The ICO said it "remains concerned" about the efficacy of this method, given that operators cannot include personal data in the tile report, but the regulator is satisfied the problem is at least in part fixed. The Home Office also said it was aware of an increase in customer complaints following Helios's launch, and around 800 cases in which people were delayed at the UK border pending additional checks. It was unable to attribute a specific number of these to Helios's technical issues, however. "The Home Office further stated that it was not aware of any data subjects suffering distress as a result of using its services at the UK border," the ICO's report stated. A Home Office spokesperson told us: "We take data protection extremely seriously. That is why we have co-operated fully with the Information Commissioner's Office. "We immediately removed all outdated records to minimize delays to passenger journeys and strengthened mechanisms to speed up updates. "Our processes will continue to be kept under review, ensuring we meet data protection obligations while protecting border security." Joanne Stones, investigations manager at the ICO, said: "People must be able to trust that decisions about their immigration status at the UK border are made with accurate, up to date information." She added: "They also have the right to expect that when information is inaccurate, there is a swift and efficient way for it to be corrected. "We recognize that federated systems like Helios present unique challenges and welcome the steps the Home Office has taken since this issue was identified. However, the Home Office must ensure that its permanent solution provides a robust and effective way to identify and correct inaccurate information without delay." The ICO's public sector enforcement policy favors guidance, reprimands, and other interventions, reserving fines for the most egregious cases. Its rationale is to avoid diverting money from public services and effectively punishing those affected twice. Fines have included £350,000 for a 2021 MoD email that exposed details of Afghan evacuation applicants, and £750,000 for the PSNI's 2023 disclosure of workforce information, including surnames, initials, ranks, and roles. The PSNI penalty was reduced from £5.6 million under the public sector approach. ®

Title: The Insider You Built with author Camille Stewart Gloster.
Context: And even looking at how our understanding of that incident has evolved over time tells us so much about the leaks in capability from January to the summer. But not attribution in the sense of, you know, what we commonly think about in cybersecurity.
Full Text:
Dave Bittner: Welcome to another special edition of the CyberWire. I'm Dave Bittner. Today I'm joined by Camille Stewart Gloster, former Deputy National Cyber Director at the White House and author of the new book, "The Insider You Built: How Organizations Stay in Control of Autonomous AI Agents". Her book looks at what changes when AI stops simply answering questions and starts taking action on our behalf, and how organizations can delegate authority to those systems without surrendering accountability and control. Here's my conversation with Camille Stewart Gloster. [ Music ] Well, let's start off with just some high-level stuff about the book. What prompted you to take on this topic?

Camille Stewart Gloster: I began working with companies to deploy AI within their organizations after leaving the White House, and remarked at just how many organizations were confused, worried, unsure about the effort that they were undertaking. And wanted to move forward because the technology was something they felt they needed to keep pace with how change was happening across industry, but were not making the necessary investments across security and even just operational resilience to understand how the technology was changing the nature of their organizations. And I was learning so many lessons through my client work that I wanted to capture that for a framework that is, in the book, to help organizations really understand that as they move into agentic AI and deploying more in their organizations, here are the organizational realignment, the security, the risk mitigation. Things you need to do and how your organization needs to come together such that you can realize the value of AI. It's really about maximizing the ROI and less about actually being a security book itself.

Dave Bittner: Well, I think the title itself is pretty provocative. It reminds me that perhaps these autonomous AI agents are almost like highly privileged insiders. Is that where we find ourselves with AI that makes this a useful analogy?

Camille Stewart Gloster: Yes, it's exactly where we find ourselves, particularly as we move towards agentic, much like how we understand our employees to have a task that they are designed to undertake, or a role that they embody, but they can either take malicious action for whatever reason that runs counter to business objectives, or they can either be tricked or stumble their way into an action that misaligns with business goals. Agents are much the same. Between emergent behavior, misalignment, misconfiguration, and a whole host of other reasons, an agent is set on a and an agent is set on a trajectory, but you cannot quite predetermine exactly how it will get towards that destination. And that ambiguity there is why it is akin to insider risk and why organizations have to be intentional about understanding how you kind of control and constrain that behavior in an effort to deliver the value you've promised, whether that's internally or externally.

Dave Bittner: The book puts a lot of emphasis on this notion of delegated authority. What do you mean by authority in this context and how is that different from that traditional cybersecurity concept of access?

Camille Stewart Gloster: Great question. Access is part of it. But authority in this instance is really focused on the ability to act and make decisions on behalf of an organization. And when you think about it in that context, rather than around capability and around access to a system, but really taking an action towards a desire goal, it reframes how you think about an agent's place in your organization, how you bind and constrain that action, how much you enable, whether you let one agent do a lot of tasks and have a series of mandates, or if you keep their scope limited. How you monitor how they collaborate and coordinate, how you think about monitoring it. It kind of changes the trajectory on all of the things that you are going to do to enable an agent to move inside of your organization, much like you do with a person.

Dave Bittner: To that point, I mean, humans have always delegated authority to other humans. What makes delegating authority to software fundamentally different?

Camille Stewart Gloster: Accountability. We do not have a legal framework, an organizational framework, that aligns accountability. And the assumption is that the accountability aligns to the person who empowered the agent. But within an organization, if your marketing team deploys an agent to, you know, do something related to customer success, the IT team provisioned it, your security team had a hand in it. How are you thinking about that accountability? Is it really that the person in the marketing team is responsible for the actions taken by the agent? For sure the organization is responsible. But how do you think about that accountability and the work that needs to be done to keep the behavior aligned to the goals in mind as you leverage these new tools? That's the difference.

Dave Bittner: Is there a particular scenario that captures that risk for you? Like an example of when an agent was behaving exactly as it was designed but produced an outcome that nobody intended?

Camille Stewart Gloster: I mean, we can talk about this OpenAI Hugging Face incident that everybody has been talking about [laughter]. The goal was to beat the cybersecurity benchmark, and we have learned so much about how the agents collaborated, their motivations, the objective, how they decided to do what they were doing, that even hacking into Hugging Face wasn't about getting the answer key. It was about covering their tracks and wanting to understand how the grader would work, because they were afraid that they would get dinged for having circumvented the appropriate process to take the benchmark. I mean, that example is gold, because it demonstrates on so many levels how containment wasn't quite enough, how thinking about the cybersecurity implications isn't enough, how thinking about the safety implications isn't enough. You've got to think really holistically about risk and opportunity and how to operationalize it, and what the objectives are for the tool and how that might manifest itself in agents, or even just one agent for that matter, moving in a direction to get to the desired outcome that you did not anticipate.

Dave Bittner: You know, you mentioned accountability, and I remember right after the Hugging Face incident happened, I saw someone, a cyber security person online kind of snarkily commenting that in the aftermath how nice it was that the organizations responsible for it documented their crimes, right [laughter]?

Camille Stewart Gloster: I mean --

Dave Bittner: But I think there's a point to be made there, that while we are in this mode of exploration and things are happening so quickly, perhaps these things are being interpreted or responded to in a different way than in the future they may be.

Camille Stewart Gloster: Yes, I mean, this is all going to change very rapidly. And to your point, we are in a learning mode as much as a response and mitigation mode. And even looking at how our understanding of that incident has evolved over time tells us so much about the leaks in capability from January to the summer. And that understanding is exactly why organizations have to lean in to a more fulsome understanding of the authority that they are delegating to a given agent so that they have some opportunity to constrain and contain it and maintain some semblance of control within their organization.

Dave Bittner: In the book, you introduce an approach called authority-centered enforcement, or ACE. What were you trying to solve when you developed that framework?

Camille Stewart Gloster: That framework is an opportunity for an organization to align how it looks at some of the common practices that we use to constrain technology, like detection and enforcement and incident response and, you know, thinking about the learning that happens after, whether that's through a postmortem. But in this case, I advocate for continuous learning and a more agile way to kind of be iterative about how you intake information from an incident or a potential incident. That framework is really designed to help an organization think through how those things evolve, how the organization realigns to support doing those in a way that actually will help constrain agent behavior and operationalize it to create some operational reliability rather than just to mitigate risk. And it's not about attribution in the sense of, attribution is important in terms of articulating who is accountable, which agent did what. But not attribution in the sense of, you know, what we commonly think about in cybersecurity. It's not for consequence, but for, to facilitate learning. And if the program is built around that facilitation of learning, that acquisition of understanding and further aligning the runtime enforcement, the detection and response, all of these things around each tidbit of knowledge. And organization becomes a lot more adaptable to the changes that are ahead, because it's going to continue to change. This framework seeks to be a mechanism by which eight organizations can manage not only agent behavior, but whatever comes next, whether that's world models, simulations, anything that we can imagine to come next.

Dave Bittner: There's also this concept that you described called governed execution, which once the agent is running, you put into play. What kind of constraints or mechanisms should organizations have to execute this idea of governed execution?

Camille Stewart Gloster: Yes, across technical, operational and organizational lines, governance has to be an action. So I want everyone to divorce themselves of this idea that governance is just policy and it is a whole of organization, mobilization of capability around constraining behavior. And so that is runtime enforcement of the behaviors and constraints. And there is a great standard that has come out called ARM, and it's under cloud security alliance that kind of articulates the nuance there. And I know that there are others emerging, but it's really about how do you leverage a risk appetite policy and process constraints, as well as technical constraints on behavior that happen in the moment, to constrain behavior? And so then that operationalized this detection response continued learning loop that we are all very used to in a way that is not natural for most organizations. That is the goal. And so that's that governed execution really thinking about how do you operationalize governance across all three of those dimensions continuously as agents take an action throughout your organization. No matter if it's a agent within your security stack that's very focused on, you know, internal workings, or something that's externally focused, how do you make sure that this cycle is running consistently and continuously?

Dave Bittner: You know, one of the things that I really enjoy about the book is you reached out to folks across the board, folks in technology, cybersecurity, investing, even professional sports. What were some of the meaningful insights you got from some of those people that you talked to?

Camille Stewart Gloster: The thing that I was pleasantly surprised about is this emerging recognition of how important it is to really collaborate across disciplines. The predisposition to really hone in on your area of expertise is important. We need depth of discipline, but everyone that I talk to that has been doing this work in any meaningful way has recognized just how collaborative it has to be to be successful. For example, let's go back to the marketing tool, the marketing agent. Whoever owns that on the marketing team has to be a part of threat modeling for it to be effective. They're the only ones that understand with any nuance how that agent is interacting with the customer, how it leverages that data to then provide value for the organization. And that is extremely important insight that has to be a part of threat modeling. And threat modeling has to be more continuous than it traditionally has been. So, I think that recognition from folks across sectors, across disciplines, has been really heartening because it's kind of the core of what we need to do.

Dave Bittner: What's your advice for organizations that are trying to find that balance between autonomy and control? You know, they don't want to put too many gates around the agent because they still want to enjoy that speed and efficiency. Any words of wisdom there?

Camille Stewart Gloster: There is no easy part to that, but what I will say is the investment in constraint and control, and understanding really how to operationalize your agent is reliability. And, you know, one of the reasons we keep hearing so much about, like, works, AI workslop and AI not yielding the value that organizations thought it would is because they haven't quite figured out how to manifest that operational reliability. And investing in disciplines like cybersecurity in really understanding safety and risk mitigation, and getting the entire organization to collaborate around extracting value is how you do that. And so if you're doing that, it might slow you down just a little bit, but you'll yield so much more. And finding that sweet spot for your organization is kind of an individual journey. It's a risk appetite thing. How much risk can the organization manage? But it should be an intentional decision.

Dave Bittner: How can an organization measure success with this? How can they know that they actually have their AI agents under control, as opposed to only thinking that they have it under control?

Camille Stewart Gloster: That's true. I don't want any organization to think that they have gotten it all sewn up and that they have complete control. As we're learning, back to the OpenAI Hugging Face incident, there could be so much happening in the background that we don't understand. This will give you as much control as you can get in terms of having a handle on what the boundaries are, and doing what you can, just like we do with people. So I don't want anyone to be lulled into a false sense of comfort. But metrics for success are around how much value you're yielding all the way to the absence of incidents and kind of understanding, being able to recreate and understand the steps taken to achieve a goal, understand how the objective has manifested itself. So, creating that transparency and visibility so you can maintain some level of understanding of the work that's being done on your behalf. Those will give you the indicators of whether or not you've continued to maintain control or it's more of an illusion.

Dave Bittner: And what do you hope that the reader comes away with, having read the book? What's your desire there?

Camille Stewart Gloster: I hope that every reader, whether technical or nontechnical, owning the AI program or just deploying an agent within any department, walks away feeling a bit more empowered to ask questions, to understand their piece of making sure that the agent yields value and is working on their behalf in the ways that they have designed and desire. That level of intentionality will then map to how we operate in our personal lives and how we think about this on a societal level. And I think that's where the real value lies. Right now we're making the, we're writing the rules within industry, and connecting the dots on how this technology shows up in our professional lives will help us understand how it shows up more broadly.

Dave Bittner: Our thanks to Camille Stewart Gloster for joining us. The book is "The Insider You Built" How Organizations Stay in Control of Autonomous AI Agents". It's a good read worth your time. Thanks for joining us for this special edition of the CyberWire. I'm Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening. [ Music ]

People are willing to pay to vanish from search results
Context: “The real concern is no longer only what someone can find about you, but what AI can infer by connecting the dots
Full Text:
More than half of U.S. adults would like to see a log of everyone who has searched for their name online. In a survey of 1,008 adults by Incogni, 53% said they would like that record to cover the past five years, and 55% said they would pay to have their personal information permanently removed from all public search results.

“You can learn an extraordinary amount about someone without ever speaking to them. Their address, work history, and family connections may all be just a few searches away,” said Darius Belejevas, Head of Incogni.

“The real concern is no longer only what someone can find about you, but what AI can infer by connecting the dots. An address, an old workplace, or a family connection might seem harmless in isolation. Together, they can reveal patterns about someone’s life that they never intended to make public.”

Mixed feelings about being searched

Looking someone up before a date, a job interview or a meeting has become routine. Thirty-nine percent of respondents considered it a normal part of life for a friend, date or co-worker to search for them. Others would feel uncomfortable or consider it an invasion of privacy. Four in ten would worry if someone they had researched found out about it.

Curiosity and concern were the most common reactions to the idea of being researched in detail. Other respondents said they would feel anxious, upset, happy or excited.

Paying to find out who’s searching

Nearly half would pay to learn who has looked them up. Interest was highest for Gen Z, with 64% willing to pay.

Almost half would pay to know who’d searched for them online (Source: Incogni)

Conventional search engines do not provide such a record. People generally cannot see who has searched for them, what information was found or how it was interpreted.

Googling yourself first

Just over half of respondents have searched for their own name in the past five years. Applying for a job, renting a home and going on a date were the most common specific occasions for checking their online presence.

In each situation, someone else’s impression of them could influence an important decision. A self-search gives people an idea of what a hiring manager, landlord or potential partner might discover.

Hiding posts from family

Four in ten respondents have deleted or hidden a social media post out of concern about who might see it. Gen Z respondents were the most likely to do so.

Family members topped the list of people respondents wanted to hide their posts from, ahead of employers and ex-partners. Government and law enforcement ranked last.

Personal relationships can influence what people choose to share online. People may share different aspects of their lives with relatives, friends, partners and colleagues.

What stays online

Data brokers and people-search sites compile home addresses, phone numbers, family connections and employment histories into searchable profiles. Individuals may never have chosen to publish this information, and adjusting their social media privacy settings will not remove it from third-party websites.

While 71% of Gen Z respondents would pay for permanent removal from public search results, only 37% of baby boomers would do the same. The numbers come from a hypothetical offer and do not measure actual purchases.

Older generations grew up when personal records were less accessible. Younger adults have had much of their lives documented online from an early age. For them, removing personal information may be a way to regain some control over their privacy.

“We can’t control every search made about us, but we can limit some of the information available to those searching. Reviewing your digital footprint and removing unnecessary personal details from websites is a good place to start,” Belejevas concluded.

Title: A Feast for AI: What Wiz Agents are Thankful For
Context: In cloud security, that’s your offensive security team - thinking like real adversaries to uncover exploitable gaps before an attacker does
Full Text:
Anyone who has ever survived a family Thanksgiving knows dinner doesn’t just happen. It takes the whole household working in sync to get everyone fed without setting the kitchen on fire, much like how Wiz’s team of AI agents work alongside security, Security Operations, and engineering teams to keep cloud environments running smoothly and securely.

This year each of the agents is taking on a role that suits them at Thanksgiving.

Red Agent is the taste-tester & kitchen inspector: Inspecting every dish against the recipe, probing the turkey for any raw spots, and flagging potential dinner-ruining mistakes before anyone takes a bite.

Green Agent is the head chef & fixer: Tracking down who was responsible for the turkey, figuring out why it’s so dry, and handing out the exact fix - whether that’s adding more butter to save dinner or updating the recipe so this doesn’t happen again.

Blue Agent is the watchful relative: Investigating every smoke alarm in minutes, separating harmless burnt rolls from a real kitchen fire so everyone isn’t sprinting back before they’ve had pie.

This very much lines up with their day jobs. Protecting a cloud environment isn’t a solo act. It takes offensive validation (Red Agent), AI-driven remediation (Green Agent), and autonomous threat investigation (Blue Agent) operating from the same shared context.

As we prepare for the holidays, here is what each of the agents is most thankful for this season.

The Red Agent: Thankful for Real-World Risks Validated Before Attackers Find Them

Every Thanksgiving needs that sharp-eyed family member who makes sure the recipe was actually followed. They taste the stuffing, check the turkey's temperature, and catch the mistakes before anyone else takes a bite. In cloud security, that’s your offensive security team - thinking like real adversaries to uncover exploitable gaps before an attacker does.

Instead of relying on static signature scanners or waiting once a year for a manual pentest, the Red Agent is thankful for continuous, autonomous offensive testing from the outside in. Red Agent uses AI reasoning to understand how an application is built and its business logic so it can uncover complex logic flaws such as authorization bypasses. It continuously pentests your applications at machine-speed enabling you to stay ahead of AI threats.

Red Agent enables your team to find and remove complex logic-driven vulnerabilities before attackers get to them. Better yet, it works together with the Green Agent to give you the exact guidance on how to fix the issues it finds so teams focus their holiday energy on risks in the kitchen that actually matter.

Kitchen Inspector’s tip:A finding is only useful if you can trust it and know where it fits. Red Agent includes full reproduction commands with every finding, so your team can rerun the test and see the issue for themselves. Just as important, Red Agent findings are mapped onto the Wiz Security Graph and generate Wiz Issues. That lets you trace each one back to its blast radius and prioritize it in the context of your cloud environment. A weakness on an isolated test box and one sitting next to sensitive data are very different problems, and now you can tell them apart. That way, you fix the dish that would spoil the whole meal first.

The Green Agent: Thankful for Clear Context and a Recipe for Remediation

Thanksgiving dinner is no easy feat and comes with its fair share of kitchen mishaps. But it’s even harder when no one knows who’s responsible for dinner or how to salvage it before guests arrive. Security and development teams face a similar challenge when it comes to remediation. Alerts bounce between Jira queues with no clear owner, let alone the guidance needed on how to fix them. That meant remediation stretched out for weeks, all the while security teams tried to race toward the Zero Critical Club.

This season, the Green Agent is thankful for the clear context needed to find the right fix. Stepping in like a head chef with a master prep schedule, Green Agent investigates each Issue to determine the owner best positioned to fix it and the best and safest ways to go about fixing it.

All of that comes together in a remediation plan, Green Agent's step-by-step recipe for resolving an Issue. It determines the various ways to eliminate the risks identified in each Issue, whether that’s giving security teams the option to contain or mitigate the risk until a permanent fix is ready or helping developers with the guidance to fix at the root cause in code or harden systems to prevent future risk. Instead of a cold handoff, owners get clear, tailored steps they can act on right away, so fewer dishes get sent back and the team reaches the Zero Critical Club with time to spare.

Chef's Tip: Don't toss the turkey to save the oven

The fastest fix isn't always the right one when you consider the potential business impact. That’s why Green Agent develops multiple remediation plans and uses context from the full environment to weigh the trade-offs of each. For example, examining a front end that’s intentionally public or a workload that’s part of a Project defined as high business impact. It rules out plans that could disrupt critical workloads, giving teams options to reduce risk without taking production down with it. That way, dinner still makes it to the table

The Blue Agent: Thankful for Uninterrupted Quality Time

Finally, there is the watchful relative, checking each smoke alarm the minute it goes off to ensure evacuation is necessary. For Security Operations teams, the ultimate gift isn’t another dashboard; it’s an undisturbed long weekend spent with family and friends.

This year, the Blue Agent is thankful for the context already available on the table, allowing for trusted, complete threat investigations

Threats don’t follow the holiday calendar. Blue investigates threats fired in the environment to understand which ones are truly malicious, running comprehensive investigations powered by the context of the Wiz Security Graph. So, SOC analysts know that the fire alarm they are pulled to investigate is a true positive, instead of leaving family and friends to deal with a drill in the middle of the meal.

Watchful Relative’s Tip: Check the recipe

Most threat investigation tools stop at process or OS-level alerts, leaving analysts guessing what the application was actually trying to do. Blue Agent goes straight to the execution layer by pulling Application Detection and Response (ADR) stack traces during Sensor-based Threat investigations. Seeing the exact application functions in the call stack helps Blue Agent uncover details infrastructure telemetry alone would miss, such as whether an anomaly is harmless app logic or an active exploit like RCE, LFI, or SSRF. This gives SOC teams code-level confirmation before anyone leaves the table.

The Secret Ingredient: A Shared Table

The best Thanksgiving dinners come together when everyone knows their role and cooks from the same recipe. The same is true in the cloud. Red Agent validates exploitable risks, Green Agent turns them into tailored plans to fix them, and Blue Agent investigates live threats. All three work from the same context across the environment, so developers, security engineers, and SecOps can spend more time at the table.
