Title: Make post-quantum cryptography updates routine with AWS-LC
Context: Standards are revised and flaws are found in implementations
Full Text:
As your organization plans upgrades to post-quantum cryptography (PQC), you should also think about cryptographic agility to more easily update algorithms used to protect your data. Changes to cryptography and related protocols aren’t new, but PQC is accelerating the pace at which organizations must add new algorithms and remove old ones to keep up with changing regulations and evolving business risk. AWS believes our key to success is standardizing on one cryptographic library that embodies three key properties: compatibility, assurance, and performance. In this blog post, you’ll learn how we think of the cost and friction of ongoing cryptographic updates in terms of these properties. You’ll learn how AWS built AWS-LC to embody these properties, thus making cryptographic upgrades straightforward and low-impact for ourselves and our customers. For custom applications where you can’t yet use AWS services and must operate your own stacks, this post also shares why you might consider using AWS-LC as your standardized library.

Every cryptographic algorithm used to protect your data today has an expiration date, even if no regulator has set one yet. Algorithms that were once the standard, such as MD5 and SHA-1, have been retired. Standards are revised and flaws are found in implementations. The move to post-quantum cryptography is the current wave of changes, with dates set by governments and regulators to complete the transition. PQC itself will progress in phases to enable hybrid and pure post-quantum algorithms and then deprecate traditional cryptography. Each change reaches your systems as a software library update, so the practical question is how often you can roll out a new version of your cryptographic library, and what each rollout costs. At AWS, we think of this cost in terms of three properties. Compatibility means an update doesn’t require application changes. Assurance means new code can be trusted when it ships, without a long bake period. Performance means a new algorithm doesn’t add so much computational overhead or latency that it gives teams a reason to wait. This post describes how AWS-LC provides each property, and how you can apply the same approach to the cryptography you own.

AWS-LC is the general-purpose cryptographic library that AWS maintains and uses across its services. It is derived from BoringSSL, which originated from OpenSSL. If you’ve called an AWS API, AWS-LC was used on the server side. Through s2n-tls, it provides hybrid post-quantum key exchange on AWS service endpoints and in services like Application Load Balancer and Network Load Balancer. It’s also the cryptography under aws-lc-rs for Rust, the default provider for rustls, and under the Amazon Corretto Crypto Provider for Java. Because so much of AWS depends on one library, we built it to be updated often. AWS-LC keeps an OpenSSL-compatible API so applications can replace algorithms without a rewrite. It uses formal verification to prove selected algorithm implementations correct. It optimizes algorithm implementations to reduce the latency and compute costs that new algorithms add. The same properties work outside AWS. For example, 1Password used AWS-LC to move its clients to hybrid post-quantum key exchange with no application code changes.

Hand off what you can, standardize what you keep

Each piece of cryptography you own is one more thing to change at every transition. By owning as little of your cryptographic stack as your constraints or requirements allow, and using AWS services to manage the rest, you can minimize your ongoing responsibility and operational risk.

If your workload relies solely on managed services like AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) and managed resources like Elastic Load Balancer or Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS), you’re already reaping the benefits of AWS-LC and the AWS shared responsibility model. You only need to keep your clients and resource configurations updated. Many organizations can rely on AWS to provide the infrastructure and basic automation, but still own and manage the endpoints and applications where most of the work happens. For these components, it’s helpful to standardize on as few cryptographic libraries as possible. With fewer libraries, your team learns each one well: how to configure it, run it, and update it. The library you standardize on also decides how often you can update it. If an update requires application changes, ships new code that no one trusts yet, or adds compute and latency, teams have a reason to wait. In the rest of this post, we show you how AWS-LC removes each of those reasons through compatibility, assurance, and performance.

Compatibility

The best library update is one that doesn’t impact your application and that your users don’t notice. Code changes happen at three points: adopting a library, adding an algorithm, and updating the library. AWS-LC keeps each one small.

Adopting AWS-LC – For TLS, AWS-LC libssl keeps an OpenSSL-compatible API, so most applications that use OpenSSL for TLS build against it with small changes. Applications that call libcrypto directly might need more work, because the AWS-LC libcrypto API differs from OpenSSL’s in places. See the porting guide for where behavior differs.

Adding an algorithm – When new algorithms are added in AWS-LC behind interfaces applications already call, s2n-tls, s2n-quic, aws-lc-rs, and the Amazon Corretto Crypto Provider adopt them automatically. Hybrid ML-KEM key exchange, for example, is enabled through existing TLS configuration APIs. For 1Password, that meant a one-line Cargo.toml change and no application code changes.

Updating the library – AWS-LC long-term support (LTS) releases keep a stable application binary interface (ABI). Applications link once, then take library updates without a rebuild. One update reaches every application on the host when each process restarts. The Amazon Linux 2027 preview uses this method to ship AWS-LC as a system library.

We built these properties so AWS services could move to AWS-LC with minimal effort. aws-lc-rs is also used by open source projects; it’s the default cryptography provider for rustls with over 100 million downloads in the past 90 days, CPython tests against AWS-LC in continuous integration, and HAProxy publishes packages built on it. Each new use surfaces problems earlier in the update process, and every fix is recorded in one codebase.

Assurance

Every new algorithm arrives as new code, and new code is where bugs and security vulnerabilities are usually found. If you can’t trust new code when it ships, you wait, and each wait delays the next change. Tests check the inputs you run, and proofs check every input. AWS-LC uses machine-checked proofs for its most critical code, including its post-quantum algorithms and parts of its classical algorithms, such as its 25519 elliptic-curve code.

AWS-LC contributes to and takes its ML-KEM and ML-DSA code from two open source projects: mlkem-native and mldsa-native. The algorithmic implementations in these projects already incorporate formal verification safeguards such as ensuring no out of bound memory access, no integer overflows, constant assembly run time, and functional correctness using tools like CBMC and HOL Light (for more information, see Verifying and optimizing post-quantum cryptography at Amazon). AWS-LC imports this code from upstream without changing it. The proofs don’t depend on instruction order, so the assembly can be re-optimized without redoing them. That prevents verification from becoming the reason a faster implementation waits. Other cryptographic implementations of the library are verified in s2n-bignum.

We use these proofs alongside testing and FIPS validation. For workloads that require FIPS 140-3, a validated module is required to allow new code to be deployed. AWS-LC FIPS 3.0 was the first cryptographic library to include ML-KEM in a FIPS 140-3 validation. ML-DSA, the NIST post-quantum signature standard (FIPS 204), is in the AWS-LC FIPS 4.0 module, and the FIPS 5.0 module includes the faster, formally verified mldsa-native implementation. Both have been submitted to NIST for validation.

Performance

A new algorithm that costs more to run gives teams a reason to delay, and across many connections a small cost per connection adds up. AWS-LC optimizes each algorithm it adds so that cost doesn’t delay the update. Amazon Science reports 2.0 to 2.4 times more ML-KEM operations per second than the reference implementations across Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance types. Earlier work applied the same approach to 25519 elliptic-curve cryptography. The optimized code is covered by the proofs described in the previous section, so speed doesn’t reduce assurance.

ML-DSA followed the same path. AWS-LC moved from its original implementation to mldsa-native, with optimized assembly for AArch64 and x86_64 platforms, and it now signs and verifies faster on both Graviton and x86 EC2 instance types. As a result, compute is no longer the main cost of post-quantum signatures: in the measurements in the following section, we show that ML-DSA-44 certificates lowered average TLS handshake latency compared with RSA-2048. What remains is size, which the next section measures.

What it costs to move

AWS services handle billions of requests every second, so anything that could affect those requests must be carefully considered. Post-quantum cryptography impacts the performance of every new TLS connection, so before we adopted ML-KEM and ML-DSA, we invested heavily in making them fast. Figure 1 shows the resulting reduction in time for both key exchange and authentication. Today, moving to PQ confidentiality has no net cost for most AWS use-cases, and PQ authentication takes less compute than the RSA certificates we use today.

Figure 1. ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-87 time per handshake, before and after AWS-LC’s native implementations, on AWS Graviton4

ML-KEM-768 key exchange decreased by over 50 percent on both the client and the server (as shown in Figure 1); we described how in Verifying and optimizing post-quantum cryptography at Amazon. In this post, we’re focusing on ML-DSA. In AWS-LC v1.49.1, ML-DSA used the original AWS-LC implementation, adapted from the reference code. In v5.10.0, it runs on mldsa-native, which implements the performance-critical kernels in hand-written Arm64 Neon assembly for AWS Graviton, including: the number-theoretic transform (NTT) and its inverse, tuned for Arm cores with the SLOTHY superoptimizer, along with pointwise multiplication, rejection sampling, and the decompose, hint, and norm-check steps of signing and verification. It also expands the public matrix four entries at a time using the AWS-LC four-way parallel SHA-3 (Keccak). These optimizations, as shown in the right half of Figure 1, reduced ML-DSA-87 signing time on the server and verification time on the client, and the same assembly is covered by the formal proofs described earlier. mldsa-native is open source, part of the PQ Code Package in the Linux Foundation’s Post-Quantum Cryptography Alliance (PQCA), and the AWS Cryptography team and Amazon Automated Reasoning Group contribute to it.

Figure 2. TLS 1.3 connection setup time by algorithm, between two AWS Graviton4 hosts in the same Availability Zone

Figure 2 shows total handshake time for various configurations, when the client and server are in the same AWS Region. For a baseline, we used TLS performance when the server prioritized ECDHE with P-256 for key exchange and RSA-2048 certificates for authentication. With the optimizations to ML-KEM, there is negligible overhead from moving to hybrid ML-KEM key exchange (the second bar from left). The hybrid key exchange preferred in AWS systems today pairs X25519 with ML-KEM-768. X25519 is faster than P-256, and that saving covers the remaining ML-KEM work, so a full connection setup takes roughly 12 microseconds more, which doesn’t meaningfully impact throughput or latency. It’s worth noting here that ML-KEM-768 introduces approximately 2.3 KB to the handshake.

PQ authentication carries more risk, because authentication is more of the handshake cost. The server signs once for each handshake, and the client verifies three signatures: the server’s handshake signature, the signature on the leaf, and the signature on the intermediate certificate. RSA-2048 signing is expensive and verification is inexpensive. ML-DSA-87 reverses that balance, shifting some work from the server to the client.

ML-DSA keys and signatures are also much larger, so the server’s handshake messages grow from 4–7 KB to 17–24 KB depending on the chosen certificate parameters. That adds certificate parsing on the client and more data to encrypt and send on the server. Within an Availability Zone, those messages still arrive in one round trip, and we measured no difference in network time between configurations.

Compared to RSA 2048, which is still prevalent today, ECDSA offers faster processing. However, both must be replaced by ML-DSA for post-quantum authentication. With the optimizations in AWS-LC, ML-DSA-44 comes close to ECDSA, and every ML-DSA parameter set is significantly faster than RSA-2048, as shown in Figure 2. As a result, we’re confident in managing the performance impact from migrating to post-quantum certificates.

Another facet of our investments in reducing performance impact is session resumption. Handshake costs apply only to new connections. Session resumption reduces how often that cost is paid. A resumed TLS 1.3 handshake authenticates with a key from the earlier session and sends no certificates or signatures, so the larger ML-DSA keys and signatures apply only to full handshakes. We’ll note here that in psk_dhe_ke mode, the resumed handshake still runs a fresh hybrid ML-KEM key exchange, which preserves forward secrecy. Now, resumption only helps if the client can present its ticket to any server behind the endpoint, so AWS has been extending support for resumption across the hosts behind its service endpoints. AWS SDKs can reuse connections across many requests, and session resumption can skip certificates and signatures entirely, which gives the most performance benefit for workloads using AWS managed services. If you’re using AWS-LC directly in your own custom applications, consider keeping session tickets enabled, prefer TLS 1.3 with psk_dhe_ke, and reuse clients so that they keep their tickets between connections.

Conclusion

Every cryptographic choice has an expiration date, so the goal isn’t to pick the right algorithm once and never replace or update it, but to make each replacement routine. Start by handing off what you can to AWS services and standardizing what you keep on as few libraries as possible. For the cryptography you own, three properties decide how quickly and how often you can implement each update. For compatibility, new algorithms arrive behind the APIs your applications already call, and long-term support releases keep a stable ABI, so adopting one takes a library update and a restart, not a rebuild. For assurance, machine-checked proofs cover a library’s most critical code, ML-KEM is inside a FIPS 140-3 validated module, and ML-DSA is in modules submitted for validation. For performance, optimized implementations keep each new algorithm from adding compute or latency that might give teams a reason to wait. Post-quantum cryptography is the change in front of us now, and it won’t be the last.

Full Text:
Welcome to this month’s AWS Security news! Organizations need current information about AWS Security developments to maintain their cloud security. This monthly digest covers key AWS Security updates. Each month, we compile new announcements, features, and resources to help you improve your security. Based on AWS Security developments, you’ll find expert perspectives in blogs, announcements of new features and capabilities, ready-to-use code samples, reference architectures, and hands-on workshops and labs to build practical security skills. Not every edition will include all of these categories, but we’ll consistently bring you the most relevant and impactful updates to help you enhance your security and governance posture.

AWS Security Blog posts

October brought 19 AWS Security Blog posts focused on the remediation flow, from a security finding to a tested fix. Learn how AI agents can find, confirm, and repair vulnerabilities, and how to add penetration testing to every deployment. You’ll also find guidance on extending existing access controls to AI agents with trusted identity propagation and preparing your signing workflows for post-quantum cryptography. The PHP2Shell posts show why patch timelines for internet-facing systems are now measured in hours, and how AWS WAF can help reduce risk while you upgrade. Other posts cover identity source changes in AWS IAM Identity Center, workload identity outside AWS, and domain-based filtering in AWS Network Firewall.

Threat detection and incident response

AWS Continuum sets a new standard in autonomous code security Authors: Alexander Greaves-Tunnell, Neha Rungta | Published: October 5, 2026 AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities achieved an 89.0 percent end-to-end success rate on the CyberGym-E2E benchmark. It found, demonstrated, and repaired vulnerabilities in real open source codebases, 23.1 percentage points above the previous public high.

Part 1 – Cybersecurity journeys: I didn’t plan this Author: Shannon Brazil | Published: October 7, 2026 The first post in a four-part Cybersecurity Awareness Month series shares how 11 AWS security professionals moved into security from unexpected backgrounds, showing there’s no single path into the field.

GuardDuty Extended Threat Detection has added five new indicators to surface attack sequences Authors: Aman Khare, Kyle Koeller | Published: October 12, 2026 Learn to use five new indicator types in Amazon GuardDuty Extended Threat Detection: vulnerability, malicious package, reachability, misconfiguration, and sensitive data. They bring signals from Amazon Inspector, Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) Reachability Analyzer, Amazon Macie, and AWS Security Hub into sequence findings, and the post shows how to add them to your incident response workflow.

Part 2 – Cybersecurity journeys: What even is this job? Author: Shannon Brazil | Published: October 13, 2026 The second post in the series covers lesser-known security roles. These include measuring risk across a million applications, building detection tools from the customer service side, and securing infrastructure launched into orbit.

Penetration testing every deployment with AWS Continuum Authors: Jigar Bhatt, Benjamin Li | Published: October 14, 2026 Learn to add AWS Continuum for penetration testing (formerly AWS Security Agent) to your continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) pipeline as a check after each deployment. It tests only the change you deployed to staging and can stop that change from reaching production when a finding meets a severity threshold you set. The post includes an example for GitHub Actions.

AWS Security Agent (now part of AWS Continuum) exploited 33 of 37 new real-world CVEs Authors: Dazhi Zhang, Hamed Soleimani | Published: October 15, 2026 AWS Continuum for penetration testing was tested against a new internal benchmark of 37 recently disclosed CVEs in live, containerized applications. Starting from a low-privilege position, it confirmed 33 of the 37 vulnerabilities end to end through the intended path, an 89.2 percent success rate.

Amazon Threat Intelligence identifies PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure in MadPot Author: CJ Moses | Published: October 21, 2026 Amazon Threat Intelligence detected activity targeting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) on its MadPot sensors four days before public disclosure. The post explains what this means for security leaders: patch critical internet-facing systems within hours, and start investigations from the earliest activity seen, not the disclosure date.

Part 3 – Cybersecurity journeys: The work behind the work Author: Shannon Brazil | Published: October 27, 2026 The third post in the series looks at the day-to-day work of AWS security professionals that rarely gets attention. October security bulletins

In October 2026, AWS published 41 security bulletins addressing vulnerabilities across open source SDKs, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, AI agent frameworks, embedded software, and widely used runtimes. The AI agent tool surface remained the main theme. An authentication bypass in Loom for AWS could allow network clients to gain administrative access to the agent control plane, and the AWS API MCP Server accepted OAuth tokens issued to other applications. Prompt-injected content could turn off secret masking in Strands Agents Tools or trigger command execution through the databases-on-aws agent plugin. The category also included cross-session conversation exposure in the Strands Agents Agent-to-Agent (A2A) server, missing authorization in the Kiro Crew WhatsApp channel, and code injection and server-side request forgery (SSRF) in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Starter Toolkit. Several broad-impact advisories called for customer action, including remote code execution in PHP web runtimes and the native Brotli decoder, a Linux kernel IPv4 TCP use-after-free issue, and recoverable eMudhra intermediate CA keys in AWS trust bundles.

Other notable issues include OS command injection in the AWS Serverless Application Model Command Line Interface (AWS SAM CLI) Terraform hook and the Amazon SageMaker Distribution startup script, SQL injection in the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) Amazon Redshift alpha constructs, an RSA padding oracle in the Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) Encryption Client for .NET, and memory-safety issues in FreeRTOS, the AWS Nitro Enclaves SDK for C, and aws-c-mqtt. Credential exposure recurred in client tooling. AWS Tools for PowerShell, the Amazon SageMaker Python SDK, and the Amazon Kinesis Producer Library wrote secrets to logs. The Amazon SageMaker Python SDK and AWS SDK for pandas also used predictably named Amazon S3 buckets without verifying bucket ownership. A common thread: tools trusted inputs they didn’t control, such as content an agent ingests, a token issued to another application, or a bucket in another account. Patches or mitigations are available for every bulletin, so upgrade promptly. For more information, see AWS Security Bulletins.

AWS samples

This month’s eight AWS samples give you deployable code that puts the remediation flow into practice. Learn how to have AI agents investigate an incident together, connect public security events to the affected lines in your code, and hold off risk at the edge until a patch is merged. Other samples show you how to run AI-assisted vulnerability scanning in isolated environments and add security requirements to specs before any code is written. You’ll also find patterns for protecting MCP servers, private VPC workloads, and browser sessions driven by AI agents, plus a dashboard for governing generative AI usage and cost.

Infrastructure security

AWS Lambda Web Functions reference architecture: Amazon CloudFront and private VPC access Learn to run a web application on AWS Lambda Web Functions behind Amazon CloudFront, using Origin Access Control so the function only accepts signed requests. A Lambda network connector lets the function reach private resources in your VPC. The sample uses Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 as the example database, with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) database authentication, so no credentials need to be stored.

Architecture patterns for MCP servers behind Amazon CloudFront Learn to run a remote Model Context Protocol (MCP) server behind Amazon CloudFront and AWS WAF using four AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) patterns, one for each origin type. The origins include Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon API Gateway, and Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). Each pattern uses the same edge protection and OAuth 2.0 authentication, applies AWS WAF rate limits to each tool and IP address, and only accepts traffic to the origin that comes through Amazon CloudFront.

Mitigating agentic bot threats with Amazon CloudFront and AWS WAF Learn to add a human verification step for browser sessions driven by AI agents. AWS WAF Bot Control flags sessions that look automated, and AWS Lambda@Edge sends them to an Amazon Rekognition Face Liveness check, which needs a live person in front of a camera. A daily limit on how often the same face can pass the check helps keep a few people from verifying many agent-controlled sessions.

Security Scanning with Claude Code on AWS Learn to deploy a separate, isolated Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) environment for each user that runs Claude Code on Amazon Bedrock, so security teams can find, triage, and fix vulnerabilities in code they own. Each environment has no inbound access and is reached through AWS Systems Manager Session Manager. Prompts, commands, and sessions are recorded in your AWS account for audit.

Specification Hardening Engine – Kiro Power Learn to add security requirements to your Kiro specs before any code is written. The Specification Hardening Engine checks EARS-format requirements against CWE and OWASP weakness categories and proposes security requirements you can trace and test. You review each proposed requirement and confirm it before it’s added to the spec.

AWS DevOps Agent traces an alarm to a faulty deployment and, using the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol, hands the code review to an agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. That agent runs an AWS Security Agent review, and its findings appear in the same investigation timeline, with a human approving every action.

Security Radar Learn to track more than 200 public security sources, including CVE records, CISA advisories, and AWS security bulletins, and match new events to the affected lines in your code. Security Radar then calls AWS Continuum to validate a patch and deliver it as a pull request. Governance and compliance

Bedrock Activity Dashboard Learn to deploy a monitoring and governance dashboard for Amazon Bedrock that tracks token use, model use, and cost by user and team. It runs 13 agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime for security, compliance, cost optimization, and usage insights. Usage data comes from Amazon CloudWatch Logs, Amazon S3, and AWS CloudTrail. The dashboard also recommends Amazon Bedrock Guardrails configurations for sensitive data and lets you reconcile chargebacks with AWS Cost Explorer reports.

Conclusion

In October, AI agents took on a larger part of the remediation flow. The posts and samples show agents that find, confirm, and repair vulnerabilities, and pipelines that test each deployment before it reaches production. The PHP2Shell event showed that activity can begin before an advisory is published. Teams can respond by prioritizing findings by evidence, patching internet-facing systems within hours, and keeping edge mitigations in place until patches roll out. The identity guidance applies existing access controls to AI agents and to workloads outside AWS through identity propagation, short-lived credentials, and centrally enforced algorithm policy. In each case, people review and approve the changes that agents propose. To stay current with AWS security updates, subscribe to the AWS Security Blog RSS feed.

Title: Black Friday Cyber Threats — Part Two: Retailers
Context: In Part One of our Black Friday Cyber Threats blog series, we examined how Black Friday creates opportunities for attackers to target consumers through fraud, impersonation,...
Full Text:
In Part One of our Black Friday Cyber Threats blog series, we examined how Black Friday creates opportunities for attackers to target consumers through fraud, impersonation, credential theft, and malware. Retailers experience many of those same threats at scale, while also contending with bot activity, business-logic abuse, operational disruption, and growing questions around AI-driven commerce.

The same conditions that make Cyber Week commercially successful, including intense demand, compressed decision-making, and massive volumes of online activity, also create opportunities for attackers to exploit both technical weaknesses and business processes at scale.

Black Friday therefore amplifies five security challenges that retailers already face throughout the year:

Automated traffic and inventory abuse: Bots drive a substantial share of seasonal online activity, creating risks ranging from credential attacks and promotional abuse to inventory hoarding, scraping, fraudulent transactions, and operational disruption.

Account takeover and authenticated-session abuse: Compromised customer accounts can expose payment methods, loyalty balances, customer information, and post-purchase workflows, while stolen browser sessions may allow attackers to operate from contexts the retailer already trusts.

Business-logic abuse: Automation enables attackers to target coupons, gift cards, loyalty programs, refunds, returns, inventory reservations, and customer-service processes at a scale that is difficult to detect through traditional fraud controls alone.

Availability and operational disruption: Peak shopping periods reduce tolerance for outages, false positives, and manual review, creating opportunities for bot-driven attacks, credential campaigns, and denial-of-service activity to affect business operations during critical revenue periods.

Data theft and extortion: Holiday trading periods concentrate revenue and operational dependence into a short timeframe, increasing the potential impact of ransomware, data theft, and extortion attempts timed to coincide with periods of heightened business pressure.

AI is influencing this environment in two distinct ways:

Generative AI enables attackers to create more convincing phishing campaigns, fraudulent listings, fake reviews, social-engineering content, and other forms of deception at greater speed and scale.

Agentic commerce introduces autonomous software capable of researching products, comparing options, and completing purchases on behalf of consumers, creating new challenges around identity, authorization, trust, and fraud prevention.

Recent incident response data suggest attackers are operating at a level of speed and scale that many organizations have not previously encountered. Arctic Wolf’s Aurora Incident Response team experienced its busiest month on record in October 2026, with cases from organizations not protected by Arctic Wolf rising 78%, as well as network intrusion cases, including ransomware, rising 96% compared with typical monthly volumes. Those trends point to a threat environment where adversaries are increasingly using automation and AI to make established attack techniques more efficient, more targeted, and easier to deploy at scale.

The emergence of shopping agents adds another layer of complexity. Retailers are beginning to encounter situations where software, rather than a human customer, may be browsing products, comparing prices, authenticating to accounts, and completing transactions. Traditional fraud controls often rely on indicators such as browsing behavior, transaction velocity, device characteristics, and network origin to distinguish legitimate shoppers from malicious automation. As agentic commerce expands, those signals become less reliable, forcing retailers to determine not only whether a customer and payment method are legitimate, but also whether the software acting on the customer’s behalf is authorized to do so.

Black Friday therefore serves as a practical example of how cyber threats are evolving. Attackers do not need entirely new techniques to increase risk. They can achieve significant impact by combining automation, AI, credential theft, fraud, and business-process abuse with the predictable operational pressures that accompany major retail events. At the same time, retailers must adapt to a future where a growing share of legitimate commercial activity may also be automated, making trust, attribution, and verification increasingly important components of security and fraud prevention.

How AI, Automation, and Fraud Are Reshaping Retail Cyber Risk

1. Automated traffic and inventory abuse

Retailers have been managing automated traffic for years, long before the current conversation around AI shopping assistants. Against that backdrop, attackers are using AI to test stolen credentials, scrape inventory data, abuse promotions, hoard high-demand products, and facilitate fraud at a scale that would be difficult to achieve manually. For retailers, the operational challenge is understanding who is behind that activity, what they are attempting to accomplish, and whether their actions align with the interests of the business and its customers.

The holiday shopping season increases the complexity. More customers are online, transaction volumes climb, and activity extends well beyond traditional business hours. Based on aggregated telemetry across our customer base, roughly 44% of alerts arrive outside the standard workday, which means a substantial portion of potential threats emerge overnight, on weekends, and during holiday periods when response teams have historically had fewer resources available.

Security teams are increasingly turning to AI to help manage that reality. As the volume of activity grows, organizations need the ability to evaluate alerts, identify suspicious behavior, correlate signals across systems, and begin investigations without waiting for someone to come online. During high-volume periods such as Black Friday and Cyber Monday, that speed becomes particularly valuable because attackers can move from initial access to follow-on activity in a matter of minutes.

Retail organizations appear to recognize that shift. In Arctic Wolf’s 2026 AI & Cybersecurity Trends Report, 95% of retail respondents reported having 24×7 monitoring coverage, the highest level of any industry surveyed. The same respondents identified secure AI adoption and preparing for the pace of AI-driven change as their top priorities over the next year, reflecting a broader understanding that both commerce and cyber threats are becoming faster, more automated, and more difficult to evaluate through human effort alone.

2. Agent identity creates a fraud-control dilemma

Agentic commerce introduces a new identity challenge for retailers because software, rather than a customer, may be navigating the shopping experience and completing transactions on the customer’s behalf.

Many fraud-detection systems were designed around assumptions about human behavior, evaluating factors such as browsing patterns, device identity, network origin, and checkout activity to determine whether a transaction appears legitimate. Authorized shopping agents may not behave like traditional customers. They may move through a site rapidly, skip intermediate steps, or operate through shared cloud infrastructure. At the same time, malicious actors are likely to adapt their own automation to resemble legitimate agents.

As a result, retailers will need new ways to establish trust, verify authorization, and maintain accountability throughout the purchasing process. The challenge extends beyond fraud prevention to questions of attribution, auditability, and dispute resolution when a transaction is later challenged by a customer.

3. Product and content manipulation

AI shopping agents rely on information they find across the internet, including product descriptions, reviews, advertisements, search results, and retailer websites. That means attackers don’t necessarily have to target the shopper directly. In some cases, influencing the information an agent sees may be enough.

A compromised product feed could direct customers to the wrong destination or display inaccurate pricing and inventory information. Fraudulent listings could be designed to appear more attractive to recommendation engines. Reviews and other user-generated content may become vehicles for manipulation, particularly if shopping agents begin relying on them more heavily when making recommendations or purchase decisions.

These aren’t entirely new problems. Retailers have spent years dealing with fake reviews, search manipulation, fraudulent listings, and advertising abuse. The difference is that AI shopping agents may consume and act on that information much faster than a human shopper would, increasing the importance of ensuring that the underlying data is accurate and trustworthy.

4. Account takeover and authenticated-session abuse

Compromised retail accounts have long been valuable to attackers because they often provide access to saved payment methods, loyalty balances, order histories, and customer account settings. The risk increases when attackers gain access to an authenticated browser session or shopping agent session, allowing them to operate from a context the retailer may already recognize as trusted.

Once inside an account, attackers can steal loyalty points and gift cards, redirect shipments, abuse promotions, initiate fraudulent purchases, manipulate refunds, or exploit trusted access to customer and supplier portals. Many of these activities can be difficult to distinguish from legitimate account activity because they occur after a successful login.

ClickFix campaigns add another dimension to this risk. Information-stealing malware is designed to collect browser credentials, session tokens, authentication artifacts, and other sensitive data that help attackers bypass traditional login controls. What begins as a consumer-focused lure can therefore have broader consequences if the compromised device belongs to an employee with access to corporate systems, supplier relationships, or business applications. In those cases, an account-compromise event can become an entry point into a much larger environment.

5. Business-logic abuse at scale

Retailers should expect automated abuse to extend well beyond payment fraud. The same technologies that help shoppers move more quickly through the buying process can also be used to exploit promotions, reserve inventory, test gift card balances, manipulate loyalty accounts, automate refund requests, and target customer service teams with convincing social engineering schemes. As more retail activity becomes digital, attackers gain additional opportunities to operate at a speed and scale that can be difficult to detect through human review alone.

At the same time, AI-powered shopping assistants are beginning to take on a greater role throughout the customer journey, from product discovery and recommendations to transaction support and post-purchase interactions. That shift introduces new challenges around identity, trust, and fraud prevention. Retailers will increasingly need to distinguish between legitimate automated activity acting on behalf of customers and malicious automation designed to abuse systems, manipulate transactions, or gain unauthorized access to accounts and services.

6. Availability and operational risk

Peak shopping periods create a difficult balancing act for retailers. Customers expect fast transactions, immediate access to promotions, and uninterrupted service, leaving little tolerance for outages, delays, or excessive verification steps. Threat actors understand that pressure and may try to exploit it through bot activity, credential attacks, fraud campaigns, and other forms of malicious automation designed to blend into legitimate customer traffic.

Recent Arctic Wolf incident response data suggests attackers are already operating at a level of speed and scale that many organizations are struggling to manage. In October 2026, the Aurora Incident Response team experienced its busiest month on record, with cases from organizations not protected by Arctic Wolf increasing 78% compared with typical monthly volumes. While that increase was not specific to retail organizations or Black Friday activity, it reflects a broader threat environment in which adversaries are using automation and AI to make established attack techniques more efficient, more targeted, and easier to deploy at scale.

7. Data Theft and Extortion Exploit Peak Operating Pressure

Black Friday concentrates transaction volume and revenue into a period when retailers have little tolerance for disruption. Threat actors can exploit that operational pressure by timing ransomware deployment, data theft, or extortion demands for holiday weekends, when response capacity may be reduced and every hour of downtime carries greater commercial impact.

The FBI and CISA have previously observed highly disruptive ransomware attacks occurring on holidays and weekends, when limited network-defense and IT capacity can give attackers additional time to expand access and deploy ransomware. Their guidance does not identify a Black Friday-specific campaign, but the underlying conditions are directly applicable to retailers operating through Thanksgiving weekend.

Modern extortion also does not require encryption. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security warns that threat actors increasingly use stolen data as the primary source of leverage, threatening disclosure or destruction even when the victim can restore systems from backups. Potential retail exposure includes customer and employee data, payment-related information, supplier records, contracts, pricing data, loyalty accounts, and internal communications.

Before Cyber Week begins, retailers should focus on controlling who and what can transact in their environment. That means distinguishing trusted shopping agents from malicious automation, strengthening authentication for high-risk actions like loyalty redemptions and address changes, and maintaining clear records of customer authorization. As AI-powered commerce grows, proving who approved a purchase may become just as important as processing the payment.

Retailers should remember that the fundamentals have not changed. Visibility, identity security, continuous monitoring, and tested response processes remain the foundation of resilience. What has changed is the speed at which attackers can operate.

Arctic Wolf’s recent incident response data and Agentic Security Operations research suggest adversaries are increasingly using automation and AI to scale familiar attack techniques. As a result, organizations need the ability to detect, investigate, and respond at machine speed while maintaining human oversight of critical decisions. The most likely Black Friday threats remain account takeover, phishing, payment fraud, malware, and business-logic abuse, but AI is making those attacks faster, easier to scale, and harder to distinguish from legitimate activity.

Title: Black Friday Cyber Threats — Part One: Consumers
Context: Fraud, credential theft, malware delivery, and social engineering all benefit when attackers can blend into trusted experiences and exploit moments when people are moving quickly
Full Text:
For millions of consumers globally, Black Friday creates exactly the kind of environment cybercriminals look for when assessing their targets, which is urgency, high transaction volume, and people clicking links, tracking packages, and hunting for deals. Rather than introducing new threats, Black Friday amplifies four risk categories that security teams already contend with year-round:

Fraud and impersonation: Fake retailers, brand-spoofing sites, fraudulent advertisements, delivery messages, and account-support scams remain the most immediate consumer threats.

Credential and session theft: Phishing, account takeover, and information-stealing malware can expose retail accounts, payment information, email, loyalty balances, and authenticated browser sessions.

Malware delivery: ClickFix and fake CAPTCHA techniques can turn shopping, coupon, and delivery lures into endpoint compromise.

Automated and agentic activity: Retailers must distinguish legitimate customers and authorized shopping agents from inventory bots, account-abuse automation, and fraud infrastructure.

AI amplifies this environment in two different ways: 1. AI can improve the quality, localization, and scale of fraudulent content and 2. Shopping agents can shorten the path from product discovery to payment.

Recent incident response data suggest attackers are operating at a level of speed and scale that many organizations have not previously encountered. Arctic Wolf’s Aurora Incident Response team experienced its busiest month on record in October 2026, with cases from organizations not protected by Arctic Wolf rising 78%, as well as network intrusion cases, including ransomware, rising 96% compared with previous months in 2026. Those trends point to a threat environment where adversaries are using automation and AI to make established attack techniques more efficient, more targeted, and easier to deploy at scale.

As transaction volume rises and shoppers make faster decisions, phishing, impersonation, credential theft, and account-takeover activity become more likely to blend into normal behavior. Black Friday therefore serves as a useful case study in how modern cyber threats evolve. Attackers do not always need new techniques. They often achieve greater impact simply by combining trusted brands, social engineering, automation, and AI to exploit predictable moments of consumer urgency.

Threats to Consumers

1. Fake stores, impersonation, and payment fraud

Consumers remain most likely to encounter fraudulent retailers, counterfeit products, deceptive advertisements, phishing messages, and false delivery notifications. The immediate objectives are usually to obtain payment, harvest credentials, collect personal information, or redirect the victim to another scam.

The large increase in overall fraud losses does not establish an equivalent increase in shopping fraud. FBI data shows that investment, business email compromise, and support fraud produced considerably higher losses than non-delivery and credit card fraud in 2025. The key takeaway is that online shopping fraud remains highly relevant during Black Friday, not that it is driving the overall increase in reported fraud losses.

2. ClickFix and fake CAPTCHA malware delivery

Some holiday scams may be looking for far more than payment information. One technique defenders are watching closely is ClickFix, a social engineering tactic that presents what appears to be a legitimate CAPTCHA, browser error, document issue, or verification step. Instead of solving a problem, the victim is instructed to copy, paste, and run a command through PowerShell, Windows Run, Command Prompt, or Terminal, effectively launching the attack themselves. Arctic Wolf has tracked the technique across multiple campaigns, including a ClickFix campaign that used an obfuscated PowerShell loader to facilitate malicious activity, a fake CAPTCHA lure delivering PsyloStealer, and the FileFix delivery method used to distribute Interlock RAT.

The approach is effective because it blends into everyday online activity. During Black Friday and the holiday shopping season, attackers have no shortage of believable scenarios to work with. A fake shopping site might ask visitors to verify they are human before accessing a limited-time sale, claim a browser extension is required to activate a coupon, or display a message saying a package tracking page, invoice, or payment verification process cannot continue until a quick troubleshooting step is completed. Those instructions ultimately direct the victim to run a command that can install malware or provide attackers with access to credentials, sensitive files, or enterprise systems.

While there is no specific reporting showing a surge in ClickFix activity tied directly to Black Friday, the technique has become an increasingly common part of the threat landscape. The success of campaigns such as those documented in Arctic Wolf’s ClickFix, PsyloStealer, and FileFix investigations demonstrates how easily threat actors can disguise malicious requests as routine troubleshooting steps. The volume of holiday shopping, package tracking, promotional emails, and payment-related activity during the season creates even more opportunities to hide those requests inside workflows that users already trust.

3. Account takeover and information theft

Compromised email accounts can enable attackers to reset passwords, intercept order confirmations, redirect deliveries, and identify other linked financial services. Stolen browser cookies and authentication tokens can further extend access by allowing attackers to hijack authenticated sessions and, in some cases, bypass password-based controls.

Black Friday increases the practical value of compromised retail accounts because they may contain:

Stored payment methods

Loyalty points and rewards

Gift-card balances

Order histories

Saved delivery addresses

Active authenticated sessions

4. AI-assisted social engineering

AI-generated text, images, advertisements, and fictitious profiles allow scammers to produce polished, localized campaigns rapidly across brands, countries, products, and delivery providers. Social media provides a high-volume distribution channel for this content: nearly 30% of consumers reporting a fraud loss in 2025 said the scam began on social media, and shopping scams accounted for more than 40% of those reports, per the FTC. The FBI has also documented criminals using generative AI to create fictitious profiles, targeted messages, celebrity endorsements, and counterfeit-product promotions at scale.

Consumers should therefore rely less on writing quality as a trust signal and more on behavioral indicators:

Unexpected urgency

Extreme discounts

Pressure to leave an official platform

Requests for cryptocurrency, gift cards, or bank transfers

Unfamiliar merchant domains

Requests to install software or browser extensions

Instructions to paste commands into system tools

5. Personal shopping agents

Personal AI agents can now browse products and complete portions of the transaction process. According to Stripe, Meta’s Muse can check out at more than one million Link-enabled businesses and can use a single-use virtual card elsewhere. The consumer is required to approve each transaction total, and Muse does not receive the underlying payment details.

Payment controls like these reduce credential exposure. Approving a transaction amount doesn’t by itself confirm the consumer is buying from the intended merchant or getting the intended product. A consumer could approve the expected amount while failing to recognize an impersonation site, counterfeit item, manipulated listing, or fraudulent seller.

Fraud, credential theft, malware delivery, and social engineering all benefit when attackers can blend into trusted experiences and exploit moments when people are moving quickly. The most effective scams rarely depend on sophisticated technical exploits. Instead, they rely on convincing users to trust a familiar brand, click a timely message, approve a transaction, install software, or follow instructions that appear legitimate. AI is making those interactions more polished and easier to scale.

Organizations focused on protecting customers and reducing cyber risk can strengthen their security posture by combining user awareness with continuous monitoring, threat detection, and incident response capabilities that help identify and contain threats before they become significant security events.

As attackers increasingly use automation and AI to accelerate established tactics, security operations must operate with greater speed, visibility, and context. Arctic Wolf helps organizations improve cyber resilience through the Aurora Superintelligence Platform, which combines human expertise with AI-driven security operations, threat intelligence, and incident response to help security teams detect, investigate, and respond to threats faster. With the Aurora Agentic SOC extending security operations through autonomous and human-guided workflows, organizations are better positioned to keep pace with an increasingly fast-moving threat landscape.

-Justin Moore, Director of Adversary Operations, Arctic Wolf

Title: Secure agentic access to AWS with Enterprise-Managed Authorization
Context: With this capability, organizations can centrally manage which applications can access Amazon Web Services (AWS) resources on behalf of their employees, without requiring users...
Full Text:
AWS Sign-In is introducing support for Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) using the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG), enabling organizations to securely authorize AI agents to access AWS MCP Server through their existing enterprise identity providers (IdPs), such as Okta. With this capability, organizations can centrally manage which applications can access Amazon Web Services (AWS) resources on behalf of their employees, without requiring users to manage additional long-term credentials or complete separate consent flows.

In our previous blog post, Introducing OAuth Support for AWS MCP Server, we introduced OAuth-based authorization, enabling AI agents to securely access AWS MCP Server through interactive sign-in or programmatic authentication using AWS credentials. EMA builds on these capabilities by enabling organizations to authorize AI agents through their existing enterprise IdPs. Because authentication to an AI application doesn’t automatically grant access to AWS resources, EMA provides a way to authorize access across these separate trust domains while maintaining existing AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions.

In this post, we explain how EMA and ID-JAG work with AWS Sign-In, discuss security best practices, and walk you through configuring Okta to authorize AI agents to access AWS MCP Server.

How Enterprise-Managed Authorization works with AWS Sign-In

Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) is an extension of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) that enables organizations to centrally manage how AI applications access protected resources on behalf of employees. EMA uses the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG), an OAuth-based authorization grant that enables enterprise IdPs to authorize access across different trust domains. Rather than requiring employees to individually authorize each MCP server, administrators can define policies in their existing IdP to control which AI applications can access specific resources.

When an employee signs in to an AI application such as Claude using their enterprise IdP, the authentication establishes their identity within Claude but doesn’t automatically grant access to AWS resources. When the AI application requests access to an MCP server, the enterprise IdP evaluates its configured access policies and issues a short-lived, signed ID-JAG assertion for the intended resource. The AI application then exchanges this assertion with the authorization server configured for the MCP server to obtain an OAuth access token, without requiring the employee to complete an additional interactive authorization flow.

For AWS MCP Server, AWS Sign-In serves as the configured OAuth authorization server. The AI application presents the ID-JAG assertion to the AWS Sign-In OAuth token endpoint. As part of the authorization process, AWS validates the assertion against the trusted IdP and uses AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) to evaluate the IAM role’s trust policy and establish the authorized role session. AWS Sign-In then issues an OAuth access token associated with the IAM role. IAM policies attached to the role determine which AWS operations the agent can perform, allowing organizations to manage agent authorization through their enterprise IdP while enforcing existing AWS permissions.

Figure 1 illustrates how an AI application, such as Claude, uses EMA with Okta and AWS Sign-In to obtain an OAuth access token and securely access AWS MCP Server using IAM role-based permissions.

Figure 1: Enterprise-Managed Authorization flow using Okta, AWS Sign-In, and AWS MCP Server

The authorization flow consists of the following steps, as illustrated in Figure 1:

Employee authentication: The employee signs in to the AI application, such as Claude, using their enterprise IdP, such as Okta, through single sign-on (SSO).

ID-JAG request: When the AI application needs to access AWS MCP Server, it requests an ID-JAG from Okta for the intended resource.

Enterprise authorization: Okta evaluates the configured access policies to determine whether the employee and AI application are authorized to access AWS MCP Server. If authorized, Okta issues a short-lived, signed ID-JAG assertion.

Token exchange with AWS Sign-In: The AI application sends the ID-JAG to the AWS Sign-In OAuth token endpoint. AWS Sign-In validates the assertion, including its issuer, signature, audience/tenant, expiration, and intended resource, and verifies the associated IAM role authorization before issuing an OAuth access token.

Access AWS MCP Server: The AI application presents the AWS-issued OAuth access token to AWS MCP Server. The server validates the token, and access to AWS resources is governed by the permissions associated with the IAM role.

Configure Enterprise-Managed Authorization using Okta and AWS Sign-In

In this section, we walk you through configuring Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) to enable an AI application, such as Claude, to securely access AWS MCP Server using an enterprise identity managed in Okta.

The configuration establishes trust between Okta and AWS, defines IAM permissions for accessing AWS resources, and configures enterprise authorization policies that govern AI application access. This walkthrough uses AWS MCP Server in the US West (Oregon) AWS Region (us-west-2).

Prerequisites

Before you begin, make sure you have the following:

An AWS account with permissions to configure IAM IdPs, roles, and policies.

An Okta organization with administrative permissions to manage applications and configure Cross-App Access policies.

An AI application, such as Claude, that supports EMA and ID-JAG.

Access to AWS MCP Server with support for OAuth-based Enterprise-Managed Authorization.

The AWS Region where you will configure the integration.

Step 0: Configure the AI application in Okta

Configure an application in Okta so that employees can sign in to the AI application through enterprise single sign-on (SSO). For this walkthrough, we use Claude as the AI application. If your organization already uses Claude with Okta SSO, you can use the existing application. This application is the requesting application when you configure Cross-App Access in Step 3.

Create the Claude SSO application: In the Okta Admin Console, go to Applications, choose Create App Integration, and create an OIDC web application, for example Claude SSO, as shown in Figure 2.

If your agent was imported through an Okta AI Agent Provider, create the OIDC application by going to Directory, AI Agents, then navigating to User access from the selected agent.

Choose the grant types: Select Authorization Code and Refresh Token. Claude uses the refresh token to request new ID-JAG assertions without asking employees to sign in again.

Add the redirect URI: Set Sign-in redirect URIs to Claude’s SSO callback URL.

Assign employees: Under Assignments, select which employees or groups can access the application.

Confirm SSO works: Check that employees can sign in to Claude through Okta before you continue.

Figure 2: Creating the Claude SSO app integration in Okta

Step 1: Configure Okta as an OIDC IdP in IAM

Create an OpenID Connect (OIDC) IdP so that AWS trusts the ID-JAG assertions that Okta issues, as shown in Figure 3.

Add the IdP: In the AWS Management Console for IAM, go to Identity providers, choose Add provider, and select OpenID Connect.

Enter the provider URL: For Provider URL, enter your Okta org URL, for example https://integrator-1234567.okta.com. Okta issues ID-JAG assertions from the org authorization server, not from a custom authorization server.

Enter the audience: For Audience, enter the AWS Sign-In authorization server for your Region, for example https://us-west-2.oauth.signin.aws, and choose Add provider.

Figure 3: Adding Okta as an OpenID Connect identity provider in IAM

Step 2: Create an IAM role and configure permissions

Create an IAM role that defines the AWS permissions granted to the AI application, as shown in Figure 4.

Create the role: In the IAM console, go to Roles, choose Create role, and select Web identity as the trusted entity type. Choose the Okta IdP from Step 1 and its audience. This creates a trust policy that allows access only through assertions from that provider.

Attach the AWS MCP Server permissions: Attach the AWS managed policy AWSMCPSignInOAuthAccessPolicy. It grants the signin:CreateOAuth2Token permission required for OAuth access to AWS MCP Server.

Attach the AWS permissions the AI application needs: Attach other IAM policies that grant only the AWS permissions required by the AI application. For this walkthrough, we use a read-only role.

Name and create the role: Enter a role name, for example OktaAwsMcpReadOnly, and choose Create role.

Copy the role ARN: You’ll enter the role Amazon Resource Name (ARN) as the Audience/tenant ID in Okta in Step 3.

Figure 4: Reviewing the IAM role and its trust policy

Step 3: Configure Cross-App Access in Okta

In the Okta Admin Console, create a resource application that represents AWS MCP Server, and then connect Claude to it. The Claude SSO App from Step 0 stays the requesting application, so you don’t enable Cross-App Access on it.

Create the AWS MCP resource application: Go to Applications, choose Create App Integration, and create an OIDC web application, for example AWS MCP (us-west-2). Okta doesn’t use this application’s sign-in redirect URI, so you can keep the default value.

Figure 5: Creating the AWS MCP resource application in Okta

Enable Cross-App Access on the resource application: On the Machine Assignments tab, edit the access method and enable Cross-App Access. Set Issuer URL to https://us-west-2.oauth.signin.aws and set Audience/tenant ID to the IAM role ARN from Step 2.

Figure 6: Enabling Cross-App Access on the AWS MCP resource application

Assign employees: On the Assignments tab, assign the employees or groups who can access AWS MCP Server through Claude.

Register Claude as an AI agent: Go to Directory, AI Agents, and choose Register AI agent. Under User access, choose Select an existing app and pick the Claude SSO App from Step 0.

Skip this step if the agent was already imported via an Okta AI Agent Provider.

Connect the AI agent to AWS MCP Server: On the AI agent page, add a resource connection with the Application resource type. Set Application instance to the AWS MCP resource application. Set the client ID registered in AWS MCP to the client ID that you configure in Claude in Step 4, for example anthropic-claude. Set Resource identifier to https://aws-mcp.us-west-2.api.aws/mcp.

Figure 7: Connecting the Claude AI agent to the AWS MCP resource application

When Claude requests access, Okta checks that the employee is assigned access and issues an ID-JAG for AWS Sign-In that carries the IAM role ARN. AWS Sign-In validates the assertion and issues an OAuth access token associated with the IAM role.

Step 4: Configure Claude to access AWS MCP Server

Add a custom connector: In Claude, open Admin settings, choose Connectors, and then choose Add, Custom connector. Enter a name and the AWS MCP Server endpoint, for example https://aws-mcp.us-west-2.api.aws/mcp.

Configure OAuth authentication: For Authentication, choose Sign in when needed. For OAuth client, choose Use your own OAuth client, enter the client ID from the resource connection in Step 3 and leave the client secret blank.

Figure 8: Adding AWS MCP Server as a custom connector in Claude

Set up managed authorization: Open the connector, and on the Configuration tab, choose Set up next to Managed authorization.

Figure 9: The connector’s Configuration tab

Configure IdP-managed access: Choose IdP-managed as the identity source and confirm that the connection checks pass. Then choose Continue, select the Claude roles that connect through managed authorization, and choose Save.

Figure 10: Setting up managed authorization with Okta as the identity source

When an employee accesses AWS MCP Server, Claude requests an ID-JAG assertion from Okta. Following successful policy evaluation, Okta issues the assertion, which Claude exchanges at the AWS Sign-In OAuth token endpoint for an OAuth access token associated with the configured IAM role. Claude uses this token to access AWS MCP Server without requiring an additional AWS sign-in.

Step 5: Validate access to AWS MCP Server

To validate the configuration:

Sign in using enterprise SSO: Sign in to the AI application using your Okta identity.

Figure 11: Signing in to Claude with SSO

Connect to AWS MCP Server: Connect the AI application to AWS MCP Server.

Verify OAuth token issuance: Confirm that Claude successfully connects to AWS MCP Server without requiring a separate AWS authorization flow. You can verify successful OAuth token issuance using AWS CloudTrail, as described in Step 6.

Validate authorized access: Perform an AWS operation permitted by the configured IAM role.

Figure 12: Calling AWS MCP Server from Claude Code

Verify access restrictions: Attempt an operation outside the IAM role’s permissions and confirm that access is denied.

You can also validate enterprise authorization policies by attempting access using an employee who is not authorized in Okta and verifying that the ID-JAG request is denied.

Step 6: Verify authorization activity using AWS CloudTrail

AWS Sign-In and AWS MCP Server integrate with AWS CloudTrail to help organizations monitor OAuth authorization activity and API requests made by AI applications. CloudTrail provides visibility into token issuance, the applications requesting access, and operations performed through AWS MCP Server.

After successfully connecting your AI application to AWS MCP Server, you can verify the authorization activity in CloudTrail:

Review the event details, including the OAuth client identifier, target resource, authorization grant type, and token issuance status, where recorded.

Best practices for securing AI agent access with EMA and AWS IAM

When configuring Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA), consider the following security recommendations to help protect AI agent access to AWS resources:

Use short-lived ID-JAG assertions: Configure your enterprise IdP to issue ID-JAG assertions with short expiration periods. This limits the time during which an assertion can be exchanged for an OAuth access token and reduces the risk associated with token exposure.

Use tenant-specific IdP issuers: In multi-tenant environments, configure tenant-specific issuer URLs to establish explicit trust relationships between AWS and the intended enterprise IdP. This helps prevent assertions issued for one tenant from being accepted in another tenant’s authorization context.

Restrict OAuth authorization using IAM condition keys: Use IAM condition keys to limit OAuth token issuance to approved AI applications, authorization flows, and AWS resources. For example, use signin:OAuthClientId to restrict access to approved AI applications, such as arn:aws:signin:::external-client/jwt-bearer/anthropic-claude and signin:OAuthGrantType to restrict the permitted grant type to urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer. Scope these permissions to the AWS MCP Server service principal to prevent unintended access to other AWS services.

Apply least-privilege IAM permissions: Grant the IAM role only the permissions required by the AI application. Use managed policies to control which AWS operations the agent can perform through AWS MCP Server, reducing the impact of unauthorized or unintended actions.

For more information about available IAM condition keys and permissions, see the AWS Sign-In condition keys reference and the AWSMCPSignInOAuthAccessPolicy documentation.

Conclusion

Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) with AWS Sign-In enables organizations to securely connect AI agents to AWS resources using their existing enterprise IdPs. By combining centralized authorization policies with IAM permissions, organizations can control which AI applications access their resources while reducing the need for employees to manage AWS credentials or complete additional authorization flows.

Using ID-JAG, AWS Sign-In exchanges enterprise-issued identity assertions for short-lived OAuth access tokens associated with IAM roles. This approach helps organizations enforce least-privilege access, reduce credential exposure, and simplify how employees securely access AWS resources through AI agents.

To get started, see the Sign-in with OAuth 2.0, Configure EMA for MCP servers, and Introducing OAuth Support for AWS MCP Server to learn more about OAuth-based access to AWS resources.
