Title: Reduce operational overhead by migrating from AWS CloudHSM to AWS KMS
Context: AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) supports the security certifications, algorithms, and performance that most AWS CloudHSM workloads require
Full Text:
AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) supports the security certifications, algorithms, and performance that most AWS CloudHSM workloads require. Organizations that migrate from AWS CloudHSM to AWS KMS have significantly reduced costs while eliminating hardware security module (HSM) provisioning, patching, and high-availability management. For a detailed comparison of both services, see AWS KMS or AWS CloudHSM: Choose the right key management solution. For payment workloads, see AWS Payment Cryptography in the following table.

Is migration right for you?

Most AWS CloudHSM workloads can migrate to AWS KMS. The following requirements might appear to need CloudHSM, but most have a resolution path:

Potential requirement

Resolution

Contractual or compliance mandate requiring single-tenant HSMs

Review your compliance documentation for explicit single-tenant language; many organizations find that it’s assumed, not mandated. Where mandated, a security review of AWS KMS typically confirms that its logical cryptographic isolation architecture satisfies the underlying intent.

Applications that rely on traditional HSM interfaces (PKCS#11, Java Cryptography Extension, OpenSSL Provider, or Key Storage Provider)

These interfaces are a communication pattern, not an architectural constraint. Contact your AWS account team to assess the refactoring effort needed for your workloads to use modern RESTful interfaces to web services.

Deprecated algorithms (TDES, PKCS#1 v1.5 with RSA) or less common operations (AES key wrapping, AES-CTR, AES-CBC)

Evaluate whether you can retire the dependency as part of your security modernization.

Over 1 billion cryptographic operations per month, where higher per-operation AWS KMS costs might favor the per-hour AWS CloudHSM cost model

Per-operation pricing is only one of several factors that affect cost. Also consider saved staff time, patching, and high-availability management. With envelope encryption (Option B in the following section), optional data key caching can further reduce API call volume.

Payment workloads using older or payment-specific cryptography (TDES, AES-CBC)

While AWS KMS embeds cryptographic best practices in a managed service, some payment systems still rely on older cryptography such as TDES. Evaluate Payment Cryptography, which supports payment use cases, including TDES-based algorithms such as CVV2, ARQC, and PIN validation. It also provides low-level algorithms, such as AES-CBC, that third-party systems might require for interoperability.

If you can resolve these requirements, it’s possible to migrate from AWS CloudHSM to AWS KMS. You can use the rest of this post to review the basic steps of migration to AWS KMS.

How migration works

Migration has three parts: updating application code to call KMS APIs, rotating or importing your cryptographic keys, and transitioning existing data. You re-encrypt previously encrypted data under KMS keys, and existing signatures remain verifiable without AWS CloudHSM. You can complete each part gradually, with zero downtime. Application refactoring is the bulk of the effort, though AI-assisted code transformation tools can reduce this work. Because you’re already refactoring application code, this migration is also an opportunity to adopt post-quantum cryptography (PQC) algorithms, discussed in the following section.

Digital signature workloads

During the transition, the AWS CloudHSM private key continues to sign existing workloads. If AWS CloudHSM lets you export (wrap) a copy of your private key, import it directly into AWS KMS to maintain continuity. For details, see How to Migrate Asymmetric Keys from CloudHSM to AWS KMS. If the key is non-exportable, create a new key pair in AWS KMS. A new asymmetric KMS key (or the imported key from CloudHSM) signs new data flowing to AWS KMS. Shift traffic from AWS CloudHSM to AWS KMS at your own pace. If you created a new key pair, export the CloudHSM public key before decommissioning and use it to verify existing signatures locally with libraries such as AWS-LC or OpenSSL as shown in Figure 1. AWS KMS doesn’t support importing public keys.

Figure 1 – Digital signature migration

Post-quantum readiness: When creating new signing keys in AWS KMS as part of this migration, consider adopting post-quantum cryptography (PQC). AWS KMS supports ML-DSA (FIPS 204), so you can begin issuing PQC signatures now rather than as a separate future effort. This matters most for long-lived signatures, such as document signing, code signing, and certificate issuance.

Durability of imported asymmetric keys: Asymmetric key material imported into AWS KMS (using ImportKeyMaterial) doesn’t have the same durability guarantees as keys generated within AWS KMS. In the unlikely event of an AWS Region-wide infrastructure failure, imported key material could become unavailable. To protect against this, create the key as a multi-Region key, then import the same key material into each replica key in other Regions. Also keep secure backups of imported private keys outside of AWS KMS. An AWS CloudHSM cluster backup is a zero-cost option; CloudHSM stores backups in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) at no additional charge. For keys created in AWS KMS (not imported), AWS KMS automatically manages durability within a Region, and multi-Region keys replicate the key material for you.

Encryption workloads

For encryption workloads, use the gradual re-encryption pattern: encrypt new data with AWS KMS while a background process re-encrypts existing data created under AWS CloudHSM keys. This achieves a zero-downtime migration. The following are two approaches to gradual re-encryption, depending on your requirements.

Option A: Direct encryption with AWS KMS API (recommended)

Call the AWS KMS Encrypt and Decrypt APIs directly (Figure 2). Your application passes plaintext to kms:Encrypt and receives a self-contained ciphertext blob. To decrypt, pass the blob to kms:Decrypt. There are no data keys to manage, no local cryptography, and no libraries beyond the AWS SDK. When decrypting, AWS KMS identifies the correct key from metadata it embeds in the ciphertext, including the key material identifier. As a result, ciphertext produced by AWS KMS is larger (by about 150 bytes) than AWS CloudHSM would produce for the same plaintext. During transition, your application must handle data encrypted by both systems. On decrypt, call kms:Decrypt first. If the ciphertext was created by kms:Encrypt, it will succeed. If it was created by CloudHSM, kms:Decrypt will return InvalidCiphertextException immediately without attempting decryption. Your application then falls back to the CloudHSM decrypt path and can optionally re-encrypt the plaintext with kms:Encrypt and store the new ciphertext. All new encrypt operations go to AWS KMS immediately; only decrypt needs the fallback until re-encryption is complete.

The following pseudocode illustrates this pattern:

def encrypt_record(record_id, record): response = kms.encrypt(KeyId=kms_key_arn, Plaintext=record) store(record_id, ciphertext=response['CiphertextBlob']) def decrypt_record(record_id): stored = fetch(record_id) try: response = kms.decrypt(CiphertextBlob=stored.ciphertext) return response['Plaintext'] except kms.exceptions.InvalidCiphertextException: # Not a KMS ciphertext - fall back to CloudHSM return cloudhsm_decrypt(stored.ciphertext)

Figure 2 – Encryption migration with AWS KMS API

More about AWS KMS encryption

AWS KMS direct encryption supports plaintext up to 4 KB per request. For larger payloads, use Option B (AWS Encryption SDK), which handles envelope encryption for you and supports data of any size.

AWS KMS also supports asymmetric encryption with RSA keys for use cases such as encrypting data destined for a specific key pair holder. This post focuses on symmetric encryption because it covers the majority of AWS CloudHSM encryption workloads.

Option B: Envelope encryption with AWS Encryption SDK

For workloads that require envelope encryption, use the AWS Encryption SDK as shown in Figure 3. Your application calls encrypt() on plaintext and decrypt() on ciphertext. The SDK manages data key generation, local 256-bit AES-GCM encryption, and serialization automatically. Its portable ciphertext format works across multiple runtimes of the AWS Encryption SDK. You can also enable data key caching to reduce calls to AWS KMS. Use this approach when you share encrypted data across services, languages, or with third parties outside of AWS.

Figure 3 – Encryption migration with AWS Encryption SDK

Migration results

A financial services company migrated their transaction data encryption from AWS CloudHSM to AWS KMS. Prior to migration, their workload ran 75 million cryptographic operations per month on three HSMs provisioned for high availability and the operational burden was 25 hours per month. After the migration, they no longer had to manage HSMs, which reduced their operational burden to near zero.

Metric

Before (AWS CloudHSM)

After (AWS KMS)

Monthly cost

$3,456 (three HSMs)

Approximately $250 (93% reduction)

Operational burden

25 hours per month (patching, certificates, and monitoring)

Near zero: no HSMs to manage

Compliance

FIPS 140-3 Level 3

Disaster recovery

Multi-Availability Zone (AZ) HSMs that they provisioned, sized, and monitored

Automatic multi-AZ availability. Optional multi-Region replication

Migration duration

–

10 weeks, zero downtime

Recommendations

We recommend the following as you migrate from AWS CloudHSM to AWS KMS.

Use AI-assisted code transformation tools to accelerate refactoring and reduce manual effort.

Run the complete migration in staging first, including re-encryption of representative data volumes.

Document specific rollback criteria. During gradual re-encryption, you can pause at any point while AWS CloudHSM continues to decrypt data that has not yet moved. Keep KMS keys enabled after a rollback, because data already re-encrypted under AWS KMS still needs them.

Design AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies, key policies, grants, and encryption context schemas before migration. Encryption context enables fine-grained audit trails not available in CloudHSM. See the AWS KMS Developer Guide for a list of log entries.

Delete CloudHSM keys only after all data is re-encrypted and verified. Before deleting, create a CloudHSM cluster backup of any keys imported into AWS KMS and export the public key of any signing key you replaced. Maintain an audit trail of the decommissioning.

Next steps

Start by auditing your current AWS CloudHSM usage: document your keys, the applications that use them, your monthly operation volume, and any compliance constraints. Use the AWS Pricing Calculator to estimate AWS KMS costs for your workload, then test a proof-of-concept migration with a non-critical application.

Conclusion

Migrating from AWS CloudHSM to AWS KMS removes the recurring work of provisioning, scaling, patching, and monitoring HSM clusters, freeing your team to focus on your application rather than the cryptographic infrastructure beneath it. You gain built-in high availability across multiple Availability Zones, with optional multi-Region replication, at a usage-based cost rather than a per-hour commitment for hardware you manage. Because the migration involves refactoring application code, it is also a natural point to adopt post-quantum signing algorithms such as ML-DSA, so you modernize your security posture in the same effort.

For implementation support, contact your AWS account team or AWS Professional Services. For API integration details, see the AWS KMS Developer Guide.

Title: Planning for 99.99 percent availability with the Amazon Cognito Plus feature plan
Context: To learn more about the features that Plus adds, see the advanced security features with threat protection
Full Text:
Amazon Cognito handles sign-in and access control for users, AI agents, and microservices with managed user directories, social and enterprise federation, and passwordless sign-in with passkeys or one-time passwords.

Sign-in is the front door to your application. If your customer identity and access management (CIAM) layer is unavailable, users can’t sign in or refresh their sessions, and they can’t reach the rest of your application. Your application’s availability directly depends on the availability of your identity layer.

Starting November 1, 2026, the Amazon Cognito Service Level Agreement (SLA) commits to a Monthly Uptime Percentage of 99.99 percent for user pools on the Plus feature plan, up from 99.9 percent. A user pool is a multi-tenant user directory that stores your users’ profiles and settings. User pools on Essentials and Lite feature plans remain at the 99.9 percent Service Commitment, while user pools already on Plus receive the new Service Commitment automatically.

This post explains why we made the change, how availability is measured, what’s in the updated SLA, how the SLA measures availability, historical availability data, and how to switch a user pool to Plus.

Why we raised the Service Commitment

Many customers use Amazon Cognito for sign-in to applications with strict availability requirements, such as patient portals and retail checkout flows. They need the services they build on to support high availability. We raised the Service Commitment for the Plus feature plan to 99.99 percent so that their identity layer is backed by an SLA that matches their commitments.

The new Service Commitment and Service Credits

For each AWS Region, during each monthly billing cycle, AWS commits to a Monthly Uptime Percentage of at least 99.99 percent for user pools on Plus, and at least 99.9 percent for user pools on Essentials and Lite. If Amazon Cognito doesn’t meet the Service Commitment for your feature plan, you may be eligible for a Service Credit, as shown in Tables 1 and 2. For full terms and exclusions, see the Amazon Cognito SLA.

What 99.99 percent means in practice

The 99.99 percent Service Commitment is a 10-times improvement over 99.9 percent. In a 30-day month, the allowable monthly downtime drops from about 43 minutes to about 4.3 minutes. For teams that set availability targets for their own applications, this gives a stronger baseline to plan against and to share with stakeholders.

How Amazon Cognito measures availability

The SLA measures availability separately for each AWS Region. Amazon Cognito divides each monthly billing cycle into 5-minute intervals and calculates the percentage of requests in each interval that don’t return an HTTP 500 or 503 error. Intervals with no requests count as 100 percent available. The Monthly Uptime Percentage is the average of these interval values over the billing cycle, minus downtime covered by the exclusions in the SLA. For the full definitions and exclusions, see the Amazon Cognito SLA.

Historical availability over the past 12 months

As we introduce the new SLA, we also looked back at the past 12 months to show how Amazon Cognito performed against the new Service Commitment. Table 3 shows monthly availability for Amazon Cognito user pools from November 2025 through October 2026.

Switch to the Plus feature plan

If your user pools use the Plus feature plan, the 99.99 percent Service Commitment applies to them starting November 1, 2026, with no action needed. If your user pools use Essentials or Lite feature plans, you can switch them to Plus in the AWS Management Console for Amazon Cognito or programmatically. Before you switch, see user pool feature plans and Amazon Cognito pricing to compare features and costs. To learn more about the features that Plus adds, see the advanced security features with threat protection.

To switch a user pool to the Plus feature plan (AWS Management Console):

Sign in to the Amazon Cognito console.

Choose User pools and then choose your user pool.

Choose Settings.

Choose the Feature plans tab.

Choose Switch to Plus.

Review your choice and then choose Confirm.

Figure 1: Amazon Cognito console Feature plans tab with the Switch to Plus button

To switch a user pool to Plus feature plan (AWS CLI):

Important: The Update-user-pool command and the UpdateUserPool API operation reset any parameter that you don’t include in the request to its default value. To avoid unintended changes to your user pool, retrieve your existing configuration first and include it in your update request.

Use the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) to retrieve your current user pool configuration with describe-user-pool:

aws cognito-idp describe-user-pool \ --user-pool-id <your-user-pool-id>

Run the update-user-pool command, including your existing configuration parameters and the Plus tier:

aws cognito-idp update-user-pool \ --user-pool-id <your-user-pool-id> \ --user-pool-tier PLUS \ <your existing configuration parameters>

If you use an AWS SDK, set UserPoolTier to PLUS in an UpdateUserPool request, and include your existing settings in the same way.

Conclusion

In this post, we shared the updated Service Commitment for Amazon Cognito user pools on the Plus feature plan, how availability is measured, and 12 months of historical data. Starting November 1, 2026, user pools on Plus are covered by a 99.99 percent Monthly Uptime Percentage Service Commitment, with no action required if you already use Plus. We plan to keep investing in the availability and resilience of Amazon Cognito.

To review the full terms, see the Amazon Cognito SLA. To learn more about the features in each plan, see user pool feature plans and advanced security features with threat protection.

Title: Microsoft's NTLM security changes trip up third-party logins
Context: The additional protections were added to address CVE-2026-118737, a vulnerability in which "improper verification of cryptographic signature in Windows Remote Procedure Call...
Full Text: Microsoft's November security updates can break authentication in some third-party applications and devices following changes to NTLM message signing. Affected systems include authentication proxy servers, single sign-on (SSO) products, and application packaging tools, the company's support notice says. The failures stem from products that claim to supply required information during NTLM authentication but return incomplete or empty data, Microsoft said: "An affected device might set the NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_TARGET_INFO flag in its CHALLENGE_MESSAGE but provide an empty or incomplete TargetInfo field." Administrators can use the notice's network trace and event log examples to identify affected products. For confirmed cases, the temporary workaround is to set the ClientAllowUnsignedNtlm Registry value to 1 on affected clients. This stops the client offering signing, backing out the new default rather than fixing the incompatible product. The recommended long-term options are a vendor update or Kerberos authentication, where supported. The value sits under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\MSV1_0 and defaults to 0, enabling clients to offer signing on non-anonymous connections. The NTLM changes arrived in the November 10 update as phase 1 in a 2-phase process. In phase 1, "Windows client devices begin offering NTLM signing on all connections by default. Servers accept both signed and unsigned clients. Auditing events identify clients not using signing." Phase 2, scheduled for May 2027, will make Windows servers require NTLM signing by default. "Clients that do not offer signing will be rejected by secure servers," Microsoft stated. Ominously, Microsoft warned that it "might remove the registry keys at a future date," so the company is not kidding about the temporary workaround thing. The additional protections were added to address CVE-2026-118737, a vulnerability in which "improper verification of cryptographic signature in Windows Remote Procedure Call Runtime allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network." NTLM is on Microsoft's hit list, having joined the Deprecated Features list in 2024. It dates back to the era of Windows NT, and Microsoft has made clear that it wants customers to move to Kerberos, which became the default in 2000. Even so, NTLM lingers on. Deprecation doesn't remove Microsoft's obligation to secure NTLM while it remains in supported Windows releases. For administrators, though, the immediate task is identifying incompatible products before temporary exceptions give way to stricter enforcement. ®

Title: Tax and technology, in sync: connected ecosystems
Your Repository's Risk Doesn't Stop at Intake
Context: That is a critical decision, but it is only one point of many where teams need visibility
Full Text:
Most repository security conversations start with a straightforward request: Should this component enter the development path?

That is a critical decision, but it is only one point of many where teams need visibility. And what about software already stored inside the organization?

Answering that question means looking beyond incoming requests to the repositories where teams publish and store software for reuse. Understanding what hosted repositories contain is the first step to seeing what may still be in circulation.

Hosted Repositories Keep Components in Circulation

A hosted repository is the authoritative location where an organization publishes and stores artifacts for teams to retrieve. Unlike a proxy repository, which fetches and caches content from an external source, a hosted repository stores content published to it.

It can contain:

Internally developed software, such as packages, libraries, container images, and build outputs.

Development versions and releases that teams publish for internal use.

Third-party components that are unavailable from a configured upstream source.

Once published, these artifacts may remain available through established development workflows. An internal library can become a shared dependency across several services. A development version may remain available while a team tests a release. A stored commercial package may be the only version available to a project with a specific requirement.

Over time, a hosted repository can hold multiple versions of a component. Teams may continue to retrieve versions that are no longer the latest release because existing builds or projects still depend on them. That makes the repository a distribution point for software other teams may use well after its initial publication.

Hosted repositories also serve different teams and workflows. The engineer who publishes an artifact may not be the person who maintains a downstream application or decides whether a new finding requires a change. Visibility into hosted contents helps connect those responsibilities: teams can see what remains available, assess the relevant findings, and decide who should follow up.

Risk Can Change After Publication

A component that met an organization's requirements when it was first published or stored may need another look as vulnerability intelligence or organizational policies change. The initial decision still matters, but it cannot provide a complete view of risk over time.

Updated intelligence can also change how an incoming component request is handled. When a request is evaluated against that intelligence and violates a configured policy, controls can block or quarantine the component before it is served through a protected proxy. That protects the intake path, but it does not assess components already stored in hosted repositories. Those require a separate review.

For example, a vulnerability disclosure may identify an affected version of a shared library after several teams have begun using it. The library itself may not have changed, but what teams know about its risk has. If that version remains available in a hosted repository, teams need to determine whether it is still in use and what action is appropriate.

Other developments can also prompt a review:

New vulnerability or component intelligence identifies a concern with a stored version.

A policy change affects whether a component is acceptable for reuse.

A team discovers that an older version is still available and may be retrieved by a build.

This does not mean every hosted component is unsafe, or that the original review was inadequate. It means a one-time decision cannot account for information that becomes available later. The relevant question is whether or not teams can identify which stored components warrant investigation, remediation, or a policy decision.

Repository governance needs to cover both new requests and the components an organization continues to store and share. That means maintaining visibility into existing hosted artifacts as well as evaluating components as they enter through managed paths.

Assess Components After Publication

Hosted repository scanning provides the complementary view: it helps teams identify current findings in selected components already stored in supported hosted repositories.

Teams can select supported repositories for monitoring, define the scan scope, and review component findings. Those results can help identify which components need attention and prioritize follow-up under organizational policies. Continuous monitoring can also surface changes as component intelligence evolves.

Coverage depends on which repositories, formats, and components are included in the scan. Teams should understand that scope so they can interpret the results accurately and know what remains outside the review.

Scanning provides visibility and supports assessment. A scan report does not itself prevent a component from being uploaded or downloaded. Teams need separate controls for those actions. See our hosted repository scanning documentation for more details.

Turn Findings Into Governance

Scanning can show teams where to look. Governance determines what happens next. Organizations should decide which hosted repositories to monitor, who reviews the findings, and how teams prioritize action when a component no longer meets policy.

A practical process can help teams:

Set the monitoring scope, including which hosted repositories are in view.

Assign responsibility for reviewing findings and coordinating follow-up.

Prioritize remediation based on policy and how a component is used.

Reassess components when relevant intelligence or organizational requirements change.

Repository findings also need context. A component's presence in a hosted repository does not establish that it was included in a particular application or release. If a finding could affect shipped software, teams can consult build records or a software bill of materials (SBOM) to determine whether that specific component version was used.

That distinction helps teams avoid both overreacting to every stored component and overlooking one because it entered the repository in the past. Repository scanning helps identify and assess hosted components. Build and release records help connect a finding to specific software.

The process also needs an owner. Platform teams may manage the repository configuration, while security teams interpret findings and application teams decide how to update or replace a component in their software. The responsibilities will vary by organization, but documenting them helps ensure that a finding leads to a decision rather than remaining an unresolved report.

Govern What Enters and What Remains

Proxy scanning helps teams assess components as they are requested. Hosted repository scanning helps them review components already stored and available for reuse. Together, these views help teams understand what enters through a managed path and what remains available over time.

The Sonatype Nexus One platform helps teams make trusted component decisions and apply governance into the build process. It connects decisions at intake with policy, remediation, and compliance workflows so teams can manage component risk as information changes. Title: Inside Agentic Offensive Frameworks: Intent IDs
Context: If a single attacker hits your environment with i14200 at 10:00 and i15100 an hour later, while your logs show only a handful of probes in between, those missing sequence...
Full Text:
“Black October” was rife with iNNNN indicators.

Barracuda: i19ghci.yml in a GitHub workflow.

Bitrise: i3694canary as an account name.

Chainstack: artex-i37257 in the attacker's artifacts.

Ardor: i63c2d.py as the persistence poller.

These IDs are Agentic Offensive Framework Intent IDs. We mentioned these IDs in our Agentic Attacks: In The Wild’s ARTEX-Harvester case, and GTIG highlighted them in ARTEX and Friends: Enter Agentic Offensive Frameworks.

We want to dissect them as a new form of harness leak that flows from agentic offensive frameworks into defender logs.

What are Intent IDs?

Intent IDs are incrementing counters in common agentic offensive frameworks. They are an internal implementation detail: the harness breaks an attack into discrete sub-goals called "intents" and assigns each one a numeric ID.

When a harness places that ID in its prompts and workspace paths, it bleeds into the attack: when the model creates a file, registers an account, pushes a GitHub workflow, or sets a User-Agent string on a target, it borrows the identifier sitting right in front of it.

There has been a proliferation of agentic offensive frameworks. We reviewed over a hundred open-source offensive harness repositories, and two families stand out for handing the LLM a numeric Intent ID that leaks into target-side artifacts:

The ARTEX family: ARTEX itself, plus public forks like Pojun (tracking current ARTEX as of v0.4.99) and AntiFox (forked from ARTEX v0.1.1).

The Cairn family: Cairn itself and descendants like sapper-v2 (a reimplementation of Cairn's design).

ARTEX

ARTEX stores intents, facts, findings, hints, and digests in one PostgreSQL table, exploration_nodes, backed by a single BIGSERIAL sequence. Each installation runs its own counter and never resets it by default.

That design produces three traits defenders see in logs:

Numbers climb across runs and targets. A fresh campaign driven from a new ARTEX installation might start in the double digits (i49 through i63 in Ardor's disclosure). A long-running, busy installation climbs into the tens or hundreds of thousands (i37257 at Chainstack).

Intent IDs are rarely seen consecutively increasing. Because facts, findings, hints, and digests draw from the same sequence as intents, consecutive intent numbers are rare.

Facts stay local; intents leak. Workers see fact IDs as bare integers in their planner snapshots. We checked 539 worker transcripts (~10,900 shell commands) from an exposed ARTEX instance. Fact IDs appeared only in local scripts and notes (e.g fact #461).

In agent/worker.go, ARTEX wires the intent ID into three places the model reads on every turn: its working directory (tasks/<task>/i<N>), its session name (exp<N>-worker-i<N>), and the "意图 id" ("intent id") field in its prompt. Pojun keeps this exact layout. AntiFox goes further: its prompt orders the agent to save its outputs under an i<id>/ subdirectory.

Cairn

Cairn separates its counters by object type and leaves a distinct fingerprint.

In services.py, Cairn formats Intent IDs as zero-padded three-digit strings (i%03d) and gives each object type its own series:

Intents: i001, i002, i003...

Facts: f001, f002, f003...

Hints: h001, h002, h003...

Projects: proj_001, proj_002...

Unlike ARTEX, Cairn resets its counters for every new project. Numbers stay small and run without gaps. On one exposed Cairn host we examined, a single project held every intent from i001 through i292.

Cairn passes {intent_id} into its explore prompt as "Current Intent", and the worker reuses it in callbacks, DTD files, webshells, and test accounts.

sapper-v2 reimplements the same i%03d/f%03d/h%03d per-project scheme.

Pacing ARTEX Intent IDs

Because an ARTEX installation's sequence increments across runs and targets without resetting by default, plotting Intent IDs against timestamps can offer analysts a pacing signal.

Linking Across IPs and Incidents

Agentic campaigns often rotate through residential proxy pools, using a new exit IP on nearly every request. Proxy rotation breaks IP-based clustering. Intent IDs cut across that noise: if activity from rotating IPs, or across separate victims, produces Intent IDs climbing at a steady rate over time, those sightings point to one ARTEX installation.

While tracking ARTEX-Harvester, we used rising Intent IDs alongside a distinctive boto3 build and proxy pool overlap to connect activity across more than a dozen organizations.

Intent IDs also survive a move between clouds. In one intrusion the attacker used stolen IAM users in AWS and a service principal in Azure. We found 36 Intent IDs on the AWS side, in SSM command comments and resource names, and 34 on the Azure side, in resource names, tags, and a role assignment description. All of them came from one climbing sequence, linking both to the same run even though the identities have nothing in common.

Deconflicting Installations

The same sequence behavior works in reverse. Because exploration_nodes.id is a single BIGSERIAL counter per database, one ARTEX installation will not assign the same Intent ID to two different intents.

This property gives analysts a rough way to separate instances:

Duplicate IDs across unrelated targets point to separate installations. Two campaigns hitting i13211 against different victims are running on different ARTEX databases, not the same one. (A single worker will reuse its own ID across multiple requests and artifacts while working a single intent, so duplicates within one engagement are expected.)

Out-of-order jumps signal a split. If a cluster of activity shows i37257 on Monday and i4100 on Tuesday, those requests are not coming from one continuous database sequence.

This deconfliction separates installations, not necessarily operators. One operator can run several ARTEX instances in parallel.

Gauging Scope from a Single Victim's Logs

Even without cross-victim visibility, the size of the gaps between Intent IDs could indicate whether your are a dedicated target or one of many.

If a single attacker hits your environment with i14200 at 10:00 and i15100 an hour later, while your logs show only a handful of probes in between, those missing sequence numbers went somewhere. Some of that gap comes from facts, findings, hints, and digests recorded against your own assets. When a jump dwarfs the activity in your logs, the same ARTEX installation is likely burning through tasks against other targets in parallel: an opportunistic, multi-target run rather than an operator focused solely on you.

These signals are lossy. Intent ID pacing is a corroborating signal, not standalone attribution:

The rate of climb is uneven. Facts, findings, hints, and digests share the sequence, and work against other targets advances the counter between sightings at one victim.

Unrelated installations collide in the same numeric ranges. Fresh deployments all pass through the low hundreds and thousands, so two unrelated operators can produce numbers that look sequential by coincidence.

Operators reset or parallelize. Rebuilding the container, wiping the database, or splitting targets across multiple ARTEX instances breaks the sequence.

Cairn resets per project. Because Cairn restarts at i001 for every new project, cross-incident pacing applies only to the ARTEX family.

Intent IDs in the Wild

Across public disclosures, exposed harness directories, and our telemetry, we cataloged hundreds of distinct Intent IDs. A few extremes show how the two designs behave at scale:

Highest Intent ID: i808807. Observed in ARTEX activity in November 2026, alongside pentest-i804759 and i806173 from the same series. An installation only reaches the 800,000s after churning through intents, facts, and findings across targets without a reset.

Lowest Intent ID: i001. The bootstrap intent of a Cairn project recovered from an exposed Cairn host. Cairn's dispatcher creates i001 automatically as a synthetic root edge connecting origin to the project's initial seed fact (f001), before worker intents begin at i002.

Longest consecutive runs:

Cairn: i001 through i292. Every intent present in a complete project graph recovered from an exposed Cairn open directory.

ARTEX: i8920 through i8923 (four in a row). Seen in artex-verify-i89xx User-Agent strings. ARTEX installations rarely string more than a few consecutive Intent IDs together because facts, findings, hints, and digests pull from the same sequence between intents.

Hunting for Harness Leaks

Intent IDs are noisy on their own, so pair i<N> with an anchor before alerting. Good anchors include prefixes like artex-, pentest-, probe, or canary in account names, User-Agents, CI workflows, and cloud resources, or leaked run-directory paths such as tasks/<task>/i<N> in command-line telemetry. Hits are useful tool markers and pacing clues, but not operator fingerprints.

Where do these leak in logs? Anywhere that the API expects user-provided context, naming, or commentary. We have already observed these IDs in:

AWS:

role session names

SSM command comments

bucket, role, user, and policy names

tags and descriptions

RDS export task IDs

KMS key descriptions and aliases

security-group names and rule descriptions

Azure and Entra:

run-command names

VM computer names

app registration names

Note: for denied calls, the names survive in error messages.

Title: Our 2026 Cybersecurity Predictions: What We Got Right, What We Got Wrong, and What Changed
Context: During a year shaped by AI-driven vulnerability discovery, however, the ability to connect a new finding with exposed systems, attacker activity, and business consequences...
Full Text:
Rapid7’s annual Security Predictions webinar returns on December 10, bringing our experts together to explore what the year ahead could hold for cybersecurity. Before sharing our predictions for 2027, we’re grading last year’s calls: that geopolitical tensions would reshape cyber threats, insider threats would dominate breach root causes, and context would become the new currency of cyber performance.

Register here for the 2027 Security Predictions webinar.

As security leaders work through their priorities for 2027, those predictions offer a useful starting point. The year reinforced several of the concerns we highlighted, while developments in attacker behavior and AI added new dimensions to the discussion. Looking at how those themes unfolded helps us understand what remains relevant and where our thinking needs to evolve.

Geopolitics shaped cyber targeting, with businesses caught in the middle

Our prediction that geopolitical fault lines would redraw the cyber battlefield earned an A-, as regional conflicts created opportunities for espionage, disruption, and public pressure throughout 2026. Cyber operations allowed adversaries to pursue those objectives below the threshold of open warfare, with commercial organizations exposed alongside government and critical infrastructure targets.

Rapid7 Intelligence tracked a spike in retaliatory activity following regional military escalations in late February. State-directed actors pursued espionage and data theft, while hacktivist personas amplified the impact. Rapid7 also assessed that stolen information was likely to be passed from state actors to hacktivist groups for public release, extending the consequences of an intrusion beyond the initial compromise.

That chain from state actor to hacktivist release makes an organization’s exposure harder to judge from its own location or industry alone. Customers, suppliers, infrastructure, and perceived political associations can attract attention, bringing a seemingly routine commercial relationship into a much wider conflict. Examining those dependencies during response exercises uncovers difficult decisions early, particularly where protecting a service or containing an incident requires agreement across security, operations, legal, and executive leadership.

Insider risk expanded beyond human users

Our prediction that insider threats would dominate breach root causes drew attention to risks ranging from employee negligence to deliberate access selling. During 2026, reporting on ransomware recruitment attempts reinforced concerns about attackers seeking cooperation from people inside organizations, while the growing use of AI agents broadened the conversation about insider risk. As agents gain access to business systems and take actions on an organization’s behalf, questions about permissions, oversight, and unintended consequences increasingly extend beyond human users.

Our blog on insider recruitment in ransomware campaigns explored an approach by Medusa to a BBC journalist, offering payment in exchange for access. It illustrated how attackers combine financial incentives, persuasion, and pressure to pursue legitimate credentials, giving organizations a concrete reason to include recruitment attempts in awareness programs and response planning.

The wider access economy also remained significant, although credentials appearing for sale do not establish that an employee willingly supplied them. External compromise and exposed systems continued to provide routes into businesses, with AI-assisted vulnerability discovery adding further pressure. Our prediction captured an important concern, while the year reinforced the need to distinguish deliberate insider cooperation from other ways attackers obtain and misuse access.

Context proved its value, although we overstated its novelty

Our prediction that context would become the new currency of cyber performance earned a B, largely because understanding an environment has always been fundamental to protecting it. During a year shaped by AI-driven vulnerability discovery, however, the ability to connect a new finding with exposed systems, attacker activity, and business consequences became particularly valuable when teams had little time to decide how to respond.

Our analysis of the ASOS incident explored that challenge after an unauthorized notification reached customers through the retailer’s own app. With the route of compromise still unclear, the incident raised questions about access to customer communications platforms and how investigators connect activity across accounts, integrations, and third-party services.

The same need for context applies to remediation, where an advisory alone cannot determine whether interrupting a critical service is justified. Teams need to know where affected technology is running, how attackers could reach it, and which mitigations are practical. Bringing asset information, threat intelligence, and operational knowledge together remains essential to making those decisions with confidence.

Bringing those lessons into our 2027 predictions

Across all three themes, the year reinforced how closely security decisions depend on understanding relationships: between organizations, between identities and access, and between technical weaknesses and business consequences. Those connections will remain relevant as AI changes how technology is used and how threats develop.

Join Rapid7’s Security Predictions webinar on December 10 to explore those shifts with our experts and consider what they could mean for your priorities in the year ahead.

Title: Ground Truth: CISO Matt Martin on Building a Real Security Program Without an Enterprise Budget
Context: Job postings demand degrees and a wall of certifications before you can apply, but attackers have none of them
Full Text:
A CISO who traded enterprise budgets for higher ed on what “creativity within constraints” really means, and the one habit worth stealing from how he leads.I have known Matt Martin for a few years, and the first thing I tell anyone about him has nothing to do with security. It is that he treats the work as a way to serve other people. I first knew Matt as the security leader who spends his own time flying to Ghana and Uganda to teach executives and students how to protect themselves. That instinct, more than any tool or certification, explains how he runs a security program.

Matt spent two decades running security organizations in financial services, including at LPL Financial, with an enterprise budget and any tool he needed. A few years ago he made a deliberate choice to take on higher ed instead, because he wanted to prove he could build a resilient security program under real constraints. Today he is the Chief Information Security and Privacy Officer at Western Carolina University.

I asked Matt to share his journey from a conference in Accra to a university in the mountains of North Carolina. His story is really about doing more with less, and right now, that is all of us.

Q. You have built real social impact into your career, sharing security knowledge and consultancy with underserved communities. How did that begin?

A. It started unexpectedly. After two decades in financial services I decided to go out on my own. The whole point was to support small and medium organizations, especially in developing countries, that could not afford the security consultancy they needed. I heard about the GC3B conference in Accra, Ghana, which was about building cyber resiliency in developing countries. They only accepted companies, so I applied as the LLC I had just started, and a few weeks later I received a letter from the government of Ghana inviting me.

I flew over not knowing a single person. The first day had a light schedule, so I hired a tour guide and he took me to see Elmina Castle and the Door of No Return. That one day changed my life. Seeing that side of the story of humanity as an adult, after growing up in the American South, connected so much for me about how tied together we all are. I carried that into every meeting at the conference.

Afterwards I developed a partnership with a nonprofit called Africa Digital Rights Hub, and it has since taken me back to run masterclasses for executives and students in Ghana and Uganda. Part of the reason Western Carolina appealed to me was that they wanted to help me expand that work.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Q. You had about three weeks between that invitation from the Ghanaian government and actually getting on the plane. What was it like to just drop everything and go?

A. It was a scramble. Three weeks to get all my immunizations, book everything, and fly to Ghana. Actually, my yellow fever vaccine wasn’t fully effective by the time I landed, I was a couple of days short, so I had to talk my way through the medical booth in the airport before I could even clear immigration.

Funny enough, it’s risk acceptance in real life. I knew my control wasn’t operating effectively yet, I understood the exposure, and I decided to go anyway. That’s the same type of call we make in security every day.

Q. I’ve heard you say that security and GRC have become an elite sport. Job postings demand degrees and a wall of certifications before you can apply, but attackers have none of them. You are largely self-taught. What has that taught you about who belongs in this field?

A. I started with a history degree, and some of the best security people I know do not have a security degree either. Think how this community started. In the beginning you couldn’t go get a degree in cybersecurity, it was creative people figuring it out as they went. There are brilliant people all over the world who could do this work and simply haven’t had the opportunity. That is why the teaching matters so much to me. There is a real chance to democratize security education and take down some of the barriers the industry has put up.

Q. You have a phrase for how you think about the work now, “creativity within constraints.” When you started in the new context of higher ed, what did you assume your constraints would be?

A. I assumed it would be budget. In financial services, I could get almost anything as long as it was reasonable. Budgets are definitely tight in higher ed, but it was not my number one problem. I needed to learn the environment.A university has done things a certain way for a long time, knowledge is meant to be open and shared, and the place can feel like family. Once I really understood the environment, I could get creative and start designing security that worked with the culture instead of against it.

Q. You’ve been candid with me that you got the first few months wrong, and I think that honesty helps other leaders even more than sharing wins. What happened?

A. I went in thinking I already knew how everything should work, and I started fixing things. I probably pushed harder than I should have before I understood the place. What I should have done was go in to learn, listen more than I talked, and document what I found before I tried to solve anything. Overseeing the security program at a large company does not mean you know how to build one everywhere.

Q. So with a small team and a tight budget, how do you actually run a real program? Walk me through the mechanics.

A. It starts with risk, not compliance. If you do risk well, compliance comes almost for free, because it tells you what you need to do and in what order. So I built a real risk register. I went to the technology leaders first and asked what was broken and what was holding them back, wrote it all down, and mapped it to a framework.

Then the honest problem is capacity. I cannot hire a team of analysts to test every control or spend weeks each year on a self-assessment. Self-attestation is not enough on its own. Anyone who has run a program knows that asking whether a control works can get you different answers depending on who you ask, so I needed real evidence, not opinions. The only way to get that at scale was to embrace automation and continuous monitoring.

Q. You have now lived on both sides. What would you take from higher ed back into a big enterprise?

A. Fiscal discipline, honestly. The habit of asking “do we really need this, or is it a nice-to-have,” and whether a given feature is three million dollars better than what we already have. In large enterprises you also end up with people inserting themselves into processes to justify a role, and everything takes longer. But look, every company of every size has something it could do better. I’ve really embraced how scarcity forces you to be more efficient.

Q. How can you judge whether someone will make a good CISO?

A. This one question tells me what I need to know: Do you know how your company makes money? Can you actually tell me how your organization makes money, or in a university, how the institution succeeds? Once you understand that, you can prioritize risk in a way that matters to the business. If you cannot answer it, you are going to protect the wrong things.

Q. What kind of CISO actually thrives in a place like higher ed?

A. You have to want to get your hands dirty. If you just want to run a team of forty and just go to meetings, it will not work, because your team is smaller and you will be doing some of the work yourself. You have to be creative enough to build things that are not the industry standard. And most of all, you have to see the business-enablement side of security, not only the technical side. You are engaging with the colleges, the chancellor, even the athletics department, and your job is to enable them. If you come in 100% security or bust, you will not last long in higher ed.

Q. Matt, thank you for this. What is on your radar right now? Is there anything you are most excited to build next?

A. Giving students a real place to learn. I want more working CISOs to share with students what the career actually looks like. Where I would love to take it is a hands-on cybersecurity lab on campus, for students to get real-world practice. I would also love to keep building the connections with universities in Africa, so students can learn from each other in both directions.

Ground truth for your program

Matt’s whole approach is a posture, not a tactic. He leads as a teacher and a collaborator, and treats security as a way to help organizations succeed rather than a roadblock.

The lesson I would take to any team, at any budget: name your real constraint before you invest against the wrong one. Matt walked in certain it was budget, and it turned out to be understanding the environment. Assume it’s money and you pour your limited resources into tools, when the real problem was one money could not solve. Get the constraint right, though, and every dollar and every control is aimed at a real business objective, which is what makes a program effective at any size.

So before your next purchase or project, ask yourself two questions: What do I actually believe my top constraint is, and how do I know? And am I about to spend against it, or around it?

Title: Electrolux Smart Boilers in Ukraine Connect to Russian Servers, Raising Privacy Concerns
Context: Researchers found Electrolux-branded smart boilers connecting to Russian servers, raising concerns about household data and privacy
Full Text:
Researchers found Electrolux-branded smart boilers connecting to Russian servers, raising concerns about household data and privacy.

A router in Ukraine recorded a water heater doing something odd. The owner, Alexander Unger, saw his Electrolux EWH 80 look up a server called mqtt.cloud.rusklimat.ru and then try to connect to it. He published the records on Facebook, including a lookup timed at 18:00 on November 23, 2026.

Mysterium VPN’s research team checked the finding. They repeated the lookup on November 25 and got the same address, 130.193.49[.]173. RIPE, the registry for Europe and Russia, lists that block under Yandex.Cloud LLC at 16 Lva Tolstogo Street in Moscow.

The server belongs to Rusklimat, a Moscow group that calls itself the leader of Russia’s climate-equipment market. Its Hommyn app uses that name to reach heaters, air conditioners and ventilation units. Developers who link such devices to Home Assistant list it as the official cloud for Ballu, Electrolux, Zanussi and Royal Thermo, and a 2025 guide on Habr says the devices contact it by default.

Rusklimat sells Electrolux-branded boilers in Russia and advertises them for Hommyn and for Yandex’s voice assistant, Alisa. Mysterium VPN adds, citing Meduza, that Ukraine struck three of Yandex’s six data centers in October 2026 and disrupted Yandex Cloud, where Rusklimat’s server runs.

“The manual for the EWH SI EEC series, hosted by the Austrian arm of the home-improvement chain Hornbach, names CladSwiss AG of Zug, Switzerland, as the manufacturer and says the boiler is made in China. It says the Electrolux name is used under license from AB Electrolux, the Swedish parent company.” reads the report published by Mysterium VPN. “It adds that the remote-control app, ClimatOn, comes from CladSwiss and isn’t provided by Electrolux.”

The manual also says the Electrolux name is used under license from AB Electrolux of Sweden, and that the remote-control app, ClimatOn, comes from CladSwiss, not Electrolux. Retailers lean on the Swedish angle: Rozetka gives Sweden as the country of brand registration, and the series is sold in Serbia, Poland and Lithuania.

This single appliance has links to five countries: Sweden, Switzerland, China, Germany, and Russia. That’s quite a complicated background for a water heater installed in someone’s bathroom.

According to CladSwiss, the data collected by its ClimatOn app should be stored in Frankfurt, Germany. Mysterium VPN also found a ClimatOn server hosted on Amazon infrastructure in Germany. This means the boiler can connect to two different servers, depending on which app the owner uses.

Both apps use the same technology platform. A developer who created software to control an Electrolux SmartInverter boiler locally found that the device identifies itself on the home network as a Syncleo device. Syncleo is based in Israel, has an office in Russia, and lists Rusklimat among its customers.

Why did a buyer in Ukraine end up on the Russian app? Mysterium VPN doesn’t know. Unger, it was told, set the boiler up with Hommyn, and a buyer of another Electrolux model wrote on Rozetka in June 2026 that the Wi-Fi worked properly only through the Russian app. Mysterium VPN has asked CladSwiss which app buyers in Ukraine and the EU are pointed to.

The Russian app knows this boiler by name. Its Google Play page shows an “Electrolux SmartInverter” in the first screenshot, and version 1.20.2 of the Android app lists 118 devices, 19 of them Electrolux, including the series named in the manual. Its privacy policy names R-Klimat LLC of Moscow as the operator and says personal data stays “exclusively within the territory” of Russia, under Russian law.

“The privacy policy bundled in the app names R-Klimat LLC of Moscow as the operator and says the app stores users’ personal information “exclusively within the territory” of Russia, under Russian law. The app is written to send sign-in details (a phone number or email address) and the name and room of each device to Rusklimat servers. It keeps device history on Yandex Cloud and sends the phone’s location to a Hommyn weather service.” continues the report. “The app also carries one fixed username and password for Rusklimat’s device server, the same in every copy. We didn’t use them and are not publishing them.”

Mysterium VPN didn’t use the credentials and won’t publish them. Neither will I.

The brand’s website points the same way. English manuals send buyers to home-comfort.com, which gives CladSwiss, at an address in Baar, Switzerland, as its contact. Its contact form asks visitors, in Russian, to let a company called RK-Region process their data under Russian federal law 152-FZ. Rusklimat’s shop names RK-Region in its payment details, and ballu.ru carries the same consent text.

Swiss register data show CladSwiss was entered in December 2019 to trade technical equipment, especially air-conditioning units. Mysterium VPN found nothing that shows who owns the company or how it connects to Rusklimat beyond these records.

What can the server see? CladSwiss’s Data Act declaration lists whether a device is on, its temperature, its operating mode and its power level, about 1 MB a day on standby and 3 MB in use. The privacy policy adds the phone’s identifier, its IP address and the names of Wi-Fi networks, plus location if the user agrees.

“A record of when a household heats water shows when people are at home. The line that carries those reports also carries commands to switch the boiler on or change its temperature. For a boiler tied to mqtt.cloud.rusklimat.ru, that line ends at a Russian company’s server in Moscow.” Mysterium VPN states. “Russia isn’t among the countries the European Commission recognizes as protecting personal data adequately, and Ukraine first ordered its internet providers to block Yandex’s services in 2017.”

The same line also carries commands to switch the boiler on or change its temperature. Mysterium VPN notes that Russia isn’t among the countries the European Commission recognizes as protecting personal data adequately.

One claim remains untested. Developers who studied a Ballu ventilation unit from the same family wrote that every unit shipped with the same cloud login and didn’t check the server’s certificate. Mysterium VPN hasn’t tested that and doesn’t know whether it applies to the boiler.

Mysterium VPN sent questions to AB Electrolux, CladSwiss and Rozetka on November 25, and none had replied at publication. AB Electrolux sold its Russian business in 2022 and said then that it had no production in Russia and wouldn’t supply the company it sold. Rusklimat’s Russian shop sells heaters under the Electrolux name today.

Mysterium VPN stresses that its findings are limited. Researchers did not connect to the servers or examine the boiler itself. They only reviewed the Hommyn app’s code, so they cannot confirm what data the device actually sends.

Users can check their router logs for connections to “rusklimat” or use DNS monitoring tools such as Pi-hole, AdGuard Home or NextDNS. Blocking the Russian server stops remote access, although local control may still work over Wi-Fi. Users can also disable the boiler’s Wi-Fi and place smart appliances on a separate guest network to keep them away from computers and phones. These checks also apply to Hommyn and ClimatOn devices from Ballu and Zanussi.

“A VPN on your phone or laptop doesn’t change where an appliance on your Wi-Fi sends its data, so the fix here sits at the router.” concludes the report.

Title: U.S. Treasury's Financial Crimes Agency Takes Some Systems Offline After Cyber Intrusion
Context: The BSA E-Filing website is still up, although some services may be temporarily unavailable
Full Text:
The U.S. Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has been hit by a cybersecurity incident that resulted in "unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems," the bureau said on Tuesday. As a precaution, it has taken some systems offline.

The bureau collects suspicious activity reports and other Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) filings from banks and other financial institutions and analyzes them to fight money laundering and terrorist financing.

The BSA E-Filing website is still up, although some services may be temporarily unavailable. The agency has not named the systems it reached or those it took offline.

To support filers affected by the disruption, the bureau is extending some filing deadlines: covered reports originally due between November 18 and December 29 can now be submitted until December 30.

A relief order issued the same day, FIN-2026-R002, applies to three groups:

Financial institutions that used Secure Direct Transfer Mode (SDTM), the channel for sending batches of BSA reports directly from their own servers, as of November 18

Companies required to file a beneficial ownership information report during the covered window

Individuals required to update a FinCEN Identifier during the same window

All other Bank Secrecy Act obligations stay in force, including the duty to monitor for suspicious transactions. The service alert says urgent suspicious activity information can still reach law enforcement through the Financial Institutions Hotline, 1-866-556-3974, which is not affected by the disruption.

The disclosure followed days of filing trouble. Filing providers reported failures in automated batch submissions beginning November 18, and the bureau posted a notice about the disruption to SDTM late last week, according to a filing outages report by the markets news site The Deep Dive.

The bureau has not said whether the intrusion caused those outages. The order grants the relief because of a "service disruption" and does not mention the cybersecurity incident.

Nor has the agency said when the access began, whether any data was viewed or taken, or who was responsible. No group has publicly claimed the intrusion so far. Those answers matter because of what the bureau holds: reports of suspicious financial activity filed by financial institutions nationwide.

The incident is not Treasury's first in recent years: in December 2024, a China-linked group used a compromised BeyondTrust API key in an earlier Treasury breach that reached department systems and documents. No link between the two incidents has been reported.

Title: Ex-OpenAI Employee Accused of Bugging Company Offices Granted $1 Million Bail
Context: A former OpenAI employee accused of concealing a covert recording device at the company's San Francisco offices will be allowed to be released from jail on a $1 million bond, a...
Full Text:
A former OpenAI employee accused of concealing a covert recording device at the company's San Francisco offices will be allowed to be released from jail on a $1 million bond, a San Francisco federal court judge ruled Tuesday.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national, was arrested on October 9, 2026, for allegedly bugging the artificial intelligence (AI) company's offices with the aim of recording sensitive conversations.

Subsequent court filings have pointed out that Alfozan was in touch on WhatsApp with a member of the Saudi royal family, as well as expressed interest in moving back to Saudi Arabia following OpenAI's initial public offering (IPO).

He has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of 5 years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by 3 years of supervised release.

"At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," the ChatGPT-maker said at the time.

Alfozan pleaded not guilty to the charges during his appearance in San Francisco federal court earlier this month.

According to CNBC, the decision comes after prosecutors told the court last week that they had "found no new evidence to support the theory that Mr. Alfozan was stealing trade secrets, or to support the speculation that he was acting as an unregistered foreign agent for Saudi Arabia."

However, they said investigators have found hundreds of audio files on the defendant's personal devices, including dozens of recordings of meetings or conversations that took place at OpenAI throughout September 2026.

Some of these involved meetings with OpenAI customers and contained material protected by attorney-client privilege, prosecutors said, adding he possessed a photograph of what's believed to be a term sheet for a "strategic partnership" between OpenAI and another company.

"What the defendant did or intended to do with those audio files remains under investigation," they said.

Under the bail conditions, Alfozan will be required to wear a GPS ankle monitor, observe a curfew from 7 p.m. to 7 a.m., stay within the Northern District of California, and avoid airports and train and bus stations. He is expected to be released on Wednesday morning.

"There is no spy story that we're talking about right now," U.S. Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse said, per The Wall Street Journal. "The government doesn't have that."

Title: Microsoft confirms authentication issues after November updates
Context: Tracked as CVE-2026-118737, this security flaw was found in the Windows Remote Procedure Call Runtime and stems from a timing-dependent authentication weakness that...
Full Text:
Microsoft has confirmed that customers may experience authentication issues after installing November security updates that address a high-severity remote code execution vulnerability.

Tracked as CVE-2026-118737, this security flaw was found in the Windows Remote Procedure Call Runtime and stems from a timing-dependent authentication weakness that unauthenticated attackers can exploit to remotely execute code without user interaction on unpatched systems.

Microsoft says the November security updates represent the first phase of NTLM message-signing improvements, which reduce exposure to relay attacks by ensuring authenticated NTLM sessions always establish a cryptographic session key and negotiate real message signing.

However, as Microsoft explained in an updated support document, the new security improvements introduced to address this vulnerability may also cause authentication failures on patched devices.

"Microsoft is aware of compatibility issues affecting some third-party apps and devices, including authentication proxy servers, single sign-on (SSO) solutions, and application packaging solutions that use NTLM authentication," it said.

"This issue can occur when such a proxy device does not correctly implement the NTLM protocol. For example, an affected device might set the NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_TARGET_INFO flag in its CHALLENGE_MESSAGE but provide an empty or incomplete TargetInfo field."

While a fix is not yet available, Microsoft said affected apps and devices return an NTLMSSP_CHALLENGE message with an empty "Target Info List" in network trace signatures or Target Machine fields with "Not Found" values in event logs.

As a temporary workaround, the company advised customers to go through the following procedure on affected systems:

Set the ClientAllowUnsignedNtlm REG_DWORD registry value under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\MSV1_0 to 1 (the value used for clients that do not offer SIGN)

Check whether the affected device or application supports a configuration that uses Kerberos authentication or whether the vendor provides a software or firmware update compatible with the NTLM signing requirements introduced by CVE-2026-118737.

If neither option is available, contact the device or software vendor to request an update that complies with the NTLM protocol requirements described in 3.1.5.1.2 Client Receives a CHALLENGE_MESSAGE from the Server.

However, Microsoft said the ClientAllowUnsignedNtlm registry setting is a short-term solution and may be removed in the future.

"Updating the affected product or using a compatible authentication configuration is the recommended long-term resolution," it noted.

Since it addressed installation issues affecting the November 2026 cumulative updates, Microsoft has also confirmed that this month's security updates are causing Windows activation failures and SQL Server performance issues.

The company is also investigating a known issue that may break printing documents with complex formatting for customers who have installed the latest Windows updates.

Unified Data

The agentic SOC starts with SIEM, and SIEM starts with data. Agents are only as good as the context they act on. Unified Agentic Investigations

The agentic SOC must scale human expertise with round-the-clock coverage for every alert. It redefines the investigation workflow to put agents at the center, with humans in control.

Security teams that simply automate linear, serial workflows end up with agents making fast, but confidently wrong, decisions. AI SOC tools built on general-purpose frontier models lack the precision needed to accurately close false positives and find the true threats hiding in the queue.

Custom Agents

Machine-speed Response

Humans approve the most critical actions, and every step is traced and auditable, so the platform can act in seconds rather than hours.

The Platform and the Engine

The shift to the agentic SOC marks a turning point in security operations, from fragmented and passive systems of record to a unified platform built to stop breaches. Visibility is only the starting point. Falcon Guardian enables security teams to enforce policies across supported AI interactions and agent activity, with controls tailored to where AI operates.

When an AI agent takes action, individual prompts, tool calls, and endpoint events tell only part of the story. A process accessing a sensitive file may appear routine on its own, but the instructions and agent activity that led to it can reveal a security threat. Security teams need to connect these events to understand what happened, why it happened, and what was affected.

Falcon Guardian, powered by CrowdStrike Agent Graph, connects agents, sessions, models, tools, skills, MCP servers, processes, files, and related security events into a unified investigative context.

The Falcon Guardian session graph reveals the causal sequence within an individual agent session, tracing instructions and tool calls through downstream execution. The Footprint View extends this understanding across related agents, users, tools, and resources to help analysts assess the scope and potential blast radius of a threat. Instead of investigating disconnected signals, security teams can trace suspicious agent behavior to its origin, understand its consequences, and determine where to respond.

Discover AI Activity and Detect Threats

Falcon Guardian brings AI security into the Falcon console to help security teams maintain visibility into AI adoption, monitor activity, and identify threats across their endpoints.

Agent Inventory reveals known and shadow AI agents, including active and dormant installations. Prompt Activity provides visibility into supported AI interactions, including the applications and models employees use. Detections bring together AI-specific threats, such as prompt injection and malicious skills, with suspicious agent behavior and Falcon endpoint detections. This helps security teams identify threats both within AI interactions and when agent activity translates into malicious system execution.

Together, these capabilities help security teams move beyond isolated AI activity logs to discover unmanaged AI, identify emerging risks, and prioritize threats that require attention.

One Architecture for Securing AI on the Endpoint

By connecting AI interactions, communications, and endpoint execution, Falcon Guardian gives security teams a more complete understanding of how AI operates and where risks emerge. With unified visibility, protection, and response across supported AI activity, organizations can govern employee use of AI, investigate threats from prompt to impact, and accelerate AI adoption with confidence.
