You Can't Defend What You Can't See: Pairing AI-Driven Security with CTEM
Context: It helps teams: Identify vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and exposures across the environment Assess how each one could realistically be exploited Prioritize the risks...
Full Text:
AI can speed up how we detect and respond. Resilience still starts with knowing where we are exposed.

Speed is not the same as readiness

In my work with security leaders, one theme keeps coming up: threats are moving faster than most programs were built to handle. Attackers automate, chain small weaknesses together, and move on newly disclosed vulnerabilities in a matter of hours.

AI is helping us keep pace. It's improving triage, cutting through alert noise, and helping analysts reach a confident answer sooner. I'm a strong believer in that value. But there is a hard truth underneath it: AI cannot protect what it cannot see.

If we don't have clear visibility into our vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and external exposures, every incident begins at a disadvantage. The tools may fire, but the team is still working out what is affected, what is reachable, and what matters most to the business.

Where CTEM fits

Continuous Threat Exposure Management (CTEM) closes that visibility gap. Instead of treating exposure as a periodic scan or an annual assessment, CTEM makes it an ongoing discipline. It helps teams:

Identify vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and exposures across the environment

Assess how each one could realistically be exploited

Prioritize the risks attackers are most likely to go after

Remediate the highest-impact issues first

The real shift is from volume to risk. Most organizations already have more findings than they can fix. The better question is not "what is wrong?" but "what could an attacker actually use, and what would it cost the business if they did?"

Get comprehensive visibility across your entire digital footprint.

Learn More

From reacting to reducing risk

A reactive posture means we are always defending against whatever showed up today. CTEM moves the work upstream. By continuously shrinking the set of exploitable weaknesses, we address high-impact exposures before they can be weaponized.

This is also a collaboration problem. Vulnerability data, application findings, cloud posture, and attack surface insights often sit in different tools owned by different teams. Bringing them into a single, risk-based remediation workflow gives everyone a shared view of what to fix first, and who owns the fix.

A layered defense, not an either/or

I don't see AI-enhanced detection and CTEM as competing investments. They cover different halves of the same problem.

AI-enhanced detection helps us spot and respond to active threats faster and with greater accuracy.

CTEM reduces the opportunities attackers have in the first place and gives responders context when something does happen.

Together they create a resilient, layered defense. When an alert fires, the team already knows which assets are exposed and which weaknesses matter most. That is the difference between responding from a position of strength and scrambling to catch up.

What AI-driven response looks like in practice

Consider a familiar scenario: an endpoint alert flags suspicious activity on an employee account, and logs from the network and the cloud show that a large volume of data is leaving the environment. Every minute matters, and in a traditional workflow most of those minutes go to gathering context rather than acting on it.

An AI-driven operation changes where the time goes. Before an analyst ever opens the case, the platform can do much of the upfront work:

Automated enrichment adds identity and asset context, history of similar activity for that client, threat intelligence, and data from integrated tools. Analysts no longer pivot across half a dozen outside sources just to understand what they are looking at.

Policy-based auto-remediation takes the actions a client has already approved, such as disabling a compromised account and revoking active sessions, so the damage stops growing while people get up to speed.

Intelligent routing assigns the case to the analyst best suited to it, based on skills, risk to the client, SLA urgency, and familiarity with the environment, instead of leaving it to whoever picks it up first.

The result is a shorter path from detection to response, and analysts who spend their time on judgment rather than data gathering.

Two principles matter as much as the speed. First, humans stay in the loop where the stakes are high. Actions that affect critical systems, such as isolating a server, should require client approval, with clear notification and a record of the decision. Second, every incident should feed back into exposure management. If a control allowed the activity, the response should include a follow-up to tighten that policy, so the same behavior is blocked next time. That is detection and exposure management working together: each response closes a gap, and the next attack has fewer places to land.

The same visibility also needs to serve different audiences. Security-mature enterprise teams want full transparency into the evidence, the actions taken, and any approvals pending. CISOs need a view of threat activity and security posture across services. Smaller organizations are better served by a plain-language summary of what happened, what it means, and what, if anything, they need to do.

Making it part of daily operations

CTEM delivers the most value when it is built into everyday security work, not run as a side project. A few practical starting points:

Know your full footprint. Build a complete inventory of cloud workloads, applications, and internet-facing assets, including the ones no one remembers deploying.

Prioritize by exploitability and business impact, not severity scores alone.

Unify findings into one remediation workflow so security, IT, and application teams work from the same list.

Measure continuously. Track how exposure shrinks over time, not just how many tickets were closed.

Feed exposure context into detection and response so analysts and AI tools both work from the full picture.

The bottom line

AI makes our teams faster. CTEM makes sure that speed is aimed at the right things. By closing critical gaps, reducing the attack surface, and staying in a constant state of readiness, we make sure that when an attack does occur, we are starting from strength, not from zero.

Title: Signal blocks AI assistants from snooping on your encrypted messages
Context: Some may consider it very convenient for their mobile operating system's agentic AI features to use their ability to look at their screen to do something like add an event to...
Full Text:
Signal, the privacy-focused encrypted messaging app, has started blocking Apple and Google's AI assistants from snooping on users' private conversations.

Some may consider it very convenient for their mobile operating system's agentic AI features to use their ability to look at their screen to do something like add an event to their calendar. They may be happy for Onscreen Awareness for Apple's Siri and Google's Gemini Intelligence to answer questions and do tasks for them.

But it's far from welcome when the screen shows an encrypted conversation that was supposed to be private.

Once a message has been captured, it could end up in a locally-stored database or uploaded to a remote server - potentially putting everyone in the chat at risk.

Signal's president, Meredith Whittaker, said in a blog post that unless proper safeguards were in place, putting AI agents into operating systems was "an existential threat to privacy at the application layer."

If you are running iOS 27 on your iPhone, Signal now blocks screenshots inside the app - which means Siri cannot read message content from the screen. A new setting called "Block Siri AI" allows users to toggle the feature on or off.

Meanwhile, on Android, Signal attempts to look where it can for an AI assistant trying to read the screen and when it spots one, automatically turns on its existing "Screen security" setting.

There are repercussions, of course, for anyone on iOS who wants to sometimes take screenshots of their own conversations, perhaps for innocent reasons. You can switch the protection off, but - as Signal warns - doing that might expose your chats to AI agents.

Furthermore, Signal admits that its efforts do not prevent every method an AI agent might use to try to read messages being sent via the app.

There is also no protection yet for Mac users, because Signal says it cannot reliably block the taking of screenshots on macOS. For that reason, the best advice if you are using the Signal desktop app on your Mac is to add it to the Excluded Apps list under System Settings > Siri.

And, of course, you need to bear in mind that there are also third-party AI agents, such as Meta's Muse, which can access sensitive data through accessibility permissions that users are encouraged to grant during setup.

Signal has called on Microsoft, Apple, and Google to to give developers an easy, well-documented way to opt their apps out of sharing data with AI agents, and to publish better technical details of how their AI features access and process data.

It is worth bearing in mind that this issue is not unique to Signal - any app that handles sensitive information faces the same problem. The difference is that Signal is publicly trying to do something about it.

As Whittaker says, "Signal is the canary in the coal mine."

Title: Impact of AI on CVEs : PROTECTION STRATEGIES
Context: By combining an AI-discovered vulnerability in the libheif image-parsing library (CVE-2026-47178) with a Linux kernel privilege escalation exploit, we turned a single malformed...
Full Text:
For enterprise software development operations, AI now handles work that was once too hard or too costly to justify, from reverse engineering and debugging to building fuzzing harnesses. Recent high profile security incidents shows how far this goes:

AI agents escaping ChatGPT sandboxes through zero-day logic flaws

Claude models breaking out of test environments while surfacing critical zero-days.

Independent researchers using LLMs to find dozens of vulnerabilities in heavily audited codebases.

Higher Volume and Lower Quality CVEs

In the first blog of this series, we explained how AI is a multiplier for security research experts, resulting in faster bug discovery and PoC development, which leaves more time for deep architectural analysis. For novices, however, it means the ability to create a large volume of low-quality CVEs that increase response time and amplify triage noise.

Published CVEs are accelerating sharply reaching 75,000 in just the first nine months of 2026

Perhaps a more serious consequence of vulnerability research with AI is “democratization” of nation state capabilities. It used to take the resources of a nation state to launch sophisticated hacks such as 0-click smartphone attacks and unauthenticated RCEs (Remote Code Execution) on enterprise servers. Using AI, these and other attacks can be launched by smaller groups such as ransomware gangs and even individual malicious actors.

Real World Evidence

This year alone, we have had more than 10+ Linux LPE (Local Privilege Escalation) vulnerabilities and have also seen multiple RCEs in popular open-source packages that power the internet, such as PHP, Chrome and Redis.

Confirmed in-the-wild exploits across major open-source projects from 2023 to October 2026

The trajectory is clear: CISOs and security teams should prepare themselves for disclosure of high severity vulnerabilities in well-known industry components by professional and amateur security researchers on a monthly basis.

Example: JFrog’s Zero-Click Chain

Exploiting a malformed image tile to achieve zero-click remote code execution

To demonstrate how AI compresses weeks of advanced exploit development into a matter of hours, our research team built a full zero-click attack chain targeting everyday desktop software. By combining an AI-discovered vulnerability in the libheif image-parsing library (CVE-2026-47178) with a Linux kernel privilege escalation exploit, we turned a single malformed image file into complete root-level system takeover without a single click from the user.

Libheif – Malicious images as an infection vector

The danger of parser vulnerabilities are well documented, , especially those that parse untrusted input sent from an attacker without user interaction. Vulnerabilities like these have been used extensively by nation-states and PSOAs (private-sector offensive actors), as well as cybercriminals, to deploy malware on systems with minimal, and in some cases, no human interaction whatsoever.

CVE-2026-47178 – Heap out-of-bounds write to popping calc

Feeling inspired by how nation-state-grade spyware infects devices, often using format parsing as the initial access vector, we started researching libheif, which is a library implementing the parsing of the HEIF image format.

Exploit flow from a malformed image tile to heap corruption and control-flow hijack

CVE-2026-47178 is a heap out-of-bounds write in the UNCI decoder in libheif that allows an attacker to overwrite virtual function pointers on the heap, thus leading to remote code execution. Leveraging AI, we discovered the vulnerability within 2 hours, as opposed to the weeks of research it would take a professional using conventional methods.

It took us another 5 hours to turn it into a reliable exploit against Debian’s File Explorer, without user interaction.

Researching & Confirming our Findings

The research environment was quite straightforward: We compiled heif-dec, the library-bundled C++ binary for parsing HEIF images using libheif with AddressSanitizer, and instructed the AI to find a heap out-of-bounds write using static analysis only and confirm its hypothesis dynamically via a crash under ASAN.

AddressSanitizer crash report confirming a heap-buffer-overflow during image decoding

The ASAN essentially acts as a truth indicator (oracle). This result tells us immediately that the LLM did not hallucinate its finding, and the finding is an actionable, real vulnerability.

We may now proceed to developing the actual exploit:

Debugger output showing a crash due to an overwritten vtable pointer from a virtual function call

Through specific heap manipulation, a technique known as heap feng shui, we successfully overwrote a virtual function pointer, a C++ object data structure, granting us direct control over the instruction pointer and completing another critical milestone. The classic convention is to set the instruction pointer to 0x41414141, to demonstrate instruction pointer control.

The final stage is to turn our control flow hijack into code execution. By default the stack is non executable, so we must utilize gadgets, or useful pieces of code that already exist in the executable’s memory space, for our needs.

Since our target was the gnome file explorer, nautilus, we decided to take a look as to how it decodes these heif images, and noticed that it uses a binary called `libheif-thumbnailer`, a binary that’s similar to libheif-dec, which uses the libheif library, alongside other libraries.

The library that’s particularly important this time is libdav1d, which is another codec. The library provided a useful gadget, akin to a one_gadget, that allows us to run `system()` with our own string specified in the `rdi` register, which is just perfect.

Now, we can run any code that we want, but not as root, and that’s the next stage.

DirtyClone – Elevating Linux LPE privileges

Now that we have remote code execution, we can begin elevating our privileges. We previously disclosed an LPE in the Linux kernel as a result of an incomplete patch of the dirtyfrag vulnerability. We won’t go in depth into the details of how the exploit works, but you can more info our previous blog post.

Exploit chain turning a corrupted vtable pointer into arbitrary code execution

The following is a summary of the attack scenario:

An attacker, using a delivery mechanism such as a messaging app (different delivery mechanism than what we outlined here), or even just downloading the file unwittingly and just navigating to the directory where the file is stored via file manager, will cause remote code execution as root.

How Can JFrog Help?

SCA scanning often begins by matching component versions against public CVE records. While this identifies potentially vulnerable dependencies, it may also report issues that are not applicable to the way a specific application uses them.

JFrog Advanced Security’s Contextual Analysis goes beyond version matching. It examines source code, binaries, configurations, and dependency paths to decide whether the vulnerable conditions are actually present, and only then reports a CVE as Applicable.

Take CVE-2026-47178 in libheif. A version match would flag every artifact that contains an affected libheif. Contextual Analysis marks it Applicable only when both conditions are met:

libheif was compiled with -DWITH_UNCOMPRESSED_CODEC=ON

the application calls the vulnerable function heif_decode_image

In the scan below, JFrog Xray found both: libheif.so.1.19.8 built with the flag, and a reference to heif_decode_image in /app/heif_app. Each piece of evidence comes with its path, offset, and symbol, so teams can verify the verdict instead of trusting it blindly. When the evidence is incomplete, Xray returns Undetermined rather than a false positive.

Validating CVE applicability through binary, function-level, and configuration evidence.

JFrog Security Research and Severity Assessment

JFrog Xray is strengthened by CVE research and enrichment from the JFrog Security Research team. Rather than treating every CVE equally, the team focuses mainly on High and Critical CVEs. For these, researchers analyze real-world exploitability, assign a JFrog Severity Score, document the conditions that determine applicability, and provide actionable remediation or mitigation guidance.

When JFrog’s analysis differs from a public CVSS rating, Xray can present a separate JFrog Severity analysis based on technical evidence and likelihood of exploitation. This gives teams another signal for prioritization instead of requiring them to rely on a single external base score.

JFrog Advanced Security complements Xray’s research-backed enrichment with Contextual Analysis. According to JFrog’s internal statistics, Contextual Analysis covered an average of 80% of High and Critical CVEs in customer scans. The same data found that an average of 85% of High and Critical findings were marked as not applicable, helping teams focus remediation on a smaller set of relevant issues. Among the NVD CVEs reassessed by JFrog researchers in 2025, JFrog’s severity assessment was lower for 96% of those rated Critical and 65% of those rated High. Together, JFrog Advanced Security’s Contextual Analysis and Xray’s research-backed severity reassessment help teams reduce CVE noise and direct remediation toward vulnerabilities that represent the greatest threat to their applications.

Take Aways

AI is uncovering real vulnerabilities faster, but also increasing false reports, inflated scores, and pressure on already overloaded maintainers and security teams. As discovery outpaces validation and patching, CVE volume and severity alone are no longer enough to guide remediation. In the AI era, the challenge is not simply finding more vulnerabilities, but identifying which findings are real, reachable, and urgent. Combining vendor guidance with contextual analysis and research-backed severity helps teams focus their limited time on the vulnerabilities that pose genuine risk.

Title: Address AI Agent Risks or Face Action, FCA Warns Financial Firms
Context: The UK’s financial regulator has warned firms that they must address cybersecurity risks from the deployment of AI agents, or face regulatory action
Full Text:
The UK’s financial regulator has warned firms that they must address cybersecurity risks from the deployment of AI agents, or face regulatory action.

The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) said that AI agents are being widely deployed in the financial services sector to improve productivity and convenience to customers.

“But these products can also blur the boundary between regulated and unregulated activity, and the protections consumers receive in relation to their finances and data,” the regulator noted.

Banks now using these AI agents to initiate transactions, move money and make investment decisions.

Without appropriate safeguards in place, such as strict access controls, agents have been observed taking dangerous actions such as gaining access to sensitive systems and data, even in pursuit of legitimate aims.

The FCA guidance, published on November 24, said that senior managers responsible for AI models deployed in a specific area of the business need to take “reasonable steps” to understand the risks arising from AI. This includes providing effective oversight and ensuring governance controls and escalation arrangements are appropriate for the risks.

Regulated financial organizations should consider any liabilities from accepting agent instructions and whether it is appropriate to accept payments instructed by an AI agent.

They should also help consumers understand the limits of financial information and advice generated by their models through clear, proportionate and consistent disclaimers.

Responsibility for complying with regulatory obligations remains with senior managers and the organization as a whole, whether the firm deploys agentic AI themselves or relies on a third-party provider, the FCA emphasized.

Read now: Bank of England, FCA and Treasury Raise Alarm Over Frontier AI

“We expect you to demonstrate that you understand the systems you use, the degree of autonomy those systems have, the risks they create and the controls necessary to manage those risks in real time and in stress situations,” the authority wrote.

“We will assess the services firms provide through agentic products, including how they develop over time, to ensure they keep to regulatory requirements,” it continued.

Failure to adhere to existing regulatory requirements, including data protection laws, will see the FCA use its powers to sanction non-compliant organizations. These powers include imposing financial penalties, prohibiting individuals from carrying out regulated activities, public censure and prosecution.

The FCA added that it welcomes early engagement from those deploying agentic AI in their products and systems, and that it offers support services including testing whether these tools meet regulatory requirements.

Context: Flags inactive service principals and unused federated apps and alerts on sensitive Entra ID changes such as app registration and owner changes Monitoring credential additions...
Full Text:
What you will learn

How ARTEX chains exposed secrets, trusted OAuth applications and Active Directory weaknesses into privileged access, why it is hard to detect, and which monitoring and credential controls limit what one identity can reach.

Delinea Labs | November 2026

On November 13, the FBI published a FLASH advisory on ARTEX, an open-source penetration testing framework that attackers have been using since at least August 2026. The framework uses multiple AI agents to automate reconnaissance, vulnerability testing, credential discovery and other stages of an intrusion. In some attacks, privileged access was reached within three hours of initial targeting.

ARTEX connects to external large language models (LLMs), divides an objective into smaller tasks and runs them through specialized agents. The agents can execute commands, analyze results and adjust their next steps based on what they find.

ARTEX relies extensively on identity-based attack techniques

Credential theft, permission testing, authentication bypass, OAuth persistence and Active Directory attacks all appear in the reported activity. An exposed credential can lead to a cloud service, then to other secrets or to applications with broader permissions. ARTEX automates finding and testing those connections.

From exposed credentials to cloud access

Since August, Microsoft has observed attackers using agentic tools to search GitHub repositories for exposed secrets. In one investigation, an agent moved from searching for credentials to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in just five minutes. Microsoft’s description of that case refers to an AI agent without naming the tool.

In several cases, the agents then obtained a token for a compromised OAuth application and used it to enumerate subscriptions, resource groups, permissions and other cloud services. They also searched Azure DevOps for secrets and used Azure VM Run Command to execute commands on virtual machines.

The agents also adapted. When an Azure Resource Manager request failed because of an incorrect API version, the agent retried with a supported version and received a successful response. Microsoft observed similar adjustments when the agents queried SQL firewall rules and Application Insights, so the attacker didn’t have to troubleshoot each failure manually.

In a separate experiment, GitGuardian planted nine secrets in a test repository and ran an ARTEX build without a dedicated secrets scanner. It found eight using standard Git and grep commands, including a credential that had been removed from the current files but remained in Git history. The model refused when asked to use the credentials, so the test showed discovery rather than exploitation.

What happens when the application is already trusted?

The ConnectWise Cloud Backup compromise showed ARTEX being used against identities that were already trusted. Microsoft linked the October campaign to Storm-0940, a China-state-aligned actor.

Storm-0940’s infrastructure was active before the application access. In a password-spraying campaign originating from an IP address that also appears in the ConnectWise indicators, Microsoft recorded more than 151,000 failed sign-ins against 327 accounts across eight organizations, peaking at 2,900 failures a minute. No successful authentication was observed.

The application access worked differently. The actor obtained credentials belonging to ConnectWise cloud applications that were already authorized to access customers’ Microsoft 365 environments.

Using ARTEX, it attempted authentication against more than 2,250 downstream tenants. Most attempts failed, but Microsoft observed successful authentication and additional activity in several customer environments. The number represents attempted access, not 2,250 confirmed compromises.

The attacker didn’t need to compromise an employee account in every organization. The stolen application credentials could be used to authenticate wherever the applications’ permissions remained valid. In one customer environment, a compromised management application assigned itself the Global Administrator role. The attacker was no longer limited to the application's original access.

Other activity modified application credentials in Microsoft Entra ID. An attacker with sufficient permissions can add another client secret or certificate and keep authenticating through that identity even after the original credential is revoked.

Beyond cloud identities

The FBI advisory also described activity targeting Active Directory and on-premise environments. Attackers enumerated more than 110,000 objects and used Kerberoasting, DCSync, and LAPS password retrieval. They also attempted lateral movement with Pass-the-Hash, Pass-the-Ticket, WinRM and Kerberos relay techniques, and endpoint protection blocked some of those attempts.

The advisory also covered unsigned SAML assertions, hard-coded administrator passwords and forged administrator tokens created with unrotated authentication keys. These findings come from multiple investigations rather than a single intrusion.

None of these techniques are new. Each still depends on conditions, such as weak service-account passwords or replication permissions, that already exist in the environment.

Same trust, different path

Our recent blog "Railway: When a build credential becomes access to customer secrets" covers an incident that started from a different place.

ConnectWise’s attacker used trust that customers had already granted. Railway’s attacker had to find the path. They did so with a build credential that led to source code and the code revealed an OIDC trust misconfiguration. Revoking the credential didn’t close that path. Railway reported AI-assisted tooling, including a harness Wiz described as similar to ARTEX, but didn’t confirm ARTEX was used.

Tooling like ARTEX speeds up both kinds of discovery. It creates neither.

What does this mean for identity security?

Detecting ARTEX specifically may be difficult. The framework uses existing penetration testing tools and legitimate cloud APIs, and agents can adjust their requests when an attempt fails.

ARTEX can automate the attack, but not the trail it leaves

The activity still generates authentication events, API calls and changes to identity configurations.

A service principal authenticating from an unfamiliar source isn’t enough on its own. Followed by unusual permission checks, secret retrieval and changes to another application’s credentials, the sequence is a much stronger indication of malicious activity. Monitoring changes to application credentials and privileged roles is most important when the initial access comes through a trusted third party.

Delinea products address some of these risks directly. Others sit with the application, the identity provider or detection tooling.

Credential rotation also has to account for what the original identity could reach. Revoking a stolen secret doesn’t remove a credential the attacker has already created or invalidate secrets retrieved from a connected system.

ARTEX adds speed to techniques defenders already know. What it exposes is how much one compromised identity can reach.

Title: The Invisible Race
Context: Braking into the first chicane at Monza, a modern Formula 1 car drops from roughly 340 kilometres an hour to less than 100 in a little over two seconds, and some 300 sensors...
Full Text:
Braking into the first chicane at Monza, a modern Formula 1 car drops from roughly 340 kilometres an hour to less than 100 in a little over two seconds, and some 300 sensors record every part of it. The brake discs pass 1,000ºC. Each tyre reports its own pressure and temperature as it loads up and flexes. Sensors track the suspension compressing, the steering angle, the throttle reopening, the airflow across the wings, and the five-g deceleration that throws the driver forward into his belts. Many of those channels sample hundreds of times a second, every second of the race. Over a single Grand Prix, a team’s two cars produce 2.3 terabytes of data — about a month of round-the-clock HD video streaming.

Almost none of it stays at the track. Where it goes, and how fast, decides a second race, one that the millions watching from Bahrain to Barcelona never see. That race runs on an unseen army of mechanics, engineers, and technicians, which every team splits into two groups: one at the garage, the other at the factory. For McLaren Racing, that means 60 people at the track, shuttling between countries and continents every weekend, and 30 more in Mission Control at the McLaren Technology Centre (MTC) in Woking, England. Those 30 stay put. Both groups matter equally, and both require instantaneous access to those 2.3 terabytes of data.

Overseeing the movement of data from garage to factory and back again is Dan Keyworth, McLaren Racing’s Executive Director of Performance Technology & Systems. “The role of my team is to get the data from the car as it’s going around the circuit and surface all that information to the engineers,” he says.

CrowdStrike splashes $44B on Zscaler, customers brace for the bill
Context: The all-stock deal, announced on Monday, will see Zscaler shareholders receive 1
Full Text: CrowdStrike has agreed to buy Zscaler for $43.9 billion in what would be the biggest cybersecurity acquisition on record, and customers are already bracing for pricier renewals. The all-stock deal, announced on Monday, will see Zscaler shareholders receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for every share they own, representing a 34 percent premium on Friday's closing price. The transaction dwarfs even Google's $32 billion acquisition of cloud security upstart Wiz. Buying Zscaler gives CrowdStrike a sizeable foothold in the network security market, where it will be going up against the likes of Palo Alto Networks and Fortinet. The plan is to combine Falcon's endpoint protection capabilities with Zscaler's zero-trust network security technology, giving customers a single platform for securing devices and the connections between them. Naturally, there's an AI angle to the biggest cyber deal in history. CrowdStrike reckons owning both technologies will allow it to keep tabs on what AI agents are doing on corporate devices, where they're connecting, and what data they're getting their hands on. CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz described the proposed combination as "cybersecurity’s operating system." The acquisition also gives CrowdStrike's salespeople plenty to get excited about. Around 8,000 Zscaler customers don't currently buy CrowdStrike's wares, and the companies already have more than 2,000 customers in common. CrowdStrike reckons it can boost its annualized revenue by around $1 billion within 30 months of closing the deal by selling more products to the two companies' existing customers. Some of those customers, however, don't sound particularly keen on being cross-sold to. Over on Reddit's r/sysadmin subreddit, news of the purchase was met with a familiar set of concerns from IT professionals who've lived through big-ticket enterprise software acquisitions before. "As a zscaler customer, this does worry me. Cost increase, forced move to Falcon, integration issues, etc," wrote one sysadmin. Another, whose organization already uses both vendors' products, added: "I think they're both great products but I imagine they'll jack up the price for our next renewal. Fun." CrowdStrike intends to make Zscaler's products available through its Falcon Flex licensing scheme, which allows customers to commit to a certain level of spending and pick and choose the products they deploy. Monday's acquisition announcement didn't spell out what the deal would mean for customers who want to continue using Zscaler alongside a rival endpoint security product. Others raised concerns about the fate of Red Canary, the managed detection and response specialist snapped up by Zscaler in August 2025. CrowdStrike already operates a competing service in Falcon Complete. There may also be some nervous employees at both companies. CrowdStrike is targeting $500 million in annual cost savings within two years of completing the acquisition, identifying datacenter infrastructure, supplier spending, and wider operations as areas where it can trim the fat. Neither company disclosed whether that would involve job cuts. Then there's the matter of putting more of the world's corporate security infrastructure in the hands of CrowdStrike, whose botched July 2024 software update took down an estimated 8.5 million Windows machines, grounding flights and disrupting hospitals, banks, and businesses worldwide. The incident gave IT departments a rather painful lesson in the risks of relying heavily on a single technology supplier. The deal is expected to close in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal 2028, assuming regulators and Zscaler shareholders give it the green light. Zscaler founder and CEO Jay Chaudhry will remain in charge of the business and take a seat on CrowdStrike's board. CrowdStrike reckons the combined business will have more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue when the deal closes. Judging by the reaction from some customers, they'll be keeping a particularly close eye on how much of that revenue comes from them. ®

We Get the Infrastructure We Pay For
Context: This essay originally appeared as part of a round table in The Free Press entitled “Is America’s Infrastructure Under Attack
Full Text:
This essay originally appeared as part of a round table in The Free Press entitled “Is America’s Infrastructure Under Attack?”

Microsoft, the FAA, banks, United Airlines, the NSA—it’s been a really bad week in cyberspace. But, amazing as it might seem, these are not related. As far as we know, they’re not the result of cyberattacks. They’re not even related to AI. (Well, that’s mostly true. The NSA will probably never tell us what went wrong.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.

Our computerized infrastructure is vulnerable and fragile. Much of it is old, and has been incrementally patched and upgraded. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense. And more and more of it is centralized: the same systems affecting many different aspects of our lives and society. In many cases, it just barely works. And when it fails, it tends to fail badly.

There are a lot of technological reasons why this is true, but they are all downstream of the economic ones. The technologies we rely on are built and maintained within our economic system—and that’s where the core problem lies.

Security, safety, resilience, redundancy, recoverability—these are all essential parts of reliable technology, but they are all costs.

More importantly, they are inefficient: costs that feel wasteful until something bad happens. Modern shareholder capitalism, and private equity in particular, squeeze all inefficiencies out of a company in pursuit of near-term profits. Competition, with multiple companies competing to do the same thing, is another inefficiency. Monopolization removes that in pursuit of near-term profits.

The result is brittle systems, single points of failure. They’re more susceptible to cyberattack—both human and AI-fueled—and more susceptible to random mistakes. The more we allow unregulated capitalism to privatize gains while socializing risks, the more we should expect these sorts of failures.

Fixing this is technical, but it’s political first. It requires changing incentives, and that involves regulation and control. “What to do” is easy; finding the political will to stand up to moneyed interests and do it is hard.

Title: Reprioritizing Automated Leads with CrowdStrike Signal
Context: In May, we pulled back the curtain on the self-learning AI models behind Automated Leads, an approach to threat detection designed to surface the subtle signs of an attack
Full Text:
In May, we pulled back the curtain on the self-learning AI models behind Automated Leads, an approach to threat detection designed to surface the subtle signs of an attack. It’s powered by CrowdStrike® Signal and delivered from the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform.

Signal (distinct from SGNL) scores every indicator by how unusual it is for that specific host. Most of these indicators are faint on their own; for example, a PowerShell download or routine administrative command. They fire too often to warrant analyst concern every time. CrowdStrike Signal looks for what genuinely stands out on a given host, whether that’s a single highly unusual indicator or a handful of weaker ones that cluster in time. It correlates them, together with any related detections, into a single lead. A lead can come together from one short burst of activity or build quietly over several days.

In September, we introduced the next step: a new prioritization layer that sits on top of CrowdStrike Signal and changes how those leads are scored and ordered. Generally available since September 9, 2026, it significantly reduces false positives while detecting more malicious activity.

The Challenge: Most Unusual Activity Is Benign

Unusual activity is everywhere, and most of it is benign: a software rollout, an administrator trying a new tool, a one-off maintenance script. Some of it is detected correctly without being an attack, such as adware or sanctioned red-team exercises. Real intrusions are rare by comparison, and they range from commodity malware to adversaries who make efforts to look like a system administrator.

For a security team with finite time, this creates a ranking problem. When unusual activity never stops, the order in which leads appear determines what gets investigated and what waits.

What’s New in CrowdStrike Signal

CrowdStrike Signal still decides what becomes a lead. The new prioritization layer decides where that lead belongs in the queue.

Previously, a lead's confidence reflected how unusual its activity was, taken as a whole. It now also reflects how closely that activity resembles what real intrusions look like. A noisy software deployment and a quiet intrusion can be equally unusual; the prioritization layer tells them apart, so the intrusion climbs the queue while the deployment drops down or out of it entirely.

What this means for your queue:

Reductions of up to 70% in lead volume, with fewer leads to review at every sensitivity setting. Some leads fall off the queue altogether; some are still available at lower thresholds, which you can choose to view with the confidence threshold control.

Better coverage of real threats: Activity that CrowdStrike threat hunters confirm as malicious still reaches the queue, and more of it does at the Moderate and Cautious settings.

How It Works: AI Agents on the Endpoint

AI agents are an emerging attack surface, and adversaries are already moving on it: The CrowdStrike 2026 Threat Hunting Report documents STARDUST CHOLLIMA poisoning AI framework packages. Agents running on tools such as Claude Code and ChatGPT Codex now run shell commands on endpoints across the business, frequently with broad permissions and without a person approving each step. While most of their actions are routine, an agent that is misused, prompt-injected, or hijacked runs the same ordinary commands an attacker would, with the full access of the user behind it. This activity can be difficult to identify as malicious.

With Automated Leads, CrowdStrike Signal can identify malicious activity without knowing whether an agent was involved. It watches what happens on the host and raises a lead when activity stands out, whether the commands came from a person, a piece of malware, or an AI agent. Recently detected Automated Leads, as detailed below, show what this looks like in practice. The intent behind the activity varied from case to case, but the path to the analyst was the same each time: The agent's actions reached the host as ordinary commands, CrowdStrike Signal correlated the activity that was out of character for that host into a lead, and the prioritization layer moved the lead to the top of the queue because the pattern matched what past intrusions also showed.

This capability complements CrowdStrike® Falcon Guardian™, which secures agents directly by discovering them, controlling which ones may run, and tracing each prompt to what happened on the system. Security teams using both can view malicious activity within agents or on the endpoint.

Title: Evo Agentic Development Security and Evo Dependency Firewall Inside NVIDIA OpenShell
Context: Every agent starts with no network access, no host files and no credentials, and it gets only what a policy grants
Full Text:
Agentic software factories are taking shape with teams starting to run fleets of coding agents the way they run CI jobs: in parallel, each one reading files, installing packages, calling APIs and opening pull requests. At that scale, the sandbox each agent runs in becomes a core security control. NVIDIA OpenShell takes the idea further than most. Every agent starts with no network access, no host files and no credentials, and it gets only what a policy grants.

A sandbox decides what an agent can reach, but once the agent is working, a second set of four questions takes over:

Are the MCP servers and skills loaded trustworthy?

Is it only calling approved tools?

Is the code it writes secure?

Is the package it installed safe?

Even a tightly locked sandbox can run a poisoned skill or pull a malicious dependency through the one door left open.

Evo Agentic Development Security (ADS) answers those questions from inside the agent's own workflow, so it travels with the agent into environments like an OpenShell sandbox. To see how Evo and OpenShell work together, we built Evo ADS and Evo Dependency Firewall into an OpenShell sandbox, and ran Claude Code against it.

What is NVIDIA OpenShell?

NVIDIA OpenShell is an open source (Apache 2.0) runtime for autonomous AI agents. NVIDIA created it and contributed it to the CNCF, where it’s now a Sandbox project. You declare what each agent can touch in a policy, and OpenShell enforces it on every file access, system call and network connection.

For agent workloads, the controls that matter most are how OpenShell scopes rules, handles credentials and treats new connections:

Rules per program, not just per host: OpenShell checks which binary opens each connection. A rule can say "only the Snyk binary may reach api.snyk.io," which limits an agent's ability to borrow Snyk's access to send data somewhere else.

Credentials the agent never sees: OpenShell holds API keys and adds them only to requests bound for approved endpoints. In our build, Claude Code's Anthropic key never enters the sandbox.

Default deny, with a review step: A new sandbox reaches nothing. When the agent tries a new host, OpenShell blocks it and drafts a rule for a human to approve.

How we built Evo into an NVIDIA OpenShell sandbox

The reference build is one OpenShell sandbox image, based on NVIDIA's own Ubuntu base, with Claude Code and four Snyk controls built in. One command (run.sh) builds the image, stores credentials in OpenShell and starts the sandbox with a pre-approved network policy. Each control in the build answers one of the four questions.

Control

What it secures

What we saw in the sandbox

Agent supply chain security (Evo ADS)

What agents use: MCP servers and skills

Found 3 MCP servers and every installed skill, and flagged each planted malicious test skill as High, including potential prompt injection scored 1000/1000

Agent behavior governance (Evo ADS)

What agents do: MCP tool calls

Evo's Allowed MCP Servers policy blocked an unapproved server mid-session; the approved one kept working

Agent output assurance (Evo ADS, powered by Snyk Studio)

What agents generate: code

Caught a SQL injection Claude wrote (CWE-89, High); the agent fixed it and the rescan found 0 issues

Evo Dependency Firewall (Experimental Preview)

What agents install: npm, PyPI packages

Served approved packages through the Snyk registry and blocked a version younger than a 7-day cooldown

Each sandbox shows up in Evo as its own machine, next to developer laptops and Docker Sandboxes, so security teams see every agent environment in one inventory.

The Docker Sandboxes kit installs Snyk when the sandbox starts. OpenShell only lets programs run from system folders such as /usr, so here Snyk is built into the image. This pattern works well for a reference architecture because the binaries are fixed at build time and checksum-verified, and nothing new is installed at runtime. We tested on OpenShell 0.1.6.

How Evo secures Claude Code inside NVIDIA OpenShell

Click through one Claude Code session in the sandbox, from setup to the results in Evo. The sections below explain each scenario in detail.

Detecting malicious agent skills and prompt injection before it runs

We planted a test skill that tells the agent to collect environment variables and send them to an outside host. Agent supply chain security scanned the sandbox at startup, flagged the skill for potential prompt injection (1000/1000) and insecure credential handling (600/1000), and pointed to the exact lines. When we asked Claude to use it anyway, the model's own safeguards stopped it. Had both of those checks failed, OpenShell would still have blocked the exfiltration, because the destination host was never in its policy.

Blocking unapproved MCP servers during an agent session

Evo's Allowed MCP Servers policy was set to block, with one local MCP server on the approved list and a second off. When Claude called a tool on the unapproved server, agent behavior governance stopped the call and named the Evo policy responsible. Calls to the approved server went through as normal. Because enforcement runs through the Claude Code agent's hooks at tool-call time, it also covers local MCP servers that never touch the network.

Fixing SQL injection in AI-generated code before the agent's turn ends

We asked Claude for a Flask /search endpoint that builds its SQL query with an f-string. Snyk Studio's Secure at Inception hook, which delivers agent output assurance, scanned the change, flagged SQL injection (CWE-89, High) and held the turn. The agent ran /snyk-fix, rewrote the query with a bound parameter, and the rescan came back clean.

Controlling npm and PyPI installs with Evo Dependency Firewall

With Evo Dependency Firewall in place, npm, pip and uv inside the sandbox can only install through the Snyk registry. Flask and lodash came through and appeared under Install requests in Evo. A package version published 3 days earlier, inside our 7-day cooldown, was refused, and Claude reported it as "Blocked by Snyk Dependency Firewall (cooldown-npm)" and offered the newest allowed version. Then we asked Claude to install straight from registry.npmjs.org. OpenShell denied it (DENIED /usr/bin/node -> registry.npmjs.org), and Claude didn't try to work around it.

How OpenShell and Evo Dependency Firewall work together

This scenario is where both products depend on each other. A dependency firewall governs the installs routed through it, so on its own it can't stop traffic that calls a public registry directly. OpenShell closes that route, but it works at the network layer and has no view of whether a package is safe. Combined, every install goes through Evo Dependency Firewall, and your policy decides what gets through.

What's next and how to get started

The reference build is a starting point, and three additions are in progress:

Snyk credentials held by OpenShell: Today the Evo push key and Snyk token are passed into the sandbox. Moving them into OpenShell providers matches how the Anthropic key is already handled.

A published image and a Brev Launchable: so teams can run the reference build without building it locally.

Destructive-action governance: extending Evo ADS beyond MCP tool calls to risky agent actions.

Want to run it yourself? This integration is in Experimental Preview. The reference build is open source, and one command builds the image, stores credentials in OpenShell and starts the sandbox. Evo Dependency Firewall is in Experimental Preview for select customers. Want to see Evo across every agent environment your teams run? Book a demo.

Title: Know the identity behind the role: Authorize and audit with trusted identity propagation
Context: Until now, TIP was available only for users who access AWS through AWS IAM Identity Center
Full Text:
Today, AWS is making it easier to grant access and audit activity based on the user or workload (a non-human caller, such as an application, service, or an automated workflow) behind an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role. Trusted identity propagation (TIP) carries the identity of the user or workload with each AWS request, so you can grant permissions to that user or workload and trace its actions in AWS CloudTrail. Until now, TIP was available only for users who access AWS through AWS IAM Identity Center. We’ve extended TIP to IAM federation and AWS IAM Roles Anywhere, making it work for users and workloads that federate directly into IAM roles or use X.509 certificates to obtain AWS credentials. We’ve also made TIP simpler to use with IAM Identity Center.

This post explains how TIP works and what’s new with this launch. It then shows two examples of how TIP improves auditability and access control based on the user or workload behind an IAM role. The post ends with how to get started depending on your preferred federation path into AWS.

How trusted identity propagation works

Customers have told us they want to control access to AWS resources and audit activity based on the user or workload behind an IAM role. Today, access control decisions apply to the role, and CloudTrail attributes each action to the role session. To give two users or workloads different access, you either create a separate role or share one role and write policies that check session attributes. Separate roles lead to role proliferation. Session attributes carry across role sessions only when you grant additional permissions, and the session doesn’t record who set each attribute.

TIP addresses this gap by attaching identity context from a trusted source, such as your identity provider (IdP), to the role session at the time of credential issuance. This identity context identifies the user or workload behind a request and can include optional claims for the session, such as a risk score or a continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) workflow name. Trusted sources include external SAML or OIDC IdPs configured for IAM federation, IAM Identity Center, and X.509 certificates configured for IAM Roles Anywhere.

After AWS attaches identity context to a role session, the context can’t be changed for the lifetime of the session. This approach gives IAM policies and audit records a stable reference to the user or workload behind each request. The context also carries forward to supported downstream requests. When a TIP session (a role session that carries identity context) assumes another role, AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) carries the context into the new role session. Similarly, when an AWS service makes a downstream request on your behalf, the request uses forward access sessions (FAS), and the FAS credentials carry the identity context from your session.

Note: TIP context propagates to a new role session only when the target role is in the account where the identity provider is configured, or if the target role is in another account in the same AWS organization. To learn how account and organization boundaries determine TIP context propagation, see Understand where TIP context propagates in the IAM User Guide.

Figure 1 shows how this flow works end-to-end. A user or workload obtains AWS credentials through one of three paths. With IAM federation, the source is a SAML assertion or OIDC token for a user or workload. With IAM Identity Center, the source is the username that IAM Identity Center receives from your identity source. With IAM Roles Anywhere, the source is an X.509 certificate for a user or workload. AWS validates the source and attaches identity context to the role session. That context stays with the session’s requests, whether the session calls an AWS service directly, assumes another role, or causes an AWS service to make downstream requests through FAS. IAM policies then evaluate the identity context to authorize requests, as the Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket policy example later in this post shows, and AWS CloudTrail records it, as the AWS Lambda example shows. With IAM outbound identity federation, the session can also request a signed JSON Web Token (JWT) that carries identity context to an external service.

Figure 1: How TIP carries identity information into authorization and audit workflows

AWS represents the identity context carried in a TIP session through three groups of context keys. The following table summarizes their purpose and points to the corresponding documentation. For details about what these context keys contain and when they appear in a TIP session, see TIP context keys in IAM policies.

Context keys

Purpose

aws:OriginIdentity/*

Identifies the user or workload that started the request and the source that issued its identity.

aws:TransactionContext/IdentityProvider/*

Carries optional claims from your IdP, such as a risk score or a CI/CD workflow name. Available only for IAM federation.

aws:IdentityCenterInstanceArn and aws:IdentityStoreArn

Identifies the IAM Identity Center instance and identity store behind a session. If you use IAM Identity Center permission sets or IAM account access manager, you can use these keys in IAM policy conditions. For example, you can allow access only to workforce users from a specific instance.

Table 1: TIP context key categories and what they represent.

aws:OriginIdentity/* is the common namespace for identity information from IAM federation, IAM Identity Center, and IAM Roles Anywhere. Across all three paths, aws:OriginIdentity/Subject identifies the user or workload that started the request, aws:OriginIdentity/SubjectType indicates whether the request was started by a user or workload, and aws:OriginIdentity/Issuer identifies the source that issued the identity. For IAM federation and IAM Roles Anywhere, aws:OriginIdentity/FederatedProviderArn also contains the Amazon Resource Name ARN) of the IAM IdP or IAM Roles Anywhere trust anchor that authenticated the identity.

IAM policies can evaluate TIP context keys when those keys are present in the request. CloudTrail records identity context in the userIdentity element of events. The userIdentity.onBehalfOf section records the user or workload identity from aws:OriginIdentity context keys, and the userIdentity.transactionContext section records IdP claims from aws:TransactionContext/IdentityProvider context keys. For field definitions and examples see Logging TIP activity with AWS CloudTrail.

Key benefits of trusted identity propagation

TIP gives you the following benefits for authorizing and auditing access based on the user or workload behind an IAM role.

Audit by identity, not only by role – CloudTrail records the user or workload behind each request.

Authorize based on who’s asking – IAM policies can grant or restrict access based on the user or workload, or on optional claims from your IdP, such as a risk score. This gives you precise access control for each session.

Rely on identity you can trust – AWS attaches identity context from a trusted source when it issues credentials. That context can’t be changed for the life of the session, and it carries forward when the session assumes another role or an AWS service makes requests on your behalf.

Use one model across federation paths – IAM federation, IAM Identity Center, and IAM Roles Anywhere share the same core aws:OriginIdentity context keys, so you write policies and review CloudTrail consistently across more than 250 supported AWS services. Across supported workflows, identity context propagates without adding the sts:SetContext permission to role trust policies.

What’s new with this launch

This launch extends TIP to IAM federation and IAM Roles Anywhere, and simplifies TIP in IAM Identity Center. You can also share identity context with services outside AWS through IAM outbound identity federation.

AWS IAM Identity Center – TIP already allows AWS applications integrated with IAM Identity Center, such as AWS Lake Formation and Amazon S3 Access Grants, to audit user activity and control access based on the user’s identity. When you enable the simplified experience, Identity Center adds a username, an identifier from your identity source, alongside the system-generated identity store user ID. This identity information is carried consistently across all access paths, including application access, account access through IAM Identity Center permission sets, and IAM account access manager. With this launch, you can now use the propagated username, mapped to the aws:OriginIdentity/Subject context key, in IAM policy conditions and view it in CloudTrail events. For more information, see Simplified experience for trusted identity propagation.

IAM federation – For users and workloads that use direct SAML or OIDC federation into IAM roles, you choose the SAML assertion field or OIDC token claim that identifies the user or workload, and TIP attaches it to the role session. You can also map optional SAML attributes or OIDC claims, such as a risk score or a CI/CD workflow name, into aws:TransactionContext/IdentityProvider/* context keys. TIP is turned on by default for new IAM IdPs, and you can turn it on for existing providers. For more information, see TIP for IAM Federation.

IAM Roles Anywhere – For users and workloads outside AWS that use X.509 certificates with IAM Roles Anywhere, TIP attaches the identity from the certificate to the role session. After IAM Roles Anywhere validates the certificate against the configured trust anchor, AWS sets aws:OriginIdentity/Subject to the certificate’s Subject common name by default, or to its URI Subject Alternative Name. TIP is turned on by default for new IAM Roles Anywhere profiles, and you can turn it on for existing profiles. For details, see Trusted identity propagation with IAM Roles Anywhere.

IAM outbound identity federation – A TIP session can now use the AWS STS GetWebIdentityToken API operation to request a signed JSON Web Toke that includes TIP session identity context for an external service. The external service validates the token and determines how to use the information. For details, see Federating AWS identities to external services.

Use identity context for auditability and access control

The following examples demonstrate two core benefits of TIP: auditability—tracing actions back to the user or workload—and access control based on that identity. In the first example, AnyCompany uses identity context logged in CloudTrail to identify the GitHub Actions workflow run that deployed new code to a production AWS Lambda function. In the second, AnyCompany uses an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket policy that grants read access only to low-risk sessions initiated from a specific IdP.

Trace a Lambda deployment to its GitHub Actions run

This example shows how TIP improves auditability: identity context in CloudTrail identifies the workload, and the specific workflow run, behind an action taken with a shared role. AnyCompany stores the backend code for its payment-processing application in the anycompany/payments-api GitHub repository. A code change merged into the repository’s main branch triggers the GitHub Actions workflow defined in .github/workflows/deploy.yml. The workflow uses GitHub OIDC federation to assume a shared CICDDeployRole role, then calls the Lambda UpdateFunctionCode API operation to deploy the new code to the production payments-api-prod function. CloudTrail records this operation as an UpdateFunctionCode20150331v2 management event.

Before TIP, the CloudTrail event shows that the CICDDeployRole/GitHubActions role session updated payments-api-prod. It doesn’t identify the GitHub repository, workflow file, or workflow run that performed the update. Investigators must match the event timestamp with GitHub records to find the responsible workflow run.

Figure 2: How TIP enables attribution of a production Lambda code update to the GitHub Actions run that performed it

AnyCompany enables TIP on its GitHub OIDC IdP. It maps the GitHub OIDC token subject to aws:OriginIdentity/Subject, configures aws:OriginIdentity/SubjectType as workload, and maps the repository, workflow_ref, and run_id claims into aws:TransactionContext/IdentityProvider/* context keys. The resulting role session identifies the workload and carries the information needed to trace the deployment to its GitHub Actions run.

With TIP, the CloudTrail management event for the Lambda UpdateFunctionCode API operation on payments-api-prod now contains the workload and workflow information:

{ "eventSource": "lambda.amazonaws.com", "eventName": "UpdateFunctionCode20150331v2", "recipientAccountId": "111122223333", "requestParameters": { "functionName": "payments-api-prod" }, "userIdentity": { "type": "AssumedRole", "arn": "arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/CICDDeployRole/GitHubActions", "onBehalfOf": { "federatedProviderArn": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com", "subject": "repo:anycompany/payments-api:environment:production", "subjectType": "workload", "issuer": "token.actions.githubusercontent.com" }, "transactionContext": { "IdentityProvider": { "repository": "anycompany/payments-api", "workflow_ref": "anycompany/payments-api/.github/workflows/deploy.yml@refs/heads/main", "run_id": "19283746550" } } } }

An investigator can now see that GitHub Actions run 19283746550 from the anycompany/payments-api repository updated the production payments-api-prod function through the deploy.yml workflow. The shared role, its trust policy, and its permissions remain unchanged. TIP adds workload and workflow attribution to the existing deployment model.

Authorize access based on session risk

This example shows how TIP supports access control: an Amazon S3 bucket policy uses a runtime risk signal from an IdP to decide, per session, whether a user of a shared role can read sensitive data. AnyCompany’s workforce users federate to AWS through an OIDC IdP and use a shared DataAccessRole to read objects from an Amazon S3 bucket. AnyCompany configures its IdP to evaluate each authentication and add a numeric risk score, from 0 to 100, to the OIDC token as a custom claim. AnyCompany enables TIP on the IAM OIDC IdP and maps the riskScore claim to the aws:TransactionContext/IdentityProvider/riskScore context key. During federation, AWS validates the token and attaches the mapped riskScore value to the role session. AWS derives aws:OriginIdentity/Issuer from the iss (issuer) claim in the OIDC token.

Before TIP, a bucket policy that grants access to DataAccessRole gives every user who assumes the role the same access, regardless of how risky their authentication was. With TIP, an S3 bucket policy can evaluate both the IdP that issued the token and the risk score carried in the session. The following policy grants read access only when the expected IdP (issuer) issued the identity, and the current session has a risk score of 30 or lower. The issuer condition prevents a riskScore value from another IdP from satisfying the policy.

Figure 3: How an S3 bucket policy uses trusted identity context to make a per-session access decision

Note: This policy example is for the IAM federation access path. Mapping SAML attributes or OIDC claims to optional aws:TransactionContext/IdentityProvider/* context keys is available only for IAM federation.

Amazon S3 bucket policy using trusted runtime context

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowLowRiskSensitiveDataRead", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/DataAccessRole" }, "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket/restricted/*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:OriginIdentity/Issuer": "idp.example.com" }, "NumericLessThanEquals": { "aws:TransactionContext/IdentityProvider/riskScore": "30" } } } ] }

The policy has two conditions: the identity must come from idp.example.com, and the session’s risk score must be 30 or lower. A low-risk session from idp.example.com satisfies both conditions. A session with a risk score above 30, a missing risk score, or a different issuer doesn’t receive access from this policy. The risk score remains fixed for the lifetime of the role session, so choose a session duration appropriate for the sensitivity of the access.

Additional considerations

Missing TIP context keys. A TIP context key is missing when the session carries no identity context or the request goes to an AWS service that doesn’t support TIP. To prevent an Allow statement from granting access when a required key is missing, use operators without IfExists, such as StringEquals or NumericLessThanEquals, as the preceding bucket policy does. Avoid operators such as StringEqualsIfExists in an Allow statement because they evaluate to true when the key is missing. In a Deny statement, add IfExists when the Deny should also apply if the key is missing. Such a Deny also applies to requests sent to AWS services that don’t support TIP, so confirm service support before adding TIP conditions. For more information, see Condition operators.

TIP conditions with cached AWS KMS data keys. Some AWS services, such as Amazon SQS, reuse cached AWS KMS data keys across requests from different sessions of the same IAM role, because the cache key is based on the role and does not include TIP context. When an AWS service reuses a cached data key, it does not send a new authorization request to AWS KMS, so AWS KMS does not evaluate the later session’s TIP context. If you use TIP context to control access to encrypted data, enforce the TIP conditions in the policy for the encrypted resource, such as an Amazon S3 bucket policy, rather than relying only on the AWS KMS key policy. For more information, see AWS KMS guidance for cached data keys.

Choose your TIP approach and get started

Your first step to getting started with TIP depends on how your users and workloads obtain AWS credentials. Use the following table to find the TIP option for your use case and get started.

Use case

TIP option

How to start

Centrally managed workforce access

IAM Identity Center

All IAM Identity Center instances can upgrade to the simplified experience for TIP. Before you upgrade, review the considerations for the simplified experience. For more information, see Simplified experience for trusted identity propagation.

Direct SAML or OIDC federation into IAM roles

IAM federation

New IAM IdPs have TIP turned on by default. For an existing IdP, turn on TIP on that provider, then map the claim that identifies the user or workload, and any optional claims your policies need, to TIP context keys. For more information see TIP for IAM Federation.

X.509-based access for users and workloads outside AWS

IAM Roles Anywhere

New profiles have TIP turned on by default. For an existing profile, enable TIP on the profile. For details, see Trusted identity propagation with IAM Roles Anywhere.

Conclusion

With this launch, TIP carries the identity of the user or workload from a trusted identity source into the role session for IAM federation, IAM Identity Center, and IAM Roles Anywhere. You can grant access based on the user or workload making the request and use CloudTrail to trace actions across more than 250 supported AWS services back to that identity. This gives you a consistent authorization and audit model across federation paths, without creating a separate role for every identity or adding the sts:SetContext permission to role trust policies.

To get started, find your federation path in the preceding table and follow the steps in the How to start column.

This subnet is assigned to a web hosting and virtual private server (VPS) provider BANATSYNC SRL with AS198364, located in Timisoara, Romania. This graph shows the DShield sensor activity over the past 90 days for this subnet and it is still ongoing as of this writing.

Using the ES|QL query listed below, starting the query from the 1 September 2026, 159 IPs from this block scanned at least once to multiple times my DShield sensors against mostly the SSH service and when found, attempted and sometimes successfully login the sensor. This analysis from this subnet started on the 5 September 2026 and capture regularly by 2 separate DShield sensors.

A review of both the firewall and cowrie logs, all IPs involved attempted to login into the SSH service with almost all (152 out 159) of them succeeding to login into the sensors using with the standard usernames (root, ubuntu, admin, etc.) using a single command (uname -s -v -n -r -m) followed by a immediate disconnection. One sensor received 127 unique IPs while the other received 134 unique IPs.

The firewall logs show some interesting characteristics with a time-to-live mostly between 45 to 52 with some exception that also include ranges between 232 to 243. In order to understand the discrepancies, I reviewed the packet capture from each sensor and found some packets where 69 IPs stared with a static IPID of 54321 and every one of them had a TTL that range between 232 to 243. All the inbound backets behaved the same way, SYN, SYN-ACK, RST targeting various ports including TCP/2323, TCP/22 and TCP/2222 where the actors/bots sometimes after multiple attemps, successfully login.

Using the logs from the DShield SIEM and selecting only the traffic with the IPID 54321 and reviewing the Vega-Lite graph, it is easy to see the activity was consistent with the previously identified 69 IPs that each time each IP would come live, the first packet was always starting with high TTL (230+) and the remainder packets were all using normal TTL related to a moderl Linux system. In order to inspect why this would be happening, using packet capture by the sensors based on matching high TTL for one specific IP address (109.160.32.146) and what appeared was interesting. Using tshark to replay the initial packet for 13 Nov 2026 started with a TTL of 239 and when that traffic responded with a reset (0x0004), the TTL was now 50. Any traffic that followed the first SYN packets all had TTL of 50 (picture below).

This is a sample of 4 IPs (DSL query below) out of the 69 that shows the first packet starting with a TTL 230+ followed by normal TTL after the activity continue. Reviewing the reports from VirusTotal of those 4 IPs [7][8][9][10] shows all the same characteristics with SSH brute-force if SSH is listening and running some commands before disconnecting.

Title: Cisco and OpenAI pitch eBPF kernel plugins as the way to tame the patchpocalypse
Context: Cisco and OpenAI have released an open-source tool called Shirudo to implement compensating controls in Linux, potentially improving security for users who can’t quickly patch...
Full Text: Cisco and OpenAI have released an open-source tool called Shirudo to implement compensating controls in Linux, potentially improving security for users who can’t quickly patch newly discovered software flaws. Shirudo relies on eBPF, the technology that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs in the Linux kernel. eBPF programs are effectively kernel plug-ins but don’t get unrestricted access to system resources. Developers have mostly used eBPF to create network functions that enable things like the open source Kubernetes observability and security tool Cilium, a Cloud Native Computing Foundation project. Cisco and OpenAI think eBPF can help organizations cope with the flood of 100,000-plus software flaws reported this year, many after the debut of AI-powered bug finders. The increased volume of flaws, and patches to fix them, is a problem for many organizations which already struggle to test fixes or find change windows in which to implement them. That problem has seen greater interest in “compensating controls” – changes to applications or infrastructure that harden them against flaws or malware, without requiring a patch. With Shirudo, Cisco and OpenAI are suggesting two things: The privileges eBPF programs enjoy make them a fine way to implement compensating controls for Linux; Agents should scan your infrastructure for vulnerabilities, then use tools like OpenAI’s Codex to write compensating controls as eBPF programs at machine speed. “Shirudo” is apparently the Japanese word for “shield,” so Cisco and OpenAI have called the eBPF programs the tool creates “shields.” The two companies envision humans checking every shield Shirudo creates before putting it into production. Shirudo is open source and available here. The two companies say they’ve already demonstrated it could mitigate the recently discovered flaws in Java without requiring downtime for an Elasticsearch implementation. Cisco and OpenAI are not alone in advocating for compensating controls. Third-party software maintenance outfits like Rimini Street have used them for years to protect software when their clients no longer have the right to access patches. VMware has introduced “virtual patching.” Palo Alto Networks and Rapid 7 also like this approach, and offer automation to develop controls. Where Cisco and OpenAI differ is their decision to make Shirudo open source, and their ambition that other players adapt and advance it. That offer is not entirely altruistic, as if Shirudo takes off it could create more demand for Codex. Cisco’s angle comes from the fact it owns Isovalent, an early champion of eBPF and the creator of both Cilium and the Tetragon sub-project on which Shirudo is based. Switchzilla is using eBPF in other products, so normalizing its use through an open source project can’t hurt. ®
