Title: MCP servers can now ship skills, run tasks, and more with Claude
Context: We're also giving servers ways to handle longer, more interactive work with Claude: Tasks and Elicitation are now generally available, and File Uploads is rolling out soon
Full Text:
Skills over MCP is now in public beta in Claude, so MCP servers can ship skills alongside their tools. We're also giving servers ways to handle longer, more interactive work with Claude: Tasks and Elicitation are now generally available, and File Uploads is rolling out soon.

Two years ago, Anthropic launched the Model Context Protocol (MCP) as a new standard for connecting AI agents to the systems where data lives. The spec has kept evolving to meet the connectivity needs of agents in production, and is becoming foundational for agentic messaging and orchestration.

With today’s updates, Claude can work with a server more like it works with another agent: learning from it, delegating to it, and exchanging input and files along the way.

Ship expertise alongside tools with Skills over MCP

Tool names and descriptions tell Claude what a server can do, but don't cover how to handle specific use cases. With Skills over MCP, servers can publish skills alongside their tools to help Claude take on longer, multi-step work. Claude loads a skill only when it's needed, keeping context use low. Skills update with the server, so developers can ship tools and guidance together and users have nothing separate to install.

Skills can cover best practices, step-by-step workflows, or even playbooks tailored to a user's account or organization. Using Skills over MCP:

Shopify helps Claude design and update a merchant's online store end to end.

HubSpot onboards customers and gets them set up in Claude.

Atlassian helps Claude draw on deep organizational context for insights and work analysis.

Carta will help Claude draft and issue equity from an uploaded document (coming soon).

Skills over MCP is in public beta in Claude and Claude Code, on by default for Pro, Max, and Ultra plans and available to Team plans once an admin enables it. Coming soon to Enterprise.

MCP servers can now take on long-running, interactive work with Claude

Agents in production are taking on longer, more consequential jobs. Servers can now support that work by running it in the background, checking in with users, and receiving files from Claude.

Hand off long-running work with Tasks. Tool calls used to have to finish before Claude could move on. With Tasks, servers can run operations that take time, or even full agent loops, while Claude keeps working and picks up the result when it's ready. Using Tasks, ZoomInfo runs deeper accounts and contact research that previously took several prompts.

Ask for input mid-call with Elicitation. Some actions need a user’s sign-off, like spending money or deleting data. With Elicitation, a server can pause to ask the user for input through a form or link, then continue where it left off. Using Elicitation:

Supabase confirms costs before creating a paid project and before running destructive SQL.

Railway asks before making potentially destructive changes, like removing a service.

GitHub has users enter a repository's name before an agent deletes it.

Tasks and Elicitation are now generally available in Claude and Claude Code for Pro, Max, and Ultra plans, and rolling out to Team and Enterprise organizations.

Send and receive files with File Uploads. Claude will be able to pass files to MCP servers, not just text. The File Uploads extension sends PDFs, spreadsheets, and images to a server without passing them through the context window.

File Uploads is rolling out soon in Claude and Claude Code to Pro, Max, Ultra, and eligible Team and Enterprise plans.

Add support to your plugins today

These features are part of the open MCP spec and its extensions, so a server that supports them works in any compatible client, not just Claude. To add support, see the docs for Skills over MCP, Tasks, Elicitation, and File Uploads.

Built on stronger foundations for connecting agents in production

Thanks to contributions from across the AI ecosystem, MCP now sees over 700 million monthly SDK downloads, and there are over 10,000 MCP connectors for Claude. We've worked with the MCP community to improve how MCP works in Claude. Over the past year, it has become:

More token efficient: Tool search loads tool definitions only when needed, which can cut the context they use by over 85% in multi-server setups.

Easier to scale: The latest MCP spec is stateless and supported across Claude products, making it easier to build servers and maintain their reliability as they grow.

Simpler to authorize: The Enterprise Managed Auth extension lets admins authorize supported servers once, so users connect automatically.

More interactive: The MCP Apps extension brings full interfaces into Claude, beside the conversation or full screen.

Together, these improvements make MCP easier to build on and adopt, and give the standard a strong base to continue evolving for the needs of agents in production.

Thank you to the MCP community

MCP is an open standard, hosted by the Agentic AI Foundation and shaped by the people who build on it. Two years of progress came from the maintainers, contributors, and developers who wrote the spec, built the SDKs, shipped servers, and added client support. Thank you for making MCP what it is today.

Title: Turn artifacts into Mac and Windows apps
Context: The "Install as app" feature is rolling out in beta in Claude for Mac and Windows
Full Text:
Starting today, you can use Claude artifacts to create, run, and share desktop apps. The "Install as app" feature is rolling out in beta in Claude for Mac and Windows.

When an artifact is installed as a Mac or Windows app, it gets its own icon and opens in its own window instead of inside Claude. You can share it with others, and it needs your permission before it can interact with your computer. You choose how much to allow.

Each app can use Claude and your connectors, and it updates automatically when the underlying artifact is edited. This simplifies the process for building and maintaining apps for both knowledge workers and developers. Requests the app makes to Claude count toward your plan’s usage limits.

Artifacts started out as a work output you’d share, like a chart or a webpage. People now use them as tools for everyday work, like a meeting prep page that regularly pulls from their calendar and email, or a tracker for the orders that need to ship that day.

If you rely on a tool for work, it should open like the rest of your apps and remind you when something needs your attention.

What installed apps can do

Installed apps can send notifications or add items to your menu bar or system tray. You choose permissions for each app, and Team and Enterprise admins can turn app permissions and full access on or off for their organization.

People at Anthropic have used these to make:

Linnet (opens in new tab), a full layered image editor

Phosphor (opens in new tab), a file manager that looks made for a movie set

Sift (opens in new tab), which sets up folder rules and uses Claude to keep your stuff organized

Tern (opens in new tab), a terminal with Claude by your side to help and explain

Vitals (opens in new tab), a menu bar and tray app for peeking at your computer’s performance

You can see more demo apps made by one of our engineers here (opens in new tab).

Permissions

There are three levels of permissions:

Default: Installed apps can only do what they’d be able to do in a browser.

App permissions: Apps can ask to use common features that Claude can tightly control, like creating always-on-top windows, listening for global shortcuts, or sending notifications.

Full computer access: Apps can ask to run programs and read, change, or delete your files without asking each time.

Your permission only covers the current version of the app, so Claude asks again after every update, even your own edits. If part of an app comes from another website, that part can change without Claude asking you again.

You can only give full access to apps you made or, on Team and Enterprise, apps made by people in your organization. Anthropic doesn’t review apps before you install them, so only give full access to apps you trust.

Getting started

Describe your app to Claude, try it as an artifact, and then click "Install as app." You don’t have to package or sign it, and it uses your Claude account, so there’s no API key or separate login.

Install as app is rolling out in beta on all plans. HIPAA-ready organizations and hybrid deployments can’t use it. It’s on by default for Team, with full access off. On Enterprise, it’s off until an owner turns it on. You need to be online and signed in to Claude to open an app. Some artifacts can’t be installed, including Claude Docs, Slides, and Sheets.

Update Claude for Mac or Windows, open an artifact you use every day, and choose "Install as app" from the Share menu.

Title: What makes a great ChatGPT app
Context: Select capabilities, don’t port your product A common first thought is to list all of your product’s features and ask, “How do we bring these into ChatGPT
Full Text:
At DevDay we introduced ChatGPT Apps — a new way to bring your product directly into ChatGPT conversations. This post builds on that launch with practical guidance for developers, PMs, and designers on how to choose the right use case and design an app that’s actually useful once it’s live. We’ll focus on how to translate your product’s strengths into clear, well-scoped capabilities the model can apply across many different conversations and user intents. If you’re looking for the original technical workflow, you can jump straight into the Apps SDK quickstart and developer docs.

We’ll cover:

What a ChatGPT app really is (and isn’t)

The three ways an app can genuinely add value

How to design for conversation and discovery

How to know whether your app is actually helping

Concrete examples and suggestions for screenshots

What a ChatGPT app actually is

When teams build their first ChatGPT app, the starting point is often:

“We already have a product. Let’s bring it into ChatGPT.”

This often starts with taking an existing web or mobile experience — screens, menus, flows — and trying to reshape it for chat. It’s a reasonable instinct; for years, “software” has meant pages, navigation, and UI scaffolding.

However, building apps for ChatGPT is a different environment. Users aren’t “opening” your app and starting on the home page. They’re having a conversation about something and the model can decide when to bring an app into that conversation. They’re entering at a point in time. In that world, the best apps look surprisingly small from the outside. They don’t try to recreate the entire product. Instead, they allow users to access a few specific powers while using the app in ChatGPT: the concrete things your product does best that the model can reuse in any conversation.

Outside of ChatGPT, your app is often the destination. Users:

Tap your icon

Enter your environment

Learn your navigation and UI patterns

Most product decisions flow from that assumption: “We own the screen.” You can invest heavily in layout, onboarding, and information architecture because users are committing to your space.

Inside ChatGPT, your app plays a different role:

It’s a capability the model can call - for both context and visual engagement.

It shows up inside an ongoing conversation.

It’s one of several tools the model may orchestrate.

That means the “unit of value” is less your overall experience and more the specific things you can help the model and user accomplish at the right moment.

A practical definition:

A ChatGPT app is a set of well defined tools that can perform tasks, trigger interactions, or access data.

This has a few implications:

You don’t need to port every feature.

You don’t need a full navigation hierarchy.

You do need a clear, compact API: a handful of operations that are easy to invoke and easy to build on.

You can think of it this way: your ChatGPT app is a toolkit the model reaches for when the user runs into a specific type of problem. The more precisely that toolkit is defined, the easier it is to use in the flow of conversation.

Once you see your app as “capabilities the model can orchestrate,” rather than “a mini version of our product,” design decisions get clearer. You start asking “What can we help with here?” instead of “Where should the user go next?”

The three ways to add real value

A simple filter for any app idea:

Know: Does it let the user work with new context or data they couldn’t see otherwise in ChatGPT?

Do: Does the app take real actions on the user’s behalf?

Show: Does the app present information in a clearer, more actionable UI than plain text?

This applies to “serious” productivity apps and to “just for fun” apps like games. A game might not help someone ship a report faster, but it still does something the base model can’t do well on its own: maintain stateful game logic, track progress, enforce rules, or render interesting views of the game world. The value is delight and engagement, but the underlying pattern is the same.

1) New things to know

Your app makes new context available within a ChatGPT conversation:

Live prices, availability, inventory

Internal metrics, logs, analytics

Specialized, subscription-gated, or niche datasets

User-specific data (accounts, history, preferences, entitlements)

Sensor data, live video streams

In practice, this often means bridging into systems where data is correct, current, and permissioned. The app becomes the “eyes and ears” of the model in your domain, and can answer questions with more authority.

2) New things to do

Your app takes actions on the user’s behalf:

Create or update records in internal tools

Send messages, tickets, approvals, notifications

Schedule, book, order, or configure things

Trigger workflows (deploy, escalate, sync data)

Play interactive games (apply rules, advance turns, track state)

Take actions in the physical world (IoT, robotics control, etc.)

Here, the app is less a source of truth and more a pair of hands. It takes the user’s intent and turns it into concrete changes in the systems your team already lives in—or, in the case of games, concrete changes in the game state that make the experience feel consistent and fair. This is where your app shifts to an agent in a meaningful way.

3) Better ways to show

An app can present information in a GUI in a ChatGPT conversation, that makes the information more digestible or more actionable:

Shortlists, comparisons, rankings

Tables, timelines, charts

Role-specific or decision-specific summaries

Visual or structured views of game state (boards, inventories, scores)

This is especially valuable when users are making choices or trade-offs. Apps can give the model a language for structure: widgets that have columns, rows, scores, and visuals that match how people actually decide—or, in games, how they understand “where they are” in the world.

If an app doesn’t clearly move the needle on at least one of know/do/show, it tends to feel like it’s not adding value beyond what users can already do in ChatGPT. Users may not complain explicitly, but it’s a missed opportunity to provide more meaningful value to the user, whether the app is meant for work or play.

Here you can see an example of an experience enhanced by an app:

An example answer from ChatGPT

This answer is helpful, however, the user may want to use an app with additional capabilities to directly browse real properties without changing context or leaving the conversation.

Answer with the Zillow app

With the Zillow app, the user has the additional ability to search live property listings, filter by criteria, and view rich property details — all without leaving the chat.

Fullscreen mode for enriched discovery

The value here is you still get rich context from the model, and also an enriched app experience that can dynamically interact with your intent. Want to ask it for homes in a specific region? With the Zillow app, the model invokes the tool on the Zillow MCP server and re-renders the UI layer.

Select capabilities, don’t port your product

A common first thought is to list all of your product’s features and ask, “How do we bring these into ChatGPT?”

On paper, that sounds thorough. In practice, it usually produces a large, fuzzy surface area that’s hard for the model to navigate and hard for users to understand. If you struggle to summarize what the app does in one sentence, the model too will have a harder time understanding it.

A more effective path:

List the core jobs-to-be-done - Identify the specific tasks or outcomes users are trying to accomplish that your product helps make possible. These are the reasons your product exists in the first place. Starting here keeps you anchored in user outcomes instead of feature checklists. Examples:

Help someone choose a home.

Empower ideas into polished presentations.

Translate intent into a delightful discovery experience.

Turn raw data into a clear, shareable report.

For each job, ask:

“Without an app, what can’t the user do within a ChatGPT conversation?”

Common answers:

Access live or private data.

Take real actions in our systems.

Get the structured or visual output users need.

This is where your unique value starts to show up. You’re no longer thinking “What can we technically expose?” but “Where are we uniquely helpful?”

Turn those gaps into a handful of clearly named operations. For example:

search_properties – return a structured list of candidate homes.

explain_metric_change – fetch relevant data and summarize likely drivers.

generate_campaign_variants – create multiple ad variants with metadata.

create_support_ticket – open a ticket and return a summary + link.

These operations are:

Concrete enough for the model to choose confidently

Simple enough to mix with other steps in a conversation

Directly tied to value, not to your entire product map

Another way to think about this: if someone on your team asked, “What are the three things we absolutely need this app to do well?” those should map almost one-to-one to your product’s capabilities.

For example, the Canva app in ChatGPT can generate an entire presentation draft and the user can enter full screen mode that matches user expectations for navigating a slide deck, but deeper slide-by-slide editing still happens in the full Canva editor.

Design for conversation and discovery

In your MCP server, you can define the description that provides the model with context when to invoke your tool, and specifically which tool calls, to perform a specific task. This helps map user intent to your tools actions.

a) Vague intent

Help me figure out where to live.

A good app response will:

Use any relevant context already in the thread.

Ask one or two clarifying questions at most, if needed.

Produce something concrete quickly — for example, a few example cities with short explanations.

The user should feel like progress has started, not like they’ve been dropped into a multi-step onboarding flow. If they have to answer five questions before seeing anything useful, many will simply stop.

Let’s take a look at how that is handled in the Canva app:

Building a full scale presentation requires context. The Canva app asks for follow up questions to get the user to synthesize what they’re looking to build.

b) Specific intent

Find 3-bedroom homes in Seattle under $1.2M near well-rated elementary schools.

Here, the app shouldn’t ask the user to repeat themselves. It should:

Parse the query.

Call the right capabilities.

Return a focused set of results with useful structure.

You can still offer refinements (“Do you care more about commute or school rating?”), but they should feel like optional tuning, not required setup.

Canva example:

When the user’s intent becomes clear and asks to generate a presentation, the model knows exactly when to call Canva and what capability to invoke.

As seen below, the tool shares a few options and also probes deeper if the user wants additional refinements:

c) No brand awareness

You can’t assume the user knows who you are.

Your first meaningful response should:

Explain your app’s role in one line (“I pull live listings and school ratings so you can compare options.”)

Deliver useful output right away.

Offer a clear next step (“Ask me to narrow by commute, neighborhood, or budget.”)

Think of it as a cold start problem: you’re introducing what you are, why you’re helpful, and how to use you — all inside one or two messages.

Build for the model as well as the user

You’re designing for two audiences:

The human in the chat

The model runtime that decides when and how to call your app

Most teams are comfortable thinking about the first. The second is newer. But if the model can’t understand what your app does or how to use it, your human-facing experience won’t get many chances to run.

There’s a third dimension that matters just as much: what user data flows through your app when the model calls it. Good app design isn’t just about clear capabilities, it’s about being disciplined in what you ask for and how you use it.

Clear, descriptive actions and parameters: Make it obvious when your app is relevant and how to call it. Use straightforward names (search_jobs, get_rate_quote, create_ticket) and spell out which params are required vs. optional and how to format them. Ambiguity is a tax on routing.

Privacy by design: Only require fields you truly need. Avoid “blob” params that scoop up extra context. Prefer minimal, structured inputs and do not use instructions like “just send the whole conversation.”

Predictable, structured outputs: Keep schemas stable; include IDs and clear field names. Pair a brief summary (“Three options that match your budget and commute time”) with a machine-friendly list ([{id, address, price, commute_minutes, school_rating, url}, …]). This lets the model talk naturally while keeping precise handles on data.

Be intentional about what you do not return: Skip sensitive internals “just in case.” Keep tokens/secrets out of user-visible paths. Redact or aggregate when full fidelity isn’t necessary.

Be explicit about what you collect and why: Ask for the minimum to do the job. When you need something sensitive (e.g., account access), say why in one sentence. Design actions and schemas so it’s obvious what’s being sent where.

Design for an ecosystem, not a walled garden

In a real ChatGPT session, your app is rarely the only one in play. The model might call on multiple apps in the same conversation.

From the user’s perspective, it’s one flow. From your perspective, it’s a reminder that you’re part of an ecosystem, not a sealed product.

A few practical consequences:

Keep actions small and focused

search_candidates, score_candidates, send_outreach

rather than a single run_full_recruiting_pipeline.

Make outputs easy to pass along

Stable IDs, clear field names, consistent structures.

Avoid hiding important information only in free-form text.

Avoid long, tunnel-like flows

Do your part of the job and hand control back to the conversation.

Let the model decide which tool should handle the next step.

If other apps (or future versions of your own app) can easily build on your outputs, you’ve set yourself up to benefit from improvements elsewhere in the ecosystem instead of competing with them.

A quick checklist

A short checklist you can run before or after building:

1. New powers

Does your app clearly know, do, or show new things?

Would users in your target scenarios notice if it stopped working?

2. Focused surface

Have you picked a small set of capabilities instead of cloning your entire product?

Are those capabilities named and scoped in ways that map cleanly to real jobs-to-be-done?

3. First interaction

Does your app handle both vague and specific prompts gracefully?

Can a new user understand your role from the first meaningful response?

Do they see value on the first turn?

4. Model-friendliness

Are actions and parameters clear and unambiguous?

Are outputs structured and consistent enough to chain and reuse?

5. Evaluation

Do you have a small, thoughtful test set with positive, negative, and edge cases?

Do you have some notion of the win rate of the app-provided answer vs. the ChatGPT answer without the app?

6. Ecosystem fit

Can other apps and the user reasonably build on your output?

Are you comfortable being one link in a multi-app chain, rather than the whole journey?

You don’t need to be perfect in every dimension to ship. But if you can answer “yes” to most of these, you’re not just putting your product inside ChatGPT, you’re giving ChatGPT real leverage in your domain — and that’s where these apps start to feel indispensable.

Title: Production monitoring with Codex
Context: Keeping in mind the principles of progressive disclosure, the access to these sources should typically be read-only, and it’s better to start with a smaller scope and broaden...
Full Text:
When an alert sounds in the middle of the night, an on-call engineer usually scrambles to their computer and starts manually searching through various sources, trying to find out what went wrong. They’ll dig through logs, metrics, and code to compare to various hypotheses: was it the recent deployment that caused the issue? A traffic spike? Dependency failure?

As Codex deployment engineers, we routinely see engineering teams struggle with slow investigations or delayed alerts due to a manual or spotty production monitoring system. Oftentimes the root cause is unclear without an exhaustive search, where the engineer on-call must manually compare what they see across multiple platforms to validate or rule out a broad range of hypothesis.

Codex can come in to help the on-call engineer right when the alert happens, sorting through all the different sources of information for them. Once it is embedded within your existing production monitoring systems, it can investigate with the tools your team already uses to triage the issue and identify its root cause.

In this demo, we walk through investigations using Grafana, Kubernetes, and Codex Security.

Incorporating Codex

Let’s go back to that alert and explore how we can integrate Codex in the process. At a high level, it’s helpful to think about what information you would give an SRE onboarding onto your production monitoring system.

1 Evidence

Trigger

Alert, incident, or operator request

2 Evidence

Collect evidence

Logs, traces, metrics, and runtime state

3 Reasoning

Correlate context

Code, deployments, configuration, and incident history

4 Reasoning

Form hypotheses

Evidence-backed causes and discriminating tests

5 Action and approval

Propose a bounded action

Specific, reversible, and linked to evidence

6 Action and approval

Human approval

A named approver authorizes the action.

If approved, apply the change.

7 Verification and learning

Verify recovery

Check trusted, agreed recovery signals.

If recovered, document the outcome.

8 Verification and learning

Document outcome

Findings, decision, result, and follow-ups

Denied: revise proposal

Not recovered: investigate

Give it the right access

The first step is to ensure that Codex has access to the relevant context needed to make a judgment, including traces, runtime state, or deployment history, and that your instructions to the agent are clear about what and where those sources are. Keeping in mind the principles of progressive disclosure, the access to these sources should typically be read-only, and it’s better to start with a smaller scope and broaden access once there’s a need for more information. To best facilitate this, you can create service accounts in those systems to maintain granular control over the resources Codex can access.

Observability platform Detects alerts and stores evidence

Codex execution environment Connects evidence, code, and tools

Model inference layer Provides OpenAI models

Proposing a fix

With this context, Codex can collate all the information across these sources to form hypotheses about the root cause. Here, the instructions should require evidence and citations for every judgment it makes, so that the reviewer will be able to easily understand the rationale behind the decisions. You can also test out having multiple agents, such as an executor agent responsible for root cause analysis (RCA) and a reviewer agent for challenging the executor’s hypotheses.

Note: If you’re interested in learning more about single vs. multi-agent setups, check out the Codex subagents guide.

The next step is to have Codex propose a bounded solution. To make sure it is evidence-based, it should draw on its RCA and the citations it used to back up its hypotheses. Ideally, the solution should also be supplemented with a rollback plan as a precautionary measure. These proposed fixes can come in the form of a report or a PR.

Reviewing and verifying recovery

As part of a human-in-the-loop workflow, a human approver should be the gatekeeper and authorize the solution. Once the change is applied, Codex can work in tandem with the human to verify recovery signals across the same sources that it was granted access to at the start of this process.

Once the incident is resolved, Codex can also assist with the postmortem and documenting the outcome.

Creating a repeatable workflow

Take this workflow through representative scenarios, such as past incidents. Each time should act like a rehearsal, an opportunity to iron out the friction points and feed the lessons learned back into improving the instructions for the next time.

Once this process has been battle-tested a few times, it’s time to take a closer look at how to make this a repeatable workflow. Turning runbooks into skills is our recommended approach to codifying this otherwise tribal knowledge.

Use what you learned in the rehearsals to refine the workflow.

Identify the context Codex needs. List the connectors Codex used to investigate the incident. Try the same incident with fewer sources and note where Codex needs more evidence to reach a conclusion.

Revise the instructions. Find the step where someone had to correct Codex. Update that step to point to the right source or supply the missing context, then run the rehearsal again.

Compare agent setups. Run the same incident with one agent, then add a reviewer. Compare how long each setup takes to identify the root cause and mitigate the incident, and how often someone has to correct it.

Once the process has been largely standardized, capture it in a Codex skill or plugin to make it reusable across different team members. The next time an alert goes off at 3 a.m., Codex can be the first one to wake up.

Title: Cisco and OpenAI Launch Shirudo, A New Project to Safeguard Agentic AI
Context: In testing against recent critical vulnerabilities “Java4shell” and the PHP flaw, Shirudo was able to write code that detected and blocked attempts to exploit both threats
Full Text:
News Summary

Defenders can start protecting systems before a permanent patch is in place. Cisco and OpenAI are making that possible through an open source effort to build infrastructure that is secure by default and defends itself.

Shirudo, an open source project built on industry-leading eBPF, helps protect running Linux systems without a reboot while teams roll out a patch.

This marks a shift from human-paced policy updates to self-defending, agent-driven security. AI agents do the legwork across the full stack, from models and data to the kernel and hardware, while people keep the keys and set the boundaries.

SAN JOSE, Calif., November 23, 2026 – Cisco (NASDAQ: CSCO) and OpenAI today launched an open source effort to make infrastructure secure by default and able to defend itself against today’s sophisticated cyber attacks. For too long, security has been a coat of paint. Cisco builds protection into the infrastructure itself, drawing on decades of building and protecting the systems the world depends on. OpenAI brings leading frontier AI research and insight into the attacks coming next. Together, they combine their insight to help anticipate AI-driven threats with the control to stop them.

Defenders must protect every part of their infrastructure, all the time. Attackers only need one machine that hasn't been patched. Shirudo is an important step toward closing that gap. The goal is infrastructure that is hardened from the moment it is built, keeps getting harder to attack, and can be restored to a known-good state if it is compromised.

“There is nothing more important than giving security teams the tools they need to match the speed of the AI-driven threats they are facing. We need self-defending infrastructure that acts at the speed of code, learns in real time, and shields itself until patches are safely rolled out,” said Jeetu Patel, Cisco President and Chief Product Officer. “Today, we’re proud to announce Shirudo with OpenAI, an important step towards that vision as we continue to collaborate with the wider community to solve the unique challenges of AI safety and security.”

“We’re giving defenders better models and tools to find and fix vulnerabilities faster, but finding a bug today doesn’t mean you can patch every system tomorrow,” said Greg Brockman, President and Co-founder of OpenAI. “We are partnering closely with Cisco on Shirudo to help teams protect the systems they need to keep running while they build and roll out a fix. So many teams rely on the same software that it makes sense to build these tools in the open. Now when one team finds a better way to protect a system, others don’t have to start from scratch.”

Shirudo: An Open Source Project from Cisco and OpenAI

Shirudo, Japanese for “shield,” uses eBPF, a technology that runs small, custom programs inside the operating system kernel without changing its source code. With it, AI agents can find a vulnerability, build a shield, and test that it stops the attack without disrupting the service. Shields go live only when the evidence says they are safe. Every shield is cryptographically signed, so the host can verify it before it runs, even if an attacker has gained administrator access.

In testing against recent critical vulnerabilities “Java4shell” and the PHP flaw, Shirudo was able to write code that detected and blocked attempts to exploit both threats. By utilizing an agentic framework, Shirudo matches the speed of AI-driven attacks as soon as a vulnerability is identified. Learn more about Shirudo here.

Cisco and OpenAI are inviting developers, researchers, and enterprises to help shape what comes next. Contribute a test that reproduces a vulnerability, run a shield against a kernel build you use, or show us where it breaks legitimate traffic. To learn more about Shirudo, visit: https://github.com/shirudo-dev/shirudo.

Title: Onboarding and offboarding: the decision you didn't know you already made
Context: Documents don't revoke access; people do, and only when they remember
Full Text:
What you will learn

Discover how automated identity management transforms onboarding and offboarding, enhancing security and efficiency while eliminating manual checklists.

The checklist nobody trusts

There's a Notion page at most companies called something like *IT Offboarding, Do Not Delete*. It was written by someone who left 18 months ago. Nobody's updated it since, because updating it means admitting nobody trusts it, and nobody has a sprint to rebuild it.This is the page someone opens on a Friday afternoon when an engineer's last day gets moved up without warning. It has 15 systems, SSH keys, database credentials, the Kubernetes cluster, the AWS console and a VPN client from 2022 that half the team forgot still exists. The page tells you where to look.

It doesn't tell you what's missing, and whatever changed since someone wrote it is exactly what's missing. Onboarding is the same checklist run forward because a new hire needs the same 15 things. Someone spends Monday morning clicking through admin panels instead of doing actual work.The real cost compounds instead of resetting with each cycle. Every manual step is a place someone assumes it's handled instead of knowing it is. Multiply that across a growing infrastructure footprint and the security posture is built on optimism.

Make identity the system of record

A runbook is a document. Documents don't revoke access; people do, and only when they remember. Tying access to identity itself, through the existing identity provider (IdP) fixes that. Add someone to the right group in Okta or Entra, and access to servers, databases, and clusters follows automatically, scoped to a role rather than assigned on a per-resource basis.Remove them, and turning off a single identity in the IdP disables everything downstream. It makes sense to treat onboarding and offboarding as an identity event rather than a checklist, because the IdP was always meant to be the system of record. Most companies just never wired it tightly enough to trust it.

Infrastructure doesn’t wait for the checklist

Infrastructure grows on its own now, and none of it shows up on that Notion page, because nobody thinks to write it down. Someone spins up a database for a proof of concept, someone else stands up a cluster to test an idea and moves on and none of it goes through an intake process because there wasn't one. That resource sits unmanaged until somebody happens to notice it.Make it a habit to scan cloud environments for new compute, database and cluster resources and bring them under management with far less manual work than registering each one by hand. This shrinks the gap between a resource existing and a resource being governed to near real time. It covers what you can broker, not a full asset inventory, and it won't surface every IAM role floating around an account.

Service accounts need a lifecycle too

Service accounts have the exact same onboarding and offboarding problem humans do, and almost nobody treats it that way. A CI/CD pipeline gets a token with more access than it needs because scoping it precisely takes an extra hour nobody has, and that token outlives the project. Nobody offboards a service account, because nobody tracked it as an employee-shaped thing to begin with.A service account created for that pipeline gets the same lifecycle discipline as a human does. It's owned and shut off in one action when the job ends. That's real, and it's a gap most access tools skip. Delinea governs the access identity uses. The underlying IAM role or Kubernetes service account still belongs to AWS, GCP, or the cluster's RBAC. A narrower claim than solving machine identity outright, and a more useful one for exactly that reason.

What building it yourself means

Building this in-house means writing and maintaining a separate integration for every system offboarding must reach: one to revoke SSH certificates, another to drop database roles, another to pull someone out of Kubernetes RBAC and another to strip cloud console access. Four integrations minimum, before discovery even enters the picture, plus a service account policy someone actually enforces instead of writing down and forgetting.It becomes a maintenance contract nobody signed, renewing every time a team adopts a new database engine or a cloud provider ships a resource type nobody's seen yet. Buying means someone else stays on the hook for keeping those integrations correct while the infrastructure changes every quarter, so the team doesn't have to.

What offboarding should look like

Go back to that Friday afternoon. The engineer's last day gets moved up, and instead of pulling up a stale Notion page and hoping to remember 15 systems, someone turns off one identity in the IdP. Any service accounts tied to that engineer get caught in the same motion. The database a contractor spun up last month is already inside the fence, found before anyone had to look for it. Nobody's checking a list and hoping. There's no list to check.

Why buy instead of build

That's the argument for buying this instead of building it. Doing it well in-house means standing up identity-tied revocation, cloud discovery and service account lifecycle management as three permanent engineering commitments, maintained forever by people who could be shipping product instead.

Title: US Cyber Director Pick Signals Shift Toward Expertise
Bluetooth brakes are broken as researchers find anyone can control them
Context: Given the importance of such control units to road safety, it’s easy to imagine how serious such a vulnerability could be if it proved to be easy to exploit, and boy, did it
Full Text: Imagine something as mission-critical as the brakes on a trailer being vulnerable to unauthorized control. One Australian manufacturer made the interesting choice of building Bluetooth into a trailer brake controller without adequately securing its critical braking functions. Anyone within Bluetooth range of an unpatched Elecbrakes trailer controller could potentially trigger its brakes or apply more braking force than intended, without needing to authenticate. The discovery comes courtesy of a pair of security researchers from Element Digital, Patrick Forck and Jeremy McCarthy. Their investigation began earlier this year when Forck was driving down the road and noticed that his physical Elecbrakes In-Car Remote had connected to someone else's trailer without pairing or prompting him. “It had connected mid-drive, without pairing or a prompt, to a brake controller that wasn’t mine, on a trailer I’d never seen, belonging to a driver who had no idea,” the researchers wrote. That one-off connection triggered a full-scale investigation by the pair. For those unfamiliar with trailer brake controllers, these devices are commonly used on larger trailers. Australian manufacturer Elecbrakes sells such controllers in Australia and New Zealand. Depending on jurisdiction, trailers over a certain weight are required to have their own braking system, which Elecbrakes manufactures. Elecbrakes offers two versions that are designed to be easier to install than traditional controllers: One that’s mounted in a vehicle, and one that is mounted directly on a trailer. That trailer-mounted unit can receive Bluetooth commands from the Elecbrakes smartphone app or a separate in-car remote. Given the importance of such control units to road safety, it’s easy to imagine how serious such a vulnerability could be if it proved to be easy to exploit, and boy, did it. Forck and McCarthy admitted they’re infrastructure security guys, not software devs, so they turned to Claude Code to dissect a decompiled copy of the Elecbrakes app, which Claude was happy to oblige. “What came back from the analysis was a map of the device’s entire Bluetooth GATT profile: 47 characteristics across four services, commands sent as plain unencrypted byte arrays, no checksums, no sequence numbers,” the researchers noted. To make matters worse, there was no authentication required for critical braking commands, even though other Bluetooth functions required pairing. Claude then built a web app that ran in Chrome which was able to access the Bluetooth controls for a nearby Elecbrakes system, and they were able to modify practically every aspect of brake control on a unit owned by one of them. Pairing failed on a few attempts, but not where it mattered: It allowed the connection without issue for actual brake control. They sent a few bytes to the brake control characteristic, and were shocked. “The electromagnetic hum at the brake drums was immediate and, frankly, a little sickening,” the pair said. “It said yes to four bytes from a total stranger then energised several tonnes’ worth of brakes and reported back that it had done so, pleased with itself.” Further experiments managed to modify braking strength based on deceleration speed as well, making it so that the trailer acted unpredictably based on the amount of force a driver applied to stop their vehicle. To say this is worse than a typical internet-connected device bug is to put it mildly - it even earned a trio of CVEs from CISA, with two of them scoring a CVSS of 9.6. “The attack surface is ‘anyone within Bluetooth range,’ the skill required is ‘can write four bytes,’ and the victim selection is ‘optional,’ ” Forck and McCarthy said. The fact AI was able to get them to that point in just a couple of days is even more concerning, they added. “This kind of research used to require a fairly rare and specific skill set,” the pair noted. “It now requires curiosity, a device you own, and an AI that can read bytecode faster than any human.” Luckily, they appear to have been dealing with a relatively responsive company in Elecbrakes - patches have been deployed for both the in-car and trailer-mounted models of their brake controllers. Installation is a manual process, we note, so if you own a controller from the company, be sure to stop and install the update. Unfortunately, Elecbrakes has a third controller out there that hasn’t been manufactured in several years, and it got skipped in the patching process. Owners of an ELBC2000 should be aware that their controller is still vulnerable, and there’s no patch available yet, as the vendor didn’t confirm that the ELBC2000 was vulnerable until the end of October, after it faced pressure from the researchers. ®

Title: Webworm Suspected of Modifying SoftEther VPN to Evade Detection and Hide Remote Access
Context: One of the tools used by the threat actor is a legitimate software called SoftEther VPN, with the bridge acting as a pathway connecting the compromised network and the attacker-...
Full Text:
The China-aligned threat actor known as Webworm is suspected to be using a custom version of the open-source SoftEther VPN Bridge tool in an attempt to remove recognizable detection fingerprints, while disguising it as network-monitoring software to establish covert remote access to compromised networks.

The modified variant "implements various tricks to hide itself from security tools," Rapid7 said in an analysis, attributing it to the adversarial collective with moderate confidence.

First publicly detailed by Broadcom-owned Symantec in September 2022, Webworm is the name assigned to a China-aligned nation-state group that has targeted government entities, IT services, and electric power companies across Russia, Georgia, Mongolia, and several other Asian nations.

One of the tools used by the threat actor is a legitimate software called SoftEther VPN, with the bridge acting as a pathway connecting the compromised network and the attacker-controlled infrastructure.

The latest findings from Rapid7 revolve around a Windows executable ("netcapa.exe"), which is a modified build of SoftEther VPN Bridge ("vpnbridge_x64.exe") version 4.44, build 9807. The modified version, rebranded as NtMonitor VPN, masquerades itself as Network Monitor Software from a company called Network Systems Solutions Inc. The artifact was uploaded to VirusTotal around mid-January 2026.

"The PDB path included in the executable reads C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\src\DebugFiles\pdb\x64_Release\vpnbridge.pdb," the cybersecurity company said. "As such, the tool doesn't hide its identity from reverse engineers, only external interactions."

The renaming is also said to be inconsistent, with many registry key paths still referencing the program as "SoftEther Project," even though a number of other occurrences of "SoftEther VPN" have been replaced by "NtMonitor VPN."

One of the most noticeable changes identified in the altered version is the use of innocuous-looking HTTP endpoints "/update/alive.cgi" and "/update/picture.cgi" to replace "/vpnsvc/vpn.cgi" and "/vpnsvc/connect.cgi," respectively, so that they look like ordinary web application activity.

It also changes the protocol watermark used by SoftEther VPN as part of the handshake process when initiating communication to help the tool distinguish protocol traffic from ordinary HTTP requests. When the connecting client is found to speak the expected protocol, it proceeds with the handshake. If the check fails, the server returns a decoy HTTP response.

The modified version swaps the GIF-based watermark used by the stock SoftEther VPN utility for a PNG-based watermark so as to bypass existing detection signatures based on the GIF watermark.

Some of the other changes introduced to the program are listed below -

Reducing a resource archive named hamcore.se2 used by SoftEther VPN to its bare minimum, as it's required to be present at runtime, and embedding it directly into the executable, causing the binary's size to increase by about 1.5 MB.

Changing the name of the configuration file from "vpn_bridge.config" to "setting.conf" and making its contents encrypted with a custom algorithm. The encrypted configuration starts with the magic bytes "RCEN" in ASCII.

What's interesting here is that the attackers have not been found to introduce any new functionality to the tool, indicating the primary focus was on stealth.

"It seems like they methodically analyzed SoftEther's detection surface and implemented counter-measures to all of the easy ways a detection engineer may target it," Rapid7 said, calling the latest evolution a hybrid approach that brings together the attacker's use of custom malware and dual-use tools.

"We are observing a sort of hybrid of the two — stock SoftEther software that is not trojanized, but rebuilt from source in a way that erases much of its detection fingerprint."

Title: Bulgaria evicts cyber snoops who lurked inside government networks for 5 years
Context: Bulgaria's Ministry of Innovation and Digital Transformation said the unauthorized and officially unattributed attackers first gained access to infrastructure used by government...
Full Text: The Ancient Thracian heartland of Bulgaria says it has shut down a cyberespionage operation that gave intruders access to government networks for five years – the longest-running known campaign against its administration. Bulgaria's Ministry of Innovation and Digital Transformation said the unauthorized and officially unattributed attackers first gained access to infrastructure used by government institutions to exchange information in 2021. It explained that the intrusion went unnoticed for so long because "the previous means of protection did not work as a single, integrated system," and that without a new, recently installed product, it may have gone undetected for much longer. "The incident was discovered thanks to the new national cybersecurity system, which for the first time provides a single picture of what is happening in state networks," the ministry added. "Without it, this activity would most likely have remained hidden for an indefinite period of time." Bulgaria acknowledged that "sensitive information related to the work of the state" was accessed, but did not specify the scale of the compromise. Innovation and Digital Transformation Minister Ivan Vasilev said attackers had downloaded more than 130 GB of data over five years. He also put the volume at 62 million pages. The Register contacted the Bulgarian government for confirmation of these numbers. The ministry said that it has not yet found any evidence that citizens' personal data was compromised, and that the affected infrastructure "will be under increased surveillance for 90 days" in case the attackers try to regain access. Vasilev said multiple international hacking groups had accessed government systems since 2021. He did not specify the names of these groups, however, nor did he name any specific countries that may have been involved. In a follow-up interview with bTV, Vasilev blamed political instability and frequent changes of ministerial leadership for leaving government systems inadequately protected. A representative of the Progressive Bulgaria party, which back in May won Bulgaria's eighth general election in five years, Vasilev said the "constant change of leadership" means "important things for the state do not actually happen." Vasilev said the intrusion was discovered over the summer as the national cybersecurity system was upgraded, and that teams had spent the past three to four months removing the attackers. ®

Title: Protect identity data with point-in-time recovery in Amazon Cognito
Context: The window accrues from the time the pool is on an eligible feature plan, and you can only recover to a point at which PITR coverage already existed
Full Text:
Amazon Cognito helps you implement secure sign-in and access control for users, microservices, and AI agents in minutes. Many of you rely on it for some of the most critical data you operate: the identities and attributes your applications use to authenticate and authorize every request. Recently, we launched point-in-time recovery (PITR) for Amazon Cognito user pools, which lets you restore a user pool to an earlier point in time if an accidental deletion, a faulty migration, or an erroneous bulk operation changes data you need. It’s turned on automatically for user pools on the eligible feature plans.

Before this launch, protecting user pool data meant building your own solution, such as exporting user attributes and group data on a schedule. That approach was time-consuming to build and operate, versioning the exports to find a clean point in time was another challenge, and reconstructing a pool from them was complicated. Users also got new sub identifiers as part of the restore process, which might break any downstream reference to the originals. Passwords, multi-factor authentication (MFA) settings, and passkeys might not be recovered, so every affected user had to reset.

In this post, we show you how to recover a user pool after an erroneous bulk operation, using the preview to review changes before you approve them.

How PITR works

On eligible user pools (see Prerequisites), Amazon Cognito now tracks changes so you can recover the pool to any point within the recovery window. The length of that window depends on your user pool feature plan. The window accrues from the time the pool is on an eligible feature plan, and you can only recover to a point at which PITR coverage already existed.

One behavior to understand is what happens to passwords during a recovery. A recovery restores passwords for users it recreates. A user who still exists and changed their password after the target time keeps the same password. The recovery doesn’t revert password changes, so users who legitimately changed their credentials don’t lose them.

A recovery is preview-based and has three steps:

Initiate a recovery to a target point in time (InitiatePointInTimeRecovery). Amazon Cognito pauses write operations to the user pool and generates a preview for your review before any changes are applied. Read operations and sign-in continue to work normally. The call returns a RestoreId.

Review the recovery preview (DescribePointInTimeRecovery). Amazon Cognito reports how many users, groups, MFA settings, and passkeys the recovery would create, update, or delete to return the pool to its state at the target time.

Approve or cancel. If the preview looks right, you approve the recovery with StartPointInTimeRecovery, and Amazon Cognito restores the pool to its state at the target time. If it doesn’t look right, you cancel it with CancelPointInTimeRecovery; no changes are applied, and write operations resume.

Prerequisites

To follow along with this post, you need:

An AWS account with an Amazon Cognito user pool on the Essentials or Plus feature plan. The recovery window is up to 1 day on Essentials and up to 14 days on Plus. The examples use a pool named anycompany-prod-user-pool in the US East (N. Virginia) AWS Region (us-east-1).

The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) configured with permissions for the Amazon Cognito user pools PITR operations.

Before you run a recovery, keep these limits in mind:

You can run one recovery at a time per user pool, and one successful recovery per 24 hours per pool.

The target time must be at least 15 minutes in the past and no earlier than the pool’s creation time.

Recovery is initiated from the pool’s primary Region and can’t start while a multi-Region replication (MRR) operation, such as replica creation or deletion, is in progress on the pool.

Recovering a user pool after an unintentional change

AnyCompany runs its user sign-in on an Amazon Cognito user pool, anycompany-prod-user-pool.

At 15:45 PDT, an operator runs a bulk change that’s supposed to set an attribute on a subset of users. A defect in the script instead deletes and modifies users. By 15:54 PDT, support receives cases of failed sign-ins and the operator halts the script. The team needs the pool as it was at 15:39 PDT. They decide to use PITR and preview the recovery before approving it.

Step 1: Start the recovery

The team initiates a recovery with a target time of 15:39 PDT by running the command in the preceding example. Figure 1 shows the same step in the console, where the team enters the target time and starts the recovery. The response includes a RestoreId that identifies this recovery throughout the workflow, along with a RestoreStatus and the RestoreTimestamp that you targeted.

aws cognito-idp initiate-point-in-time-recovery \ --user-pool-id us-east-1_EXAMPLE \ --restore-timestamp 2026-10-28T22:39:00Z

Figure 1: Initiating a recovery to a target point in time

Step 2: Review the recovery preview

DescribePointInTimeRecovery returns the Restoration for this RestoreId, including a RestorePreview that summarizes how many entities will be affected if the pool is returned to the target time. The team reviews the preview and confirms the number of affected users matches the scope.

aws cognito-idp describe-point-in-time-recovery \ --user-pool-id us-east-1_EXAMPLE \ --restore-id a69b8c1e-9866-441d-EXAMPLE11111

In this case, the preview reports 16 users to create and 5 users to update, as the following sample response shows. Figure 2 shows the same preview in the console, with the create, update, and delete counts for users, groups, MFA settings, and passkeys. These numbers match the scope of the bulk operation, so the team continues. If the preview had shown unexpected changes, the team could cancel the recovery with no changes applied.

{ "Restoration": { "RestoreId": "a7c41e92-0d3b-4f6a-EXAMPLE11111", "RestorePreview": [ { "Entity": "Users", "CreateCount": 16, "DeleteCount": 0, "UpdateCount": 5 }, { "Entity": "Groups", "CreateCount": 0, "DeleteCount": 0, "UpdateCount": 0 }, { "Entity": "User MFAs", "CreateCount": 0, "DeleteCount": 0, "UpdateCount": 0 }, { "Entity": "Passkeys", "CreateCount": 0, "DeleteCount": 0, "UpdateCount": 0 } ], "RestoreStatus": "PREVIEW_GENERATED", "RestoreTimestamp": 1793227140, "TriggerTimestamp": 1793228700 } }

Figure 2: Reviewing the recovery preview before applying

Step 3: Approve the recovery

If the preview is correct, the team approves the recovery with the command in the following example, and Amazon Cognito restores anycompany-prod-user-pool to its 15:39 PDT state. Figure 3 shows the approval step in the console, and Figure 4 shows the confirmation that appears after the recovery starts. Writes to the user pool resume automatically after the recovery completes or is canceled.

aws cognito-idp start-point-in-time-recovery \ --user-pool-id us-east-1_EXAMPLE \ --restore-id a7c41e92-0d3b-4f6a-EXAMPLE11111

Figure 3: Approving the recovery

Figure 4: Recovery confirmation

aws cognito-idp cancel-point-in-time-recovery \ --user-pool-id us-east-1_EXAMPLE \ --restore-id a7c41e92-0d3b-4f6a-EXAMPLE11111

Your application integration doesn’t change

Because PITR rolls back the data in your existing user pool rather than creating a new one, your application integration doesn’t need any changes. A recovery restores user data and leaves your user pool configuration in place, so configuration changes you made after the recovery point are preserved. For example, a custom attribute you added to the schema, an AWS Lambda trigger you updated, or a password policy you tightened stays as it is. The user pool ID also stays the same, and so do your app client IDs and secrets, managed login and domain, identity provider and SAML/OIDC configurations, and the provider Amazon Resource Names (ARNs) that services such as Amazon API Gateway and Application Load Balancer use to validate tokens. Recreated users keep the same sub identifiers, so downstream references to them keep working.

How PITR complements multi-Region replication

Multi-Region replication and PITR address different failure modes. Multi-Region replication keeps a synchronized replica of your user pool in another Region, so if the primary Region is impaired, you can fail over traffic to a replica Region with minimal downtime. PITR helps with data problems, such as erroneous bulk operations that corrupt your user pool’s state. You roll back to any point within your recovery window without changing your application integration.

Security considerations

A recovery changes the identity data that every sign-in and authorization decision depends on, so treat recovery permissions like any other high-impact administrative access.

Separate who initiates a recovery from who approves it. Because initiating and approving are separate API actions, you can assign them to different AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles. Give an operator the permission InitiatePointInTimeRecovery, and give an approver the permission StartPointInTimeRecovery. Both permissions need DescribePointInTimeRecovery and ListPointInTimeRecoveries to review the preview, and CancelPointInTimeRecovery to stop a recovery. IAM keeps the two permissions on separate roles, but it doesn’t stop one person from assuming both. Assign the roles to different people or teams, and grant the approver role only for the duration of an approved change.

Treat initiating a recovery as sensitive. Initiating a recovery pauses write operations on the user pool until the recovery is approved or canceled. If no action is taken within 24 hours, the preview automatically cancels and write operations are resumed. While writes are paused, users can’t sign up, reset their passwords, or update their profiles. A user pool also allows only one successful recovery per 24 hours, so an unauthorized recovery uses up a recovery you might need for a real incident.

Review restored users after a recovery. A recovery recreates users who were deleted after the target time, including users you removed on purpose, such as employees who have left or compromised accounts. After a recovery completes, check the recreated users against your incident timeline. Disable any that should stay removed and revoke their sessions with AdminUserGlobalSignOut.

Monitor recovery activity. Amazon Cognito records PITR API calls in AWS CloudTrail. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that notifies your security team whenever InitiatePointInTimeRecovery or StartPointInTimeRecovery is called, so that no recovery goes unnoticed.

Pricing

PITR is included at no additional charge in eligible feature plans with a recovery window of up to 1 day on the Essentials feature plan and up to 14 days on the Plus feature plan.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed you how to recover an Amazon Cognito user pool after an erroneous bulk operation with PITR, from reviewing the changes in a preview to approving the recovery. PITR provides protection for your users’ identities, with no custom export-and-restore pipeline to build or operate. Because the recovery happens in place on the same user pool, your application integration keeps working unchanged. PITR is already enabled for eligible user pools. Before you need it, separate the initiate and approve permissions, add an alert on recovery calls, and practice the preview workflow on a test pool.

Title: Got the next big thing in AI security? Pitch it at CPX and win!
Context: The theme is AI in cyber security: using AI to stop attacks, or securing AI itself
Full Text:
Cyber security startups, do you think you have the next big thing in AI? We want to see it. Check Point Software kicks off our fifth global Innovation Sandbox Competition, in Las Vegas and Vienna, in February 2027.

Innovation has been part of Check Point’s DNA for more than 30 years. Today we’re continuing that with our fifth global Innovation Sandbox Competition, held at our CPX events in Las Vegas and Vienna in February 2027. Compete for the chance to give a five-minute pitch on our main stage, in front of thousands of Check Point customers and partners, and to announce your win with us in a joint press release.

In summary

The CPX 2027 Innovation Sandbox is a free, live pitch competition for cyber security startups. The theme is AI in cyber security: using AI to stop attacks, or securing AI itself. You pitch for five minutes to Check Point leadership, C-level security buyers, and industry judges. Winners give a keynote on the CPX main stage. Intent to compete is due November 30, 2026.

Key takeaways

Two competitions: CPX AMER in Las Vegas, February 9–11, 2027, and CPX EMEA in Vienna, February 23–25, 2027

Theme: how your company disrupts cyber security with AI

Pitches run five minutes, at every round

Winners get a main-stage keynote, a joint press release, and a video of their keynote

Entry is free

An optional Start-up sponsorship adds visibility at CPX alongside your entry

Confirm your intent to compete by November 30, 2026

Inside the competition

We asked Brian Linder, Head of Check Point’s Office of the CTO, who runs the Innovation Sandbox competition, what startups need to know before they enter.

What is the Innovation Sandbox?

It’s a live startup pitch competition at CPX, Check Point’s annual conference. Startups pitch to Check Point leadership, C-level security buyers, and industry judges. “The prize is the stage,” Linder says. “Winners get a keynote in front of the full CPX audience. And entry is free.”

Where and when does it happen?

At two CPX events: Las Vegas, February 9–11, 2027, and Vienna, February 23–25, 2027. Startups can enter one or both, and a win in Las Vegas doesn’t rule you out in Vienna. “Yes, absolutely,” Linder says, when asked if a winner can compete again.

What are you looking for this year?

The 2027 theme is AI in cyber security, either using AI to stop attacks or securing AI itself.”We want AI that really powers the product,” Linder says. “Not AI as a buzzword.”

How do the judges score a pitch?

The opening round asks three questions. Did the judges understand the problem, and does it matter? Is the product meaningfully different? Is AI driving the innovation?

Finalists face a higher bar. “Is this a problem we’d fund now, and did you state it early?” Linder says. “Why you, and not the incumbents or the other AI startups?” Judges also look at whether the AI is core and novel or a thin wrapper on a general large language model (LLM), whether the team sounds credible about accuracy and limits, and whether the story lands in five minutes.

Five minutes isn’t long.

“That’s the point,” Linder says. The limit applies at every stage: the video submission, every judging round, and the winning keynote. “At five minutes, the mic goes off.”

How does judging work?

After passing prequalification, there are three rounds of judging at the CPX event. First comes a live audience vote on the Innovation Stage, with four or five Check Point judges. Next, CISOs in the C-level Executive Session judge. The final round is a private roundtable with four or five Check Point executives.

Winners are named that night and give their keynote the next morning.

What do winners take home?

A five-minute keynote on the CPX main stage on the final day, with up to two winners per event. Check Point also works with winners on a joint press release.”We send the CPX production video of the keynote a few days after the event,” Linder says. “Winners can use it freely in their own marketing.”

Who has competed before?

Some familiar names. Demisto won in 2018 and was acquired by Palo Alto Networks the next year. Axonius won in 2019. Prompt Security won in 2024 and was later acquired by SentinelOne. Veriti competed in 2024, and Check Point acquired it in 2025. Torq won in 2025.

Past years drew 10 to 15 startups. For 2027, Linder is aiming for about 15 per event, and returning competitors are welcome. “We encourage it,” he says.

Does it cost anything to enter?

No. Entry is free, and each competing startup’s speaker gets a complimentary CPX conference pass.

Fast-track your visibility with a Start-up sponsorship

To complement your competition entry, we offer a Start-up sponsorship level at CPX. It’s designed for emerging cyber security innovators with strong strategic alignment with Check Point. It puts your company in front of customers and industry leaders throughout the event, alongside your pitch and a possible main-stage win. To learn more, contact [email protected].

How to enter

Confirm your intent to compete by November 30, 2026, for both events. Send your speaker bio and photo, company logo, session abstract, and answers to two questions: what makes you unique, and who your competitors are. Your deck and pitch video follow later. They’re due January 26, 2027, for Las Vegas and February 9, 2027, for Vienna.

For more information, and to join the competitions, contact [email protected].

Title: CrowdStrike to Acquire Zscaler in Record $44 Billion Deal
Context: The news follows an announcement in September 2026 where the two firms expanded their partnership with Zscaler to be included in CrowdStrike’s Project QuiltWorks, an industry-...
Full Text:
Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike has announced its intention to acquire cloud-based security firm Zscaler for approximately $43.9bn. If concluded, the transaction will represent the biggest ever acquisition in the cybersecurity market.

The deal expected to expand CrowdStrike's total addressable market by more than $185bn, while creating opportunities for the company to cross-sell its Falcon platform to approximately 8000 Zscaler customers.

Under the terms of the agreement, Zscaler shareholders will receive 1.135 shares of CrowdStrike common stock for each share of Zscaler common stock they own.

The transaction is expected to close in the second half of CrowdStrike’s fiscal year 2028, subject to the relevant approvals.

The proposed deal would beat Google’s acquisition of Wiz for $32bn, which was concluded in March 2026, as the most valuable cybersecurity M&A transaction of all time.

Zscaler Deal Brings Network Security into CrowdStrike Fold

With the acquisition of Zscaler, CrowdStrike will enter network security, complementing its endpoint security offerings.

“Security used to be about keeping the adversary out. Today, safety is required to let AI in,” said George Kurtz, CEO and founder of CrowdStrike. “The network used to connect people to places. Now it connects agents to data.”

He added that with the acquisition of Zscaler, CrowdStrike will be building “cybersecurity’s operating system,” which includes a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI and enable agentic applications to run safely.

“We see a path to become the largest AI safety and security company the world has ever seen,” Kurtz said.

Jay Chaudhry, CEO, chairman, and founder of Zscaler, added that the agreement will also accelerate Zscaler’s ability to bring its “Zero Trust Everywhere” to a larger customer base.

Once the deal is closed, CrowdStrike will offer Zscaler’s Zero Trust SASE, security for AI, and data protection as part of the Falcon platform.

Additionally, the data from CrowdStrike’s Falcon and Zscaler’s Zero Trust Exchange will converge into a single dataset. This will allow CrowdStrike’s SafeMind frontier security models to train on the adversary’s full attack path.

The news follows an announcement in September 2026 where the two firms expanded their partnership with Zscaler to be included in CrowdStrike’s Project QuiltWorks, an industry-wide initiative which aims to improve information sharing and coordinated defense against AI-powered cyber threats.

In 2026, CrowdStrike has expanded its portfolio through several acquisitions, including identity management startup SGNL, acquired early in the year for approximately $740m, and AI security specialist Pangea, which it acquired on September 16 for a reported $260m.

Title: AI Runtime Security in Kubernetes: How Do You Prove Enforcement Works?
Context: How should the first 90 days establish AI runtime enforcement
Full Text:
How should the first 90 days establish AI runtime enforcement?

Use three signed approval gates to turn a limited pilot into a tested enforcement scope. The calendar organizes the work; reviewed evidence determines whether each stage is complete.

Days 1 to 30: Establish the baseline Inventory workload identities, cloud permissions, accessible credentials and observed connections. Keep existing protections active while proposed additional controls run in audit mode.

Review the activity that would have been blocked with the application owner. Distinguish required dependencies from access that was simply available. The first gate requires an agreed inventory and reviewed baseline, with the accountable security leader approving the scope.

Days 31 to 60: Reduce authority and resolve exceptions

Give agents dedicated identities and restrict permissions to required resources. Separate the authority to read from the authority to act, with application approval for consequential operations. Define permitted workload connections using the reviewed baseline.

Resolve expected policy violations and give every accepted exception an owner and expiry date. The second gate requires approval of the proposed enforcement scope and remaining exceptions.

Days 61 to 90: Enforce and test the controls

Enable reviewed policies and conduct a controlled exercise using test transactions. Demonstrate that a prohibited action is denied by the intended control and that an approved workflow completes. Test application approval checks separately from workload restrictions.

Validate containment and recovery, then retrieve the relevant evidence. The final gate requires documented results and security leadership approval before expanding to additional namespaces.

Title: Signal Moves to Block  iOS and Android AI Agents From Reading Chats
Context: Meredith Whittaker, president of the Signal Foundation, outlined the measures in a November 20 blog post, calling AI agents woven into operating systems, such as Google Gemini...
Full Text:
Signal has moved to stop AI agents built into iOS and Android from capturing users' chats, warning that it could not control anything they collected.

Meredith Whittaker, president of the Signal Foundation, outlined the measures in a November 20 blog post, calling AI agents woven into operating systems, such as Google Gemini on Android and Apple's Siri AI, "an existential threat to Signal."

Protections Vary by Platform

On Android, it said Screen security, an existing setting, would switch on automatically when Signal spotted an AI assistant trying to read the screen. Signal explained that because there are multiple versions of Android beyond Google, for many vendors, there is no reliable way to detect when a screenshot was attempted if screenshots are already disabled. Signal said it chose detection over blocking all screenshots, which would have impacted the user experiance.

Users could turn the protection off, though Signal warned this could leave their messages, and their contacts', open to AI agents. Blocking screenshots also does not stop agents from reading data already stored on a device, Signal said.

On iOS 27, Signal said it was preventing screenshots and showed a setting called "Block Siri AI."

However, on macOS 27, Signal said it had no dependable way to stop screenshots and that Apple's screen-protection options covered only streaming and copy-protected media. It advised users to add Signal to the Siri Excluded Apps list.

In 2025, Signal began blocking screenshots by default on Windows 11 to keep out Microsoft Recall, which takes screenshots every few seconds and stores their text in a searchable database that Signal said could keep even disappearing messages indefinitely.

Read more on AI agent security: 65% of Enterprises Have Seen AI Agents Act Out of Scope

Signal Presses Platform Makers for an Opt-Out

Signal also pointed to third-party agents such as Meta Muse, which it said were using accessibility settings to reach app data. Those settings let apps read and control the screen and are designed for assistive tools.

It asked Apple, Google and Microsoft for a documented way for apps to opt out of AI access to their screens, files, notifications and other system features without breaking how they work, plus clearer documentation of how agents handle data.

Signal said confidential computing, which protects data while it is processed, fell short because AI providers would still decide how much privacy users got. Google and Apple were engaging with Signal, which said it was "cautiously optimistic" about some major operating system providers.

Whittaker said Signal's developers had put significant effort into forensic analysis of Android and iOS to learn how AI systems reached app data, and that the lack of documentation made strong privacy harder to build.
