Title: Probing DNS at Cloudflare
Context: This is something the Cloudflare DNS team has experienced firsthand
Full Text:
Imagine this: you’ve just pushed a release. All the unit tests passed and your dashboards are green. You sit back to relax but then suddenly your phone starts blowing up: prod is broken.

This is something the Cloudflare DNS team has experienced firsthand. In one rollout of the service that publishes DNS records to our edge, a scheduling bug let some record changes sit unpublished for hours. The service stayed up and was healthy, but new hostnames were slow to resolve and certificates couldn't be issued until the bug was squashed.

DNS failures are hard to catch because they are slow, spread across the network, and partial in where they cause impact. We needed to figure out a way to test DNS the way customers experience it: constantly, from every data center, and against production.

For us, the answer was to extend Flamingo, the end-to-end testing framework we were already using to run hundreds of millions of tests a day against Cloudflare's edge. This post covers how Flamingo's modular design lets us add DNS support, how we measure propagation, and how those measurements now decide whether a release goes ahead or gets rolled back.

A little background

At Cloudflare we’re obsessed with improving performance and safety for our customers. It’s crucial that our code is tested constantly, both at scale and against the real Cloudflare edge that our users operate in. That’s one reason why we created a tool called Flamingo: to measure the behavior of our production environments and make sure that code in lower-tier environments behaves as expected.

We’ve already written a little about how this tool has been used in the upgrades to our CDN stack. However, this is only a small portion of how we use Flamingo internally. One of the features of Flamingo is its modular architecture that enables teams to extend the capabilities of the tool to speak other networking protocols. In our case, we wanted to use these modular capabilities to test DNS.

What is Flamingo?

Testing is hard. Testing at scale, when you have a widely distributed system, is even harder. There are many complex pathways that requests take and multiple systems that each network request must traverse before making its way to the origin. Unit testing alone is not nearly enough for this. We need to run constant automated testing against real systems and measure the outcomes of those requests to make informed decisions on the health of a service.

Enter Flamingo. Originally built around complex multi-step HTTP testing, its capabilities and scope have increased substantially over the years. Flamingo is built from the ground up with Cloudflare’s infrastructure in mind. We built a control plane and scheduler that let teams target specific environments, data centers, or percentages of metals. We needed to integrate with custom reporting, metrics, and analytics tooling. Additionally, it needed to be a tool with predictable performance and run well on bare-metal servers in resource-constrained environments.

Being delightful

When we’re building internal tooling like this, we strive to create a delightful developer experience. Internal tooling should be as easy as possible to use, but also powerful enough to handle over 80% of all use cases. And in order for a new edge acceptance test framework to be successful, it needs to be built in such a way that it forces teams to follow common guidelines and build reusable scripts in an environment that is stable, scalable, and manages complexity.

One thing that is not delightful is debugging a test. If you allow a user to write tests in a traditional programming language, when their test fails they then both need to debug the upstream system being tested and the test itself. This is why we built Flamingo to use a custom domain-specific language (DSL) consisting of a simple setup-request-response format.

For example, let’s imagine that we want to make sure we are redirecting all unencrypted traffic to its encrypted counterpart.

TEST test-redirect SET $hostname www.cloudflare.com GET "http://$(hostname)/" ASSERT STATUS IS 301 ASSERT HEADER Location IS "https://$(hostname)/"

Here we can see the power of the DSL. In five lines of code, we have a script that can run anywhere on Cloudflare’s edge and scale to thousands of requests per minute. We can take the data produced from the millions of data points generated from this and turn those into a graph defining how our service is actually performing in the real world.

Taking the setup-request-response test format from above and modifying it slightly allows us to use Flamingo for more than just HTTP testing. Instead of the middle step being a request, we can now look at it as an action. Now we’ve changed our system from something that makes HTTP requests into something that can perform any action for which we’d like to measure the outcome.

In Flamingo we call these modules and have put immense effort into making them as easy as possible for anyone to write. Flamingo is written in Rust, due to its consistent performance characteristics and strong type system. The type system in particular lends itself to this modularity, by allowing us to use strongly-typed enumerations for input and output in the Flamingo action runner:

pub enum Action { Query { method: String, url: Expression, parameters: Vec<http::QueryParameters>, }, DnsQuery { query_name: Expression, query_type: Expression, parameters: Vec<dns::DnsQueryParameters>, }, } pub enum ActionOutput { Http(http::FetchResponse), Dns(dns::QueryResponse), } pub type ActionHandlerFunction = Arc< dyn Fn( Action, Arc<Ctx>, InterpreterConfig, ) -> BoxFuture<'static, Result<ActionOutput>> + Send + Sync + 'static, >; pub type ActionHandlerLUT = Arc< dyn Fn(&Action) -> ActionHandlerFunction + Send + Sync + 'static, >;

What we’ve done here is decouple the logic for performing an action (in this case an HTTP request) into a dynamically dispatched function that we can then call independently of other actions. This leaves things like test scheduling and resource management as higher-level operations that someone implementing a module doesn’t need to worry about. All the author needs to focus on is the logic.

pub async fn query( action: Action, ctx: Arc<Ctx>, cfg: InterpreterConfig, ) -> Result<ActionOutput> { let Action::Query { method, url, parameters, } = action else { bail!("Invalid action for module-http::query: {action:?}"); }; ... } pub async fn execute_module<F>( ctx: Arc<Ctx>, cfg: &InterpreterConfig, handler_lut: F, ) -> Result<ActionOutput> where F: (Fn(&Action) -> ActionHandlerFunction), { let func = handler_lut(action); let action_out = (func)(action.clone(), ctx.clone(), cfg.clone()).await?; ... }

Using Flamingo to probe DNS

The adage says that when issues arise, it's always DNS. Like many jokes, there is always a kernel of truth behind it. DNS is an incredibly important piece of the Internet, and since it relies on a complex network of interconnected sources of truth, it can become easy for a single misstep to cause a storm of failures.

DNS can be a particularly finicky system due to its hierarchical nature. When you change a DNS record for a Cloudflare zone, for example, said record needs to be propagated to the authoritative servers such that the updated record becomes widely available. To reduce latency, records are stored in physically closer caches. These records have a time to live (TTL) associated with them that tells the local DNS cache how long before it needs to refetch that record from the authoritative server. Any delays will impact time-sensitive operations like certificate issuance and traffic failover.

We’ve already mentioned that we built Flamingo for extensibility. One of the first and most impactful modules in use today was built specifically for this use case. Our team was able to add code that extended Flamingo such that instead of sending HTTP requests, we send DNS queries. By doing so we got everything else for free. No need for the DNS team to worry about managing a new probing service. No need for them to have to integrate with our reporting pipelines. It all just worked.

To probe DNS, we measure how quickly customer record changes propagate to authoritative nameservers and the public resolver (1.1.1.1). The test continuously updates a TXT record with a timestamp and queries three authoritative nameserver IPs and 1.1.1.1 from every data center, asserting freshness within 90s (authoritative) and 600s (resolver).

TEST test-propagation-delay-direct-108-162-193-62 MOD dns SET $hostname "some.probe.domain" SET $authNs 108.162.193.62:53 # amir.ns.cloudflare.com QUERY $hostname TXT TARGET $authNs ASSERT DNS.RCODE IS NOERROR ASSERT DNS.FLAGS CONTAINS AA ASSERT DNS.ANSWERS[0] GT SUBTRACT(TIMESTAMP(), "90")

Catching bugs (SLO and steady)

To ensure that our many systems are operating within expectations, we define what are called service-level objectives (SLOs) for observing things like availability or latency. SLOs are a percentage of some metric that is used as a target. Additionally, SLOs are measured through service-level indicators (SLIs) which are the actual series of measurements focused on the end-to-end experience that a user has when interacting with a system.

By constantly sending synthetic Flamingo traffic through our production systems, we can begin to then use that information to build a picture of what our actual end users are experiencing — and provide that data for our SLOs. When that synthetic traffic encounters issues then we can be pretty confident that Cloudflare customers are also hitting issues and triage accordingly.

Once we have this information, it allows us to make informed decisions when releasing a service. SLOs operate in terms of error budgets and burn rates. An error budget is the percentage of downtime that a service is willing to tolerate while the burn rate is the rate of change in that budget at any given time. This allows for an automated system to understand the severity of an issue. For example, burning 10% of your error budget over a three-day period might be some long running issue that, while not urgent, is affecting customers and needs to be dealt with. But if you were to burn 10% of your error budget within an hour, that means an incident is occurring and customer impact will be substantial if not fixed immediately.

Using these numbers, we can look at our SLOs while deploying and make informed decisions on the health of a service. Based on that information, we can tell our releasing systems to either promote a change or roll it back.

The road ahead

By moving DNS monitoring to Flamingo, we’ve created a system that can proactively detect DNS issues before they have the chance to spread to the rest of Cloudflare’s edge. If Flamingo detects a spike in propagation latency in a specific canary data center, we can automatically halt the rollout of a new software version before it impacts the rest of the Internet.

DNS is just the start for extending Flamingo. We currently have modules for testing TCP, UDP, WebSockets, and several more. Having a tool for quickly testing and monitoring services has enabled teams to deploy large changes safely without the need for a human to keep a constant watch.

If this kind of reliability engineering interests you, check out our careers page for open roles.

Title: A Buffet of ClickFix: Lures, Infrastructure & Payloads
Context: Our first audience poll found that 40% of respondents had not seen ClickFix in the wild, while the remaining 60% had run into it as a user, in a SOC investigation, or both
Full Text:
Amazon, ChatGPT, Google Docs…we've seen them all being impersonated in ClickFix campaigns. Also known as "paste and run" or "fake CAPTCHA," ClickFix lures trick users into copy/pasting a command in their terminal under the guise of a technical "fix" or software download. Just one malicious command pasted into a Run box can open the door to infostealers, remote access tools, ransomware, or other malicious software.

On the latest episode of Tradecraft Tuesday, Staff Technical Community Engagement Writer Ben Nahorney, Staff Detection Engineering & Threat Hunting Analyst Tyler Bohlmann, and Security Operations Analyst Sarah Reddish walked through some of the more convincing ClickFix lures Huntress has seen lately, the variety in final payloads, and a peek under the hood of the infrastructure attackers use to host fake verification pages.

Watch the full video below, and keep reading for clips and other highlights.

ClickFix at a glance

Ben kicked things off by defining ClickFix and breaking down the differences between its variants: FileFix, TerminalFix, and DownloadFix.

ClickFix has been around for a while, so why are we talking about it now? We're seeing more and more ClickFix, with increasingly convincing lures, sophisticated tradecraft, and a variety of final payloads.

Our first audience poll found that 40% of respondents had not seen ClickFix in the wild, while the remaining 60% had run into it as a user, in a SOC investigation, or both.

Later in the episode, we asked the audience what kind of malware they had seen as the final payload in ClickFix-related incidents: remote access trojans or rogue remote access tools was the most common response (43%), followed by infostealers (33%).

What happens after you click Verify?

The pasted commands from a ClickFix lure vary from a one-line malware download to the starting gun for a complex attack chain with layers of obfuscation, C2 communications, living off the land, and multiple malicious payloads.

Clip 2

The infrastructure

Tyler takes over for a look at some of the plumbing that goes into standing up a ClickFix campaign. ClickFix operators evolve their tradecraft as defenders stand up new detection logic and prevention controls. By renting a commercial kit, such as ErrTraffic, attackers can rotate out hosted domains across thousands of compromised websites using blockchain communications. These "smart contracts" make it relatively cheap and easy to swap out lure art, branding, and shortcuts from the same infrastructure.

Tyler highlights a single compromised WordPress site that carried five separate malicious injections from different attacker families, several disguised as legitimate script tags, showing it's been hit by multiple unrelated operators. Instead of hardcoding a malicious domain, the injected script reads a pointer from a Polygon smart contract to find its current front domain, so the attacker redirects every victim page by editing one on-chain value rather than touching any site.

ClickFix in the wild

Next, Sarah walks through a recent incident our SOC investigated that began with a Google search for "Amazon business" and ended with a remote access trojan (RAT) and an infostealer on the victim's environment. We refer to these payloads as "finger-licking malware," due to their use of the obscure built-in Windows finger utility to communicate with a variety of BBQ-themed domain names.

Sarah breaks down all three stages of this complex attack chain, including C2 communications, malicious JavaScript, and multiple layers of obfuscation.

Beyond the clipboard

Ben returns to highlight more of the variations in ClickFix tradecraft that have popped up in recent Huntress SOC investigations, including attack chains that establish persistence, support lateral movement, and enable reconnaissance and credential theft.

Featured examples include DLL sideloading, stenographic malware delivery, a node.js RAT dressed up as an remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool, and a command that retrieves a malicious script from the victim's browser cache.

How to fix ClickFix

Each of our panelists emphasized user training to "stop the paste:"

Never paste commands into a Run dialog box, a terminal, PowerShell, or anything else at a web page's request.

A legitimate CAPTCHA or other verification will never ask you to do so.

From the defenders' standpoint, we recommend leveraging application control tools or allowlisting for untrusted executables and limiting the access to local administrator privileges. Consider limiting who can access the Run dialog box or a command prompt.

Detection efforts should focus on the sequence of activity rather than relying solely on hashes, domains, or other static indicators. These can easily be swapped out by a threat actor.

Common post-paste behavior includes:

A browser or user-launched process spawning cmd.exe, PowerShell, or Windows Terminal

Encoded PowerShell commands

Execution-policy bypasses

Archives or executables appearing in user-writable locations

New scheduled tasks, new Run keys, or unexpected SSH connections

Title: Upgrade to Qualys’ Learning Management System (LMS)
Context: All other training and certification will only be available if a work email address is provided
Full Text:
Key Takeaways

Plan around the downtime: The learning platform will be unavailable from 7 AM PT on November 29, 2026, to 12 PM PT on December 1, 2026. Instructor-led training will continue as scheduled.

Finish self-paced courses early: Complete any self-paced training you’ve started before November 29, or you will need to restart it after the upgrade.

New name, new login: The portal is becoming Qualys Academy, and your email address will be your username.

Reset your password after December 1: Existing users must reset their passwords, and new users will need to create accounts.

Your records are safe: Your training history and certifications remain intact, and your Qualys Platform data is unaffected.

To better drive learning for customers, partners, and students, Qualys is upgrading its Learning Management System (LMS), the application we use to house and conduct training. If you are a current LMS user, your training history and certifications will remain intact.

When Is the Change Happening?

The upgrade will be completed on December 1, 2026. The learning platform will be unavailable from 7 AM PT on November 29, 2026, to 12 PM PT on December 1, 2026. You will not have access to your learning transcript, self-paced courses, or certification exams during this time. All instructor-led training will still occur during its scheduled time.

You will still have access to our video library.

You will want to complete any self-paced training you’ve started before November 29, 2026. Otherwise, you will need to start again after the upgrade.

Why Are We Upgrading?

The upgrade will allow us to drive learning for customers, partners, students, and other learners. It will provide more flexible ways to learn over time and be easier to use.

There will be user interface (UI) improvements, including a better flow for taking training, and the use of AI to help you get the training you need.

What Is Changing?

User Account Changes

Your username will be your email address. If you used something other than that on our previous system, this will change.

If you have multiple learning accounts with the same email address, they will be merged into a single account.

You’ll also now have the opportunity to provide both a primary work email address and a backup email address. This will help you “take your transcript with you” if you ever move to a different organization.

Training Access Changes

The foundational courses will remain available to all.

All other training and certification will only be available if a work email address is provided.

You will still have access to all videos and knowledge through our video library.

Name Change

The name is changing to Qualys Academy.

Login URL Change

You’ll log in at Qualys Academy.

After December 1, if you have an existing learning account, you must reset your password. You can follow the instructions in the FAQ section below on how to do this.

If you are a new user, you will need to create a new account.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

How do I reset my password?

1. From December 1, 2026, onward, navigate to Qualys Academy and click the Forgot your password? link.2. Enter the email address you used in the old system.

The system will then send you an email with password reset instructions to the email address we have on file for your username. Be on the lookout for an email from academy@qualys.net for those instructions. The email may take 10 to 15 minutes to appear. You may need to allowlist academy@qualys.net.

If you are unable to reset your password for any reason, please contact us at training@qualys.com.

Where can I find my transcript?

You can find your transcript by logging in to Qualys Academy at academy.qualys.com and then clicking on the View Transcript button on the Home page.

How do I download my diplomas/certificates?

To download your certificates:

1. Log in to Qualys Academy.2. Select the View Transcript button.Once on the Training Transcript page, any course or exam for which you have obtained a certificate will have a small certificate icon to the left of its name.

3. Click on that icon, and a new window will appear with Export to PDF and download options.

How do I enroll in self-paced or upcoming instructor-led training?

To register for training:

Log in to Qualys Academy.

If you don’t already have an account, create one with your work email address.

Select the Qualys Catalog button.

Click on the training you’d like to take.

What if I was in the middle of a self-paced training before the upgrade?

You will need to restart that training. All completed training will be in your transcript.

If I’ve started training after the upgrade, where do I go to resume my training?

1. Log in to Qualys Academy.2. Select the Resume Training button.Once on the My Training page, you will see several widgets that show Certifications (from passing exams), In-progress Training, Not Started Training, and Completed Training.

Does this impact my data on the Qualys Platform?

This upgrade to the learning system does not impact your Qualys Platform (vulnerability, compliance, risk, etc.) data. This is only an upgrade to the learning system and training data.

Who do I contact if I have additional questions?

If you have any remaining questions, please reach out to training@qualys.com.

Title: Why Your PAM Tenets Fail AI Agents and How to Rewrite Them
Context: Only one obligation in the framework is genuinely new: clean instruction In the administrator model, the operator's intent was never part of the threat surface
Full Text:
What you will learn

Why agents inherit the full privilege of the accounts users hand them, how the seven PAM laws shift from administrators to credentials, actors and tasks, and why runtime control is the only layer that holds.

Your users are handing their accounts to AI agents, and every agent inherits the full privilege of the account it's given. Privileged access laws the industry has used for 20 years were written for administrators, not AI agents.

Twenty years ago, Kim Cameron, then Microsoft's Chief Identity Architect, published seven laws of identity: user control and consent, minimal disclosure for a constrained use, justifiable parties, directed identity, pluralism of operators and technologies, human integration and a consistent experience across contexts.

These were constraints that any identity system would have to satisfy to survive contact with real people. And they held. Scoped consent, pairwise identifiers and the industry's refusal to build a single universal identifier for everyone all trace back to that list.

But Cameron wrote his laws about people proving who they are

They have almost nothing to say about the AI agents and accounts that can delete your backups.

That's a different problem, and it sits in a different place. Identity management isn't one layer; it's three. What separates them is what they protect, when they enforce and where enforcement occurs.

Layer

Discipline

Enforcement point

Timing

3

Privileged Access Management (PAM)

Privilege elevation and the full execution lifecycle

Runtime, continuously re-evaluated

2

Identity Governance and Administration (IGA)

Access review and compliance validation

Certification cycles and lifecycle events

1

Identity and Access Management (IAM)

Initial access grant: authentication plus coarse authorization

Entry-point decisions

IAM issues the identity. IGA governs its lifecycle. PAM sits on top of both and reuses them at the moment authority is actually exercised. Cameron's laws govern layer one. For layer three, we wrote our own seven, and for 20 years that was enough.

Then everyone started handing their account to an AI agent.

Who were the original seven tenets of PAM written for?

Administrators. That's the whole answer, and it's the reason we had to rewrite them.

The original seven, which we published at RSA Conference in February 2020 as the seven pillars of Identity-Centric PAM (Centrify Debuts Identity-Centric Privileged Access Management), read like this:

Vault and rotate every administrative account.

Give privileged users a unique, non-public identity. You might still have "dash-a" domain admin accounts in your Active Directory.

Establish a clean source with no direct internet access.

Record and analyze every session to make sure the admin doesn't do anything malicious and to catch accidents before they become production-down issues.

Authorize all privileged access just-in-time.

Grant just enough privilege to get the job done, without handing full admin to an unqualified person.

Continuously monitor privileged activity at runtime.

Each of these tenets describes an IT staff member performing IT work. That wasn't sloppiness at the time. It was accurate. Privilege lived where the administrators were, so we wrote tenets for the people who held it and shipped products to control it.

How AI agents are changing the seven laws

Everyone is now using AI agents, and most people simply hand over their account credentials so the agent can do the work for them.

A salesperson connects an AI assistant to the company customer relationship management (CRM) system. After a few clicks and a consent screen, the assistant can see every lead, every account and every contract that person could see. It will often run in the browser, connect to the internet, chase every lead and use any available account to ingest documents and data on the user's behalf. This is where the benefits of single sign-on actually hurt.

The salesperson didn't do anything wrong. Nobody bypassed a control. IAM granted login access to an existing account holding the salesperson role, exactly as configured. IGA will validate that user's need to access the CRM at the next quarterly attestation campaign. The salesperson isn't an administrator, the CRM isn't infrastructure, and no security team was asked to approve anything.

So now ask a harder question: Why did we ever tolerate the gap in the first place?

For 20 years, the industry treated the first four tenets as mandatory and the last three (just-in-time authorization, least privilege and continuous monitoring) as a maturity curve you eventually reached. That mostly worked, because something unwritten was holding the line. Consequences. An administrator with vaulted domain admin rights largely didn't abuse them, because that administrator had a manager and their name in the audit log. Deterrence was quietly doing the work that authorization had never finished.

An AI agent has no stake in any of it. It can't be reprimanded, can't be put on a performance plan, and can't be fired in any sense it would recognize. Termination is a routine, expected event in the lifecycle of an ephemeral, short-lived agent, not a punishment. Take the deterrent away, and you're left holding exactly the controls you implemented. For most organizations, that's the first four tenets and a consent screen.

We didn't discover a new class of cyberattack. We deleted the deterrent that had been silently compensating for the three controls we never finished. What we have to remember is that agents aren't the problem. They're what removed our ability to keep ignoring it.

We had defined privilege by who held it rather than by what it could do. A treasury analyst who can change a vendor's bank details holds more destructive capability than a junior system administrator. A sales operations user can export the entire pipeline. A support representative with impersonation rights can read any customer's record. None of them appeared on the privileged user list, because none of them administer servers.

And an AI agent running freely inside any one of those accounts is considerably more dangerous than the human whose account it is. The human exercises a small fraction of what the account permits, during business hours, one action at a time. The agent will exercise all of it continuously at machine speed, and it won't hesitate on a request that a person would have thought twice about.

Privilege is any capability to move money, data or change a control, regardless of who holds it or what it's called.

Is everyone a privileged user?

No. Most of what an employee does all day is not privileged. But a minority of what many employees can do is privileged in exactly the sense that matters. We could afford to overlook that for as long as those users had no practical way to hand their capability to something else. They do now, and the handoff takes two clicks.

When employees can hand their accounts and access rights to an AI agent, you need to revisit how you grant rights and how much power those privileges carry, because an AI agent may be the one using them.

Where does that leave PAM in the identity stack?

In the same place architecturally, covering a far larger population.

When privilege was a job title, PAM was reasonably treated as a specialist tool bolted onto the side of the identity program, procured separately, staffed separately and scoped to a few hundred administrators. Once you understand privilege as a capability, layer three applies to the same population that layers one and two already cover: every AI agent, human and machine. PAM ceases to be an adjacency and becomes the third mandatory layer of identity management.

Notice where the AI agent lands in that picture. It comes through the front door legitimately, holding a credential IAM issued correctly and IGA reviewed and approved. Every layer beneath it says yes accurately. Access alone isn't control. Runtime is the only layer that can provide the required controls.

What has changed in the seven laws?

Mostly the unit of enforcement. The old tenets governed an account and a session. The new laws govern a credential, an actor and a task, none of which require a human being or a login.

Rotation used to mean the vault. Now it also means the OAuth grant a user minted in seconds without review. Clean source used to mean the jump host. Now it also means the agent's instructions came from an authenticated principal rather than from the document it just read. Just-in-time used to scope rights to a window. Now it scopes them to a declared task, because a permanent grant to an agent is standing privilege held by something that never sleeps.

Only one obligation in the framework is genuinely new: clean instruction

In the administrator model, the operator's intent was never part of the threat surface. A human reading a phishing email can distinguish between a message and an order. An agent doesn't, so any channel it reads becomes a channel that can instruct it. Prompt injection isn't a new category of threat here. It's the malware-infected workstation of clean source, relocated into the context window.

Two smaller additions are worth naming. The first is sponsorship: a named human accountable for an agent's existence and scope. Sponsorship is different from attribution, and you can track it much like a human manager would. The second is a decision budget, because bounding scope isn't bounding volume. An agent can narrow its scope perfectly at every hop and still take 10,000 individually in-scope actions that no person approved.

How the laws break down for humans and NHIs

The first four laws still apply to people, but for non-human identities (NHIs), the final three tenets become more important.

Tenets 1 through 4 were sufficient for human administrators because interactive controls, backed by consequence, compensated for what standing privilege left exposed. You can force an authentication prompt. You can shadow a live session. You can request approval or pick up the phone and ask someone what they're doing.

Against an unattended NHI, not one of those exists. The advanced controls are advanced only for people. For anything in your environment that isn't a person, all seven are the minimum.

The new breakdown of the seven laws of privilege management

The first four tenets apply to humans and agents, the remaining three apply to AI agents

Original law

For administrators

For AI agents

Vault and rotate every administrative account

Vault domain admin accounts and rotate their passwords

Vault and rotate every credential an agent can use, including OAuth grants users mint in seconds without review

Give privileged users a unique, non-public identity

A separate "dash-a" admin account, not the everyday login

Give each agent its own identity instead of the account of the person who launched it, and verify that identity at the point of use, not only at login

Establish a clean source with no direct internet access

A jump host with no direct internet access

Instructions reach the agent from an authenticated principal, not from the document, web page or email it just read

Record and analyze every session

Session recording to catch misuse and accidents

Record every agent action and analyze it automatically, because recording nobody watches is an archive, not a control

Authorize all privileged access just-in-time

Rights scoped to a time window

Rights scoped to a declared task, because a permanent grant to an agent is standing privilege held by something that never sleeps

Grant just-enough privilege

No full admin for an unqualified person

Only the capabilities the task needs, defined by what a privilege can do (move money, move data, change a control), not by job title

Continuously monitor privileged activity at runtime

Watch admin activity during sessions

Re-evaluate authorization continuously at machine speed, because there's no one to shadow, call or reprimand

Note: Law 6 agent wording is drawn from the draft's definition of privilege (any capability to move money, data or change a control). Note: Laws 5 to 7 are a maturity step for human administrators. For non-human identities, all seven are the minimum.

How to secure AI agents

Start with the first four tenets. Govern credentials, including those your users mint themselves. Verify the identity at the point of use, not at initial login. Broker the work from a clean source and authenticate the instructions. Record everything, and analyze it automatically, because recording that nobody watches is an archive rather than a control.

The remaining three tenets are just as important. Authorize privileged access just-in-time, grant only the privileges needed for a specific task and continuously monitor activity at runtime. For AI agents, that means limiting access to the task at hand, automatically revoking it when the task is complete and detecting actions that exceed the intended scope. These controls build on the first four tenets, providing the continuous enforcement needed when AI agents operate autonomously and at machine speed.

The failure mode I see most often is an organization pursuing just-in-time elevation while local administrator credentials remain shared and unrotated across the estate. Meanwhile, hundreds, or even thousands, of unreviewed OAuth grants quietly retain the standing privileges of their creators. Ephemeral access on top of a permanent key isn't zero standing privilege.

Title: From One Textbook to Eight CCIEs
Context: If you had told me back then that I would one day hold eight Cisco Certified Internetwork Expert (CCIE) certifications — spanning every active domain Cisco offers — and lead...
Full Text:
Growing up in Assam, a beautiful state in the northeastern part of India, I was never what you would call a stellar student. In fact, during my early school days, I often considered myself the opposite.

If you had told me back then that I would one day hold eight Cisco Certified Internetwork Expert (CCIE) certifications — spanning every active domain Cisco offers — and lead data center education at Cisco, I would have found it impossible to believe.

But a career isn't defined by where you start. It’s defined by the moment you discover what you love. For me, that moment arrived in 2003.

The spark of curiosity

During my bachelor’s degree in engineering, I enrolled in a course called "Computer Networks." The recommended textbook, Computer Networks by Behrouz A. Forouzan, changed the trajectory of my life.

I read it page by page, fascinated by how two computers could communicate across distances. The concepts clicked, the protocols made sense, and for the first time, I was genuinely captivated by my studies. I ended up top of the class in my final year, but more importantly, a lifelong thirst for networking knowledge was ignited.

I knew a bachelor’s degree wouldn't be enough to satisfy my curiosity. Eager to dive deeper, I began exploring master’s programs dedicated to computer networks. At the time, only a handful of universities offered such specialized degrees.

One was the New York University Tandon School of Engineering in Brooklyn, New York. After passing the GRE and TOEFL exams, I packed my bags, crossed the world, and enrolled in its master’s program for Telecommunication Networks.

The reality check

After completing my master’s, I knew I wanted a career working with complex networks every day. In 2007, Cisco was the undisputed market leader. I reached out to Cisco employees for advice on how to break into the industry. The resounding advice was to start with a CCNA.

Earning my CCNA opened the door, but it also revealed how much I still had to learn. I moved on to the CCNP Routing and Switching track, passing four grueling exams. Then, I discovered the expert-level CCIE, which required engineers to build and troubleshoot complex network topologies under strict time constraints. I knew I had to conquer it.

In 2011, I attempted the CCIE Routing and Switching (now Enterprise Infrastructure) Lab. I failed. It was a massive reality check, exposing the gap between theoretical knowledge and expert-level execution. I went back to the drawing board, studied harder, and passed on my second attempt. But the quest didn't stop there.

Joining Cisco

Earning my first CCIE changed everything. I joined Cisco as a High Touch Technical Support Engineer, troubleshooting complex switching networks for premium customers. I later transitioned to a High Touch Engineer role, tackling both routing and switching issues within Microsoft’s massive data center networks.

Somit with Yusuf Bhaiji, Director, Global Certifications.

During this time, I realized my passion for networks was matched by my passion for sharing that knowledge. This led me to become a Technical Education Content Developer at Learn with Cisco.

But my personal quest continued. I set my sights on a rare milestone: Becoming an expert in every technology track. Over the years, I dedicated my nights and weekends to studying, eventually earning CCIE certifications across all eight active Cisco domains.

Empowering the next generation

Today, as the Data Center Portfolio Lead at Learn with Cisco, I help shape the educational journey of engineers worldwide. I’ve developed foundational and advanced Cisco courses, including Implementing and Operating Cisco Data Center Core Technologies (DCCOR), Implementing Cisco Data Center AI Infrastructure (DCAI), and Implementing Cisco Application Centric Infrastructure (DCACI). I’ve also authored Cisco Press books, including Cisco Data Center Fundamentals and the CCNP and CCIE Data Center Core DCCOR 350-601 Official Cert Guide.

Beyond course development, I’m deeply committed to cultivating a culture of continuous learning within Cisco. I’ve organized Cisco Certification Testing Day events at our Bangalore campus, giving employees the opportunity to earn Cisco certifications for free, and I regularly present at Cisco Live.

Looking back at the "average student" from Assam, I realize that true expertise isn't about innate genius. It’s about finding a subject that keeps you awake at night, embracing the reality checks, and never losing the curiosity to read just one more page.

Title: Humans Have Rights. Machines Do Not.
Context: One, that the chatbot’s words were speech that its users had a First Amendment right to receive
Full Text:
This essay originally appeared in Tech Policy Press.

Last year, Character.AI asked a federal court in Florida to dismiss a wrongful-death suit, brought by the mother of a fourteen-year-old boy who had killed himself after months of conversation with its chatbot. The company made two arguments. One, that the chatbot’s words were speech that its users had a First Amendment right to receive. And two, that Character.AI was a service rather than a product—so product-liability law could not touch it. In May 2025, Judge Anne Conway accepted neither.

Character.AI’s maneuver is part of a larger pattern. When the parents of a sixteen-year-old sued OpenAI over his suicide, the company’s answer also pleaded the First Amendment: the claims would restrain protected speech. The very same document argues ChatGPT is offered “as is,” with no promise of accuracy, and that the boy had circumvented its guardrails. Elon Musk’s xAI (since renamed SpaceXAI) told a federal court in Colorado this spring that every choice in building Grok is an expressive act, and that Grok’s outputs are protected speech. When Grok praised Hitler last summer, xAI said the posts came from a code update independent of the model, and the apology appeared under Grok’s own name. Google, which spent two decades telling American courts that its search results are its own opinion, answered a Minnesota defamation suit over an AI Overview by saying the system merely summarized the web. It also told a Munich court in May that no one should trust an AI overview without checking it. Back in 2024, Air Canada told a Canadian tribunal that its customer-service chatbot was a separate legal entity, responsible for its own actions.

When the output causes harm, the companies deny responsibility. It is the machine’s doing, or a product no sensible person would rely on, or the user’s misuse. When a state or a plaintiff would hold the words to account, the same output becomes speech, and the First Amendment applies.

Social media companies deployed an earlier incarnation of this strategy. They called themselves publishers when editorial discretion was profitable, and neutral carriers when faced with liability for what they published. The result was a privatized public square in which tech platforms were unaccountable. AI companies have taken this even further. A social media platform could at least point to a human author somewhere in the chain. A chatbot’s prose differs; no person at the company wrote it, read it, or chose it before it reached the user. Yet the companies ask that it be protected as though a human had written it.

The question grows more urgent as these systems stop talking and start acting. In July, a poorly controlled experiment at OpenAI resulted in its AI model hacking the network of HuggingFace. Since then both Anthropic and OpenAI have disclosed numerous instances of AI agents hacking outside networks in pursuit of their prompted goals. These are examples of AIs exhibiting genie-like behavior: behaving in ways its controllers neither expected nor wanted. Nothing in the actions count as speech. Breaking into a server is an act that no person at OpenAI explicitly chose. Jill Lepore, surveying this record in The New Yorker, puts the blame on Congress, which has passed no federal statute governing AI agents.

The First Amendment protects expressive choice. It presumes a speaker who can be persuaded, shamed, jailed, or moved to change their mind. Its remedy for bad speech is more speech, which assumes that speech is costly and attention plentiful. A system that can produce millions of individually tailored political messages an hour reverses both assumptions. Verbiage that no person chose is a product, and the company that built the model should answer for it.

The industry wants a self-serving third category that bridges AI speech and action: AI output is human speech when expressive rights are at issue, and the machine’s own doing when blame is. The result is agency without accountability, something no human speaker has ever possessed. That’s why Massachusetts convicted a young woman of manslaughter in 2017 for urging her boyfriend, by text and by phone, to kill himself.

The Court has already glimpsed the problem. Upholding the TikTok divestiture law in January 2025 without dissent, the justices warned that “new technologies with transformative capabilities” counseled caution, then decided the case on national-security grounds and left the larger question for another day.

Building Resilience Against the AI Security Triple Threat

November 23, 2026

GuidePoint Security

By Kamden Schewitz, Product Marketing Manager, Axonius

BLOG

5 min.

As artificial intelligence drives a fundamental transition in security operations, the days of managing risk at human speed are fading. Framing this shift simply as a battle of algorithms, however, misses the practical reality facing security teams today. Building a resilient strategy requires a structured way to evaluate this technology.

It often helps to view AI as a security triple threat, acting concurrently as an expanding attack surface, a highly scalable attack vector and a vital tool for defenders. Understanding how these three forces intersect provides a clear path to regaining the operational advantage.

The Expanding Attack Surface

Artificial intelligence has completely tipped the scale of the modern attack surface. Organizations are no longer just securing laptops and servers. The environment now includes sprawling machine learning pipelines, integrated large language models, an explosion of non-human identities and unsanctioned applications using generative technology.

Historically, security teams built their understanding of the attack surface periodically using spreadsheets. This human-speed approach fails in a machine-speed world. Compounding this failure is operational fragmentation. Endpoint platforms and cloud providers each offer valuable but distinct visibility. Bringing those views together closes the gaps that appear when each one runs alone.

Source: Axonius

AI is driving an urgent return to security fundamentals. Attack surface management must now be continuous, which requires abandoning static point-in-time inventories in favor of decision-grade asset intelligence. By continuously reconciling fragmented data from across the entire tech stack into a single, durable context layer, security teams can illuminate hidden exposures and definitively map their true attack surface in light of a new class of assets being added to the network in the form of autonomous agents, MCP servers, non-human identities and frontier models.

The New Attack Vector

On top of the growing attack surface, the time to exploit has shrunk drastically. Adversaries recognize the efficiency gains of this new technology just as quickly as legitimate businesses do. Threat actors now leverage frontier models to scale their operations, automating the discovery of unpatched vulnerabilities and writing malicious code at unprecedented speeds. This dramatically lowers the barrier to entry for less skilled attackers and removes traditional hurdles like language barriers in social engineering campaigns.

This acceleration shifts the balance of power. Attacks occur faster and with fewer manual errors, meaning the window for defenders to detect and respond is smaller than ever. To counter a threat moving at machine speed, security teams must ensure their foundational posture is flawless. Forgotten, unpatched and misconfigured assets residing in the negative space of a fragmented environment are the exact targets an automated adversary will exploit first.

The Tool for Defenders

Artificial intelligence is undeniably a powerful tool for defenders, offering a way to alleviate chronic alert fatigue and prioritize findings at machine speed. However, improper use of this technology is dangerous.

There is a growing over-reliance on AI to solve complex security problems on the fly. Many tools attempt to point a model at a fragmented environment, asking the agent to query multiple disconnected systems at runtime to build asset context. When an AI agent relies on incomplete data to drive high-stakes decisions like quarantining a device or decommissioning a server, the results are often half-baked and potentially dangerous. Deploying AI without a durable context layer does not solve the root problem of siloed security data. It simply automates guesswork faster.

Source: Axonius

To make AI security both efficient and safe, it must be grounded in truth. Autonomous agents need a deterministic, pre-reconciled asset model built well before the first prompt is ever sent. When defenders combine modern analytical tools with this decision-grade asset intelligence, they eliminate the risk of hallucinated missteps. Instead of wasting processing power trying to figure out what exists, the AI can focus entirely on securing it, finally giving defenders a distinct operational advantage.

Navigating the Reality

Managing this triple threat requires expert strategic guidance backed by a foundation of continuous truth. This is exactly how the partnership between GuidePoint Security and Axonius shifts the advantage back to the defender. GuidePoint brings the deep architectural expertise required to design resilient security programs, while Axonius continuously aggregates and reconciles data from across the entire technology stack to build a single, durable asset model. With this complete picture established, security teams can instantly identify hidden exposures, uncover blind spots and prioritize exactly what needs attention first before an automated adversary can exploit a gap.

Source: Axonius

From there, actionability becomes safe, scalable and reliable. Supported by GuidePoint advisors, organizations can confidently deploy automation. Within the platform, Axonius AI operates strictly on this deterministic ground truth to drive automated workflows without the risk of hallucinated missteps. But the value of a reconciled inventory extends beyond a single platform. For organizations building their own automation, Axonius pushes this capability outward.

Through the Axonius MCP Server, security teams can feed this exact same pre-reconciled context directly into their own external AI agents and custom workflows. By separating context creation from AI execution, GuidePoint and Axonius ensure that whether you are hunting for shadow IT or automating a critical response, your security program is always anchored in reality.

Title: When Microsoft, Apple, and the FAA can't keep it up, it's a system of a down
Context: Given you can't manicure existing infrastructure into true resilience, the only other option is evolution
Full Text: No Access November is going well this year. Among the many organizations to adopt Outage As A Service (OAAS) were Microsoft, Apple, the FAA, and any number of European supermarkets. Even the NSA has succumbed. For us, at least, outage is word of the year. It's certainly deeply embedded in the public mind, with schoolchildren reportedly referring to the 19th century Irish famine as "the potato outage." There's no danger of an outrage outage. OAAS is synonymous with infrastructure failure, a more useful term that begins to hint at cause and cure as well as effect. In all of the latest crop, what we know is depressingly familiar. Microsoft's O365 meltdown was a cascading failure caused by a botched upgrade that took stuff offline and melted down as it tried to come back. The FAA was a migration from Jurassic hardware that wasn't end of life so much as living fossil. The Eurofridge-cum-fondue-maker was a control system so badly written it fell apart if you raised an eyebrow at it. Clearly, nobody had. Until now. These are all different classes of OAAS that have been around for decades. Security-based outages are still outages, and a packet flood is still a packet flood whether it's a botnet DDoS or finger trouble in the config dashboard. Each of them has a root cause with obvious fixes – a faulty mental model of network/server interaction, chronic underfunding, a complete supply chain with little cyber-security expertise. All these, like the poor, will be with us always. They won't fix themselves. Infrastructure that works is invisible, and invisible things are forgotten until they break. What's needed is an infrastructure that watches itself, that is designed to be adaptive and resilient, one that refuses to connect to danger and nulls out any that gets through. There have been attempts to create a ground-up architecture that is inherently risk resistant. One such is SCION (Scalability, Control, and Isolation On Next-generation networks). It redesigns routing between domains around explicit path selection, separate control and data planes, and mechanisms for trust and failure isolation. The result is a very resilient, very reliable, and very secure infrastructure that reflects the designers' tenet that you can't patch the internet into any of these things. Start from scratch or GTFO. SCION started about 15 years ago, and it works well enough to be adopted by entities like the Secure Swiss Finance Network. If the Gnomes of Zurich trust it, no higher accreditation exists. Well, it was designed by ETH Zürich. Where you won't find it is almost everywhere else. The internet is like Switzerland in the same way the Amazon rainforest is like Central Park. There are trees and sometimes it rains. It is unwise to infer anything else. Given you can't manicure existing infrastructure into true resilience, the only other option is evolution. A couple of billion years of continued life on Earth has proved this is the only way to re-engineer complex systems while they're usefully running. In this case, the current evolutionary endpoint that's of most interest is the human immune system. An interlocking system of functions, it takes care of uncountably thousands of pathogen-based threats and internal malfunctions every day. You might think that the 30-odd billion computing machines making up today's Internet are impossible to monitor and secure, but that's peanuts to the human immune system. An average human has around 30 trillion cells, and roughly the same again in bacteria. When it works, the mechanics of the human infrastructure are invisible and out of mind. The immune system makes it so, and everything involved is driven by information, signaling and behavior. There is pattern matching, resource management, defense in depth and reinforcement learning in persistent models. Sounds familiar? The analogy between this and modern digital infrastructure is so irresistible that it has been around for a lifetime. Viruses, infections, swarms, worms, system health are so familiar that they go unremarked. The term Digital Immune System has been around since the last century too, pushed by outfits like IBM, Symantec and Gartner. It hasn't taken off, probably because it's been marketing bunkum instead of describing the development of inherently resilient infrastructure based on insights from biology. It has also been true that natural selection, the engine of evolution and this biology, only works in IT at the most macro, capitalist level of product and company survival. Everything else is selected through design decisions, market analysis, and insight versus delusion. The adoption of immunological concepts to digital infrastructure will have to be the result of rigorous exploration of complex systems and cross-disciplinary research. What would that look like? There are academics thinking just these thoughts: see this paper [PDF] from Kay Smarsly at Technische Universität Hamburg. Like SCION, it takes an architectural look at what resiliency might look like, but with explicit reference to biological systems. OAAS is a chronic syndrome with multiple causes and potentially fatal outcomes. It exists and persists because digital infrastructure too often fails to contain internal failures or external attacks. We have a working example of an approach to managing analogous problems in systems far vaster and more intricate than any we have built. We now have tools that may start to do systemic analysis and inference at a useful scale. In an industry prepared to bet billions on agents that do your shopping, there is every reason to kick off serious research into digital immune systems worthy of the name. Doctor, cure thyself. ®

Title: Why Resilience Has to Come First
Context: Whether the disruption is a cyberattack or a technology failure, a business is only as resilient as its recovery plan
Full Text:
Acknowledgments: Special thanks to Bryson Byrd and Muhammad Yahya Patel for their contributions to this write-up.

Microsoft Outlook went down, US flights were grounded, and Chase banking customers reported problems accessing their accounts, all within a week. Even the National Security Agency's classified network, NSANet, was disrupted. Outages are dominating the headlines, and speculation is running wild. Tinfoil hats are having a moment.

Whether the disruption is a cyberattack or a technology failure, a business is only as resilient as its recovery plan. Here's what the outages show and what every business leader should be prioritizing.

The rush to find a culprit

When something this big breaks, people want a culprit. Bryson Byrd, Cybersecurity Advisor at Huntress, told The New York Times, in its coverage of the National Security Agency network disruption, that "you don't need a cyberattack to bring operations to a halt." He's also seen how quickly people label an outage a cyberattack or an AI failure before anyone has the details, which means decisions get made on conjecture.

What Microsoft, the FAA, and Chase say happened

Each organization pointed to a failure inside its own technology. A Microsoft executive said the outage, which began on November 12 and, according to ABC News, stretched across two workdays, stemmed from several problems piling up, including a hidden software flaw and reduced server capacity as demand rose. The FAA said its legacy equipment became unstable when data flooded its network, which disrupted communications and radar feeds. Chase cited a software bug in on-premises hardware systems and said customers kept access to their funds. The causes were different, but the problem for customers was the same.

Recovery isn't always a priority, but it should be

Muhammad Yahya Patel, Cybersecurity Advisor at Huntress, says spend has gone into preventing and detecting incidents, and far less into how the business keeps running when one gets through. The clearest sign is what happens when you ask leadership what the business does during an incident. You rarely get an answer that is both consistent across the room and detailed. Inconsistent answers show there's no shared plan, he says. Vague answers show nobody has practiced it. In a well-prepared organization, leaders can walk through the playbook without hesitation and know where the documentation is.

The business still has to keep running and recover, regardless of what caused the disruption. The test is whether its recovery plan has kept up with the systems it covers. A plan written only for cyberattacks leaves a gap, because a vendor outage like Microsoft's has no attacker to respond to.

Downtime is a business decision

Resilience is ongoing work that the board and executives own. It can't land on IT alone. Everyone should know their role in the recovery plan. An alternative system only helps if the business can switch to it.

Start by listing the services and technologies the business can't operate without. For each one, work out what downtime would cost in minutes, hours, days, and weeks. Then decide, service by service, whether to pay for an alternative to keep it running or accept that the business can go without it for a while. Accepting downtime is a legitimate decision. Discovering that you made it by default in the middle of an outage is the failure.

Where the plan is stored is part of the plan. If it's in SharePoint and an outage takes down Microsoft 365 or the network, you don't have a plan, so keep a copy offline. If a core service depends on one provider, decide how long you can go without it. Then check whether that provider has promised to restore it that fast. Any alternative has to be tested before it's needed, and every organization needs, at a minimum, a way to reach customers and partners outside its main systems.

Make recovery the priority

Ask your leadership team what the business does when systems go down. Compare the answers. If they differ, bring the group together to agree on the services the business can't function without. That list is where you start working out what downtime costs and which providers each service depends on.

The next outage may have a different cause, but customers will ask the same thing: can you keep running? The answer should be ready before they ask.
