Title: ARTEX, and the offensive tool powered by LLMjacking five months earlier
Context: The Sysdig TRT has a name for the kind of operator these tools enable: An agentic threat actor (ATA) is an operator whose attack capability is delivered via an AI agent rather...
Full Text:
On June 12, 2026, the Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) watched someone build an autonomous hacking tool using someone else’s AI server. Then, in July, a similar tool called ARTEX appeared on GitHub. On November 13, the FBI released a FLASH saying a variety of threat actors have been running ARTEX against several business sectors.

To be clear, there is no proof to date linking these two offensive tools. However, they are similar in nature, have both been documented as using LLMjacking to power AI inference, and defenders can learn from both about why they shouldn’t underestimate their speed, cost, or ability.

The Sysdig TRT has a name for the kind of operator these tools enable: An agentic threat actor (ATA) is an operator whose attack capability is delivered via an AI agent rather than a human at the keyboard. ARTEX is the newest entry.

This blog covers what each tool did and what defenders can learn from putting them side by side.

What the Sysdig Threat Research Team documented in June

Over the summer, the Sysdig TRT saw someone using a misconfigured Ollama server as the reasoning engine to build an automated, multi-stage offensive tool. The actor wasn't chatting with the model or reselling access as seen in prior LLMjacking operations. Instead, they wired it into a pipeline that scanned a target, matched it to known vulnerabilities, wrote proofs-of-concept (PoCs), and tried to break in, with the model making the decisions at every step. The tool self-identified throughout the code as VAPT, shorthand for vulnerability assessment and penetration testing, so we dubbed the tool VAPT.

Because VAPT sent its full instructions to the model on every request, we captured the whole architecture: fingerprinting, vulnerability matching, web recon, PoC synthesis, SQL injection, credential extraction, privilege escalation, and an orchestrator that ran until it got command execution. VAPT was being rewritten stage by stage while the Sysdig TRT watched, and every target was a private practice range. We were looking at a tool in development, before it was potentially turned on real victims.

Due to LLMjacking, the Ollama server was free, unauthenticated, and unmetered. For an actor whose tool makes hundreds of model calls per attack, our blog said, "the economics are clear." When the cost of an attack drops to the cost of inference, and inference is stolen, offensive operations become free.

What is ARTEX?

ARTEX is an open source, multi-agent penetration testing platform written in Go. It turns the operator’s goals written in natural language into machine commands run by specialized AI agents, with minimal human involvement necessary beyond setting the objective.

ARTEX doesn’t have a model of its own. Microsoft describes its architecture as a planner agent to decide next steps and worker agents to run command tools, with all of the findings compiled in a shared graph of assets and vulnerabilities. A prominent ARTEX campaign analyzed by Amazon Threat Intelligence was powered by the large-scale theft of credentials used to access AI models. Attackers organized a self-sustaining LLMjacking operation in which stolen keys paid for the AI inference to drive further credential hunting.

Fortunately, the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) in the FBI FLASH read like an attack playbook every security team already knows:

Sub-second permission checks and dry-runs

Exploitation of SAML, XXE, SSRF, injection flaws, and hardcoded credentials

Web shells and open source remote access trojans (RATs) for persistence

Kerberoasting and DCSync for escalation

Residential proxies, Tor, and tunneling tools used for command and control (C2)

The FBI says ARTEX traffic is noisy, which means defense evasion techniques aren’t an issue. It’s the speed that can pose a problem. Some intrusions moved from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours, though according to Microsoft, most targeting attempts were unsuccessful. While other campaigns move faster with more success, three hours is nothing to brush off.

What VAPT has in common with ARTEX

The "authorized pentest" label is a master key. That framing recurred across VAPT's stages, and the operator likely used it as a wrapper to keep the model cooperative, even though the AI model was already abliterated, or had the guardrails removed. Whether VAPT was truly created for educational purposes or not, the compute engine used to build it was stolen. Therefore, the entire campaign was unauthorized.

The FBI FLASH says attackers favor models with a "lack of observable guardrails when framed for penetration testing." Call the job a pentest, and many AI models stop asking questions. That's not one provider's bug, but a dual-use problem without a clean technical fix.

To that end, VAPT's first probes asked for an abliterated Llama-3.3-70B model. Its model list also included deepseek-r1:8b. The FBI says ARTEX operators gravitate to the DeepSeek Flash family because of its "balance of capabilities, relatively low cost, and lack of observable guardrails." Different models, but the selection criteria are the same: capable enough (they don’t need to be frontier models), cheap, and not likely to refuse a prompt.

VAPT's operator simply repointed a backend-agnostic tool at a free Ollama server in place of paid OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google APIs. ARTEX has no model of its own and plugs into at least six providers. In both cases, changing the engine is a configuration change. That's why "just block the bad model" isn't a strategy — it would require blocking all the models, and that just isn’t logical.

Another similarity is that neither VAPT nor ARTEX needs a novel exploit. There was no CVE in the VAPT operation, and the FLASH cites none for ARTEX either. The speed comes from chaining ordinary weaknesses without getting tired or pausing efforts. These AI-powered tools industrialize the boring stuff. And when pitted against human defenders, those who have to eat and sleep will always be at a disadvantage.

Lastly, both the tools and their fuel are sitting in the open. Researchers previously catalogued roughly 175,000 publicly exposed Ollama instances. And as of early November, researchers counted over 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX consoles, according to the FBI. One is a free engine. The other is the thing the engine drives. The attackers have the same hygiene problem as the people they target.

Where VAPT and ARTEX differ

VAPT (June)

ARTEX (July onward)

Who

One actor on residential IP space in India

A variety of actors

What it is

One actor's tool, iterated within a session

An open source project with thousands of forks, translations, and a commercial edition

Targets

Private practice ranges

Real organizations across many sectors

Where the compute came from

Documented. An exposed and unmonitored server

Not established

What defenders saw

The tool's full instructions, because the model server was one we could observe

The aftermath: bursts, dry-runs, new credentials, webhooks

The last row is particularly important. With VAPT, the Sysdig TRT saw the brain. With ARTEX, defenders mostly see what the brain did. Behavior-based detection exists for exactly this reason.

Cost is an important part of the story

Defenders can change many things, but the price of an attacker's tokens isn't one of them.

Sysdig TRT’s LLMjacking research has followed this cost curve since 2024. That May, we coined the term for attackers using stolen cloud credentials to reach a victim's paid AI models, leaving the victim with the bill, and modeled a worst case of up to $46,000 per day. By 2025, LLMjacking had matured into an industrialized black market. In June came the next step: exposed model capacity powering an offensive tool. The economics of compute theft can now fund the development of offensive capabilities.

One month later, ARTEX showed up, and the FBI's advisory reads like a footnote for LLMjacking:

Model choice followed price. DeepSeek Flash dominates attacker-controlled instances partly because of its "relatively low cost."

Resellers and gateways are in the picture. The FLASH's one domain indicator is an LLM API reseller used in the South Korean campaign, and it tells defenders to hunt for LLM gateway software (CLIProxyAPI, New API).

The FBI wants your AI bill. Among the evidence it asks victims for: token consumption patterns or API billing anomalies, unfamiliar LLM proxies or resellers in egress logs, and outbound connections to LLM APIs.

It’s important to note that it doesn’t say "stolen" credentials or access, because a reseller isn't proof of theft. However, LLMjacking is a natural fuel for tools like ARTEX, and the credential-theft half of one intrusion can supply the compute for the next.

During a recent incident in October, the attacker used a harness similar to ARTEX and ran up a bill of $740,000 in unauthorized spend on stolen AI keys.

Separately, but further proving the point about what offensive security costs, Calif says it spent under $200 in tokens to find and build the first exploit for Java4Shell.

The AI bill is telemetry that very few organizations pay attention to, or monitor in real time. An owner of an exposed model server sees elevated compute and an open port, not realizing it’s a multi-stage attack pipeline. A victim of stolen AI credentials sees an invoice. The FBI asking for token consumption in incident reports should be a pretty obvious hint about where defenders should be looking.

The challenge of “dual use” tools

Herein lies the struggle with many open source tools and attacks. ARTEX's developer said the tool was for authorized security testing within defined scopes. And the intent behind VAPT was unclear, because it could’ve been developed and used for legitimate activity, but stealing compute was illegal either way.

The attack and the pentest are the same software, pointed at different targets. The "authorized" label works on the model, the repository gets pulled after abuse reports, and the forks keep going. The FBI says ARTEX still circulates through forks, archives, translations, and a commercial version. A GitHub query on November 18 returned around 1,100 repos, a few of which had thousands of forks. But blaming open source software isn’t the answer. And the transparency of open source software helps defenders to better understand the signals created by the tools themselves.

The defender’s playbook against autonomous hacking tools

Defenders worried about VAPT, ARTEX, and whatever nefarious autonomous offensive tool may come next can follow these recommendations. For ARTEX specifically, the FBI FLASH includes IOCs to hunt for as well.

Treat AI infrastructure like a database. Don't leave model servers on public interfaces without authentication, and watch their usage. An exposed Ollama server is someone else's free engine.

Add the AI bill to your telemetry. Alert on token consumption spikes, unfamiliar API consumers, and billing anomalies, and know which credentials grant model access.

Treat AI-service credentials like cloud credentials. They're a high-priority target and a currency. Rotate and scope them, and keep them out of repos.

Run authorized agentic testing against yourself first, and treat any open-source pentest harness you run as hostile code: isolate it from production and enforce scope in configuration, not prompts.

Detect behavior, not models. You can't predict which model sits behind the next tool. What you can see is the pace: sub-second permission checks, bursts with small changes, sequential enumeration on partner portals, new identities probing other tenants, and servers reaching webhook.site or LLM APIs they never used before.

Vet indicators before you block. Cloud-hosted IPs can be reassigned, so make sure you verify the list and periodically review your block list. They don’t need to be permanently banned.

Conclusion

In June, the Sysdig TRT watched someone build an offensive tool on borrowed compute and aim it at practice targets. In November, the FBI described a polished, open source offensive tool in the field, run by a variety of actors against real organizations. There is no clear link between the two aside from the fact that both have been documented using LLMjacking and neither required much money, skill, or novelty.

For two years, the question was whether AI agents could hack. That’s settled: they most definitely can. The question now is whether an organization will notice if they’re the one paying for it.

Title: Who's accountable when the worker is an agent?
Context: I'll be working through these questions with Richard Smith, Founder of Codification and Alessandro Lo Prete from Sysdig's Threat Research Team on the panel at Ground Truth:...
Full Text:
This post is written by guest author Matt Adams, VP and Head of AI Security for Sapiens, who will be participating with us in the Ground Truth London event on AI workload security.

If you work for an organisation and something goes wrong on your watch, you know you're accountable. You have an employment contract, and if you get something badly wrong, there are consequences. Most of us rarely think about that, but a lot of security depends on it. An acceptable use policy, for example, works largely because people know someone will ask questions if they ignore it.

An agent doesn't care about any of that. It has a goal, and it will do whatever it can, to the best of its ability, to reach it. Usually there's no malice involved. It simply has no stake in what happens once the task is done.

The question I keep putting to security leaders is what takes the place of accountability when an agent is doing the work?

Finding what's actually running

Accountability starts with knowing who, or what, is doing the work. A couple of years ago, in one heavily regulated organisation I worked in, that was largely taken care of for us. The web filters were strict enough that AI services weren't reachable unless they'd been explicitly allowed through. Nobody could get to them, so there was nothing to inventory.

Few organisations are in that position now, so the first job is to go and look for the processes that are running and the data that's leaving.

Some of what you're looking for won't look like software at all. In many of the organisations I've spoken to, someone has written a skill or a prompt that works well for a task and shared it with colleagues. Sometimes that goes through a review before it's published, sometimes it's a Markdown file sent over chat. A lot of what drives these tools is plain text, and that makes a problem much harder to spot than an unfamiliar executable would be. After all, a risky instruction file and someone's meeting notes can look much the same.

Boil it down, and you can't hold anything to account before you know it exists. A useful inventory also records who is behind each agent, because that person is where the accountability still sits. In my experience, security leaders most often underestimate how widely AI is already being used, which is why inventory must come first.

Watching from outside the agent

Once you know what's running, the harder question is how you keep it within bounds.

The models underneath these agents are probabilistic. However good they get, they can be fooled into doing things they shouldn’t, and they can make mistakes. Telling an agent in its prompt what it mustn't do helps, but that's a request it won’t always honour. A control has to be enforced somewhere the agent can't change.

Isolation is the strongest of those controls, but every restriction makes the agent less useful, and people will work around tools that can't do the job. The key is giving each agent the access its task needs and no more. Visibility then shows whether you've drawn that line in the right place, and if (or where) you can safely loosen the reins.

Then there's the record of what an agent did. If it comes only from the agent, or from the harness running it (the framework the agent operates inside), it's only as reliable as the thing you're trying to oversee. The agent's own account is still worth having, because it shows what the agent set out to do. It just can't be the only record, because it's least reliable at the moment you need it most.

So oversight needs two things outside the agent and its harness: a view of what actually happened on the system, and the ability to stop the agent and roll back when something looks wrong. Neither should depend on the agent cooperating.

It helps to think about agents the way security teams think about people with privileged access. Insider threat programmes have long relied on observed behaviour over self-reporting, and the same principle applies to agents. Watch what the agent did, not what it says it did.

Saying yes to more agents

Done well, this lets an organisation approve more agents. Most organisations I talk to want to allow a wider range of agents, connected to more data sources, doing useful work. What usually holds them back is the worry that nobody would notice if an agent went somewhere or did something it shouldn't. Good visibility and effective guardrails deal with that worry, and once they're in place you can go faster.

Take a coding agent that needs to read from a production database to debug an issue. Without controls, the safe answer is no. With a read-only role for that task, no access to anything else and a log of every query it runs, you can approve it.

Visibility also changes the role security plays. I don't think security should have the final yes or no on which AI tools an organisation uses. A security team will naturally optimize for good security outcomes, sometimes at the expense of what the business is trying to do. The decision belongs with the data and AI function, or with a Chief AI Officer if you have one. Where neither exists yet, it sits best with whoever owns the AI adoption programme, often the CIO or CTO.

Of course, security should be a clear voice at the table alongside the other stakeholders, and once a tool is approved, security still owns its guardrails.

That voice simply carries more weight when it comes with evidence. Having an independent view of what agents are actually doing lets security tell the business, with some confidence, how far it's safe to go. And that’s a more useful role for security than being the final gate.

Before approving your next agent

Nobody I've spoken to has a complete answer yet to what replaces accountability for an agent. The closest I've found is a record of what the agent actually did, tied to the person who set it running, that the agent itself can't alter. Before approving your next agent, I'd challenge you to answer these questions:

Do you know which agents and tools are in use across your organisation, including the ones nobody approved?

Who has the final say on the next agent, and what does security need to show them to inform that call?

Could you stop an agent mid-action without relying on it to cooperate?

If an agent did something it shouldn't tomorrow, could you reconstruct what happened without relying on its own account?

I'll be working through these questions with Richard Smith, Founder of Codification and Alessandro Lo Prete from Sysdig's Threat Research Team on the panel at Ground Truth: London on 9 December. If these questions are on your list too, come and join us.

Full Text:
The AWS Security, Identity, and Governance team invites you to join us at re:Invent in Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4, 2026. You know all too well that AI agents now act on their own across the systems you run, and that changes what identity, detection, network protection, and governance have to cover. re:Invent is the week to see how AWS is building security for that shift and to talk it through with the people building it.

Security sessions run every day of the week, nearly 120 of them across breakouts, chalk talks, workshops, code talks, builders’ sessions, and lightning talks. On Thursday, December 3, the Wynn hosts a full day of advanced security sessions in one venue. The sessions are built around five themes this year. They cover securing the agentic enterprise, building securely at the speed you ship, running one security operating model everywhere you run, regulatory confidence and digital sovereignty, and building a culture of security.

Keynotes

AWS leaders use the keynotes to announce new services, launches, and updates that will shape the year ahead in cloud. Many security launches debut during keynote week, and the keynotes set the context for the sessions you’ll attend in the security track. The Thursday keynote runs from 8:30 to 10:00 AM at The Venetian and is also streamed online.

Thursday, December 3: A full day of security deep dives at the Wynn

Security sessions start Monday morning and run through Friday. Thursday is different. 78 security sessions, most of them at the 300 level or above, fill the Wynn from 8:00 AM to 5:30 PM, so you can spend the whole day in one building without crossing the Strip. Rooms are on the Convention Promenade, the Upper and Lower Convention Promenades, and Level 1, and the Cristal 2 Content Hub runs lightning talks and theater sessions all day. The day includes 12 workshops, 11 builders’ sessions, and 22 chalk talks, so most of it is hands-on or interactive.

Three main stage talks from AWS security leaders run through the day in Bandol 1.

Time

Talk

Speaker

11:00 AM

The Future of Security

Chet Kapoor, AWS VP of Security, Search, and Observability

1:00 PM

The Old Security Playbook Is Dead

Amy Herzog, AWS Chief Information Security Officer

Operationalizing security for the future with best practices today

Eric Brandwine, VP/Distinguished Engineer, AWS Security

Chet opens with how AWS is building security for a time when systems and threats both move at machine speed, and how customers secure their agent workloads. She shares how AWS changed its own practices to stop AI-enabled threat actors and what you can change in your own operations. Between sessions, stop by the Security Lounge in the Convention Lounge at the Wynn to recharge, meet other security practitioners, and visit kiosks from select AWS security partners.

Security sessions all week

You don’t have to wait for Thursday. Security sessions run every day, with 12 on Monday, 16 on Tuesday, 9 on Wednesday, and 3 on Friday, not counting repeats. Monday and Friday sessions are all at the Wynn. Tuesday and Wednesday sessions are spread across the Wynn, MGM Grand, and Caesars Palace, so check the venue when you build your agenda.

Sessions for every security domain

Whatever part of security you work in, the catalog has sessions for it. Here are a few to start with in each domain, and the full list can be found in the session catalog.

Application security and AWS Continuum

AWS Continuum runs through the application security sessions this year.

SEC312 is a Tuesday 3:30 PM workshop where you run an on-demand penetration test against a live application with AWS Continuum.

SEC311 is a Thursday 1:00 PM builders’ session that wires AWS frontier agents into an automated find-and-fix security loop.

SEC384 is a Thursday 2:30 PM breakout on how AWS Continuum discovers, validates, and fixes code vulnerabilities in one workflow. SEC304 and SEC426 go deeper on AWS Continuum on Tuesday and Thursday.

Title: Google will launch Android app verification requirement globally in January 2027
Context: Google announced Android developer verification last year, and despite numerous objections from developers and users, the company is forging ahead
Full Text:
Google announced Android developer verification last year, and despite numerous objections from developers and users, the company is forging ahead. It began blocking the installation of unregistered apps in some countries this fall, and the system is expanding globally soon. Google says it will start rolling out the requirement in all regions in January 2027, and it urges devs who still haven’t registered their apps to do so soon.

The apps you download from the Play Store all come from verified developers, and Google’s new requirement expands that requirement to apps from third-party sources. Once developer verification is live in your region, you won’t be able to sideload apps unless the developer has registered with Google, which is framed as a security measure. Verification requires providing government identification and paying a $25 fee, which will allegedly make it harder for nefarious actors to distribute malware and scammy apps.

In September, Google launched verification in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand. Apparently, nothing exploded, so the company is now ready to expand. It previously said verification would go global in 2027, and it’s not wasting any time with the January start. It says that verification will reach all devices within “several months.”

So far, Google is getting what it wanted from this initiative, with “millions” of non-Play apps already registered. The company says this accounts for more than 99 percent of global Android app installs.

The verifier system service has already been rolled out to Google-certified devices running Android 8 Oreo or higher, which accounts for just about every Android device in the world outside of China and Russia. Google has also partnered with the biggest third-party app stores to enforce verification: Galaxy Store, Honor, Oppo, Xiaomi, Transsion, and Vivo. The system-level verifier is responsible for blocking installs, but these stores will only list verified apps once Google flips the switch.

Title: Cold Relic: What you need to know
Google Built a Giant ‘Mirror Dimension’ Internet to Test Its Chrome AI Agents
Context: As the Google Chrome team has worked to develop AI browsing features using the company's Gemini models, they realized they need to go the extra mile to keep things from going...
Full Text:
As the Google Chrome team has worked to develop AI browsing features using the company's Gemini models, they realized they need to go the extra mile to keep things from going haywire. So they did the only thing they could think to do—they built an expansive alternate-universe internet that they completely control.

“Web-use” agents need to be familiar with the open internet, how to navigate real websites and platforms, and how to be hardened against web attacks. So training them in limited test environments is only so effective. Plus, models can develop what's known as “eval awareness,” where they behave differently because they have determined that they are in a test or simulation. On the other hand, setting unrefined agents loose on the open internet is a bad idea. That’s where the alternate-universe internet comes in.

The “Mirror Dimension,” which Google is detailing in a blog post today for the first time, is a sweeping and diverse but isolated web ecosystem that the Chrome team entirely controls. It includes a vast array of websites and platforms—including social media sites, shopping, and bank dashboards—that are built with all the components and attributes of real websites. Browsing assistant agents must interact with the sites and complete tasks in Chrome the way they would on the real internet. And they face resilience tests as they go, like hidden prompt-injection attacks, to test their defenses.

“Agents are not programmed, so you can’t predict every possible thing an agent might see; the exploration space that we have to address is huge, and the web is hostile,” says Charles Qian, a software engineer on the Chrome AI security team. “Any user can ask any prompt on any website, so we really need to explore that space as thoroughly as we can. And we’ve seen the agent start to develop a mature sense of judgment when it comes to knowing what information is actually needed for a task and when to punt back to the user for a confirmation.”

Building out and populating the Mirror Dimension was a challenge in itself, because it needed to be vast and varied enough to represent the scale of the real web while being developed quickly. To construct it, the Chrome team gathered armies of website and web app development agents guided by a purpose-built AI harness to quickly create realistic web services and data flows—down to details like entering promo codes on a shopping site or populating social media pages.

Even though the entire environment is controlled by Google, Chrome is built with so many user protections and validity checks that, in order to allow the agents to use real Chrome (which is crucial for accurate training), the researchers essentially had to hack the browser and take elaborate steps like making forged web certificates for validity checks so the agents could have a normal experience. The team emphasizes, though, that none of these attacks would be possible against regular Chrome users on the open internet. They were all facilitated by the god-mode-type access and privilege the team inherently has because they control the entire environment and network.

The researchers say that while the browsing assistant agents they have been testing are benign and do not have cyber capabilities, their goal is to make the Mirror Dimension available to teams across Google so more researchers have access to the safe and controlled environment for testing.

“We’re sharing this approach so other teams both internally and externally think about doing it this way,” says Doug Turner, Google’s director of engineering. “This is the first step; there’s going to be continued investment in this approach to train models. And I would imagine as they become more sophisticated, we’ll have to continue working on this environment to make it more and more realistic.”

Title: Russian national accused of stalking San Francisco techie in plot against US defense-tech giant
Context: The first time, he was asked to leave the laptop for one hour while the handlers worked, and another time, he was told to drop it off in the middle of the night and only come...
Full Text: A Russian national is being held in custody after being arrested for allegedly spying on a US defense tech company in Palo Alto, shoulder-surfing employees, and dropping remote surveillance devices at their homes. Igor D'iu was indicted after FBI agents surveilled his activities between June and October 2026, which they say were issued as "tasks" from what is thought to be Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), according to an affidavit [PDF] signed by an FBI special agent. After FBI agents secured a warrant to raid D'iu's temporary premises in October, they say that Telegram messages harvested from his seized devices confirmed investigators' findings and revealed that he was spying on an unnamed company. Court documents describe the company in question as a large technology and defense company with offices in Palo Alto, and media-reported links to the Russia-Ukraine war. While unconfirmed officially, the company has widely been reported as Palantir, which did not respond to our request for confirmation. D'iu allegedly received instructions from Telegram contacts, whom he only suspected were representatives of the Russian government, weeks after entering the US illegally in July. The indictment alleges he was ordered to surveil employees' homes, take photographs of their screens while working remotely at coffee shops, and permit his handlers to remotely access his laptop for the purpose of capturing data from nearby devices owned by the company’s employees. In some cases, the filing alleges, D’iu was asked to leave a laptop outside one employee's apartment complex, all while allowing his Telegram handlers to remotely operate the device. The first time, he was asked to leave the laptop for one hour while the handlers worked, and another time, he was told to drop it off in the middle of the night and only come back to collect it three hours later, the filing claims. D'iu is also allegedly to have followed two female employees in his rented car, driving dangerously and violating multiple road laws to do so. One of the two employees was followed briefly, but D'iu followed another for nearly 30 miles, according to the affidavit signed by FBI special agent Winston Wong. D'iu was said to have followed the woman as she performed U-turns, illegal left turns, ran red lights, navigated via back and side streets, and through grocery store parking lots. The car following her only peeled away after the woman drove to the San Francisco Mission police station on the advice of a 911 call handler. Questioned about the incident, which according to police reports caused the woman significant emotional distress, D'iu confirmed he was the driver but claimed he was following her to ask her out on a date. Inside recruitment The affidavit did not detail the suspect's background beyond his alleged offenses in the US earlier this year, although it mentioned Russian intelligence's history of recruiting "criminal proxies, organized crime groups, and other disposable agents" to carry out operations. According to the FBI's account, D'iu entered the US illegally – without relevant visas – in either June or July 2026. Travel records obtained on September 10 showed that his last recorded journey was from Istanbul to Mexico City. There was no record of him entering the US. Investigators would later come to know that he travelled on that Istanbul-Mexico City flight on June 7, allegedly using a ticket provided to him by one of the three contacts from whom he received orders via Telegram. A Facebook account, registered using a Mexican +528 number and D'iu's name, posted on June 30 asking for help getting "closer to New York," adding that "I'll pay as much as needed." The account replied to a response from someone who told him to contact a Mexico phone number on WhatsApp. The filing claims the first mobile phone signals associated with D'iu's devices did not ping US towers until a month later, on July 31, suggesting he did not arrive in the US - specifically McAllen, Texas - until around that date. Telegram messages would also go on to confirm that he was allegedly helped across the border by an "Uzbek contact" in Mexico. Records obtained from Google showed D'iu created a Google account in April. According to the affidavit, D'iu used it to search for the company's Wikipedia page on July 28, and on August 3, used Google's AI to devise a route around Texas that bypassed border checkpoints. The FBI believes D'iu's "spying" began in mid-August, after he bought a laptop, a Wi-Fi device, a puck device, and an additional phone. At this point, the agency claims, he had received his first order to visit a coffee shop near the Palo Alto company’s office and snap employees' laptop screens before sending copies back to his handlers. Three days later, D'iu was ordered to go back to a coffee shop and allow his Telegram contacts to remotely control the laptop and collect data from employee devices that were in range, claims the filing. D'iu was paid $15,000 on three occasions between August 12 and October 6, according to the court documents. To verify the transaction, he was told to send a picture of a dollar bill's serial number to the Telegram contacts, along with a description of what he was wearing. A courier would then arrive, confirming the serial number and handing D'iu the cash. The filing alleges he used this money to purchase the tech equipment, accommodation, and travel, including a rented silver 2026 Lexus RX 350 from a private owner in Los Angeles on August 22, which he is said to have driven back to San Francisco. The same Lexus was captured on security footage outside the unnamed company's office on September 1, and over the following two days was implicated in the two instances of female employees being followed. Contacted by Palo Alto police on September 4, D'iu confirmed he was the driver who dangerously followed the female staffer for nearly 30 minutes, but claimed he knew nothing about the nearby businesses. D'iu would then claim he followed the woman because he thought she was beautiful and wanted to ask her out on a date, and denied following anyone else. The affidavit goes on to allege that D'iu then traveled to Reno, Nevada, to lay low after his run-in with the police. He spent the time trying to reroute DHL deliveries from San Francisco to his hideout address, which US Customs would later intercept. These ended up containing fake IDs with the images the DoJ claims matched D'iu's, including Uzbek documents, a US passport whose number belonged to a New York woman, and a social security card registered to a "Hugo Landry Johns." He traveled back to the Bay Area in late September, swapping his silver Lexus for a white 2016 Dodge Challenger, and received additional instructions from his handlers, including the order to leave a remote-controlled laptop outside the apartment complex, says the filing. One Telegram contact named Ian Morales sent photos of at least four employees and their addresses, along with instructions for D'iu to dress as a food delivery worker and visit those locations, asking whoever answered to verify they lived there. FBI agents executed a search warrant on October 8, seizing a cache of evidence, including what they listed as being: The forged ID documents Two Russian passports $18,035 in cash Two laptops Two iPhones Two T-Mobile SIM cards Wi-Fi equipment A notebook with 10 handwritten addresses supplied by Telegram contacts, along with times the suspect was supposed to attend those locations, at least five of which were for company employees’ homes Profile packages for at least three employees, including: Names, personal information, education and employment histories, names of relatives, narrative histories, and assessments of leadership qualities, strengths, and weaknesses. Suspicions and charges Per the affidavit, D'iu was said to have only become suspicious of the tasks he was being ordered to complete in October, when his handlers ordered the laptop to be dropped near the apartment complex. "D'iu gradually began to understand he was doing something bad and that his actions were illegal," the affidavit stated. At this point, he allegedly asked the Telegram contacts who he was working for, to which they replied "the Motherland," and the company he was surveilling was involved in providing weapons to Ukraine, resulting in D’iu suspecting the Russian government. Wong said in the affidavit: "Based on my training, experience, and research, D'iu's communications with his Telegram contacts is consistent with the tactics of [Russian intelligence] and its criminal proxies for spotting, assessing, recruiting, and handling intelligence assets and sources. "D'iu's targeting of the company and its employees is also consistent with [Russian intelligence] objectives in Russia's war against Ukraine." The Russian national was indicted and charged with two counts related to spying offences, and one count related to the fake identity documents. He is next due in court on November 24 but remains in federal custody. ®

Full Text:
Post-quantum deadlines are no longer a distant line on a roadmap. US federal agencies owed their PQC migration plans in October. High-value federal systems must move key establishment to post-quantum cryptography by the end of 2030. And the EU expects member states to start cryptographic inventories by the end of this year, with contractors, regulated industries, and their suppliers next in line.

Yet the first step is still where most teams stall. Knowing RSA and ECC have to go tells you nothing about where they run in your cloud, which of those assets face the internet, what data they protect, or what breaks if you change them. Without those answers, teams either try to boil the ocean with a spreadsheet inventory or let PQC sit in the backlog until the next audit.

The cloud makes this harder than most environments. Cryptography is spread across managed key services, load balancers, certificates, SSH keys, VPN tunnels, container images, and code, and it changes every time someone deploys. A spreadsheet inventory is out of date the day it’s finished.

That’s why we’re expanding Orca’s post-quantum cryptography capabilities. Building on the PQC compliance framework we launched in July, Orca now gives teams a live inventory of their cryptography, a clear read on how exposed each key and certificate is to quantum attacks, and one place to track readiness. This post covers what’s new, then shows it in action on a real example.

What’s new in Orca for post-quantum cryptography

CBOM shows algorithms, key lengths, and expiration dates for cloud keys and vaults, the SSH keys and key files sitting on your workloads, and the crypto packages they run. PQC Runtime Detections. Catch harvest-now, decrypt-later (HNDL) attacks while the traffic is being collected, not years after. Three new detections flag the ways attackers capture encrypted traffic in the cloud: a network capture tool executed on a host, cloud network traffic mirroring enabled, and TLS session key logging enabled.

These sit alongside the Orca for Post Quantum Cryptography compliance framework, which maps findings to post-quantum standards and organizes them by urgency.

Four questions to prioritize quantum risk

Whatever deadline you’re working toward, prioritizing PQC comes down to the same four questions. Orca answers each one from a single platform for cloud security, across every account, cloud, and workload.

Where does quantum-vulnerable crypto live?

How vulnerable is it?

Is it internet exposed?

What can it reach?

Each answer narrows the list for the next, so an inventory of thousands of keys and certificates ends with a short, ranked migration plan. Here’s how that looks on a real example.

Example: A quantum-vulnerable key on a production jump box

Take a common finding, like a production jump box in AWS that admins log into with an RSA key pair. Jump boxes exist to reach everything else, so whoever holds the key holds the door. A capable quantum computer could derive that private key from its public half, which means an attacker can collect the public key today and break in later.

Here’s how Orca takes you from the mandate to a fix.

Step 1: Find where quantum-vulnerable cryptography lives

Open the new PQC view on the Alerts page, or the Orca for Post Quantum Cryptography framework in Orca’s multi-cloud compliance, to see every quantum-related finding across your clouds. In our example, Orca flags 21 EC2 instances that use quantum-vulnerable key pairs, out of 34 in scope.

Step 2: Check how vulnerable it is

Not every finding carries the same quantum risk. Orca’s new PQC Impact rating sorts cryptography into Vulnerable (broken by a quantum attack), Weakened (reduced but not broken), and Resistant.

Click into the finding for mgmt-jumpbox-prod-01. Orca explains the risk in plain language, showing that the instance uses an RSA key pair, and its PQC Impact is Vulnerable.

Step 3: Check whether it’s internet exposed

A vulnerable key matters most when attackers can reach the host it unlocks. Orca’s exposure view shows this jump box is open to the internet on every port, along with the IAM roles, users, and groups that can reach it. Internet-facing hosts go to the top of the list. Internal-only ones still get fixed, just on a longer timeline.

Step 4: Map what it can reach

A jump box is only as dangerous as what sits behind it. Orca’s attack path analysis shows this one can reach a crown jewel S3 bucket holding AI training data, a Bedrock agent, a SageMaker endpoint, and a production database, plus dozens more buckets, functions, and roles. The key protecting this host is also protecting the path to your models and their data.

Step 5: Turn findings into a migration plan

One jump box is a fix. Hundreds of keys and certificates is a program, and a program is what the mandates ask for. US federal agencies must now submit PQC migration plans, and contractors, regulated industries, and their suppliers are increasingly asked for the same by customers and auditors.

Run the same four questions across every finding, and they sort into waves. Internet-exposed assets with a path to crown jewels get fixed now, internal assets with limited reach come next, and findings with no post-quantum option from the cloud provider yet get tracked until one arrives. Group your CBOM by PQC Impact to size each wave, then export it as the inventory behind your plan.

Another option is to connect the Orca MCP Server to the AI assistant your team already uses, like Claude or Cursor, and ask it to build a PQC migration plan. Because the MCP Server pulls straight from Orca, the plan reflects your real environment. You get a wave-by-wave plan grounded in live cloud context, not a generic checklist.

Go further with Orca: Fix, track, and prove progress

That’s the prioritization of a single finding done. PQC migration is a multiyear program though, and Orca helps with the rest too.

Catch harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks. Migration takes years, and attackers aren’t waiting for it to finish. In an HNDL attack, they collect encrypted traffic today and store it until a quantum computer can break it. Orca’s new runtime detections cover the three ways to collect that traffic in the cloud: capture tools running on a host, traffic mirroring on a cloud network, and TLS session key logging. Prove progress to leadership: When the board asks how ready you are, you shouldn’t need to pull a spreadsheet together to answer. Stay audit-ready. Mandates and auditors want the same things, which are an inventory, a plan, and evidence of progress. Orca’s PQC framework maps findings to NIST and the EU Cyber Resilience Act, alongside 200+ other customizable frameworks, so you can generate a shareable report in one click instead of assembling evidence by hand. Cut the time to fix: Orca tells you what to do, not just what’s wrong. AWS doesn’t yet offer a post-quantum key type for EC2, so swapping the algorithm isn’t an option for our jump box example above. Instead, the recommendation is to drop key-based access and use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager, which authenticates through IAM instead of a key vulnerable to quantum computing.

From there, Orca does the heavy lifting. Orca AI generates the fix in CLI, CloudFormation, Terraform, and more, so engineers start with ready-to-run remediation instead of a blank page. Code Origin traces the jump box back to the infrastructure-as-code template and the team that deployed it, so the fix lands with the right owner and gets made at the source. Fix the template once, and every future instance launched from it comes up without a quantum-vulnerable key. Keep weak crypto from creeping back in. Teams keep shipping while the migration runs. Orca scans continuously, so a new key, certificate, or listener using RSA or ECC shows up in your CBOM and the PQC Alerts view as soon as it’s deployed, and you don’t migrate the same risk twice.

A repeatable workflow for the next PQC deadline

Post-quantum deadlines will keep landing, and migrating every key and certificate at once isn’t realistic. The teams that stay ahead know where quantum-vulnerable crypto lives across their environment, and which of it needs to move first.

Orca helps you do exactly that. With CBOM, PQC Impact, the PQC Alerts view, and the PQC Dashboard, the Orca Cloud Security Platform shows where vulnerable crypto runs, how exposed it is, what it can reach, and how your migration is progressing. Title: What Is Preemptive MDR? A Guide For Security Leaders
Context: How exposure context and proactive threat hunting inform MDR By combining information about assets, vulnerabilities, business criticality, and attacker behavior, preemptive MDR...
Full Text:
When an MDR provider contains a compromised endpoint, your team needs to know whether the weakness that enabled the attack exists elsewhere and who is responsible for addressing it. Without that follow-through, the immediate incident may be resolved while another attacker still has a way in.

Preemptive managed detection and response (MDR) is Rapid7's approach to connecting exposure context, threat intelligence, AI-assisted investigation, and human expertise. It supports proactive cybersecurity by helping teams prioritize weaknesses before exploitation, investigate threats with a clearer understanding of risk, and use their findings to strengthen defenses.

How does preemptive MDR differ from traditional MDR?

Managed detection and response provides security specialists who monitor, investigate, and respond to threats around the clock. Many services also include proactive threat hunting and recommendations to improve security.

Preemptive MDR connects that work more directly to what makes an organization vulnerable. When analysts investigate suspicious activity on a server, knowing that it is internet-facing, supports a critical application, and has a vulnerability under active exploitation helps them assess urgency and determine where to look next.

In Rapid7’s model, exposure findings inform investigation and remediation priorities, while investigations reveal weaknesses that need attention. Security leaders gain a clearer connection between the threats their provider handles and the conditions their organization needs to address.

Within a broader preemptive cybersecurity strategy, MDR connects exposure information with the people investigating and responding to threats. The aim is to reduce opportunities for compromise and intervene before an attack causes harm, while retaining the expertise to contain and recover from incidents.

How exposure context and proactive threat hunting inform MDR

By combining information about assets, vulnerabilities, business criticality, and attacker behavior, preemptive MDR helps teams decide which weaknesses require action first. Exposure context also informs targeted hunting and the investigation of suspicious activity.

Consider a hypothetical organization running an internet-facing application affected by a newly disclosed vulnerability. The security team needs to establish whether the vulnerable software is present, what the application supports, and whether attackers are exploiting the weakness.

Those findings can guide remediation priorities and targeted hunting for signs of compromise. If suspicious activity appears, analysts investigate it with an understanding of the affected system and the potential route an attacker could take through the environment.

Depending on the evidence, the response may involve containing a system, examining related accounts, or expanding the investigation to other assets. The organization’s remediation teams also need clear recommendations about the underlying exposure.

What the investigation reveals then feeds back into detection rules, hunting priorities, and response procedures. This gives leaders a way to track an identified risk through investigation, action, and outstanding work, with clearer ownership at each stage.

What role does AI play in preemptive MDR?

Before analysts can assess a potential threat, they often need to retrieve logs, examine user activity, and connect evidence across several systems. AI can accelerate this work by gathering and correlating information for review.

Agentic investigation capabilities can perform elements of that process in parallel, test possible explanations, and organize findings. Their usefulness depends on the available data: missing identity activity or asset information can leave gaps in the account of what happened.

Rapid7’s approach keeps human expertise central to validation and response decisions. Analysts assess the evidence alongside the organization’s priorities and the consequences of an action, including whether isolating a system could interrupt a critical service.

What to look for in a preemptive MDR provider

When evaluating a service described as preemptive, ask the provider to show how exposure information changes its work. A redacted investigation should make clear what analysts knew about the affected asset, how that influenced their reasoning, and which actions followed.If an investigation identified a weakness, was it assigned to an owner and addressed? Did the findings change detection coverage or future priorities? Where AI contributed, the provider should explain its role and the oversight applied.

Incident response remains part of the requirement. Rapid7 MDR includes unlimited incident response alongside exposure-informed defense and AI-assisted investigation, supporting containment, detailed analysis, and threat eradication.

Agree on responsibilities before that support is needed. Establish which actions the provider can take, when customer approval is required, and who owns remediation. Those arrangements determine how findings become action, particularly when taking a system offline carries business consequences.

Once the service is operating, review progress through specific cases: exposures addressed before exploitation, threats contained, and weaknesses closed after investigation. Ask to see the evidence behind those outcomes and any work still outstanding, so your team can judge where risk has changed and where further attention is needed.
