Title: The risks of device code authentication for AI coding agents
Context: Detection and disruption availability depend on the supported configuration, required telemetry, identity integration, and deployment prerequisites
Full Text:
In this article

From a familiar phishing technique to an AI coding agent

How the attack works

One approval, four ways the impact can spread

Turning a phishing attempt into a Defender signal

Mitigation and protection guidance

References

Learn More

Device code phishing has become a recurring route to account takeover. Instead of stealing a password, an attacker persuades someone to approve a sign-in on a legitimate site simply by entering a code. The resulting access often can reach email, files, or other cloud services, depending on the account and the permissions granted. Notable earlier campaigns such as EvilTokens show how readily this technique can be scaled to do real damage. Microsoft worked hard with partners in industry and law enforcement to disrupt EvilTokens in September 2026.

That led us to a different question: what else can an attacker do with a phished device code authorization? What happens when the same trick targets an AI agent rather than a mailbox?

We used GitHub Copilot CLI as an illustrative example. Depending on its configuration, it can work with code, run commands on a user’s machine, retain context across sessions, and allow an active session to be steered remotely. Like many command-line tools, it supports the OAuth device flow for sign-in. The phishing technique itself is not specific to GitHub or Copilot CLI: any public client that supports the device flow can be abused the same way, and the attacker chooses the requested scopes when starting the flow.

We explored this scenario in a controlled lab simulation. A victim test account approved a GitHub device-code request initiated by an attacker client we controlled. With that approval, we were able to analyze four possible outcomes:

Steer an active Copilot CLI session remotely, if the user has enabled remote control and organization policy allows it, and, subject to local permissions and approval settings, have the agent run commands on the user’s machine.

Add misleading entries to the agent’s memory that could influence later interactions.

Read Copilot CLI sessions that were synchronized to the cloud.

Access private repositories available to the affected account.

These are proof-of-concept results showing how existing features, working as designed, could be abused after a phished authorization; they are not attacks we have observed in the wild. These outcomes require the victim user to approve a device code request initiated by the attacker; each outcome also depends on the account permissions and enabled features described below.

Later in this post, we show how Microsoft Defender helps detect these attacks by connecting phishing attempts with GitHub authentication activity, and how organizations can disrupt suspicious access to protect affected identities.

From a familiar phishing technique to an AI coding agent

The OAuth device flow helps clients such as command-line tools sign in without displaying a full browser. A client requests a short code; the user enters it on the service’s verification page; the requesting client receives access after approval. In device code phishing, the attacker starts the request and persuades someone else to approve it.

Microsoft has reported device code phishing against accounts in several campaigns, including Storm-2372, an AI-enabled campaign in 2026, and EvilTokens. Those cases motivated us to examine a different target: a coding agent that can work with repositories and, when remote control is enabled, expose an active session to remote interaction.

The remainder of this post describes a controlled GitHub Copilot CLI simulation; we have not observed the four outcomes below in those campaigns or in the wild.

How the attack works

Figure 1. A user approves a legitimate GitHub device-code request that was initiated by the attacker-controlled client. Conceptual illustration.

Initiate: The attacker starts a device-code sign-in request. In our simulation, we used the Copilot CLI client, but any device-flow client could be used.

Lure: The attacker sends the short code and GitHub verification link to the user, for example under the pretext of an IT request or a Copilot license check. The verification page is genuinely hosted by GitHub; the legitimate domain alone does not establish who initiated the request.

Approve: The user opens the GitHub page, signs in if needed, and approves the request. This is the social engineering step.

Sign in: After approval, the attacker-controlled client completes the sign-in automatically.

Operate: The attacker can act within the permissions granted to the application and the resources available to the affected account.

The request behind the code

The following example shows the initial HTTP request to GitHub’s device authorization endpoint. The Copilot CLI client identifier is public; it is not a client secret. The attacker sends the short code returned by GitHub to the user. Once the user approves it, the requesting client signs in without another manual step.

GitHub Device Code Authentication (Simplified) Endpoint: GitHub Device Authorization Endpoint Client ID: Requested scopes:

The request looks legitimate

The user signs in on the real GitHub site, not a lookalike page. A familiar domain therefore cannot tell the user whether the request was theirs. An authorization also appears under a legitimate application name; the name alone cannot distinguish the attacker-controlled client from an expected sign-in.

One approval, four ways the impact can spread

The device code approval was only the starting point. What an attacker could do next depended on the account’s permissions, enabled features, memory settings, and whether an active session could be controlled remotely.

Figure 2. Four possible outcomes in the lab, each subject to the account’s permissions and enabled features. Conceptual illustration.

1. An attacker can steer an enabled remote session

Copilot CLI supports remote steering of an active interactive session when the user has enabled remote control for that session and organization policy allows it. In our lab, the attacker-controlled client used the test account’s authorization to interact with a remotely controllable session. The agent ran a command on the test machine, subject to the session’s approval prompts and local operating-system permissions. This demonstrates misuse of an authorized remote-session capability working as designed; it is not unauthenticated remote code execution and does not apply when remote control is disabled, the session is not running, or the machine is offline.

Figure 3. Remote-session misuse is bounded by the local machine’s permissions and approval controls. Conceptual illustration.

2. Memory can carry the attack forward

Copilot Memory can retain repository facts and user preferences. In the simulation, we added misleading entries using the agent’s /memory command. If those entries are used in later interactions, the effects can outlast the initial sign-in. The behavior depends on which memory features and policies are enabled.

Figure 4. Misleading memory can affect later agent interactions. Conceptual illustration.

3. Synced sessions reveal earlier context

Where cloud session storage is enabled, we could read the test account’s synced Copilot CLI sessions, including sessions from before the simulation. They may contain code snippets, file paths, architecture discussions, and other work context. For Copilot Business and Enterprise, availability depends on the organization’s session-storage policy; syncing a session does not itself enable remote control.

4. Repository access follows the account

In the lab, the authorization let us access private repositories available to the test account. The request included the repo scope along with read:user, read:org, gist, and codespace. These scopes are chosen by the client that starts the flow; the resulting repository access reflects the requested scopes and the account’s permissions, not a property of Copilot CLI itself. The potential exposure is bounded by the account’s repository access, which can include application code and infrastructure definitions.

A phishing message, a click, and a GitHub authorization can each look unremarkable on their own. The challenge for defenders is recognizing when they belong to the same attempted takeover. The legitimate verification page is part of the story, not evidence that the request was safe.

Turning a phishing attempt into a Defender signal

Microsoft Defender helps organizations detect and respond to device code phishing targeting GitHub accounts. With the GitHub Enterprise Cloud connector enabled in Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps, organizations gain visibility into GitHub activity that can support investigations of suspicious authorization patterns.

As part of our research, we developed two detections for suspected GitHub Copilot CLI device code phishing, covering attacks delivered through email and Microsoft Teams.

These detections correlate suspicious messages and clicks with subsequent GitHub OAuth token creation and regeneration events, helping identify potentially unauthorized Copilot CLI authorizations that might otherwise appear legitimate. Microsoft Defender XDR customers can refer to the list of applicable detections below.

Microsoft Defender coverage

Observed activity

Tactic

Microsoft Defender XDR: Suspected GitHub Copilot CLI device code phishing via email

Suspected device code phishing delivered through email, potentially resulting in unauthorized GitHub Copilot CLI access.

Initial Access / Credential Access

Microsoft Defender XDR: Suspected GitHub Copilot CLI device code phishing via Microsoft Teams

Suspected device code phishing delivered through Microsoft Teams, potentially resulting in unauthorized GitHub Copilot CLI access

Initial Access / Credential Access

Beyond detection, we also developed a disruption action for GitHub Enterprise Managed Users (EMU). This action suspends the affected managed identity through the organization’s identity provider, interrupting the attacker’s access. We validated this capability in our research environment.

Responders should also review and revoke unexpected OAuth authorizations, verify that access is blocked, and investigate potentially affected sessions, repositories, and saved memory.

Together, these capabilities help security teams move from identifying a potential phishing attempt to containing the affected identity. Detection and disruption availability depend on the supported configuration, required telemetry, identity integration, and deployment prerequisites.

Figure 5. Microsoft Defender alert generated for suspected GitHub Copilot CLI device code phishing via email. Figure 6. Research model for identifying and containing the affected managed identity. Conceptual illustration.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Make the approval rule clear to everyone who uses developer and AI tools: enter a device code only for a sign-in you initiated yourself. An unexpected request to “verify” GitHub or activate Copilot should be treated as a phishing attempt, even if the page is hosted on github.com. GitHub’s own verification page warns users never to use a code sent by someone else.

Configure Safe Links policies in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 for email and verify Safe Links protection for Microsoft Teams. These protections can help with malicious links and provide investigation context; a legitimate GitHub verification URL still requires the user to recognize an unsolicited code request.

Review GitHub Copilot CLI session settings. For organization-provided seats, GitHub’s “Store local sessions in the Cloud” policy determines whether sessions can be stored and remotely controlled. Choose the least permissive setting that supports your workflows. Remote control also requires an active, online interactive session.

Review authorized OAuth applications in GitHub account settings and revoke authorizations that are unexpected or no longer needed. Limit repository access with appropriate organization roles so an affected account cannot reach more code than its work requires.

If Copilot Memory is enabled, use GitHub’s memory-management controls to review and remove suspicious repository facts or user preferences. Disabling memory does not automatically delete entries already stored, so review the saved content during incident response.

Connect GitHub Enterprise Cloud to Defender for Cloud Apps and validate the activity available in your environment before relying on it for investigations.

Remember: A legitimate sign-in can still be the wrong one

The most striking part of this simulation was how little needed to look suspicious. The user visited the real GitHub site and approved a normal-looking request. Yet the approval belonged to a client the user had not started. From there, the consequences depended on what that identity could access and which Copilot CLI capabilities were enabled.

That is why this is more than a story about a code. As AI agents gain access to repositories, session history, and local tools, the impact of a phished authorization increasingly depends on what those agents can reach.

A legitimate verification page does not mean the request is safe. Users should approve only device-code requests they initiated. Organizations should regularly review and revoke unexpected GitHub OAuth authorizations, restrict Copilot session and memory settings to what their workflows require, and validate GitHub activity visibility in Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps to support investigations.

Ultimately, protecting against device code phishing requires both user awareness and the ability to connect suspicious authorization activity to the phishing attempt that preceded it.

These mappings describe behaviors demonstrated in the proof-of-concept simulation, not an attributed campaign.

T1566.002 – Phishing: Spearphishing Link (Initial Access). In the tested email delivery, a link led the user to the device authorization page and prompted approval.

T1528 – Steal Application Access Token (Credential Access). After the test account approved the request, the attacker-controlled client obtained an OAuth token.

This seems like a good thing:

Google Deepmind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees­a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself.

Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world’s communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind’s formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code.

[…]

The DeepMind analysis did not find any new vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and showed that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work.

Alternate link.

Details:

First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code.

Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human ­ just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most.

Title: Why threat hunting should matter to every board
Context: If your organisation can’t answer that question, it may have gaps in its visibility or detection capability
Full Text:
Boards should have confidence that their organisation can detect and investigate emerging cyber threats, including activity that existing security alerts may miss.

Organisations use a range of cyber security controls. They use security products, receive threat intelligence and monitor alerts from trusted providers. Many have well-developed processes for responding to known threats. But these measures can’t tell you everything about your ability to detect an attack.

When a new attacker technique is identified, ask: could we detect this technique if it was used against us?

If your organisation can’t answer that question, it may have gaps in its visibility or detection capability.

As attackers use AI to operate at greater speed and scale, identifying and addressing these gaps becomes increasingly important. Organisations need to be able to identify signs of malicious activity early, rather than relying solely on detecting an attack once its effects become apparent.

Threat hunting can help organisations test their ability to detect relevant attacker activity and expose gaps in their defences.

This blog is for boards of organisations that monitor their systems for cyber threats, either themselves or through a third-party provider. It explains why threat hunting matters as threats evolve, and how boards can support their organisation to learn from what it finds and turn those insights into stronger cyber defences.

Title: Why Traditional SCA Tools Cannot Keep Up With AI-Generated Code
Context: Why Scan-and-Review Can Become a Bottleneck A scan can identify a vulnerable or policy-violating component, but detection is only the start of the work
Full Text:
AI coding tools generate and revise code in seconds. They can also make dependency decisions along the way in selecting packages and versions, adding frameworks, or changing how an application uses existing components.

Each choice becomes part of the software supply chain and adds something teams need to evaluate. Many traditional software composition analysis (SCA) workflows assess those choices after they enter the codebase when a pull request or build triggers a scan.

As AI tools introduce or modify dependencies more frequently, that scan-and-review process can lag behind development.

SCA remains essential for understanding and managing the components in software. But to keep pace with AI-assisted development, teams need to pair scanning with up-to-date component intelligence and policy guidance at the point where developers and AI tools choose dependencies.

AI Adds More Dependency Decisions to Every Change

AI-generated code is often discussed in terms of whether or not it contains vulnerabilities. That is only part of the security picture. An AI coding tool can introduce a package, select a version, or modify an existing dependency, often faster than developers can review them individually.

In traditional SCA workflows, that analysis begins after a dependency has been selected: a developer adds a package, a pull request or build triggers a scan, and the team reviews the findings. That approach can work when component changes arrive at a pace people can absorb. It becomes harder when coding assistants and agents generate changes continuously, sometimes introducing several dependencies in a single task.

The more dependency decisions AI makes, the more important it is that each choice is based on reliable, current information. Without that context, unsuitable packages or versions can add risk, review, and remediation work downstream.

AI Recommendations Need Current Context

A model's knowledge may not reflect current package releases, vulnerabilities, licensing details, or project health.

Without that context, it may:

Suggest an outdated version when a more current release is available.

Recommend a package or version that does not exist.

Choose a component that conflicts with organizational policies or license requirements.

Developers and AI tools need current component intelligence to evaluate those choices. We explain how to bring that context into AI-assisted workflows in our guidance on safer development.

A dependency graph can also grow beyond the package a developer sees in a code suggestion. A direct dependency may bring in transitive components, and a project may span several languages or ecosystems.

In our recent analysis of AI and shift-left security, we compared a Spring Framework project with 764 open source components in its dependency tree to an agentically developed project with 2,543 dependencies across four languages. These examples do not represent every project, but they illustrate how quickly the review surface can expand.

The result is not simply "more code," but a larger, changing dependency surface that teams must evaluate, often with less time and visibility.

Why Scan-and-Review Can Become a Bottleneck

A scan can identify a vulnerable or policy-violating component, but detection is only the start of the work.

Teams still need to determine if the finding applies to their use, how urgent it is, whether or not an acceptable alternative exists, and how to update without breaking the application. If every new finding requires an individual investigation, a faster development workflow can create a longer security queue.

Several gaps tend to emerge:

The decision has already been made. A scan in a pull request or CI pipeline may flag a component after it has been added to the code. The team now needs to remove or replace it, potentially reworking code that depends on it.

Finding volume grows faster than review capacity. More dependency changes can generate more alerts. If teams cannot distinguish urgent exposure from lower-priority findings, important work competes with routine triage.

The scan may lack decision context. A result tells the team that a component has a risk, but developers also need current information about versions, maintenance, licenses, and organizational policies to choose a suitable alternative.

Manual review does not scale with automated changes. Security teams and maintainers cannot review every dependency choice one by one when assistants and agents can produce many changes across teams and repositories.

Late remediation creates rework. Replacing a dependency after implementation or testing may require code changes, new tests, and another round of review. That can erase some of the time AI saved during initial development.

These pressures reflect the AI productivity paradox in which speeding up code creation does not automatically speed up review, testing, security, or release. If those stages cannot absorb the additional volume, more output can mean more work waiting in queues.

Move Component Guidance Closer to the Choice

Rather than waiting for a scan to run, teams can give developers and AI coding tools and AI systems current component intelligence as they choose dependencies.

That guidance should help answer practical questions before a dependency becomes part of an application:

Does this component and version exist, and is it maintained?

Are there known vulnerabilities or malware concerns?

What license does it use, and does it meet the organization's licensing requirements?

Does the choice meet the organization's policies?

Is there a safer or more suitable version that is compatible with the application?

AI tools need that information in a form they can use during development. That lets them check component details as they make recommendations.

This does not remove the need for developer judgment. Teams still need to set policies, review exceptions, and understand how dependencies are used. The goal is to give developers and AI tools reliable information to make better initial choices and reduce the number of avoidable issues that reach a later review queue.

Keep Scanning as Part of a Layered Approach

Earlier guidance and later-stage analysis solve different problems. AI-assisted development calls for safeguards across the SDLC. Context at the point of choice can prevent some risky or noncompliant dependencies from entering a codebase.

Automated workflows can also update dependencies or prepare changes for developer review. SCA scans remain important for identifying issues in existing applications, surfacing newly disclosed vulnerabilities, and helping teams respond as component risk changes.

Modern SCA can extend beyond scanning with component intelligence and policy guidance at selection, along with automation for dependency updates and remediation.

A practical workflow:

Gives developers and AI coding tools access to current component and vulnerability information.

Applies organizational policies consistently across human and AI-assisted development.

Offers clear alternatives and remediation guidance when a recommendation raises concerns.

Continues scanning code and builds to catch problems that earlier controls miss.

Maintains an accurate view of application dependencies so teams can assess impact when new risks emerge.

This approach keeps security controls close to development without turning every change into a manual approval process. It also recognizes that no single scan or decision point can account for every risk throughout a component's lifecycle.

Build at AI Speed With Better Dependency Decisions

AI can make software development faster, but every new component still raises questions about security, maintenance, licensing, and policy. When teams answer those questions only after a scan or review, that added speed can create more triage and rework.

To keep pace, teams need SCA that goes beyond scanning to guide dependency selection and support ongoing management and remediation.

Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes
Context: In the first, it completed a calculation that physicists set up more than 20 years ago, but which had never been solved
Full Text:
Claude has solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes and the search for a theory of quantum gravity. In the first, it completed a calculation that physicists set up more than 20 years ago, but which had never been solved. Claude’s result showed that a sudden transition associated with the formation of black holes persists even where spacetime no longer has a definite shape. In the second, Claude found the exact limit of the simplest version of a technique used to test candidate theories of quantum gravity. This post explains both findings, first in plain terms and then in more technical detail. The preprints are available here and here.

Introduction

Modern physics rests on two frameworks: general relativity and quantum mechanics. General relativity describes very large things, like stars; quantum mechanics describes very small things, such as atoms. Both are astonishingly good at predicting how the universe behaves, but they’re mathematically incompatible. Finding a theory that unites them—“quantum gravity”—is one of the field’s biggest goals. Black holes are a natural testing ground, because they’re one of the few areas where both relativity and quantum mechanics matter—they pack immense mass into a very small space.

One of the most useful tools for studying quantum gravity is called holographic duality. The real universe has three dimensions of space and one of time, which relativity combines into four-dimensional spacetime. But physicists studying quantum gravity often work with simpler model universes that they can understand in more detail.

The basic idea of holographic duality is that some of these theoretical universes can be described in two ways: as a complete universe with gravity and spacetime, and in quantum terms, with no gravity at all, “written” on the universe’s outer boundary. Just as a real hologram encodes a 3D image on a 2D plane, the quantum model encodes all the information of the universe in one dimension fewer (a universe with four dimensions of space, for instance, can be fully described by a quantum theory with three). This lets physicists turn hard questions about gravity into questions about quantum physics, which are sometimes easier to answer.

The first problem Claude solved concerns what happens when you heat up one of these theoretical universes. At low temperatures, the universe fills up with a gas of particles. Above a certain temperature, a black hole forms instead. In 1983, Stephen Hawking and Don Page showed that this switch is abrupt: it’s a phase transition, similar to how water suddenly boils at 100°C. But Hawking and Page’s calculation relies on general relativity, which holds only when the universe is vast, compared with the tiny scale at which that description breaks down. As the theoretical universe shrinks toward that smaller scale, spacetime loses any definite shape and becomes blurry, and nobody knows how to do the calculation on the gravity side of the duality. On the quantum side, though, the same situation can be calculated, at least in principle.

In 1999, physicists found that there was a phase transition in that regime as well. But they didn’t know whether it was abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth. In 2003, a group of physicists set out the calculation that would settle the question, but it was extremely complex and was never completed. Claude did it by running a small research group of copies of itself, in which it worked out almost every piece of the calculation independently and checked its math against known results. It showed that the phase transition is abrupt. The same sudden switch appears at both extremes, suggesting that black hole formation isn’t just a feature of relativity but is actually built into the underlying quantum theory.

The second problem concerns a simplified theoretical universe with two dimensions of space instead of three. This universe is straightforward enough to study in detail, but still has black holes and other mysteries similar to those of our own universe. Even in this simpler universe, physicists don’t know how to create a full theory of quantum gravity, so they approach it from the other direction: rather than building a single, correct theory, they try to rule out wrong ones by showing that they are internally inconsistent. This method is called bootstrapping.

Since 2009, physicists have used a version of this method to set a ceiling on how heavy the lightest black hole in such a universe could be. Any theory that breaks the ceiling is ruled out, and each lowering of the ceiling narrows the search. Results from numerical calculations hinted at where the best possible ceiling lay, but they couldn’t prove it, and the best proven ceiling was well short of what the numerical results suggested.

Claude Fable 5.2 noticed a pattern in the numerical results that physicists had missed and borrowed a method from elsewhere in math and physics to calculate the precise ceiling for the simplest version of this technique and prove that it could not be lowered. It doesn’t identify the correct theory, but it may point physicists in the right direction.

Neither result describes our own universe directly, and neither has practical applications, but both contribute to a long-running theoretical effort to understand how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together.

In the rest of this post, we explain in more detail what each problem was and what Claude did to solve them.

A note about Claude’s methods

In August, an Anthropic researcher, Hongbin Chen, was testing Claude’s capabilities as a side project. He asked Claude to draw up a list of interesting open problems in theoretical physics, specifically focusing on black holes and the bootstrap method. Claude came back hours later with 22 candidates, and Hongbin set up separate agents to work on each one; they could read each other’s progress posts and collaborate when working on related problems. The agents ran in the background, with no special setup, for about six weeks.

The agents solved the two problems in this post. One was the Hawking-Page phase transition, the question of when a hot gas turns into a black hole. Weeks after one of the agents reached a solution, a physicist, who had independently used Claude to tackle the same problem, shared his result, and a colleague realized that Hongbin’s agent had reached the same answer earlier. The two solutions used different methods, so they were a useful check on each other.

The modular bootstrap result came from several agents. The one that was assigned the problem spotted the pattern in the numerical results when surveying the bootstrap literature, and another one—which was working on a mathematically related problem about how tightly spheres can be packed into a high-dimensional space—turned that pattern into a method. It found that this method reproduced a sphere-packing result recently proved by an OpenAI model. Claude then applied the same method to the bootstrap problem, which an earlier Claude agent had tried, and failed, to solve in 61 parallel attempts. Two other agents also independently arrived at the same answer. One half of the final proof, showing that the ceiling can’t be lowered, follows the strategy of the OpenAI proof. In September, the results were formally verified in Lean, a computerized proof checker. Claude then wrote the paper with minimal guidance, and a physicist checked every main result.

The Hawking-Page transition

To understand the first problem, we need to start with something much more familiar: a walk through New York City.

Imagine that you’re heading from Penn Station to the High Line entrance on West 30th Street and 10th Avenue, and there are two equally good routes. You could walk west along West 33rd Street and turn south, or head south first and then walk west along West 30th Street. Either way, you have to pick one. In the quantum world, though, that’s not true: a particle can take both routes simultaneously.

This is most clearly demonstrated in the famous double-slit experiment. In this test, you fire particles, one at a time, at a barrier cut with two narrow slits, and record where, on a screen behind it, each one lands. Each particle lands at a particular point on the screen, as a particle should. But as you fire more of them, they build up a pattern of stripes that would only be possible if each one had passed through both slits, like a wave.

To predict what a quantum particle will do more generally, physicists have to add up every path it could possibly take, known as its possible histories. Not every history counts equally; some contribute far more to the sum than others. It’s an extravagant and mysterious way to describe how a single particle behaves, but it’s also one of the most successful ideas in physics.

This approach, known as the “sum over histories,” is well established for particles and anything made of them. But what about gravity? Einstein showed that gravity is a consequence of curved spacetime: objects with mass bend space and time around them, and we feel that bending as gravity. In a quantum theory of gravity, therefore, what gets summed over is the shape of spacetime itself, rather than just the paths of particles moving through it. To make predictions in a quantum theory of gravity, we would have to add up every shape that the universe could possibly take, and nobody yet knows how to do that. Much of modern quantum gravity research is an attempt to work it out.

Hawking and Page found a case where this sum is simple enough to handle but still interesting. To explain Hawking and Page’s work, we need to imagine a different kind of universe, called anti-de Sitter spacetime. Imagine you’re standing in a giant bowl. No matter how hard you throw an object, it will always roll back to the place you threw it from.

Our universe isn’t like that. The difference comes down to a quantity called the cosmological constant, which describes the energy of empty space. In our universe, this energy is positive, which makes space expand ever faster. In anti-de Sitter spacetime, the energy is negative, so everything is pulled back to where it started. Hawking and Page chose this universe for their calculation because of how it behaves when it heats up: the bowl keeps heat in so it can stay at a steady temperature.

At any given temperature, two histories matter far more than all the others. Here, a “history” means an entire version of the universe: a particular shape of spacetime, along with everything in it. In one, the bowl is filled with an ordinary gas of particles—including gravitons, the particles believed to carry gravity. In the other, it contains a black hole. Whichever contributes more to the sum is, in effect, what we would observe—it “wins.” At low temperatures, the gas history wins, and the universe is full of gas; at high temperatures, the black-hole history wins, and the universe contains a black hole. At one particular temperature—which physicists now call the Hawking-Page temperature—the universe switches abruptly from one to the other. This is the phase transition.

It’s a rare case where we can see two very different shapes of spacetime competing in the sum over histories, and can say which one wins.

This is where the holographic principle enters the story. In the 1970s, Jacob Bekenstein and Hawking found that the amount of information a black hole can hold is proportional to its surface area, not to its volume. That’s very different from ordinary matter, where every bit of volume holds roughly the same amount of information.

In the early 1990s, Gerard ’t Hooft and Leonard Susskind proposed that this idea applies to gravity in general—that everything inside a region of space can be fully described by the information on its boundary, just as a flat hologram can display a three-dimensional image. In 1997, Juan Maldacena formalized the idea further. Gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl, he argued, is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory of particles, with no gravity at all, existing on the rim of the bowl (the universe’s outer boundary). These are the gravity side and the quantum side of the duality we described in the introduction—they’re two languages for describing the same underlying reality.

In the case Claude studied, the quantum theory on the rim is called N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. It’s related to the theories that describe how particles interact in the real universe, but it has extra symmetries that make it much easier for physicists to work with. (Claude has worked with this theory before, calculating how particles interact within it to a new level of precision.) Since the gravity side predicts two histories competing with each other, the obvious question is: does N=4 super Yang-Mills theory (the quantum side) show the same thing?

For now, physicists can analyze this theory in detail only when its particles barely interact with each other, a condition known as weak coupling. This is the opposite end of the spectrum from where Hawking and Page’s gravitational calculation works. Weak coupling on the quantum side corresponds to the small, blurry universe on the gravity side. So there was no guarantee that any of Hawking and Page’s findings would hold there.

Remarkably, they do. Bo Sundborg in 1999, and after him Ofer Aharony, Joseph Marsano, Shiraz Minwalla, Kyriakos Papadodimas, and Mark Van Raamsdonk, showed that even at weak coupling, the theory on the rim goes through a transition as it heats up. This is its counterpart of the switch from gas to black hole inside the bowl. But it was still unknown whether this transition is abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth and gradual.

When particles barely interact, physicists have to calculate how they behave one step at a time. They start with a simplified version of the theory in which particles don’t interact at all. Then they add a series of corrections, each more precise and harder to compute than the last. Physicists call these steps loops. In 2003, Aharony and his colleagues realized that whether the phase transition was an abrupt jump, as Hawking and Page predicted, or gradual, hinged on a single number that appeared only three loops in. Computing that number involves many thousands of terms, known as diagrams—far too many to work through by hand. In 2005, the same group completed the calculation for a simpler cousin of the theory and found an abrupt transition. But the version for N=4 super Yang-Mills, more than 10 times larger, was never completed.

The scale of the computational problem, while daunting, wasn’t the only obstacle to completing the calculation. There was a conceptual issue, as well: naively adding up all the parts of the calculation gives an infinite answer, and those infinities have to be tamed carefully to extract a meaningful result.

To solve the problem, Claude ran a small research group of agents, all copies of itself. Almost every piece of the calculation was done twice, by agents acting independently. For extra consistency checks, parts of the calculation could also be compared to previous results in the literature.

The result Claude found is an abrupt jump as the temperature rises, exactly analogous to what Hawking and Page had found using the sum over spacetime histories. The emerging picture is very simple: the transition is abrupt at both weak and strong coupling—the blurry and the smooth ends, in the gravity description. The most natural possibility is that it stays abrupt everywhere in between.

This is a beautiful outcome. It shows that a calculation using the sum over histories in gravity qualitatively matches the behavior of an ordinary quantum theory with no gravity at all.

Many open questions remain. The abrupt transition Claude found is very much like the one we see whenever we boil water. One interesting feature of abrupt transitions is that the losing side of the competition can survive for a while: for instance, water can be superheated above 100°C without boiling, as you could see for yourself if you were to put a cup of extremely pure water in the microwave. (But please don’t do this; it’s dangerous, and Anthropic would rather not be responsible for an epidemic of scalded readers.)

Something similar happens here. Above the Hawking-Page temperature, the hot gas of gravitons and other particles can survive for a long time in a superheated state. But at a higher temperature it can no longer survive: this is another transition, the Hagedorn transition, which is a characteristic signature of string theory. On the gravity side, that transition has many interesting properties of its own, and it would be valuable to check in detail whether they also appear in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory.

Another open question concerns the other possible histories of spacetime. Hawking and Page considered three: one in which their model universe is filled with gas, one that contains a large black hole, and one containing a smaller black hole that never comes to dominate the sum over histories. In principle, there are many more possible histories. As far as anyone knows, none of them ever dominates. But given certain changes to the starting conditions—if the universe is set spinning, for instance, or given a fixed amount of energy or charge—then some of these histories do take over. Working out exactly which ones win, and when, is an interesting problem for the future.

The modular bootstrap

As we saw earlier, one useful model universe has just two dimensions of space and one of time: it’s called “3D gravity” because it describes gravity in three spacetime dimensions. According to the principle of holographic duality, 3D gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory living on the bowl’s rim.

As a model, 3D gravity is much simpler than the real thing, but it still allows for black holes and many of the same mysteries. It provides a useful laboratory for studying the sum over spacetime histories. It’s also a good place to test the idea that spacetime isn’t a basic ingredient of the universe, but emerges from something deeper. In general relativity, black holes look smooth. But in quantum gravity, if you zoom in to the smallest scales—the Planck length, around 10-35 meters, where quantum effects on gravity become impossible to ignore—black holes are made of an enormous number of tiny, individual building blocks. Physicists believe the same is true in our own, four-dimensional universe, but the 3D version is much easier to analyze with holographic duality.

Claude’s results build on a method called the bootstrap, a general strategy for solving quantum theories. Counterintuitively, the strategy doesn’t try to solve a theory directly. For 3D gravity, that isn’t even possible, because nobody knows how to define the theory precisely. Instead, the bootstrap rules theories out by showing that they contradict themselves. Physicists scan over all possible quantum theories and try to eliminate them one by one.

Remarkably, in many cases this method makes it possible to pinpoint a single quantum theory and calculate precisely how it behaves. The requirements of relativity and quantum mechanics are so demanding, and so delicately balanced, that together they rule out every alternative. In 2012, the bootstrap was used to solve a quantum field theory called the 3D critical Ising model, a simple model of magnetism that also describes water at the point where liquid and vapor become indistinguishable. Since then, it has been applied to many different quantum systems.

In 2009, Simeon Hellerman introduced a technique called the modular bootstrap, which applies the bootstrap method to 3D gravity. Its goal is to rule out inconsistent theories of quantum gravity in three spacetime dimensions. By combining it with other bootstrap methods, physicists hope to eventually eliminate every inconsistent theory. Whatever is left must be consistent. There could be no consistent theories, or just one, or whole families of them. Any of these outcomes would be interesting, because it would help us understand what spacetime looks like at the Planck scale in this simplified universe, and give us hints about the Planck scale in our own.

Here’s how the modular bootstrap works. 3D gravity in anti-de Sitter spacetime has a quantity called the central charge (c), which roughly counts how many microscopic building blocks the universe is made of. When general relativity holds, c is very large, because large black holes contain an enormous number of building blocks. A second quantity, M₁, is the mass of the lightest black hole. To run the bootstrap, physicists scan over every possible theory, with every possible value of c and M₁, and look for inconsistencies.

To understand how that search works, we need to go back to the sum over spacetime histories. In 3D gravity, that means adding up different 3D shapes of spacetime. They can be simple, like a ball, or more complicated, like the donut and two-holed donut in the figure below. The spacetime is the inside of the shape—the dough inside the donut. Its surface, like the rim of the bowl in the earlier section, is where the quantum theory is “written,” in one fewer dimension.

The modular bootstrap starts with a spacetime shaped like an ordinary, one-holed donut, or torus. There are two different ways to interpret this shape, depending on which direction we call “time” and which we call “space.” In the first, the long direction around the hole is time and the other, shorter loop, around the tube, is space. In the second, they’re swapped: the long loop is space and the shorter loop is time.

In calculations like these, the length of the time loop sets the temperature: the shorter the loop, the hotter the universe. So swapping the two loops trades a cold universe for a hot one. The two interpretations correspond to the two competing histories that Hawking and Page studied. In 3D gravity there are no gravitons, but there is a transition similar to the one that Claude analyzed in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory.

Now we come to the crucial step. In relativity, space and time are on an equal footing. So it can’t matter which loop we label space and which we label time. As far as relativity is concerned, the two interpretations are equivalent, and the physics must be the same for every possible experiment.

Quantum mechanics, however, treats time differently from space. To calculate anything, you pick a direction to call time and track how the system evolves along it. So, when we calculate observable quantities in quantum gravity, the two interpretations of the donut lead to calculations that look very different. But in relativity, it doesn’t matter which loop is called time, so the two calculations have to give exactly the same answer.

If we knew the theory of 3D quantum gravity, we could do both calculations and confirm that they match. We don’t, but with the bootstrap method, that isn’t a problem. Physicists scan over the possible values of c (the number of building blocks) and M₁ (the mass of the lightest black hole). For each pair of values, they try to prove that the theory would be inconsistent—that the two calculations on the donut couldn’t possibly give the same answer. This involves searching for a special mathematical object called a bootstrap functional. If physicists find one, then the theory is inconsistent, and those values are ruled out.

The hope, supported by the bootstrap’s successes elsewhere, is that combining this approach with other bootstrap methods will eventually rule out most possible theories of 3D quantum gravity. The theories left standing would be the only ones consistent with both gravity and quantum mechanics. Physicists could then use them to explore some of the biggest questions in quantum gravity: is there only one theory? Does it rely on string theory, or are there alternatives? What are black holes made of at the microscopic level, and how do we sum over spacetime histories?

This strategy can work in principle, but it’s very difficult in practice, because bootstrap functionals are hard to find. What matters for quantum gravity is what happens when c is large—but the larger c gets, the harder the search becomes. In the original paper on the modular bootstrap, Hellerman proved that in any consistent theory of 3D gravity, M₁ can be no larger than c/6, up to small corrections. Theories with a heavier lightest black hole can’t possibly be consistent with both gravity and quantum mechanics.

The goal of the modular bootstrap is to push this ceiling as low as possible, pinning down how heavy the lightest black hole can be. Physicists write the ceiling as M₁ ≤ c/Λ. A lower ceiling means a larger number Λ. The results below, including Claude’s, concern the simplest and most-studied version of the method, which ignores how the black holes spin.

Over the past 15 years, physicists have worked to lower the ceiling and pin down the theory as tightly as possible. There are two ways to do this. One is analytical—building a bootstrap functional by hand, with pen-and-paper mathematics. The other is numerical—using computers to search for functionals and optimize them. The results of these numerical calculations suggested that the modular bootstrap could push the ceiling down to about c/9.1. But these calculations get harder as c grows, so they couldn’t settle the question. On the analytical side, Tom Hartman, Dalimil Mazáč, and Leonardo Rastelli proved a ceiling of c/8.5, but because this was higher than the numerical results had suggested, this clearly wasn’t the best the modular bootstrap could do. Since then, just how tightly the modular bootstrap can constrain quantum gravity has remained an open question.

Claude set about solving the problem by running numerical experiments and reproducing results from the literature. In doing so, it noticed a pattern that physicists had so far missed, involving the way the numerical ceiling shifted slightly as c grew. Based on that pattern, Claude developed a hypothesis about the behavior of the bootstrap functional, using a mathematical tool called a spectral curve. Spectral curves are well known in other areas of mathematics and physics, but had never been applied to this problem. Claude found the spectral curve that governs the modular bootstrap at large values of c. It then used it to prove that the lightest black hole in 3D quantum gravity can be no heavier than c/Λ, where Λ is given by an exact formula and is approximately 9.1266. It also proved that this ceiling is optimal: it’s the lowest this version of the modular bootstrap can ever go. Claude delivered the solution across four research notes, which it later merged into a single paper.

This is one of the first times the bootstrap has been used to derive an exact result in the regime of quantum gravity where black holes matter. It also shows that this version of the method can’t, on its own, push the ceiling down to c/12, the mass at which black holes first appear; that will take other ingredients. Although it doesn’t pin down the theory of quantum gravity in three dimensions by itself, it provides a starting point and helps to narrow the search.

Conclusion

These two results show Claude doing two very different kinds of research. The first is a known calculation that physicists had set aside for two decades, because the work was too long and error-prone to complete by hand. The second required a new idea: spotting a pattern others had missed and bringing in a mathematical tool from another area of physics. Both were carried out largely autonomously. Neither result settles the question of quantum gravity, or even comes close to doing so, but each pushes physics forward in a longstanding area of research.

Context: For us, the outcome was a service that could handle launch
Full Text:
MAKING THE SERVICE LEGIBLE TO CLAUDE

My colleague Felix Rieseberg recently wrote a tutorial on being more ambitious with models. His main idea is to raise the "altitude" you prompt Claude at: ask for the outcome you want, not the individual task.

So instead of asking Claude to fix individual crashes, you ask it to make your app crash-free. (Our own apps aren't all the way there yet, but this is how we're making real progress.) To work at that altitude, though, you have to set up your code so Claude can pull crash reports on its own and run a harness that reproduces each crash and checks the fix.

For us, the outcome was a service that could handle launch. To get there, we did two things to make the service as legible to Claude as we could:

A diagnostic loop. Claude read the telemetry on every iteration and added whatever it thought was missing.

Legible technology choices. We picked a runtime and dependencies so any number Claude measured traced back to code we wrote.

A diagnostic loop

Every iteration, Claude read the telemetry and added whatever it thought was missing. Writing telemetry by hand is tedious, so in practice most telemetry would go in after something broke. Now Claude just writes it as it goes.

Memory is the best example.

Early in the harness run, one large doc was using about 3 GB on its pod (not a fun number to see). Claude’s first stab at fixing it was to shrink one of our caches so our server would evict docs sooner. The next harness run showed the memory was actually in a separate cache inside one of our dependencies, so Claude dropped the change.

From there Claude kept narrowing it down with finer-grained memory profiling. Eventually it found that every keystroke was copying the doc into several different data structures, adding a few MB each time. Claude switched those structures to copy-on-write, so they now share one reference instead of each holding its own copy.

After about three days of iterating, that doc topped out around 180 MB, and our estimate of what we’d need for launch dropped from more than 500 memory-optimized pods to about 50.

Legible technology choices

We were picky about the service’s runtime and dependencies. We wanted any number Claude measured to trace back to code we wrote.

This is because our models hill climb best with a clean signal. We expected a garbage collector to add noise, because memory and latency shift on the collector’s schedule.

Two choices helped the most.

We wrote the service in Rust. With no garbage collector, all of a doc’s memory sits in structures we defined, so when it grew, Claude could point to the one responsible, change it, and see whether memory came down on the next iteration. We have great Go tooling at Anthropic too, and we didn’t bake off the two languages, so this is our experience with Rust. What I did appreciate, coming from past work in Go, was how little I had to think about memory sticking around after my code was done with it.

We also kept dependencies to a minimum. Every library brings data structures we didn’t write and can’t easily account for. For the few we really needed, we vendored the code so we could read and measure it ourselves.

Rust is hard for people to write, and a few years ago that would have weighed heavily on the choice. Claude writes it and most other languages fine, so that matters a lot less now.

Title: Linked billing on the Claude Platform
Context: With linked billing, platforms can: Launch faster
Full Text:
Today we're introducing linked billing on the Claude Platform in beta. Third-party platforms, such as coding agents and workflow automation tools, can let their end customers pay for Claude API usage without sharing an API key. End customers keep their existing Anthropic billing and set their own spend limits, and platforms get a simpler, more secure way to offer Claude.

A more secure alternative to sharing API keys

Paying for Claude API usage on a third-party platform usually means sharing an API key, which works like a password: anyone who has the key can make requests billed to the customer, so the platform has to keep it safe.With linked billing, customers link their Claude Platform organization instead, and usage is billed directly to it. No API key changes hands, so platforms have no customer keys to store, encrypt or rotate, and customers’ API keys never leave their organization.

Platforms can see usage for each linked customer. Customers approve each linked platform, set a spend limit, and can unlink at any time.

Platforms can offer Claude to customers without building the billing

Linked billing gives platforms a new way to offer Claude to their customers. Platforms send requests, and Anthropic bills the end customers directly. With linked billing, platforms can:

Launch faster. Anthropic hosts the approval flow and the billing, so there’s no metering or invoicing to build.

Understand usage by customer. Get each linked customer’s request count, token usage and models used in Console, or programmatically with the Usage and Cost Analytics API (beta).

Choose who pays. Decide on each request whether the platform or the end customer pays, so platforms can pass Claude API costs to customers or cover some features themselves by product or instance.

Customers get more visibility and control

Customers can easily link to platforms using Anthropic’s hosted flow. They can then draw down from their existing Anthropic commitment, or pay as they go. With linked billing, customers can also:

Link once for the whole organization. A Console user with an Owner, Admin, or Billing role approves the link, so it works the same for individual developers and large teams.

Set limits for each platform. Customers can set a monthly spend limit for each platform, or a default that applies to each one.

See where API spend goes. Console shows spend for each linked platform.

Unlink at any time. Customers can unlink directly from Console.

Requests run in the platform’s organization, so settings in the customer’s organization, such as IP allowlists, encryption keys, and data retention, don’t apply.Platforms that support linked billing today include Asana, ClickHouse, Factory, Gumloop, Harness, Higgsfield AI, Kilo Code, Linear, Major, Mintlify, Omni, OpenArt, Niteshift, Railway, Ramp, Runlayer, Tessera, Tines, and Warp.

Getting started

Linked billing is available today in beta on the Claude Platform. Third-party platforms can add support by creating an app in Console and following the steps in the docs. Claude Platform customers can link their organization from any supported platform, and find platforms that offer linked billing on Claude Marketplace.

If you were planning to do any banking today, good luck.

Customers of many major financial institutions experienced unspecified technical issues on Monday as thousands of reports flooded the uptime-tracking website Downdetector.com from people saying that they had issues using their banks in some way.

It is currently unclear which systems are having issues. However, the problem may stem from technical difficulties at JPMorganChase, the top retail bank that holds over 10 percent of all US deposits, did identify a specific issue.

“JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems—there is no evidence this is cyber-related,” says JPMorganChase spokesperson Pablo Rodriguez. “It is taking longer than usual to service some customers.”

Rodriguez adds that the bank is not experiencing a “systemic issue” but that “other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us.” The spokesperson adds that customers “still have access to their accounts and funds” and that the bank is working to resolve the issues.

Apparent issues with the banks, credit unions, fintech apps, and credit card companies appear to begin around 9:30 am ET and peaked at around 2 pm ET. Many people also reported issues using Zelle, the peer-to-peer money-transfer system adopted by major banks. However, in a statement, Zelle denied its systems were the cause of the reported outages while acknowledging that issues at banks may impact people’s ability to use Zelle.

“Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should,” a Zelle spokesperson says in a statement. “Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds. Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds.”

US Bank spokesperson Jeffrey Shelman also says the financial institution’s systems “are not directly impacted.” Shelman adds, however, that “clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.”

Seth Eisen, senior vice president of communications at MasterCard, says, “Our network is operating normally.” A Visa spokesperson says the company is aware of the ongoing payments issue, but that Visa’s systems are operating normally too.

According to reports on Downdetector, which is sourced to user reports rather than official statements, the issues on Monday also impacted customers of Bank of America, Capital One, Wells Fargo, TD Bank, Navy Credit Federal Union, and more. These companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

U.S. airline operations return to normal. Microsoft unpacks last week’s outage. Commerce Secretary Lutnick defends less stringent export controls on advanced AI chips. Italy fines Meta 887 million dollars for privacy violations. Telegram’s new widgets may deliver a RAT. The FBI warns of ARTEX pen testing abuse. Refrigeration controllers see opportunistic scanning. Publicly available AI models dramatically accelerate vulnerability discovery. Monday business briefing. Our guest is Patrick Coughlin, CEO and Co-Founder of Savi Security, sharing how shopping fraud has industrialized in the AI era. A refrigerator company learns it’s secretly leading the laundry revolution.

Today is Monday November 16th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

U.S. airline operations return to normal.

U.S. airline operations are largely returning to normal following a rare four-hour nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA on Friday, November 13, which caused thousands of cancellations and stranding travelers into the weekend.

Officials confirmed the disruption was not caused by a cyberattack, attributing it instead to aging telecom infrastructure and legacy hardware. Specifically, an L3Harris contractor upgrading copper wire to fiber replaced a Cisco 600-series router manufactured between 2001 and 2006. The faulty router began flooding the network with login attempts, spreading instability across 17 FAA facilities and prompting the agency to halt flights out of an abundance of caution while 3,500 planes were airborne.

In response, the Trump administration increased its funding request for air traffic control modernization to $30 billion, noting that a previous $12.5 billion allocation is insufficient. However, Democratic lawmakers pointed out that only $1 billion of those initial funds have been spent so far, demanding accountability at an upcoming congressional briefing.

Microsoft unpacks last week’s outage.

Microsoft has traced last week's nearly 24-hour global Microsoft 365 outage to a latent Windows defect in its cloud networking gateway servers. According to Redmond's preliminary incident report, the bug, introduced via a server-specific fix deployed back in July, caused severe "lock contention," where competing internal processes exhausted processor and memory capacity on newer, multi-core hardware.

The defect remained hidden for over three months until a shift in Microsoft Teams traffic collided with a 14 percent reduction in server capacity. As servers crashed, automated failover systems rerouted connections to healthy endpoints, triggering a cascading failure that rendered over 80 percent of servers unresponsive and severely disrupted Exchange Online.

Engineers eventually mitigated the crisis by rolling back the faulty connection-handling update and gradually restoring traffic. While Microsoft confirms customer Windows devices were unaffected and require no configuration changes, the incident underscores how automated recovery mechanisms can inadvertently amplify systemic cloud failures.

Commerce Secretary Lutnick defends less stringent export controls on advanced AI chips.

According to The New York Times, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been advocating for less stringent export controls on advanced artificial intelligence chips, rules that directly affect Southeast Asian data centers with financial ties to his former firm, Cantor Fitzgerald.

While the US bans the direct sale of cutting-edge Nvidia chips to China, Chinese tech firms can legally rent computing power from facilities in countries like Malaysia, Indonesia, and Thailand. Lutnick, who transferred leadership and ownership of Cantor Fitzgerald to his sons, has pushed to limit new regulations to only seven countries, exempt existing data centers, and require government notifications rather than strict licenses.

Cantor Fitzgerald has arranged major financing for several of these data center operators, including Singapore-based Bitdeer, which plans to supply Nvidia computing power to Chinese tech giant Tencent. National security analysts and Democratic lawmakers have raised concerns over potential conflicts of interest and warned that narrower rules will allow Beijing to easily bypass restrictions.

Conversely, a Commerce Department spokeswoman stated that Lutnick bases his policy decisions strictly on US national interests, does not discuss department matters with his sons, and has complied with all federal ethics agreements. Furthermore, proponents of a lighter regulatory touch argue that overly broad restrictions could stifle American innovation and harm US companies like Nvidia.

Italy fines Meta 887 million dollars for privacy violations.

Italy’s data protection authority has fined Meta 805 million euros, roughly 887 million US dollars, for accessing Android users’ photos, videos, and metadata without specific consent or proper notification.

According to the regulator, the violation stems from Facebook’s gallery suggestions feature, introduced in 2023. The app bundled camera roll access into a single, generic authorization prompt, leaving roughly 20 million Italian users unaware they were permitting Facebook to scan their personal galleries for post ideas. Regulators noted the infringement remains ongoing for users who have not updated their apps, and cited Meta’s lack of cooperation during the investigation when calculating the penalty.

Meta announced it will appeal, calling the fine disproportionate. Moving forward, Menlo Park must implement a separate, transparent consent prompt detailing how gallery data is accessed and how users can opt out.

Telegram’s new widgets may deliver a RAT.

Kaspersky warns that a remote code execution vulnerability in Telegram’s newly launched widgets feature may have been exploited in the wild to deliver WebRAT, a Rust-based trojan also known as Salat Stealer. According to the Russian security firm, visiting compromised Telegram channels triggered a hidden PowerShell script to install the malware, which steals cryptocurrency wallets and Telegram account data.

The alert follows proof-of-concept videos from researchers at V12 demonstrating exploits against Telegram’s Android and Windows clients, which they attribute to running the QuickJS JavaScript engine without a sandbox.

While Kaspersky advises users against launching widgets until patched, Telegram CEO Pavel Durov dismissed the claims, stating users cannot be hacked merely by receiving a message and confirming that server-side patches have already resolved the underlying scenario.

The FBI warns of ARTEX pen testing abuse.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation has issued a Flash notice warning that threat actors are increasingly weaponizing ARTEX, an open-source, artificial intelligence-driven penetration testing framework, to execute rapid, global cyber intrusions. Since at least August 2026, attackers have used the tool to target sectors including finance, government, defense, and healthcare, compromising over two thousand downstream tenants in a ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply chain breach and stealing data on roughly 67,000 individuals from South Korean financial institutions.

Released on GitHub in July 2026, ARTEX plugs into external large language models to automate reconnaissance and exploitation, enabling some intrusions to achieve privileged access in under three hours. According to the FBI, attackers predominantly pair the framework with Chinese-origin models like DeepSeek Flash due to low costs and minimal guardrails.

Although the creator removed the original repository in October following widespread abuse, community forks and commercial variants continue to proliferate. The Bureau notes that ARTEX’s speed leaves defenders little time to respond, urging organizations to bolster defenses on overlooked portals and third-party integrations.

Refrigeration controllers see opportunistic scanning.

Threat actors began attempting to exploit newly disclosed vulnerabilities in Copeland’s XWEB EVO refrigeration controllers less than two hours after the flaws went public, according to security firm VulnCheck.

Researchers uncovered 14 flaws, each capable of yielding root privileges, after similar controllers were targeted in an October attack on 700 French supermarkets that France attributed to Iran. While nine vulnerabilities affect older firmware, five impact the latest builds, including predictable daily passwords derived from the device's exposed MAC address. Because Copeland ended support for the XWEB EVO line in March 2026, these flaws will not be patched.

VulnCheck’s sensors detected opportunistic scanning targeting unauthenticated flaws on November 12 and 13. With nearly 2,000 hosts exposed online, researchers urge operators to isolate these legacy devices behind a VPN and migrate to supported models.

Publicly available AI models dramatically accelerate vulnerability discovery.

Cybersecurity firm Forescout Technologies reports that publicly available artificial intelligence models can dramatically accelerate vulnerability discovery in critical infrastructure software on a tight budget.

Using a custom AI-assisted research harness to examine 10 popular TCP/IP stacks, Forescout researchers compressed roughly nine months of work into just 90 hours, combining 10 hours of AI scanning with 80 hours of manual validation. The effort uncovered 99 flaws, including 66 zero-day vulnerabilities, at a static analysis cost of roughly $935, or $2.58 per finding. (Researchers noted binary analysis proved six times costlier and twice as slow as source-code review.)

Forescout VP of Research Daniel dos Santos warned that while AI still requires human expertise, it fundamentally alters vulnerability economics, allowing defenders and attackers alike to find embedded software bugs faster and cheaper.

Monday business briefing.

Venture capital and mergers and acquisitions in the cybersecurity sector remain heavily focused on artificial intelligence, cloud security, and managed services, according to recent industry announcements.

On the funding front, Israeli AI detection and response platform Daylight led the pack with an $80 million Series B round backed by Goldman Sachs Alternatives. Fellow Israeli startups also saw major investments as Bay emerged from stealth with $50 million, cloud backup provider Dreeze raised $33 million, and SecOps platform Brava secured $15 million. Meanwhile, US firms Lazarus AI and WhiteMatter raised $43 million and $20 million respectively, and Italian automation startup CyberKord closed $3 million.

In M&A activity spanning four countries, compliance platform Vanta agreed to acquire Israeli agentic security firm Pillar Security, while Cogent acquired AI penetration testing startup Specular. Elsewhere, ShorePoint absorbed federal contracts from Coalfire Federal, while managed security and consulting consolidation saw acquisitions by Brite, ASI Solutions, Entech, and Saepio.

A refrigerator company learns it’s secretly leading the laundry revolution.

Stirling Marathon, a modest appliance maker in Elora, Ontario, recently learned it was poised to revolutionize the North American laundry industry. There was just one minor catch: the company only makes refrigerators, freezers, and coolers.

According to CBC News, the sudden surge in fame was courtesy of an artificial intelligence scam. Fraudsters blended legitimate company marketing photos with AI-generated footage on YouTube to hawk a fictitious "bombshell" washing machine called "the Keel."

Customer service representative Jordan Cuddihy first realized something was amiss on a Wednesday morning after fielding puzzled inquiries from across the continent, and watching hopeful bargain-hunters physically show up at the facility. A quick Google search revealed the phantom appliance, prompting YouTube to eventually pull the plug on both the video and the channel. For Stirling Marathon, it was a brief, unsolicited brush with industrial disruption, proving that in the age of AI, you don’t actually need to manufacture a product to generate buzz.
